title: The American Declaration of Freedom in Space
full_text:
(
printed page 70767)
Proclamation 11079 of November 3, 2026
The American Declaration of Freedom in Space
A Proclamation
It is America's destiny to explore and expand our frontiers beyond Earth to the farthest depths of space. Today, my Administration reaffirms that our solar system and all of outer space beyond Earth are the province of all humans, and that our Nation will lead the way in the exploration, development, use, and settlement of these new frontiers—forging an interplanetary civilization founded on the enduring and inalienable rights of freedom and individual liberty.
From the intrepid Apollo 11 astronauts who took humanity's first steps on the Moon to the pioneering rovers that explored the surface of Mars, the United States has always blazed a trail into the great unknown, shattering boundaries and pushing mankind to extraordinary new heights. Behind each triumph are generations of astronauts, scientists, engineers, and workers whose tireless dedication and unmatched ingenuity turn impossible dreams into reality.
Under my leadership, the United States is once again writing a bold new chapter in space exploration. This past April, the Artemis II mission successfully carried astronauts around the Moon and farther from Earth than any human had ever traveled before. This historic voyage is only the beginning. Next summer, Artemis III will undertake one of the most complex and consequential test flight campaigns in the history of our Nation's space program.
This proud legacy of innovation is our sacred inheritance, and our Nation bears the solemn responsibility to advance it by continuing to open new horizons of exploration and discovery. Through the landmark Executive Orders and directives I have signed, we are reinvigorating human spaceflight, unleashing a competitive and thriving commercial space industry, and ensuring American space superiority for all eternity. We will return to the Moon by 2028, lay the foundation for a permanent American lunar presence, and hasten the day when an American becomes the first human to set foot on the red dunes of Mars. Together, we will build the facilities, develop the resources, and establish a permanent presence in space to extend the reach of American exploration, preserve our frontier spirit, and strengthen our national security for centuries to come. The nation that leads in space will shape the future of humanity—and that nation will be the United States of America.
Today, we renew our solemn and righteous mission to propel humanity toward the farthest reaches of the universe. We reaffirm that the United States will lead the way in this bold endeavor, for the nation with the best scientific understanding of space, the most advanced space economy, and the greatest spacefaring citizens, will be the most prosperous nation for centuries to come. Above all, we pledge to carry our sacred values of faith and freedom wherever we journey, so that freedom may forever ring among the stars and beyond.
NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of America, by virtue of the authority vested in me by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, do hereby proclaim that the solar system
(
printed page 70768)
and all of outer space beyond Earth are the province of all humans and are open to exploration, development, use, and the establishment of a permanent presence by American citizens consistent with United States law and the international obligations of the United States.
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this third day of November, in the year of our Lord two thousand twenty-six, and of the Independence of the United States of America the two hundred and fifty-first.

FR Doc. 2026-22789
Filed 11-5-26; 11:15 am]

title: Anti-Communism Week, 2026
full_text:
Proclamation 11078 of November 3, 2026
Anti-Communism Week, 2026
A Proclamation
For more than a century, human freedom has been threatened by communist and socialist ideologies that eliminate individual opportunity, subjugate individuals to the state, and extinguish the God-given rights upon which free nations are built. This Anti-Communism Week, we are reminded of the devastating consequences of state control over human thought, creativity, and political expression, resulting in suffering, poverty, exploitation, violence, and misery for millions, and we renew our commitment to protect the sacred values of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness from the chains of tyranny.
Our Republic was founded upon the enduring conviction that our rights are inherent, our liberties are sacred, and our Government derives its just powers from the consent of the governed. These principles have defined our national character for over 250 years and continue to distinguish our way of life from that of all other countries on Earth.
Today, however, our American experiment faces renewed threats as socialist, communist, and radical leftist ideologies find increased expression in our Nation. We must remain vigilant in defending the principles that sustain our Republic and ensure the lessons of history are never forgotten nor repeated. Under my leadership, America will never fall victim to these evil ideologies, and the United States will never become a communist country.
The story of America is, above all, a story of a Nation uniting as one, standing up to tyranny, and charting its own destiny as a free and self-governing Republic. As President, I will always protect the founding principles for which so many fought and died. Together, we will defend our Constitution, which protects our freedoms; uphold the dignity of every individual; strengthen the free market, which has made us the most prosperous country ever to exist; and ensure that the promise of America remains alive and well for generations to come.
This week, we honor the victims of socialism and communism by remembering their lives, defending the freedoms that were denied, renewing our resolve to safeguard the Republic entrusted to us, and reminding ourselves that what we have created as a Nation stands as the greatest testament to human freedom in the history of the world.
NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of America, by virtue of the authority vested in me by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, do hereby proclaim the week of November 1 through November 7 as Anti-Communism Week. I call upon all Americans to stand firm in their defense against any threat to the American way of life and to protect our burning flame of liberty from the darkness of communism.
(
printed page 70766)
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this third day of November, in the year of our Lord two thousand twenty-six, and of the Independence of the United States of America the two hundred and fifty-first.

AGENCY:
Securities and Exchange Commission.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission” or the “SEC”) is amending the definitions of “small business” and “small organization” (collectively, “small entities”) that are used in connection with Commission rulemaking under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (the “Investment Company Act”) and the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 (the “Advisers Act”). These definitions concern regulatory requirements applicable to registered investment companies and business development companies (collectively, “funds”) as well as investment advisers. The definitions are used specifically for purposes of the Regulatory Flexibility Act (the “RFA”), which requires the Commission to consider the impact of its regulations on small entities. The amendments are designed to modernize the definitions, by increasing certain asset-based thresholds, including a mechanism for periodic future inflation adjustments, and eliminating the threshold based on total assets for advisers. In connection with these amendments, the Commission is making conforming amendments to Form ADV as well as the rule that allows certain small SEC-registered advisers to apply for a continuing hardship exemption from making Advisers Act filings electronically.
DATES:
This final rule was published in the
Federal Register
on November 6, 2026.
Final amendments to
17 CFR 270.0-10
(“rule 0-10”) and
17 CFR 275.0-7
(“rule 0-7”) are effective February 4, 2027.
Final amendments to
17 CFR 275.203-3
(“rule 203-3”) and
17 CFR 279.1
(“Form ADV”) are effective, and have a compliance date of, February 4, 2027.

I. Introduction
We are adopting amendments to Commission rules that define a “small entity” under the RFA for funds and investment advisers by raising the asset thresholds contained in both definitions.
[
3
]
Specifically, the amendments to the Investment Company Act rule (rule 0-10) will increase the net asset threshold for
(
printed page 69956)
funds to be considered “small” from $50 million to $10 billion and replace the “group of related investment companies” definition in the rule with “family of investment companies,” as that term is currently used in Form N-CEN. We are also adopting amendments to the Advisers Act rule (rule 0-7) that will increase the amount of regulatory assets under management (“RAUM”) below which an adviser is considered small from $25 million to $1 billion, eliminate the $5 million total assets threshold provision from the definition, and make conforming amendments to the adviser control relationship threshold to reflect the increased adviser RAUM threshold in the definition. Additionally, the amendments to Investment Company Act rule 0-10 and Advisers Act rule 0-7 will provide a mechanism for future inflation adjustments to the thresholds. Finally, the Commission is making conforming amendments to Form ADV and Advisers Act rule 203-3(b) for hardship exemptions to implement the amended adviser RAUM threshold. The final rules reflect comments the Commission received on amendments it proposed in January 2026 and will help the Commission more appropriately promote the effectiveness and efficiency of its regulations, with the goal of minimizing significant economic impact on small entities, consistent with the RFA.
[
4
]
A. Background
The Commission has a longstanding commitment to understanding and addressing the concerns of small entities and has established the Office of Small Business Policy in the Division of Corporation Finance, the Office of the Advocate for Small Business Capital Formation, and the Small Business Capital Formation Advisory Committee to be responsive to such concerns.
[
5
]
In the context of rulemaking, the Commission tailors its regulations to the relevant characteristics of regulated entities and weighs the impact of its rules on small entities, including through performing analyses under the RFA.
[
6
]
A purpose of the RFA is to promote the effectiveness and efficiency of regulations, including through consideration of alternative regulatory approaches, with the goal of minimizing the significant economic impact on small entities consistent with the stated objectives of applicable statutes.
[
7
]
The Commission is required to determine if a rulemaking is likely to have a “significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities” under the RFA.
[
8
]
Unless the Commission certifies that the rulemaking will not have such an impact, the Commission is required to conduct a regulatory flexibility analysis both during the proposal and final stages of adopting a rule.
[
9
]
The Small Business Act gives the Administrator of the U.S. Small Business Administration (the “SBA”) authority to establish small business size standards for all Federal agencies, in the absence of other specific statutory authority.
[
10
]
An agency may nevertheless prescribe its own small business size standard pursuant to section 601(3) of the RFA if, as described in
13 CFR 121.903(c)
, the agency consults with the SBA Office of Advocacy and the size standard will be used for the sole purpose of performing an RFA analysis.
[
11
]
Allowing agencies to establish their own definitions for the terms “small business,” “small organization,” and “small governmental jurisdiction” for purposes of the RFA analyses gives agencies flexibility in applying the provisions of the RFA.
[
12
]
In 1982, the Commission adopted rule 0-10 for investment companies and rule 0-7 for investment advisers to define “small business” and “small organization” for purposes of Commission rulemakings under the Investment Company Act and Advisers Act, respectively.
[
13
]
These definitions were last amended in 1998
[
14
]
and, in connection with outreach to small entities, the Commission has subsequently received requests to update the definitions.
[
15
]
Under rule 0-10, an investment company is deemed a small entity if it, together with other investment companies in the same group of related investment companies, has net assets of $50 million or less as of the end of its most recent fiscal year.
[
16
]
A group of related investment companies is defined, with respect to management companies, as two or more management companies (including series thereof) that (i) hold themselves out to investors as related companies for purposes of investment and investor services; and (ii) either (1) have a common investment adviser or have investment advisers that are affiliated persons of each other; or (2) have a common administrator.
[
17
]
Under rule 0-7, an investment adviser is deemed a small entity if it: (i) has RAUM
[
18
]
of less than $25 million (the “RAUM Threshold”);
[
19
]
(ii) did not have total assets
[
20
]
of $5 million or more on the last day of the most recent fiscal year (the “Total Assets Threshold”); and (iii) does not control, is not controlled by, and is not under common control with (a “control relationship”) another investment adviser that has assets under management of $25 million or more, or
(
printed page 69957)
any person (other than a natural person) that had total assets of $5 million or more on the last day of the most recent fiscal year (the “Control Relationship Threshold”).
In January 2026, the Commission proposed amendments to the investment company and investment adviser “small entity” definitions. Specifically, the Commission proposed to:
Amend rule 0-10 for funds to: (i) increase the net asset threshold for funds from $50 million to $10 billion; and (ii) refer, for purposes of aggregating the net assets of related funds, to a “family of investment companies” as that term is used in Item B.5 of Form N-CEN rather than to a “group of related investment companies” as used in the current rule;
Amend rule 0-7 for investment advisers to increase the RAUM Threshold below which an investment adviser is considered to be a “small entity” from $25 million to $1 billion and to conform the assets under management threshold in the Control Relationship Threshold with the revisions made to the RAUM Threshold;
Amend Form ADV to revise the instructions and Item 12 of Part 1A of Form ADV, including through making conforming changes to Form ADV, and amend rule 203-3 providing a continuing hardship exemption from electronic filing requirements; and
Amend rule 0-10 and rule 0-7 to allow the Commission to make subsequent inflation adjustments to the asset thresholds in these rules by order every 10 years in accordance with an inflation adjustment mechanism.
The Commission also requested comment on whether to amend the Total Assets Threshold, as well as the total assets threshold contained in the Control Relationship Threshold, in rule 0-7.
The Commission received approximately 20 comments on the proposed amendments. Commenters generally supported the proposal's goal to modernize the “small entity” definitions.
[
21
]
These commenters noted that the current rules are out of date and stated that the proposed amendments would help calibrate the Commission's analysis of the regulatory and compliance costs for small entities under the RFA.
[
22
]
Some commenters suggested modifications to the proposal, such as a higher fund net asset threshold, alternative non-RAUM Thresholds, different mechanisms for future threshold adjustments, elimination of the adviser Total Assets Threshold, or different treatment of certain entities.
[
23
]
Some commenters expressed concern that the proposal would diminish investor protections and suggested lower asset thresholds.
[
24
]
After consideration of the comments received, and as discussed in more detail below, the Commission is adopting the amendments largely as proposed but with some modifications in response to comments.
B. Overview of the Final Amendments
We are amending the definitions of “small business” and “small organization” under the Investment Company Act and the Advisers Act for purposes of the RFA, largely as proposed, but with modifications:
Raising the Fund Net Asset Threshold. As proposed, the Commission is raising the net asset threshold for funds from $50 million to $10 billion.
[
25
]
Amending the Fund Group Definition. As proposed, the Commission is, for purposes of aggregating the net assets of related funds, replacing the term “group of related investment companies” with “family of investment companies” as that term is used in Item B.5 of Form N-CEN.
Raising the Adviser RAUM Threshold. As proposed, the Commission is raising the RAUM Threshold from $25 million to $1 billion, and making conforming amendments to the Control Relationship Threshold to reflect the increased RAUM Threshold.
[
26
]
In a change from the proposal, the Commission is amending the Control Relationship Threshold to help advisers understand how to calculate the threshold.
Eliminating the Adviser Total Assets Threshold. In a change from the proposal, the Commission is eliminating the $5 million Total Assets Threshold, and making conforming amendments to the Control Relationship Threshold to reflect that the Commission is eliminating the Total Assets Threshold.
Periodic Inflation Adjustments. As proposed, the Commission is amending rule 0-10 and rule 0-7 to allow the Commission to make subsequent inflation adjustments to the asset thresholds by order every 10 years in accordance with the inflation adjustment mechanism set forth in section II.C below (the “Inflation Adjustment Mechanism”).
Conforming Amendments to Form ADV and the Hardship Exemption Rule. As proposed, the Commission is making conforming amendments to Form ADV, the uniform application for investment adviser registration and report form by exempt reporting advisers, and rule 203-3(b), which sets forth conditions for certain small SEC-registered advisers to apply for a continuing hardship exemption from the requirement to make Advisers Act filings electronically with the Investment Adviser Registration Depository (the “IARD”).
[
27
]
The amendments are designed to reflect the Commission's amendments to the RAUM Threshold, the Control Relationship Threshold, and their corresponding periodic Inflation Adjustment Mechanism. In a change from the proposal, the Commission is also making additional conforming amendments to Form ADV and rule 203-3(b) to reflect the determination at adoption to eliminate the Total Assets Threshold.
Smaller firms play an important role in the asset management industry.
[
28
]
We are mindful that smaller firms may face disproportionate compliance burdens compared to larger firms.
[
29
]
For example, compliance costs—such as staff time, recordkeeping, cybersecurity costs, and reliance on outside expertise or market data—often do not scale with firm size,
[
30
]
and have increased, while client fees have decreased.
[
31
]
We also are mindful that failure to consider the impact of regulations on small entities could risk reducing innovation, competitiveness, and new market
(
printed page 69958)
participants.
[
32
]
The Commission tailors its regulations to the relevant characteristics of regulated entities and weighs the impact of its rules on small entities, including through performing regulatory flexibility analysis under the RFA.
The final amendments are designed to help ensure the Commission's RFA analyses capture a more meaningful population of “small entities” so the Commission can continue to address the special concerns of small businesses. Updating the definitions of “small business” and “small organization” is appropriate to reflect the substantial growth in, and distribution of, regulatory assets under management and net assets over the decades since these thresholds were set.
[
33
]
The updates to the definitions reflect more reliable and consistent metrics for whether an adviser or fund is small, compared to those in the current rules.
Some commenters stated that the proposed amendments would classify too many funds or advisers as small (effectively leading the Commission to prioritize benefits of large funds and advisers instead of truly small funds and advisers),
[
34
]
or otherwise could result in regulatory arbitrage between investment advisers and broker-dealers
[
35
]
and diminish investor protections.
[
36
]
As explained below, the final amendments will not classify too many funds or advisers as small. The final amendments also will not diminish investor protections. Designating an entity as a small entity does not reduce investor protection. Investor protection is a concern regardless of the size of an entity. The purpose of the small entity definition is, in part, to ensure that the Commission considers whether its rules are appropriately calibrated so that smaller entities are not subject to regulations that may be disproportionately burdensome relative to the benefits or improvements in investor protection. The final amendments will enhance the Commission's rulemaking process by helping ensure the RFA analyses reflect current economic realities by incorporating the evolution of adviser and fund growth since the rules were first adopted, as other commenters stated.
[
37
]
One commenter stated that the proposal did not appear to evaluate the investor-protection consequences of the proposed amendments and asserted the proposal focused primarily on industry size, rather than regulatory risk or compliance capacity. It outlined certain areas that the Commission should quantify and analyze in this regard, in particular to focus any regulatory relief on genuinely small entities and in a risk-based manner.
[
38
]
Because the final amendments primarily affect the process by which the Commission considers potential impacts on small entities, including benefits and costs of future rulemaking on small entities, the final amendments will not have any immediate impact on investor protection. Rather, the final amendments will require the Commission to consider and address the potential impacts of future rulemaking on small entities, including effects on investor protection.
Separately, the methodology for the proposed thresholds reflects that advisory fees are generally scaled with an adviser's assets under management, where greater advisory fees can support an increased compliance capacity. The updated thresholds also will allow the Commission to more appropriately address in future rulemakings, in a risk-based manner, concerns that are unique to those entities that should be deemed small entities in view of the growth in assets since the rules were adopted and the appropriateness of any regulatory accommodations that may be provided to small entities.
While conducting RFA analyses in future rulemakings, the Commission can take into account any potential for regulatory arbitrage between broker-dealers and investment advisers and adjust its future rules accordingly. The Commission carefully weighs the economic impact of its rules on all regulated entities, including small businesses, and tailors its regulations to the relevant characteristics of the particular entities regulated. In this way, the Commission works to meet its mandate under the Federal securities laws while at the same time considering any potentially disproportionate costs and regulatory burdens for small entities. The Commission intends to continue this careful, measured regulation that addresses small business concerns within the protections of the Federal securities laws.
II. Discussion
A. Amendments to Rule 0-10 Under the Investment Company Act
1. Raising the Net Asset Threshold
The Commission is amending the net asset threshold for small funds, as proposed. The final rule will amend paragraph (a) of rule 0-10 to increase the net asset threshold from $50 million to $10 billion and, as discussed in more detail in section II.C below, establish a mechanism to inflation-adjust this figure every ten years. The increase accounts for the overall growth in the fund industry since the $50 million threshold was originally set in 1982.
[
39
]
At that time, 62.4% of funds were deemed “small entities,” but by 2024, the share of funds deemed “small entities” had fallen to 0.6%.
[
40
]
Raising the net asset threshold in rule 0-10 to reflect growth in the investment company industry over the past decades will improve the utility of RFA analyses by more closely reflecting the population of funds that does not have the same competitive advantages as larger fund families (for instance, due to economies of scale when these larger families perform certain compliance and other operational functions in-house).
[
41
]
It also will more closely reflect the population of funds that does not have the same negotiating power as larger
(
printed page 69959)
fund families when retaining service providers to perform compliance and operational functions.
In determining how to calibrate the amended threshold, the Commission considered the distribution of assets across individual funds and fund families, with the goal of ensuring that the proportion of funds that may face greater challenges in complying with Commission regulations due to their size be included in the small entity definition. Specifically, the Commission analyzed data reported on Form N-CEN to sort families of investment companies into percentiles according to their cumulative average total net assets. The Commission further analyzed this data to determine the percentage of individual funds and the percentage of average total net assets represented by each percentile.
[
42
]
At proposal, the Commission estimated that, as of December 2024, fund families at or below the 80th percentile threshold of $10.04 billion in net assets accounted for 22.91% of individual funds and only 2.13% of fund assets.
[
43
]
The analysis that formed the basis for the proposed threshold reflects that the assets of the investment company industry are heavily concentrated at the largest fund families, and these largest fund families not only manage a large majority of assets in the industry, but also account for a majority of the individual funds.
[
44
]
Most commenters supported generally raising the net asset threshold from the current level to account for growth in the industry.
[
45
]
Several commenters supported raising the net asset threshold to $10 billion in particular, stating that this threshold appropriately reflects current market size and structure.
[
46
]
One of the commenters specifically expressed its support for the distribution-based methodology used to reach the proposed $10 billion threshold for funds.
[
47
]
This commenter, while supporting the proposal, further encouraged the Commission to adjust the threshold to $12 billion to account for growth in the industry since the date of the data underlying the proposal. Some other commenters expressed concerns that $10 billion is too high, one of whom requested that the Commission quantify and analyze the investor-protection consequences of the higher threshold and another expressed concerns about the effects of entities with billions of dollars in assets being deemed to be “small” (
i.e.,
very large firms could receive regulatory accommodations intended for smaller firms with limited regulatory capacity, which the commenter indicated could cause smaller firms to lose the advantages the RFA provides them and have negative investor protection consequences).
[
48
]
One commenter suggested adjusting the thresholds adopted in the 1998 amendments for inflation, resulting in a $100 million threshold, or alternatively using the SBA's small entity standard based on $40 million in gross receipts.
[
49
]
Another commenter, asserting that the proposed threshold is too high, suggested defining “small entities” as those at or below the 20th percentile of aggregate fund family net assets using a distribution methodology based on Form N-CEN data.
[
50
]
After considering these comments, we are, as proposed, raising the net asset threshold to $10 billion for funds. We agree with commenters' statements that the increased threshold would better reflect the growth in the fund industry and aid the Commission's analysis of regulatory and compliance costs on small funds.
[
51
]
Based on analysis of the distribution of data discussed above, we are adopting a “small entity” definition that incorporates a $10 billion net asset threshold, which continues to correspond to the 80th percentile threshold in that distribution-based analysis.
[
52
]
While the amended threshold will deem some relatively large individual funds “small” for purposes of the RFA, such an outcome is consistent with the economies of scale rationale for aggregating funds within a family. A single large fund with no other related funds will bear similar regulatory costs to several smaller, related funds that collectively represent a similar level of net assets. Therefore, aggregating assets across fund families reflects the Commission's understanding that funds within a complex typically use the same administrative, management, and compliance systems to oversee all the funds within the complex, so fees imposed on the fund by the adviser or administrator typically reflect economies of scale that the adviser or administrator achieves from managing other funds.
While the Commission seeks to ensure that funds and fund families that may face greater challenges with regulatory compliance due to their size be deemed small entities, we are also mindful that setting the threshold too high has the potential to be counterproductive and to undermine the purpose of the Commission's RFA analyses. A higher threshold would result in a larger pool of small entities and therefore would increase the number of small entities needed to be affected by a rule for the rule to “have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities,” which could lead to fewer RFA analyses being performed.
[
53
]
Setting the threshold too high might also inadvertently lead to the Commission overlooking issues that concern the smallest entities when the Commission attempts to tailor its rules, and instead focusing primarily on issues of more general concern to the industry. Such an outcome might have the potential to perpetuate larger funds' advantages in the market, to the detriment of the smaller funds that the RFA was designed to protect.
[
54
]
Accordingly, the Commission's amended threshold is meant to identify a level below which a meaningful proportion of funds would be deemed small entities, but above which the size of, and concentration of assets in, fund families increases to such an extent that treating individual funds within those families as small entities would not be consistent with the goals of the RFA. We are therefore not adopting a smaller threshold than the proposed $10 billion threshold. We are also therefore not adopting a threshold of $12 billion as one commenter suggested. We do not believe this change from the proposed
(
printed page 69960)
approach, based on one-year market movements, would be appropriate, as the proposed threshold was designed to be stable and flexible enough to guide Commission analysis for the next 10 years and not to reflect short-term market fluctuations.
We are not adjusting the current threshold for inflation, as some commenters suggested, but rather are retaining the proposed distribution-based methodology as the basis for the final rules' threshold adjustment. A net asset threshold of $100 million (the result of inflation-adjusting the current rule's threshold) would cover less than 3% of funds and less than .03% of fund assets and would constrain future Commission analysis of small entity issues to this limited group.
[
55
]
Further, we are not adopting a threshold based on a gross receipts analysis. As discussed in the Proposing Release, gross receipts are not well suited to the fund industry, primarily because the Commission does not have or collect data for gross receipts of registered investment companies.
[
56
]
As the Proposing Release also discussed, funds primarily generate revenue through capital appreciation and other investment returns rather than receipts from the sale of goods or services, and a fund's investment returns may be attributable primarily to its particular investment strategy, meaning that two funds of identical size but pursuing different investment strategies may produce vastly different returns.
[
57
]
Commenters did not address or dispute these rationales for using an approach other than a gross receipts analysis.
We are also not adopting an approach that defines small entities as fund families with net assets at or below the 20th percentile as determined annually. A commenter recommended the Commission amend the Control Relationship Threshold to provide a special rule for insurance companies, so that an insurance company's affiliated institutional advisers would not be cumulated with an insurance company's affiliated retail advisers.

This commenter stated that institutional advisers and retail advisers involve substantially different infrastructures, systems, and regulatory requirements, they do not share management or advisory personnel, they have distinct costs and burdens, and there are few opportunities for economies of scale between them. The commenter expressed concern that a retail adviser may be disproportionately and unfairly impacted by changes in Commission regulation if its assets under management are cumulated with an institutional adviser merely due to common control.
We are not persuaded to provide a special rule for insurance companies, so that an insurance company's affiliated institutional advisers would not be cumulated with an insurance company's affiliated retail advisers. Currently, the requirements in rule 0-7 do not distinguish between retail advisers and institutional advisers. We are not persuaded that advisers should be treated differently under rule 0-7 solely based on the fact that they are affiliated with an insurance company. We disagree with this commenter's assertion that an adviser's retail and institutional advisory businesses involve substantially different regulatory requirements. Retail and institutional advisory businesses involve substantially similar regulatory requirements, because both are subject to the Advisers Act, and the rules thereunder, among other things which do not generally differentiate between the type of client. Even if affiliated advisers choose different infrastructures, systems, management, or advisory personnel, there remain opportunities for economies of scale concerning compliance with and operation under the Advisers Act and the rules thereunder, even if some particular provisions do not apply to each adviser. Therefore, we disagree with the commenter's assertion that a retail adviser would be disproportionately or unfairly impacted by changes in Commission regulation if its assets under management are cumulated with an institutional adviser due to common control.

C. Periodic Future Adjustments
The final amendments to rules 0-10 and 0-7 will, as proposed, provide an Inflation Adjustment Mechanism for periodic future adjustments of the asset-based thresholds used in these rules' small entity definitions.
[
170
]
Specifically, the amendments provide that the Commission will issue an order every ten years adjusting: (i) the net asset threshold in the investment company small entity definition; and (ii) in the investment adviser small entity definition, the RAUM Threshold (which will also now have the effect of adjusting the Control Relationship Threshold). As proposed, the final amendments to rule 0-10 and rule 0-7 will require that the adjustment of the asset-based thresholds be calculated by reference to the Personal Consumption Expenditures Chain-Type Price Index (the “PCE Index”).
[
171
]
The final amendments providing the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism will require rounding the investment company small entity net asset threshold to the nearest multiple of $1,000,000,000 and rounding the investment adviser small entity RAUM Threshold (and thus the Control Relationship Threshold) to the nearest multiple of $100,000,000.
[
172
]
In order to adjust the asset-based thresholds for the “small entity” definitions as discussed above, the Commission considered an analysis of the distribution of fund and adviser assets and the growth in these assets over time. As described in the Proposing Release, however, these amended thresholds may become less useful over time due to growth in markets and any subsequent changes in the fund and adviser industries. The proposed Inflation Adjustment Mechanism was designed to ensure that the thresholds are adjusted every ten years, because the adjustment would be required by rule and effected through a Commission order.
Some commenters supported the proposed inflation adjustments.
[
173
]
Other commenters supported the goal of periodic adjustments, but expressed concern about the details of the proposal.
[
174
]
For example, some commenters recommended the Commission use a shorter cadence for adjustments, such as five or seven years, to ensure that the thresholds remain reasonable.
[
175
]
Some commenters recommended using an adjustment mechanism they consider more relevant than inflation, such as a broad-based index of asset prices,
[
176
]
or the proposal's own asset-based distribution
(
printed page 69969)
analysis for RAUM and net asset percentiles.
[
177
]
After considering comments, we are adopting the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism substantially as proposed.
[
178
]
Adjustments that the Commission makes mechanically by order could help maintain the thresholds at levels that reflect the buying power of money over time, without the need for Commission action through rulemaking.
[
179
]
We expect, as discussed in the Proposing Release and by commenters, that the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism will prevent the thresholds in the small entity definitions from becoming less meaningful over time on account of anticipated changes in dollar value.
[
180
]
Specifically, because a fund's or adviser's size is related to its ability to bear compliance costs, adjusting the asset-based thresholds is designed to account for potential increases in those compliance costs.
While certain comments recommended a shorter adjustment cadence, the final amendments' Inflation Adjustment Mechanism reflects the same ten-year cadence as proposed. Given the distributions of different-sized entities for funds and investment advisers, inflationary changes over shorter periods would generally not result in a meaningfully different set of funds and investment advisers being considered small entities under their respective definitions.
[
181
]
Likewise, after considering comments recommending an adjustment mechanism based on a metric other than inflation, we are adopting this aspect of the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism as proposed. We acknowledge that inflation may not perfectly represent growth in the fund and adviser industries. Nevertheless, as discussed above, our view continues to be that inflation adjustment is the most appropriate mechanism for periodically and mechanically adjusting the asset thresholds and implementing the adjustments by order. Inflation, unlike the asset-based distribution analysis mechanisms described by commenters, is a known factor for which a precise value can reliably be derived from a defined index. Periodically adjusting the thresholds to a set percentile from a distribution analysis would similarly be inappropriate. The percentile that resulted from the distribution analysis performed in the Proposing Release is particular to that data and set of facts and, therefore, is not necessarily indicative of the proportion of funds or advisers that should be deemed small entities in the future. In addition, performing the same or similar analysis to determine a future percentile based on then-current data would involve a level of analysis that would require a future rulemaking rather than an adjustment by Commission order. Similarly, we do not consider using a broad-based index of asset prices as the basis for adjustment as suggested by commenters to be appropriate in light of the breadth of fund and adviser strategies. Any one particular index of asset prices would not be appropriate for certain strategies, and if multiple indexes were used, this could result in different levels of adjustment depending on the index, as well as operational complexity.
It is possible, but less predictable, that the asset-based thresholds may become less useful over time even taking the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism we are adopting into account (for example, with the advent of market events, changes in the makeup or distribution of size of the fund or adviser markets, or other industry changes). In this case, the Commission could consider performing appropriate analyses to propose amendments to the thresholds again in the future independent of the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism. Similarly, in the future, the Commission also could consider proposing a periodic adjustment approach using analysis other than one based on the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism.

III. Economic Analysis
The Commission is mindful of the economic effects, including the costs and benefits, of its rules. The Commission has a long-held focus on small entities when engaged in rulemaking. A purpose of the RFA is to promote the effectiveness and efficiency of regulations, including through consideration of alternative regulatory approaches, with the goal of minimizing
(
printed page 69970)
the significant economic impact on small entities consistent with the stated objectives of applicable statutes.
[
185
]
The Commission is required to determine if a rulemaking is likely to have a “significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities” under the RFA.
[
186
]
In applicable rulemakings, the Commission's definitions of “small entities” determine the scope of the regulatory flexibility analyses conducted at the proposal and final stages. The updated definitions are expected to better tailor the Commission's analyses of the specific regulatory challenges faced by small entities by expanding the scope of the analyses that the Commission conducts under the RFA. These analyses, in turn, are expected to better inform the Commission of the regulatory impacts faced by small entities so that it may consider adapting its rulemaking accordingly.
[
187
]
To the extent such adaptations to future rulemakings will occur, the use of the amended definitions of “small entities” in RFA analyses could result in different benefits and costs of such rulemakings.
[
188
]
For example, if the Commission, informed by the more tailored RFA analyses, determined to scope fewer small entities into future rulemakings or tailor obligations imposed by such rulemakings differently for small entities, there could be lower compliance costs imposed on such entities.
In addition to these indirect effects, the final rule will have direct economic effects arising in situations where the updated small entity definitions affect the application of existing Commission rules and regulations. Currently, the Commission's definition of “small entity” under the RFA is incorporated into the Commission's other rules and regulations only in connection with an adviser's responses to Form ADV (and this release is implementing corresponding amendments to the form) and to rule 203-3(b). We thus consider the effects of the updated definition as it relates to the use of that definition in Form ADV, as well as the effects of the other associated changes to the form and to rule 203-3(b).

(b) For purposes of this section,
control
means the power, directly or indirectly, to direct the management or policies of a person, whether through ownership of securities, by contract, or otherwise.
(1) A person is presumed to control a corporation if the person:
(i) Directly or indirectly has the right to vote 25 percent or more of a class of the corporation's voting securities; or
(ii) Has the power to sell or direct the sale of 25 percent or more of a class of the corporation's voting securities.
(2) A person is presumed to control a partnership if the person has the right to receive upon dissolution, or has contributed, 25 percent or more of the capital of the partnership.
(3) A person is presumed to control a limited liability company (LLC) if the person:
(i) Directly or indirectly has the right to vote 25 percent or more of a class of the interests of the LLC;
(ii) Has the right to receive upon dissolution, or has contributed, 25 percent or more of the capital of the LLC; or
(iii) Is an elected manager of the LLC.
(4) A person is presumed to control a trust if the person is a trustee or managing agent of the trust.
(c) The dollar amount specified in paragraph (a) of this section shall be adjusted by order of the Commission, issued on or about March 1, 2037, and approximately every ten years thereafter. The adjusted dollar amount established in such orders shall be computed by:
(1) Dividing the year-end value of the Personal Consumption Expenditures Chain-Type Price Index (or any successor index thereto), as published by the United States Department of Commerce, for the calendar year preceding the calendar year in which the order is being issued, by the year-end value of such index (or successor) for the calendar year 2027; and
(2) Multiplying $1 billion times the quotient obtained in paragraph (c)(1) of this section and rounding the product to the nearest multiple of $100 million.

title: Medicare Program: Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment and Ambulatory Surgical Center Payment Systems; and Quality Reporting Programs; including the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program and Ambulatory Surgical Center Quality Program; Request for Information on Strengthening the Standardization and Comparability of Hospital Price Transparency (HPT) Data; Prior Authorization; Accrediting Organization (AO) Deeming for Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA); and Notices of Closure of Teaching Hospitals and Opportunities To Apply for Available Slots
abstract: This final rule with comment period revises the Medicare Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) and the Medicare Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) payment system for calendar year 2027 based on our continuing experience with these systems. We also describe the changes to the amounts and factors used to determine the payment rates for Medicare services paid under the OPPS and those paid under the ASC payment systems. In addition, this final rule with comment period updates and refines the requirements for the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program and the Ambulatory Surgical Center Quality Reporting Program. There are no changes to the Rural Emergency Hospital Quality Reporting Program. We finalized the expansion of the prior authorization requirement to include additional Botulinum Toxin Injection services. We also finalized implementation of certain provisions of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, for off-campus outpatient departments of a provider. In addition, this final rule with comment period announces notices of closure of teaching hospitals and opportunities to apply for available slots. Additionally, we finalized the policy that hospital accrediting organizations (AOs) with deeming authority may assess compliance with certain Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA) administrative requirements under 42 CFR 489.20 during accreditation and reaccreditation surveys.
dates: Effective Date: The provisions of this rule are effective January 1, 2027.

AGENCY:
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Final rule with comment period.
SUMMARY:
This final rule with comment period revises the Medicare Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) and the Medicare Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) payment system for calendar year 2027 based on our continuing experience with these systems. We also describe the changes to the amounts and factors used to determine the payment rates for Medicare services paid under the OPPS and those paid under the ASC payment systems. In addition, this final rule with comment period updates and refines the requirements for the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program and the Ambulatory Surgical Center Quality Reporting Program. There are no changes to the Rural Emergency Hospital Quality Reporting Program. We finalized the expansion of the prior authorization requirement to include additional Botulinum Toxin Injection services. We also finalized implementation of certain provisions of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, for off-campus outpatient departments of a provider. In addition, this final rule with comment period announces notices of closure of teaching hospitals and opportunities to apply for available slots. Additionally, we finalized the policy that hospital accrediting organizations (AOs) with deeming authority may assess compliance with certain Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA) administrative requirements under
42 CFR 489.20
during accreditation and reaccreditation surveys.
DATES:
Effective Date:
The provisions of this rule are effective January 1, 2027.

I. Summary and Background
A. Executive Summary of This Document
1. Purpose
In this final rule with comment period, we are updating the payment policies and payment rates for services furnished to Medicare beneficiaries in hospital outpatient departments (HOPDs) and ambulatory surgical centers (ASCs), beginning January 1, 2027. Section 1833(t) of the Social Security Act (the Act) requires us to annually review and update the payment rates for services payable under the Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS). Specifically, section 1833(t)(9)(A) of the Act requires the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (the Secretary) to review certain components of the OPPS not less often than annually, and to revise the groups, the relative payment weights, and the wage and other adjustments to take into account changes in medical practice, changes in technology, and the addition of new services, new cost data, and other relevant information and factors. In addition, under section 1833(i)(2)(D)(v) of the Act, we annually review and update the ASC payment rates. This final rule with comment period also includes additional policy changes made in accordance with our experience with the OPPS and the ASC payment system and recent changes in our statutory authority. We describe these and various other statutory authorities in the relevant sections of this final rule with comment period. In addition, this final rule with comment period announces the closure of a teaching hospital and the opportunity to apply for available slots. In addition, this final rule with comment period updates and refines requirements for the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program and the Ambulatory Surgical Center Quality Reporting Program. There are no changes to the Rural Emergency Hospital Quality Reporting Program. We finalized the expansion of the prior authorization requirement to include additional Botulinum Toxin Injection services. This final rule with comment period also includes changes to implement certain provisions of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, for off-campus outpatient departments of a provider. Additionally, we are finalizing a policy that hospital

accreditation organizations (AOs) with deeming authority may assess compliance with certain EMTALA administrative requirements under
42 CFR 489.20
during accreditation and reaccreditation surveys.
2. Summary of the Major Provisions
OPPS Update:
For CY 2027, we are increasing the payment rates under the OPPS by an outpatient department (OPD) fee schedule increase factor of 2.3 percent. This increase factor is based on the inpatient hospital market basket percentage increase of 3.2 percent for inpatient services paid under the hospital inpatient prospective payment system (IPPS), reduced by the productivity adjustment of 0.9 percentage point. Based on this update, we estimate that total payments to OPPS providers (including beneficiary cost sharing and estimated changes in enrollment, utilization, and case mix) for calendar year (CY) 2027 will be approximately $114.4 billion, an increase of approximately $11 billion compared to estimated CY 2026 OPPS payments.
We are continuing to implement the statutory 2.0 percentage point reduction in payments for hospitals that fail to meet the hospital outpatient quality reporting requirements by applying a reporting factor of 0.9804 to the OPPS payments and copayments for all applicable services. Under the final 340B remedy offset, payments for services at hospitals subject to the 340B remedy offset will be reduced by 2.0 percentage points.
ASC Payment Update:
For CYs 2019 through 2023, we adopted a policy to update the ASC payment system using the hospital market basket update. In light of the impact of the COVID-19 public health emergency (PHE) on healthcare utilization, we extended our policy to update the ASC payment system using the hospital market basket update an additional 2 years—through CYs 2024 and 2025. For CY 2026, we extended this interim period an additional year—through CY 2026. In this final rule, we are extending our utilization of the hospital market basket update as the update factor for the ASC payment system for one additional year (through CY 2027). Using the hospital market basket update, for CY 2027, we are increasing payment rates under the ASC payment system by 2.3 percent for ASCs that meet the quality reporting requirements under the ASCQR Program. This increase is based on a hospital market basket percentage increase of 3.2 percent reduced by a final productivity adjustment of 0.9 percentage point. Based on this update, we estimate that total payments to ASCs (including beneficiary cost sharing and estimated changes in enrollment, utilization, and case-mix) for CY 2027 will be approximately $9.9 billion, an increase of approximately $560 million compared to estimated CY 2026 Medicare payments.
Adjustment for Cost-of-Living in Alaska and Hawaii:
For CY 2027, we are establishing a cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for outpatient hospital services provided in Alaska and Hawaii that applies the same COLA factors as finalized in the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule for FY 2027 for hospitals located in these States.
Device Pass-Through Payment Applications:
For CY 2027, we received 19 complete applications for device pass-through payments. We sought public comment on 13 applications (six applicants withdrew) and are approving device pass-through payment status for nine applications. We are also denying device pass-through payment status for four applications in this final rule with comment period.
Changes to the List of ASC Covered Surgical Procedures and Ancillary Services Lists:
For CY 2027, we are continuing to expand the ASC covered procedures list (CPL) by adding 618 codes to the ASC CPL that were recommended by interested parties or were finalized for removal from the IPO list for CY 2027.
Changes to the Inpatient Only (IPO) List:
We are continuing to phase out the IPO list by removing 637 services from the auditory, digestive, endocrine, female genital, hemic and lymphatic systems, integumentary, male genital, maternity care and delivery, mediastinum and diaphragm, respiratory and urinary clinical families from the IPO list for CY 2027.
Cross-Program Updates for the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting and Ambulatory Surgical Center Quality Reporting Programs:
We are removing the Appropriate Follow-Up Interval for Normal Colonoscopy in Average Risk Patients measure from the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting and Ambulatory Surgical Center Quality Reporting Programs.
Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program:
In addition to finalizing the cross-program proposal to remove the Appropriate Follow-Up Interval for Normal Colonoscopy in Average Risk Patients measure, we are updating and refining validation and validation reconsideration procedures, including policies applicable to electronic clinical quality measures (eCQMs).
Rural Emergency Hospital Quality Reporting Program:
We are not making any updates to the Rural Emergency Hospital Quality Reporting Program in this final rule with comment period.
Ambulatory Surgical Center Quality Reporting Program:
We are finalizing the cross-program measure proposal to remove the Appropriate Follow-Up Interval for Normal Colonoscopy in Average Risk Patients measure.
Expansion of Category for Hospital Outpatient Department Prior Authorization Process:
We added Botulinum Toxin Injection codes to the existing category of services subject to the Hospital Outpatient Department prior authorization process for dates of service on or after July 1, 2027.
Partial Hospitalization and Intensive Outpatient Programs:
We are updating the Partial Hospitalization Program (PHP) and Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP) payment rates for CY 2027 using the methodology we finalized in CY 2026.
Payment Adjustment for 340B-Acquired Drugs Based on Results of the Medicare OPPS Drug Acquisition Cost Survey:
Section 1833(t)(14)(D)(ii) of the Act requires the Secretary to periodically conduct surveys of hospital acquisition costs for each specified covered outpatient drug for use in setting the payment rates for such drugs. Additionally, on April 18, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order (E.O.) 14273, “Lowering Drug Prices by Once Again Putting Americans First”. Section 5 of the E.O., “Appropriately Accounting for Acquisition Costs of Drugs in Medicare”, which directs the Secretary of HHS to publish in the
Federal Register
a plan to conduct a survey under section 1833(t)(14)(D)(ii) of the Act so he can determine the hospital acquisition cost for covered outpatient drugs at hospital outpatient departments. Accordingly, from January 1, 2026 through April 7, 2026, we conducted a survey of the acquisition costs for each separately payable drug acquired by all hospitals paid under the OPPS. Taking the survey results into account, for CY 2027 we are paying ASP minus 28 percent for 340B acquired drugs. Statute requires that this policy be implemented in a budget neutral manner, so this will increase OPPS payments for non-drug services by an equivalent amount, which is estimated to be a 7.50 percent increase to non-drug service payments for this final rule with comment period.

3. Summary of Costs and Benefits
In section XXVI. of this final rule with comment period, we provide a detailed analysis of the regulatory and Federalism impacts that the changes will have on affected entities and beneficiaries. Key estimated impacts are described below.
a. Impacts of all OPPS Changes
Table 112 in section XXVI.C. of this final rule with comment period displays the distributional impact of all the OPPS changes on various groups of hospitals and CMHCs for CY 2027 compared to all estimated OPPS payments in CY 2026. We estimate that the finalized policies in this final rule with comment period will result in a 1.7 percent increase in OPPS payments to providers for services. We estimate that total OPPS payments for CY 2027, including beneficiary cost-sharing, to the approximately 3,600 facilities paid under the OPPS (including general acute care hospitals, children's hospitals, cancer hospitals, and CMHCs) will increase by approximately $1.78 billion compared to CY 2026 payments due to the OPD update, excluding changes in enrollment, utilization, and case-mix. However, for providers subject to the 340B remedy offset, the 340B remedy offset is estimated to reduce payments by $1.6 billion in CY 2027.
We estimated the isolated impact of our OPPS policies on CMHCs because CMHCs have historically only been paid for partial hospitalization services under the OPPS. Beginning CY 2024, they are also paid for IOP services under the OPPS. Based on our policy to calculate CMHC PHP and IOP costs based on 40 percent of the corresponding proposed hospital-based PHP and IOP costs, we estimate a 29.0 percent increase in CY 2027 payments to CMHCs relative to their CY 2026 payments.
b. Impacts of the Updated Wage Index
We estimate that our update of the wage indexes based on the fiscal year (FY) 2027 IPPS final rule wage indexes will result in no change for urban hospitals under the OPPS and a 0.3 percent increase for rural hospitals. These wage indexes include continued utilization of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) labor market area delineations based on 2020 Decennial Census data, with updates, as discussed in section II.C. of this final rule with comment period.
c. Impacts of the Rural Adjustment and the Cancer Hospital Payment Adjustment
For CY 2027, we will continue to provide additional payments to cancer hospitals so that a cancer hospital's payment-to-cost ratio (PCR) after the additional payments is equal to the weighted average PCR for the other OPPS hospitals using the most recently submitted or settled cost report data. Section 16002(b) of the 21st Century Cures Act requires that this weighted average PCR be reduced by 1.0 percentage point. For CY 2027, we are targeting PCR of 0.88 to determine the CY 2027 cancer hospital payment adjustment to be paid at cost report settlement. That is, the payment adjustments would be the additional payments needed to result in a PCR equal to 0.88 for each cancer hospital.
There are no significant impacts of our CY 2027 payment policies for hospitals that are eligible for the rural sole community hospital adjustment, as we are maintaining the current policy in the CY 2027 OPPS.
d. Impacts of the OPD Fee Schedule Increase Factor
For the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC, we are establishing an OPD fee schedule increase factor of 2.3 percent and applying that increase factor to the conversion factor for CY 2026. As a result of the OPD fee schedule increase factor and other budget neutrality adjustments, we estimate that urban hospitals will experience an increase in payments of 2.0 percent and that rural hospitals will experience an increase in payments of 5.6 percent. Classifying hospitals by teaching status, we estimate non-teaching hospitals will experience an increase in payments of 6.5 percent, minor teaching hospitals will experience an increase in payments of 3.5 percent, and major teaching hospitals will experience a decrease in payments of 2.0 percent. We also classified hospitals by the type of ownership. We estimate that hospitals with voluntary ownership will experience an increase of 2.1 percent in payments, while hospitals with government ownership will experience a decrease of 1.1 percent in payments. We estimate that hospitals with proprietary ownership will experience an increase of 10.5 percent in payments.

In an effort to ensure that Medicare and its beneficiaries pay appropriately for services and to encourage more efficient delivery of care, the Congress mandated replacement of the reasonable cost-based payment methodology with a prospective payment system (PPS). Under the OPPS, we generally pay for hospital Part B services on a rate-per-service basis that varies according to the APC group to which the service is assigned. We use the Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System (HCPCS) (which includes certain Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes) to identify and group the services within each APC. The OPPS includes payment for most hospital outpatient services, except those identified in section I.C. of this final rule with comment period. Section 1833(t)(1)(B) of the Act provides for payment under the OPPS for hospital outpatient services designated by the Secretary (which includes partial hospitalization services furnished by CMHCs), and certain inpatient hospital services that are paid under Medicare Part B.
The OPPS rate is an unadjusted national payment amount that includes the Medicare payment and the beneficiary copayment. This rate is divided into a labor-related amount and a nonlabor-related amount. The labor-related amount is adjusted for area wage differences using the hospital inpatient wage index value for the locality in which the hospital or CMHC is located.
All services and items within an APC group are comparable clinically and with respect to resource use, as required by section 1833(t)(2)(B) of the Act. In accordance with section 1833(t)(2)(B) of the Act, subject to certain exceptions, items and services within an APC group cannot be considered comparable with respect to the use of resources if the highest median cost (or mean cost, if elected by the Secretary) for an item or service in the APC group is more than 2 times greater than the lowest median cost (or mean cost, if elected by the Secretary) for an item or service within the same APC group (referred to as the “2 times rule”). In implementing this provision, we generally use the cost of the item or service assigned to an APC group.
For new technology items and services, special payments under the OPPS may be made in one of two ways. Section 1833(t)(6) of the Act provides for temporary additional payments, which we refer to as “transitional pass-through payments”, for at least 2 but not more than 3 years for certain drugs, biological agents, brachytherapy devices used for the treatment of cancer, and categories of other medical devices. For new technology services that are not eligible for transitional pass-through payments, and for which we lack sufficient clinical information and cost data to appropriately assign them to a clinical APC group, we have established special APC groups based on costs, which we refer to as New Technology APCs. These New Technology APCs are designated by cost bands which allow
(
printed page 70289)
us to provide appropriate and consistent payment for designated new procedures that are not yet reflected in our claims data. Similar to pass-through payments, an assignment to a New Technology APC is generally temporary; that is, we retain a service within a New Technology APC until we acquire sufficient data to assign it to a clinically appropriate APC group.
C. Excluded OPPS Services and Hospitals
Section 1833(t)(1)(B)(i) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to designate the hospital outpatient services that are paid under the OPPS. While most hospital outpatient services are payable under the OPPS, section 1833(t)(1)(B)(iv) of the Act excludes payment for ambulance, physical and occupational therapy, and speech-language pathology services, for which payment is made under a fee schedule. It also excludes screening mammography, diagnostic mammography, and effective January 1, 2011, an annual wellness visit providing personalized prevention plan services. The Secretary exercises the authority granted under the statute to also exclude from the OPPS certain services that are paid under fee schedules or other payment systems. Such excluded services include, for example, the professional services of physicians and nonphysician practitioners paid under the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (MPFS); certain laboratory services paid under the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (CLFS); services for beneficiaries with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) that are paid under the ESRD prospective payment system; and services and procedures that require an inpatient stay that are paid under the hospital IPPS. In addition, section 1833(t)(1)(B)(v) of the Act does not include applicable items and services (as defined in subparagraph (A) of paragraph (21)) that are furnished on or after January 1, 2017, by an off-campus outpatient department of a provider (as defined in subparagraph (B) of paragraph (21)). We set forth the services that are excluded from payment under the OPPS in regulations at
42 CFR 419.22
.
Under § 419.20(b) of the regulations, we specify the types of hospitals that are excluded from payment under the OPPS. These excluded hospitals are:
Critical access hospitals (CAHs);
Hospitals located in Maryland and paid under Maryland's All-Payer or Total Cost of Care Model;
Hospitals located outside of the 50 States, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico;
Indian Health Service (IHS) hospitals; and
Rural emergency hospitals (REHs).

E. Advisory Panel on Hospital Outpatient Payment (the HOP Panel or the Panel)
1. Authority of the Panel
Section 1833(t)(9)(A) of the Act, as amended by section 201(h) of
Public Law 106-113
, and redesignated by section 202(a)(2) of
Public Law 106-113
, requires that we consult with an expert outside advisory panel composed of an appropriate selection of representatives of providers to annually review (and advise the Secretary concerning) the clinical integrity of the payment groups and their weights under the OPPS. In CY 2000, based on section 1833(t)(9)(A) of the Act, the Secretary established the Advisory Panel on Ambulatory Payment Classification Groups (APC Panel) to fulfill this requirement. In CY 2011, based on section 222 of the Public Health Service Act (the PHS Act), which gives discretionary authority to the Secretary to convene advisory councils and committees, the Secretary expanded the panel's scope to include the supervision of hospital outpatient therapeutic services in addition to the APC groups and weights. To reflect this new role of the panel, the Secretary changed the panel's name to the Advisory Panel on Hospital Outpatient Payment (the HOP Panel). The HOP Panel is not restricted to using data compiled by CMS, and in conducting its review, it may use data collected or developed by organizations outside the Department.
2. Establishment of the Panel
On November 21, 2000, the Secretary signed the initial charter establishing the Panel, and, at that time, named the APC Panel. This expert panel is composed of appropriate representatives of providers (currently employed full-time, not as consultants, in their respective areas of expertise) who review clinical data and advise CMS about the clinical integrity of the APC groups and their payment weights. Since CY 2012, the Panel also is charged with advising the Secretary on the appropriate level of supervision for individual hospital outpatient therapeutic services. The Panel is technical in nature, and it is governed by the provisions of the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA). The current charter specifies, among other requirements, that the Panel—
May advise on the clinical integrity of Ambulatory Payment Classification (APC) groups and their associated weights;
May advise on the appropriate supervision level for hospital outpatient services;
May advise on OPPS APC rates for ASC covered surgical procedures;
Continues to be technical in nature;

For CY 2027, we proposed to continue to use the hospital-specific overall ancillary and departmental cost-to-charge ratios (CCRs) to convert charges to estimated costs through application of a revenue code-to-cost center
(

To calculate the APC costs on which the proposed CY 2027 APC payment rates are based, we calculated hospital-specific departmental CCRs for each hospital for which we had CY 2025 claims data by comparing these claims data to the most recently available hospital cost reports, which, in most cases, are from CY 2024. For the proposed CY 2027 OPPS payment rates, we used the set of claims processed during CY 2025. We applied the hospital-specific CCR to the hospital's charges at the most detailed level possible, based on a revenue code-to-cost center crosswalk that contains a hierarchy of CCRs used to estimate costs from charges for each revenue code. In accordance with our longstanding policy, similar to our finalized policy for CY 2026 OPPS ratesetting, we proposed to calculate CCRs for the standard cost centers—cost centers with a predefined label—and nonstandard cost centers—cost centers defined by a hospital—accepted by the electronic cost report database. In general, the most detailed level at which we calculate CCRs is the hospital-specific departmental level.

a. Calculation of Single Procedure APC Criteria-Based Costs
(1) Blood and Blood Products
Since the implementation of the OPPS in August 2000, we have made separate payments for blood and blood products through APCs rather than packaging payment for them into payments for the procedures with which they are administered. Hospital payments for the costs of blood and blood products, as well as for the costs of collecting,
(
printed page 70292)
processing, and storing blood and blood products, are made through the OPPS payments for specific blood product APCs.
We proposed to continue to establish payment rates for blood and blood products using our blood-specific CCR methodology (
90 FR 53457
), which utilizes actual or simulated CCRs from the most recently available hospital cost reports to convert hospital charges for blood and blood products to costs. This methodology has been our standard ratesetting methodology for blood and blood products since CY 2005. It was developed in response to data analysis indicating that there was a significant difference in CCRs for those hospitals with and without blood-specific cost centers and past public comments indicating that the former OPPS policy of defaulting to the overall hospital CCR for hospitals not reporting a blood-specific cost center often resulted in an underestimation of the true hospital costs for blood and blood products. To address the differences in CCRs and to better reflect hospitals' costs, our methodology simulates blood CCRs for each hospital that does not report a blood cost center by calculating the ratio of the blood-specific CCRs to hospitals' overall CCRs for those hospitals that do report costs and charges for blood cost centers and applies this mean ratio to the overall CCRs of hospitals not reporting costs and charges for blood cost centers on their cost reports. We proposed to calculate the costs upon which the proposed payment rates for blood and blood products are based using the actual blood-specific CCR for hospitals that reported costs and charges for a blood cost center and a hospital-specific, simulated, blood-specific CCR for hospitals that did not report costs and charges for a blood cost center.
We continue to believe that the hospital-specific, simulated, blood-specific CCR methodology takes into account the unique charging and cost accounting structure of each hospital, as it better responds to the absence of a blood-specific CCR for a hospital than alternative methodologies, such as defaulting to the overall hospital CCR or applying an average blood-specific CCR across hospitals. This methodology also yields more accurate estimated costs for these products and results in payment rates for blood and blood products that appropriately reflect the relative estimated costs of these products for hospitals without blood cost centers and for these blood products in general (
91 FR 41742
).

A C-APC is defined as a classification for the provision of a primary service and all adjunctive services provided to support the delivery of the primary service. We established C-APCs as a category broadly for OPPS payment and implemented 25 C-APCs beginning in CY 2015 (

;

Under our C-APC policy, we designate a service described by a HCPCS code assigned to a C-APC as the primary service when the service is identified by OPPS status indicator “J1”. When such a primary service is reported on a hospital outpatient claim, taking into consideration the few exceptions that are discussed below, we make payment for all other items and services reported on the hospital outpatient claim as being integral, ancillary, supportive, dependent, and adjunctive to the primary service (hereinafter collectively referred to as “adjunctive services”) and representing components of a complete comprehensive service (

and

This results in a single prospective payment for each of the primary, comprehensive services based on the costs of all reported services at the claim level. One example of a primary service would be a partial mastectomy, and an example of a secondary service packaged into that primary service would be a radiation therapy procedure.
Services excluded from the C-APC policy under the OPPS include services that are not covered OPD services, services that cannot, by statute, be paid for under the OPPS, and services that are required by statute to be separately paid. This includes certain mammography and ambulance services that are not covered OPD services in accordance with section 1833(t)(1)(B)(iv) of the Act; brachytherapy seeds, which also are required by statute to receive separate payment under section 1833(t)(2)(H) of the Act; pass-through payment drugs and devices, which also require separate payment under section 1833(t)(6) of the Act; self-administered drugs (SADs) that are not otherwise packaged as supplies because they are not covered under Medicare Part B under section 1861(s)(2)(B) of the Act; and certain preventive services (
