55. Cystourethroscopy With Lithotripsy and Vacuum Aspiration of Kidney, HCPCS Codes C9761 and C0814 (APCs 5375 and 5376)
HCPCS code C9761 (
Cystourethroscopy, with ureteroscopy and/or pyeloscopy, with lithotripsy, and ureteral catheterization for steerable vacuum aspiration of the kidney, collecting system, ureter, bladder, and urethra if necessary, with use of steerable ureteral catheter or suction-integrated ureteroscope
) became effective October 1, 2020 and describes a minimally invasive procedure used to break up and remove kidney stone fragments and dust by use of a continuous irrigation and vacuum system. The long descriptor was revised in CY 2023 to include “must use a steerable ureteral catheter” and we further revised the long descriptor to include “suction-integrated ureteroscope” effective July 1, 2026, after meeting with the specialty society.
We also established HCPCS code C8014 (Cystourethroscopy, with ureteroscopy and/or pyeloscopy, with lithotripsy, including use of a suction enabled ureteral access sheath, with irrigation (if performed) effective July 1, 2026, to describe these cystourethroscopy procedures where a suction-enabled ureteral access sheath is used to vacuum kidney stone fragments. We assigned HCPCS code C8014 to APC 5375 (Level 5 Urology and Related Procedures) and status indicator `J1' as we believe this procedure with this device has clinical and resource similarities to other procedures assigned to APC 5375.
For CY 2027, the OPPS payment rates are proposed based on available CY 2025 claims data. For the CY 2027 proposed rule, we found a total of 3,516 single frequency claims and a geometric mean cost of approximately $9,472 for HCPCS code C9761. For CY 2027, we proposed to maintain the APC assignment of 5376 (Level 6 Urology and Related Procedures) and status indicator of `J1' for HCPCS code C9761.
For CY 2027, we proposed to maintain the APC and status indicator assignment for HCPCS code C8014. We currently have no claims data for ratesetting purposes as this is a new code.
We received public comments on these two HCPCS codes. Below is a summary of the comments and our responses.
Comment:
A commenter suggested that we consolidate both C-codes into one single technology-neutral code to describe suction-assisted ureteroscopic and/or pyeloscopic lithotripsy and if we did not consolidate the two C-codes, provide exclusive coding instructions for each of these HCPCS codes. The commenter explained that both of these C-codes describe suction-assisted stone-fragment evacuation during cystourethroscopy with ureteroscopy and/or pyeloscopy with lithotripsy and are furnished during the same procedure, through the same anatomic pathway, and for the same purpose. The commenter believes the device distinction is not enough of a meaningful difference to require separate HCPCS codes or have a different APC assignment. The commenter cites studies supporting their position that the performance between a flexible and navigable suction access sheath (FANS) and the CVAC system described by C9761. The commenter then went on to say that if CMS continues to maintain both HCPCS codes, C9761 and C8014 should be assigned to the same APC. The commenter requested that CMS publish clear coding instructions with illustrative examples distinguishing between the three types of devices: (1) a suction-enabled ureteral access sheath (
i.e.,
FANS); (2) a steerable vacuum-aspiration ureteral catheter (
i.e.,
CVAC system); and (3) a suction-integrated ureteroscope noting that additional coding guidance would support accurate coding and reduce claims denials.
Another commenter requested that we reassign C8014 to APC 5376 (Level 6 Urology and Related Services stating that the reassignment would be more appropriate, both clinically and based on resource utilization. The commenter noted that there are a number of complex kidney stone procedures in APC 5376, including HCPCS code C9761. The commenter believes that because we do not yet have claims data available for C8014 for our standard geometric mean cost (GMC) methodology, clinical coherence with existing APC assignments should receive significant consideration in evaluating the appropriate APC placement, such as C9761 as a crosswalk. In addition, the commenter provided their analysis of claims data to support their belief that C8014 would be more appropriately assigned to APC 5376.
Another commenter supported the creation of HCPCS code C8014 and its APC assignment to APC 5375 (Level 5 Urology and Related Services). They believe that the creation of this code will help CMS measure utilization, resources, and costs separately from the service described by HCPCS code C9761
(
printed page 70418)
and refine payment as we begin to have claims data.
The commenter expressed concerns regarding the revised long descriptor for C9761 stating that the revised language causes some further confusion with cases involving a suction-capable ureteroscope (also commonly referred to as a direct in-scope suction (DISS) ureteroscope), with or without a suction-enabled ureteral access sheath. The commenter requested clarification regarding the term “integrated” and suggested that there be a documentation-based framework that articulates three different care pathways to distinguish the type of technology used (or not used), including (1) the standard ureteroscopy/lithotripsy pathway; (2) the suction-enabled access sheath pathway; and (3) the steerable-vacuum aspiration pathway. The commenter states that the clinical literature does not support the equivalency of suction-capable ureteroscopes and suction-enabled access sheaths are equivalent to the steerable renal vacuum-aspiration service represented by HCPCS code C9761.
This commenter believes that our coding clarification should distinguish the device predicate from the service predicate and further clarification is necessary for payment accuracy, beneficiary protection, and program integrity. The commenter suggests that HCPCS C9761 is coded when the services actually provided are less resource intensive. To remedy these concerns, the commenter requested that CMS issue provider communication explaining the three types of care pathways to distinguish the types of technology used and define “suction-integrated ureteroscope” in functional terms, or in the alternative, revise the current long descriptors to provide clarity regarding the service described by the code.
Response:
We appreciate the input and recommendations from the interested parties. Over the years we have heard from interested parties regarding concerns about providers utilizing HCPCS code C9761 to describe the ureteroscopy/lithotripsy procedure with a suction-enabled ureteral access sheath and the potential program integrity concerns that raises when C9761 is assigned to a higher APC because of the underlying device costs. To remedy these concerns, we created C8014 to specifically describe the ureteroscopy/lithotripsy procedures with suction-enabled sheaths and assigned it to what we believe is an appropriate APC. We then heard from the American Urological Association who then informed us that there is a third type of device (suction-integrated ureteroscope) that is used to vacuum stone fragments during ureteroscopy/lithotripsy procedures. As a result, we revised the descriptor language to include this device in the descriptor for C9761.
We do not believe that we should at this time consolidate these two HCPCS codes into one single technology neutral code and assign it to APC 5376. While we understand the rationale, we do not want to create further coding confusion since we just created C8014 to distinguish suction-enabled sheaths from steerable vacuum catheters and suction-integrated ureteroscopes. We believe the descriptor language is clear and that there is enough of a difference in costs that warrants separate coding. In addition, we do not believe both HCPCS codes should be assigned to the same APC.
In response to the comments regarding coding guidance and MLN education, we have stated in past rules that we do not provide coding guidance, as it is out of scope for the OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
89 FR 94122
) and if hospitals have questions about appropriate coding that they cannot resolve on their own, the appropriate first step would be to review the HCPCS codes or consult their Medicare Administrative Contractor (MAC) for their jurisdiction. We refer readers to MLN Matters MM14477 (OPPS July 2026 Update) for information regarding the creation of C8014 and the descriptor revision for C9761.
In summary, after consideration of the public comments we received, we are finalizing our proposal without modification, to assign HCPCS code C9761 to APC 5376 (Level 6 Urology and Related Procedures) and a status indicator of `J1' and HCPCS code C8014 to APC 5375 (Level 5 Urology and Related Procedures) and a status indicator of `J1'. As we do every year, we will monitor the claims data and reevaluate the APC assignments for these codes in the next rulemaking cycle to determine if more appropriate APC assignments are warranted.
The final CY 2027 payment rates for these codes can be found in Addendum B to this final rule with comment period. 2. New Device Pass-Through Applications for CY 2027
a. Background
Section 1833(t)(6) of the Act provides pass-through payments for devices, and section 1833(t)(6)(B) of the Act requires CMS to use categories to determine the eligibility of devices for pass-through payments. As part of implementing the statute through regulations, we continue to believe that pass-through payments for devices that offer substantial clinical improvement are important to ensure that hospitals can provide Medicare beneficiaries with access to the advantages of the new technology. Conversely, we have noted that the need for additional payments for devices that offer little or no clinical improvement over previously existing devices is less apparent. In such cases, these devices can still be used by hospitals, and hospitals will be paid for them through appropriate APC payment. Moreover, a goal is to target pass-through payments for devices where cost considerations are most likely to interfere with patient
(
printed page 70426)
access (
66 FR 55852
;
67 FR 66782
; and
70 FR 68629
).
As specified in regulations at § 419.66(b)(1) through (3), to be eligible for transitional pass-through payment under the OPPS, a device must meet the following criteria:
If required by FDA, the device must have received FDA approval or clearance (except for a device that has received an FDA investigational device exemption (IDE) and has been classified as a Category B device by FDA), or meet another appropriate FDA exemption; and the pass-through payment application must be submitted within 3 years from the date of the initial FDA marketing authorization, if required, unless there is a documented, verifiable delay in U.S. market availability after FDA marketing authorization is granted, in which case CMS will consider the pass-through payment application if it is submitted within 3 years from the date of market availability;
The device is determined to be reasonable and necessary for the diagnosis or treatment of an illness or injury or to improve the functioning of a malformed body part, as required by section 1862(a)(1)(A) of the Act; and
The device is an integral part of the service furnished, is used for one patient only, comes in contact with human tissue, and is surgically implanted or inserted (either permanently or temporarily), or applied in or on a wound or other skin lesion.
As finalized in CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, skin substitutes with an approved Biologics License Application (BLA) will be considered under transitional drug pass-through payment status, and skin substitutes with FDA Premarket approval (PMA) or FDA 510(k) clearance will continue to be evaluated under transitional device pass-through payment status (
90 FR 53636
).
In addition, according to § 419.66(b)(4), a device is not eligible to be considered for device pass-through payment if it is any of the following: (1) equipment, an instrument, apparatus, implement, or item of this type for which depreciation and financing expenses are recovered as depreciable assets as defined in Chapter 1 of the Medicare Provider Reimbursement Manual (CMS Pub. 15-1); or (2) a material or supply furnished incident to a service (for example, a suture, customized surgical kit, or clip, other than a radiological site marker).
Separately, we use the following criteria, under § 419.66(c), to determine whether a new category of pass-through payment devices should be established. The device to be included in the new category must—
Not be appropriately described by an existing category or by any category previously in effect established for transitional pass-through payments, and was not being paid for as an outpatient service as of December 31, 1996;
Have an average cost that is not “insignificant” relative to the payment amount for the procedure or service with which the device is associated as determined under § 419.66(d) by demonstrating: (1) the estimated average reasonable cost of devices in the category exceeds 25 percent of the applicable APC payment amount for the service related to the category of devices; (2) the estimated average reasonable cost of the devices in the category exceeds the cost of the device-related portion of the APC payment amount for the related service by at least 25 percent; and (3) the difference between the estimated average reasonable cost of the devices in the category and the portion of the APC payment amount for the device exceeds 10 percent of the APC payment amount for the related service (with the exception of brachytherapy and temperature-monitored cryoablation, which are exempt from the cost requirements as specified at § 419.66(c)(3) and (e)).
To meet the cost criterion for device pass-through payment status, a device must pass all three tests of the cost criterion for at least one APC. We generally use the lowest APC payment rate applicable for use with the nominated device when we assess whether a device meets the cost significance criterion, thus increasing the probability the device will pass the cost significance test (
69 FR 65775
), and we calculate the device offset amount at the HCPCS/CPT code level (
81 FR 79657
); and
Demonstrate a substantial clinical improvement, that is, the device to be included in the category has demonstrated that it will substantially improve the diagnosis or treatment of an illness or injury or improve the functioning of a malformed body part compared to the benefits of a device or devices in a previously established category or other available treatment, or, for devices for which pass-through payment status will begin on or after January 1, 2020, as an alternative pathway to demonstrating substantial clinical improvement, a device is part of the FDA's Breakthrough Devices Program and has received marketing authorization for the indication covered by the Breakthrough Device designation.
In the CY 2016 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we changed our device pass-through evaluation and determination process. Device pass-through applications are still submitted to CMS through the quarterly process, but the applications are subject to notice and comment rulemaking in the next applicable OPPS annual rulemaking cycle. Under this process, all applications preliminarily approved during quarterly review will automatically be included in the next applicable OPPS annual rulemaking cycle, while applicants whose submissions are not approved during quarterly review will have the option of being included in the next applicable OPPS annual rulemaking cycle or withdrawing their application from consideration. Under this notice-and-comment process, applicants may submit new evidence, such as clinical trial results published in a peer-reviewed journal or other materials, for consideration during the public comment process for the proposed rule. This process allows those applications that we are able to determine meet all of the criteria for device pass-through payment under the quarterly review process to receive timely pass-through payment status, while still allowing for a transparent, public review process for all applications (

The applicant stated that the Altius® System consists of the (1) Altius® Implantable Pulse Generator (IPG), which is implanted in the abdomen; (2) Altius® Cuff Electrode Leads; (3) Altius® Battery Charger and alternating current (AC) adapter; (4) Altius® Patient Controller, which allows the patient to activate the IPG to initiate therapy; (5) Programming Wand, which is used by the provider to program and set stimulus therapy parameters; and (6) Programmer Application Personal Computer (PAPC), which includes physician programming software. The applicant is seeking a new device category for transitional pass-through payment status for only the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components of the Altius® System. The applicant stated that the Altius® IPG is a rechargeable neurotransmitter device that is implanted in the abdomen and when activated, generates a continuous high frequency, high amplitude alternating current electrical stimulus (5kHz and 10kHz) via the Altius® Cuff Electrode Leads, which are circumferentially wrapped, anchored, and implanted around the nerve(s). Per the applicant, the “alternating” nature of the delivered electrical stimulus refers to the direct electrical stimulation of the circumferential electrodes within a lead distributed in an alternating fashion across these electrodes.

We received the application for device pass-through payment status for the Altius® System within 3 years of the date of FDA PMA approval. Based on our review of the application, we have determined that the Altius® System meets the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1) and that the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components meet the eligibility criteria at § 419.66(b)(3) and (4).
In the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, we noted regarding the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1), with respect to the Altius® IPG and Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components, that the applicant stated that no existing (current or previous) device pass-through payment categories appropriately describe the nominated device components. Per the applicant, the existing pass-through codes C1778 (Lead, neurostimulator (implantable)) and C1822 (Generator, neurostimulator (implantable), high frequency, with rechargeable battery and charging system) do not describe the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components because these codes (1) are not specifically indicated for treating chronic intractable lower limb amputation pain; (2) are not capable of delivering continuous, high amplitude, high frequency alternating current; (3) do not use circumferentially wrapped and anchored cuff electrode leads to provide direct energy delivery to the targeted nerves; and (4) do not allow for physician-pre-programmed therapy delivery controlled by the patient using the patient stimulation controller. The applicant also stated that devices described by C1778 do not make direct contact with the target nerve; instead, they deliver stimulation to the general region of the pain, unlike the Altius® Cuff Electrode Leads. The applicant added that existing devices described by C1822 deliver low-amplitude, rectangular pulses per second to general or peripheral areas to increase nerve activity and produce pain relief, whereas the Altius® IPG provides continuous, high-amplitude sinusoidal waveform stimulation to decrease target nerve activity and produce on-demand pain relief. The applicant stated that the Altius® System, including the Altius® IPG and Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components, is the only FDA-authorized neuromodulation system indicated as an aid in the management of chronic intractable phantom and residual lower limb post-amputation pain in adult amputees.
Based on the description the applicant provided, we stated that the Altius® IPG is a rechargeable neurotransmitter device that generates a continuous high frequency, high amplitude alternating electrical stimulus (5kHz and 10kHz) via the Altius® Cuff Electrode Leads, which are circumferentially wrapped, anchored, and implanted around the nerve(s), and therefore, could be appropriately described by C1778 (Lead, neurostimulator (implantable)) and C1822 (Generator, neurostimulator (implantable), high frequency, with rechargeable battery and charging system), respectively. Specifically, we stated our belief that the pass-through payment category C1778 may appropriately describe the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead component because the pass-through payment category describes any device that is an implantable neurostimulator lead. Additionally, we stated our belief that the pass-through payment category C1822 may appropriately describe the Altius® IPG because the category includes implantable neurostimulator pulse generators that deliver high-frequency stimulation (including approximately 10 kHz) and are rechargeable using an external charging system. Further, we stated that C1822 does not describe the amplitude, pulse frequency, or waveform of the stimulation generated by the device. We noted that CMS does not establish pass-through device categories for the purpose of describing specific devices, but rather, device categories are intended to encompass all devices that can be appropriately described by a category. In this context, we stated that we believed that the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components may be appropriately described by C1778 and C1822. We also stated that, after reviewing the information provided by the applicant, we were unable to determine that the Altius® System, inclusive of the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components, meets the device category eligibility criteria, and therefore, we proposed to deny transitional pass-through payment status for CY 2027.
We invited public comment on whether the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components meet the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1). We also invited public comments on our proposal to deny transitional pass-through payment status for the Altius® System, inclusive of the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components for CY 2027.

Comment:
The applicant and many commenters requested that CMS approve device pass-through payment for the Altius® System. The applicant and these commenters stated that denying pass-through payment for the Altius® System would create major financial barriers for hospitals and surgical centers, resulting in fewer offering the device, and therefore, limiting Medicare patients' access to a proven, non-opioid treatment for severe post-amputation pain. In addition, the applicant and commenters stated that the Altius® System offers a meaningful safety and quality-of-life benefit, as well as directly supporting CMS and the broader public health system's ongoing priorities to expand non-opioid pain therapies.
The applicant and commenters stated that they believe there are no existing device categories or categories previously in effect that appropriately describe the Altius® System. In response to our concerns that the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components may be appropriately described by C1778 and C1822, the applicant and commenters stated that, in the proposed rule, CMS misclassified the Altius® System under C codes for legacy spinal cord stimulation (SCS) and peripheral nerve stimulation (PNS) devices, specifically C1778 (Lead, neurostimulator implantable) and C1822 (generator, neurostimulator (implantable), high frequency, with rechargeable battery and charging system). The applicant and commenters stated that neither C1778 and C1822, nor any existing neurostimulator codes, adequately describe the Altius® System because it is a fundamentally new type of device. The applicant and commenters
(
printed page 70432)
reiterated that the Altius® System is an FDA Breakthrough-designated therapy engineered specifically to deliver an on-demand, high-frequency, high-amplitude alternating current and circumferential electric nerve conduction block.
The applicant and several commenters stated that the Altius® System represents a distinct technology class defined by a unique mechanism of action (neurostimulation that results in a complete electrical nerve block), a unique electrode design (360° circumferential cuff surgically wrapped around the sciatic nerve or its main branches through a dedicated open surgical implant), and a unique energy delivery profile (high blocking amplitude in a continuous alternating current (5-10k Hz) in 30 minute). The applicant and commenters compared the Altius® System's mechanism of action to that of legacy SCS and PNS devices which rely on percutaneous leads placed near a nerve that stimulate the nerve at a low amplitude and frequency (10-100 Hz) in discrete pulses using a field effect to produce paresthesia intended to mask pain. The applicant and commenters stated that paresthesia cannot override the constant, high-frequency ectopic firing of a damaged peripheral neuroma, eventually rendering these legacy devices ineffective. The applicant and commenters stated that the Altius® System deadens nerve endings in a completely different way than current peripheral and spinal cord stimulators, and, as a result, no existing device categories describe the nominated device and its novel therapy. The applicant and commenters further explained that implanting the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead, a full circumferential cuff, requires an open surgical procedure under general anesthesia in an ambulatory surgical center or hospital outpatient department, rather than the quick needle-based placement used for standard leads done in office.
In addition, the applicant stated that existing OPPS Ambulatory Payment Classifications (APCs) for general neurostimulators reflect low-cost, percutaneously-inserted needle lead systems and do not cover the additional expenses associated with the Altius® System. The applicant stated that, by stating C1822 appropriately describes the Altius® IPG, CMS is equating high-frequency spinal cord generators that deliver low-amplitude pulsed direct current into the epidural space to alter central gating without blocking nerve conduction with the Altius® IPG's high-amplitude alternating current generator that produces a true peripheral nerve conduction block. According to the applicant, by stating that C1778 appropriately describes the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components, CMS is also equating percutaneous lead wires place adjacent to tissues with the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead's 360-degree cuff electrode that is surgically wrapped around the sciatic nerve. The applicant concluded that grouping the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components under legacy SCS and PNS codes (C1822 and C1778) mischaracterizes the Altius® System's physics, biology, and clinical reality. The applicant further suggested that CMS create the following new device category code that would appropriately describe the Altius® System: neurostimulator system, peripheral, circumferential nerve block, includes an implanted rechargeable pulse generator (high frequency, high amplitude, alternating current), implanted cuff electrode(s) (wrapped around nerve), and patient controller.
Another commenter stated that the existing HCPCS device categories, including C1778 and C1822 appropriately describe the Altius® System and its components. The commenter stated that, as CMS noted, C1822 does not describe a specific amplitude, pulse frequency, or waveform generated by a device. The commenter stated that rather, HCPCS device categories are intended to encompass all devices that share the relevant functional and technological characteristics, not to distinguish among individual products based on proprietary design features. Further, the commenter stated that the Altius® System's lead design does not appear to be sufficiently unique to warrant creation of a new device category. Per the commenter, other commercially available neurostimulation systems utilize leads that wrap around and anchor to a target nerve. The commenter stated, for example, that LivaNova's VNS Therapy
TM
System employs a helical lead that coils around the vagus nerve and is secured in place, demonstrating that circumferential nerve-wrapping lead designs are already present in the market and can be appropriately accommodated within existing neurostimulator lead categories. The commenter concluded that distinctions resting on a device's approved indication, electrode geometry, stimulation parameters, control interface, or the physiologic direction of its effect do not identify anything absent from the current HCPCS framework nor is the analysis altered by Breakthrough Device Designation, which affects only the requirement to demonstrate substantial clinical improvement and does not displace the pass-through requirement at § 419.66(c)(1).
Response:
We appreciate the applicant's and commenters' input. After consideration of the public comments we received and further review of the application, we agree with the applicant that there is no existing device category, or category previously in effect, that appropriately describes a neurostimulator system that uses high-frequency, alternating current.
In the proposed rule, we also invited public comment on whether the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components meet the cost criterion at § 419.66(d).
We did not receive any comments regarding whether the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components meet the cost significance criteria as described at § 419.66(d). Based on our findings from the first, second, and third cost significant tests, we continue to believe the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components meet the cost significance criteria specified at § 419.66(d).
After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the device pass-through application, we have determined that the Altius® System, inclusive of the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components, meets the requirements for device pass-through status described at § 419.66. Therefore, we are approving the Altius® System for device pass-through payment status effective January 1, 2027, under the alternative pathway for devices that have an FDA Breakthrough Device designation and FDA marketing authorization for the indication covered by the Breakthrough Device designation.

Comment:
The applicant submitted a public comment in support of device pass-through payments for the ProSense® Cryoablation System, noting that the nominated device meets all the transitional device pass-through payment criteria. The applicant also stated that transitional pass-through payment is intended to reduce financial disincentives and for new technology to be adopted so that it provides a substantial clinical improvement to Medicare beneficiaries. The applicant stated that the population for which FDA authorized the ProSense® Cryoablation System is primarily the Medicare population, and without transitional pass-through payment, hospitals face a disincentive to adopt the only FDA-authorized, non-surgical local treatment for low-risk breast cancer, particularly for women for whom surgery is an unsuitable option. In addition, the applicant stated that CMS establishing a device category effective January 1, 2027, would allow Medicare beneficiaries access to the ProSense® Cryoablation System while hospitals are making adoption decisions.
With respect to the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1), the applicant requested that CMS recognize October 3, 2025, as the initial date of FDA marketing authorization and the beginning of the newness period for the ProSense® Cryoablation System. The applicant reiterated that FDA granted the ProSense® Cryoablation System De Novo classification on October 3, 2025, and maintained that this is the initial date of FDA authorization for purposes of device pass-through payment status. The applicant also noted that it submitted its application for transitional pass-through payment on December 26, 2025, within three years of this date. The applicant stated that FDA classified the ProSense® Cryoablation System as a new generic device type under a newly created classification regulation (
21 CFR 878.4355
): cryoablation device for local treatment of low-risk breast cancer. The applicant added that FDA assigned this device type a new product code, QXW (DEN220077), consistent with section 513(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act which states that the classification shall be the initial classification of the device.
According to the applicant, federal regulations (
21 CFR 860.200(a)
) state that the purpose of the De Novo process is to classify devices for which there is no legally marketed device on which to base a review of substantial equivalence. The applicant stated that because FDA granted the ProSense® Cryoablation System De Novo authorization, rather than 510(k) clearance, FDA has already determined that there is no legally marketed predicate device for the nominated device. The applicant further stated that FDA's De Novo order created a device type, a classification regulation, and a product code that did not previously exist, and it imposed special controls, including a 400-patient, 30-site post-market surveillance study, that apply to no prior cryoablation clearance. Additionally, the applicant stated that it is inappropriate for CMS to extrapolate to previous 510(k) devices when FDA has already determined that the device qualifies for De Novo classification. The applicant concluded that CMS should use October 3, 2025, as the initial date of FDA marketing authorization, and recognize that the ProSense® Cryoablation System meets the criteria for the transitional pass-through payment.
Response:
We appreciate the applicant's input. After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, we continue to believe that the ProSense® Cryoablation System, including the nominated Prosense® Cryoprobe, received FDA marketing authorization prior to the October 3, 2025 De Novo classification. As previously discussed, the current ProSense® Cryoablation System was included in K183213, cleared on December 20, 2019, and that clearance identified the previously cleared IceSense
TM
3 System in K102360 as its predicate. As we stated in the proposed rule, in the K183213 clearance, FDA stated that the ProSense® Cryoablation System is a rebranding of the IceSense
TM
3 single-probe system in K102360, with the same hardware and software components. Additionally, FDA stated that it analyzed and determined that the hardware and software changes introduced since the IceSense
TM
3 System clearance on November 29, 2010 did not require new 510(k) premarket notifications. The current system and cryoablation technology are traceable through FDA clearances issued on November 18, 2005 (K052530), November 29, 2010 (K102360), and December 20, 2019 (K183213). Therefore, the ProSense® Cryoablation System does not meet the newness criterion described at § 419.66(b)(1) because we received the ProSense® Cryoablation System application for device pass-through payment on December 26, 2025, which is not within 3 years of these prior FDA marketing authorizations.
While the applicant stated that the ProSense® Cryoablation System De Novo classification on October 3, 2025 established a new device type, classification regulation, and product code, and that FDA's order states that the classification is the initial classification of the device, it appears that this De Novo authorization established a new FDA classification for the device when used for the treatment of certain patients with low-risk breast cancer. Therefore, it does not constitute the initial FDA marketing authorization of this device technology for the purposes of § 419.66(b)(1), because this device technology, including the nominated cryoprobe, had previously received FDA marketing authorization with different indications for use. Although we recognize FDA's regulatory responsibility for determining the appropriate pathway for marketing authorization, CMS applies the requirements at § 419.66(b)(1) in determining whether a device technology meets the newness criterion for device pass-through payment, which does not depend on the type of FDA marketing authorization.
Because we have not received information demonstrating that the device itself is sufficiently different from the previously cleared ProSense® Cryoablation System such that October 3, 2025 should not be considered its initial FDA marketing authorization for purposes of § 419.66(b)(1), we continue to believe that the October 3, 2025, De Novo classification does not restart the newness period.
After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, the ProSense® Cryoablation System does not meet the newness criterion to be considered for device pass-through payment. Therefore, in this final rule with comment period, we will not address whether the technology meets the remaining criteria required for device pass-through payment. We are not approving the ProSense® Cryoablation System for device pass-through payment status for CY 2027 because the technology does not meet the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1).

We stated we had several concerns with this study.
Firstly, we stated we were concerned that the study does not provide a comparison to a control group, such as patients treated with standard graft-to-vein sutured anastomosis. Without a comparison to currently available treatments, particularly in the clinical setting where it is most likely to be used, we stated we were unable to assess whether the EndoForce
TM

To demonstrate substantial clinical improvement, we stated we consider supporting evidence, preferably published peer-reviewed clinical trials, that show improved clinical outcomes, such as reduction in mortality, complications, subsequent interventions, future hospitalizations, recovery time, pain, or a more rapid beneficial resolution of the disease process compared to other currently available treatments.
Secondly, we were concerned that the smaller patient population and study design of Burgess et al. (2024), and the lack of stratification by key clinical factors known to affect AVG outcomes, may limit both the reliability of the cumulative patency findings and the generalizability of results to the Medicare population. We stated that stratification factors, such as coronary artery disease, hypertension status, and ipsilateral access placement, which have all been shown to be associated with thrombosis, need for intervention, and cumulative patency would be helpful to assess the outcomes.
In addition, we stated it was unclear to what extent any improvement in cumulative patency is due to use of the EndoForce
TM

TM

Specifically, we stated that Burgess et al. (2024) reports a 6-month cumulative patency of 92 percent in its patient population and compares it to the 80 percent rate reported in Halbert et al. In contrast, we stated that Burgess et al. (2024) analyzed ESRD patients between 2018 and 2021. Thus, we questioned whether the results in Halbert et al. (2024). Similarly, we stated that Harms et al. (2016) is a retrospective study of 599 patients treated between January 2006 and December 2011, and Woodside et al. We noted that these studies reflect earlier clinical practices and patient populations that differ from those in Burgess et al. (2024), which evaluated patients between 2018 and 2021. We stated that Burgess et al. (2024) compared its reported intervention rate of 1.22 per patient-year to higher rates reported in Harms et al. (2016) and Woodside et al. Moreover, we noted patient populations varied across studies, and it is unclear how these differences may have affected intervention rates per patient-year. We stated, for example, Burgess et al. However, we continue to have several of the concerns listed in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule. TM

We expressed concern in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule that Burgess et al. (2024) lacked stratification by key clinical factors known to affect AVG outcomes, and therefore, there are insufficient data to rule out the possibility that factors other than EndoForce
TM
may also have impacted cumulative and primary unassisted patency. (2026) studies, and the percentages of those who were male, white, diabetic, with hypertension, cardiovascular disease, or current tobacco use. However, we note that other risk factors, such as prior catheter use, low albumin, an elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) level, low fetuin-A, low diastolic blood pressure, hemoglobin <10 g/dL, peripheral artery disease, and low initial intra-access blood flow (< 650 mL/min), have also been associated with decreased patency.

Even tools developed using automated image-based approaches remain constrained by figure quality and rasterization artifacts. Errors introduced during digitization can propagate and affect downstream analyses, such as treatment effect estimation and meta-analysis. Another recent study found that pixelation and color blending could degrade coordinate accuracy, introducing noise during digitization.
[
69
]
The study also found visual representations of censoring to be another common source of errors. Specifically, when censoring ticks are missing or poorly resolved, algorithms may misplace event timings, leading to biased survival estimates. Dense clustering of early censoring marks can obscure later events or make digitization unreliable. Because a 6-month patency point sits exactly in this early, censoring-dense region, we are concerned that these limitations may have important implications for the Astor et al. (2026) and Halbert et al. (2020) meta-analyses. We remain concerned about the quality of these abstracted data and the potential impact on the pooled 6-month patency among currently available AVGs, and uncertain whether the results reported by Astor et al. (2026) and Halbert et al. (2020) indicate that EndoForce
TM
produced better clinical outcomes than the AVGs with a standard sutured venous anastomosis. Regarding Astor et al. (2026), it also remains unclear whether the difference between the 6-month cumulative patency rates of 92 percent in Burgess et al. (2024) and 86 percent in the 12 studies reporting numerical values was statistically significant.
We continue to have concerns about the appropriateness of comparing EndoForce
TM
's effects on patency with those of AVFs. We agree with the commenter who stated that AVF is not a viable permanent-access strategy for some patients, that current KDOQI guidance
[
70
]
emphasizes a patient-centered approach based on vessel characteristics, comorbidities, anticipated dialysis needs, and patient circumstances rather than an absolute `fistula first' approach, and that the substantial clinical improvement inquiry should ask whether EndoForce
TM
improves treatment relative to the conventional, surgically created graft-to-vein anastomosis it replaces, not whether an AVG created with EndoForce
TM
is superior to an AVF in a patient for whom an AVF is otherwise appropriate. Accordingly, comparisons between EndoForce
TM
and AVFs do not directly address whether EndoForce
TM
provides substantial clinical improvement over existing technologies.
In response to our concern that Kramer et al. (2026) was not sufficiently powered to assess patency at 180 days post-implantation among patients with ESRD who needed hemodialysis, the applicant stated that the study did not claim that its results were statistically significant and a commenter noted that CMS should nevertheless treat the results as clinically meaningful. However, we maintain our concern that a comparison of the results from Kramer et al. (2026) to other studies could be confounded by differences between the studies, and we remain uncertain whether any difference in intervention rates or patency can be attributed to the use of EndoForce
TM
alone.
A commenter noted that CMS's prior application of the substantial clinical improvement standard supports granting the EndoForce
TM
System transitional pass-through payment status despite meaningful evidentiary limitations, because the evidence supports the technology producing a clinically important benefit. We disagree that the prior approvals cited by the commenter establish that EndoForce
TM
System meets the substantial clinical improvement criterion. We note that we assess each application on its own merits based on the evidence submitted. Our concerns regarding the evidence supporting this application are discussed previously. We refer to the full details of our rationale regarding other applications in the respective final rules.
After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, the EndoForce
TM
System does not meet the substantial clinical improvement criterion to be considered for device pass-through payment. Therefore, in this final rule with comment period, we will not address whether the technology meets the remaining criterion required for device pass-through payment. We are not approving the EndoForce
TM
System for device pass-through payment status for CY 2027 because the technology does not meet the substantial clinical improvement criterion at § 419.66(c)(2).

TM

We appreciate the applicant and commenter's input. After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, we continue to believe that C1713 appropriately describes the LINK

After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, the LINK

B. Device-Intensive Procedures
1. Background
Under the OPPS, prior to CY 2017, device-intensive status for procedures was determined at the APC level for APCs with a device offset percentage greater than 40 percent (
79 FR 66795
). Beginning in CY 2017, CMS began determining device-intensive status at the HCPCS code level. In assigning device-intensive status to an APC prior to CY 2017, the device costs of all the procedures within the APC were calculated and the geometric mean device offset of all of the procedures had to exceed 40 percent. Almost all of the procedures assigned to device-intensive APCs utilized devices, and the device costs for the associated HCPCS codes exceeded the 40 percent threshold. The no cost/full credit and partial credit device policy (
79 FR 66872
through
66873
) applies to device-intensive procedures and is discussed in detail in section IV.B.4. of the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC proposed rule. A related device policy was the requirement that certain procedures assigned to device-intensive APCs require the reporting of a device code on the claim (
80 FR 70422
) and is discussed in detail in section IV.B.3. of the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC proposed rule. For further background information on the device-intensive APC policy, we refer readers to the CY 2016 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
80 FR 70421
through
70426
).
a. HCPCS Code-Level Device-Intensive Determination
As stated earlier, prior to CY 2017, under the device-intensive methodology we assigned device-intensive status to all procedures requiring the implantation of a device that were assigned to an APC with a device offset greater than 40 percent and, beginning in CY 2015, that met the three criteria as listed. Historically, the device-intensive designation was at the APC level and applied to the applicable procedures within that APC. In the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
81 FR 79658
), we changed our methodology to assign device-intensive status at the individual HCPCS code level rather than at the APC level. Under this policy, a procedure could be assigned device-intensive status regardless of its APC assignment, and device-intensive APC designations were no longer applied under the OPPS or the ASC payment system.
We believe that a HCPCS code-level device offset is, in most cases, a better representation of a procedure's device cost than an APC-wide average device offset based on the average device offset of all of the procedures assigned to an APC. Unlike a device offset calculated at the APC level, which is a weighted average offset for all devices used in all of the procedures assigned to an APC, a HCPCS code-level device offset is calculated using only claims for a single HCPCS code. We believe that this methodological change results in a more accurate representation of the cost attributable to implantation of a high-cost device, which ensures consistent device-intensive designation of procedures with a significant device cost. Further, we believe a HCPCS code-level device offset removes inappropriate device-intensive status for procedures without a significant device cost that are granted such status because of their APC assignment.
(
printed page 70462)
Under our existing policy, procedures that meet the criteria listed in section IV.C.1.b. of this final rule with comment period are identified as device-intensive procedures and are subject to all the policies applicable to procedures assigned device-intensive status under our established methodology, including our policies on device edits and no cost/full credit and partial credit devices discussed in sections IV.C.3. and IV.C.4. of this final rule with comment period.
b. Use of the Three Criteria To Designate Device-Intensive Procedures
We clarified our established policy in the CY 2018 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
82 FR 52474
), where we explained that device-intensive procedures require the implantation of a device and additionally are subject to the following criteria:
All procedures must involve implantable devices that would be reported if device insertion procedures were performed.
The required devices must be surgically inserted or implanted devices that remain in the patient's body after the conclusion of the procedure (at least temporarily); and
The device offset amount must be significant, which is defined as exceeding 40 percent of the procedure's mean cost.
We changed our policy to apply these three criteria to determine whether procedures qualify as device-intensive in the CY 2015 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
79 FR 66926
), where we stated that we would apply the no cost/full credit and partial credit device policy—which includes the three criteria listed previously—to all device-intensive procedures beginning in CY 2015. We reiterated this position in the CY 2016 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
80 FR 70424
), where we explained that we were finalizing our proposal to continue using the three criteria established in the CY 2007 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period for determining the APCs to which the CY 2016 device intensive policy will apply. Under the policies we adopted in CYs 2015, 2016, and 2017, all procedures that require the implantation of a device and meet the previously described criteria are assigned device-intensive status, regardless of their APC placement.
2. Device-Intensive Procedure Policy
As part of our effort to better capture costs for procedures with significant device costs, in the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
83 FR 58944
through
58948
), for CY 2019, we modified our criteria for device-intensive procedures. We had heard from interested parties that the criteria excluded some procedures that interested parties believed should qualify as device-intensive procedures. Specifically, we were persuaded by interested party arguments that procedures requiring expensive surgically inserted or implanted devices that are not capital equipment should qualify as device-intensive procedures, regardless of whether the device remains in the patient's body after the conclusion of the procedure. We agreed that a broader definition of device-intensive procedures was warranted and made two modifications to the criteria for CY 2019 (
83 FR 58948
). First, we allowed procedures that involve surgically inserted or implanted single-use devices that meet the device offset percentage threshold to qualify as device-intensive procedures, regardless of whether the device remains in the patient's body after the conclusion of the procedure. We established this policy because we no longer believe that whether a device remains in the patient's body should affect a procedure's designation as a device-intensive procedure, as such devices could, nonetheless, comprise a large portion of the cost of the applicable procedure. Second, we modified our criteria to lower the device offset percentage threshold from 40 percent to 30 percent, to allow a greater number of procedures to qualify as device intensive. We stated that we believed allowing these additional procedures to qualify for device-intensive status would help ensure these procedures receive more appropriate payment in the ASC setting, which would help encourage the provision of these services in the ASC setting. In addition, we stated that this change would help to ensure that more procedures containing relatively high-cost devices are subject to the device edits, which leads to more correctly coded claims and greater accuracy in our claims data. Specifically, for CY 2019 and subsequent years, we finalized that device-intensive procedures will be subject to the following criteria:
All procedures must involve implantable devices assigned a CPT or HCPCS code;
The required devices (including single-use devices) must be surgically inserted or implanted; and
The device offset amount must be significant, which is defined as exceeding 30 percent of the procedure's mean cost (
83 FR 58945
).
In addition, to further align the device-intensive policy with the criteria used for device pass-through payment status, we finalized, for CY 2019 and subsequent years, that for purposes of satisfying the device-intensive criteria, a device-intensive procedure must involve a device that:
Has received FDA marketing authorization, or has received an FDA IDE and has been classified as a Category B device by FDA in accordance with §§405.203 through 405.207 and 405.211 through 405.215, or meets another appropriate FDA exemption from premarket review;
Is an integral part of the service furnished;
Is used for one patient only;
Comes in contact with human tissue;
Is surgically implanted or inserted (either permanently or temporarily); and
Is not either of the following:
++ Equipment, an instrument, apparatus, implement, or item of the type for which depreciation and financing expenses are recovered as depreciable assets as defined in Chapter 1 of the Medicare Provider Reimbursement Manual (CMS Pub. 15-1); or
++ A material or supply furnished incident to a service (for example, a suture, customized surgical kit, scalpel, or clip, other than a radiological site marker) (
83 FR 58945
).
In addition, for new HCPCS codes describing procedures requiring the implantation of devices that do not yet have associated claims data, in the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
81 FR 79658
), we finalized a policy for CY 2017 to apply device-intensive status with a default device offset set at 41 percent for new HCPCS codes describing procedures requiring the implantation or insertion of a device that did not yet have associated claims data until claims data are available to establish the HCPCS code-level device offset for the procedures. This default device offset amount of 41 percent was not calculated from claims data; instead, it was applied as a default until claims data were available upon which to calculate an actual device offset for the new code. The purpose of applying the 41-percent default device offset to new codes that describe procedures that implant or insert devices was to ensure ASC access for new procedures until claims data become available.
As discussed in the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC proposed rule and final rule with comment period (
83 FR 37108
through
37109
and
83 FR 58945
through
58946
, respectively), in accordance with our policy stated previously to lower the device offset percentage threshold for procedures to qualify as device-
(
printed page 70463)
intensive from greater than 40 percent to greater than 30 percent, for CY 2019 and subsequent years, we modified this policy to apply a 31-percent default device offset to new HCPCS codes describing procedures requiring the implantation of a device that do not yet have associated claims data until claims data are available to establish the HCPCS code-level device offset for the procedures. In conjunction with the policy to lower the default device offset from 41 percent to 31 percent, we continued our current policy of, in certain rare instances (for example, in the case of a very expensive implantable device), temporarily assigning a higher offset percentage if warranted by additional information such as pricing data from a device manufacturer (
81 FR 79658
). Once claims data are available for a new procedure requiring the implantation or insertion of a device, device-intensive status is applied to the code if the HCPCS code-level device offset is greater than 30 percent, according to our policy of determining device-intensive status by calculating the HCPCS code-level device offset.
In addition, in the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we clarified that since the adoption of our policy in effect as of CY 2018, the associated claims data used for purposes of determining whether or not to apply the default device offset are the associated claims data for either the new HCPCS code or any predecessor code, as described by CPT coding guidance, for the new HCPCS code. Additionally, for CY 2019 and subsequent years, in limited instances where a new HCPCS code does not have a predecessor code as defined by CPT, but describes a procedure that was previously described by an existing code, we use clinical discretion to identify HCPCS codes that are clinically related or similar to the new HCPCS code but are not officially recognized as a predecessor code by CPT, and to use the claims data of the clinically related or similar code(s) for purposes of determining whether or not to apply the default device offset to the new HCPCS code (
83 FR 58946
).
Clinically related and similar procedures for purposes of this policy are procedures that have few or no clinical differences and use the same devices as the new HCPCS code. In addition, clinically related and similar codes for purposes of this policy are codes that either currently or previously describe the procedure described by the new HCPCS code. Under this policy, claims data from clinically related and similar codes are included as associated claims data for a new code, and where an existing HCPCS code is found to be clinically related or similar to a new HCPCS code, we apply the device offset percentage derived from the existing clinically related or similar HCPCS code's claims data to the new HCPCS code for determining the device offset percentage. We stated that we believe that claims data for HCPCS codes describing procedures that have minor differences from the procedures described by new HCPCS codes will provide an accurate depiction of the cost relationship between the procedure and the device(s) that are used, and will be appropriate to use to set a new code's device offset percentage, in the same way that predecessor codes are used.
If a new HCPCS code has multiple predecessor codes, the claims data for the predecessor code that has the highest individual HCPCS-level device offset percentage is used to determine whether the new HCPCS code qualifies for device-intensive status. Similarly, in the event that a new HCPCS code does not have a predecessor code but has multiple clinically related or similar codes, the claims data for the clinically related or similar code that has the highest individual HCPCS level device offset percentage is used to determine whether the new HCPCS code qualifies for device-intensive status.
In the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
89 FR 94214
through
92419
), we finalized a change to our methodology for applying default device offset percentages for new device-intensive procedures. Under our previous policy, if a new CPT/HCPCS code did not have available claims data, either from the new HCPCS code or any predecessor code or clinically-similar code that uses the same device, and the CPT/HCPCS code otherwise met our criteria for device-intensive status, we would apply a default device offset percentage of 31 percent. However, we were aware of certain situations where the default device offset amount might not adequately reflect the existing device portion of the procedure's costs when compared to the cost of similar devices. A potential large difference between the default device offset amount and the device portion of similar devices might impede our ability to accurately remove device offset amounts from new device-intensive procedures under the OPPS and to set payment rates for device-intensive procedures under the ASC payment system.
Therefore, for CY 2025 and subsequent CYs, we finalized our proposal to modify our default device offset percentage policy for new device-intensive procedures. Specifically, for new CPT/HCPCS codes that both describe a procedure that requires the surgical implantation or insertion of a single-use device that exceeds 30 percent of the procedure's cost and that meets our requirements of a device as described here and lack claims data (from either the new HCPCS code or any predecessor code or clinically-similar code that uses the same device), we would apply a default device offset percentage that is the greater of 31 percent or the device offset percentage of the APC to which the procedure has been assigned. We stated that we still believe that a HCPCS code-level device offset is, in most cases, a more accurate representation of a procedure's device cost than an APC-wide average device offset based on the average device offset of all the procedures assigned to an APC. However, because newer device-intensive procedures lack claims data, we believe the APC-wide average device offset percentage is, in many cases, a better reflection of the estimated device costs of the procedure than a default 31 percent offset. Additionally, there can be instances where the typical device costs of procedures in an APC can be significantly greater than the 31 percent default device offset. For these reasons, we finalized our modification to our default device offset percentage for new device-intensive procedures. This methodological change was finalized for both the OPPS and ASC Payment System for CY 2025 and subsequent CYs and applies to new procedures assigned to clinical APCs, but not to new procedures assigned to New Technology APCs.

2. Proposed Device-Intensive Procedure Policy
We proposed to continue the CY 2026 device-intensive procedure policies for CY 2027. Specifically, we proposed to continue use of HCPCS code-level device-intensive determination and three criteria to designate device-intensive procedures, in accordance with existing policies. We also proposed to continue our device-intensive procedure policy, our proposed use of CY 2025 claims information for determining device offset percentages and assigning device-intensive status, and our proposed default device offset policy for determining device offset percentages in the absence of claims data for device-intensive procedures (

). We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters requested that CMS designate CPT code 52282 (Cystourethroscopy, with insertion of permanent urethral stent) as device-intensive and establish its CY 2027 device offset using manufacturer invoice data. The commenters stated that the historical claims are not representative because no FDA-approved permanent prostatic urethral stent was commercially available in the United States for approximately a decade, making the proposed zero device offset unreliable.
Response:
As discussed in section III. of this final rule with comment period, we agree with the commenters that no FDA-approved permanent prostatic urethral stent had been available on the U.S. market for approximately 9 years before FDA approved such a device through the premarket approval application process in late 2025. Therefore, we believe that the CY 2025 claims data for CPT code 52282 do not accurately reflect the device and service costs associated with inserting a permanent prostatic urethral stent and are not an appropriate data source for calculating the device offset percentage for CPT code 52282. In the absence of representative CY 2025 claims data, we are accepting the commenters' recommendation to assign device-intensive status to CPT code 52282 for CY 2027. We are not accepting the commenters' recommendation to use manufacturer invoice data to calculate the device offset percentage. Instead, we will apply our default device offset methodology to CPT code 52282 for CY 2027.
Comment:
Several commenters opposed removing device-intensive status from CPT code 55882 (Ablation of prostate tissue, transurethral, using thermal ultrasound, including magnetic resonance imaging guidance for, and monitoring of, tissue ablation; with insertion of transurethral ultrasound transducer for delivery of thermal ultrasound, including suprapubic tube placement and placement of an endorectal cooling device, when performed) for CY 2027 under the ASC payment system. The commenters stated that the TULSA procedure requires proprietary, single-use transurethral ultrasound and endorectal cooling devices that are integral to the service, contact human tissue, and are temporarily inserted into the patient. They stated that the proposed offset is distorted by incomplete device reporting, noting that the average invoice cost of $8,089 represents approximately 49 percent of the proposed $16,366 geometric mean cost. The commenters also reported that claims identifying C1889 produced offsets above the 30-percent threshold, whereas many hospitals reported little or no device cost. They requested a 49-percent device offset based on documented acquisition costs.
Response:
CPT code 55882 became effective January 1, 2025. In reviewing these comments, we discovered that we had correctly assigned device-intensive status to this procedure under the ASC payment system but had inadvertently not assigned device-intensive status to this procedure under the OPPS. In general, a new CPT code that meets our criteria for device-intensive status and is separately payable in both the OPPS and ASC payment system should be designated as device-intensive under both the OPPS and the ASC payment system. (Once claims data is available, differences in the claims data available under the two systems' ratesetting methodologies may result in a procedure receiving device-intensive status under the ASC payment system but not under the OPPS.)
The incomplete reporting of devices associated with CPT code 55882 under the OPPS underscores the importance of our device edits policy for device-intensive procedures. In the absence of an applicable device edit, we do not believe it would be appropriate to selectively determine which claims to use to calculate the device offset percentage; instead, we believe it is appropriate to rely on a full year of claims data during which CPT code 55882 is subject to the device edits policy. Therefore, because usable CY 2025 claims data are unavailable for CPT code 55882, we are accepting the commenters' recommendation to maintain device-intensive status for the code for CY 2027 and will apply our device edits and device credits policies to the procedure beginning in CY 2027 by assigning the procedure device-intensive status for both the ASC and OPPS settings. We are not accepting the commenters' recommendation to calculate the device offset percentage using acquisition-cost data and will instead apply our default device offset methodology.

The commenters stated that the procedure requires implantation of a single-use integrated sacral neuromodulation system and that the manufacturer-reported device cost of $18,500 represents approximately 83.5 percent of the proposed APC payment. The commenters stated that the two claims apparently used to determine device-intensive status were invalid or

printed page 70465)
unrepresentative because the code had status indicator “E1” until the device received FDA approval in June 2025 and commercial use did not begin until after November 2025. We agree with the commenters that we should disregard CY 2025 claims for CPT code 0786T. As we stated previously, in the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
89 FR 94218

Since CPT code 0786T was assigned a status indicator of “E1” for all of CY 2025, under our current policy, we will continue to assign CPT code 0786T device-intensive status for CY 2027 and will apply a device offset percentage based on our default device offset methodology.
Comment:
Several commenters requested that we designate CPT code 0730T (Trabeculotomy by laser, including optical coherence tomography (OCT) guidance) as device intensive and apply a 65-percent device offset. The commenters explained that the procedure requires two proprietary, single-use optical interfaces that contact the cornea and are integral to OCT-guided imaging and laser treatment under a CMS-approved Category B IDE study. The commenters stated that the combined $3,750 acquisition cost represents approximately 65 percent of the proposed geometric mean cost for APC 5493 and therefore exceeds the 30-percent device-cost threshold.
Response:
CPT code 0730T describes a minimally invasive glaucoma surgical procedure that reduces intraocular pressure by improving aqueous outflow. Specifically, CPT code 0730T describes a laser trabeculotomy procedure that noninvasively creates a channel through the trabecular meshwork, unlike other laser trabeculoplasty procedures that apply laser energy to stimulate biological changes that improve aqueous outflow. We are not accepting the commenter's recommendation to treat the patient interface system as a device for purposes of determining device-intensive status. Our criteria for device-intensive status require that a device be surgically inserted or implanted into the patient. In the CY 2006 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
70 FR 68629
through
68630
), we explained that the surgical insertion or implantation criterion encompasses devices inserted or implanted through a natural or surgically created orifice, as well as devices inserted or implanted through a surgically created incision. We do not consider placement beneath the eyelid and against the ocular surface to constitute insertion through a natural or surgically created orifice or incision. Therefore, we do not consider the patient interface system associated with CPT code 0730T to be an insertable medical device for purposes of device-intensive status.
Comment:
Several commenters requested that we expand device-intensive policy to permit CPT codes 0686T (Histotripsy (
i.e.,
non-thermal ablation via acoustic energy delivery) of malignant hepatocellular tissue, including image guidance) and 0888T (Histotripsy (
i.e.,
non-thermal ablation via acoustic energy delivery) of malignant renal tissue, including imaging guidance), which describe histotripsy of liver and kidney tumors, respectively, to qualify based on the cost of a nonimplantable “single patient use device” applied to the patient's skin. The commenters stated that the device will cost $7,500 in CY 2027 and stated that both procedures satisfy the 30-percent device-cost threshold, notwithstanding that the device is neither surgically inserted nor implanted. The commenters stated that revising the policy and increasing payment would facilitate beneficiary access to noninvasive histotripsy in the lower-cost ASC setting.
Response:
While we understand the commenters' concerns regarding payment adequacy for capital-intensive procedures furnished in the ASC setting and may consider these concerns in future rulemaking, we did not propose revising the eligibility criteria for device-intensive procedures. We believe that expanding the definition of device-intensive procedures to include high-cost items that contact a patient's skin, but are not surgically implanted/inserted, could have significant unintended consequences for both the OPPS and the ASC payment system. Therefore, we are not accepting the commenters' recommendations.
Comment:
A commenter opposed the proposed device offset percentage for CPT code 0885T (Colonoscopy, flexible, with initial transendoscopic mechanical dilation (
e.g.,
nondrug-coated balloon) followed by therapeutic drug delivery by drug-coated balloon catheter for colonic stricture, including fluoroscopic guidance, when performed) and requested that we continue to assign device-intensive status. The commenter stated that the three claims used to calculate the proposed offsets were erroneous because the ProTractX3 drug-coated balloon was available only through company-funded IDE trials and the facilities submitting the claims were not trial participants. The commenter requested that in the absence of sufficient claims data, the procedure should be assigned the APC-level device offset percentage under the OPPS.
Response:
We rely on hospitals to accurately report device costs associated with procedures. However, based on this comment and other public comments raising concern with determining device intensive status for services with very few claims, we believe that in instances where a procedure has very few claims upon which to determine device intensive status it would be appropriate to apply a low volume methodology for device intensive status which we are finalizing for this CY 2027 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period and which is discussed further later in this section of the preamble.
Under this low volume policy for device-intensive procedures, for procedures assigned device-intensive status in the current year with fewer than 10 claims in the ratesetting year, we will use the greater of: (1) the device offset percentage calculated from the available claims; or (2) the device offset percentage calculated under our default methodology, which is the greater of 31 percent or the device offset percentage of the APC to which the procedure is assigned.
Given the limited number of claims—three claims for this final rule with comment period—the device offset percentage of CPT code 0885T would fall under this low volume policy for device-intensive procedures and would be assigned a default device offset of 34.95 percent based on the APC-wide device offset of APC 5331 (Complex GI Procedures).

balloon dilation); maxillary sinus ostium, transnasal or via canine fossa), noting that the associated device costs exceed the 30-percent threshold. The commenters requested that we also designate CPT codes 31296 (Nasal/sinus endoscopy, surgical, with dilation (

balloon dilation); frontal and sphenoid sinus ostia) as device

Comment:
A commenter opposed CMS's proposal to increase the device offset percentage for APC 5231 (Level 1 ICD and Similar Procedures) from 58 percent to 79 percent.
