We received public comments on our survey response rate and respondent characteristics. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Two commenters raised concerns about the creation of the refined hospital population, especially in relation to analysis of the survey response rate. A commenter pointed out that the refinements resulted in a larger increase in the response rate for non-340B hospitals (from 34.9 percent to 53.3 percent) than for 340B hospitals (from 23.1 percent to 28.6 percent).
Response:
The population of 4,494 CCNs that CMS initially identified for ODACS eligibility was intended to be maximally inclusive in order to identify all entities paid under the OPPS that could have purchased survey-relevant outpatient drugs during the ODACS study period. However, further claims analysis revealed that a subset of the 4,494 eligible CCNs did not submit any OPPS claims for survey-relevant HCPCS codes during the study period. Many of these entities, which were predominantly subunits or non-acute care hospitals, also did not submit an ODACS response or submitted a response reporting zero drug acquisitions. These observations are not unexpected given that many subunits likely acquire their outpatient drugs in conjunction with their parent unit and some non-acute care entities do not acquire or administer the specific outpatient drugs included in the survey at all.
To create a population with evidence of survey-relevant OPPS drug utilization—either via their ODACS response or claims data—CMS applied two refinements. CMS refers readers to Section 3.1.2 of the ODACS Technical Report for details on these refinements and their impact on the hospital population. Consequently, the refined population of 3,147 CCNs more precisely reflects the universe of hospitals with meaningful and relevant outpatient acquisition volume for drugs included in the survey and, in turn, better focuses on the universe of hospitals that would be impacted by the proposed policy change.
The survey response rate changes as a result of these refinements because the denominator of response rate changes. The response rate is calculated as the number of CCNs that submitted an ODACS response divided by all survey-eligible CCNs. In the initial population, the denominator of 4,494 CCNs yields a response rate of 29.8 percent ; in the refined population, the denominator of 3,147 CCNs yields a response rate of 41.4 percent. CMS believes that the refined population response rate of 41.4 percent better represents the share of hospitals that reported acquiring surveyed NDCs out of all hospitals that could have reasonably been expected to report OPPS acquisitions of the surveyed NDCs. These refinements had a larger impact on the non-340B response rate only because the vast majority of subunits and non-acute care entities in the initial population are non-340B entities.
Comment:
Many commenters contended that the response rate, especially from 340B hospitals, does not meet section 1833(t)(14)(D)(iii) of the Act's statutory threshold of a “large sample of hospitals” and is therefore too low to justify the proposed policy change. One commenter cited the 2005 acquisition cost survey conducted by GAO, which aimed to receive responses from 1,000 hospitals after sampling 1,400 hospitals out of an initially eligible 3,450 hospitals, to justify a 29.8 percent response rate as meeting the requirement for a large sample. Some commenters also linked the response rate to concerns over data representativeness, arguing that because the response rate among 340B hospitals was lower than among non-340B hospitals, it calls into question the representativeness and comparability of the 340B and non-340B respondent populations.
Response:
We note that CMS sampled more hospitals than the GAO. Rather than limit the survey to a subset of hospitals, CMS ensured through its methodology that the maximum number of hospitals could participate and fulfill their statutory obligation to respond to the survey. For a discussion of this statutory requirement, see the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule (
90 FR 53764-53765
). Nowhere in statutory language is “a large sample of hospitals” defined nor is a particular threshold set for achieving “a large sample of hospitals.” Moreover, determining adequate sample size in any survey-based quantitative analysis is a complex challenge that involves evaluating factors unique to that analysis, including the sampling design, population size, and population variability. For instance, the 2005 GAO survey design employed a stratified random sampling methodology that explicitly sampled from the initial hospital population; therefore, applying a threshold of 29.8 percent is not comparable to CMS's ODACS survey design, which did not employ a sampling methodology. Rather, CMS invited all 4,494 hospitals identified as paid under the OPPS to respond to the survey and contribute any acquisition data for surveyed NDCs. A response-rate floor defined for a stratified sample does not have an established meaning for a census survey.
Consistent with generally accepted statistical practice, sample size sufficiency was evaluated through the calculation of confidence intervals (CIs) and IPW adjustment rather than seeking to meet an arbitrary threshold. CMS notes that a smaller sample size does not necessarily make a sample less representative; rather, representativeness is governed by response mechanism instead of sample size. Large samples can be more skewed in certain characteristics, yielding potentially larger biases. This possibility is why CMS performed IPW adjustment and statistical diagnostic tests to understand and account for potential sample size and data representativeness issues. The IPW adjustment and calculation of CIs indicated that the response rate yielded sufficiently precise estimates of hospitals' acquisition costs. As we explained in Section 3.5.2 of the ODACS Technical Report, to evaluate whether the number of survey responses received was sufficient to produce statistically valid estimates of hospitals' acquisition costs, we calculated CIs for both unadjusted and IPW adjusted acquisition cost margins. The CIs provide measures of whether the response rate adequately captures true population results. When response rate is insufficiently low, CIs are wide due to the high degree of uncertainty regarding where the true result lies. Conversely, when response rate is sufficient, CIs narrow as uncertainty lessens. CMS calculated the CIs using a bootstrap methodology. First, the full dataset of survey records (after applying data refinements and excluding geometric mean outliers) was repeatedly sampled with replacement using hospitals as the sample unit; acquisition cost margins were recalculated for each repeated sample. This process was repeated 10,000 times to generate distributions of unadjusted and IPW-adjusted acquisition cost margin estimates. Finally, the 95% CIs were identified for each margin estimate using the 2.5th percentile as the lower bound and the 97.5th percentile as the upper bound.
We reported the impact of IPW adjustment and CI calculation on acquisition cost margins in Section 4.4.2 of the ODACS Technical Report which described that applying IPW adjustment had minimal impact on acquisition cost margins for either non-340B or 340B acquired drugs. For drugs acquired outside the 340B Program, hospitals' survey-reported acquisition costs were 2.7 percent above the mean ASP before
(
printed page 70514)
IPW adjustment and 2.8 percent above the mean ASP after IPW adjustment. For drugs acquired through the 340B Program, hospitals' survey-reported acquisition costs were 33.4 percent below the mean ASP before IPW adjustment and 33.1% below the mean ASP after IPW adjustment (Table 67). The consistency between unadjusted and IPW-adjusted results supports the robustness and representativeness of the acquisition cost margins derived from survey responses.
The 95 percent CIs for both unadjusted and IPW-adjusted acquisition cost margins did not substantially differ from each other, indicating that the weighting adjustment had minimal impact on the resulting estimates. For non-340B drugs, the CIs spanned 3.8 percent below the mean ASP to 6.9 percent above the mean ASP for the unadjusted margin and between 1.6 percent below the mean ASP to 6.5 percent above the mean ASP for the IPW-adjusted margin. For 340B-acquired drugs, the CIs were much narrower and spanned 34.7 percent to 32.3 percent below the mean ASP for the unadjusted margin and from 34.3 percent to 32.1 percent below the mean ASP for the IPW-adjusted margin.
The narrow CIs for 340B-acquired drugs support the statistical validity of the survey results on 340B drugs and indicate that the received sample is sufficiently large to produce reliable estimates of hospital outpatient drug acquisition costs for 340B drugs. The CIs for the non-340B drugs span a wider range of potential acquisition cost margins, which is expected given the greater distributional spread in the survey data for non-340B drugs.
Comment:
Many commenters noted slight differences in composition between the respondent population and overall population of survey-eligible hospitals along observable hospital characteristics. Some alleged that CMS had not demonstrated data representativeness for groups of their interest such as major teaching hospitals, rural hospitals, and high-volume purchasers. Other commenters also requested more information about representation along particular stratifications (
e.g.,
payer mix and patient populations) and for particular groups (
e.g.,
rural referral centers, Disproportionate Share Hospital [DSH] status), expressing concern that there could be differences in population composition along these factors that were not considered. Finally, some commenters raised concerns that the outlier trimming and data exclusions could disproportionately impact certain hospital characteristics, impairing representativeness.
Response:
CMS previously published results that evaluated data representativeness along many of the hospital characteristics mentioned by commenters, including, hospital size, geographic rurality and location, 340B participation, academic teaching status, and OPPS drug claims volume. CMS refers readers to Table 6 of the ODACS Technical Report for these results. CMS acknowledges that the population composition differed slightly across some of these characteristics between the respondent population and the overall survey-eligible population. These differences are precisely why CMS applied IPW, a widely used statistical technique that reweights received data to account for under- or overrepresentation of particular hospital characteristics such that the weighted sample replicates the characteristics of the overall population. Applying IPW adjustment had minimal impact on acquisition cost margins for non-340B and 340B-acquired drugs, supporting the robustness and representativeness of the acquisition cost margins derived from survey responses. CMS refers readers to Section 4.4.2 of the ODACS Technical Report for a full discussion of the IPW adjustment methodology and results.
To address commenters' concerns that the respondent population is not representative along additional hospital characteristics not previously discussed, CMS conducted further analysis of the population by share of Medicare patients, DSH percentage, and hospital type. Unadjusted results show that the respondent population does not meaningfully differ from the overall population of survey-eligible hospitals by either Medicare share or DSH percentage, two indices of payer mix and patient population. When stratifying by hospital type, the respondent population is composed of slightly more IPPS hospitals and slightly fewer RRCs or RRC/SCHs, relative to all survey-eligible hospitals. CMS then integrated these three new variables as covariates in our IPW adjustment, and their inclusion had no impact on existing acquisition cost margins for either 340B-acquired or non-340B drugs.
Comment:
Many commenters raised concerns that CMS's IPW adjustment methodology does not adequately address the risks of nonresponse bias and therefore does not ensure representativeness of the resulting acquisition cost margins. Commenters noted that IPW adjustment, which uses observable hospital characteristics to reweight population composition, can be insufficient if either or both of (i) the likelihood of survey response and (ii) drug acquisition costs are influenced by unobservable factors. Commenters offered various examples of potential unobservable factors that could hypothetically be exerting influence, including administrative complexity, drug purchasing arrangements, health system affiliation, and access to bulk purchasing discounts. As such,
(
printed page 70515)
commenters stated that CMS lacks evidence that the adjustors and covariates are able to close potential gaps in responses or acquisition costs. Additionally, some commenters stated that the narrow confidence intervals produced by the margin analyses indicate consistency among the respondent hospitals but do not demonstrate that the respondents accurately reflect the population as a whole. Finally, one commenter questioned why CMS did not report the distribution of respondents by OPPS drug volume quintile after IPW adjustment.
Response:
As CMS describes below, we believe the acquisition cost data received are representative of acquisition costs among the eligible hospital population. We acknowledge that to sufficiently account for all determinants of hospital response and acquisition cost is a complex challenge given that acquisition costs for nonrespondents are, by definition, unobservable. CMS conducted an internal analysis to address concerns about nonresponse bias, with the specific goal of addressing whether nonresponse is correlated with acquisition costs. We used cost-to-charge ratios (CCR) from hospital cost reports and claim line charges from each providers' Fee-For-Service (FFS) drug claims data to create a proxy measure of acquisition cost that could be evaluated for the full population of survey-eligible hospitals. This analysis found that, for the 340B hospital population, respondents and nonrespondents had no statistically significant difference in costs, and the magnitude of the difference was close to zero, suggesting that a hospital's cost burden was not associated with their likelihood of response. CMS believes the consistency of proxy drug acquisition costs among respondents and nonrespondents supports the conclusion that the narrow confidence intervals obtained through the analysis do not simply reflect a homogenous respondent group, but rather are consistent with a sample that is representative of the eligible hospital population in terms of acquisition cost.
CMS conducted other tests to ensure the appropriateness of the IPW model and its covariates. First, we ran diagnostics on the distribution of estimated propensity scores and the resulting weights. In none of our IPW models did the estimated response probabilities fall below 10 percent; this is within the range where weight instability is not a concern and implies that weight trimming or truncation is not necessary. Second, CMS calculated Kish's effective sample size for each model, a diagnostic that summarizes how concentrated influence is across the weighted sample (a value close to the actual sample size indicates that weights are spread evenly across hospitals, while a value near 1 would indicate the estimate is driven by a single observation). In all cases, the effective sample size was close to the actual sample size, indicating that no small set of high-weight hospitals exerted disproportionate influence on the results.
As to why CMS did not report the distribution of respondents by OPPS drug volume quintile after IPW adjustment, OPPS drug volume quintile was highly correlated with the hospital size (bed count) quintile variable; given this, OPPS drug volume quintile was not included as a covariate in the IPW adjustment model to avoid collinearity issues. To address this comment, CMS also tested whether the final IPW weights balance the observed OPPS drug volume quintiles. We found that the reweighted sample effectively replicates the distribution of the OPPS drug volume quintiles in the population, even when this variable was not directly included. See Table 60.
(2) Margins Between Survey-Reported Hospital Acquisition Costs and Volume-Weighted ASP
Using the methodology, refinements, and processes discussed throughout Section (2)(b) Data Analysis and Methodology, we evaluated the received survey data to determine the difference between hospitals' survey-reported acquisition costs and ASP-based Medicare payment amounts. We first identified the percent margin between aggregate acquisition costs and volume-weighted ASP for both non-340B and 340B drug acquisitions, then performed an analogous calculation to identify the margin between 340B ceiling prices and ASP as additional context for the 340B acquisition cost margins. Next, we tested alternate methodological specifications to evaluate whether these margins varied depending on the methods used. Finally, we stratified margins by individual therapeutic classes to identify possible variation in acquisition costs relative to ASP along drug type.
The survey provides valuable information regarding hospitals' drug acquisition costs. Following the GAO recommendation to validate Medicare payment rates using hospital acquisition costs, we assessed the survey data for trends where acquisition cost did not align with Medicare payment. The most immediately evident difference was between Medicare payment rates and acquisition cost data for 340B-acquired drugs by 340B-participating hospitals. Based on the survey response data and applying the methodologies discussed previously, we found that for drugs acquired through the 340B Program, hospitals' reported acquisition costs during the specified time period were approximately 33.4 percent below both the mean and the median ASP. For drugs acquired outside of the 340B Program, hospitals' survey-reported acquisition costs during the specified time period were approximately 2.7 percent above the mean ASP and 2.8 percent above the median ASP.
To help validate these findings, we compared aggregate 340B ceiling prices for drugs included in the survey during the corresponding survey period to ASP amounts.

Based on this analysis, during the survey study period 340B ceiling prices were, in aggregate, 28.0 percent below the mean ASP and 29.2 percent below the median ASP, respectively. These findings help validate the survey response data for 340B-acquired drugs, as the ceiling price average discount is generally representative of the maximum acquisition cost and minimum discount, though hospitals can negotiate additional discounts resulting in a sub-ceiling acquisition cost. This is reflected in the survey results where the aggregate 340B acquisition cost margin is approximately 33.4 percent below the mean ASP—several percentage points lower than the aggregate ceiling price margin of 28.0 percent below the mean ASP.

Comment:
Several commenters discussed concerns regarding variation in acquisition costs by individual drug and/or therapeutic class, pointing out that a single adjustment to ASP may lead to underpayment for certain drugs and overpayment for others. Response:
As we noted in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, we considered calculating payment rates derived from individual acquisition cost amounts for 340B drugs; however, given the dynamic nature of drug pricing, we concluded that it would be more appropriate to apply a single discount factor to ASP. We also explained that we believed that this approach would be more appropriate as ASP is also dynamic in nature. ASP changes over time (quarter to quarter), so tying the payment amount to an average discount of ASP results in a more accurate payment amount, by quarter, than if hospitals had to wait until the next survey cycle. Each drug HCPCS code has its own specific payment rate calculated that is unique to the drug described by the applicable HCPCS code. We indicated that we would apply an average discount, calculated as described under V.B.9.b. and V.B.9.c.(2). of the proposed rule, to the drug-specific ASP amount. This would make our proposed payment rate specific to the average acquisition cost for the drug. We also stated that applying the payment rate in this manner would allow for this average discount to apply to newly calculated ASPs as they are updated on a quarterly basis. We further explained that it would not be practical to calculate a drug-specific payment rate for each NDC, and each HCPCS code, based on the survey data, as the survey-collected data is based on a snapshot in time and would not reflect future changes in average acquisition costs. Therefore, as drug prices change, we believe it is appropriate and reasonable to continue to update the calculated ASPs and then to reduce payments by an appropriate percentage of ASP to better align payment with the average cost of the drug.
With respect to commenters' observation that a single adjustment to ASP may lead to underpayment for certain drugs and overpayment for others, we emphasize that the purpose of our policy is to better align payment for 340B-acquired drugs with their acquisition costs in the aggregate, not to ensure that hospitals receive a payment amount greater than the cost of acquisition for every drug purchase. This approach is not unique to the policy for 340B-acquired drugs; because the OPPS is a prospective payment system, payment for an individual item or service may be more or less than a hospital's cost in any specific case. We would additionally note that the alternative payment rate that we are finalizing, ASP minus 28 percent, is greater than the ASP minus 33.4 percent amount demonstrated by the survey and would therefore partially mitigate commenters' concerns.
We also note that payment rates are already set on a drug-by-drug basis using the ASP methodology, and this policy will similarly reflect the differing acquisition costs of specific drugs. The percentage adjustment applied to ASP has never been tailored to individual HCPCS codes and this policy is consistent with that longstanding approach. Further, CMS chose to
(

volume-weight the proposed ASP percentage adjustment to reflect the relative utilization and differing margins of individual drugs.
CMS performed an additional variation of the IPW analysis in an effort to further address concerns about differences in drug utilization mix across providers. For those drug classes that displayed differences between the two groups, we included variables measuring each respondent's utilization of the drug classes of interest into the IPW adjustment. The introduction of these drug mix variables showed no impact on the existing aggregate margins, indicating that differing drug mix across providers does not appear to be exerting undue influence on the comparisons of acquisition costs to ASP.
(3) Application of Population Weight Adjustment and Calculation of Confidence Intervals To Assess Statistical Validity
In accordance with section 1833(t)(14)(D)(iii) of the Act, after completing initial analysis of survey respondents' acquisition costs, we evaluated whether survey respondents comprised a large sample that is sufficient to generate statistically significant and representative estimates of hospitals' acquisition costs. To do so, we conducted sensitivity analyses using inverse probability weighting (IPW) and confidence intervals, which we believe support the statutory objective of obtaining acquisition cost estimates from survey responses that are accurate and representative of the outpatient drug acquisition costs incurred by all hospitals paid under the OPPS.
(i) IPW Methodology
IPW is a widely used statistical technique in survey research
[
120 121 122 123 124
]
to ensure that sample data produce estimates that accurately represent the population of interest. We applied IPW to account for the potential underrepresentation or overrepresentation of hospitals with particular characteristics among survey respondents and to evaluate whether acquisition cost margins derived from survey responses sufficiently reflected outpatient drug acquisition costs for all OPPS hospitals.
For purposes of the IPW analysis, we constructed respondent and nonrespondent populations that align with the refined hospital population discussed previously in (1) Survey Response Rate and Respondent Characteristics. We defined the respondent population as hospitals that submitted a survey response reporting the purchase of at least one surveyed NDC during the survey study period. We defined the nonrespondent population as survey-eligible hospitals that did not submit a survey response but billed at least one Fee-For-Service outpatient claim associated with a survey-relevant HCPCS code during the same period. Because acquisition cost margins were calculated separately for drugs purchased through the 340B Program and drugs purchased outside the 340B Program, we further stratified hospitals based on evidence of 340B drug use. Hospitals were identified as 340B participants using HRSA's 340B OPAIS enrollment information and claims submitted with 340B modifiers. Hospitals that neither submitted an ODACS response nor billed relevant outpatient claims during the survey period were excluded from the IPW-adjusted population. Subunits were collapsed with their corresponding parent unit prior to constructing the respondent and nonrespondent populations.
After identifying the respondent and nonrespondent groups, we calculated response propensity scores using logistic regression models based on observed hospital characteristics, including number of beds, teaching hospital status, geographic rurality, and Census division. Propensity scores were estimated separately for hospitals purchasing drugs outside the 340B Program and hospitals purchasing drugs through the 340B Program. A higher propensity score means that the hospital was more likely to submit a survey response; a lower propensity score means that the hospital was less likely to submit a survey response.
We then calculated inverse probability weights equal to the inverse of each hospital's estimated probability of responding to the survey. Hospitals with a higher likelihood of responding received smaller weights, while hospitals with a lower likelihood of responding received larger weights. The weights were used to adjust for differential representation of hospital characteristics between the respondent sample and the broader population of survey-eligible hospitals. Down-weighting hospitals with a high probability of response (which are overrepresented in the received sample) while upweighting CCNs with a low probability of response (which are underrepresented in the received sample) accounted for the differential representation of hospital characteristics in the sample as compared to the full population.
Finally, we calculated the IPW-adjusted acquisition cost margins by first applying the calculated weights to hospitals' average acquisition costs and corresponding ASP-based payment amounts, then recalculating aggregate acquisition cost margins by finding the difference between the IPW-adjusted acquisition costs and IPW-adjusted ASP-based payment and then dividing that difference by the IPW-adjusted ASP-based payment. We also applied the same methodology when calculating IPW-adjusted margins between acquisition costs and 340B ceiling prices.
(ii) Confidence Intervals Methodology
To evaluate whether the number of survey responses was sufficient to produce statistically valid estimates of hospitals' acquisition costs, we calculated confidence intervals for both unadjusted and IPW-adjusted acquisition cost margins. The confidence intervals provide measures of whether the survey response rate adequately captures true population-level results. When response rate is insufficiently low, confidence intervals are very wide due to the high degree of uncertainty regarding where the true result lies. Conversely, when response rate is sufficient, confidence intervals become narrower as uncertainty lessens.
We calculated confidence intervals using a bootstrap methodology. Specifically, we repeatedly sampled with replacement from the original survey dataset and recalculated acquisition cost margins for each repeated sample. We repeated this process 10,000 times to generate distributions of unadjusted and IPW-adjusted acquisition cost margin estimates. We then identified the 95 percent confidence intervals for each acquisition cost margin estimate using the 2.5th percentile as the lower bound and the 97.5th percentile as the upper bound.
(
printed page 70521)
(iii) Results of Population Weight Adjustments and Confidence Intervals From ODACS Data
Application of inverse probability weighting improved the alignment between the distribution of respondent hospital characteristics and the broader population of survey-eligible hospitals. We found that IPW-adjusted respondent characteristics more closely resembled the full population across measures such as rural/urban, teaching status, Census division, and 340B participation (Table 71).
(
printed page 70522)
(iv) Weighted Adjusted Acquisition Cost Margins
We found that application of IPW had minimal impact on estimated acquisition cost margins for either non-340B drugs or 340B-acquired drugs. For drugs acquired outside the 340B Program, the analysis conducted estimated that acquisition costs were approximately 2.7 percent above the mean ASP prior to IPW adjustment and approximately 2.8 percent above the mean ASP after IPW adjustment. For drugs acquired through the 340B Program, the analysis estimated that acquisition costs were approximately 33.4 percent below the mean ASP prior to IPW adjustment and approximately 33.1 percent below the mean ASP after IPW adjustment. The consistency between unadjusted and IPW-adjusted results supports the robustness and representativeness of the acquisition cost margins derived from survey responses (Table 72).
The 95 percent confidence intervals for both unadjusted and IPW-adjusted acquisition cost margins were not substantially different from each other, indicating the weighting adjustment had minimal impact on the resulting estimates. For non-340B drugs, the confidence intervals ranged from approximately 3.8 percent below the mean ASP to 6.9 percent above the mean ASP for unadjusted margin and between 1.6 percent below the mean ASP to 6.5 percent above the mean ASP for the IPW-adjusted margin. For 340B-acquired drugs, the confidence intervals were much narrower and ranged from approximately 34.7 percent to 32.3 percent below the mean ASP for the unadjusted margin and from 34.3 percent to 32.1 percent below the mean ASP for the IPW-adjusted margin (Table 72).
We believe the relatively narrow confidence intervals for 340B-acquired drugs support the statistical validity of the survey results on 340B drugs and indicate that the received sample is sufficiently large to produce reliable estimates of hospital outpatient drug acquisition costs for 340B drugs. We note that the confidence intervals for the non-340B drugs span a wider range of potential acquisition cost margins. This is expected given the greater distributional spread in the survey data for non-340B drugs, as discussed in this section V.B.2.8. of this final rule with comment period.

Response:
CMS thanks the commenter for raising this consideration. CMS did not volume-weight the mean ASP payment rate for two key reasons. First, the ASP payment rates for most drugs did not vary substantially across the quarters in the study period, so volume-weighting was not needed to make the mean ASP an appropriate measure. Additionally, drugs may not be acquired in the same quarter as they are administered, leading to potential misalignment between hospitals' acquisition cost and the applicable ASP payment rate. Still, CMS did perform additional analyses comparing reported acquisitions costs to the minimum, or lowest, payment rate published for each HCPCS during the study period in order to construct lower bound estimates of the margin between ASP and hospitals' acquisition costs. These analyses revealed only a small impact on the aggregate margins.

]
Thus, CMS proceeded with comparisons to the

mean ASP as more representative of average payment rate during the study period.
Comment:
Some commenters took issue with CMS's selected methodology to weight each drug's ASP by the total number of NDC units reported by all respondents. A commenter stated that because NDCs reported in higher volume have a greater impact on aggregate acquisition cost margins, these margins would be biased if respondents do not reflect the overall survey-eligible population. Another commenter compared the selected methodology with an alternate approach that CMS considered to weight by OPPS claims volume, contending that the latter is more appropriate because it would better reflect the services that would be impacted by the proposed 340B-acquired drug payment change. Commenters noted that the two methodologies yielded slightly different aggregate acquisition cost margin results and contended that CMS had arbitrarily chosen to weight by survey-reported unit volume without sufficient justification.
Response:
CMS is unpersuaded by arguments that volume-weighting by survey-reported unit volume is inappropriate. Rather, this approach ensured that the ASPs for NDCs that represented a larger share of total survey-reported purchasing activity were proportionally represented in the estimated acquisition cost margins. Of key importance is the fact that hospitals' acquisition cost survey data captures all outpatient drug purchases, making weighting by survey volume necessary for internal consistency, whereas volume-weighting by OPPS unit volume only reflects Medicare FFS drug utilization. Additionally, there can be time lags between when a hospital purchased a drug and when it is administered, which would lead to misalignments between survey-reported unit volume for drugs purchased during the surveyed time period and OPPS claims volume for drugs billed during the surveyed time period. Accordingly, CMS believes that the selected volume-weighting method should consider all reported utilization volume, not just that for Medicare FFS beneficiaries, and ensure alignment with the surveyed time period to enable fair comparisons between survey-reported acquisitions and equivalent Medicare payment amounts. CMS does not find it problematic that the acquisition cost margins differ slightly between weighting methodologies. Slight divergences are to be expected given that unit volume is not identical between survey responses and billed claims for the two reasons listed above, and CMS believes that the merits of selecting the survey-reported unit volume weighting approach have been sufficiently justified. Finally, CMS refers readers to the discussion of representativeness analyses in section V.B.8.c. of this final rule with comment period to address concerns regarding potential respondent bias related to drug utilization volume.

July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025), their applicability to the current and future Federal drug-pricing landscape is limited given continued evolution in policymaking (
e.g.,
the forthcoming implementation of negotiated Maximum Fair Prices for selected Part B drugs and ongoing consideration of alternative mechanisms for effectuating 340B ceiling prices) and the impact of these developments on hospitals' financial environment.
Response:
CMS notes that all survey analyses inherently represent a point-in-time estimate based on when data were collected. Lengthening the surveyed time period would have increased the administrative burden for hospitals to complete the survey, given increased time necessary to review their purchasing records and aggregate data. Additionally, drugs may experience shortage or supply chain interruptions in any year and the Federal drug policymaking landscape is in continuous evolution, making it impossible to designate a particular time period as “normal” or baseline market conditions against which to form comparisons. CMS notes that the surveyed time period of one year (July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025) aligns with the GAO-selected time period of one year (July 1, 2003 to June 30, 2004).
Comment:
Some commenters pointed to CMS's discussion of the five exclusions applied to remove anomalous or duplicative survey records as evidence that the received data were low quality. A commenter specifically cited that 8.9 percent of all received records were excluded due to these criteria, alleging that this represented a large share of total records.
Response:
Records that were excluded due to meeting at least one of the five criteria listed in Section 3.3 of the ODACS Technical Report do not necessarily represent inaccurate or low-quality data. In many cases, these records reflect drug- and context-specific misunderstandings of or misalignments with the exact survey design rather than being indicative of larger data quality issues. CMS refers readers to Section 3.3 of the ODACS Technical Report for discussion of each situation and possible explanations underlying these observed anomalies. For the exclusion described in section 3.3.5 specifically, CMS notes that not all responses for affected clotting factor and respiratory therapy NDCs displayed the unit-misalignment issue, but were removed to avoid potential selection bias from specifically excluding those survey records with units reported in IU or MG; therefore, this exclusion removes more than just records featuring the anomaly. Nevertheless, CMS elected to remove records in these five exclusion criteria to promote data alignment with the stated survey design and ensure consistency in analyzing the data.
These five specific exclusions, associated with likely misunderstandings of the exact survey design, resulted in exclusions that only composed a small share of total records. After applying these data restrictions, 146,117 records remained, 91.1 percent of the original records received, with which CMS calculated acquisition cost margins. Moreover, these 146,117 records detail the acquisition cost of drugs that comprise approximately 97 percent of payment for survey-relevant outpatient drugs from July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025. Compared to this preponderance of data retained, these five data restrictions excluded a small share of total records.
Comment:
Many commenters requested additional detail on CMS's methodology (including outlier identification and weighting), sensitivity analyses, representativeness of the survey data, and IPW model specifications. Numerous commenters also requested the release of the survey instrument and data collected, with or without anonymization applied.
Response:
Hospitals were assured that their acquisition cost data would remain confidential as part of the ODACS data collection and analysis process, and this protection will be honored. Publishing de-identified survey data with anonymized hospital characteristics appended still presents an immense confidentiality risk due to the small number of respondent hospitals identified in multiple specific categories (
e.g.,
rural hospitals in specific Census regions). For details on methodology and results, CMS refers commenters to the ODACS Technical Report. Further, CMS has provided additional detail on methods and analysis results in comment response throughout this final rule with comment period.
C. CY 2027 OPPS Payment Methodology for 340B Purchased Drugs Based on Survey Results
As described previously, section 1833(t)(14)(D)(ii) of the Act requires the Secretary to conduct periodic surveys to determine the hospital acquisition cost for each SCOD for use in setting the payment rates for SCODs under section 1833(t)(14)(A) of the Act. Section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act provides that the payment amount for a SCOD for a year is equal to the average acquisition cost for the drug (which at the option of the Secretary, may vary by hospital group) as determined by the Secretary, taking into account the survey data collected under subparagraph (D) of section 1833(t)(14) of the Act. Based on our analysis of the survey data, the most immediately evident and significant difference found between Medicare payment and acquisition cost was for 340B drugs acquired by 340B-participating hospitals, where the selected methodology shows that aggregate acquisition costs were approximately ASP minus 33.4 percent. This indicates average acquisition costs that were 37.2 percent lower than the general OPPS payment rate (ASP plus six percent). These results clearly demonstrate that ASP plus 6 percent is not an appropriate payment proxy for hospitals that acquire drugs through the 340B Program. Consequently, we proposed to adjust the OPPS payment policy for 340B drugs to better align payment with the acquisition costs demonstrated by the survey. Specifically, for CY 2027, we proposed to pay for drugs acquired under the 340B Program at ASP minus 33.4 percent.
Conversely, for non-340B drugs, after taking into account the survey data, we proposed to maintain the current payment rate, which is generally ASP plus 6 percent, under the authority at section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act. As displayed in Table 67, the heterogeneity in acquisition costs for non-340B drugs is slightly greater than for 340B drugs; this variation has led us to believe this area warrants additional analysis by CMS and input from interested parties. The results of the survey for non-340B drugs generally indicate lower acquisition costs than current OPPS payment; however, the
(
printed page 70527)
discrepancy is not as clear and significant as with 340B drugs. Therefore, we are continuing to analyze the data from this survey, aligning those reported costs with hospital claims billing patterns, to see if any additional significant trends exist that merit further adjustments to OPPS payment policy in future years. We are also assessing billing patterns among those hospitals that did not respond. Finally, we collected and analyzed information on non-NDC-specific GPO discounts that hospitals receive and are still considering how these discounts could be factored into future analysis and policymaking. We will consider these issues for future rulemaking.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.

These commenters stated that aligning the 340B payment rate more closely with hospitals' actual acquisition costs, as reflected by the survey data, would improve the accuracy of Medicare payment, reduce incentives to choose more expensive drugs or shift drug administration to higher-cost settings, promote transparency and accountability, direct statutorily-required budget-neutral savings toward non-drug OPPS services and help ensure beneficiaries share in the value of 340B discounts through lower cost sharing. A commenter stated that CMS's findings are consistent with analyses from the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC) and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS OIG) showing that Medicare payments for 340B-acquired drugs have substantially exceeded 340B drug acquisition costs. Another commenter stated that this policy reflects that Federal payment rates should rest on evidence of what something actually costs. A commenter stated that the survey made evident that the acquisition cost for SCODs through the 340B Program is far lower than the statutory default rate of ASP plus six percent and that with this clear survey data, CMS is required to set payment based on the average acquisition cost for 340B-acquired drugs. We thank commenters for their support.

Further, this policy ensures that the reduced drug costs, and associated reduced drug cost sharing obligations, are passed directly to the beneficiaries that these hospitals serve. We acknowledge that some hospitals will potentially experience greater reductions to drug payments than increases to non-drug items and services as a consequence of our policy. However, that does not change our statutory obligation under section 1833(t)(14) of the Act to conduct a survey of drug acquisition costs and adjust payment rates taking those costs into account.

Response:
We disagree that we have failed to account for the effect of the proposal in formulating and proposing our policy, and we do not agree with commenters that our proposed policy is contrary to the Congressional intent behind the 340B program. We are fulfilling our statutory obligation under section 1833(t)(14) of the Act to periodically conduct a survey of hospital acquisition costs and use the resulting data to inform payment rates. The purpose of the proposed policy is to better align our payment amounts for 340B-acquired drugs with their actual acquisition costs as demonstrated by the survey.

Many of these commenters additionally referenced “severe financial headwinds” that they are experiencing due to a variety of past and impending economic factors.
Response:
We recognize that the cumulative economic effect of the policies we are proposing for CY 2027, along with the financial circumstances hospitals have faced over the past few years, may be significant for some hospitals. However, we believe these effects must be balanced against the windfalls hospitals received previously that we are statutorily obligated and/or have the discretion to recover, our obligations under section 1833(t)(14) of the Act to periodically conduct surveys of hospitals' drug acquisition costs and take that data into account in setting payment rates, and our responsibility to adopt methods to control unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services.
Comment:
Many commenters urged us to delay or phase-in (or both) the implementation of the proposal. Commenters suggested that delaying implementation would provide additional time for CMS to conduct a more complete hospital-level impact analysis of the combined effect of the 340B drug payment proposal, the remedy proposal and the site neutral proposal and other OPPS payment changes. Another commenter suggested that CMS could use the delay to establish a limit on how much money hospitals could lose if they rely heavily on 340B drugs and develop a methodology that would ensure a more equitable distribution of the savings resulting from the proposed payment reduction. Commenters also noted that an implementation delay would provide interested parties with additional time to comment on the payment proposal and underlying survey. Commenters also stated that it would give hospitals time to adapt to the financial impact of the policy and help avoid abrupt disruptions to patient services.
Response:
We understand commenters' emphasis on taking a measured approach to implementing the proposal. However, we believe that the payment misalignment that our proposed policy will address has been in effect for many years and it is important to implement this policy now that we have conducted the required survey and have data clearly demonstrating that the existing payment rate for 340B-acquired drugs is not even close to a representative proxy for the cost of their acquisition. Given the extent of the payment misalignment identified by the survey results and the length of time the misalignment has likely been in place, we think that delaying or phasing-in the changes would be inconsistent with our obligations under section 1833(t)(14) of the Act and our goal of ensuring that Medicare and Medicare beneficiaries are paying for drugs commensurate with the cost of their acquisition.
Comment:
Many commenters opposed the proposal on the grounds that it would establish a dangerous precedent that non-Medicare payers might follow. These commenters stressed that Medicare payment policies often influence other entities, such as Medicaid or commercial payers, to “piggyback” off CMS' payment decisions. These commenters expressed concern that this would fundamentally undermine the purpose and effectiveness of the 340B program to financially assist hospitals that serve a high volume of low-income patients.
Response:
We do not have control over how our proposed policy might influence other non-CMS payers in the future. What those other payers may or may not do in the future would not be a valid reason for us to refrain from better aligning OPPS payment for 340B-acquired drugs with their acquisition costs as demonstrated by the survey, consistent with section 1833(t)(14)(iii)(I) of the Act.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern about the indirect implications of the proposal to pay ASP minus 33.4 percent for 340B-acquired drugs for providers that contract with Medicare Advantage (MA) organizations. Commenters stated that MA organizations and private PBMs
(
printed page 70529)
will cite these OPPS rate reductions as justification to impose their own cuts for 340B drugs, further weakening the ability to utilize 340B savings. Commenters urged CMS to clarify that the proposed payment methodology of ASP minus 33.4 percent, including any downstream budget neutral impacts, is Original Medicare (OM) payment policy and does not itself establish, require or permit a corresponding payment reduction under MA contracts.
Response:
We appreciate feedback on this issue. CMS establishes payment policies and payment rates for services payable under OM through a separate, distinct process that is not directly related to terms of private contracting arrangements between MA organizations and providers. Further, section 1854(a)(6)(B)(iii) of the Act prohibits CMS from requiring an MA organization to contract with a particular hospital, physician, or other entity to furnish items and services, including 340B-acquired drugs, or requiring a particular price structure for payment under such a contract. Providers and MA organizations may engage in dispute resolution under existing contracts and any contract negotiations or re-negotiations independently of CMS. MAOs must pay non-contract providers or facilities for services and items at least the amount they would have received under OM payment rules, in accordance with section 1852(a)(2) of the Act.
1. Statistically Significant Estimate
Under section 1833(t)(14)(D)(iii) of the Act, the periodic surveys conducted by the Secretary under section 1833(t)(14)(D)(ii) of the Act must “have a large sample of hospitals that is sufficient to generate a statistically significant estimate of the average hospital acquisition cost for each specified covered outpatient drug.” Our survey results meet this standard, particularly because hospital acquisition cost is a price measure.
[
130
]
Reliable price measures require far less sampling than quantity or revenue measures because markets tend to compress this distribution of prices across transactions but do not compress the distribution of quantities or expenditures.
[
131
]
While hospital acquisition cost for a branded drug would not be exactly equal across hospitals in the 340B Program, it would not differ by a factor of 1000 and rarely even a factor of 2. Because the standard errors of the 340B-hospital sample mean and the non-340B-hospital sample mean are each proportional to the standard deviation of the underlying population, a compressed price distribution translates directly into small standard errors and high statistical significance.
[
132
]
As discussed previously and shown in Table 74, the 95 percent confidence intervals for 340B drugs were relatively narrow, ranging from approximately 34.7 percent to 32.3 percent below ASP for the unadjusted margin and from approximately 34.3 percent to 32.1 percent below ASP for the IPW-adjusted margin. These results support the statistical validity of the estimated acquisition cost margins and indicate that the survey data provide reliable estimates of the acquisition cost discounts realized by 340B hospitals relative to ASP. These sampling requirements for price measurement are well known in national accounting. For example, the Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics measures prices for the Consumer Price Index (CPI) using about 100,000 commodity-and-service price observations per month, while the Producer Price Index (PPI) uses approximately 64,000 monthly price quotations from about 16,000 establishments.
[
133
]
These samples are tiny relative to the transactions they are designed to represent: the CPI commodity-and-service sample alone is less than 0.01 percent of such payments.
[
134
]
In our efforts to obtain data from a statistically significant sample of hospitals paid under the OPPS, we initially included for survey participation 100 percent of OPPS hospitals. From this, we received replies from 53.3 percent of non-340B hospitals and 28.6 percent of 340B hospitals. These response rates are similar to past surveys of health care providers as determined by a separate meta-analysis
[
135
]
and have resulted in sample sizes that show significant differences in acquisition costs between the two hospital categories.
[
136
]
While we applied data cleaning to exclude specific survey records with anomalous or implausible data, very few hospitals were excluded from our population: only 27 subunits that reported identical and duplicative data to their parent unit. Additionally, while we applied refinements to narrow the population of hospitals to only those who either responded to the survey or had OPPS claims for survey-relevant HCPCS codes, these refinements did not remove any hospital with relevant data from analysis. These efforts were undertaken to maintain the largest possible pool of hospitals and data to evaluate. It is our view based on efforts to sensitivity test the responses and reweight the findings that the conclusion of statistical difference in the average acquisition costs for 340B and non-340B hospitals would likely not change.
Comment:
Multiple commenters concurred with CMS that the survey generated a statistically significant estimate. One commenter stated that:
CMS opened the survey to all hospitals that received OPPS payments for outpatient drugs during the survey period. Because this survey was meant to determine hospital acquisition costs for outpatient drugs paid under OPPS, this is the correct universe. As explained in the survey, 3,147 entities were eligible to complete it. Of these, 1,343 (42.7%) submitted a response and 1,304 reported acquisitions of one of the surveyed drugs. While the statutory text “a large sample” has no objective meaning, nor does it have any statistical definition, expert judgment is called for to determine whether the CMS survey's sample would qualify. There are several
(
printed page 70530)
reasons to believe it does. For one, this sample is larger than the original GAO survey conducted in 2005. In that survey, the original, official survey conducted as required by statute, only 1,157 hospitals responded. GAO determined that this sample was “reliable for estimating [Specified Covered Outpatient Drugs] prices.” It went on to say that estimates of prices were more precise for drugs purchased by many hospitals. Further, the responding hospitals included hospitals across the relevant categories defined by GAO and frequently used in health care policy, such as teaching and non-teaching, urban and rural. Because each category was represented in the final sample, there was data CMS was able to use to transform the results such that they would match the population of hospitals, similar to how political polls feature weights such that they can reflect an entire voting population.
Another commenter stated that:
CMS employed a census-based approach that sought information from all hospitals relevant to the proposed policy and ultimately obtained responses from a substantial number of hospitals, generating what [the commenter] understands to be the largest volume of acquisition cost data for hospital outpatient drugs ever collected in connection with the Medicare program. After applying appropriate data-cleaning and validation procedures, CMS used inverse probability weighting to account for differential response rates among hospital types and evaluated the resulting estimates using established statistical techniques. Importantly, the survey produced a narrow 95 percent confidence interval for the acquisition cost of 340B-acquired drugs, with estimates ranging only from ASP minus 32.3 percent to ASP minus 34.7 percent (a range of only 2.4 percentage points). CMS calculated these confidence intervals using 10,000 bootstrap replications, a sound and established statistical technique designed to assess the precision and reliability of survey estimates. The narrowness of this confidence interval confirms that the survey data are reliable and sufficiently precise for purposes of informing CMS's determination of the average acquisition cost of 340B-acquired drugs and implementing an acquisition-cost-based payment methodology. Moreover, CMS's approach to addressing nonrespondents likely results in a more conservative estimate of the discount associated with 340B-acquired drugs and therefore is favorable to 340B hospitals. CMS used inverse probability weighting to ensure that responding hospitals appropriately represented nonresponding hospitals in the overall population, a methodology that is widely accepted and that improved the representativeness of the final sample. To the extent that 340B hospitals with the lowest acquisition costs were less likely to respond, CMS's weighting methodology would tend to increase estimated acquisition costs for 340B-discounted drugs relative to the acquisition costs that might have been observed had all hospitals responded. Thus, if anything, the survey methodology is more likely to overstate average acquisition costs for 340B-acquired drugs than understate them. Taken together, the survey's large volume of data, rigorous weighting methodology, and narrow confidence intervals provide strong support for CMS's conclusion that the survey generated a statistically significant and reliable estimate of the average acquisition cost of 340B-acquired drugs.
Finally, a third commenter found the survey to be
[. . .]methodologically sound and has response rates that compare favorably to other drug cost surveys, such as the National Average Drug Acquisition Cost (NADAC) survey, which CMS has relied on for over a decade as the accepted benchmark for Medicaid fee-for-service pharmacy reimbursement. The ODACS identified 4,494 survey-eligible hospitals and all valid survey responses were used in the analysis. Of the initial population, 43.6 percent of hospitals submitted a response. This design and response profile appears robust when compared to NADAC. NADAC similarly collects voluntary, invoice-level net acquisition cost data from a random monthly sample of independent and chain retail community pharmacies but only 18-24 percent of surveyed pharmacies respond to the monthly survey request, a response rate below the 41.4 to 43.6 percent range achieved by the ODACS. The ODACS's methodology and point estimates provide compelling evidence for reducing 340B drug payment rates under OPPS.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support. We concur with their assessment that our survey meets and exceeds the statutory standard.
Comment:
Many commenters contended that CMS did not meet statutorily specified requirements to “conduct a survey . . . to determine the hospital acquisition cost for each specified covered outpatient drug” and raised concerns that the survey did not “have a large sample of hospitals that is sufficient to generate a statistically significant estimate of the average hospital acquisition cost for each specified covered outpatient drug.” Commenters pointed to the fact that drugs for which fewer than 10 survey responses were received were dropped from the final margin calculations as evidence that CMS did not demonstrate that the survey sample was large enough to support statistically significant estimates of the average acquisition cost for each, individual outpatient drug.
Response:
We disagree with the statement that the survey lacked adequate breadth and achieved an insufficient response rate to analyze the universe of specified covered outpatient drugs in a statistically significant manner. To the contrary, CMS fulfilled its statutory duties to request, collect, and analyze data for each specified covered outpatient drug. CMS gave nearly 4,500 hospitals the opportunity to submit their acquisition cost data for consideration. The survey included 1,843 NDCs for outpatient drugs and biological products, corresponding to 519 HCPCS codes. All but 10 drugs with nonzero outpatient claims utilization received at least one survey response. The drugs that received at least one survey response represent virtually all Medicare use and spending, comprising 99.9 percent of payment for survey-relevant outpatient drugs from July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025. The fact that some low-volume drugs received fewer responses—consistent with their utilization patterns in practice—does not invalidate the data collected by the survey instrument or make it inapplicable for policymaking.
Commenters referenced the fact that outlier identification required the exclusion of drugs with fewer than 10 hospitals reporting acquisitions. While CMS excluded drugs that received fewer than 10 survey responses in the process of outlier identification, this enabled us to retain the vast majority of HCPCS codes during this stage of analysis, particularly in the context of overall use and spending. Even with this restriction applied, we retained observations for drugs representing 93.8 percent of Medicare payment for survey-relevant outpatient drugs from July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025. CMS also reiterates that outlier identification and trimming is only one aspect of the survey analysis process, and extensive analyses were performed upon the full population of data received.
Section 1833(t)(14)(D)(iii) of the Act requires that the survey have a “large sample of hospitals that is sufficient to generate a statistically significant estimate of the average hospital acquisition cost for each specified covered outpatient drug” but does not
(
printed page 70531)
specify how this is to be determined. While GAO deemed a response rate of 1,000 out of 3,450 eligible hospitals would meet the requirement for a large sample when designing the initial surveys in 2004 and 2005, their assessment—specific to their survey design and constraints at the time—does not constitute a specific, authoritative response rate that all subsequent surveys must precisely meet. We reiterate that our survey design invited 100 percent of the 4,494 eligible hospitals to participate, and approximately 41 percent of the refined population of 3,147 hospitals reported acquiring surveyed drugs. Additionally, the volume of data collected overall through ODACS is substantially larger than what was collected in GAO's initial surveys: GAO only considered 53 non-radiopharmaceutical outpatient drug HCPCS codes in their surveys of hospitals' reported acquisition costs, a tenth of the number of Part B drug HCPCS codes that were analyzed through ODACS. As such, our survey greatly exceeds the comprehensiveness of GAO's survey in terms of included hospitals and drugs. Furthermore, as detailed in section V.B.8.b of this final rule, the data received in the CMS survey produced statistically significant results—particularly for 340B-acquired drugs—that are representative of the overall survey-eligible population as shown through the IPW and confidence interval analyses among other factors cited in this final rule. Detailed discussion of the statistical significance of the data collected through ODACS can be found in the ODACS Technical Report and elsewhere in this final rule.
2. Grouping Hospitals by 340B Covered Entity Status
Section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to set the amount of payment for SCODs at an amount equal “to the average acquisition cost for the drug for that year (which, at the option of the Secretary, may vary by hospital group (as defined by the Secretary based on volume of covered OPD services or other relevant characteristics)), as determined by the Secretary taking into account the hospital acquisition cost survey data under subparagraph (D).”
In accordance with this authority, we proposed to vary the amount of payment for 340B-acquired drugs by the group of hospitals that are enrolled in the 340B Program as 340B covered entity hospitals because their drug acquisition costs vary significantly from those not enrolled in that program. The significant drug acquisition cost discounts that 340B covered entity hospitals receive for 340B-acquired drugs enable these hospitals to acquire drugs at much lower costs than non-340B hospitals incur for the same drugs. Accordingly, we proposed to use 340B covered entity status as a relevant characteristic to group hospitals for purposes of payment based on average acquisition cost under section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act. Therefore, for 340B drugs acquired by 340B covered entity hospitals, we proposed changes to better align Medicare payment with average acquisition cost for the drug as specified in statute.
As discussed in more detail below, for drugs not acquired through the 340B Program, we proposed that 340B and non-340B hospitals would continue to receive payment at a payment rate that is generally ASP plus 6 percent.
We acknowledged (
91 FR 41888
) we could set a single payment rate for a drug for a hospital group (such as 340B hospitals) regardless of whether the drug was acquired through the 340B Program, but that does not align with our intent to more appropriately align payment with acquisition costs. As such, we are only applying the reduced payment rate to drugs acquired through the 340B Program by the hospital group defined as 340B hospitals, as this most appropriately aligns payment with acquisition cost of drugs of this hospital group. For non-340B drugs acquired by 340B hospitals, we proposed that payment will not be adjusted. We sought comment on these proposals. Specifically, we sought comment on our proposal to use 340B covered entity status as a relevant characteristic to group hospitals for purposes of payment based on average acquisition cost under section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act and our proposal to vary the amount of payment for 340B-acquired drugs by the group of hospitals that are enrolled in the 340B Program to more appropriately align payment with the average acquisition cost for the drug.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters supported our proposal to vary the amount of payment for 340B-acquired drugs by the group of hospitals that are enrolled in the 340B Program. These commenters stated that doing so would better align payment for these drugs with their acquisition cost, resulting in more accurate Medicare payment and reduced beneficiary copayment for these drugs.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support.
Comment:
Many commenters stated that CMS lacks the authority under section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act to vary payments by groups defined by 340B Program participation. These commenters characterized CMS' proposal to do so as arbitrary and capricious, contrary to the text of the Medicare statute, and not in accordance with
5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A)
. These commenters recognized the Secretary's authority under section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) to vary payment “by hospital group (as defined by the Secretary based on volume of covered OPD services or other relevant characteristics)” but stated that 340B status is not a relevant characteristic. They stated that 340B status is not a relevant characteristic because 340B Program participation designations are not CMS hospital groups, but rather determinations made by a separate agency unrelated to Medicare program considerations. They stated that the intent of Congress was never to include participation in the 340B Program, a Federal program codified in another statute, the Public Health Service Act, as a characteristic that should be used to vary payment. One of these commenters stated that:
If Congress intended 340B participation to be used as a factor to differentiate Medicare drug payment, it would have included it as one of the relevant characteristics in establishing the SCOD payment rate methodology, given that in passing the [Medicare Modernization Act] in 2003, the 340B program had already been in existence for over a decade. That is, Congress well knew that 340B hospitals had lower acquisition costs. In passing the 340B statute, Congress intended that the 340B program would function by allowing covered entities to purchase these drugs at lower costs and to retain the difference between reimbursement and the drug purchase price as a way to allow them to `stretch scarce Federal resources as far as possible, reaching
(
printed page 70532)
more eligible patients and providing more comprehensive services.'
In support of their argument, the commenter pointed to the absence of 340B status on CMS enrollment forms, GAO reports from 2004 and 2005 in which the GAO did not include 340B participation as a relevant characteristic when examining differences in hospital acquisition costs, and Congress's exclusion of 340B prices from the calculation of ASP under section 1847A(c)(2)(A) of the Act.
Response:
We do not agree that we lack the authority under section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act to vary payments by groups defined by 340B Program participation. Section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to establish appropriate Medicare OPPS payment rates for covered outpatient drugs equal to the average acquisition cost for the drug for that year (which, at the option of the Secretary, may vary by hospital group (as defined by the Secretary based on volume of covered OPD services or other relevant characteristics)), as determined by the Secretary taking into account the hospital acquisition cost survey data under subparagraph (D). As demonstrated by its plain language, the best reading of the statute is that it delegates significant discretionary authority to the Secretary. We do not see anything in the statute that would limit the Secretary's discretion in the manner described by commenters. The Secretary is generally empowered to define hospital groups “based on volume of covered OPD services or other relevant characteristics” and there is nothing in section 1833(t)(14) of the Act or elsewhere to indicate the Secretary is foreclosed from defining a hospital group based on a hospital's voluntary participation in a program (the 340B Program) that has a direct and significant effect on the hospital's ability to acquire drugs at a substantial discount.
As described earlier in this section, we assessed a variety of hospital characteristics, such as hospital size, 340B participation status, ODACS drug purchase volume, outpatient drug claims billing volume, rurality, geographic location, GPO membership, GPO discount amount, and teaching status. Our detailed analysis found that 340B drug acquisition resulted in a nearly 40 percent differential from current Medicare payment, by far the most significant discrepancy between current Medicare payment and hospital acquisition cost, clearly making 340B status a relevant characteristic[ ] for purposes of varying OPPS payment.
After consideration of public comments we are finalizing our proposal to vary the amount of payment for 340B-acquired drugs by the group of hospitals that are enrolled in the 340B Program as 340B covered entity hospitals.
3. Applying a Single Reduction Percentage to ASP for 340B-Acquired Drugs
Section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act provides that the payment amount for a SCOD for a year is equal to the average acquisition cost for the drug “as determined by the Secretary taking into account” the survey data collected under subparagraph (D). In accordance with this authority, we proposed to apply a single discount factor to ASP for drugs acquired by 340B hospitals in lieu of calculating individual acquisition cost amounts for 340B-acquired drugs. Applying a single discount factor to ASP creates a standardized payment reduction. Conversely, calculating individual acquisition costs links reimbursement directly to the exact, variable purchase prices hospitals pay for specific 340B drugs.
We considered calculating payment rates derived from individual acquisition cost amounts for 340B drugs; however, given the dynamic nature of drug pricing we concluded that it would be more appropriate to apply a single discount factor to ASP. We believe this is more appropriate as ASP is also dynamic in nature. ASP changes over time (quarter to quarter), so tying the payment amount to an average discount of ASP results in a more accurate payment amount, by quarter, than if hospitals had to wait until the next survey cycle.
Each drug HCPCS code has its own specific payment rate calculated that is unique to the drug described by the applicable HCPCS code. We would apply an average discount, calculated as described previously under V.B.9.b. and V.B.9.c.(2). of this final rule with comment period, to the drug-specific ASP amount. This makes our proposed payment rate specific to the average acquisition cost for the drug. Applying the payment rate in this manner also allows for this average discount to apply to newly calculated ASPs as they are updated on a quarterly basis. It would not be practical to calculate a drug-specific payment rate for each NDC, and each HCPCS code, based on the survey data, as the survey-collected data is based on a snapshot in time and would not reflect future changes in average acquisition costs. Therefore, as drug prices change, we believe it is appropriate and reasonable to continue to update the calculated ASPs and then to reduce payments by an appropriate percentage of ASP to better align payment with the average cost of the drug.
As an alternative to establishing one aggregate discount amount based on survey data, we considered establishing one aggregate discount amount based on 340B ceiling prices from HRSA.

Under this alternative, we would use HRSA's 340B ceiling price data, rather than survey data, to calculate an average discount. As described previously, when assessing the 340B ceiling price, we calculated an analogous acquisition cost margin of ASP minus 28 percent for 340B drugs, which was calculated as the difference between the 340B ceiling price for each NDC in the survey and ASPs that were volume-weighted by 340B OPPS claims data utilization during the duration of the survey. We believed this could be a reasonable alternative to our proposal, as it is based on objective data, can be updated regularly (such as quarterly or annually) with the release of new ceiling prices and new claims utilization data, and significantly diminishes the discrepancy between Medicare payment and hospital acquisition costs for these drugs. We sought comment on this alternative to set OPPS payment for 340B acquired drugs at ASP minus 28.0 percent, per the methodology described to calculate this OPPS claims volume weighted mean margin of the 340B ceiling price from ASP. We note this figure is volume-weighted using OPPS claims data for the duration of the survey, but we also solicited comment on volume-weighting this average based on the claims data available for the applicable calendar year in which the policy would be effective. For example, for the CY 2027 rule, this would be volume-weighted based on claims data available for that year's rule, which would be claims data from CY 2025. At the end of this section in the proposed rule, we also provide estimated impacts of this alternative policy proposal of ASP minus 28 percent based on the 340B ceiling price data, so interested parties were aware of these impacts if CMS

The proposal will reduce Medicare and beneficiary spending that exceeds hospitals' acquisition costs, advancing both program integrity and beneficiary affordability.” Another commenter agreed with CMS that the proposed payment rate for 340B-acquired drugs “more accurately reflects the hospital acquisition cost, and we respectfully urge CMS to finalize this proposed payment change.”
Response:
We thank commenters for their support.

We disagree that section 1833(t)(14) of the Act requires CMS to calculate and set payment rates for each specified covered outpatient drug. While the statute indicates that data should be collected for specific drugs, it is not prescriptive regarding how that data should ultimately be used to set payment rates. Payment rates are already set on a drug-by-drug basis using the ASP methodology, and this will continue to be the manner in which payment rates for individual drugs are set. The percentage adjustment applied to the ASP (ASP plus six percent) has never been tailored to individual HCPCS codes; this policy mirrors that approach. Therefore, as drug prices change, we believe it is appropriate and reasonable to continue to update the calculated ASPs and then to reduce payments by an appropriate percentage of ASP to better align payment with the average cost of the drug.

Response:
We agree with commenters that our alternative approach would have several advantages compared to our proposed survey-data-based approach. We also think that this approach is appropriate based on the survey results, which, as we noted previously, found that hospitals' survey-reported 340B acquisition costs were at least 28.9 percent below the mean ASP for drugs in all high-spending therapeutic classes (that is, those with more than $100 million in reported acquisition costs).
We thank the commenters for their comments regarding updating the ceiling price payment rate weighted by claims volume for the applicable calendar year, in this case 2025 claims for CY 2027 rulemaking, rather than claims data from the duration of the survey. We appreciate the commenters' suggestions to phase-in in our policy; however. as we stated previously, we believe that the payment misalignment that our proposed policy would address has been in effect for many years and it is important to implement this policy without delay now that we have conducted the required survey and have data clearly demonstrating that the existing payment rate for 340B-acquired drugs is so far out of line as a representative proxy for the cost of their acquisition.

We disagree that the statute or the Supreme Court's decision in

requires us to set payment rates using the hospital acquisition cost survey data as a precondition to vary payment by hospital group. Section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act requires the Secretary to “take into account” the hospital acquisition cost survey data.
