We have taken into account the hospital acquisition cost survey data; indeed, it is our thorough analysis of that data that demonstrates (1) the clear and substantial discrepancy between current payment for 340B-acquired drugs and acquisition cost for 340B drugs that requires a prompt and reasonable solution, and (2) that a payment rate of ASP minus 28 percent would reflect a reasonable and conservative estimate of the average acquisition costs for 340B drugs for 340B hospitals given the survey results shows an average acquisition cost of ASP minus 33.4 percent. This is consistent with the approach we adopted in response to the GAO's survey in 2006. When the GAO conducted their survey and released their report, CMS did not use the survey data to directly set drug payment rates prospectively. In its report, the GAO stated that “[t]o ensure that Medicare payments for SCOD products are based on sufficiently accurate data, we recommend that the Secretary . . . validate, on an occasional basis, manufacturers' reported drug ASPs as a measure of hospitals' acquisition costs using a survey of hospitals or other method that CMS determines to be similarly accurate and efficient.”

CMS conducted the survey and the survey demonstrated that (1) current Medicare payment for 340B-acquired drugs is not based on sufficiently accurate data, as evidenced by the nearly 40-percent discrepancy between average acquisition cost and Medicare payment; and (2) that ASP minus 28 percent would reflect a reasonable and conservative estimate of the discounts 340B hospitals receive on 340B drugs.
We acknowledge that 340B ceiling prices are the maximum prices that pharmaceutical manufacturers can charge hospitals participating in the 340B Program. However, we do not agree that renders them unsuitable to inform Medicare payment rates.
Comment:
A few commenters stated that the existence of the two alternatives suggests that neither should be adopted. According to these commenters, the two alternatives constitute “materially different estimates” from Federal data sources, which underscore both the uncertainty surrounding the underlying analysis and the limitations of using a single national average discount assumption to establish payment rates for a highly diverse set of drugs and providers.
Response:
We do not agree with commenters' assessment of the two alternatives. We acknowledge their differing natures; however, we do not believe that they signify uncertainty in our analysis or limitations in using a single national average discount to establish payment rates for 340B-acquired drugs. In fact, we believe that the relative uniformity of these two estimates of ASP minus 28.0 percent and ASP minus 33.4 percent augers for the validity and accuracy of these two estimates, with the ASP minus 28.0 percent estimate naturally and predictably reflecting a slightly more conservative estimate of the discounts 340B hospitals receive on 340B-acquired drugs.
Comment:
A commenter preferred the proposed ASP minus 33.4 percent methodology over the alternative ASP minus 28 percent approach because it is grounded directly in observed hospital acquisition costs. The commenter observed that while an ASP minus 28 percent methodology might slightly lessen the fiscal impact of the revised policy, the acquisition-cost survey provides a more direct empirical foundation than an alternative derived from estimates of statutory ceiling prices.
Response:
We agree with the commenter that the proposed ASP minus 33.4 percent methodology has several advantages in comparison to the ASP minus 28 percent alternative in that it is based on real world acquisition cost data and would more fully capture the discount hospitals are receiving. However, as previously discussed, we believe ceiling price payment methodology volume-weighted by OPPS claims data is a reasonable alternative, as it is based on objective data, can be updated regularly (at least annually, and perhaps quarterly in the future as we gain more experience with this process) with the release of new ceiling prices and new claims utilization data, and significantly diminishes the discrepancy between Medicare payment and hospital acquisition costs for these drugs. It is a reasonable, empirically based payment methodology and the accuracy of our estimate is reinforced by the survey finding similar, but slightly larger, average discounts for 340B drugs acquired by 340B hospitals.
After consideration of public comments received and after taking into account the hospital acquisition cost survey data, we are finalizing our alternative proposal to set OPPS payment for 340B-acquired drugs at ASP minus 28 percent based on 340B ceiling price data and we are revising
42 CFR 419.41(d)
and adding a new paragraph (k) to implement this payment change. While we believe both alternatives to be excellent proxies for hospitals' acquisition costs for 340B-acquired drugs, we think that the virtues of setting the payment rate for 340B drugs acquired by 340B hospitals at ASP minus 28 percent based on the 340B ceiling data as validated by the ODACS outweigh the advantages of using the ASP minus 33.4 percent payment rate based on the survey data alone. ASP minus 28 percent is based on objective data, is a reasonable and conservative estimate of hospital 340B drug acquisition costs as validated by the ODACS, and is responsive to commenters' concerns that a payment rate of ASP minus 33.4 percent would result in too significant of a payment reduction and would inhibit beneficiary access to these drugs. ASP minus 28 percent is also in line with the minimum discount by major therapeutic class CMS found from the ODACS, where the acquisition costs varied from a high of ASP minus 28.8 percent to a low of ASP minus 71.4 percent. Additionally, our 95 percent confidence interval analyses of the survey data determined that acquisition costs fell between ASP minus 34.7 percent and ASP minus 32.3 percent. When including the IPW analysis, this 95
(
printed page 70535)
percent confidence interval became ASP minus 34.3 to minus 32.1 percent. It additionally is in line with the average acquisition costs stratified by various hospital characteristics as shown in Table 70. Specifically, and as previously discussed, we assessed the survey data by drug acquisition volume, OPPS drug billing volume, hospital size (number of beds), geographic rurality, census region, teaching status, share of Medicare patients, disproportionate share percent, and hospital type. Through all of these different hospital characteristics, assessing both the mean and median results, the margin drops as low as ASP minus 39.7 percent, and as high as ASP minus 30.3 percent. Through these 96 permutations of the data, these tight ranges not only support the integrity of the survey results but also make the ceiling price alternative that we are adopting reasonable and should help alleviate any commenter concerns that the payment rate based on the survey data is inappropriate.
We note that in the event that our authority under section 1833(t)(14) of the Act was determined to not provide sufficient flexibility to utilize the 340B ceiling price data as validated by the ODACS to set a payment rate of ASP minus 28 percent for 340B-acquired drugs for CY 2027, we believe the payment rate of ASP minus 33.4 percent—as determined by the average 340B drug acquisition cost in the ODACS—to be a better, more accurate determination of such hospital acquisitions costs than our prior policy of ASP plus 6 percent.
4. Add-On Payment for 340B Drugs
Under the OPPS, Medicare pays separately payable drugs at rates that approximate their acquisition costs, such as at ASP or WAC. These drugs may also receive an add-on payment. Under the OPPS, section 1833(t)(14)(E) of the Act authorizes, but does not require, the Secretary to make an adjustment to payment rates for SCODs to take into account overhead and related expenses, such as pharmacy services and handling costs. Because we took a prudent approach in estimating the average acquisition costs for 340B-acquired drugs, we did not believe that it was necessary to establish an add-on for overhead and handling as we believed that a conservative estimate may already account for the costs of overhead. We also believed that hospitals would likely negotiate additional discounts that will render an additional add-on payment unnecessary. This approach also aligned with the requirement under section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii) of the Act to pay at the average acquisition cost. Therefore, for CY 2027 and subsequent years, we proposed to pay for 340B drugs acquired under the 340B Program by 340B hospitals at ASP minus 33.4 percent with no add-on payment. We sought comment on our proposal to not include an add-on payment.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.

A commenter supported our proposal not to provide an add-on. This commenter cautioned CMS about layering additional payments onto the survey-derived amount without clear evidence that they represent costs not already captured in the methodology. The commenter found our proposal reasonable “insofar as the underlying acquisition-cost estimate already provides an appropriate approximation of hospitals' costs associated with obtaining these drugs. A separate adjustment should require evidence of a distinct and material expense rather than become another mechanism through which the gap between Medicare reimbursement and acquisition cost gradually reemerges.”
Response:
We thank the commenter for their support.

Many commenters objected to our proposal not to include an add-on payment for overhead and handling and faulted our proposed payment methodology for failing to capture all of the costs associated with furnishing a drug and complying with the 340B Program. A commenter emphasized the importance of the add-on payment for hospitals dispensing high-cost cellular and gene therapy products, including CAR-T therapies, that require specialized apheresis and cell-processing capacity; chain-of-custody and chain-of-identity protocols; and compliance with many additional requirements.
Many commenters disagreed with our rationale for not establishing an add-on. In the proposed rule we stated that an add-on was unnecessary because (1) we took a prudent approach in estimating the average acquisition costs for 340B-acquired drugs and we believe that that prudent estimate of acquisition cost may already account for overhead and (2) we believe that hospitals will likely negotiate additional discounts. A commenter characterized the decision as arbitrary and capricious, stating that CMS provides no justification for the exclusion and “merely states that its cost estimate may already account for the costs of overhead, a weak statement that undermines confidence in the adequacy of the resulting payment rate.” Several commenters shared their view that CMS' assumption that hospitals will likely negotiate additional discounts was inconsistent with market realities. A few commenters alleged that, in setting the payment rate, CMS failed to account for how cost structures vary dramatically across different types of hospitals.

Many commenters emphasized that acquisition costs and overhead costs are two separate measures and that in setting the payment rate CMS conflated the reported acquisition costs with overhead costs. A commenter pointed out that the current payment rate of ASP plus 6 percent contains the average sales price (a proxy for acquisition cost) plus a 6 percent add-on for overhead costs and that in the survey, CMS collected only a hospital's total net acquisition cost for a drug defined as “the total amount paid by the hospital inclusive of all discounts, rebates, and price concessions applicable at the NDC level.” The commenter stated that hospitals were not instructed to report any additional costs that they incurred to administer the drugs, such as overhead, pharmacy services, and handling costs.

Response:
We acknowledge the many costs that are associated with the delivery of a drug; however, as we have explained, we believe that, due to our prudent approach in determining an average acquisition cost, our proposed payment amount for 340B-acquired drugs does not support CMS exercising its discretion to include an add-on or adjustment in payment for overhead costs. Many of the costs mentioned by commenters are standard operating costs of hospitals and healthcare facilities and are not necessarily related to the cost of the drug. Additionally, as we are finalizing the alternative ASP minus 28 percent payment rate, a significantly conservative average acquisition cost, it is not necessary to provide an add-on. Finally, an add-on percentage, such as a 6 percent add-on to ASP, can create incentives for some providers to choose higher-priced products over lower-priced products even when the two products are clinically equivalent.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to not include an add-on payment for 340B-acquired drugs.
5. 340B Payment Policy for Drugs for Which ASP Is Unavailable
Section 1847A of the Act establishes the average sales price (ASP) methodology, which provides the amount payable for drugs and biologicals described in section 1842(o)(1)(C) of the Act furnished on or after January 1, 2005. Based on this, our historic policy has been to pay for most drugs at ASP plus 6 percent. There are some situations, however, where it is not possible to pay ASP because, for example, a drug is sufficiently new so there is no sales data available upon which to derive an average. In these situations, our historic policy has been to pay for the drug according to the following hierarchy: In general, if ASP information is not available, payment is based on the WAC with WAC plus 6 percent. If WAC information also is not available, then payment is based on AWP with 95 percent of AWP being paid. If AWP is not available, then payment is based on Mean Unit Cost (MUC). And if MUC is not available, then payment is based on the invoice price.
Consistent with this policy, starting in CY 2027, we proposed that payment for 340B drugs when ASP is unavailable mirrors CMS's historic payment policies for drugs paid under OPPS. If ASP information is not available, payment is based on the WAC, with WAC minus 33.4 percent. If WAC information also is not available, we proposed a payment rate of 59.69
[
139
]
percent of AWP. This percent was calculated by first reducing the original 95 percent of AWP price by 6 percent to generate a value that is similar to WAC with no percentage markup. Then we applied the 33.4 percent reduction WAC-similar AWP value to obtain the 59.69 percent of AWP, which is similar to either ASP minus 33.4 percent or WAC minus 33.4 percent. For 340B drugs paid based on MUC, we proposed to continue to pay them at 100 percent of MUC. These MUC-based payments are calculated based on hospital claims data, which already account for hospital acquisition costs and do not need to be discounted further. Similarly, we proposed to continue to pay for invoice priced 340B drugs at the invoice amount as the invoice price amount should already reflect the 340B discount. We sought comment on this proposal.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
One commenter requested clarification as to whether we are proposing to pay MUC only for 340B drugs for which ASP is unavailable or are we also proposing to pay for 340B drugs for which ASP is available but is paid under the MUC under non-340B settings. Another commenter noted that while ASP minus 33.4 percent appears to be higher than most proposed MUC-based rates for CY 2027, applying different reimbursement methodologies to 340B-acquired drugs, biologics, and diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals without pass-through status that are subject to MUC-based payment may create additional confusion for hospitals. The commenter requested that CMS provide additional clarification, as needed, in the CY 2027 OPPS Final Rule.
Response:
If ASP information is not available, payment is based on the WAC. If WAC information also is not available, payment is based on AWP. If AWP is not available, then payment is based on arithmetic MUC. If MUC is not available, then payment is based on invoice pricing. However, certain products, such as nonpass-through diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals with claims data, will continue to be paid based on arithmetic MUC as discussed in this final rule with comment period. MUC-based payments are calculated based on hospital claims data, including 340B and non-340B drugs, which
(
printed page 70537)
already account for hospital acquisition costs and do not need to be discounted further. If we were to discount this payment rate, then we would be accounting for 340B discounts twice.
After consideration of these public comments, we are finalizing our payment hierarchy for when ASP is not available as proposed: If ASP information is not available, payment will be based on the WAC; if WAC information is not available, payment will be based on AWP; if AWP is not available, payment will be based on MUC; and if MUC is not available, payment will be based on the invoice price. However, given our adoption of the proposed alternative of ASP minus 28 percent, we are not finalizing the reduction amounts that we proposed for WAC and AWP. Consistent with the reduction amount we are adopting, we are finalizing WAC minus 28 percent and 64.53 percent of AWP. We are finalizing our proposal to pay 100 percent of MUC for 340B drugs paid based on MUC and the invoice amount for invoiced priced 340B drugs as proposed.
6. Applicability
We proposed to apply our proposed policy to pay for drugs acquired under the 340B Program at ASP minus 33.4 percent to all separately payable drugs, biologicals, biosimilars and radiopharmaceuticals acquired under the 340B Program. This approach would establish a uniform payment policy consistent with our historic OPPS payment policy of paying the same payment rate for SCODs and non-SCODs. We noted our proposal to apply this policy to separately payable drugs and biologicals that are not SCODs was a policy proposal rather than a statutory requirement. We note that the survey included both SCODs and drugs and biologicals that we have historically treated as SCODs for payment purposes. We have treated non-SCOD drugs as SCODs for payment purposes since CY 2006. We sought comment on this proposal.
The payment policy would not apply to vaccines, as they are excluded from the 340B Program; drugs with transitional pass-through payment status, which are paid under section 1833(t)(6)(D) of the Act; and non-opioid pain management drugs as defined under section 1833(t)(16)(G) of the Act, as we believe reducing payment for those drugs would be inconsistent with statutory instructions on payment amount for those qualifying products. As previously described in the information collection request approved by OMB under the PRA, CMS may continue to validate the results of this survey on a periodic basis; for example, perhaps as often as every 4 years. We sought comment on this proposal. Specifically, we sought comment on the proposal that the policy to pay for drugs acquired under the 340B Program at ASP minus 33.4 percent would apply to all separately payable drugs, biologicals, biosimilars and radiopharmaceuticals acquired under the 340B Program, and would not apply to vaccines, drugs with transitional pass-through payment status and non-opioid pain management drugs.
Additionally, as we proposed to apply a single discount factor to the ASP for 340B-acquired drugs in lieu of calculating individual acquisition cost amounts for 340B-acquired drugs, we believed it was appropriate to apply this payment adjustment using the single discount factor to existing and new drugs that are paid under the OPPS.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that CMS lacks the statutory authority to apply a 340B-differentiated rate to drugs that are not SCODs. These commenters point to section 1833(t)(14)(B) of the Act which defines a SCOD as “a covered outpatient drug (as defined in section 1927(k)(2)) for which a separate ambulatory payment classification group (APC) has been established and that is (I) a radiopharmaceutical agent; or (II) a drug or biological for which payment was made [on a pass-through basis] on or before December 31, 2002” and excludes drugs that first received pass-through payment on or after January 1, 2003. These commenters state that if CMS wants to apply the ASP minus 33.4 percent rate to separately payable drugs not meeting this definition (
i.e.,
drugs CMS has historically treated as SCODs), then CMS must identify, drug by drug or class by class, the statutory authority on which that differential rests. A commenter requested that CMS enumerate in the final rule which HCPCS codes CMS treats as SCODs and state the authority applied to each separately payable drug outside that definition.
Response:
We disagree that we lack the statutory authority to apply our proposed payment policy to drugs that we have historically treated as SCODs. We note that in the event that our authority under section 1833(t) of the Act was determined not to be sufficient to adjust payment for 340B-acquired SCODs to ASP minus 28 percent, we would continue to apply an adjusted payment rate for 340B-acquirednon-SCODs. Similarly, we note that in the event that our authority under the Act was determined not to be sufficient to adjust payment for 340B-acquired non-SCODs, we would continue to apply an adjusted payment rate for 340B-acquired SCODs.
Comment:
Most commenters who commented on our proposal not to apply the payment adjustment to vaccines, drugs with transitional pass-through payment status, and qualifying non-opioid pain management drugs under section 1833(t)(16)(G) of the Act supported it. One commenter thanked CMS for recognizing that failing to exempt NOPAIN Act-qualifying drugs would undercut—or severely limit—the underlying policy goal of increasing use of and access to non-addictive pain management approaches. Similarly, another commenter expressed strong support for our proposal not to apply the payment adjustment to qualifying non-opioid pain management drugs under section 1833(t)(16)(G) of the Act because applying an additional 340B payment adjustment to these products would be inconsistent with the statutory framework governing payment for eligible non-opioid treatments. The commenter stated that finalizing the exclusion would help preserve the integrity of the separate payment policy established by Congress, ensure that qualifying non-opioid products continue to be reimbursed in a manner consistent with the statutory methodology applicable to them and help ensure Medicare beneficiaries retain access to clinically appropriate alternatives to opioids.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS confirm that the proposed policy does not apply to 340B-acquired diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals with pass-through status.
Response:
Please see section V.A. of this final rule with comment period for discussion of pass-through payment for drugs, biologicals, biosimilars, and radiopharmaceuticals. As previously discussed, the payment policy would not apply to drugs with transitional pass-through payment status, which are paid under section 1833(t)(6)(D) of the Act, as we believe reducing payment for those drugs would be inconsistent with statutory instructions on payment amount for those qualifying products. However, we will continue to monitor the effects of this policy and will consider changes as appropriate.
Comment:
A commenter requested clarification as to how drugs will be treated during the calendar year in
(
printed page 70538)
which their temporary pass-through status expires. Will the drug remain excluded for the remainder of that year or become subject to the reduced payment rate upon expiration? A few commenters expressed concern that drugs graduating from pass-through status would be underpaid due to such drugs accruing little or no inflation penalty and having a ceiling price of 23.1 percent upon expiration. A commenter recommended establishing a smaller reimbursement reduction for drugs leaving temporary pass-through status. Another suggested a minimum three-year delay of application of the reduction to drugs graduating from pass-through status.
Response:
CMS operationalizes pass-through expiration on a quarterly basis as discussed in section V.A. of this final rule with comment period. Once pass-through expires, the applicable payment rate would be effective the following quarter.
Comment:
One commenter expressed concern about the proposal to exclude drugs with transitional pass-through status from the proposed payment adjustment for 340B-acquired drugs. This commenter requested that CMS acknowledge that the exclusion could result in significant payment differentials among therapies treating the same condition where some drugs qualify for transitional pass-through status and others do not. The commenter referenced studies demonstrating that payment differentials among clinically competing products can significantly affect product utilization at 340B covered entities during periods of differential reimbursement. The commenter suggested that CMS consider available authorities, including its equitable adjustment authority under section 1833(t)(2)(E) of the Act, to mitigate these disparities and promote a more uniform payment policy by January 1, 2027. The commenter additionally requested that CMS acknowledge that covered entities maintain flexibility and may purchase outside of the 340B Program on a drug-by-drug basis at prices above the 340B ceiling price and code those claims accordingly, which would trigger reimbursement at the standard OPPS rate.
Response:
We thank the commenter for bringing this matter to our attention and we acknowledge the potential for the payment disparities they have identified. We anticipate examining this issue in annual rulemaking in the near future and we welcome engagement from interested parties as to how we might do so. If hospitals follow all required guidance and regulations, they may purchase outside of the 340B program as necessary. Readers should follow the finalized billing modifier requirements as discussed later in this section and comply with all relevant requirements to ensure proper payment. We remind readers that dispensing or furnishing drugs solely to take advantage of differences in reimbursement structures, rather than based on the patient's medical needs, may raise concerns under applicable federal fraud and abuse laws. Such conduct may also implicate section 1156(a)(1) of the Act, which states that items and services provided by a hospital for which payment may be sought under Medicare “will be provided economically and only when, and to the extent, medically necessary.”

Multiple commenters suggested additional drugs for CMS to consider excluding from the proposed payment policy. Several commenters suggested that biosimilars should be excluded. These commenters contended that biosimilars are fundamentally different from both single-source drugs and innovator biologics and should not be subject to a payment adjustment derived from a survey methodology that does not adequately account for their unique market characteristics. A commenter suggested that, if not exempted, the payment adjustment should be reduced for biosimilars because reimbursing biosimilars at the same reduced rate as their reference or originator products would eliminate an important financial incentive for covered entities to preferentially use lower-cost biosimilars over more expensive originator products. A few commenters expressed concern that applying the reduction to biosimilars would be inconsistent with requirements of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), which directs CMS to provide a payment rate of ASP plus 8 percent. A few commenters suggested that radiopharmaceuticals be excluded. A of these commenters recommended that CMS exempt therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals pending a targeted analysis of radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT)-specific costs. One commenter recommended that CMS exclude plasma protein therapies from the payment adjustment given the unique facets of plasma protein therapies and the dependence of Medicare beneficiaries on them. The commenter alleges that both Congress and CMS have previously recognized the unique aspects of plasma protein therapies by excluding them from previous reimbursement initiatives. The commenter cited as examples CMS's implementation of the competitive acquisition program, in which it excluded certain plasma protein therapies (
e.g.,
blood clotting factors and immune globulin products), and the statutory exclusion from the Medicare drug pricing negotiation program for products derived from human whole blood or plasma. A commenter suggested oncology drugs. Another commenter suggested cell and gene therapies. This commenter stated that cell and gene therapies are materially different from the mature, higher-volume drugs that likely drive the aggregate 340B acquisition-cost estimate. These therapies are newly launched, patient-specific or otherwise operationally complex, used in very small populations, and frequently supported by too few survey observations to establish a reliable product-level acquisition cost. Other commenters did not recommend a specific class of drug be excluded but rather drugs in shortage or with documented supply vulnerabilities or drugs with limited manufacturer competition where reimbursement reductions could threaten market sustainability. Another commenter suggested exempting drugs whose Medicare spending per beneficiary exceeds $100,000 annually. In the commenter's view this exemption would protect beneficiary access to therapies that cost more than $100,000 annually, such as advanced oncology, immunotherapy, rare disease, and specialty biologic treatments. The commenter stated that applying the proposed payment adjustment to these high-cost drugs would make it very difficult for hospitals to acquire them, particularly given the continued price increases from pharmaceutical companies. Using an annual treatment-cost threshold would provide a transparent, objective, and administratively feasible approach that relies on data already available to CMS while protecting access to the therapies most critical to vulnerable Medicare beneficiaries.
Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback and analysis of our proposed policy. While we understand drug payment and pricing is a dynamic issue, we believe the most ideal policy is one that is consistent and universal to the extent possible.
Comment:
Two commenters suggested that Drugs Covered as Preventive Services (DCAPS), which include HIV PrEP medicines, be excluded because they are covered and reimbursed under a separate statutory framework from traditional Medicare Part B drugs.
(
printed page 70539)
Response:
We thank the commenters for their suggestion. While the OPPS payment for DCAPS mirrors the amounts set forth in the fee schedule established under section 1833(a)(1)(W)(ii) of the Act, DCAPS furnished in HOPDs are paid under section 1833(t) of the Act, not section 1833(a)(1) of the Act. Section 1833(a)(1) of the Act sets forth payment amounts for services described in section 1832(a)(1) of the Act, which excludes medical and other health services (including additional preventive services) furnished by a provider of services (including a hospital). Rather, DCAPS furnished in HOPDs are described in section 1832(a)(2)(B) of the Act—medical and other health services furnished by providers of services. Section 1833(a)(2)(B)(iii) of the Act provides that services described in 1832(a)(2) of the Act (with exceptions not relevant here) are paid an amount determined under section 1833(t) of the Act—that is, the OPPS. In the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC final rule (
89 FR 94295
to 94304), we finalized an OPPS payment amount for DCAPS, codified at § 419.41(j), that was consistent with the fee schedule established under section 1833(a)(1)(W)(ii) of the Act; we did not, however, establish a policy to pay for DCAPS under the section 1833(a)(1)(W)(ii) fee schedule itself. DCAPS furnished in a HOPD are thus paid under the OPPS, and not under section 1833(a)(1)(W)(ii) of the Act.
However, the OPPS DCAPS payment framework is separate and distinct from the payment methodologies set forth at section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) and (II) of the Act. We did not propose to revise the OPPS payment methodology applicable to DCAPS. As such, DCAPS are not subject to our finalized 340B payment adjustment made pursuant to our authority at 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act at this time. We may consider revisions to the OPPS DCAPS payment methodology in future rulemaking.
Comment:
We received a few comments relating to periodic revalidation of the survey. All commenters supported CMS periodically revalidating the survey. A commenter said CMS should periodically repeat or otherwise validate the survey so that the adjustment reflects changes in purchasing patterns, discounts, and the composition of the 340B market rather than allowing a one-time estimate to become a permanent payment convention. Another commenter, noting CMS's reporting that it had received a number of responses, many of which appeared to be coordinated form letters declining to provide their acquisition data, stated that an annual survey would diminish the leverage of a single year's non-response. Another commenter pointed out that an annual survey cadence would create a more durable evidentiary record for future OPPS rulemaking and would help ensure that payment policy remains responsive to changes in drug pricing, utilization, and provider purchasing behavior. Finally, one commenter acknowledged the administrative burden of an annual survey on hospitals and CMS but noted that the survey infrastructure now exists, and the marginal burden of a repeat administration is materially lower than the burden of conducting the survey the first time. Response:
We appreciate the commenters' suggestions and will take them into account for future rulemaking. Comment:
A few commenters stated that the survey window was too short.
Response:
We disagree with commenters that the survey window was too short. It ran for fourteen weeks (January 1, 2026 through April 7, 2026), was supported by two pre-survey training webinars, a dedicated phone line and email address for technical support, a dedicated web page featuring multiple guidance documents (FAQs, user guides, fact sheets, etc.) and featured a survey instrument designed to minimize, to the extent reasonably possible, the amount of effort necessary for hospitals to collect and report the required information to CMS. Hospitals were put on notice as early as April 2025 with the President's Executive Order that a survey was coming, nearly a year prior to the survey close date, with the majority of the survey requirements being available with the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC proposed rule with comment period published in July 2025.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to apply our payment proposal to all separately payable drugs, biologicals, biosimilars and radiopharmaceuticals acquired under the 340B Program as proposed, with exceptions as discussed. We are also finalizing our proposal to not apply the payment proposal to vaccines, drugs with transitional pass-through payment status and non-opioid pain management drugs as proposed.
7. Beneficiary Copayments
An important consequence of our final policy is that it will reduce Medicare beneficiaries' copayments for Medicare Part B drugs. Medicare beneficiaries are liable for a copayment that is typically equal to 20 percent of the OPPS payment rate, which is currently generally ASP plus 6 percent (regardless of the 340B purchase price for the drug). As the survey demonstrates, in some cases, beneficiary coinsurance alone exceeds the amount the hospital paid to acquire the drug under the 340B Program. For example, Lupron Depot (NDC 00074-3663-03) had a mean adjusted ASP of $4,690.08 compared to an average 340B acquisition cost of $667.94, excluding outliers and responses above the 340B ceiling price, yielding an absolute margin of −$4,022.14 and a percent margin of −85.8 percent. As the drug is paid at ASP plus 6 percent, the payment rate for one package of the NDC averaged $4,971.49, of which a beneficiary would pay 20 percent, or $994.30. Therefore, a beneficiary's copay would be over $300 above the average hospital's 340B acquisition cost. During the ODACS study period, 3,544 beneficiaries had an OPPS claim for Lupron Depot, meaning that a sizeable beneficiary population is affected by these high coinsurance amounts. This is also not a small sample size aberration: 137 hospitals reported purchasing this drug through the 340B Program (after excluding outliers and responses above the 340B ceiling price).
Additionally, sections 11101 and 11102 of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) (
Pub. L. 117-169
, enacted August 16, 2022) established requirements under which drug manufacturers must pay inflation rebates if they raise their prices for certain drugs payable under Part B and/or covered under Part D faster than the rate of inflation. Specifically, section 11101 of the IRA amended section
(
printed page 70540)
1847A (i) of the Act, which establishes a requirement for drug manufacturers to pay rebates into the Federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund for Part B rebatable drugs for each calendar quarter beginning on or after January 1, 2023, if the specified amount, as determined under section 1847A(i)(3)(A)(ii) of the Act, exceeds the inflation-adjusted payment amount, which is calculated as set forth in section 1847A(i)(3)(C) of the Act. Pursuant to section 1847A(i)(5) of the Act, the IRA also provides for an adjustment to the beneficiary coinsurance amount in cases where the price of a Part B rebatable drug increases faster than the rate of inflation such that the beneficiary coinsurance is calculated based on the lower inflation-adjusted payment amount instead of the applicable payment amount.
Section 11101(b) of the IRA amended section 1833(t)(8) of the Act by adding a new subparagraph (F) to modify OPPS copayments for Part B rebatable drugs. In the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we codified the OPPS program payment and cost sharing amounts for Part B rebatable drugs as required by section 1833(t)(8)(F) of the Act by adding a new paragraph (e) to § 419.41, which states in the case of a rebatable drug (as defined in section 1847A(i)(2)(A) of the Act), except if such drug does not have a copayment amount as a result of application of section 1833(t)(8)(E) of the Act, for which payment is not packaged into payment for a covered OPD service (or group of services) furnished on or after April 1, 2023, and the payment for such drug under the outpatient prospective payment system is the same as the amount for a calendar quarter under section 1847A(i)(3)(A)(ii)(I) of the Act, in lieu of the calculation of the copayment amount and the Medicare program payment amount otherwise applicable under § 419.41(d) (other than application of the limitation described in paragraph § 419.41(c)(4)(i)), the copayment and Medicare program payment amounts determined under §§ 410.152(m) and 489.30(b)(6) of this chapter shall apply. In the CY 2025 PFS final rule, we codified policies regarding the computation of the inflation-adjusted beneficiary coinsurance, including § 427.201, which specifies that the methodology set forth in § 427.201(b) will be used to calculate the inflation-adjusted beneficiary coinsurance and associated Medicare payment percentage for Part B rebatable drugs as set forth in §§ 410.152(m), 419.41(e), and 489.30(b)(6). The methodology at § 427.201(b) ensures that coinsurance adjustments are not applied in a manner that would increase beneficiary coinsurance. For additional details on this coinsurance policy, we refer readers to the full discussion at
89 FR 98237
and
98238
.
Under section 1833(t)(8)(F) of the Act and current OPPS regulations at § 419.41(e), beneficiary coinsurance is adjusted for Part B rebatable drugs paid under the OPPS only where a Part B rebatable drug is paid the same as the amount for a calendar quarter under section 1847A(i)(3)(A)(ii)(I) of the Act—that is, for single source drugs and biologicals, paid 106 percent of the lesser of ASP or WAC, and for biosimilar biological products, paid the amount determined under section 1847A(b)(8) of the Act. Because, as proposed, separately payable, nonpass-through, 340B-acquired drugs would be paid an amount other than the amount under section 1847A(i)(3)(A)(ii)(I) of the Act, the coinsurance adjustment provisions of the Medicare Part B Inflation Rebate Program would not apply to separately payable, nonpass-through, 340B-acquired drugs under the proposed payment policy. We believed this was appropriate and consistent with the statutory intent of the Medicare Part B Inflation Rebate Program, as the coinsurance adjustment at section 1847A(i)(5) of the Act is intended to reduce the coinsurance amount to equal that of 20 percent of the inflation-adjusted payment amount described at section 1847A(i)(3)(C) of the Act, and we expected that the applicable coinsurance under the payment proposal for 340B-acquired drugs would likely be lower than 20 percent of such inflation-adjusted payment amount. We sought comment on the interaction between coinsurance adjustments under section 1847A(i)(5) of the Act and the proposed policy to pay for drugs acquired under the 340B Program at ASP minus 33.4 percent.
We anticipated that our proposed policy to pay for separately paid drugs acquired under the 340B Program at ASP minus 33.4 percent would collectively reduce beneficiary copayments by an estimated $1.15 billion for CY 2027.
We received public comments. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters appreciated the effect of the proposed policy on reducing beneficiary copayments.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support.
Comment:
Many commenters challenged our statement that the proposed payment adjustment would reduce copayments for Medicare beneficiaries. In their view we failed to disclose that due to budget neutrality Medicare beneficiaries will pay higher copayments for all non-drug Part B items and services by roughly the same amount. Consequently, in these commenters' view, the out-of-pocket burden on patients is redistributed, not decreased, by the proposed policy. One of these commenters recommended that CMS calculate and report the net impact on beneficiary spending across the complete episode of care, rather than presenting the drug-specific reduction as though it were a direct reduction in total patient expense. A few commenters found fault with the example we cited of a drug, Lupron Depot, for which the beneficiary copayment exceeded the 340B price paid by the hospital. A commenter stated that this one illustration was insufficient data to draw any conclusions about the reliability of CMS' estimation of beneficiary savings. Another commenter stated that the observation that beneficiary cost-sharing sometimes exceeded a hospital's 340B purchase price describes the intended design of the 340B statute, in which the differential between acquisition cost and payer reimbursement is the mechanism by which Congress chose to fund safety-net care.
Response:
We thank the commenters for expressing their concerns. As we acknowledged throughout the proposed rule and this final rule, including the regulatory impact section, this policy will largely be implemented in a budget neutral manner. From an individual beneficiary experience, their reduced payment for 340B drugs will be substantial and noticeable. We also emphasize that our proposal to apply this reduction to non-excepted, off-campus PBDs will not be budget neutralized and therefore will generate savings for beneficiaries.
Comment:
Some commenters expressed concern that the proposed payment adjustment would arbitrarily create cost-sharing disparities between Medicare beneficiaries. These commenters pointed out that while a beneficiary who receives a Part B drug at a 340B hospital will see reduced coinsurance liability for that drug, a beneficiary receiving the identical drug at a non-340B hospital will face higher coinsurance despite having the same coverage via Medicare. Some of these commenters said that this disparity could result in a distortion of the beneficiary experience. Since beneficiary out-of-pocket liability would vary significantly by facility status,
(
printed page 70541)
patients would be steered toward specific health systems based on financial incentives rather than quality, provider access, or clinical outcomes. Similarly, these commenters contend, this payment structure would place a disproportionate burden on beneficiaries whose care needs are driven by procedures, diagnostic scans, or emergency visits rather than specialty Part B drugs.
Response:
The intent of our proposed policy is to better align payment for 340B-acquired drugs with their acquisition costs as demonstrated by the ODACS. A consequence of that increased accuracy is that beneficiaries will pay more accurate copayments. We do not think that it would be appropriate to continue to pay what we now know to be less accurate rates for drugs, and make beneficiaries pay higher copays for those drugs, simply to maintain parity in beneficiaries' copayment experience between 340B and non-340B hospitals. With respect to the proposed reduction having a disproportionate effect on beneficiaries whose care needs are driven by non-drug items and services, we reiterate our response to the previous comment. We note that the 340B program in general is outside the scope of this final rule with comment period.
Comment:
One commenter stated that because the large majority of Part B coinsurance is paid not by beneficiaries out of pocket but by supplemental coverage, including Medigap, employer wrap plans, and Medicaid, realized out-of-pocket savings to beneficiaries are a fraction of the amount cited by CMS. The commenter additionally noted that budget neutrality requires an increase of approximately 8.44 percent in the conversion factor for non-drug services, which raises beneficiary coinsurance on every non-drug outpatient service at every OPPS hospital and that the proposed rule nowhere nets this offsetting increase against the claimed drug savings.
Response:
We note that, even though many beneficiaries have supplemental coverage, beneficiaries often pay a premium for such supplemental coverage and those plans make coinsurance payments for the beneficiary. Thus, to the extent Medicare would be lessening the coinsurance amount such supplemental plans would have to make, we would expect the price of such plans to decrease or otherwise reflect these lower costs in the future, thereby lowering the amount that beneficiaries pay for supplemental plan coverage. Further, for the millions of Medicare beneficiaries who do not have supplemental coverage at all or who have a supplemental plan that does not cover all of a beneficiary's cost-sharing obligation, the proposed policy would directly lower out-of-pocket spending for 340B-acquired drugs for those beneficiaries. We also note that the budget neutral nature of this policy is required by statute.
We thank commenters for their input. As we indicated above, we are revising
42 CFR 419.41(d)
and adding a new paragraph (k) to implement our finalized policy to pay ASP minus 28 percent for all separately payable drugs, biologicals, biosimilars and radiopharmaceuticals acquired under the 340B Program . We anticipate that this policy will collectively reduce beneficiary copayments for drugs by an estimated $1.1 billion for CY 2027.
8. 340B Payment Policy Exemptions
We proposed to exempt children's hospitals and PPS-exempt cancer hospitals from our proposed policy to adjust OPPS payments for drugs acquired under the 340B Program. In accordance with section 1833(t)(7)(D)(ii) of the Act, we make transitional outpatient payments (TOPs) to both children's and PPS-exempt cancer hospitals. This means that these hospitals are permanently held harmless to their “pre-BBA amount,” and they receive hold harmless payments to ensure that they do not receive a payment that is lower in amount under the OPPS than the payment amount they would have received before implementation of the OPPS. Accordingly, if we were to reduce drug payments to these hospitals on a per claim basis, it is very likely that the reduction in payment would be paid back to these hospitals at cost report settlement, given the TOPs structure. Consequently, we believe it is appropriate to exempt children's and PPS-exempt cancer hospitals from the alternative 340B drug payment methodology.
In addition to the children's and PPS-exempt cancer hospitals, Medicare has long recognized the particularly unique needs of rural communities and the financial challenges rural hospital providers face. Across the various Medicare payment systems, CMS has established a number of special payment provisions for rural providers to maintain access to care and to deliver high quality care to beneficiaries in rural areas. With respect to the OPPS, section 1833(t)(13) of the Act provided the Secretary with the authority to make an adjustment to OPPS payments for rural hospitals, effective January 1, 2006, if justified by a study of the difference in costs by APC between hospitals in rural areas and hospitals in urban areas. Our analysis showed a difference in costs for rural SCHs. Therefore, for the CY 2006 OPPS, we finalized a payment adjustment for rural SCHs of 7.1 percent for all services and procedures paid under the OPPS, excluding separately payable drugs and biologicals, brachytherapy sources, and devices paid under the pass-through payment policy, in accordance with section 1833(t)(13)(B) of the Act. We have continued this 7.1 percent payment adjustment since 2006.
For CY 2027 and subsequent years, we proposed that rural sole community hospitals (as described under the regulations at
42 CFR 412.92
and designated as rural for Medicare purposes), children's hospitals, and PPS-exempt cancer hospitals would be exempted from the 340B payment adjustment and that these hospitals would continue to generally be paid ASP plus 6 percent for drugs. We stated that we may revisit our policy to exempt rural SCHs, as well as other hospital designations for exemption from the 340B drug payment adjustment, in future rulemaking.

9. 340B Payment Policy for Drugs Furnished by Nonexcepted Off-Campus Departments of a Hospital
In the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
81 FR 79699

Pub. L. 114-74

As a general matter, under sections 1833(t)(1)(B)(v) and (t)(21) of the Act, applicable items and services furnished by certain off-campus outpatient departments of a provider on or after January 1, 2017, are not considered covered OPD services as defined under section 1833(t)(1)(B) of the Act for purposes of payment under the OPPS and will instead be paid “under the applicable payment system” under Medicare Part B if the requirements for such payment are otherwise met. We indicated that, in order to be considered part of a hospital, an off-campus department of a hospital must meet the provider-based criteria established under
42 CFR 413.65
. Accordingly, we refer to an “off-campus outpatient department of a provider,” which is the term used in section 603 of the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015, as an “off-campus outpatient provider-based department” or an “off-campus PBD.” For a detailed discussion of the legislative history and statutory authority related to payments under section 603 of the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015, we refer readers to the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
81 FR 79699
through
79719
) and interim final rule with comment period (
81 FR 79720
through
79729
).
To implement the amendments made by section 603 of
Public Law 114-74
, we issued an interim final rule with comment period (
81 FR 79720
), which accompanied the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period to establish the PFS as the “applicable payment system” that applies in most cases, and we established payment rates under the PFS for those nonexcepted items and services furnished by nonexcepted off-campus PBDs. Specifically, we established a PFS relativity adjuster that is applied to the OPPS rate for the billed nonexcepted items and services furnished in a nonexcepted off-campus PBD to calculate payment rates under the PFS. The PFS relativity adjuster reflects the estimated overall difference between the payment that would otherwise be made to a hospital under the OPPS for the nonexcepted items and services furnished in nonexcepted off-campus PBDs and the resource-based payment under the PFS for the technical aspect of those services with reference to the difference between the facility and nonfacility (office) rates and policies under the PFS. The current PFS relativity adjuster is set at 40 percent of the amount that would have been paid under the OPPS (
90 FR 53770
). These PFS rates include the same packaging rules that are unique to the hospital outpatient setting under the OPPS, including the packaging of drugs that are unconditionally packaged under the OPPS. This includes packaging certain drugs and biologicals that would ordinarily be separately payable under the PFS when furnished in the physician office setting. For a full discussion of our initial implementation of section 603, we refer readers to the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
81 FR 79699
through
79719
) and the interim final rule with comment period (79720 through 79729). For a detailed discussion of the current PFS relativity adjuster related to payments under section 603, we refer readers to the CY 2018 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
82 FR 52356
through
52637

through

We note that, ordinarily, Medicare pays for drugs and biologicals furnished in the physician's office setting at ASP plus 6 percent. This is because section 1842(o)(1)(A) of the Act provides that if a physician's, supplier's, or any other person's bill or request for payment for services includes a charge for a drug or biological for which payment may be made under Medicare Part B and the drug or biological is not paid on a cost or prospective payment basis as otherwise provided in this part, the amount for the drug or biological is equal to the following: The amount provided under section 1847, section 1847A, section 1847B, or section 1881(b)(13) of the Act, as the case may be for the drug or biological.
Generally, in the hospital outpatient department setting, low-cost drugs and biologicals are packaged into the payment for other services billed under the OPPS. Separately payable drugs (1) have pass-through payment status, (2) have a cost per day exceeding a threshold, or (3) are not policy-packaged or packaged in a C-APC. As described in sections V.A. and V.B. of this final rule with comment period, section 1847A of the Act establishes the ASP methodology, which is used for payment for drugs and biologicals described in section 1842(o)(1)(C) of the Act furnished on or after January 1, 2005. The ASP methodology, as applied under the OPPS, uses several sources of data as a basis for payment, including the ASP, the WAC, and the AWP (
90 FR 53682
). As noted in section V.B. of this final rule with comment period, since CY 2013, our policy has been to pay for separately payable drugs and biologicals at ASP plus 6 percent in accordance with section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(II) of the Act (the statutory default) (
90 FR 53702
). Consequently, in the case of services furnished in a hospital outpatient department, Medicare has historically paid ASP plus 6 percent for separately payable Part B drugs and biologicals. For a detailed discussion of our current OPPS drug payment policies, we refer readers to the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
90 FR 53697
through
53766
).
(
printed page 70544)
As a general matter, in the nonexcepted off-campus PBD setting, we pay hospitals under the PFS for all drugs and biologicals that are packaged under the OPPS based on a percentage of the OPPS payment rate, which is determined using the PFS relativity adjuster. Because OPPS packaging rules apply to the PFS payments to nonexcepted off-campus PBDs, the PFS payment for some nonexcepted items and services that are packaged includes payment for some drugs and biologicals that would be separately billable under the PFS if a similar service had been furnished in the office-based setting. As we noted in the CY 2017 final rule with comment period, in analyzing the term “applicable payment system,” we considered whether and how the requirements for payment could be met under alternative payment systems in order to pay for nonexcepted items and services, and considered several payment systems under which payment is made for similar items and services (
81 FR 79712
). Because the PFS relativity adjuster that is applied to calculate payment to hospitals for nonexcepted items and services furnished in nonexcepted off-campus PBDs is based on a percentage (40 percent) of the amount determined under the OPPS for a particular item or service, and the OPPS is a prospective payment system, we believed that items and services furnished by nonexcepted off-campus PBDs paid under the PFS were payable on a prospective payment basis. Therefore, we believed we had flexibility to pay for separately payable drugs and biologicals furnished in nonexcepted off-campus PBDs at an amount other than the amount dictated by sections 1842(o)(1)(C) and 1847A of the Act.
As discussed previously, our proposal to adjust the payment rate for separately payable drugs and biologicals (other than vaccines, drugs on pass-through payment status and non-opioid pain management drugs) acquired under the 340B Program from ASP plus 6 percent to ASP minus 33.4 percent would apply to separately payable drugs and biologicals paid under the OPPS. Under sections 1833(t)(1)(B)(v) and (t)(21) of the Act, however, nonexcepted items and services furnished by nonexcepted off-campus PBDs are not covered outpatient department services and, therefore, are not payable under the OPPS. This means that, absent our inclusion of them in our proposed policy, nonexcepted off-campus PBDs would not be subject to the payment changes we proposed. Because hospitals can, in some cases, acquire drugs and biologicals under the 340B Program for use in nonexcepted off-campus PBDs, we believe that not adjusting payment for these departments would present a significant incongruity between the payment amounts for these drugs depending upon where (for example, excepted or nonexcepted PBD) they are furnished. This incongruity would distort the relative accuracy of the resource-based payment amounts under the site-specific PFS rates and could result in significant perverse incentives for hospitals to acquire drugs, biologicals, biosimilars, and radiopharmaceuticals under the 340B Program and avoid Medicare payment adjustments that account for the discount by providing these drugs to patients predominantly in nonexcepted off-campus PBDs. It would also undermine our goals of reducing beneficiary cost-sharing for these drugs and biologicals and moving towards site neutrality through the section 603 amendments to section 1833(t) of the Act. To avoid such perverse incentives and the resulting distortions, we proposed for CY 2027 and subsequent years, to pay an amount equal to ASP minus 33.4 percent, or equivalent, for drugs, biologicals, biosimilars, and radiopharmaceuticals acquired under the 340B Program that are furnished by nonexcepted off-campus PBDs.
Consistent with the approach to budget neutrality we adopted when we previously implemented a reduction for 340B-acquired drugs furnished by nonexcepted off-campus PBDs (
83 FR 59021
) and our approach to budget neutrality for items and services provided by nonexcepted off-campus PBDs generally (
83 FR 58832
), these adjusted payments would not be budget neutralized.

10. Billing Modifiers
To effectuate the payment adjustment for 340B-acquired drugs, we proposed that, beginning January 1, 2027, providers who are not exempted from the 340B payment adjustment would report modifier “JG” (Drug or biological acquired with 340B Drug Pricing Program Discount) to identify if a drug was acquired under the 340B Program. The phrase “acquired under the 340B Program” would include all drugs acquired under the 340B Program or Prime Vendor Program, regardless of the level of discount applied to the drug. Drugs that were not acquired under the 340B Program would not be reported with the modifier “JG.” For separately payable drugs (status indicator “K”), application of modifier “JG” would trigger a payment adjustment such that the 340B-acquired drug is paid at ASP minus 33.4 percent.
We additionally proposed that, beginning January 1, 2027, for drugs or providers that are exempted from the 340B drug payment policy for CY 2027, which include pass-through drugs (status indicator “G”), non-opioid treatment for pain relief drugs authorized under section 4135 of the CAA, 2023 (status indicator “K1”), rural SCHs, children's hospitals, and PPS-exempt cancer hospitals, should not report modifier ”JG.” Instead, these exempted providers should report the informational modifier “TB” (Drug or Biological Acquired With 340B Drug Pricing Program Discount, Reported for Informational Purposes) to identify OPPS separately payable drugs purchased with a 340B discount. The informational modifier “TB” will facilitate the collection and tracking of 340B claims data for OPPS providers that are exempted from the payment adjustment in CY 2027. However, use of modifier “TB” will not trigger a payment adjustment, and these providers will generally receive ASP plus 6 percent for separately payable drugs furnished in CY 2027, even if such drugs were acquired under the 340B Program.
We also proposed that, beginning January 1, 2027, all providers report a distinct modifier to identify drugs and biologicals that were not acquired under the 340B Program. Specifically, we proposed to establish a new modifier, designated in the proposed rule with the placeholder modifier code “XX” (Drug or biological not acquired under the 340B Drug Pricing Program), which would be required to be reported for all separately payable drugs that were purchased outside of the 340B Program.
The requirement to use modifier “XX” would apply to all providers paid under the OPPS, including excepted and nonexcepted off-campus PBDs. Reporting the modifiers “XX,” “JG,” or “TB” for applicable drugs would ensure that all drug claims are consistently categorized as either 340B-acquired or non-340B-acquired. We believe that requiring the use of modifier “XX” for non-340B drugs will improve the completeness and consistency of claims data, facilitate program integrity and oversight, and enhance our ability to monitor acquisition patterns across providers. The use of modifier “XX” would not trigger a payment adjustment and such drugs would continue to be paid at the applicable OPPS rate (generally ASP plus 6 percent for separately payable drugs) consistent with existing policy. In summary, we proposed all separately paid drug claims reported under the OPPS would be reported with a modifier of either “JG,” “TB,” or “XX” (Table 75). We solicited comment on our proposal to require all separately paid drug claims to be reported with a modifier of either “JG,” “TB,” or “XX.”
As stated in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, we believe the addition of this new modifier is consistent with the decisions that hospitals are already making (is the drug a 340B-acquired drug or a non-340B-acquired drug) when billing for these drugs. As previously mentioned, we believe requiring the use of modifier “XX” for non-340B drugs will improve the completeness and consistency of claims data—this requirement could even decrease burden on hospitals as it may improve the accuracy of billing, thus decreasing the need for hospitals to reprocess claims that were billed incorrectly. We requested comment as to whether the addition of modifier “XX” would create unnecessary, undue burden for hospitals.
(
printed page 70546)
Additionally, we acknowledged this billing modifier proposal would have implications for how we identify billing units of drugs acquired through the 340B Program under the Medicare Part B Drug Inflation Rebate Program. In the CY 2025 Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) final rule (
89 FR 98583
), we codified at § 427.303(b)(1)(iv) that we will exclude from Part B rebate calculations separately payable billing units in claim lines for institutional claims that are billed with the “TB” modifier for claims with dates of service on or after January 1, 2025. As we stated in the proposed rule, establishing a requirement to use the “JG” modifier, in addition to the requirement to use the “TB” modifier would necessitate changes to how we identify 340B units to exclude from Part B rebate calculations.
Consequently, we proposed a conforming change at § 427.303(b)(1)(iv) to reflect proposed changes to the requirements to use billing modifiers for 340B-acquired drugs as described in section V.B.10. of this final rule with comment period. Specifically, to account for these billing modifier proposals, at § 427.303(b)(1)(iv), we proposed to add “or successor billing modifiers to identify 340B units.” This means, for the purposes of Part B inflation rebate calculations, we would exclude billing units acquired under the 340B Program as identified through separately payable units in claim lines billed with the “TB” modifier, or successor billing modifiers to identify 340B units for 340B-acquired drugs, for claims with dates of service on or after January 1, 2025. Therefore, as a matter of operations, effective January 1, 2027, CMS would identify separately payable billing units in claim lines billed with the “TB” modifier and proposed “JG” modifier. We recognized that policy amendments for the Medicare Prescription Drug Inflation Rebate Program are typically proposed in the PFS; however, we believed it was appropriate to propose an amendment to § 427.303(b)(1)(iv) in the OPPS/ASC proposed rule due to timing differences in the publication of the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule relative to the OPPS/ASC proposed rule and to ensure we are able to appropriately exclude 340B units from Part B rebate calculations starting January 1, 2027.
