D. CY 2027 OPPS Payment Methodology for Non-340B-Acquired Drugs Based on ODACS
CMS analyzed acquisition cost data collected through the ODACS for drugs acquired outside the 340B Program and evaluated several methodologies for estimating the relationship between hospitals' acquisition costs and ASP-based payment amounts as previously discussed in this section.
Using our preferred proposed methodology, which calculates acquisition cost margins using the geometric mean of survey-reported acquisition costs, we estimate that hospitals' acquisition costs for non-340B drugs were approximately 2.7 percent above ASP during the survey period. However, we recognize that acquisition costs reported through the survey may not fully reflect all manufacturer rebates, chargebacks, administrative fees, or other post-purchase price concessions received by hospitals, as we have not included GPO discounts into the ASP plus 2.7 percent figure. Therefore, even ASP plus 2.7 percent, the reported acquisition costs, may overstate hospitals' net acquisition costs. As a result, the estimated margin of ASP plus 2.7 percent may, in part, reflect differences in how manufacturer
(
printed page 70549)
rebates and other retrospective discounts were reported rather than solely the underlying acquisition costs of the drugs.
The survey results for non-340B drugs exhibit greater variation than the survey results for 340B-acquired drugs. As a result, the confidence intervals for the estimated non-340B acquisition cost margins span a slightly wider range of potential values. We believe this finding is expected given the diversity of purchasing arrangements, contracting structures, and acquisition channels available to hospitals when acquiring drugs outside the 340B Program. The broader distribution of survey-reported acquisition costs suggests greater uncertainty regarding the precise average acquisition cost margin for non-340B drugs relative to the margin observed for 340B-acquired drugs.
Although the survey data suggest that hospitals' acquisition costs for non-340B drugs may be lower on average from the current payment rate of ASP plus 6 percent, the survey results are subject to slightly greater variability and may be affected by differences in the reporting of manufacturer rebates and other price concessions. Consequently, we believe the survey data should be interpreted further as we assess the need for a payment rate change for non-340B drugs.
Given the need to further consider the non-340B survey results for the reasons mentioned, including the range of reasonable acquisition cost estimates supported by the data, we did not propose to establish a survey-based payment rate for non-340B drugs. Rather, for CY 2027, after taking into account the survey results, we proposed to continue paying separately payable non-340B drugs, biologicals, biosimilars, and radiopharmaceuticals as we do in CY 2026, which is generally at a rate of ASP plus 6 percent. We believe this approach appropriately considers the survey findings, including the uncertainty associated with manufacturer rebate reporting and the broader distribution of acquisition cost estimates, while maintaining stability in payment rates and allowing CMS to continue evaluating acquisition cost information obtained through its survey authority under section 1833(t)(14)(D)(ii) of the Act.
Under the same survey-based methodology proposed for determining payment for 340B-acquired drugs, such an approach for non-340B drugs would be based on the geometric mean acquisition cost estimate derived from the survey data, resulting in a payment rate of approximately ASP plus 2.7 percent. In the case of the 340B-acquired drugs, the discrepancy between acquisition cost and Medicare payment is substantial and obviously apparent; however, the discrepancy between acquisition cost and Medicare payment for non-340B acquired drugs is much less significant. Therefore, we proposed to continue paying for non-340B acquired drugs at a rate of ASP plus 6 percent. We also intended to continue evaluating the acquisition cost survey data for non-340B-acquired drugs and noted we may consider the results of this analysis in future rulemaking.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters supported our proposal to maintain the current payment rate for CY 2027 for separately payable drugs and biologicals without pass-through payment status that are not acquired under the 340B Program. These commenters stated that this method of payment makes hospital reimbursement predictable, accurate, and maintains parity with the physician office setting. One of these commenters stated that applying a payment change to non-340B drugs on the strength of data that is more widely dispersed than the data for 340B drugs would introduce risk for products that are dispensed infrequently as compared to non-orphan drugs. Several of these commenters cautioned CMS against future reductions to non-340B drugs. A commenter opined that applying any reimbursement reductions for drug purchases would be particularly difficult to justify because non-340B hospitals generally acquire drugs without the substantial discounts available through the 340B Program. Multiple commenters observed that since survey reported acquisition costs were only 2.7 percent above the mean ASP and 2.8 percent above the median ASP, that this means that for any given non-340B drug, it is likely that ASP will be roughly the same as the non-340B purchase price.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support. With respect to future payment adjustments to non-340B drugs, as we indicated in the proposed rule, we are continuing to evaluate the survey data.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern with the asymmetry of applying survey findings to reduce OPPS payment for 340B drugs but not to adjust payment for non-340B drugs. One commenter alleged that this demonstrates that CMS is “applying the survey aggressively when it produces savings but disregards it where application would reduce payment to non-340B hospitals.” The commenter contends that this inconsistency undermines our rationale that payments should reflect actual acquisition cost. The commenter also pointed out that the failure to reduce OPPS payments for non-340B drugs will create a situation where non-340B hospitals will see their total OPPS reimbursements increase due to budget neutrality. The commenter finds this outcome to be unfair and discriminatory based on 340B status. The commenter contends that the proposed payment rate will result in an underpayment for some 340B drugs since the 340B discount can range from 23.1 percent to 100 percent depending on manufacturers' actions. CMS' proposal to apply a single ASP percentage reduction of 33.4 percent to all drugs supposedly will underpay hospitals for 340B drugs subject to any discount above 33.4 percent. The commenter says that based on this underpayment of some 340B drugs, they will choose to not dispense a 340B drug to patients where the 340B payment would result in an underpayment. Instead, the commenter will purchase those drugs at the list price (wholesale acquisition cost), submit the claim without a 340B modifier, and receive the ASP plus 6 percent payment. It is the commenter's belief that other hospitals and health systems will do the same thing, which will significantly impact CMS proposed budget savings of $5.7 billion from this proposed payment adjustment.
Response:
We acknowledge that we are proposing to adjust payment for 340B-acquired drugs but not for non-340B-acquired drugs in CY 2027. However, this asymmetry is simply the result of our analysis of the survey data in conjunction with ceiling prices required under the 340B Program for which there is no corollary outside of that program. As we explained in the proposed rule, based on the respective confidence intervals for 340B and non-340B drugs, we believe it is appropriate to move forward with an adjustment for 340B-acquired drugs in CY 2027 but to continue to study the data with respect to non-340B-acquired drugs. We disagree with the commenter that we are discriminating against 340B hospitals in doing so. We are better aligning our payment for 340B-acquired drugs with the cost of their acquisition, as demonstrated by the survey and supported by ceiling-price data, in compliance with section 1833(t)(14) of the Act and we are budget neutralizing that payment adjustment in compliance with our statutory budget neutrality
(
printed page 70550)
obligations. The nearly 40 percent discrepancy for 340B-acquired drugs is so drastic and obvious it needs to be addressed immediately; however, the preliminary non-340B average acquisition cost is only a few percentage points away from the current payment rate and warrants additional consideration before proposing changes, especially considering there is no non-340B corollary to 340B ceiling prices.
Comment:
One commenter suggested that, based on the confidence interval spread for 340B drugs, CMS should conclude that the current payment rate for non-340B drugs is in fact the current payment rate for non-340B drugs (ASP plus 6 percent). Alternatively, the commenter indicated that they also supported our determination in the proposed rule that hospital acquisition data is not currently available for non-340B drugs such that payment under section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(II) (
i.e.,
ASP plus 6 percent) continues to be appropriate.
Response:
We thank the commenter for their suggestion and for their support of our proposal to pay ASP plus 6 percent for non-340B-acquired drugs for CY 2027. As we indicated in the proposed rule, we continue to evaluate acquisition cost information obtained through CMS's survey authority under section 1833(t)(14)(D)(ii) of the Act.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to continue paying for non-340B-acquired drugs at a rate of ASP plus 6 percent for CY 2027.
E. Summary
In summary, after consideration of public comments received, for the reasons discussed above, we are not finalizing our proposal for CY 2027 and subsequent years to pay for drugs acquired under the 340B Program at ASP minus 33.4 percent. Instead, we are finalizing our alternative proposal for CY 2027 and subsequent years to pay for drugs acquired under the 340B Program at ASP minus 28 percent and are revising
42 CFR 419.41(d)
and adding a new paragraph (k) to implement this payment change. We are finalizing our proposal to pay for drugs acquired outside of the 340B Program at ASP plus 6 percent. We are also finalizing our proposal to exempt rural SCHs, PPS-exempt cancer hospitals and children's hospitals from the 340B Payment Policy for CY 2027 and subsequent years. We are also finalizing our proposal that hospitals paid under the OPPS, other than a type of hospital excluded from the OPPS (such as CAHs or REHs) or exempted from the 340B drug payment policy for CY 2027, are required to report modifier “JG” on the same claim line as the drug HCPCS code to identify a 340B-acquired drug; the modifier “TB” for all pass-through drugs, non-opioid treatment for pain relief drugs, and 340B-acquired drugs reported by rural SCHs, children's hospitals and PPS-exempt cancer hospitals for informational purposes; and the modifier “XX” (finalized as “ND”) for all drugs that were not acquired through the 340B Program. We note these payment policies apply to both excepted and non-excepted provider-based departments of a hospital. Finally, we are finalizing our proposal with modification to make a conforming change to § 427.303(b)(1)(iv) to ensure our process to identify 340B units for purposes of Part B inflation rebate calculations aligns with our proposed 340B modifier billing requirements. All of these finalized proposals are effective January 1, 2027.
F. Budget Neutrality
As we proposed the previously defined payment adjustments through our authority under section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act, we also proposed making this adjustment in a budget neutral manner. To maintain budget neutrality within the OPPS, we estimated that OPPS payment for 340B-acquired drugs would be reduced by approximately $4.85 billion in CY 2027; however, these payments would be redistributed in an equal offsetting amount to all hospitals paid under the OPPS through increased payment rates for non-drug items and services furnished by all hospitals paid under the OPPS. Specifically, the redistributed dollars would increase the conversion factor for OPPS non-drug items and services by 8.44 percent for CY 2027.
We also estimated the alternative methodology previously described to pay 340B-acquired drugs at ASP minus 28 percent, which is the average acquisition cost calculated from the 340B ceiling prices and volume weighted by OPPS utilization data. Through this method, we estimated that OPPS payment for 340B-acquired drugs would be reduced by approximately $4.68 billion in CY 2027. Specifically, the redistributed dollars would increase the conversion factor for OPPS non-drug items and services by 8.14 percent for CY 2027.
For additional details on our proposed budget neutral implementation of this policy, please see section II.B. of this final rule with comment period.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters acknowledged our statutory obligation to budget neutralize our proposed payment adjustment. One commenter stated that “this adjustment is both appropriate and required.”
Response:
We thank commenters for recognizing our statutory obligation to budget neutralize our proposed payment adjustment.
Comment:
Several commenters supported budget neutralizing our proposed payment adjustment due to the benefit the budget-neutral redistribution would provide to many hospitals, including those serving rural and underserved communities. One of these commenters expressed disappointment that physician practices would not receive the corresponding increase in OPPS payment for non-drug items and services. The commenter opined that payment under the Medicare PFS continues to lag OPPS payment for many comparable services and stated that this distributional effect underscores the need for CMS, through PFS rulemaking, to ensure that payment to independent physician practices reflects the realistic cost of furnishing high-quality care and supports continued beneficiary access.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support. With respect to the commenter's suggestion that we address differences in payment between the PFS and the OPPS, as acknowledged by the commenter this issue is outside the scope of this rulemaking.
Comment:
Several commenters, including MedPAC, supported reducing payment for 340B-acquired drugs generally but lamented our statutory obligation to budget neutralize those reductions. These commenters disliked its effect of increasing beneficiary copayments for non-drug items and services and contributing to greater differences in Medicare's payment rates for those services delivered in both the hospital and office settings. These commenters urged us to work with Congress to enable us to implement the payment adjustment in a non-budget neutral manner.
Response:
We thank MedPAC and the other commenters for their feedback and will take their suggestion under consideration for future rulemaking, if applicable.
Comment:
Many commenters requested that CMS recalculate the budget-neutrality adjustment on an annual basis, using OPPS claims data from the prior year to ensure the policy is implemented in a fully budget neutral manner. These commenters pointed to
(
printed page 70551)
the implementation of our previous 340B payment policy and stated that because we did not recalculate the budget neutrality adjustment to account for volume changes in drug claims and non-drug claims over the duration of that policy, the original adjustment did not reflect actual claims.
Response:
We are fully implementing budget neutrality for CY 2027. We will consider recalculating the budget-neutrality adjustment on an annual basis for future rulemaking.
Comment:
Many commenters claimed that budget neutrality does not require a uniform redistribution across hospitals and that CMS should prioritize “essential hospitals,” “true safety-net hospitals,” teaching hospitals, non-exempted children's hospitals, “hospitals that demonstrably serve the greatest numbers of Medicare beneficiaries, Medicaid beneficiaries, dual-eligible individuals, and low-income patients,” and “hospitals whose operations and missions are consistent with the intent of the 340B Program, particularly nonprofit hospitals with a demonstrated commitment to providing charity care and serving underserved populations” in the budget neutral redistribution.
Response:
While we recognize the commenters' concerns regarding the effect of budget neutrality on the hospital types they list, we note that the purpose of the 340B Payment Policy is not to replace the 340B Program. We have attempted to address some of these concerns through the finalized exemptions for rural sole community hospitals, PPS-exempt cancer hospitals, and children's hospitals.
Comment:
Many commenters observed that the 8.44 percent increase to payment for non-drug items and services would not make all hospitals whole. The commenters state that hospitals with substantial 340B drug volume would experience a drug payment reduction, while hospitals with comparatively little or no 340B exposure would receive the benefit of the increased payments for non-drug services. A commenter stated “[t]here is no assurance that the hospital will recover what it loses.” Another commenter observed that “[a] hospital that experiences a substantial reduction in drug payments will not necessarily receive sufficient additional reimbursement through non-drug services to offset its actual losses. CMS should therefore evaluate budget neutrality at the hospital level and by hospital type rather than relying solely upon aggregate OPPS neutrality.”
Response:
We acknowledge that some hospitals will potentially experience greater reductions to drug payments than increases to non-drug items and services as a consequence of our policy. However, that does not change our statutory obligation under section 1833(t)(14) of the Act to conduct a survey of drug acquisition costs and adjust payment rates taking those costs into account.
Comment:
A commenter expressed concern about APC calibration. The commenter stated that “[w]hile CMS anticipates that reductions in 340B drug reimbursement will be offset through corresponding increases in payment for non-drug OPPS services, hospitals must have confidence that the APC recalibration accurately and fully reflects the funds removed from 340B drug reimbursement. However, CMS has not demonstrated that the resulting redistribution appropriately reflects the hospitals, service lines, and patient populations most affected by the proposed drug payment reductions. Because reductions in drug reimbursement and increases in APC payments are not distributed uniformly across providers and service lines, the effects of the proposal are likely to vary considerably across hospitals and clinical programs. Therefore, CMS should provide greater transparency regarding both the calculation of the budget neutrality adjustment and the distributional impact of the proposal to ensure that hospitals can appropriately evaluate its effects.”
Response:
We agree that it is important to provide transparency in calculating budget neutrality for this finalized payment adjustment. For this reason, we have provided discussion throughout the proposed and final rules regarding the calculations and impact involved. We further note that we provide a separate column describing the impacts of the budget neutral distribution for this adjustment for various categories of OPPS providers in section XXVII of this final rule.
Comment:
Many commenters requested that we conduct additional analyses and release additional information relating to budget neutrality before finalizing our proposal. Multiple commenters requested CMS conduct and publish a detailed analysis of the proposal's impact on 340B hospitals, safety-net providers, access to care, and essential outpatient services before finalizing the policy. A commenter suggested that CMS publish hospital-specific net-impact estimates before finalizing the policy and establish protections for hospitals facing material losses. The commenter additionally requested that CMS evaluate whether the redistribution changes incentives to furnish complex outpatient therapies or affects access in communities already experiencing hospital financial stress. Another commenter requested that CMS publish a combined beneficiary cost-sharing analysis that nets the claimed drug coinsurance savings against the coinsurance increases produced by the budget-neutral conversion factor adjustment.
Another commenter alleged that CMS provided no explanation of its methodology for calculating the impact of the payment reductions and included no accompanying data files providing the data that went into its calculation of the aggregate impact. The commenter stated that “[i]t is imperative that prior to implementing a policy of such magnitude, CMS be transparent in its methodology for modeling the cut and the corresponding budget neutrality adjustment, so that interested parties can replicate these models and verify CMS' calculations. CMS should publish its methodology for modeling the impact, which would include how CMS identified 340B hospitals and 340B drugs, including which data sources it used. CMS should also publish a hospital-level impact file with the results of the payment cut.”
Response:
We thank commenters for their many suggestions for information for us to release and analyses for us to conduct prior to finalizing our proposal. As we have noted previously; however, we believe that the payment misalignment that our policy will address has been in effect for many years and it is important to implement this policy without delay now that we have conducted the required survey and have data clearly demonstrating that the existing payment rate for 340B-acquired drugs is not even close to a representative proxy for the cost of their acquisition. With respect to the commenter's suggestion to establish protections for hospitals facing material losses, as we discussed in our earlier response to a commenter, we have attempted to address some of these concerns through the finalized exemptions for rural sole community hospitals, PPS-exempt cancer hospitals, and children's hospitals. We also note that with respect to potential future impacts, our budget neutrality calculations are based on what exists in the claims data and the direct changes associated with policy. We do not predict behavioral changes or hospital decisions as a result of those policies. With respect to beneficiary cost savings, these savings are likely to stay flat or increase, saving beneficiaries more as a result. As is true of any update, there will be some redistribution of
(
printed page 70552)
copayments because the 20 percent beneficiary cost sharing for drugs gets “transferred” over as 20 percent into the broader OPPS through the conversion factor budget neutrality adjustment for the 340B policy. That budget neutrality adjustment will make many of the overall OPPS payment rates and their associated copayments higher. OPPS cost-sharing for a service is capped at the applicable Part A hospital inpatient deductible amount for that year for each service. That means that when OPPS payments and therefore their associated copayments, increase relative to that fixed amount, more services are likely to get capped at the inpatient deductible amount. Finally, we note that the impact file includes all proposed/final budget neutrality adjustments and updates, as well as the 340B remedy where applicable. The impact analysis looks at the existing claims, applies the proposed/finalized policies but not does not consider behavioral changes or provider decision making.
We thank commenters for their input. We estimate that OPPS payment for 340B-acquired drugs will be reduced by approximately $4.65 billion in CY 2027 as a result of our adoption of this policy. When factoring in our finalized policy for 340B drug payment in non-excepted PBDs, our total estimated reduction in 340B drug spending is $5.45 billion for CY 2027, which includes both Medicare and beneficiary payments.
G. Final Payment Rates for Skin Substitute APCs
In the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we finalized a policy to separately pay for skin substitute products as incident-to supplies in the physician office, hospital outpatient, and ambulatory surgical center settings effective January 1, 2026 (
90 FR 53729
through
53748
). We excluded skin substitutes approved as biological products under section 351 of the PHS Act, which would continue to be paid consistent with section 1847A of the Act, from our policy to pay for skin substitute products as incident-to-supplies. As part of this final policy, we assigned sheet-form skin substitute products to one of three clinical APCs we created on “FDA regulatory categories”:
[
141
]
APC 6000 (PMA Skin Substitute Products), APC 6001 (510(k) Skin Substitute Products), and APC 6002 (361 HCT/P Skin Substitute Products). For CY 2026, we set an initial payment rate of $127.14/cm
2
for APCs 6000 (PMA Skin Substitute Products), 6001 (510(k) Skin Substitute Products), and 6002 (361 HCT/P Skin Substitute Products). In the event ASP data was not available for a particular product, we stated we would use the outpatient hospital MUC data. If MUC was not available, we stated we would use the product's WAC or 89.6 percent of AWP if WAC was also unavailable. We also believe that updating the payment rates for CY 2027, before the impacts of the payment policy are reflected in the CY 2026 claims that will be used for CY 2028 OPPS/ASC and PFS rulemakings, could result in payment disruptions or introduce unnecessary volatility. We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Commenters generally supported finalizing a single blended payment rate for CY 2027. Commenters supported a period of stable payment to ensure beneficiary access to skin substitute products.
(
printed page 70553)
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support.
Comment:
Some commenters did not support continuing to pay for sheet-form skin substitute products at the $127.14/cm
2
payment rate for CY 2027 as proposed. Some commenters believed that the proposed payment rate is punitive and overcorrects for abuses seen in the skin substitute space. Commenters suggested that targeted program integrity tools directed at improper billing patterns rather than an across-the-board payment reduction that applies to both compliant and noncompliant providers would more precisely address CMS's concerns without impacting access to medically necessary care. Several commenters requested that CMS finalize a payment rate that is more reflective of the costs and utilization volume for skin substitute products. 2
and $715.45/cm

90 FR 53728
through
53748
).

2
payment rate for sheet-form skin substitute products paid under the OPPS.
Comment:
Several commenters requested CMS evaluate utilization patterns following the implementation of the revised $127.14/cm
2
rate and to monitor beneficiary access and distinguish reductions in inappropriate utilization from reductions in clinically appropriate utilization. Commenters requested that we review the available 2026 claims data to assess changes in several measures, including utilization rates of skin substitute products by site of service; clinical outcomes for patients with chronic, non-healing wounds, and utilization rates of medical visits.

We thank the commenters for their suggestions. CMS is generally interested in better understanding the effects of all of our payment policies, including potential impacts to beneficiary access and clinically appropriate utilization. Comment:
Several commenters requested that CMS update the payment rate for skin substitute products using a defined inflation index, such as the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) or the Medicare Economic Index, rather than recalculating them based on new ASP data. Commenters thought updating the payment rate annually for inflation would keep reimbursement aligned with rising costs and help ensure continued beneficiary access to advanced wound care technologies.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters for their input. We believe that, over time, the ASP data we are collecting will more accurately reflect the market impacts of our policy to treat skin substitute products as incident-to supplies. By relying on ASP, payment updates will be responsive to changes in the actual cost of skin substitute products as a result of market pressures, whereas an index like the CPI-U is a general inflation measure that does not account for pricing dynamics. Therefore, we believe that updating the payment rates, based on ASP data will more likely result in payment rates that reflect the changing dynamics of the market rather than anchoring the cost to the initial payment rate for CY 2026, and finalized payment rate for CY 2027, based on data collected prior to the implementation of this policy. We thank the commenters for their input and perspective on this issue. (
printed page 70554)
substitute products by FDA regulatory category. A commenter noted that because FDA regulatory requirements and pathways evolve over time, using regulatory history as a permanent basis for payment differentiation would also create arbitrary disparities among products that serve the same clinical purpose today, based solely on when and how each product entered the market. The commenter recommended that CMS should base any future payment distinctions on demonstrated clinical performance and resource costs, not regulatory classification. Response:
We thank the commenters for their input. We continue to believe that categorizing skin substitute products by FDA regulatory pathway remains appropriate at this time. We note, however, that under the finalized policy, for CY 2027, all sheet-form skin substitute products would be paid at the same $127.14/cm
2
rate. We continue to believe that it is premature to adjust the payment rate for skin substitute products because updated use patterns reflecting the CY 2026 policy changes are not yet available. We will continue to analyze claims data as it becomes available and will propose any changes in payment through the rulemaking process.
Comment:
We received several comments requesting that we align payment for non-sheet form skin substitutes with payment for sheet-form skin substitute products. Specifically, commenters requested that CMS change the status indicator of the non-sheet application codes (HCPCS codes G0681-G0684) from “N” to “T” to allow for payment, and assign the non-sheet application codes to the same APCs as the sheet-form application codes (CPT codes 15271-15278). Specifically, commenters requested that CMS assign HCPCS code G0681 to APC 5053 (Level 3 Skin Procedures) and HCPCS code G0683 to APC 5054 (Level 4 Skin Procedures). HCPCS codes G0682 and G0684, which describe add-on codes, should be treated the same as the sheet-form application add-on codes (CPT codes 15272, 15274, 15276, and 15278) and be assigned to status indicator “N,” per the commenters. In addition, commenters requested that CMS pay separately for non-sheet skin substitute products to align with payment for sheet-form skin substitute products. Commenters believed that non-sheet products service similar clinical purposes as sheet products, and, therefore, aligning for non-sheet forms and sheet-forms recognizes the clinical non-sheet forms offer, preserves physician flexibility to select the best product for each patient, supports innovation, ensures skin substitute products are evaluated on therapeutic value rather than disadvantaged by coding or reimbursement policy, and maintains site neutrality with products applied in the physician office setting.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their input. Payment for application of non-sheet skin substitute products could benefit from parity with payment for the application of sheet form skin substitute products, and not doing so could fail to appropriately recognize the resource costs expended when applying non-sheet products. Accordingly, we are not finalizing our proposal to maintain the status indicator of “N” for HCPCS codes G0681 and G0683. For CY 2027, we are finalizing to change the status indicator for HCPCS codes G0681 and G0683 from “N” to “T” and assign G0681 to APC 5053 (Level 3 Skin Procedures) and G0683 to APC 5054 (Level 4 Skin Procedures), consistent with the APC assignments for the analogous sheet form application codes (CPT codes 15271 through 15278). We are finalizing assignment of status indicator “N” to add-on codes G0682 and G0684, consistent with the treatment of the sheet form application add-on codes (CPT codes 15272, 15274, 15276, and 15278), as proposed. The final CY 2027 payment rates can be found in Addendum B to this final rule with comment via the internet on the CMS website. In addition, we refer readers to Addendum D1 of this final rule with comment period for the status indicator definitions for all codes reported under the OPPS. Addendum D1 can also be found via the internet on the CMS website. As previously discussed, we will continue to monitor the effects of this policy in general, including this newly finalized aspect.
We are not finalizing separate payment for non-sheet skin substitute products at this time. Non-sheet products are not manufactured, applied, or measured in the same standardized manner as sheet form products, which are billed in per cm
2
units. Because of these differences, we believe it is more appropriate to continue packaging payment for non-sheet form products under the OPPS. We recognize the interest commenters have expressed in separate payment for non-sheet form skin substitute products, and we will continue to consider the issue of separate payment for non-sheet products moving forward.
Comment:

Response:
We thank the commenter for this suggestion and will take it into consideration. One difficulty with the commenter's request is that non-sheet products cover a wide range of physical forms and may not share a common structure the way sheet-form skin substitute products do. We note that we have described the form of some non-sheet skin substitute products in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC Final Rule as gels, powders, liquids, injectables, 3D-printed constructs, etc. (

We do not believe it is appropriate to except

We appreciate the input from the commenters. H. Add-On Payment for Technetium-99m (Tc-99m) Derived From Domestically Produced Molybdenum-99 (Mo-99)
As discussed in prior rulemaking, in collaboration with the Department of Energy, National Nuclear Security Administration (DOE/NNSA), CMS provided an additional payment of $10 for the marginal cost for Tc-99m produced by non-Highly Enriched Uranium (HEU) sources in an effort to support access to Technetium-99m (Tc-99m), a critical radioisotope used in the majority of diagnostic imaging services, and produced through the radioactive decay of molybdenum-99 (Mo-99) from CY 2013 to CY 2025. We stated that we believe such an adjustment would ensure equitable payments in light of market influences, cost differentials, and cost variations and their potential to create significant payment inequities among hospitals (
77 FR 68323
). Accordingly, we established HCPCS code Q9969 (Tc-99m from non-highly enriched uranium source, full cost recovery add-on per study dose) to describe the Tc-99m radioisotope produced by non-HEU methods and used in a diagnostic procedure.
In January 2022, the Secretary of Energy issued a certification that stated that there is a sufficient global supply of non-HEU-sourced Mo-99 to meet the needs of patients in the United States (
86 FR 73270
). Additionally, in March 2023, the last major global producer of Mo-99 converted from HEU to low-enriched uranium (LEU) targets, and all Mo-99 used in the United States is now produced without HEU. As such, in the CY 2024 OPPS final rule with comment period (
88 FR 81803
), we adopted a policy to end the additional $10 add-on payment described by HCPCS code Q9969 for non-HEU-sourced Tc-99m at the end of CY 2025. We explained that given that all Mo-99 used in the U.S. is now produced without HEU, we believe that starting in CY 2026 the Medicare claims data utilized to set payment rates would only include claims for diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals that utilized non-HEU-sourced Tc-99m, meaning the data would reflect the full cost of the Tc-99m diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals that providers would use in CY 2026. That being the case, we believe there would no longer be a need for the additional $10 add-on payment for non-HEU-sourced Tc-99m for CY 2026 or future years.
In the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC proposed rule with comment period (
89 FR 59377
through
59378
), we shared that the Department of Energy and other interested parties raised another issue
(
printed page 70556)
affecting the domestic supply chain for Mo-99 and Tc-99 that, left unaddressed, could also cause payment inequity among outpatient hospital providers. We noted that foreign Mo-99 production has historically been subsidized by foreign governments, resulting in prices below the true cost of production. These artificially low, foreign government-subsidized prices have created a disincentive for domestic investments in Mo-99 production infrastructure and a barrier to entry for new producers, including U.S. companies, which in turn has resulted in unreliable production and periodic shortages. Subsequently, using our equitable adjustment authority under section 1833(t)(2)(E) of the Act, we proposed and finalized a policy to address the payment inequity resulting from the higher cost of Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99 by establishing a new add-on payment of $10 per dose for radiopharmaceuticals that use Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99 starting on January 1, 2026. Furthermore, we stated that the Department of Energy, National Nuclear Security Administration (DOE/NNSA) would establish the criteria to certify whether the Tc-99m radiopharmaceutical dose is derived from domestically produced Mo-99 and eligible for the add-on payment, which would be included in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC proposed rule with comment period. We also stated that we would continue to develop the technical implementation of this additional payment after a definition for domestically produced Tc-99m radiopharmaceutical was established, including any requirements for providers to document that the Tc-99m radiopharmaceutical used in a procedure was domestically produced and could qualify to receive the add-on payment. Additionally, we stated that our intent was to have the regulatory framework for this policy in place prior to the domestic production of Mo-99 and Tc-99m, to increase provider awareness of the availability of additional payments for domestically sourced Tc-99m radiopharmaceuticals. Likewise, producers of domestic Mo-99 would have certainty that the Medicare OPPS payment policy takes into account the additional costs of Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99.
a. Criteria for Classifying a Tc-99m Radiopharmaceutical Dose as Domestically Produced
In the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
90 FR 53751-53755
), for purposes of the add-on payment for radiopharmaceuticals that use Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99, we finalized our definition of a domestically produced dose of Tc-99m as a dose of Tc-99m generated from domestically produced Mo-99. We also finalized the following definitions:
Domestically produced dose of Tc-99m:
A dose of Tc-99m generated from domestically produced Mo-99;
Domestically produced Mo-99:
Mo-99 that was both irradiated and processed in the U.S.;
Irradiated:
The process of bombarding a uranium or molybdenum target with radiation in order to produce Mo-99, and to specify that irradiation is typically performed with a nuclear reactor or particle accelerator;
Processed:
In this context, processed refers to the purification of Mo-99 from irradiated material.
Additionally, we finalized a policy that a dose of Tc-99m generated from Mo-99 that was irradiated or processed outside the U.S. would not qualify for this add-on payment, even if the Mo-99 was loaded into a Tc-99m generator in the U.S. or if the Tc-99m was eluted at a radiopharmacy in the U.S. We also finalized the codification of the aforementioned definitions and references for domestically produced Mo-99 to § 419.49 to specify when a dose of Tc-99m generated from domestically produced Mo-99 could be eligible for the add-on payment.
b. Coding and Documentation for the Add-On Payment for Tc-99m Derived From Domestically Produced Mo-99
In the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
90 FR 53751-53755
), we also finalized the establishment of HCPCS C-code C9176 (Tc-99m from domestically produced non-HEU Mo-99, [minimum 50 percent], full cost recovery add-on, per study dose), effective January 1, 2026. Hospitals may report HCPCS code C9176 once per dose, along with any diagnostic scan or scans furnished using Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99, if they can certify that at least 50 percent of the Mo-99 in the Tc-99m generator used to produce the Tc-99m was domestically produced Mo-99. We also finalized the implementation plan, including the $10 per-dose add-on payment and the certification and tracking approach described in the CY 2026 rulemaking.
For CY 2027, we did not propose any changes to the add-on payment policy for radiopharmaceuticals that use Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99. We received public comments regarding this policy, which we summarize and respond to below.
Comment:
Although we did not propose any changes to the add-on payment for radiopharmaceuticals that use Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99 for CY 2027, we received comments regarding the policy. One commenter supported continuation of the $10 per-dose add-on payment and HCPCS code C9176, stating that the policy helps account for the higher costs associated with domestic production and supports investment in a more secure and resilient domestic Mo-99 supply chain. The commenter also encouraged CMS to continue monitoring whether the $10 add-on payment remains sufficient over time in light of production, compliance, transportation, and supply-chain costs.
Another commenter opposed continuation of the add-on payment and urged CMS to discontinue the policy for CY 2027. The commenter stated that the add-on payment does not effectively incentivize domestic Mo-99 production because payments are made to hospitals rather than directly to domestic producers and expressed concern that hospitals may have difficulty identifying when a dose qualifies for the add-on payment. The commenter also stated that the policy could disrupt existing Tc-99m supply and distribution arrangements, including generator contracting, and potentially affect patient access, particularly in rural communities.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback. As discussed in the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we established the $10 per-dose add-on payment using our equitable adjustment authority under section 1833(t)(2)(E) of the Act to address the payment inequity resulting from the higher cost of Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99. In the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we finalized the implementation framework for this policy, including the criteria for a domestically produced dose of Tc-99m, the 50-percent threshold for domestically produced Mo-99, and HCPCS code C9176.
We continue to believe that the add-on payment appropriately accounts for the additional costs to hospital outpatient departments associated with utilizing Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99. As we explained in prior rulemaking, establishing the payment framework in advance of domestic production provides hospitals with information regarding the availability of additional payment for qualifying doses and provides domestic producers with greater certainty that Medicare OPPS
(
printed page 70557)
payment policy takes into account the additional costs associated with domestic production. After a consideration of the comments received, noting we did not propose changes to this policy for CY 2027, we are continuing the existing policy without modification.
We appreciate commenters' perspectives regarding the amount of the add-on payment, implementation of the policy, and potential effects on the Mo-99 and Tc-99m supply chain. We will continue to monitor relevant information regarding the implementation of the policy, including information regarding the costs associated with domestically produced Mo-99 and the availability of Tc-99m, and may consider whether future refinements are warranted.
VI. Estimate of OPPS Transitional Pass-Through Spending for Drugs, Biologicals, Radiopharmaceuticals, and Devices
A. Amount of Additional Payment and Limit on Aggregate Annual Adjustment
Section 1833(t)(6)(E) of the Act limits the total projected amount of transitional pass-through payment for drugs, biologicals, and categories of devices for a given year to an “applicable percentage,” currently not to exceed 2.0 percent of total program payments estimated to be made for all covered services under the OPPS furnished for that year. If we estimate before the beginning of the calendar year that the total amount of pass-through payments in that year would exceed the applicable percentage, section 1833(t)(6)(E)(iii) of the Act requires a uniform prospective reduction in the amount of each of the transitional pass-through payments made in that year to ensure that the limit is not exceeded. We estimate the pass-through spending to determine whether payments exceed the applicable percentage and the appropriate pro rata reduction to the conversion factor for the projected level of pass-through spending in the following year to ensure that total estimated pass-through spending for the prospective payment year is budget neutral, as required by section 1833(t)(6)(E) of the Act.
For devices, developing a proposed estimate of pass-through spending in CY 2027 entails estimating spending for two groups of items. The first group of items consists of device categories that are currently eligible for pass-through payment and that will continue to be eligible for pass-through payment in CY 2027. The CY 2008 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
72 FR 66778
) describes the methodology we have used in previous years to develop the pass-through spending estimate for known device categories continuing into the applicable update year. The second group of items consists of devices that we know are newly eligible, or project may be newly eligible, for device pass-through payment in the remaining quarters of CY 2026 or beginning in CY 2027. The sum of the proposed CY 2027 pass-through spending estimates for these two groups of device categories equals the proposed total CY 2027 pass-through spending estimate for device categories with pass-through payment status. We determined the device pass-through estimated payments for each device category based on the amount of payment as required by section 1833(t)(6)(D)(ii) of the Act, and as outlined in previous rules, including the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
90 FR 53766
through
53769
). We noted that, beginning in CY 2010, the pass-through evaluation process and pass-through payment methodology for implantable biologicals newly approved for pass-through payment beginning on or after January 1, 2010, that are surgically inserted or implanted (through a surgical incision or a natural orifice) use the device pass-through process and payment methodology (
74 FR 60476
). As has been our past practice (
76 FR 74335
), we include an estimate of any implantable biologicals eligible for pass-through payment in our estimate of pass-through spending for devices. Similarly, we finalized a policy in CY 2015 that applications for pass-through payment for skin substitutes and similar products be evaluated using the medical device pass-through process and payment methodology (
79 FR 66885
through
66888
). In CY 2026, we finalized a policy to consider skin substitutes with an approved Biologics License Application (BLA) under transitional drug pass-through payment status, while skin substitutes with FDA Premarket Approval or FDA 510(k) clearance continue to be evaluated under transitional device pass-through payment status (
90 FR 53636
). Therefore, for CY 2027, we also proposed to include an estimate of any skin substitutes and similar products with FDA Premarket Approval or FDA 510(k) clearance in our estimate of pass-through spending for devices and skin substitutes with an approved BLA under transitional drug pass-through spending for drugs and biologicals.
For drugs and biologicals eligible for pass-through payment, section 1833(t)(6)(D)(i) of the Act establishes the pass-through payment amount as the amount by which the amount authorized under section 1842(o) of the Act (or, if the drug or biological is covered under a competitive acquisition contract under section 1847B of the Act, an amount determined by the Secretary equal to the average price for the drug or biological for all competitive acquisition areas and year established under such section as calculated and adjusted by the Secretary) exceeds the portion of the otherwise applicable fee schedule amount that the Secretary determines is associated with the drug or biological. Consistent with current policy, we proposed to apply a rate of ASP plus 6 percent to most drugs and biologicals for CY 2027, and therefore our estimate of drug and biological pass-through payment for CY 2027 for this group of items was $12.2 million.
Payment for certain drugs,

VIII. Payment for Partial Hospitalization and Intensive Outpatient Services
Since CY 2000, Medicare has paid for partial hospitalization program (PHP) services under the OPPS. Beginning in CY 2024, as authorized by section 4124 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act (CAA), 2023 (
Pub. L. 117-328

Additional background on the partial hospitalization and intensive outpatient benefits is included in the following paragraphs.
We note that some commenters made comments on PHP and IOP topics that were not discussed in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule. These topics are out of scope for purposes of this notice and comment rulemaking, but we will consider these comments as we consider these issues for future rulemaking.
A. Background
1. Partial Hospitalization
A partial hospitalization program (PHP) is an intensive outpatient program of psychiatric services provided as an alternative to inpatient psychiatric care for individuals who have an acute mental illness, which includes, but is not limited to, conditions such as depression, schizophrenia, and substance use disorders (SUD). Section 1861(ff)(1) of the Act defines partial hospitalization services as the items and services described in paragraph (2) prescribed by a physician for an individual determined (not less frequently than monthly) by a physician to have a need for such services for a minimum of 20 hours per week and provided under a program described in paragraph (3) under the supervision of a physician pursuant to an individualized, written plan of treatment established and periodically reviewed by a physician (in consultation with appropriate staff participating in such program), which sets forth the physician's diagnosis, the type, amount, frequency, and duration of the items and services provided under the plan, and the goals for treatment under the plan.
Section 1861(ff)(2) of the Act describes the items and services included in partial hospitalization program services. Section 1861(ff)(3)(A) of the Act specifies that a PHP is a program furnished by a hospital to its outpatients or by a CMHC, as a distinct and organized intensive ambulatory treatment service, offering less than 24-hour-daily care, in a location other than an individual's home or inpatient or residential setting. Section 1861(ff)(3)(B) of the Act defines a CMHC for purposes of this benefit. We refer readers to sections 1833(t)(1)(B)(i), 1833(t)(2)(B), 1833(t)(2)(C), and 1833(t)(9)(A) of the Act and
42 CFR 419.21
, for additional information regarding PHP.

Section 4124(b) of the CAA, 2023, amended section 1861(ff) of the Act, establishing Medicare coverage for intensive outpatient services effective for items and services furnished on or after January 1, 2024. An intensive outpatient program (IOP) is a distinct and organized program of psychiatric services for individuals who have an acute mental illness, which includes, but is not limited to, conditions such as depression, schizophrenia, and SUD. Intensive outpatient services are not required to be provided in lieu of inpatient hospitalization. Section 1861(ff)(4) of the Act defines intensive outpatient services as the items and services described in section 1861(ff)(2) of the Act prescribed by a physician for an individual determined (not less
(

Section 1861(ff)(2) of the Act describes the items and services included in intensive outpatient services. Section 1861(ff)(4)(C) of the Act specifies that an IOP is a program furnished by a hospital to its outpatients, by a CMHC, by a Federally qualified health center (FQHC), or by a rural health clinic (RHC) as distinct and organized intensive ambulatory treatment service, offering less than 24-hour-daily care, in a location other than an individual's home or inpatient or residential setting. B. Coding and Billing for PHP and IOP Services Under the OPPS
In the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we finalized a billing requirement that all providers use condition code 41 to indicate that a claim is for partial hospitalization services and use condition code 92 to identify intensive outpatient claims, effective January 1, 2024. Since the statutory definitions of both IOP and PHP generally include the same types of items and services covered, we stated in the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period that we believe it is appropriate to align the programs using a consistent list of services, so that level of intensity would be the only differentiating factor between partial hospitalization services and intensive outpatient services. The use of condition codes 41 for PHP claims and 92 for IOP claims allows us to differentiate between these services for billing purposes.
We recognize that the level of intensity of mental health services that a patient requires may vary over time; therefore, we believe utilizing a consolidated list of HCPCS codes to identify services under both the IOP and PHP benefits supports a smooth transition for patients when a change in the intensity of their services is necessary to best meet their needs. For example, a patient receiving IOP services may experience an acute mental health need that necessitates more intense services through a PHP. Alternatively, an IOP patient that no longer requires the level of intensity provided by the IOP can access less intense mental health services, such as individual mental health services. The full list of HCPCs codes recognized under the PHP and IOP benefits can be found in the Medicare Claims Processing internet Only Manual, Chapter 4, sections 260.1 and 261.1, respectively, and their subsections, available at
https://www.cms.gov/​regulations-and-guidance/​guidance/​manuals/​downloads/​clm104c04.pdf
