Commenters stated that CMS therefore had not demonstrated that reducing payment for imaging without contrast services would result in a reduction in volume rather than simply lower Medicare payment for the same volume or potentially lead to additional utilization.
Commenters pointed to CMS's experience with the sustainable growth rate methodology and other prior discussions of volume control as evidence that reducing unit payment does not necessarily result in lower utilization. Commenters therefore stated that the proposed methodology is not reasonably designed to control unnecessary increases in volume as required under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their input. We disagree that the possibility that a provider could respond to a reduction in payment by increasing volume means that our volume control method is not reasonably designed to control unnecessary increases in volume. As we explained in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period in response to similar comments (
90 FR 53811
), our volume control method is specifically designed to address unnecessary increases in OPD volume that result from site-of-service payment differentials. By applying a PFS-equivalent payment rate, the method removes the payment differential that creates an incentive to furnish a service in the higher-paid OPD setting when the
(
printed page 70607)
same service can safely be furnished in a lower-cost setting.
We recognize that changes in payment may affect provider behavior in different ways. However, the relevant incentive addressed by this policy is the additional Medicare payment available when an imaging without contrast service is furnished in an excepted off-campus PBD rather than in a physician office or non-excepted off-campus PBD. Once payment for the service furnished in the excepted off-campus PBD is aligned with the PFS-equivalent payment applicable in the lower-paid setting, the financial incentive to furnish the service in the excepted off-campus PBD solely because of the higher OPPS payment is removed. We therefore continue to believe that applying the PFS-equivalent payment rate is an appropriate method to control the unnecessary increase in volume attributable to that payment differential.
We also do not believe that commenters' references to the sustainable growth rate (SGR) methodology lead to a different conclusion. The SGR established an aggregate spending target under the PFS and adjusted physician payment updates based on whether aggregate expenditures exceeded that target. Our volume control method does not establish an aggregate expenditure target or reduce payment in response to providers exceeding a predetermined volume benchmark. Rather, it prospectively addresses a specific payment differential that we have determined is a substantial cause of unnecessary increases in covered OPD services by eliminating that differential for the affected services.
We will continue to monitor utilization following implementation of this policy, as we have done for our clinic visit and drug administration volume control policies. We continue to believe that prospectively applying the PFS-equivalent payment rate to imaging without contrast services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs is an appropriate method under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act to control unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services.
Comment:
Several commenters requested additional information and implementation guidance regarding how the volume control method for imaging without contrast services would be operationalized. Commenters requested that CMS clearly identify the HCPCS codes subject to the policy and explain how changes in HCPCS coding or APC assignments would affect application of the volume control method in future years.
Commenters also requested clarification regarding the treatment of imaging services paid through the multiple imaging composite APCs and encounters involving multiple imaging services. Commenters requested CMS to clarify how the PFS-equivalent payment methodology would apply when imaging without contrast services are furnished together with other imaging services, including services that may not otherwise be subject to the volume control method, and how the policy would interact with existing OPPS packaging and composite payment policies.
Some commenters also requested sufficient implementation guidance and lead time for hospitals to update billing, claims-processing, financial, and other operational systems before the policy takes effect.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' requests for additional implementation guidance. As finalized in this rule, the volume control method applies to imaging without contrast services assigned to APCs 5521 through 5524, as well as imaging without contrast services paid through the applicable multiple imaging composite APCs (APCs 8004, 8005, and 8007), when furnished by an off-campus PBD excepted from section 1833(t)(21) of the Act and billed with the “PO” modifier. We identify the applicable HCPCS codes and their APC assignments through the applicable OPPS Addenda, consistent with our usual process for publishing annual OPPS payment information.
We also clarify that this policy does not change the existing OPPS packaging or composite APC policies. Where an imaging without contrast service is otherwise paid through a composite APC under the OPPS, the existing requirements for determining whether the composite payment applies will continue to apply. When the applicable imaging without contrast composite APC is paid for a service furnished by an excepted off-campus PBD, the payment for that composite APC will be subject to the volume control method finalized in this rule. Similarly, existing OPPS packaging rules will continue to determine whether other items and services furnished during the encounter are separately payable or packaged.
The volume control method does not change hospitals' existing requirements for reporting the “PO” modifier for services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs. Rather, the modifier will continue to identify services furnished by these departments for purposes of applying the appropriate payment methodology. Services furnished in other settings or not otherwise within the scope of the volume control method will continue to be paid under the applicable Medicare payment methodology.
We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding implementation and the need for hospitals to update their billing and operational systems. The policy will be implemented through the annual OPPS payment system and associated claims-processing instructions, consistent with our established processes for implementing annual OPPS payment changes. We believe these existing mechanisms provide an appropriate framework for communicating the HCPCS and APC information necessary to implement the policy.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to use our authority under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act to apply an amount equal to the site-specific PFS payment rate for non-excepted items and services furnished by a non-excepted off-campus PBD (the PFS payment rate) for HCPCS codes assigned to the imaging without contrast APCs or paid through the imaging without contrast composite APCs, when provided at an off-campus PBD excepted from section 1833(t)(21) of the Act (departments that bill the modifier “PO” on claim lines) without modification. In addition, we are finalizing our proposal to implement this policy in a non-budget neutral manner without modification. We will monitor the impacts of this policy to ensure that beneficiaries continue to have access to quality care.
9. Exemption for Rural Sole Community Hospitals
As stated previously, we proposed to expand our method to control unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services by paying a PFS-equivalent payment rate for imaging without contrast services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs. We believe that this policy is an appropriate method for controlling unnecessary volume of imaging without contrast services in excepted off-campus PBDs because beneficiaries can generally safely receive these same services in a lower-cost setting but instead may receive care in a higher-cost setting due to payment incentives. In these cases, we maintain that, similar to the clinic visit volume control policy established in the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
83 FR 59004
through
59015
) and the drug administration volume control policy established in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
90 FR 53806
through
53821
), to the extent
(

similar services can be safely provided in more than one setting, we do not believe it is appropriate for the Medicare program to pay more for these services in one setting than another. We continue to believe the difference in payment for these services is a significant factor in the shift in services from the freestanding physician's office setting to the hospital OPD.
In the CY 2023 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
87 FR 72047
through
72051
) and the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
90 FR 53821
through
53824
), we finalized exemptions to our clinic visit and drug administration volume control policies for PBDs of rural SCHs. In those rules, we explained that rural SCHs have historically received special payment treatment to account for their higher costs and the disproportionately harmful impact that payment reductions could have on them. a. Special Payment Treatment for Rural SCHs
Across the various Medicare payment systems, CMS has established several special payment provisions for rural providers to ensure access to high quality care for beneficiaries in rural areas. CMS administers several statutory hospital payment designations in which rural or isolated hospitals that meet specified eligibility criteria receive higher reimbursement for hospital services than they otherwise would receive under Medicare's standard payment methodologies. A rural hospital may qualify as a Critical Access Hospital (CAH),

and Rural Referral Centers (RRCs),

which qualify these hospitals for additional payments or exemptions. Not all rural or isolated hospitals receive special payment treatment under the OPPS. For instance, CAHs are not paid under the OPPS and are reimbursed at 101 percent of reasonable costs for outpatient services.
Rural SCHs are a hospital type that has received special payment treatment under the OPPS to account for their higher costs and the disproportionately harmful impact that payment reductions could have on them. In the CY 2006 OPPS final rule with comment period (
70 FR 68556
through

Our analysis revealed that rural SCHs had significantly higher costs per unit than urban hospitals. We have continued to adjust payments for rural SCHs by 7.1 percent each year since 2006. As discussed in section II.E. of this final rule with comment period, for CY 2027 we proposed to continue the current policy of utilizing a 7.1 percent payment adjustment for rural SCHs.
As noted previously, in the CY 2023 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (

Commenters were generally supportive of this proposal and noted that rural SCHs are typically the chief, if not sole, source of community outpatient care for rural residents and stated that this exemption would be vital to ensuring continued access to the care they need. Some commenters stated that the exemption should be extended to other types of hospitals, including urban SCHs. In that rule, we explained that our analysis did not find that urban SCHs had the additional resource costs for covered OPD services that rural SCHs have and only finalized applying the clinic visit policy exemption to rural SCHs (

However, because our historical analysis did not demonstrate that these facilities had the additional resource costs that rural SCHs do, we did not finalize any exemptions beyond our exception for rural SCHs (

90 FR 53822
), and we proposed to extend it to our proposed imaging without contrast policy for similar reasons. Specifically, we proposed to exempt rural SCHs from payment of the site-specific PFS-equivalent payment for imaging without contrast services, as described by APCs 5521 through 5524, 8004, 8005, and 8007, when furnished at an off-campus PBD exempted from section 1833(t)(21) of the Act (departments that bill the modifier “PO” on claim lines). Under the proposed policy, a rural SCH would continue to bill services in APCs 5521 through 5524, 8004, 8005, and 8007 with the “PO” modifier for CY 2027 and the payment rate for such services would continue to be the full OPPS payment without the PFS relativity adjuster.
This exemption would result in higher payments to excepted off-campus PBDs of rural SCHs compared to if rural SCHs were subject to the proposed volume control method. By exempting rural SCHs, the Medicare payments for these services would remain at the OPPS level. We note, however, that these figures do not represent increases in costs to Medicare or the beneficiaries above the current policy, as our proposed exemption would maintain current payment rates at excepted off-campus PBDs of rural SCHs of 107.1 percent of the OPPS payment rate for these services. These figures are solely for the purpose of comparing potential savings from this policy.
We invited comments on all aspects of the proposed exemption for rural SCHs from the method to control unnecessary volume of imaging without contrast services. Specifically, we requested comments on whether such an exemption was appropriate for rural SCHs; what the impact on SCHs would be, should we finalize the method without an exemption for rural SCHs; and whether we should consider any other hospital types for an exemption to any of the three policies to control unnecessary volume of outpatient services at off-campus PBDs. Additionally, we requested comments on whether the current exemptions for rural SCHs from the method to control unnecessary volume of clinic visit and drug administration services remained appropriate.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
The majority of commenters supported our proposal to exempt rural Sole Community Hospitals (rural SCHs) from payment of the site-specific Medicare PFS-equivalent payment for any HCPCS codes assigned to the imaging without contrast APCs or paid through the imaging without contrast composite APCs, when furnished at an off-campus PBD excepted from section 1833(t)(21) of the Act (departments that bill the modifier “PO” on claim lines). Several commenters opposed the volume control method generally but stated that should CMS finalize the policy, CMS should also finalize the proposed exemption for rural SCHs. Commenters stated that rural SCHs have higher costs, operate with limited financial and workforce resources, and are important for maintaining access to care in rural areas where alternative sources of imaging services may be limited. Commenters also stated that applying the volume control method to rural SCHs could result in reduced service availability or require beneficiaries to travel greater distances for care. One commenter opposed a broad exemption for all rural SCHs and recommended that CMS instead target the exemption to independent rural hospitals or hospitals that demonstrate greater financial vulnerability. The commenter stated that some rural SCHs are affiliated with large health systems and may be better positioned to absorb payment reductions than independent hospitals.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support of the proposed exemption for rural SCHs. As discussed in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule (
91 FR 41918
), and consistent with our historical analysis that indicated rural SCHs have higher costs, we agree that their financial health is vital to ensure continued access to care in rural areas. We acknowledge the nuanced perspective that many commenters took in supporting the proposed exemption while disagreeing with the volume control methodology overall.
We appreciate the commenter's recommendation that any exemption be targeted to independent rural hospitals or hospitals demonstrating greater financial vulnerability. However, as we stated in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
90 FR 53823
), we believe the rural SCH designation generally indicates that a hospital has additional costs and is vital for access in rural areas. We do not believe that the exemption should be limited to independent hospitals, as rural SCHs that are part of larger health systems may also face similarly heightened costs. We continue to believe that these considerations support exempting rural SCHs from the volume control method. We intend to continue to monitor costs at rural SCHs and to ensure that this exemption continues to be warranted for our volume control policies.
Comment:
Several commenters supported the proposed rural SCH exemption but recommended that CMS extend the exemption to additional types of hospitals and providers. Commenters recommended exemptions for, among others, all rural hospitals, Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs), Rural Emergency Hospitals (REHs), Medicare Dependent Hospitals (MDHs), Rural Referral Centers, low-volume hospitals, safety-net hospitals, hospitals serving Health Professional Shortage Areas or Medically Underserved Areas, Qualifying Disadvantaged Hospitals, children's hospitals, and other geographically isolated or essential providers. Commenters generally stated that hospitals other than rural SCHs may face similar financial, workforce, and geographic challenges and may likewise be important for maintaining beneficiary access to imaging services in communities where alternative sites of care are limited.
Some commenters also recommended exempting hospitals that have reclassified as rural. Other commenters recommended exempting children's hospitals, noting their generally limited Medicare utilization and expressing concern regarding the potential effects of the policy on pediatric access.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' recommendations regarding additional types of hospitals and providers for which they believe further exemptions would be warranted. We note that CAHs
(
printed page 70610)
and REHs are not subject to the volume control method finalized in this rule, and therefore an exemption for these hospital types is not necessary.
We also appreciate commenters' discussion of rural reclassifications and clarify that the exemption for rural SCHs includes SCHs that have reclassified as rural, consistent with our rural SCH exemptions from the clinic visit and drug administration volume control methods.
We appreciate commenters' recommendation to exempt children's hospitals based on their generally limited Medicare utilization and concerns regarding pediatric access. We recognize the unique role that children's hospitals play in furnishing specialized pediatric care and appreciate commenters' interest in ensuring that Medicare payment policies do not adversely affect access to these services. We also recognize that children's hospitals generally have limited Medicare utilization, which may limit the overall impact of this policy on these hospitals. Based on the information available to us, we do not believe that a separate exemption for children's hospitals is necessary at this time. As discussed previously, the policy does not prevent a physician from determining that the hospital outpatient setting is clinically appropriate for a particular beneficiary. We will continue to consider the effects of our volume control policies on different types of hospitals and beneficiary access to care and may consider whether additional exemptions are appropriate in future rulemaking.
With respect to the other hospital types suggested by commenters, as we discussed in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule and in prior rulemaking (
90 FR 53823
), our historical analysis has found that rural SCHs have higher costs, which we believe is appropriate to consider when developing a payment policy such as this. Rural SCHs have historically received special treatment under the OPPS due to these higher costs. As we stated in the CY 2023 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
87 FR 72047
through
72051
), we believe exempting rural SCHs, which have demonstrated additional resource costs, is appropriate to ensure these hospitals can remain open to serve the beneficiaries who rely on them for their care.
We proposed a narrow exemption largely based upon the historical treatment and documented additional resource costs of rural SCHs under the OPPS. We continue to believe in the underlying principles of the volume control method, and that same rationale continues to justify application of the volume control method for imaging without contrast services to other hospitals subject to this policy. Where differences in payment lead to unnecessary increases in the volume of covered outpatient department services, we remain concerned that shifts in the site of care increase beneficiary cost-sharing liability because Medicare payment rates for the same or similar services are generally higher in hospital outpatient departments than in physician offices.
We share commenters' concerns about maintaining access to care in rural and medically vulnerable communities, including concerns regarding pediatric access. However, we do not believe that commenters provided sufficient reasoning or data to demonstrate that the other hospital types subject to this policy have the additional resource costs that our historical analysis has demonstrated for rural SCHs and therefore should also be exempted from this OPPS payment policy. We will continue to study access and costs to determine whether further exemptions to the volume control policy are appropriate in future rulemaking.
Comment:
Some commenters recommended that CMS use criteria other than hospital type in determining whether a provider should qualify for an exemption. Commenters suggested considering factors such as geographic isolation, the availability of alternative imaging providers, beneficiary travel times, financial vulnerability, local workforce shortages, and the role of a hospital in maintaining access to essential services. Some commenters recommended that CMS monitor the effects of the policy on beneficiary access, including changes in imaging availability, wait times, travel distances, and service volumes, particularly in rural and underserved communities.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' thoughtful suggestions regarding alternative criteria for determining whether an exemption may be appropriate. As discussed previously, for purposes of this policy we believe that the rural SCH designation provides an appropriate basis for the exemption because of the historical treatment and documented additional resource costs of rural SCHs under the OPPS. We are not adopting additional exemption criteria at this time. We will, however, consider commenters' suggestions as we continue to evaluate the effects of our volume control policies and whether additional exemptions may be appropriate in future rulemaking.
We also appreciate commenters' concerns regarding beneficiary access. Consistent with our approach to the clinic visit and drug administration volume control policies, we will continue to monitor the effects of this change in Medicare payment policy, including the volume of these types of OPD services and beneficiary access to care, including for beneficiaries with disabilities, and may revisit the policy in future rulemaking.
Comment:
Some commenters recommended that CMS exempt certain imaging services or clinical circumstances from the volume control method based on the type of service furnished or the needs of the patient. Several commenters recommended exempting preventive and screening imaging services from the volume control method based on concerns regarding beneficiary access to recommended screening and early detection services. As discussed previously in this section, commenters specifically identified certain preventive and screening services included in the imaging without contrast APCs and recommended that CMS exclude these services from the policy.
Other commenters recommended exemptions for certain oncology-related imaging services. One commenter requested that CMS exempt diagnostic and procedural imaging directly associated with planned or same-day interventional oncology procedures, including pre- and post-procedural imaging used for treatment planning, procedural guidance, or assessment following a procedure. Other commenters recommended exemptions or other protections for imaging furnished to high-acuity oncology patients or imaging that is integrated with specialty oncology care, stating that these services may require hospital-level clinical infrastructure, specialized staff, immediate access to other hospital resources, or coordination with other services furnished as part of the patient's treatment.
Some commenters also raised concerns that applying the volume control method to imaging without contrast services, while imaging services furnished with contrast or an enhancing agent would not be subject to the policy, could create a payment incentive affecting the use of contrast or enhancing agents. Commenters specifically noted that ultrasound enhancing agents may be clinically appropriate for certain echocardiography services but stated that the decision to use an enhancing agent should be based on the clinical needs of the patient rather than differences in payment. Commenters expressed concern that increased use of
(
printed page 70611)
enhancing agents in response to payment differences could also increase costs associated with the agent, intravenous access, nursing, and other related resources.
Some commenters more generally recommended exempting imaging furnished as part of a medically complex diagnostic workup, imaging integrated with same-day procedures requiring hospital-level resources, or services that rely on hospital infrastructure or specialty resources. Commenters stated that these circumstances may involve medically-complex beneficiaries or additional resources that are not available in freestanding imaging facilities or physician offices.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' thoughtful suggestions regarding exemptions for particular imaging services or clinical circumstances. As we stated in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period in response to similar recommendations regarding drug administration services (
90 FR 53824
), we are concerned that exempting a small subset of services from the volume control methodology could inadvertently incentivize an increase in the provision of those services in the higher cost setting of care. Furthermore, we do not believe that commenters have provided a clear clinical justification for exempting certain imaging without contrast services while leaving other imaging without contrast services non-exempted. We believe it would be most transparent to propose any service-specific exceptions through notice-and-comment rulemaking.
We address commenters' recommendations regarding preventive and screening imaging services in detail previously in this section. As discussed there, we recognize the important role that preventive services play in identifying disease at an earlier stage and improving health outcomes for Medicare beneficiaries, but we do not believe that the preventive nature of a service, by itself, warrants exclusion from the volume control method.
We also appreciate commenters' concerns regarding the potential for differences in payment to affect the use of contrast or enhancing agents. We agree that the decision to use a contrast or enhancing agent should be based on the clinical needs of the beneficiary and not on differences in Medicare payment. The volume control method finalized in this rule does not change the clinical criteria for determining when the use of a contrast or enhancing agent is appropriate. As discussed previously, our policy is intended to remove a payment incentive that we believe contributes to unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services, not to influence clinical decisions regarding how an imaging service should be furnished. We will monitor utilization following implementation of this policy and may consider changes in utilization patterns, including the use of contrast or enhancing agents, as part of our evaluation of the effects of the volume control method.
With respect to commenters' recommendations regarding imaging furnished to high-acuity or medically complex patients, imaging furnished in connection with planned or same-day procedures, or imaging furnished as part of integrated oncology care or other complex episodes of care, we appreciate that OPDs serve unique patient populations and provide services to medically complex beneficiaries. However, we do not believe that these circumstances demonstrate the need for higher payment for all imaging without contrast services furnished to these beneficiaries or in connection with these episodes of care. The fact that an imaging service is furnished on the same day as, or in connection with, another hospital service also does not necessarily establish that the imaging service itself requires the hospital outpatient setting or should be excluded from the volume control method. Our policy does not prevent a physician from determining that an OPD is the appropriate setting for a particular beneficiary based on the beneficiary's clinical needs.
We also are not certain how we would reliably identify the particular patients, services, or clinical circumstances suggested by commenters for purposes of administering an exemption. We appreciate commenters' input and may consider these suggestions in future rulemaking.
Comment:
Several commenters discussed the impact of the proposed method to control volume for imaging without contrast services on PPS-exempt cancer hospitals. Commenters noted that payments to PPS-exempt cancer hospitals are subject to the cancer hospital payment adjustment based on a payment-to-cost ratio and stated that reducing OPPS payment for imaging without contrast services could indirectly affect payments to these hospitals through the payment-to-cost ratio methodology.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' discussion of the impact of this policy on PPS-exempt cancer hospitals. We note that any reduction in the initial OPPS payment to a PPS-exempt cancer hospital as a result of this policy would lower the hospital's payment-to-cost ratio and would result in a corresponding increase in the cancer hospital payment adjustment at cost report settlement. We therefore do not believe that the application of the volume control method to imaging without contrast services warrants a separate exemption for PPS-exempt cancer hospitals.
We also recognize that this policy may affect the target payment-to-cost ratio used in determining the cancer hospital payment adjustment because the target payment-to-cost ratio is based on the payment-to-cost ratios of hospitals paid under the OPPS other than PPS-exempt cancer hospitals. We believe the effect of this policy on the target payment-to-cost ratio, through its effect on non-cancer hospitals' payment-to-cost ratios, would be relatively small. Moreover, because we believe the reduced payment for imaging without contrast services furnished by non-cancer hospitals subject to this policy is appropriate, we likewise believe that any resulting effect on the target payment-to-cost ratio is appropriate.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to exempt rural Sole Community Hospitals (rural SCHs) from payment of the site-specific Medicare PFS-equivalent payment for any HCPCS codes assigned to the imaging without contrast APCs or paid through the imaging without contrast composite APCs, when furnished at an off-campus PBD excepted from section 1833(t)(21) of the Act (departments that bill the modifier “PO” on claim lines). We believe that exempting rural SCHs from the volume control policy for imaging without contrast services will help to maintain access to care in rural areas by ensuring rural providers are paid for imaging without contrast services provided at off-campus PBDs at the same rate paid when the service is furnished in on-campus departments. Finalizing this policy also aligns with the special payment treatment rural SCHs receive under the OPPS. We will continue to monitor the effects of this change in Medicare payment policy.
B. OPPS Payments for SaMS Diagnostic Services
1. Payment for Software as a Medical Service (SaMS)
In recent years, there have been rapid developments in the use of software-based technologies with novel functionalities to support clinical decision-making in the outpatient and physician office settings. New clinical software, which includes clinical
(
printed page 70612)
decision support software, clinical risk modeling, and computer aided detection (CAD), is becoming increasingly available to providers. These technologies often perform data analysis of diagnostic images from patients, relying on complex algorithms or statistical predictive modeling to aid in the diagnosis or treatment planning of a patient's condition. In previous rulemaking, we have referred to these algorithm-driven services that assist practitioners in making clinical assessments or diagnoses as Software as a Service (SaaS). Unlike prescription digital therapeutics (PDTs), for example PDTs that provide cognitive behavioral therapy to treat substance disorders or chronic insomnia, SaaS technologies as we refer to them do not currently treat illnesses or patient injuries. SaaS is also separate from remote patient monitoring (RPM) and remote therapeutic monitoring (RTM), which are digital healthcare tools for tracking patient data outside traditional office settings (
90 FR 49394
). For CY 2027, we proposed-a change in terminology. We noted that we now understand that in other industries, the existing SaaS terminology is used for general cloud-based computing service models outside of a health care context, which may cause confusion as we are using it to describe specific services that provide a medical function for purposes of OPPS/ASC Medicare payment policy. To dispel any ambiguity and clarify that distinction, we proposed to change our terminology from SaaS to Software as a Medical Service (SaMS) to refer to software-based technologies that support clinical decision making through algorithmic analysis, including those that provide clinical or diagnostic functionality. We welcomed public comments on the proposed change in terminology.
CMS has been evaluating how to develop a comprehensive and consistent approach to SaMS payment for several years with the novel and evolving nature of these technologies. We have sought public input through two comment solicitations (
87 FR 72035
through
87 FR 72036
,
89 FR 94129
through
89 FR 94131
) and expressed our objective to seek a payment strategy that aligns with our agency's mission to increase quality, improve health, reduce costs, and strengthen the healthcare system. However, questions remain regarding how best to structure payment for these services. One challenge is that current Medicare Part B payment systems for SaMS, including in the OPPS, are primarily designed to pay for services that rely on material resources, rather than technologies whose value is driven by proprietary algorithms and scalable, non-material costs. This creates difficulties in establishing appropriate valuation methodologies, as the current cost-based system often offers only limited transparency into underlying costs and may not effectively constrain pricing. Another challenge is determining how to account for the various ways in which these technologies are acquired and billed by hospital OPDs, particularly in cases with subscription- or license-based arrangements, as well as per-use or “per-click” fees, which raises concerns regarding program integrity.
As coding for SaMS continues to rapidly increase and technologies evolve, establishing a consistent and timely payment methodology for these services is a priority. New SaMS technologies are continuing to be introduced to the market, each often accompanied by unique CPT codes reflecting their proprietary algorithms or specific characteristics. Interested parties are frequently seeking Medicare payment and coding for SaMS technologies through the new technology APC process or requesting clinical APC assignments. As a result, CMS is continuously assessing and evaluating payment for SaMS through different pathways. As we consider this policy, we want to ensure that we are moving toward a more standardized approach that reduces payment rate variation across similar technologies.
Given the growing need for a comprehensive and tailored payment methodology, as we work to gather additional data to better understand and more fully address the inherent payment challenges in this area, we proposed an interim payment policy for SaMS for CY 2027 while we examine a range of approaches to payment for these kinds of technologies. Specifically, we proposed to assign SaMS technologies to new technology APCs for CY 2027. We propose
d
to designate 36 HCPCS codes as SaMS services and reassign the proposed designated SaMS services that are currently paid separately (assigned to status indicator “S”) under clinical APCs, to new technology APCs that closely align with their current CY 2026 payment rates. We proposed to assign the separately paid SaMS technologies to new technology APCs because we believed that the existing clinical APC structure did not adequately accommodate SaMS. We believed that the new technology APCs were more appropriate to accommodate SaMS on a temporary basis, as there have historically been placements under the OPPS that allow us to provide consistent payment for new procedures that are not yet reflected in our claims data or for which we lack sufficient clinical information and cost data until we can identify an appropriate clinical APC. In certain circumstances, we have also assigned some services to new technology APCs through rulemaking, even when they have not met the specific regulatory criteria (
66 FR 59897
through
59903
) or have not applied for new technology APC assignment through the subregulatory process. For example, we have assigned certain services to new technology APCs in special cases where an appropriate clinical APC to which to assign the service does not exist. In the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we maintained the new technology APC assignment for HCPCS codes G2082 and G2083 because we did not believe there was an appropriate clinical APC to which to assign the service (
90 FR 53551
). This proposed approach of assigning SaMS services to the same APC series would allow CMS to take the first step towards standardization and applying a consistent payment methodology across these services as we consider more comprehensive long-term approaches, including those that may better align payment with clinical outcomes.
We also believed it was important to distinguish SaMS technologies from other services that are assigned to new technology APCs because not all new services assigned to new technology APCs are SaMS technologies. Therefore, we proposed to create a new status indicator under OPPS specifically for SaMS technologies. For CY 2027, we proposed to create status indicator “O1” (Software as a Medical Service, Paid under OPPS; separate APC payment) and assign all services that we proposed to designate as SaMS to status indicator “O1.” Functionally, we proposed for status indicator “O1” to have the same payment specifications as status indicator “S,” to allow for separate payment. We requested public comment on this proposal. We also requested public comment regarding whether a new status indicator with the same specification as status indicator “T” (Procedure or service subject to multiple procedure discounting) would provide more appropriate payment for these services while addressing any potential program integrity concerns.
For CY 2027, we proposed to designate the HCPCS codes listed in Table 83 as SaMS technologies. Of these, we proposed to assign 21 HCPCS codes to new technology APCs from clinical APCs, maintaining approximate
(
printed page 70613)
payment rate continuity with CY 2026 payment, and status indicator “O1”. Table 84
provides the list of HCPCS codes and proposed new technology APC and status indicator assignments for CY 2027. For SaMS that are already assigned to new technology APCs for CY 2026, we proposed to continue to assign these services to new technology APCs for CY 2027 while proposing to update the status indicator assignment to “O1” to designate these technologies as SaMS. We refer readers to section III.C. of the proposed rule-(
91 FR 41803
through
91 FR 41807
) for a discussion on our proposals for SaMS technologies that are currently assigned to new technology APCs for CY 2026.
We note that there are a small number of technologies we consider to be SaMS that are currently paid under the OPPS and assigned to an OPPS status indicator of “Q1” (STV-Packaged Codes; Paid under OPPS), indicating that the service is conditionally packaged. Services assigned to an OPPS status indicator of “Q1” will receive packaged payment when furnished with a significant procedure but will be separately paid when the service appears on the claim without a significant procedure. Because services assigned to new technology APCs are exempt from C-APC packaging policies, we did not believe it would be appropriate to propose to assign SaMS HCPCS codes that are currently conditionally packaged for CY 2026 to new technology APCs with status indicator “S” (Procedure or Service, Not Discounted When Multiple) to indicate separate payment. As an alternative, we considered unconditionally packaging SaMS services that are currently assigned to status indicator “Q1” by proposing to assign the services a status indicator of “N” (Items and Services Packaged into APC Rates). However, we stated that we believe proposing to unconditionally package payment for CY 2027 for SaMS technologies that are currently conditionally packaged under the OPPS may have resulted in interruptions to patient access. Given that we intended for this policy to be a first step towards more comprehensive payment policy changes and sought to minimize disruption, we believed it was more appropriate to propose to maintain the clinical APC and status indicator assignments for these codes. Therefore, for CY 2027, we proposed to maintain the clinical APC and status indicator assignments for SaMS that are currently conditionally packaged under the OPPS.
Similarly, there are other HCPCS codes that describe SaMS assigned to status indicator “E1” (Items, codes, and services not covered by any Medicare outpatient benefit category; statutorily excluded; not reasonable and necessary), status indicator “N” (Items or services packaged into APC rates), or status indicator “M” (Items and services not billable to the FI or MAC). Since these are not separately paid services under the OPPS for CY 2026, for CY 2027, we proposed to maintain the OPPS status indicators to which they are currently assigned.
We provided a table with the various SaMS HCPCS codes that were impacted by our proposals. Table 83 provides the proposed CY 2027 APC and status indicator assignments for codes we proposed to designate as SaMS services and that are currently assigned to clinical APCs or are not separately paid under the OPPS for CY 2026. We referred readers to section III.C. of the proposed rule for a discussion on the proposed CY 2027 payment rates for SaMS codes that are currently assigned to new technology APCs for CY 2026. In addition, we referred readers to Addendum B of the proposed rule for proposed CY 2027 OPPS payment rates and status indicators for HCPCS codes that we proposed to designate as SaMS. We requested comment on our proposals, including the list of HCPCS codes we proposed to designate as SaMS and that we proposed to reassign to new technology APCs for CY 2027, including whether there were any additional HCPCS codes we should consider.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters supported the proposed terminology change from SaaS to SaMS. One commenter explained that the proposed terminology would clarify the distinction between clinical algorithms and generic cloud tooling. A commenter requested that we clarify whether the transition to SaMS is intended solely as a naming convention or whether it reflects broader distinctions regarding the scope, classification, valuation or payment treatment of these technologies.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support. The terminology change from SaaS to SaMS seeks to clarify, as one commenter explained, the distinction between clinical algorithms used to furnish these services and generic cloud tooling.
Based on the comments received, for CY 2027, we are finalizing our proposal to change the terminology for these algorithm-based software services that are paid under Medicare from “SaaS” to “SaMS.”
Comment:
Many commenters requested clarification regarding the types of services that would be considered SaMS for purposes of this policy. For example, commenters asked whether remote care delivery or non-device clinical decision support (CDS) would be considered SaMS for purposes of separate payment. Similarly, we received comments regarding how CMS will distinguish separately paid software that supports clinical decision making from software that provides broader operational, administrative, or business functions. One commenter specifically requested that we expand our scope of services that we designate as SaMS to include those that perform analyses on structured clinical data conforming to recognized interoperability standards such that super intelligence-enabled comprehensive clinical trial eligibility analysis would be payable under the OPPS.
[
173
]
Response:
We thank the commenters for their interest in better understanding the scope of our policy. Regarding whether we would consider remote care delivery services as SaMS for purposes of this policy, we refer the commenter to our proposal where we specified that SaMS is separate from RPM and RTM, which are digital health tools for remotely tracking patient data. Furthermore, software that includes broader operational, administrative, or business functions, including clinical trial eligibility analysis, would not be considered SaMS under current policy. These kinds of software services can provide operational efficiencies but would not have a Medicare benefit category to allow for separate payment under OPPS.
We also appreciate commenters' input regarding whether CMS would consider non-device CDS as SaMS. The 36 services that we proposed to designate as SaMS, and that we previously referred to as SaaS, are regulated by the FDA as devices and therefore would not be considered non-device CDS. We note that although SaMS described in this section of this final rule with comment period (section X.B.1.), are required to have FDA marketing authorization to receive Medicare payment, “SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests,” which are described in the following section of this final rule with comment period (section X.B.2.), currently do not require FDA marketing authorization in order to receive payment. As the CY
(
printed page 70614)
2027 SaMS policy is an interim policy that seeks to maintain payment for CY 2027, we are declining to expand the scope of our policy to include non-device CDS at this time, although we note that there are existing non-device CDS services assigned to clinical APCs for CY 2026. We will consider expanding and further clarifying the scope of the SaMS policy for future rulemaking.
Comment:
We received several comments requesting information on CMS's process for identifying the 36 proposed HCPCS codes to be designated as SaMS. Commenters requested that we adopt, in the future, specific criteria that CMS will use to determine whether a service is payable as a SaMS under OPPS. For example, a commenter requested that we include the definitions and criteria from the recently updated Appendix S, effective June 2026, available via the AMA's website to identify SaMS codes. Other commenters requested that we identify SaMS codes based on functionality rather than input modality. We also received comments requesting that CMS align its clinical or diagnostic functionality criteria with the definitions that are used by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for their review of indications for use and device descriptions in their guidance documents and clearance processes.
Response:
We appreciate the comments. To identify the 36 proposed SaMS CPT codes, we examined all CPT codes currently paid under the OPPS to determine which codes aligned with the SaMS terminology provided in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, specifically “software-based technologies that support clinical decision making through algorithmic analysis, including those that provide clinical or diagnostic functionality” as a framework. We excluded RTM, RPM, non-device CDS, and services that we did not believe would fall under a Medicare benefit category, including those that are administrative in function. For instance, software that serves as the infrastructure that the provider uses to furnish another separately paid service.
Given the interim nature of the proposed policy, we will take the criteria concerns raised by the commenters, including establishing specific criteria for SaMS service for purposes of payment under the OPPS, into consideration for future rulemaking. We welcome public engagement from interested parties on these issues, including whether there are services that should be designated as SaMS in the future.
Comment:
We received a significant number of comments and requests from various interested parties regarding the proposed APC and status indicator assignments for certain SaMS services. Some of the requests included services that we did not identify as SaMS for the proposed rule and interested parties requested that they be added to the SaMS list. Others requested to maintain the clinical APC assignments for specific services we identified as SaMS versus assigning them to new technology APCs. A third category of requests included services that we identified as SaMS and assigned to new technology APCs, but interested parties requested different new technology APC assignments. We also received several comments requesting for certain services to be designated as SaMS and assigned to status indicator “O1” for CY 2027. A summary of the SaMS APC Specific requests and our responses are below.
We also note that since the CY 2027 proposed rule was published, the AMA revised their `release and effective date' calendar for new category III CPT codes. The new category III CPT codes that were going to be effective January 1, 2027, became effective October 1, 2026. New category III CPT codes with January 1, 2027, effective dates that we had designated as SaMS for the proposed rule, were assigned to clinical APCs and status indicators for the October 2026 update.
We received several comments requesting for certain services to be designated as SaMS and assigned to status indicator “O1” for CY 2027.
a. Biomechanical Computed Tomography (BCT) Analysis, CPT Code 0554T
Biomechanical Computed Tomography (BCT) analysis involves the use of a previous CT scan that is used by a computer software program to measure both the bone strength and bone mineral density of the hip or spine region. These services are described by CPT codes 0554T, 0555T, 0556T, 0557T, 0558T, and 0743T. CPT code 0554T is currently assigned to status indicator `M' (Items and Services Not Billable to the MAC. Not paid under OPPS). We received public comment on this service.
Comment: A commenter requested we designate CPT code 0554T
(Bone strength and fracture risk using finite element analysis of functional data and bone-mineral density utilizing data from a computed tomography scan; retrieval and transmission of the scan data, assessment of bone strength and fracture risk and bone-mineral density, interpretation and report)
as a SaMS. The commenter stated that since the other BCT codes (0555T, 0556T, 0557T, 0558T, 0743T) were designated as SaMS, it may be appropriate to designate CPT code 0554T as SaMS, although the commenter noted that the payment for CPT code 0554T is the sum of the payment for CPT codes 0555T-0557T.

2. SaMS Analyses Performed on Laboratory Tests
In recent years, we have seen an increase in laboratory tests that combine laboratory analyses, such as genomic sequencing or immunoassays, with computer algorithms to produce a clinical test result. The AMA CPT Editorial Panel created a category called Multi-Analyte Assays with Algorithmic Analysis (MAAA's), to categorize test codes that combined laboratory analyses with computer algorithms to generate clinical information. More recently, however, we are seeing the development of distinct algorithmic analyses alone with distinct CPT codes.
For example, when the genomic sequencing of an individual is performed, this sequencing will likely only need to be performed once by a laboratory. However, once the genomic sequence has been generated, the subsequent algorithmic analyses of that sequence data can be performed an infinite number of times to produce a wide range of results and/or diagnostic or risk-related information. These secondary analyses of original genomic sequences can be proprietary and unique to a single laboratory but could also be conducted at a range of settings. For purposes of this final rule with comment period, we are referring to subsequent stand-alone algorithmic analyses as “SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests”.
As discussed in the proposed rule, currently, certain SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests are treated as clinical diagnostic laboratory tests (CDLTs) and paid under the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (CLFS) (
91 FR 41925
). Section 1861(s) of the Act specifies items and services included as “medical and other health services” under Part B, including diagnostic X-ray tests, diagnostic laboratory tests, and other diagnostic tests as described in section 1861(s)(3) of the Act. Sections 1833(h) and 1834A of the Act and the implementing regulations at
42 CFR part 414, subpart G
,
set
forth the CLFS rate setting methodologies for CDLTs. We stated in the proposed rule that we do not believe it is appropriate to consider these secondary algorithmic analyses, when performed alone, to be CDLTs or establish CLFS payment rates for these analyses because we believe these secondary algorithmic analyses may not currently require laboratory services or entities, regulated by CLIA, to perform them. Our position is that the secondary analyses, which have distinct CPT codes,
[
174
]
are “other diagnostic tests” under section 1861(s)(3) of the Act as opposed to “diagnostic laboratory tests.” As noted previously, Medicare will not pay for CDLTs on the CLFS unless they are furnished by laboratories that meet applicable certification requirements. Tests that examine materials derived from the human body are assigned to and paid under the CLFS only when furnished by such certified laboratories in accordance with
42 CFR 410.32(d)
. Because SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests are downstream evaluations of the data generated by a prior laboratory test, which are described by distinct CPT codes, an entity that performs only algorithmic analyses of previously
(
printed page 70628)
sequenced data may not meet the definition of a “laboratory” under
42 CFR 493.2
or qualify for payment under CLFS. We believe SaMS that evaluate data generated by a prior laboratory test should not be treated as CDLTs for Medicare payment purposes.
As discussed in the proposed rule, we are also concerned that paying for these analyses based on existing CLFS payment methodologies may create significant vulnerabilities for the Medicare program, due to the lack of data transparency and CDLTs not being subject to beneficiary cost-sharing or budget neutrality.
42 CFR 414.508
outlines the rate setting methodologies CMS uses to set payment rates for new tests on the CLFS. Under § 414.508(b), CMS determines the payment amount based on either crosswalking or gapfilling methodologies until applicable information is available to establish a payment amount under the methodology described in § 414.507(b). Crosswalking is used if it is determined that a new CDLT is comparable to an existing test, multiple existing test codes, or a portion of an existing test code. Gapfilling is used when no comparable existing CDLT is available. Public consultation for payment for a new clinical diagnostic laboratory test is required in determining payment amounts, receiving public comments and recommendations (and data on which the recommendations are based) as well as recommendations from the Medicare Advisory Panel on Clinical Diagnostic Laboratory Tests (CDLTs) per § 414.506. A significant challenge to the rate setting process for CMS is receiving transparent data from laboratories outlining resource costs of a test, particularly for the algorithmic portions of tests that are combined with other analytes. In the past, laboratories have explained to CMS that the algorithmic components of laboratory tests are highly proprietary and details cannot be shared. Thus, CMS has worked with the limited information available on the details of methods or resources for the algorithmic portions of tests or analyses and has thus far relied on other laboratory methods provided in the CPT descriptor (
i.e.,
NGS sequencing, RT-PCR, or DNA methylation analysis). As CMS has gathered more information on SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests, we now believe that since these analyses are entirely computer-based, comparison based on laboratory methodologies is not appropriate. We believe that these analyses are substantially similar to other SaMS already paid under the OPPS. Additionally, in contrast to the OPPS, the CLFS generally does not include beneficiary cost-sharing or budget neutrality adjustments, which limits transparency regarding pricing and creates challenges for ensuring appropriate valuation of these services.
CMS has an interest in ensuring that services that are fundamentally similar are paid for and treated in the same way, regardless of the setting of care in which the service is furnished. Since we believe SaMS perform algorithmic analyses on previously generated data, we believe SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests are substantively similar to other SaMS technologies that are currently paid under the OPPS. Accordingly, we believe that whether the SaMS performs algorithmic analyses of an imaging test (
e.g.
CT scan) or whether it performs an algorithmic analysis on data generated from a laboratory test, all algorithmic analyses should be treated consistently from a payment perspective. We believe that this uniform approach for SaMS technologies would promote stability and predictability in payment for similar services.
Finally, we note that CMS and CDC issued a Request for Information (RFI) on July 16, 2026, regarding CLIA regulations, the results of which may be used to help inform the agencies as to what types of action, if any, should be taken to update the existing CLIA regulations through future comment and rulemaking (
91 FR 43586
). The RFI closed for comments on September 15, 2026. CMS may refine SaMS payment and policies based on RFI responses and make changes in future rulemaking.
For CY 2027, as an interim first step to address concerns described above, we proposed to assign 10 HCPCS codes describing various SaMS analysis performed on laboratory tests to new technology APCs under the OPPS, using the latest available CLFS data to crosswalk to new technology APCs with payment rates that closely approximate the current CY 2026 CLFS payment rates for these codes. We note that SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests would not currently require FDA marketing authorization in order to receive payment under OPPS. SaMS payment policies may be refined in future rulemaking. We explained that the proposed payment rates for SaMS performed on prior laboratory tests cannot be expected to align exactly with current CLFS payment rates because assignment to new technology APCs is based on established cost bands rather than individual test-specific payment amounts. For example, if a HCPCS code is currently paid $430.17 under the CLFS, the appropriate new technology APC assignment under this proposal would be APC 1506 (New Technology—Level 6 ($401-$500)), which has a standardized payment rate of $450.50, rather than receiving a payment rate that exactly matches the current CLFS amount. We noted that, under this proposal, SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests would be paid separately by being assigned to new technology APCs with the newly proposed status indicator “O1” (Software as a Medical Service, Paid under OPPS; separate APC payment) for CY 2027. These 10 HCPCS codes were identified based on the CPT descriptor for the code. We noted that, if there were no laboratory methods included in the code descriptor, and only an algorithmic analysis was described, we identified the code as a SaMS analysis performed on a laboratory test. We invited public comment on this proposed list and any other similar analyses that should be removed from the CLFS and paid under the OPPS.
In addition, for CY 2027 and subsequent years, we proposed to assign any new SaMS analyses performed on laboratory test codes to new technology APCs for payment under the OPPS. We requested public comment on these proposals, including the list of 10 HCPCS codes that we identified as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests and any additional HCPCS codes that we should designate as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests and pay under the OPPS rather than the CLFS. We stated that CMS may finalize a policy that includes such payment for additional HCPCS codes in the final rule based on public comment.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.

We thank the commenters for their support and note that we will consider these comments as we continue to refine this payment policy.

Commenters requested that CMS establish a payment mechanism for these services when the patient is not seen in a hospital outpatient department, noting that as proposed, the framework would leave no payment mechanism for a substantial share of medically necessary testing. Commenters also requested that CMS assign substantively comparable specimen-based algorithmic analyses to consistent new technology APCs and state the basis for APC assignment, and that CMS establish a defined, confidential process through which laboratories may submit cost and clinical outcomes data to support valuation as CMS develops a more comprehensive payment methodology. One commenter supported the proposal but requested that CMS defer changes to CLFS payment for algorithm-only laboratory analyses until the necessary coding, regulatory, and operational infrastructure has been established.
Response:
We appreciate the suggestion to be transparent and thoughtful in the implementation of this policy. We believe that publicly proposing this policy in the proposed rule, inviting comments, and addressing those comments in this rule has made this process transparent. We also appreciate the recommendation to evaluate the clinical benefit of SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests. We remind readers that our goal in this rulemaking cycle is to establish the category of SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests and the general payment mechanism for those services under the OPPS. Regarding a request to establish a separate confidential process through which laboratories may submit cost and clinical data, we remind commenters that we are available to meet with interested parties where information may be shared with CMS. However, because payment rates are finalized through the notice-and-comment rulemaking process, which requires providing the underlying reasoning for our proposals and final policy, establishing a separate confidential process would not be compatible with the existing rulemaking process. Further, finalizing this policy would not eliminate Medicare payment for these services, or prohibit certain facilities from billing Medicare, but rather, it would define how these services would be paid under the OPPS. For the purposes of maintaining stability, particularly for the HCPCS codes we proposed to remove from the CLFS and place in an APC category, we chose to assign APC levels based on the CY 2026 CLFS payment rates to avoid any considerable payment disruption. As we continue to develop this policy, we will consider possible methods for evaluating the APC assignment for new SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests. We do not believe that it is appropriate to delay the movement of SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests from the CLFS to the OPPS, given the speed at which SaMS technologies are developing and the goal of having a consistent policy across payment systems for similar services. These services will be paid for under existing and well-established Medicare payment mechanisms, depending on the place of service (that is, hospital outpatient departments or physician offices).

For example, both SaMS currently paid under the OPPS and SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests perform algorithm-based analyses on existing data. We anticipate that resource costs may be similar between these kinds of services. The fact that a service has historically been billed and paid as a single, integrated CDLT on the CLFS does not mean that each component of that service must continue to be paid as such, particularly where the analytical component is distinguishable from the data-generating component as provided by the HCPCS code descriptor, both in the resources required to perform it and in the manner in which its costs are incurred. 3. Summary of CY 2027 SaMS Final Payment Policies
In summary, for CY 2027, we are finalizing the following interim payment policies. First, we are finalizing a terminology change from SaaS to SaMS to more accurately describe algorithm-based software services. Second, we are creating a new status indicator “O1” (Software as a Medical Service, paid under OPPS; separate APC payment) to designate SaMS that are payable under the OPPS. Third, we are finalizing assignment of all SaMS assigned to status indicator “O1” to a new technology APC. For CY 2027, we are maintaining the payment rates consistent for SaMS assigned to status indicator “O1” from CY 2026 OPPS rates. In addition, we are finalizing our proposal to use the term “SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests” to describe stand-alone algorithmic analyses of data generated by a prior laboratory test. Although the services we have designated as SaMS in section X.B.1. of the final rule with comment period are required to have FDA marketing authorization to receive Medicare payment, “SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests do not currently require FDA marketing authorization in order to receive payment under OPPS. While these secondary analyses are currently paid for under the CLFS as “diagnostic laboratory tests” under section 1861(s)(3), (16), and (17) of the Act, for CY 2027, we are finalizing our position that these services are “other diagnostic tests” and, therefore, will be paid under OPPS under section 1861(s)(3) of the Act. Specifically, we are finalizing payment for 14 SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests from the CLFS to the OPPS by assigning the codes to new technology APCs that align with current CY 2026 CLFS payment rates.
C. Adjustment for Cost-of-Living in Alaska and Hawaii
We have heard from a variety of interested parties about the particularly difficult cost environment facing hospitals located in Alaska and Hawaii. These challenges stem from the unique circumstances of those geographies, including dependency on outside goods and components, remote locations and transportation challenges, and other factors inherent to providing healthcare in these non-contiguous States.
A review of the available cost report data used in OPPS ratesetting highlights these issues. We stated in the proposed rule that we observed a number of hospitals in Alaska and Hawaii with payment-to-cost ratios (PCRs) that range from 0.6 to 0.7, significantly below the average PCR for OPPS hospitals of 0.89 used as an initial target for the cancer hospital adjustment discussed in section II.F. of the proposed rule. In addition, the overall ancillary cost-to-charge ratios for several hospitals located in these States are higher than average, indicating that there are higher costs relative to what those hospitals charge for the outpatient services they provide compared to other OPPS hospitals.
Under the IPPS, section 1886(d)(5)(H) of the Act provides discretionary authority to the Secretary to make adjustments as the Secretary deems appropriate to take into account the unique circumstances of hospitals located in Alaska and Hawaii. To account for higher non-labor-related costs for these two States in the IPPS, we apply an adjustment factor to the nonlabor-related portion of the standardized amount for hospitals in Alaska and Hawaii. For FY 2011 and in prior fiscal years, we used the most recent cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) factors obtained from the U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM) website at
https://www.opm.gov/​policy-data-oversight/​pay-leave/​pay-systems/​nonforeign-areas/​#url=​COLA-Rates
to update this nonlabor portion.
In the FY 2013 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule, we established a methodology to update the COLA factors for Alaska and Hawaii that were published by the U.S. OPM every 4 years (coinciding with the update to the labor-related share of the IPPS market basket), beginning in FY 2014. We refer readers to the FY 2013 IPPS/LTCH PPS proposed and final rules for additional background and a detailed description of this methodology (

Based on the policy finalized in the FY 2013 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule, we utilized these COLA factors for FYs 2022 through 2025 to adjust the nonlabor-related portion of the standardized amount for hospitals located in Alaska and Hawaii.
As we discussed in the proposed rule, in general, under the IPPS methodology, we updated the 2009 OPM COLA factors by a comparison of the growth in the CPIs for the areas of Urban Alaska and Urban Hawaii, relative to the growth in the CPI for the average U.S. city as published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). We used the comparison of the growth in the overall CPI relative to the growth in the CPI for those areas to update the COLA factors for all areas in Alaska and Hawaii, respectively, because BLS publishes CPI data for only Urban Alaska and Urban Hawaii. Using the respective CPI commodities index and CPI services index, and using the approximate commodities/services shares obtained from the IPPS market basket, we created reweighted CPIs for each of the respective areas to reflect the underlying composition of the IPPS market basket nonlabor-related share. Lastly, we exercised our discretionary authority to adjust payments to hospitals in Alaska and Hawaii by including the statutorily mandated cap of 25 percent that was applied when determining OPM's COLA factors. We think this same logic would apply to adopting the IPPS COLA policy for hospital outpatient services in Alaska and Hawaii, as additional nonlabor costs that apply to hospital inpatient services provided in these States likely also apply to hospital outpatient services in these States. Further, not addressing the discrepancy between the IPPS and OPPS adjustment to account for nonlabor related costs would potentially continue a disincentive to provide services in the hospital outpatient setting due to the adjustment only applying to inpatient services.
Based on our review of the costs of providing outpatient services in these States and our general practice of applying consistent policies across the inpatient and outpatient hospital settings where possible, we proposed to use the equitable adjustment authority provided by section 1833(t)(2)(E) of the Act to propose to apply the IPPS COLA factors to the nonlabor share of OPPS payment amounts for hospitals located in Alaska and Hawaii for CY 2027 and future years. We note that for OPPS payments for which there is no wage adjustable portion, we proposed to apply the COLA to the full OPPS payment, as would be the case for status indicator assignments of “G,” “H,” “K,” “R,” and “U”.

As previously discussed in this section, Table H-01 of the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule lists the IPPS COLA factors finalized for FY 2027 for the OPM designated areas of Alaska and Hawaii (
91 FR 50389

Under the OPPS, section 1833(t)(2)(E) of the Act grants the Secretary the authority to establish equitable adjustments as necessary, and we proposed to use that authority to establish a COLA for outpatient hospital services provided in Alaska and Hawaii that mirrors the COLA provided for inpatient hospital services provided in these States. Associated with this proposed policy, we also proposed to add conforming regulation text changes by adding subsection (l) to § 419.43. This new subsection describes the cost-of-living adjustment to the nonlabor portion of the OPPS payment amounts for hospitals located in Alaska and Hawaii. Finally, we noted that under our authority at section 1833(t)(2)(E) of the Act this adjustment would be budget neutral, and stated that the associated budget neutrality adjustment is discussed in section II.B. of the proposed rule.

Response:

(
printed page 70638)
between the inpatient and outpatient hospital payment systems.

91 FR 50388

Comment:
One commenter believed that the COLA would establish an asymmetry in which hospitals receiving low wages would contribute to financing the COLA through OPPS budget neutrality without receiving comparable recognition for their geographic circumstances. The commenter asked CMS to explain this difference or provide more substantial relief through modifying budget neutrality for the OPPS wage-index transitional exception to specifically apply to hospitals above the 75th percentile of wage indexes.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's concerns but do not agree that the COLA and wage-index policies create the asserted asymmetry. The hospital wage index and COLA apply to address different cost categories and payment portions. The wage index is used to adjust the portion of the OPPS payment that is labor-related to account for different geographic levels of hospital wage costs. The COLA is designed to adjust the portion of payments not related to labor costs, so as to account for the distinct nonlabor costs of furnishing services in Alaska and Hawaii.
The presence of a nonlabor COLA for Alaska and Hawaii thus does not indicate that the wage-index methodology is failing to recognize geographic variation in labor costs elsewhere. Hospitals outside Alaska and Hawaii continue to receive wage index and other geographic adjustments applicable to them under both the IPPS and OPPS.
Section 1833(t)(2)(E) of the Act mandates that equitable adjustments are made in a budget-neutral manner, requiring that associated changes do not affect estimated aggregate OPPS expenditures. We do not believe that it is appropriate to budget neutralize specifically to hospitals with wage indexes above the 75th percentile. Developing wage index budget neutrality in this manner would result in different wage indexes between the IPPS and OPPS, we believe that it is important to maintain alignment of the IPPS and OPPS wage indexes,
We therefore do not believe that establishing the COLA in the OPPS necessitates implementation of an additional wage index adjustment or altering the calculation of budget neutrality with regards to the wage index and its associated adjustments. For a detailed discussion of the wage index, please see section II.C. of this final rule with comment period.
Comment:
Commenters agreed that circumstances in Alaska and Hawaii lead to higher non-labor costs, but stated that rural communities in other States also have geographic barriers to access care, shortages of health care workers, long travelling distances, transportation limitations, and other access limitations. One commenter stated, in general, that CMS allow for regional variation for cost-of-living.
Response:
The OPPS addresses certain geographic differences through other payment policies, including application of the hospital wage index to the labor-related portion of the OPPS payment, the rural sole community hospital adjustment, geographic reclassification, and the out-migration adjustment. The OPPS COLA policy serves a narrower purpose. It recognizes the unique non-labor costs experienced by hospitals in the two non-contiguous states, Alaksa and Hawaii, and aligns the OPPS treatment of those costs with the longstanding IPPS policy.
After consideration of the public comments and for the reasons discussed, we are finalizing our proposal to apply the finalized IPPS COLA factors to the non-labor portion of OPPS payment for hospitals located in Alaska and Hawaii for CY 2027 and future years. We are also finalizing the proposed conforming regulation text changes at
42 CFR 419.43(l)
and the associated budget neutrality adjustment as discussed in section II.B. of this final rule with comment period.
