b. Electronic Clinical Quality Measures
In the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule (
91 FR 41966
), we proposed extending the educational review process established for chart-abstracted measure validation to eCQM validation beginning with validation affecting the CY 2030 payment determination (that is, starting with validated data from CY 2027). We believe that expanding the educational review process to include eCQMs would allow hospitals to better understand the processes and data for eCQM validation.
Hospitals may request an educational review if they believe they have been scored incorrectly or if they have questions about their validation of eCQMs. A hospital would have 30 calendar days from the date the validation results are made available to contact CMS' Validation Support Contractor requesting a written explanation of its performance. Because hospitals receive eCQM validation results on an annual basis, they would have the opportunity to request an educational review once annually. Upon receipt of an educational review request, we would review the requested data elements and written justifications provided by the hospital. We would also provide the results of the eCQM validation educational review to the requesting hospital, including our findings of whether the scores were correct or incorrect, through a CMS-approved secure file transmission process (currently, UFM/MFT). If the results of a validation educational review determine that the original validation score was incorrect, the corrected score would be used to compute the final validation score and confidence interval at the end of each calendar year.
In the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule (
91 FR 41966
), we proposed to codify this policy by revising §  419.46(f)(4) to include eCQMs. As proposed, §  419.46(f)(4) would indicate that hospitals selected for validation may request an educational review within 30 calendar days from the date validation results are made available. Under the proposed revisions to § 419.46(f)(4), if the results of an educational review indicate one or more measures were incorrectly scored, the corrected validation score would be used to compute the final validation score used for payment determination. We refer readers to section XXIV.A. of this final rule with comment period for more information on the burden estimates associated with these proposals.
We invited public comment on these validation of Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program data proposals, including eCQM validation into the existing validation processes for chart-abstracted measures, reducing the validation selection pool from 500 to up to 400 hospitals, applying targeting criteria to eCQMs, updating the number of cases for chart-abstracted and eCQM validation, transitioning from a 2-year to a 3-year cycle between the reporting period and the payment determination year to align submission quarters, extending the electronic file submissions policy to eCQM medical records requests, establishing the eCQM validation scoring method, and expanding the educational review process.
Comments Regarding Electronic Clinical Quality Measure Data Validation
Comment:
Many commenters supported efforts to reduce reporting burden and streamline Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program requirements to improve facility accountability and the reliability of submitted data, especially as CMS continues to expand the use of electronic measures. Some commenters appreciated CMS' efforts to use consistent definitions, confidence intervals, sampling methodologies, and reconsideration procedures across inpatient and outpatient programs to reduce administrative complexity, promote greater consistency in program oversight, and allow hospitals to focus resources on improving data quality and patient care rather than navigating varying validation requirements.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support and agree that streamlining our requirements and aligning them across programs reduces burden while promoting data accuracy and reliability across measure types.
Comment:
A commenter stated that the administrative workload associated with eCQM reporting and validation can be substantial, particularly for small and rural facilities with limited staff to support internal compliance, information technology, data analytics, or quality reporting, and recommended that CMS should provide special support for these facilities.
Response:
We understand concerns regarding the impact on hospitals with limited health IT resources available. We acknowledge that introducing eCQM validation affects burden; however, we believe the benefits of ensuring that hospitals report accurate data outweigh the increase in burden as these data are made publicly available for consumer use. We refer readers to section XXIV.A. of this final rule with comment period for more information on the burden estimates associated with our validation policies. We have sought to reduce overall burden by reducing the total number of hospitals selected and focusing on a more targeted selection of hospitals via our targeting criteria.
Comment:
A commenter suggested expanding the scope of data validation to include claims-based measures as the commenter stated CMS' existing audit processes are focused on improper payment identification rather than measure validity.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's recommendation. Our validation processes relate to assessing the accuracy of quality data that hospitals themselves abstract, calculate, or submit to CMS based on agreement rate. For claims-based measures, we can retrieve necessary information to calculate the quality measures from our own claims databases. Medicare claims are subject to audit for improper payment, system edits, and other program integrity activities to help ensure claims data are supported, compliant, and suitable for payment and secondary uses including quality measure calculations. Additionally, all our measures, including claims-based measures, undergo the rigorous measure development lifecycle outlined at the CMS Measures Management System website,
[
205
]
which includes measure
(
printed page 70693)
testing and reliability analysis which evaluates whether a measure is repeatable and stable.
We are finalizing the proposal to begin validating each eCQM in the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program when there is a full year of data available for that measure.
Comments Regarding Changes to Selection Process for Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program Validation
Comment:
Many commenters supported reducing the hospital selection pool from 500 to up to 400 hospitals, of which up to 200 hospitals are randomly selected and up to 200 hospitals are selected based on targeting criteria. Several commenters stated that the change to more targeted selection would help lower-performing hospitals improve based on targeted interventions, while allowing already higher-performing hospitals to continue performing well without additional burden.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support and agree that rebalancing the number of hospitals selected by targeting criteria would more effectively and efficiently direct validation program resources to assessing agreement rates for hospitals that evidence data accuracy concerns.
Comment:
A commenter expressed concern that a smaller overall validation sample would not provide the same level of confidence in program-wide data quality and recommended that CMS ensure that there are no unintended consequences.
Response:
We recognize that sampling a smaller number of hospitals increases the estimate of variability for the overall data. Since the overall performance on chart-abstracted measures is consistently high across hospitals, there is little true variation to detect for those measures, and confidence remains high regarding overall data quality for chart-abstracted reporting. As eCQMs are newer to the validation process, we have less historical experience to draw upon; this is one of the reasons we believe it is important to begin validating eCQM data now, so that we can build a similar evidentiary basis over time. In determining the number of hospitals eligible for selection for validation, we seek to balance burden with a validation approach that assesses data quality across both measure types. Our many years of experience validating hospital measure data in the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program, Hospital Inpatient Quality Reporting Program, and Hospital-Acquired Condition Reduction Program, including observed validation results and failure rates based on agreement rates, demonstrates that a larger selection pool is not necessary. Additionally, retaining the selection pool at its current size of up to 500 hospitals would yield only a marginal improvement in the precision of our population-level confidence estimate, while placing additional administrative burden on approximately 100 more hospitals each year. Consistent with the statistical principle underlying our approach to Hospital Inpatient Quality Reporting Program sample sizing, the precision gained from increasing a sample size beyond a certain point diminishes relative to the administrative burden of doing so. We believe the pool of up to 400 hospitals appropriately balances maintaining robust program-wide confidence with minimizing unnecessary burden on additional hospitals.
We will continue to monitor the number of hospitals passing validation and if the pass rate falls to a level where we can no longer be confident in the agreement rates of hospitals participating in the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program, we will address this issue in future rulemaking.
Comment:
A few commenters did not support the requirement that any hospital selected for validation must submit both chart-abstracted and eCQM data as this could increase administrative burden on health systems. Instead, a commenter recommended limiting the audit of hospitals selected under targeted criteria to the specific data modality that triggered the selection.
Response:
We interpret these comments to mean that commenters are concerned about the burden of submitting data required to validate both eCQMs and chart-abstracted measures. While there may be some instances of increased burden for specific hospitals, we disagree with the commenters that this approach is more burdensome for the majority of hospitals. Requiring selected hospitals to submit documentation for both measure types allows us to maintain oversight of data quality across the full range of measures subject to validation and helps ensure that the continued expansion of eCQMs in the measure set of the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program does not result in reduced attention to the accuracy and reliability of chart-abstracted data. While our proposed policy would add the requirement for selected hospitals to submit eCQMs in addition to chart-abstracted measures, the total number of validated measures remains low as chart-abstracted measures have been phased out and eCQMs are phased in. We note in section XIV. of this final rule with comment period, we are removing the Appropriate Follow-Up Interval for Normal Colonoscopy in Average Risk Patients measure which, while not validated, will reduce hospital burden. After this removal, there will be one remaining chart-abstracted measure in the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program, the Head Computed Tomography (CT) or Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) Scan Results for Acute Ischemic Stroke or Hemorrhagic Stroke Patients who Received Head CT or MRI Scan Interpretation Within 45 minutes of Arrival measure.
We are finalizing the proposal to update the validation selection pool and application of existing targeting criteria to eCQMs.
Comments Regarding Case Selection for Validation
Comment:
A few commenters supported reducing the quarterly validation requirements for chart-abstracted measures from 12 cases and validating up to 8 cases per measure to accommodate validation of both chart-abstracted measures and eCQMs.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support and agree that the change promotes data accuracy while balancing burden. As discussed further in our response to comments below, based on the results of a power analysis, we are finalizing an even greater reduction—up to 7 cases per quarter (28 cases annually) per applicable measure, rather than the up to 8 cases per quarter (32 cases annually) that was proposed.
Comment:
A commenter opposed establishing a validation sample size of up to 32 cases per measure annually due to the commenter's concern regarding the increase in burden as new measures are added to the program. Instead, the commenter advised implementing a fixed, aggregate hospital-level cap across all measures combined to maintain rigorous, statistically sound audit oversight without placing increasing strain on health care operations.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's concern regarding the cumulative burden associated with validating an increasing number of measures over time. We note that one of the goals of the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program is to move forward in the least burdensome manner possible, while maintaining a parsimonious set of the most
(
printed page 70694)
meaningful quality measures and continuing to incentivize improvement in the quality of care provided to patients. We carefully evaluate each measure proposed for adoption to ensure that its benefits outweigh the cumulative burden of requirements across the program, including data validation policies.
In light of this comment, and consistent with a power analysis conducted to evaluate whether the proposed sample size could be reduced without compromising validation accuracy, we are finalizing a sample size of up to 28 cases annually per applicable measure (up to 7 cases per quarter), rather than the up to 32 cases per measure (up to 8 cases per quarter) that was proposed. This represents a 12.5 percent reduction in the annual case burden relative to our proposal. Our analysis found that a sample size of 28 cases produced agreement with historical hospital classifications of 98.4 percent, with a false-pass rate of 0.1 percent and a false-fail rate of 1.6 percent, indicating that this reduced sample size continues to provide a reliable and statistically sound basis for validation while reducing burden on hospitals. We also note that our analysis found that approximately 89.9 percent of requested cases were available for sampling in the modeled scenario; we will continue to monitor case availability as we implement this change and will address any issues in future rulemaking if warranted.
We decline to adopt the commenter's alternative recommendation of a fixed, aggregate hospital-level cap across all measures combined. While our validation scoring methodology computes a confidence interval using the results from a hospital's applicable measures combined at the hospital level, we continue to believe that establishing a minimum number of cases per measure, rather than a single aggregate cap, better ensures that each individual measure is adequately represented within that combined sample, particularly as additional eCQMs become eligible for validation over time. A fixed aggregate cap could result in a disproportionately small number of cases being drawn from any individual measure, which would reduce our ability to detect measure-specific reporting or specification issues even though the overall hospital-level score remains statistically sound. We will continue to monitor the cumulative impact of this policy as new measures are added to the program and will consider further refinements in future rulemaking as appropriate.

Response:
We thank commenters for their support and agree that this alignment creates simplicity.
Comment:

We understand the commenter's concern that $3.00 per chart may not cover the full time and materials associated with record submission. ) as well as the reimbursement rate across other quality reporting programs, such as the Hospital Inpatient Quality Reporting Program (
78 FR 50956
) and Inpatient Psychiatric Facilities Quality Reporting Program (

We are finalizing the same file submission process for eCQMs as chart-abstracted measures.
Comments Regarding Submission Quarters
Comment:
A few commenters supported aligning submission quarters across both measure types by moving to a 3-year cycle as this alignment should make it easier for hospitals to track their validation activities and allow CMS sufficient time to complete the validation and review process.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support and agree that this alignment adds simplicity while allowing sufficient time to complete validation activities.
Comment:
A commenter stated that moving from a 2-year to a 3-year cycle between the reporting period and payment determination appears unnecessary, particularly as CMS continues to transition toward more eCQMs.
Response:
The shift to a 3-year cycle between the reporting period and payment determination is operationally necessary as we adopt eCQMs. Since eCQMs are reported on an annual basis, a 3-year cycle allows sufficient time to complete sampling, medical record abstraction, confidence interval calculation, and educational reviews following the data reporting deadline. As the annual eCQM submission deadline for the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program is May 15, there is not enough time to request and receive records from selected hospitals, validate an entire year's worth of eCQM data, and calculate the confidence interval by August when we select hospitals for the next payment determination's validation cycle. By shifting to a 3-year cycle, we can effectively include eCQMs and provide an educational review opportunity for eCQMs and the last quarter of chart-abstracted measures. Currently, if a hospital's Q4 educational review determines that a record was incorrectly scored, there is not sufficient time to include that corrected score into the end-of-year confidence interval calculation before the calculation must be finalized for payment determination. As we further leverage Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources® (FHIR®)
[
206
]
for eCQMs, we will consider opportunities to expedite the data validation cycle in the future.
Comment:
A commenter supported CMS' effort to reduce administrative burden by exempting hospitals for validation from being reselected within the subsequent year but believed many hospitals would prefer the possibility of consecutive year selection rather than having a single set of validation results place their annual payment update at risk across multiple payment determinations. Another commenter stated that applying CY 2029 validation findings for chart-abstracted measures to CY 2030 validation findings creates a double jeopardy concern for a single year's validation results.
Response:
We interpret these comments to mean the commenters are concerned about CY 2027 chart-abstracted data validation impacting their annual payment update for CY 2029 and CY 2030. We wish to clarify that a hospital would not be validated again for the CY 2030 payment determination if they were already selected for CY 2029 payment determination data validation so that validation findings of CY 2027 chart-abstracted data would not affect more than one year's payment determination.
Comment:
A commenter asked CMS to provide a clear explanation of how hospitals selected during the transition year will be treated. Another commenter asked CMS to ensure that the criteria
(
printed page 70695)
used to select hospitals for eCQM validation are transparent, consistently applied, and clearly communicated in advance.
Response:
For the transition year (that is, validation of CY 2027 data for the CY 2030 payment determination), up to 200 hospitals would be randomly selected and up to 200 hospitals would be selected using the targeting criteria at § 419.46(f)(3)(i) through (v), but only if the hospital did not participate in validation affecting the CY 2029 payment determination. In other words, all hospitals selected for validation affecting the CY 2029 payment determination would be excluded from reselection for validation affecting the CY 2030 payment determination to avoid validating the same CY 2027 chart-abstracted data over again. After the transition year affecting the CY 2030 payment determination, up to 200 hospitals would be randomly selected and up to 200 hospitals would be selected using the targeting criteria at § 419.46(f)(3)(i) through (v).
We are finalizing the transition from validation results affecting payment 2 years after the reporting period to 3 years after the reporting period beginning with the CY 2030 payment determination.
Comments Regarding the Scoring Method
Comment:
A few commenters supported applying the same scoring methodology process to eCQMs as chart-abstracted measures as it balances administrative simplicity while acknowledging that eCQMs and the data that inform them are different in nature from chart-abstracted measures.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support and agree that this alignment creates simplicity.
Comment:
A commenter suggested shifting the focus of assessing the validity of the data elements to evaluating whether the level of data accuracy is sufficient for a measure to produce valid results. They stated that a minimum threshold at a 75 percent level of data accuracy may not result in a measure with either reasonable validity or reliability, and the public and the provider community need a higher level of assurance that the measure results reflect the quality of care of a facility as opposed to the accuracy of a number of data elements. A commenter asked for clarity on which record elements CMS will use to adjudicate a match.
Response:
We confirm that data validation scoring is at the measure level as the commenter recommends, not the individual data element level. While individual data elements are assessed during the data validation process to confirm that a clinical event actually occurred, was documented appropriately in the source records, was interpreted correctly, and was mapped correctly into reporting fields, the validation score for the measure reflects whether the CMS validation process obtained the same measure outcome as the hospital's original submission. If the CMS validation process does not obtain the same measure outcome, then the case may be considered a mismatch. Applying an upper bound of a 90 percent two-sided confidence interval with a 75 percent lower bound threshold level accounts for sampling variability, reflects a reasonable standard of data accuracy, and aligns with existing validation thresholds for chart-abstracted measures while allowing for legitimate differences in hospital data implementation. However, we will consider increasing the threshold in future rulemaking as hospitals gain further experience with eCQM reporting over time.
Comment:
Many commenters supported validation overall but recommended modifications to the validation processes to include eCQMs. Several commenters recommended validating eCQMs after one or two full years of mandatory reporting of data or providing an initial reporting-only year as a phased implementation to provide health systems with the necessary operational runway to establish, test, and stabilize electronic data extraction workflows before being subjected to formal audits and financial penalties. If CMS did a reporting-only year as recommended, commenters also suggested that CMS conduct targeted validation activities. These commenters indicated that results from an initial reporting-only year could provide hospitals with educational feedback regarding identified issues to allow hospitals to identify documentation deficiencies, data abstraction concerns, measure logic inconsistencies, and submission errors and better ensure that validation results accurately reflect performance rather than implementation challenges. A commenter emphasized that clear communication regarding expectations, common validation errors, and areas requiring corrective action will improve reporting accuracy and help ensure validation activities function as a quality improvement tool rather than solely a compliance exercise.
Many commenters expressed concern with beginning validation with CY 2027 reporting period data for the STEMI eCQM due to issues in accurately identifying patients in the numerator and denominator and concerns that the current measure logic is not designed well for electronic data capture. Several commenters stated that the two denominator exceptions for the CY 2026 reporting period are helpful, but challenging to implement, which further complicates efforts to improve accuracy of STEMI data capture. A few commenters asked CMS to ensure that validation methodologies adequately account for the complexity of emergency cardiovascular care workflows, including data originating from emergency medical service systems, transferring facilities, emergency departments, and cardiac catheterization laboratories.
Several commenters who were concerned about beginning validation of the STEMI eCQM with CY 2027 reporting period data also supported a reporting-only period or delaying scoring until electronic capture of STEMI is mature. Another commenter recommended delaying validation activities until hospitals have completed at least one full reporting cycle using the revised STEMI eCQM specifications.
Response:
We appreciate commenters raising these concerns and sharing their recommendations. We agree with commenters that delaying the timeline for eCQM validation and providing an opportunity for educational review would allow hospitals to gain experience with measure requirements and identify deficiencies before validation scores affect payment. We also recognize that STEMI care, by its nature, is fast-moving and frequently spans multiple clinicians and care settings, including the emergency department, the cardiac catheterization laboratory, and interpreting cardiology services, which can present documentation and systems integration challenges. We believe the measure is appropriately designed for electronic capture as the eCQM is endorsed by the consensus-based entity
[
207
]
and underwent the rigorous measure development lifecycle outlined at the CMS Measures Management System website,
[
208
]
to ensure the measure is precisely specified, feasible, valid, and reliable. However, we acknowledge that the STEMI eCQM specifications were
(
printed page 70696)
recently revised, and we agree with commenters that payment penalties associated with validation scores should be delayed for the STEMI eCQM as initial scores may reflect challenges with implementing recent measure updates rather than the true accuracy of hospital STEMI eCQM submissions.
Based on commenter concerns about the STEMI eCQM and data issues during the first year of mandatory implementation of any eCQM, we are finalizing the data validation policy with a modification to delay payment penalties associated with validation scores until an eCQM has been mandatory in the program for one year of reporting. During the first full year of mandatory reporting, validation scores will only be used to provide selected hospitals with an opportunity for educational review, and payment penalties will only be assessed if a hospital does not submit requested records. If a hospital does not submit at least 75 percent of the requested records for the applicable eCQM under validation, the hospital will fail validation even during this unscored period. This modification allows at least one full reporting cycle using the revised STEMI eCQM specifications before a payment impact and provides an opportunity for educational feedback to identify and resolve errors before validation score results may affect payment.
As an example of how the finalized policy will be applied, the STEMI eCQM validation for the CY 2027 reporting period impacting the CY 2030 payment determination will serve as an educational review opportunity, with a payment penalty only for failure to submit at least 75 percent of the requested records. For the CY 2028 reporting period impacting the CY 2031 payment determination, payment penalties for the STEMI eCQM validation will be based on attaining at least a 75 percent validation score for eCQM data validation.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed that eCQM performance and reporting are heavily dependent upon EHR configuration, vendor programming, data mapping, and interoperability among health information systems. These commenters stated that this means CMS should ensure that validation findings appropriately distinguish hospital reporting issues from technology-related discrepancies that may be outside a hospital's direct control, particularly as CMS moves towards automated and FHIR®-based measurement.
Specifically, a few commenters did not support treating missing or flawed medical records as mismatches, stating that eCQM discrepancies often stem from vendor specification updates, structured data mapping, or electronic file transmission protocols, which would unfairly penalize facilities for circumstances unrelated to actual measure accuracy. A commenter recommended that CMS instead establish an eCQM-specific validation scoring framework that accommodates electronic data architecture nuances and provide a technical remediation window prior to impacting annual payment determinations. Another commenter encouraged CMS to consider alternative approaches, including a grace period, an exception process for circumstances outside a hospital's control, or, in the case of unavailable records, a separate classification that does not automatically equate unavailable records with measure inaccuracy.
Response:
We understand that hospitals rely on measure developers and EHR vendors for eCQM reporting. However, we do not agree that records unavailable for validation should be excluded from the calculation of the validation score. The purpose of validation is to assess whether the CMS validation process obtains the same measure outcomes as the hospital's original submission. If a record is not received or does not contain the necessary information, then we cannot determine that the reported result agrees with the medical records, so it causes a mismatch. Yet, we recognize that data mapping and data quality issues may arise with eCQM implementation. The 75 percent scoring threshold is intended to account for sampling variability and reasonable differences in hospital data implementation while maintaining a reasonable standard for data accuracy. Our modification to delay any payment penalties associated with validation scores until an eCQM has been mandatory in the program for one year of reporting also allows additional time for hospitals and their vendors to resolve data reporting issues.
After consideration of the public comments we received, we are finalizing our proposal that a minimum score of 75 percent accuracy will be required for the hospital to pass the eCQM validation requirement with a modification to delay the payment penalties associated with the eCQM validation score until the second full year an eCQM has been mandatory in the program. During the first full year of mandatory reporting, validation scores will only be used to provide selected hospitals with an opportunity for educational review, and payment penalties will only be assessed if a hospital does not submit requested records. If a hospital does not submit at least 75 percent of the requested records for the applicable eCQM under validation, the hospital will fail validation even during this unscored period.
Comments Regarding the Educational Review Process
Comment:
A few commenters supported expanding the educational review process to eCQMs and allowing educational results from all four quarters of chart-abstracted measure validation to be included in the final validation scores. These commenters stated that hospitals should have a meaningful opportunity to identify and resolve questions or errors in their validation results before those results affect payment.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support and agree that educational reviews are a meaningful opportunity to address questions and errors in validation results.
We are finalizing the educational review process to include the last quarter of chart-abstracted measures and to integrate eCQMs into the final validation scores.

F. Payment Reduction for Hospitals That Fail To Meet the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting (OQR) Program Requirements for the CY 2027 Payment Determination
1. Background
Section 1833(t)(17) of the Act, which applies to subsection (d) hospitals (as defined under section 1886(d)(1)(B) of the Act), states that hospitals that fail to report data required to be submitted on measures selected by the Secretary, in the form and manner, and at a time, specified by the Secretary will incur a 2.0-percentage point reduction to their OPD fee schedule increase factor; that is, the annual payment update factor. Section 1833(t)(17)(A)(ii) of the Act specifies that any reduction applies only to the payment year involved and will not be taken into account in computing the applicable OPD fee schedule increase factor for a subsequent year.
The application of a reduced OPD fee schedule increase factor results in reduced national unadjusted payment rates that apply to certain outpatient items and services provided by hospitals that are required to report outpatient quality data in order to receive the full payment update factor and that fail to meet the Hospital OQR Program requirements. Hospitals that meet the reporting requirements receive the full OPPS payment update without the reduction. For a more detailed discussion of how this payment reduction was initially implemented, we refer readers to the CY 2009 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
73 FR 68769
through
68772
).
The national unadjusted payment rates for many services paid under the OPPS equal the product of the OPPS conversion factor and the scaled relative payment weight for the APC to which the service is assigned. The OPPS conversion factor, which is updated annually by the OPD fee schedule increase factor, is used to calculate the OPPS payment rate for services with the following status indicators (listed in Addendum B to this final rule with comment period, which is available via the internet on the CMS website): “J1”, “J2”, “P”, “Q1”, “Q2”, “Q3”, “R”, “S”, “T”, “V”, or “U”. Payment for all services assigned to these status indicators will be subject to the reduction of the national unadjusted payment rates for hospitals that fail to meet Hospital OQR Program requirements, with the exception of services assigned to New Technology APCs with assigned status indicator “S” or “T”. We refer readers to the CY 2009 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
73 FR 68770
through
68771
) for a discussion of this policy. In the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
81 FR 79796
), we clarified that the reporting ratio does not apply to codes with status indicator “Q4” because services and procedures coded with status indicator “Q4” are either packaged or paid through the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule and are never paid separately through the OPPS.
The OPD fee schedule increase factor is an input into the OPPS conversion factor, which is used to calculate OPPS payment rates. To reduce the OPD fee schedule increase factor for hospitals that fail to meet reporting requirements, we calculate two conversion factors—a full market basket conversion factor (that is, the full conversion factor), and a reduced market basket conversion factor (that is, the reduced conversion factor). We then calculate a reduction ratio by dividing the reduced conversion factor by the full conversion factor. We refer to this reduction ratio as the “reporting ratio” to indicate that it applies to payment for hospitals that fail to meet their reporting requirements. Applying this reporting ratio to the OPPS payment amounts results in reduced national unadjusted payment rates that are mathematically equivalent to the reduced national unadjusted payment rates that would result if we multiplied the scaled OPPS relative payment weights by the reduced conversion factor. For example, to determine the reduced national unadjusted payment rates that applied to hospitals that failed to meet their quality reporting requirements for the CY 2010 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we multiplied the final full national unadjusted payment
(
printed page 70699)
rate found in Addendum B of the CY 2010 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period by the CY 2010 OPPS final rule with comment period reporting ratio of 0.980 (
74 FR 60642
).
We note that the only difference in the calculation for the full conversion factor and the calculation for the reduced conversion factor is that the full conversion factor uses the full OPD update, and the reduced conversion factor uses the reduced OPD update. The baseline OPPS conversion factor calculation is the same since all other adjustments would be applied to both conversion factor calculations. Therefore, our standard approach of calculating the reporting ratio as described earlier in this section is equivalent to dividing the reduced OPD update factor by that of the full OPD update factor. In other words:
Full Conversion Factor = Baseline OPPS conversion factor * (1 + OPD update factor)
Reduced Conversion Factor = Baseline OPPS conversion factor * (1 + OPD update factor−0.02)
Reporting Ratio = Reduced Conversion Factor/Full Conversion Factor
Which is equivalent to:
Reporting Ratio = (1 + OPD Update factor−0.02)/(1 + OPD update factor)
In the CY 2009 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
73 FR 68771
through
68772
), we established a policy that the Medicare beneficiary's minimum unadjusted copayment and national unadjusted copayment for a service to which a reduced national unadjusted payment rate applies would each equal the product of the reporting ratio and the national unadjusted copayment or the minimum unadjusted copayment, as applicable, for the service. Under this policy, we apply the reporting ratio to both the minimum unadjusted copayment and national unadjusted copayment for services provided by hospitals that receive the payment reduction for failure to meet the Hospital OQR Program reporting requirements. This application of the reporting ratio to the national unadjusted and minimum unadjusted copayments is calculated according to § 419.41 of our regulations, prior to any adjustment for a hospital's failure to meet the quality reporting standards according to § 419.43(h). Beneficiaries and secondary payers thereby share in the reduction of payments to these hospitals.
In the CY 2009 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (

For example, the following standard adjustments apply to the reduced national unadjusted payment rates: the wage index adjustment, the multiple procedure adjustment, the interrupted procedure adjustment, the rural sole community hospital adjustment, and the adjustment for devices furnished with full or partial credit or without cost. Similarly, OPPS outlier payments made for high cost and complex procedures will continue to be made when outlier criteria are met. For hospitals that fail to meet the quality data reporting requirements, the hospitals' costs are compared to the reduced payments for purposes of outlier eligibility and payment calculation. C. Request for Information on Stratification of the All-Cause Hospital Transfer/Admission Measure
We previously adopted the All-Cause Hospital Transfer/Admission measure in the ASC Quality Reporting Program in the CY 2012 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
76 FR 74499
). The All-Cause Hospital Transfer/Admission measure is an outcome measure that assesses the rate of patients receiving care in an ASC who require transfer to a hospital or admission to a hospital upon discharge from the ASC. Currently, the measure does not distinguish the phase of care in which a transfer occurs (pre-procedure, intra-procedure, or post-procedure).
[
209
]
As reported in MedPAC's 2025 Report to Congress, extracapsular cataract removal with intraocular lens insertion was the most common Medicare Fee-for-Service procedure performed by ASCs in 2023, accounting for 19 percent of all ASC Fee-for-Service volume. In addition, a substantial number of ASCs that bill Medicare specialize in a single clinical area, with gastroenterology and ophthalmology among the most common specialties providing services to Medicare beneficiaries.
[
210
]
A recent retrospective study which examined the causes and timing of direct hospital transfers from an ophthalmology-specific surgery center over a 2-year period reported that about 77 percent of hospital transfers were associated with concerns identified prior to the induction of anesthesia, including transfers identified in the preoperative area or upon connection to monitoring equipment in the operating room.
[
211
]
Nearly 23 percent of these transfers were directly related to anesthesia or the surgical procedure, including events occurring during induction or intraoperatively. These findings suggest that the majority of hospital transfers from ophthalmology-specific ASCs could be occurring preoperatively rather than procedural complications. While many of these events occur prior to anesthesia induction, they are often identified during anesthesia-led pre-procedure evaluation, reflecting important safety checks in patient assessment.
[
212
]
Based on these findings and discussions with interested parties, we considered whether adding a phase-of-care stratification relative to the surgical encounter (for example, pre-procedure, intra-procedure, and post-procedure) could improve the interpretability and usefulness of the All-Cause Hospital Transfer/Admission measure in the ASC Quality Reporting Program. The current measure reports an overall rate of transfers/admissions and does not specify when during the ASC encounter the need for transfer/admission is identified. Stratification by phase of care would improve attribution and interpretability across the diverse range of ASC services, including nonoperative procedures such as those associated with pain management, for hospital transfers/admissions associated with ASC care.
It is important to measure and monitor transfers/admissions that occur pre-procedure, intra-procedure, and post-procedure, as each stratum could provide insight into care processes between facilities. Pre-procedure events may reflect the effectiveness of pre-procedure evaluation, patient selection, and escalation or transfer processes, while intra-procedure and post-procedure events may be more closely associated with anesthesia administration, the procedure itself, and immediate recovery, including complications that arise during or after the ASC encounter. A phase-of-care stratification may also provide more comprehensive information to support beneficiary decision-making and patient safety monitoring.
We sought public comment on clinically meaningful and operationally feasible approaches for including a phase-of-care stratification for the All-Cause Hospital Transfer/Admission measure. Specifically, we requested input on potential stratification frameworks, including appropriate time anchors, their operational definitions, and the corresponding time windows that could be used to define each stratification category.
We received public comments on these topics. The following is a summary of the comments we received:
Comment:
Many commenters supported stratifying the All-Cause Hospital Transfer/Admission measure by phase of care, stating that the current measure combines events occurring under different clinical circumstances and therefore provides limited information about when or why a transfer or admission occurred. Many commenters stated that phase-of-care stratification could improve the measure's usefulness and ease of interpretation, support attribution and quality improvement, and provide more meaningful information about patient safety and the circumstances surrounding transfers. Several commenters specifically noted that preoperative transfers may reflect the identification of previously unrecognized clinical conditions, appropriate patient selection, or other safety-related clinical decisions rather than complications associated with the procedure.
Many commenters recommended distinguishing transfers occurring during the pre-procedure, intra-procedure, and post-procedure phases, although commenters differed regarding the precise definitions and boundaries.
(
printed page 70703)
Several commenters recommended using specific clinical or workflow events, including anesthesia or procedure start, procedure completion, entry into or exit from the operating or procedural setting, arrival in recovery, and discharge, as phase boundaries. A commenter specifically recommended using procedure start and stop times rather than anesthesia start and stop times because not all procedures involve anesthesia and an anesthesia-based anchor could limit completeness and comparability. A few commenters recommended determining the phase based on when the condition or need for transfer is first identified rather than when the patient physically leaves the ASC, while a few commenters proposed broader groupings, including combining intra- and post-procedure events. A commenter also recommended that CMS partner with measure developers and other interested parties to design and test methods for stratification.
Many commenters supported stratification while emphasizing that CMS should address potential unintended consequences in developing and using the measure. Several commenters recommended accounting for patient complexity, case mix, procedural risk, clinical context, or differences among patients, procedures, and facilities to avoid misleading comparisons or inappropriate attribution. Several commenters also emphasized that the measure should not create incentives to avoid, delay, or otherwise discourage medically appropriate transfers or treatment of patients with greater clinical complexity. A commenter further cautioned against attributing events to ASCs when they are not reasonably within the facility's control, noting that pre-procedure transfers may result from incomplete clearance, changes in patient condition, or appropriate referral decisions, while post-discharge hospital encounters may reflect unrelated acute illness, patient non-adherence, chronic conditions, or other events not reasonably predictable or preventable by the ASC. Several commenters raised concerns about validity, reliability, attribution, statistical stability, or the need for testing before phase-specific results are used for comparison, payment, public reporting, or other consequential purposes; a few commenters specifically raised concerns about small numbers or statistically unstable phase-specific rates.
Several commenters recommended considering information beyond phase of care to provide additional context for interpreting transfers and admissions. A few commenters recommended including information about the reason for or appropriateness of a transfer, including distinctions between potentially preventable events and medically appropriate escalation of care. A few commenters recommended consideration of downstream outcomes or information available from other care settings, while a few commenters recommended including additional patient, procedure, facility, or other characteristics because phase of care alone may not fully explain differences in transfer or admission rates. Several commenters also addressed implementation and data requirements. A few commenters recommended using information already available in clinical documentation, claims, or other existing data infrastructure where possible to limit additional reporting requirements. A few commenters recommended clear definitions, guidance, or examples to support consistent implementation, and a few commenters emphasized the need for consistently recorded or structured data to support reliable phase classification.
Several commenters raised concerns about how phase-specific results would be reported and used. A few commenters recommended limiting public reporting, comparison, payment, or other consequential uses until the methodology is established or the results are sufficiently reliable, while a few commenters expressed concern that patients or other users could misunderstand phase-specific results and recommended clear explanations to support appropriate interpretation. A few commenters recommended retaining the overall All-Cause Hospital Transfer/Admission measure while adding phase-of-care stratified results. A commenter stated that retaining the overall measure would preserve information for public reporting and consumer decision-making, while another commenter stated that it would preserve a broad patient-safety signal while providing additional context about the circumstances contributing to that signal.
A few commenters did not support phase-of-care stratification at this time or questioned whether stratification by phase of care alone would provide sufficiently meaningful or actionable information. A few commenters cited differences in phase-specific transfer rates across datasets. Specifically, a commenter cited their own internal data aggregated across more than a thousand ASCs where most transfers occurred postoperatively, which contrasted from the study from a single-specialty ophthalmology ASC in which the majority occurred preoperatively.
[
213
]
The commenter stated that these differences raised questions about whether phase-only stratification alone would be meaningful, and suggested further stratification by single-specialty or multi-specialty status, case type, and characteristics of the patient population may be needed to produce actionable information. One of these commenters supplied the example of a single facility with a high pre-surgery transfer rate to support this view. The same commenter also questioned whether the additional burden of phase-of-care stratification would provide information sufficiently useful and valuable to warrant the effort. A commenter recommended that CMS remove the All-Cause Hospital Transfer/Admission measure altogether to reduce administrative burden and streamline reporting requirements.
Response:
We appreciate all the comments on this topic. While we are not responding to specific comments in response to the RFI in this final rule, we believe that this input is very valuable and will continue to take such comments into account for a potential future stratification of the All-Cause Hospital Transfer/Admission measure that may be proposed in future rulemaking.

XVIII. Accrediting Organization (AO) Deeming Authority for the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA)
A. Background
The Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA) was enacted in 1986 and codified at section 1867 of the Act (
42 U.S.C. 1395dd
) to address concerns regarding the inappropriate transfer of, or refusal to treat individuals with emergency medical conditions who are seeking emergency department care, commonly referred to as “patient dumping.” EMTALA applies to hospitals that participate in Medicare and operate emergency departments, including critical access hospitals (CAHs) and rural emergency hospitals (REHs). For purposes of this discussion, the term “hospitals” includes CAHs and REHs. To enroll and be qualified to participate in Medicare under section 1866(a)(1)(I) of the Act (
42 U.S.C. 1395cc(a)(1)(I)
), all such hospitals must agree to comply with EMTALA's statutory and regulatory requirements, among other applicable requirements.
Section 1867 of the Act establishes the three core obligations of EMTALA.
First, when an individual comes to a hospital's emergency department and requests examination or treatment, the hospital must provide an appropriate medical screening examination to determine whether an emergency medical condition exists.
Second, if the hospital determines that the individual has an emergency medical condition, the hospital must provide either necessary stabilizing treatment within its capability or arrange for an appropriate transfer to another medical facility. Note, when assessing whether there is an emergency medical condition with respect to a pregnant woman, consideration has to be given to whether the condition places the health of the woman or the unborn child in serious jeopardy, and with respect to a pregnant woman having contractions, it requires consideration of whether a transfer would pose a threat to the health or safety of the woman or the unborn child.
Third, hospitals with specialized capabilities or facilities shall not refuse to accept appropriate transfers of individuals requiring such capabilities or facilities if the receiving hospital has the capacity to treat the individual. The statute also authorizes the imposition by the Office of Inspector General (OIG) of civil monetary penalties against hospitals and physicians and, for physicians, exclusion from participation in Federal health care programs for violations, and permits the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) to impose involuntary termination of a hospital's Medicare provider agreement for non-compliance in accordance with
42 CFR 489.53
.
CMS has implemented EMTALA through regulations at
42 CFR 489.20
and
489.24
, which address two distinct categories of obligations. Section 489.20(l), (m), (q) and (r) sets forth administrative requirements, including to post EMTALA signage, maintain a central log of individuals who present to the emergency department, retain transfer records for 5 years, and maintain an on-call physician list. These administrative obligations support transparency, documentation, and accountability in emergency care operations. These requirements are provider agreement commitments and obligations hospitals accept as a condition of Medicare participation under section 1866(a)(1)(I) of the Act. They are distinct from the substantive individual care protections at § 489.24.
Section 489.24 implements the statute's substantive protection requirements for individuals who present to the emergency department and request examination or treatment, including detailed provisions governing the provision of appropriate medical screening examinations, stabilizing treatment, appropriate transfers, and receiving hospital responsibilities. These requirements reflect the core protections established by section 1867 of the Act and are directly enforceable by CMS and/or the OIG.
Enforcement of EMTALA has historically occurred through complaint investigations conducted by State Survey Agencies (SAs) under CMS direction. Pursuant to § 488.6, CMS “deems” a hospital to meet Medicare requirements if it is accredited by an AO with a hospital accreditation program approved by CMS. CMS will approve such organizations if it finds that its standards and survey processes provide reasonable assurance that accredited entities meet or exceed applicable Medicare requirements. Hospitals accredited by such AOs are deemed to meet the Medicare Conditions of Participation (CoPs) but are subject to CMS validation surveys and complaint investigations in accordance with existing CMS policies and procedures. More than 90 percent of Medicare-participating hospitals (excluding CAHs and REHs) and more than 40 percent of CAHs, independent of hospitals, are accredited by AOs with CMS-approved accreditation programs. At this time, no REHs are deemed to meet requirements through a CMS-approved accreditation program.
We proposed that if an AO identifies EMTALA deficiencies at § 489.24 during an accreditation or reaccreditation survey, the matter must be referred to the CMS location for further review and possible SA investigation. If an AO identifies EMTALA deficiencies at § 489.20(l), (m), (q) and (r), they would require the hospital or CAH to submit an acceptable Plan of Correction (PoC) addressing how it would come into compliance with the cited EMTALA requirements. If the PoC is accepted and the hospital has returned to compliance, then no further enforcement action would be taken. If the PoC is rejected, the AO would be required to contact the CMS location for further review. Under § 488.5(a)(4)(ix), AOs are already required to notify CMS timely if an AO survey identifies an “immediate jeopardy.” The proposed EMTALA requirement would augment the already-existing reporting requirement. If a complaint alleging an EMTALA violation is received by CMS (or the SA acting under an agreement pursuant to section 1864 of the Act), it would be triaged to determine its investigation
(
printed page 70706)
priority level. The SA or CMS conducts an onsite investigation, and if a violation is identified, a deficiency is cited and the survey findings are documented. Currently the CMS location refers § 489.24 violations to the OIG, which has independent statutory authority to impose civil money penalties against hospitals and physicians, and potential exclusion of physicians from Federal health care programs. CMS retains the authority to terminate a hospital's Medicare provider agreement for EMTALA noncompliance at § 489.53.
In CY 2025, we issued 1,071 EMTALA citations for violations of the two applicable regulations, underscoring the need for Medicare-participating hospitals to comply with emergency care obligations. Of these, 521 citations were issued under § 489.20 requirements, 530 citations were issued under § 489.24, and 20 citations were issued under both §§ 489.20 and 489.24. Section 489.24 is the more expansive regulation governing the specific medical screening, stabilization, and transfer requirements hospitals must fulfill when an individual requests emergency care. Administrative compliance under § 489.20 appears to be a leading indicator of overall EMTALA program integrity. A hospital that cannot maintain accurate on-call logs, post required notices, or retain transfer documentation is a hospital whose broader EMTALA compliance posture warrants closer scrutiny. Including a structured, thorough review of § 489.20 requirements into every hospital survey is essential to fulfilling the protective intent of EMTALA. The inclusion of the requirements at § 489.20(l), (m), (q) and (r) into the accreditation and reaccreditation survey process mean that AOs would assess whether hospitals are maintaining the documentation, recordkeeping, and operational safeguards that support transparency and accountability in emergency care. Because these obligations are record-based and procedural, we proposed to review AO survey processes as part of our hospital accreditation program approval to check that EMTALA requirements are included within the existing accreditation framework.
It should be noted that findings related to potential § 489.24 violations must be referred to CMS for SA investigation and those findings would continue to follow existing public disclosure procedures applicable to complaint-based SA investigations, which are separate from AO accreditation survey reports. Section 1865(b) of the Act explicitly permits the Secretary to publicly disclose AO surveys and information related to them to the extent that such surveys and information relate to an enforcement action taken by the Secretary.
Our regulations at
42 CFR part 488
govern AO approval and oversight. The proposal we are finalizing in this rule will operate within section 1865 of the Act and part 488 statutory and regulatory structures by integrating review of EMTALA's administrative requirements into existing accreditation organization processes for accrediting and re-accrediting hospitals, while preserving CMS and OIG enforcement authority over EMTALA's core statutory protections under section 1867 of the Act. We anticipate several benefits associated with this change. First, integrating EMTALA administrative review into accreditation and CMS or state survey agency certification surveys would minimize operational disruption for hospitals. Rather than undergoing separate review processes triggered by administrative deficiencies, hospitals will be able to address these requirements within the structured accreditation or state survey framework.
Second, this policy may improve compliance consistent with the documentation and operational safeguards at § 489.20(l), (m), (q) and (r). Because these requirements are record-based and procedural in nature, they are well-suited to routine survey evaluation. Regular review during accreditation and recertification surveys may enhance sustained compliance.
Third, this final rule with comment period will allow SAs to concentrate more resources on complaint-based investigations involving potential violations of § 489.24, including issues related to appropriate medical screening examinations, stabilizing treatment, and appropriate transfers. These investigations often require case-specific fact-finding and clinical review, and preserving SA capacity for these activities supports effective enforcement of EMTALA's core protections.
Nothing in this final rule with comment period alters a hospital's obligations under Federal civil rights conscience (protections) laws, or the authority of the HHS Office for Civil Rights to enforce those laws.
B. CMS Approval of Accreditation Organizations
We proposed to clarify at § 488.5(a) that an AO with a CMS-approved accrediting program for hospitals under section 1865 of the Act may assess compliance with the EMTALA-related administrative requirements set forth at § 489.20(l), (m), (q) and (r) as part of their hospital initial accreditation and reaccreditation surveys, which must be completed no later than 36 months after the prior accreditation effective date consistent with § 488.5(a)(4), for those provider types. This proposal was limited to AOs conducting initial accreditation or reaccreditation surveys within the scope of their existing CMS-approved accrediting programs. This amendment would formally require CMS-approved AOs to include review of these specified EMTALA obligations into the existing accreditation framework, while preserving CMS' direct enforcement authority over EMTALA's core statutory protections.
As proposed, AOs would evaluate hospital compliance with the administrative commitments codified at § 489.20(l), (m), (q) and (r), including requirements to post appropriate EMTALA signage; maintain a central log of individuals who present to the emergency department; retain transfer records for a period of 5 years; and maintain an on-call physician list to ensure availability of specialty services. These obligations are documentary and administrative in nature, are well-established in regulation, and are conducive to structured review within the context of accreditation and reaccreditation surveys.
If an AO identified noncompliance with any of the EMTALA administrative requirements at § 489.20(l), (m), (q) and (r), the AO would cite the deficiency and address it through its established procedures, consistent with the procedures it used to address other Medicare deficiencies identified during accreditation and reaccreditation surveys. This would include requiring corrective action plans, monitoring compliance, and reporting findings to CMS in accordance with existing oversight and validation protocols. CMS would retain ultimate oversight responsibility and could take additional action as appropriate under its survey and enforcement authorities.
We believe that the administrative requirements at § 489.20(l), (m), (q) and (r) are appropriate for evaluation during initial accreditation and reaccreditation surveys. Integrating review of these provisions into the AO survey process would promote more consistent monitoring of established documentation and recordkeeping obligations, reduce duplicative investigations triggered solely by administrative concerns, and minimize disruption to hospital operations. At the same time, this approach would allow SAs to concentrate their resources on complaint-based investigations
(
printed page 70707)
involving potential violations of § 489.24.
To implement this proposal, we proposed to revise § 488.5 by adding a new paragraph (a)(23), laying out the AO's responsibility to include the EMTALA administrative requirements into its accreditation standards and survey processes and to identify and address noncompliance with those provisions within the deeming framework.
C. Evaluation of Accreditation Authority Request
AOs would have to document the procedures used to assess compliance with these requirements and would be required to cite and address any identified deficiencies through their established accreditation procedures, consistent with the procedures used to address Medicare deficiencies identified during accreditation and reaccreditation surveys.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Commenters generally supported CMS's proposal to have AOs review administrative EMTALA requirements (signage, logs, transfer records, and on-call lists) during accreditation surveys, provided CMS retains ultimate enforcement authority over substantive EMTALA protections.
Response:
We appreciate the broad support for this proposal and confirm that this rule does not delegate authority over substantive EMTALA determinations, including allegations involving inadequate screening, failure to stabilize, or improper transfer to AOs. CMS and SAs will continue to investigate and adjudicate all substantive EMTALA complaints and immediate jeopardy findings as well as review and investigate AO referrals regarding the administrative EMTALA requirements. The scope of AO review under this rule is limited to the administrative elements specified in the proposed rule. We are finalizing as proposed, with the clarifications discussed below.
Comment:
Two commenters recommended a transition period, suggesting through at least CY2028 before full implementation, to allow AOs, SAs, and hospitals time to align processes.
Response:
The AOs with hospital deeming programs will need to first submit applications to update their accreditation programs to include review of the EMTALA administrative requirements and submit them to CMS for approval before an AO can start surveying for the EMTALA administrative requirements. Accordingly, we do not believe a transition period is needed.
Comment:
Two commenters raised concerns that expanded AO survey responsibilities could result in duplicative or conflicting requirements if not applied consistently across AOs and SAs.
Response:
We intend to issue standardized interpretive guidance and survey protocols specific to the administrative EMTALA elements, which all approved AO accreditation programs should include in their own standards. This guidance will clearly delineate the respective roles of AOs, SAs, and hospitals: AOs with hospital deeming programs will assess the specified administrative documentation and postings during regular accreditation and reaccreditation surveys, while SAs will retain jurisdiction over complaint-driven and substantive EMTALA investigations.
In addition, our guidance will affirm that compliance with the administrative requirements at § 489.20(l), (m), (q), and (r) is distinct from, and does not establish compliance with, Federal civil rights conscience (protections) laws; and that individuals retain the right to file a complaint with the HHS Office for Civil Rights. OCR staff are available to review the civil rights content of that material at CMS's request.
Comment:
One commenter requested rigorous reviewer qualifications and EMTALA-specific training for AO surveyors and cautioned against shifting hospital-level administrative compliance burden onto individual physicians.
Response:
We agree that surveyor competency is essential to consistent application of these requirements. We will require AOs to demonstrate that surveyors assigned to EMTALA administrative reviews have completed CMS-approved EMTALA training prior to conducting these assessments, as a condition of AO approval. We also clarify that the administrative requirements addressed by this rule are hospital-level requirements. Nothing in this rule shifts EMTALA compliance responsibility from the hospital to individual physicians, and we do not intend for AO findings related to these administrative requirements to be used as a basis for adverse action against individual practitioners.
Comment:
Several commenters cautioned against “scope creep,” urging that AO reviews remain confined to administrative requirements and not expand into substantive EMTALA screening or stabilization determinations, and called for a single, nationally standardized enforcement framework.
Response:
We confirm that the scope of AO survey activity under this rule is limited to the administrative requirements and does not extend to clinical screening, stabilization, or transfer-decision review requirements at § 489.24, which remain within CMS and SA exclusive investigation authority.
Comment:
One commenter recommended that CMS apply lessons learned from AOs' prior experience with EMTALA-adjacent survey activity.
Response:
We will draw on existing AO deeming experience, including prior CMS validation surveys and complaint outcome data, to inform the interpretive guidance and training requirements discussed previously, and will continue to use our validation survey process to monitor AO performance on these administrative EMTALA elements after implementation.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing these provisions as proposed.
