B. Controlling Unnecessary Increases in the Volume of Covered OPD Services
In accordance with § 419.83(b), we proposed to expand prior authorization requirements to include additional Botulinum Toxin Injection services. The eight additional Botulinum Toxin Injection codes would be included in the existing list at proposed revised § 419.83(a)(2) and would require prior authorization for services provided on or after July 1, 2027. Additionally, to improve readability and brevity, we proposed to remove effective date language from the regulatory text and revise the section numbering. The former paragraphs (a)(1)(i) through (v), (a)(2)(i) and (ii), and (a)(3) would be redesignated as paragraphs (a)(1) through (8).
1. Expansion of Service Category
The additional Botulinum Toxin Injection codes that would require prior authorization beginning on July 1, 2027, are those identified by the HCPCS codes in Table 102. For ease of reference, in Table 102 we have included the 2020, 2021, and 2023 Final Lists of Outpatient Services that Require Prior Authorization, covering the five initial service categories, two additional service categories, and one more service category, respectively. As we mentioned previously, we proposed to include additional codes in the existing Botulinum Toxin Injections service category that was established through the CY 2020 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period.
2. Basis for Expanding Service Category
As part of our responsibility to protect the Medicare Trust Funds, we routinely analyze data associated with all aspects of the Medicare program. This responsibility includes monitoring the total amount or types of claims submitted by providers; analyzing the claims data to assess the growth in the number of claims submitted over time (for example, monthly and annually, among other intervals); and conducting comparisons of the data with other relevant data, such as the total number of Medicare beneficiaries served by providers, to help ensure the continued appropriateness of payment for services furnished in the hospital OPD setting.
In proposing the addition of these new services, we reviewed over 100 million OPD claims from 2017 through 2024. We determined that, on average, the number of OPD claims submitted for payment to the Medicare program decreased yearly by 1.1 percent. This reflects a decrease from approximately 114 million OPD claims submitted for payment in 2017 to approximately 104 million claims submitted for payment in 2024, with claim counts rounded for reporting purposes. The 1.1 percent decrease in overall OPD claims annually represents a decrease compared to the 0.6 percent increase identified in the CY 2023 OPPS/ASC proposed rule when we looked at the period from 2012 through 2021. Our analysis also showed that the Medicare allowed amount (the amount Medicare would pay for services regardless of external variables, such as beneficiary plan differences, deductibles, and appeals) for overall OPD claims increased from approximately $53.1 billion in 2017 to approximately $69.8 billion in 2024, representing an average annualized growth rate of 3.5 percent. Again, this is a decrease when compared to the 4.2 percent rate of growth identified in the CY 2023 OPPS/ASC proposed rule from 2012 through 2021. This analysis provides a benchmark regarding overall Medicare spending trends for OPD services during the same period.
In contrast to overall OPD utilization trends, utilization of all Botulinum Toxin Injection codes listed in Table 102 (2027 List of Additional Outpatient Department Services That Require Prior Authorization) has grown at a notably higher rate. This difference suggests that these services are increasing faster than overall OPD utilization, which warrants further review to ensure appropriate utilization. Our analysis of Integrated Data Repository (IDR)
[
219
]
data showed that claim volume for Botulinum Toxin Injection codes listed in Table 102 increased by 42.8 percent overall between 2017 and 2024
[
220
]
, based on a direct comparison of claims volume in 2017 and 2024, and there was a 4.6 percent average annualized growth rate increase during the same time period. Specifically, claims volume for the additional Botulinum Toxin Injection codes increased from approximately 43,500 claims submitted for payment in 2017 to approximately 62,103 claims submitted for payment in 2024. By comparison, the overall OPD claims volume decreased by 8.3 percent between 2017 and 2024
[
221
]
, based on a direct comparison of total OPD claims in 2017 and 2024, and by the 1.1 percent average annualized rate decrease in OPD claims submitted for payment during the same time period. We also examined claims for each of the seven injection procedure codes proposed for addition to the prior authorization list. Between 2017 and 2024, claims containing HCPCS CPT 64611 increased from 2,788 to 5,124, or 83.8 percent. Claims containing CPT 64616 increased from 15,502 to 22,934 (47.9 percent); CPT 64617 from 3,573 to 3,951 (10.6 percent); CPT 64642 from 12,469 to 17,914 (43.7 percent); CPT 64644 from 9,913 to 14,303 (44.3 percent); CPT 64646 from 1,970 to 2,914 (47.9 percent); and CPT 64647 from 322 to 355 (10.2 percent). CPT codes 64616, 64642, and 64644 had the largest increases in the number of claims.
We also recognize that additional FDA-approved indications for botulinum toxin products during this period may have contributed to some increase in utilization. We reviewed new FDA-approved indications from 2017 through 2024 and principal diagnoses on botulinum toxin injection claims. Claims potentially related to expanded indications increased from 1,731 in 2017 to 3,354 in 2024 but remained a small share of the claims analyzed. However, the newly approved
(
printed page 70709)
indications represent a limited number of additional clinical uses and are not expected to account for the full magnitude of the observed increase in utilization, suggesting that other factors may also be contributing. Accordingly, we do not believe that expanded indications alone fully explain the magnitude of the observed growth, which suggests that other factors may also be contributing to increased utilization. Specifically, overall OPD claims decreased from approximately 114 million unique claims in 2017 to approximately 104 million unique claims in 2024. The codes included in our proposal represent approximately $102 million in annual Medicare payments and constitute a subset of overall botulinum toxin utilization selected based on observed utilization volume, growth trends, and program integrity considerations.
When analyzing the data, we took the COVID-19 Public Health Emergency (PHE) into consideration. As a result of the PHE, health care use and spending dropped sharply due to cancellations of elective and non-emergency care to increase hospital capacity and social distancing measures to reduce the community spread of the coronavirus. Consequently, the claims data for CY 2020 showed a notable decrease in volume of services compared to the previous year. This decline in CY 2020 due to the PHE is reflected in the overall trend for the 2017 through 2024 period, including calculations of the 1.1 percent average annualized decrease in OPD claims submitted for payment over the 2017 through 2024 period discussed previously, which is based on year-over-year changes across all years in the period, including CY 2020. Although a decline in utilization was observed in CY 2020, claims volume for these services increased significantly in subsequent years and exceeded levels that would have been reasonably expected based on overall OPD utilization trends. Accordingly, we do not believe any claim decreases resulting from the PHE affect our conclusion that there were “unnecessary increases in the volume of covered” claims for these services. This determination is based on several considerations, including utilization growth for Botulinum Toxin Injection services substantially exceeding overall OPD utilization trends during the same period, despite overall OPD claims volume declining. In addition, the increased utilization persisted over multiple years rather than reflecting a temporary fluctuation. CMS also reviewed potential explanations for the increase in utilization, including changes in clinical need, coding changes, and other factors that could reasonably explain sustained growth in service volume, but did not identify sufficient evidence to account for the magnitude of the increase observed. CMS further considered broader program integrity concerns, including billing patterns and utilization trends that may indicate a risk of unnecessary utilization.
Our conclusion that increases in volume for Botulinum Toxin Injections are unnecessary is based not only on data specific to these services but also on a comparison of the rate of increase for these procedures to the overall trends for all OPD services. We believe that comparing the utilization rate for specific services to the overall Medicare OPD utilization trends is generally an appropriate method for identifying unnecessary increases in volume, particularly when there are no legitimate clinical or coding reasons for the changes. The Medicare allowed amount analysis discussed above provides additional information regarding broader Medicare spending trends during the same period. As we have stated in the previous OPPS/ASC final rules with comment period, we believe that prior authorization is an effective mechanism to ensure Medicare beneficiaries receive medically necessary care while protecting the Medicare Trust Funds from unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD Services without adding onerous new documentation requirements. Therefore, we believe prior authorization for these additional codes will be an effective method for controlling unnecessary increases in the volume of these services and expect that it will reduce the instances in which Medicare pays for services that are determined not to be medically necessary. This will also serve as a tool within CMS' broad program integrity strategy to address potential fraud, waste, and abuse. We requested comments on the addition of these new services, specifically on the potential for unintended clinical consequences that may result from this addition.
We received 122 public comments on this proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed support for CMS's efforts to improve interoperability, streamline prior authorization, and reduce administrative burden.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support of CMS's efforts to improve interoperability, streamline prior authorization processes, promote appropriate utilization of Medicare resources, and reduce administrative burden. We remain committed to improving the efficiency of prior authorization processes while supporting appropriate access to care.
Comment:
A couple of commenters noted that consumers may be unable to determine whether a service requires prior authorization.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' concern regarding access to information about prior authorization requirements. Regarding Medicare Fee-for-Service, prior authorization requirements apply only to certain items and services. CMS and the Medicare Administrative Contractors (MACs) make information regarding applicable prior authorization requirements publicly available. In addition, MAC websites generally provide tools or searchable resources that allow providers to determine whether a particular service or procedure is subject to prior authorization requirements. Accordingly, providers can consult the applicable MAC's resources to identify whether prior authorization is required for a service before it is furnished.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS require or encourage the use of structured, auditable, clinician-owned clinical logic frameworks for prior authorization while preserving licensed clinician oversight of final determinations. The commenter also recommended clinician-owned, auditable governance for SI-assisted prior authorization decisions and cited recent developments involving the WISeR Model as an example of the importance of transparency and clinical accountability in SI-enabled utilization management. The commenter urged CMS to consider these principles as it implements the hospital OPD program.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's recommendations regarding the use of structured, auditable clinical logic frameworks in prior authorization processes while maintaining licensed clinician authority over final determinations. The hospital OPD prior authorization program has been operational since 2020. We will consider the comments regarding transparency, auditability, interoperability, and clinician oversight as we evaluate policies for the hospital OPD program and future rulemaking. To the extent the comment references the WISeR Model, that model is a separate CMS Innovation Center (CMMI) model and is outside the scope of this rulemaking. Comments specific to the
(
printed page 70710)
WISeR Model should be directed to
WISeR@cms.hhs.gov
.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS include standards-based, FHIR/mCODE-enabled prior authorization using validated software as a medical service (SaMS) and pilot a structured submission pathway with automated approvals and gold-carding for qualifying providers.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's recommendations regarding the use of standards-based, interoperable technologies and automated processes to streamline prior authorization and reduce provider burden. We also appreciate the commenter's suggestions regarding structured submission pathways and exemptions, sometimes called “gold carding,” for qualifying providers. Although it is beyond the scope of our proposal, we note that the hospital OPD prior authorization process currently includes an exemption from prior authorization requirements for qualifying providers that demonstrate a high level of compliance with Medicare requirements. Under
42 CFR 419.83(c)
, CMS may exempt a provider that demonstrates compliance with Medicare coverage, coding, and payment rules. Under the current annual assessment process, a provider that submits at least 10 prior authorization requests and receives provisional affirmations for at least 90 percent of its initial requests may qualify for an exemption from submitting further requests while the exemption is in effect. CMS continues to assess exempt providers' compliance and may withdraw an exemption.
The commenter's recommendations regarding FHIR/mCODE-enabled prior authorization, validated software as a medical service (SaMS), structured submission pathways, and automated approvals are also beyond the scope of the proposed expansion of the hospital OPD prior authorization process. We note, however, that MACs may accept prior authorization requests submitted using FHIR-based approaches, as applicable. We will consider these comments as we continue to evaluate opportunities to improve and streamline prior authorization processes.
Comment:
Several commenters raised concerns regarding prior authorization for services outside the scope of the proposed expansion. One commenter expressed concerns regarding prior authorization for botulinum toxin injections used to treat certain urologic conditions. Other commenters opposed existing prior authorization requirements for cervical fusion with disc removal, facet joint interventions, and implanted spinal neurostimulator services. Another commenter urged CMS to exercise caution in any future expansion of prior authorization to metabolic and bariatric surgery services, citing potential treatment delays, patient harm, and administrative burden.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' concerns. The proposal addressed in this rule is limited to the eight additional Botulinum Toxin Injection codes identified in the proposed rule. The procedure used for botulinum toxin injection into the bladder is not among the eight additional codes proposed for inclusion in the hospital OPD prior authorization process. In addition, we did not propose changes to the existing prior authorization requirements for cervical fusion with disc removal, facet joint interventions, or implanted spinal neurostimulator services, nor did we propose to expand prior authorization to additional metabolic and bariatric surgery services. Therefore, comments and recommendations concerning prior authorization for these services are outside the scope of this rulemaking.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS issue implementation guidance sufficiently in advance of July 1, 2027, effective date for the additional botulinum toxin injection codes to allow hospitals adequate time to update prior authorization workflows and avoid disruptions to patient care.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's request. We intend to provide education and implementation guidance well in advance of the July 1, 2027, effective date to support provider preparation and facilitate implementation of the expanded prior authorization requirements. CMS currently provides guidance, educational resources, and program updates for the hospital OPD prior authorization program on the program's website, including the Operational Guide, Frequently Asked Questions, applicable HCPCS lists, and information regarding changes to program requirements and implementation timelines
[
222
]
. We intend to update these resources, as appropriate, and provide additional information through established CMS and MAC communication channels.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern that expanding prior authorization to additional botulinum toxin injection services could delay medically necessary treatment and adversely affect beneficiary access and outcomes. Commenters emphasized that these services are used to treat chronic neurologic and other disabling conditions and stated that treatment delays could result in worsening symptoms, pain, functional decline, or other complications. Some commenters noted particular concerns for beneficiaries with significant disabilities and those in rural or underserved areas.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' concerns regarding potential delays in access to medically necessary botulinum toxin injection services and the resulting impact on beneficiaries. We recognize the importance of timely treatment, particularly for beneficiaries with significant functional impairments. The Medicare prior authorization process includes established review timeframes designed to support timely access to medically necessary services. Prior authorization requests are generally reviewed within 7 calendar days for standard requests, though the average review time over the past year was 3.6 days, and expedited review within 2 business days is available when a delay could seriously jeopardize the beneficiary's life, health, or ability to regain maximum function. In addition, as noted in response to the previous comment, providers who demonstrated compliance with Medicare coverage requirements through their prior authorization affirmation rate may qualify for an exemption from prior authorization. We believe these safeguards help address concerns regarding timely beneficiary access while supporting appropriate Medicare program oversight.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that botulinum toxin injections are recurring, individualized treatments and expressed concern that requiring prior authorization for each treatment cycle could disrupt established treatment plans. Commenters also noted that a beneficiary's clinical condition and treatment needs may change between authorization and the date of service, requiring practitioners to modify the muscles treated or applicable procedure code. Commenters recommended streamlined renewals, longer authorization periods or multi-cycle authorizations for established patients, and flexibility to accommodate clinically necessary changes in treatment.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' concerns regarding the recurring and individualized nature of botulinum toxin treatment, continuity of care, and the need for clinical flexibility. Prior authorization is intended to ensure that Medicare
(
printed page 70711)
coverage, coding, and payment requirements are met before services are furnished and is not intended to interfere with the treating practitioner's clinical judgment or delay medically necessary care. We recognize that a beneficiary's clinical condition and treatment needs may change between submission of a prior authorization request and the date of service. We considered commenters' recommendations regarding flexibility for clinically necessary changes, streamlined authorization for established patients, and consideration of ongoing treatment in determining whether and how to finalize the proposal. We will continue to evaluate implementation of the prior authorization requirements and consider appropriate operational flexibilities and safeguards to support timely access to medically necessary services while protecting the Medicare Trust Funds.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern that expanding prior authorization would increase administrative burden on hospitals, physicians, and clinical staff, diverting resources from patient care. Commenters stated that the burden may include preparing and tracking requests, submitting additional documentation, responding to non-affirmations, resubmitting requests, and pursuing further review. Some commenters questioned whether CMS's burden estimates fully account for the clinical and administrative staff time associated with these activities.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' concerns regarding the administrative burden associated with prior authorization. We recognize the importance of minimizing unnecessary burden on providers and beneficiaries while supporting appropriate utilization of Medicare services. Prior authorization does not establish new Medicare coverage or documentation requirements; rather, it requires documentation supporting applicable Medicare coverage, coding, and payment requirements to be submitted before the service is furnished.
As discussed in the Collection of Information Requirements section of this final rule, we estimate that the average time for office clerical activities associated with preparing and submitting a prior authorization request is 30 minutes, which is equivalent to the time estimated for prepayment or postpayment medical review. We continue to believe that 30 minutes represents a reasonable average estimate of the time needed to prepare and submit a prior authorization request. We acknowledge that the actual time associated with an individual request may vary depending on the circumstances, including whether additional documentation or resubmission is necessary.
We will continue to monitor the program, including its impact on providers and beneficiaries.
Comment:
Several commenters questioned whether increased utilization of botulinum toxin injection services demonstrates unnecessary or inappropriate utilization. Commenters stated that utilization growth may reflect factors such as expanded indications, evolving clinical practice, improved access, changes in the Medicare population, or shifts in site of service. Commenters recommended that CMS conduct additional analysis and use more targeted program integrity approaches, such as focused medical review, provider education, Targeted Probe and Educate, post-payment review, or data-driven review of providers or utilization patterns presenting greater program integrity risk, rather than broadly expanding prior authorization.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' concerns regarding the basis for the proposed expansion. We agree that increased utilization, standing alone, does not establish that services are medically unnecessary or improperly billed. We recognize that utilization trends may be influenced by a variety of factors, including changes in approved indications, clinical practice, beneficiary access, the Medicare population, and site of service. As discussed in the proposed rule, we identified a significant increase in utilization of these services relative to overall hospital OPD utilization during the same period and acknowledged that expanded FDA-approved indications may have contributed to some of this growth. While increased utilization does not, by itself, demonstrate that services are medically unnecessary or improperly billed, the magnitude of the utilization increase supports additional oversight to ensure that applicable Medicare coverage, coding, and payment requirements are met.
We also appreciate the recommendations to use more targeted program integrity approaches. CMS uses a variety of program integrity tools based on the circumstances. Prior authorization allows CMS to review documentation before the service is furnished and the claim is submitted for payment to determine whether applicable Medicare requirements are met. It does not establish new coverage requirements or change existing Medicare coverage criteria. We believe prior authorization is an appropriate program integrity tool in these circumstances.
Comment:
Several commenters recommended that, if CMS finalizes the proposed expansion, it adopts safeguards to minimize administrative burden and disruptions in care. Recommendations included expedited review, clear and consistent criteria, streamlined processes for established patients, reduced or standardized documentation, provider exemptions for demonstrated compliance, electronic prior authorization workflows, timely appeals, and monitoring and public reporting of denials, processing times, treatment delays, beneficiary access, and other program outcomes.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' recommendations regarding safeguards to minimize administrative burden and disruptions in care. We recognize the importance of minimizing unnecessary administrative burden and avoiding disruptions in medically necessary care while ensuring that Medicare coverage, coding, and payment requirements are met.
The hospital OPD prior authorization process includes safeguards intended to reduce burden and protect beneficiary access to care. For example, the process provides for expedited review when a delay could seriously jeopardize a beneficiary's life, health, or ability to regain maximum function. This standard is not limited to the situations in which the beneficiary is recovering from an acute event. The process also includes an exemption from prior authorization requirements for qualifying providers that demonstrate a high level of compliance with Medicare requirements.
We will continue to monitor the hospital OPD prior authorization process and consider opportunities to improve transparency, automation, and standardized electronic workflows while maintaining appropriate program integrity safeguards.
Comment:
Several commenters asserted that CMS lacks statutory authority to expand prior authorization to the additional hospital OPD botulinum toxin injection services. The commenters argued that section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act does not authorize CMS to impose prior authorization requirements for hospital outpatient services.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' concerns. We disagree that we lack authority to establish prior authorization requirements for these hospital OPD services. Section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act requires the
(
printed page 70712)
Secretary to develop a method for controlling unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services. Thus, where, as here, we have determined that there have been unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services, section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act gives us authority to utilize prior authorization as a method to control those unnecessary increases. The hospital OPD prior authorization process is an appropriate exercise of this authority because it provides a mechanism to ensure that Medicare payment requirements are met before services are furnished and claims are submitted. Prior authorization does not prohibit or limit coverage of medically necessary botulinum toxin injection services that meet applicable Medicare coverage, coding, and payment requirements.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to add eight Botulinum Toxin Injection codes to the hospital OPD prior authorization process.

XX. Codification of Section 6225 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 for the Requirements for Provider-Based Status (§§ 413.65 and 419.23)
A. Background
Section 1861(u) of the Act lists the types of facilities that are regarded as providers of services but does not use or define the term “provider-based”. Since the beginning of the Medicare program, however, some providers, referred to as
main providers,
have functioned as a single entity while owning and operating multiple subordinate facilities that were treated as part of the main provider for Medicare purposes (as related to, for instance, payment; certification; coverage; and/or billing). With this treatment, compared to being treated as a freestanding facility, provider-based facilities might experience a number of advantages, including most notably, increased payments from Medicare. Therefore, we have maintained that having clear criteria for treating a facility as provider-based, as opposed to operating as a freestanding facility, is important because failure to properly distinguish between the two risks inaccurate program payments, which can result in provider overpayments and increased beneficiary coinsurance liability, with no commensurate benefit to the Medicare program or its beneficiaries. Section 413.65 specifies the criteria for treating a facility as provider-based and the requirements for a CMS determination of provider-based status, including an attestation by the provider that the facility meets the provider-based criteria. Provider compliance with provider-based rules is mandatory, but since the passage of the Medicare, Medicaid, and SCHIP Benefits Improvement and Protection Act (BIPA) of 2000 (
Pub. L. 106-554
, App'x F), a provider has needed to submit an attestation only if it wishes to obtain a CMS determination of provider-based status.
B. Requirements at Section 6225 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026
Section 6225 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (CAA, 2026),
Public Law 119-75
, enacted on February 3, 2026, amends section 1833(t) of the Act by adding new paragraph (23). In brief, section 6225 of the CAA, 2026 will prohibit Medicare payments under the OPPS beginning January 1, 2028, unless off-campus outpatient departments of a provider bill using a separate National Provider Identifier (NPI) and the main provider has submitted an attestation that the departments meet the provisions at § 413.65. As noted previously, although provider compliance with provider-based rules is mandatory, payment had not been conditioned on verification of such compliance.
Section 1833(t)(23)(A) of the Act, as added by section 6225 of the CAA, 2026, specifies that no payment may be made under that subsection (or under an applicable payment system pursuant to
(
printed page 70716)
paragraph (21) of section 1833(t) of the Act) for items and services furnished on or after January 1, 2028, by an off-campus outpatient department of a provider unless that department has obtained, and the items and services are billed under, an NPI that is separate from the NPI of the main provider; the main provider has submitted to the Secretary, during the 2-year period ending on the date such items and services are furnished, an initial provider-based status attestation that the off-campus outpatient department is compliant with the requirements described in section § 413.65 (or a successor regulation); and the main provider has submitted a subsequent attestation within the timeframe specified by the Secretary. The initial attestation may include an attestation submitted in accordance with existing § 413.65(b)(3) until the Secretary establishes the new attestation submission process, which is discussed further below.
New section 1833(t)(23)(B)(i) of the Act requires the Secretary, through notice and comment rulemaking, to establish a process for each provider with an off-campus outpatient department to submit an initial and subsequent attestation, for the review of each such attestation and for the determination, through site visits, remote audits, or other means (as determined appropriate by the Secretary), whether each off-campus outpatient department is compliant with the requirements described in subparagraph (A). In addition, new section 1833(t)(23)(C) of the Act defines an “off-campus outpatient department of a provider” for purposes of paragraph (23) as a department of a provider (as defined in § 413.65) that is not located on the campus (also defined in § 413.65) of the main provider or is not within the distance described in such definition of campus from a remote location of a hospital (also defined in § 413.65).
C. Modifications To Implement the Provisions of Section 6225 of the CAA, 2026
1. Modification to the Hospital OPPS Regulations
As discussed previously, section 1833(t)(23)(A) of the Act, as added by section 6225 of the CAA, 2026, specifies that no payment may be made under the OPPS for items and services furnished on or after January 1, 2028, by an off-campus outpatient department of a provider unless that department has obtained, and the items and services are billed under, an NPI that is separate from the NPI of the main provider; the main provider has submitted to the Secretary, during the 2-year period ending on the date such items and services are furnished, an initial provider-based status attestation that the off-campus outpatient department is compliant with the requirements described in section § 413.65; and the main provider has submitted a subsequent attestation within the timeframe specified by the Secretary. In the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule (
91 FR 41981
), we proposed to add new section § 419.23 to codify this requirement. (We note the proposed changes to the provider-based regulations at § 413.65 to implement the attestation requirements are discussed in the next section. We also note, as discussed in greater detail in the next section, we proposed that prior to submitting an attestation, providers must obtain an NPI for each provider-based department.) Public comments on our proposals and our responses are discussed in the subsequent sections.
2. Modifications to the Provider-Based Regulations at § 413.65
In the proposed rule (
91 FR 41980
through
41984
), we proposed changes to the provider-based regulations at § 413.65 to implement the new requirements in section 6225 of the CAA, 2026. First, we proposed the addition of a new entry in the list of definitions in § 413.65(a)(2) for an “Off-campus outpatient department of a provider”. We currently define a “department of a provider” as a facility or organization that is either created by, or acquired by, a main provider for the purpose of furnishing health care services of the same type as those furnished by the main provider under the name, ownership, and financial and administrative control of the main provider. The definition of a department of a provider does not include rural health clinics (RHCs) or, except as specified in § 413.65(n), Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs). In accordance with the statutory definition provided in section 1833(t)(23)(C) of the Act, we proposed to add a new definition to paragraph (a)(2) describing an off-campus outpatient department of a provider as a department of a provider that is not located on the campus of the main provider or within 250 yards of a remote location of a hospital. Under this proposed definition, facilities or organizations that are not located on the campus of the main provider would be considered off-campus for provider-based purposes. This would include remote locations of a hospital, which are defined in § 413.65 as facilities that provide inpatient services in a location off the campus of a main provider. Remote locations are often referred to as secondary or subordinate “multi-campus” locations of a hospital, and in most cases operate in a substantially similar manner as the main provider. Section 6225 of the CAA, 2026, adding section 1833(t)(23)(C) to the Act, defines an “off-campus outpatient department of a provider” as neither being on the campus of the main provider, nor within the distance specified in the definition of campus of a remote location of a hospital.
Comment:
A commenter requested CMS clarify whether the relevant remote location encompasses the broader area surrounding the inpatient facility or is limited to the specific building or buildings providing inpatient services.
Response:
As discussed previously, the term “remote location of a hospital” is defined by regulation and it means, in part, a facility that provides inpatient hospital services under the name, ownership, and financial and administrative control of the main provider (see § 413.65(a)(2)). Remote locations are subject to the additional provider-based status requirements applicable to “off-campus” facilities at § 413.65(e). The “campus” definition at § 413.65(a)(2) applies to the physical area encompassing the main buildings of the main provider. We believe the inclusion of the 250-yard limit in section 1833(t)(23)(C) of the Act is intended as an alternative for an on-campus designation for purposes of section 6225 of the CAA, 2026. For this reason, we proposed to amend the regulations to clarify that any outpatient department that is located within 250 yards of a remote location facility would not be included in the definition of an “off-campus outpatient department of a provider” (and therefore would not be subject to the attestation or separate NPI requirements).
Comment:
We received a few comments requesting CMS provide additional clarification on how the measurement from a remote location would be implemented. Specifically, a commenter inquired from what point of the remote location facility would the measurement be taken, and whether certain structures, like awning, walkways, etc., would be acceptable starting points for measurement.
Response:
We understand the commenters' interest in this issue. Section 1833(t)(23)(C) of the Act, as added by 6225 of the CAA, 2026, refers to the distance specified in the definition of campus, which is codified at § 413.65(a)(2). In the campus definition, any area or structure within 250 yards of a main building of the
(
printed page 70717)
hospital is considered on-campus for purposes of applying the provider-based regulations. We proposed that, for purposes of implementing section 6225 of the CAA, 2026, we would add a new definition to paragraph (a)(2) describing which facilities or organizations would be considered off-campus outpatient departments of a provider (
91 FR 41981
). Under the proposal, any facility on the campus of the main provider or within 250 yards of a remote location of a hospital would
not
meet the regulatory definition of an “off-campus outpatient department of a provider”, and would therefore not be subject to the attestation or separate NPI requirements. We did not propose any modification to the definition of a campus in the proposed rule. Based on current practices, the 250-yard measurement could begin at any point of the remote location facility that provides patient care. Typically, when making provider-based on-campus determinations, we have reviewed publicly available satellite mapping software to make these determinations, using straight-line measurements from the main building to the nearest point of the potential provider-based department. In some cases, applicants may supply additional survey material to assist in this measurement process using a submission process designed by CMS. We would expect to follow the same practice in deciding whether a facility meets the requirements of section 6225 of the CAA, 2026. Regarding the inclusion of certain features, like awnings or walkway overhangs, we believe that non-structural components are not consistent with the definition of a remote location of a hospital and would not be an appropriate measuring point.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing the definition of “off-campus outpatient department of a provider” as proposed, without modification.
Section 413.65(e) includes additional requirements applicable to off-campus facilities or organizations. These requirements apply to all off-campus outpatient facilities, including those that are in close proximity to (and often within the same building as) inpatient remote locations. The implementation of section 603 of the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 (
Pub. L. 114-74
) in the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
81 FR 79699
through
79719
) and interim final rule with comment period (
81 FR 79720
through
79729
), however, excepted outpatient departments located within 250 yards of a remote location from payment policy implications for off-campus departments. Given the definition of an “off-campus outpatient department of a provider” in section 603 of the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 and section 6225 of the CAA, 2026 separates outpatient departments located outside the regulatorily-specified distance of a remote location of a hospital and provider off-campus outpatient departments, we stated in the proposed rule that we believe that it would be appropriate to distinguish off-campus requirements from those for hospital outpatient departments that are within 250 yards of a remote location of the main provider (
91 FR 41981
). Therefore, we proposed to revise § 413.65(e) to specifically exclude outpatient departments located within 250 yards of a remote location of a hospital, and to revise § 413.65(b)(3)(ii), (g)(1)(i), and (h) to append “or within 250 yards of a remote location of a hospital” to the references of being on the campus of the main provider. We stated we believe these proposed conforming changes would better clarify which facilities are affected by the new legislation and would better align the current provider-based rules with statutory provisions regarding the distinction between on- and off-campus locations and services. In addition, we proposed to make a technical change to § 413.65(g)(1)(i) and (ii) to revise “treated by Medicare” to “treated by CMS” consistent with the other proposals discussed in this section.
Comment:
A commenter urged CMS not to finalize the proposed revisions to § 413.65(e) that would treat outpatient departments located within 250 yards of a hospital's remote location as located on the main provider's campus. The commenter requested that CMS preserve the existing standard to provide stability and avoid imposing any unnecessary burden beyond those required by statute.
Response:
We believe the commenter misunderstood the effect of the proposal to revise § 413.65(e) to exclude outpatient departments located within 250 yards of a remote location of a hospital (
91 FR 41981
). Currently, remote locations of a hospital are considered to be “off-campus”, along with any outpatient departments located in close proximity to the inpatient facility that is the remote location of the hospital. Any off-campus facilities are currently subject to the additional applicable off-campus requirements of § 413.65(e), because they are not considered to be located on the main provider's campus. As stated previously, we believe these proposed conforming changes would better align the current provider-based rules with statutory provisions regarding the distinction between on- and off-campus locations and services. Our proposal to revise § 413.65(e) would exclude outpatient departments located within 250 yards of a remote location of a hospital from the additional provider-based status requirements applicable to off-campus facilities, so our proposal would reduce regulatory burden on outpatient departments that are within 250 yards of a remote location of a hospital.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing these revisions as proposed.
In the proposed rule (
91 FR 41981
), we proposed to add new section § 419.23 to codify the separate NPI and attestation requirements for payment under the OPPS for items and services furnished on or after January 1, 2028. In addition, we proposed to add a reference in § 413.65 to the new mandatory attestation requirements required by section 6225 of the CAA, 2026 and proposed a maximum 5-year timeframe for any subsequent attestation(s) (
91 FR 41981
). Specifically, we proposed to add § 413.65(b)(6) to state that, as of January 1, 2028, a main provider must submit an initial attestation of provider-based status for each of its off-campus outpatient departments within the 2-year period prior to furnishing services, and subsequent attestation(s) within a period not to exceed 5 years thereafter (
91 FR 41981
). We stated that we anticipate addressing the subsequent attestation requirement in the 2028 rulemaking cycle; nonetheless, we welcomed comments on the subsequent attestation (
91 FR 41982
). For all off-campus outpatient departments providing services on or before January 1, 2028, we proposed initial attestations must be submitted between January 1, 2026 and December 31, 2027, and off-campus outpatient departments that begin providing services after January 1, 2028 must submit an attestation within the 2 years prior to when the billed services are delivered. Subsequent attestation(s) would be submitted at an interval to be specified by CMS and not to exceed 5 years thereafter. In addition, we proposed providers that submit initial attestations within the 2-year period prior to January 1, 2028, would meet the attestation requirements of section 6225 of the CAA, 2026, even if they have not received a provider-based status determination from CMS by January 1, 2028. We also sought comments on an initial mandatory attestation for provider departments that received a determination of provider-based status prior to January 1, 2026,
(
printed page 70718)
and remain in compliance with all applicable provisions of § 413.65. For these departments, we stated that we were considering having the authorized official attest with a letter to CMS with evidence of CMS determination attached affirming its continued compliance with § 413.65.
Comment:
Numerous commenters strongly opposed the mandatory NPI and attestation requirements, citing administrative burden and payment disruption concerns and requested CMS consider a longer implementation timeline than what is currently required by law. They additionally recommended establishing a “good-faith” correction period or exercising enforcement discretion due to downstream operational impacts on hospital billing, NPI assignments, and system testing and updates. A commenter stated that the separate NPI required for an off-campus outpatient department of a provider under the provisions of section 6225 of the CAA, 2026 be consistently reflected on both the hospital's facility claim (paid under the OPPS or applicable payment system under 1833(t)(21)) and the associated physician's professional claim (paid under the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (PFS)) to allow for a “cross-claim linkage”.
Response:
We acknowledge the commenters' opposition to the mandated separate NPI and attestation requirements, particularly as related to anticipated administrative burden and payment disruption concerns. The statute establishes January 1, 2028, as the date on which CMS must stop making payments for items and services furnished at an off-campus outpatient department of a provider unless the NPI and attestation requirements are met. Specifically, section 1833(t)(23)(A) of the Act sets forth the requirements for payment for items and services “furnished on or after January 1, 2028, by an off-campus outpatient department of a provider.” Failure to meet the separate NPI or attestation requirements would affect payments for the items and services furnished by a specific off-campus outpatient department of a provider, not all OPPS payments to the main provider. As discussed throughout this section, we have sought to minimize the burden on providers in complying with the requirements of section 6225 of the CAA, 2026 while also maintaining appropriate oversight, and will continue to make every effort in doing so. As we implement these provisions, such efforts will include the development of billing, enrollment, and other subregulatory guidance. However, we will monitor implementation progress and may consider these suggestions for future rulemaking. We may consider the commenter's feedback regarding the cross-claim linkage on related professional claims in the development of future billing or other subregulatory guidance.
Comment:
Commenters questioned whether multiple hospital services operating at the same physical address require separate NPIs or may be covered by a single NPI, and whether an off-campus location providing multiple hospital services (such as providing both laboratory and radiology services) would need separate NPIs for each service line. Another commenter requested CMS provide clarity on how the location designation in the Provider Enrollment, Chain, and Ownership System (PECOS) would impact the NPI assignment. For example, whether multiple off-campus provider-based departments located at the same address but with separate identifiers (
e.g.
room numbers or suite numbers) assigned in PECOS would require a separate NPI for each off-campus provider-based department. Some comments requested clarity on whether hospitals should obtain NPIs by the physical address level, based on how the location is designated in PECOS, or by each individual department.
Response:
For purposes of the requirements of section 6225 of the CAA, 2026, and consistent with § 413.65(a)(2), “department of a provider” is identified by the hospital's submission of its physical facility location in the enrollment system—its street address, including suite or floor number, where applicable. A single off-campus location operating at one address is one “department of a provider” and, therefore, needs only one NPI even if multiple types of services are being provided there. For example, a hospital with an off-campus location providing both laboratory and radiology services would obtain one NPI for that location, not separate NPIs per service line.
Comment:
Other comments related to the separate NPI requirement included concerns that separate NPIs for off-campus provider-based departments could conflict with CMS requirements to combine same-day outpatient services on a single claim because the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) standard claim format permits only one billing NPI. Some commenters also expressed concern about potential Medicare Advantage (MA) implications of new department-specific NPIs. Commenters stated that new NPIs could trigger new prior authorization requirements for MA patients, disrupt coordination of benefits, and cause supplemental insurance claim denials due to NPI mismatches. Commenters further argued that requiring separate NPIs undermines HIPAA's goal of a single provider identifier and urged CMS to clarify that department-specific NPIs are administrative requirements only and do not indicate new independent provider entities.
Response:
The establishment or use of an NPI to satisfy the requirements of section 6225 of the CAA, 2026 does not, by itself, change the nature of the department, which remains a provider-based department of the hospital. To address certain issues mentioned in the comments, we are taking measures to allow the entry of multiple NPIs within a claim—the claim level NPI of the hospital plus the service line NPIs for the various services provided during a given day.
We will continue to consider commenters' feedback—including concerns about burden and operational challenges—as the agency develops policies and subregulatory guidance for implementing the NPI requirement.
Comment:
Commenters generally supported our proposals related to timing of the initial attestation, including the proposal to submit initial attestations in the 2-year period prior to January 1, 2028, and the proposal that initial attestations submitted by January 1, 2028 will meet the requirement even if CMS has not issued a provider-based determination by that date. Some commenters recommended that attestation approvals granted prior to January 1, 2026, be “grandfathered” as having met the initial attestation requirement. Other commenters requested that the initial attestation requirement be limited to new off-campus outpatient departments of a provider. Another commenter urged CMS to tie the initial attestation deadline to the existing Form CMS-855A enrollment activation date, such as 60 days following that enrollment activation date. The commenter stated that it is “administratively irrational” to require a provider-based attestation prior to this enrollment activation since the facility does not yet legally exist within the Medicare system. A commenter requested that CMS clarify in the regulation text at § 419.23 that claims for services provided at a department with a complete, timely attestation under review will continue to be paid without interruption.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' feedback on our proposals related to the timing of the initial attestation, and are finalizing them, with one modification discussed below. Specifically, we are
(
printed page 70719)
finalizing our proposal that for departments providing services on or before January 1, 2028, initial attestations must be submitted between January 1, 2026 and December 31, 2027; for departments beginning services after January 1, 2028, initial attestations must be submitted within the 2 years prior to delivering billed services; and providers submitting initial attestations within the required 2-year period will meet the initial attestation requirement, even if a provider-based status determination has not been received by that date. Based on feedback from commenters, we are adding paragraph (c) to § 419.23 to clarify that a provider satisfies the submission requirement at paragraph (a)(2) of this section even if CMS has not made a determination of provider-based status before the first day on which the outpatient department renders services.
Regarding attestation approvals granted prior to January 1, 2026, section 6225 of the CAA, 2026 specifies the timing for the initial attestation by requiring that payment cannot be made for items or services furnished on or after January 1, 2028 by an off-campus outpatient department of a provider unless such provider has submitted an initial provider-based attestation “during the 2 year period ending on the date such items or services are so furnished.” Although attestations submitted before the statutory “2 year period” deadline do not meet the initial attestation requirement, our streamlined attestation process aims to reduce provider burden.
Regarding the request to use the Form CMS-855A enrollment activation date as the deadline for the initial attestation, under current procedures a Form CMS-855A must be submitted, reviewed by the MAC, and assigned an effective date of enrollment activation before an off-campus outpatient department of a provider can be added to a provider's enrollment record. However, as previously discussed, the provisions of section 6225 of the CAA, 2026 specify the timing for the initial attestation, tying it to the date the items or services for which payment is being sought are furnished. We appreciate the commenter's concern and encourage providers to take into account the time needed to add a potential provider-based off-campus outpatient department to their enrollment record when considering when to submit an initial attestation within the statutory 2-year period.
Comment:
Several commenters requested CMS modify the proposed maximum 5-year timeframe for the required subsequent attestation to reduce the overall burden on hospitals. Some suggested a timeframe of seven to ten years, and some requested a timeframe of no less than 10 years. Another commenter expressed the importance of maintaining provider-based compliance for equitable payment policy, and suggested CMS implement a shorter timeframe, such as 3 years or upon a change in ownership, for the subsequent attestation. Many commenters recommended requiring only one subsequent attestation after the initial attestation, or only requiring periodic re-attestations in specified circumstances, such as when there is a material change in the relationship between the hospital and its off-campus provider-based department, a change in ownership, or a management contract change. A commenter also requested CMS clarify when the proposed 5-year “countdown” for the subsequent attestation would begin, such as when the initial attestation is submitted or when CMS issues the provider-based status determination.
A commenter stated that CMS should establish the subsequent (post-CY 2028) attestation cadence in the final rule, rather than deferring it to future rulemaking or guidance, to provide adequate lead time for compliance planning.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' feedback. In response to the comment regarding the start of the subsequent attestation timeline, we are clarifying that the time-period for the subsequent attestation would begin on the date the attestation is submitted as we believe this is the most consistent with the statute.
At this time, we continue to believe that a maximum 5-year subsequent attestation period is an appropriate timeframe to balance provider burden while ensuring continued provider-based compliance. As we gain experience with these new requirements, we may revisit this policy, including commenters' suggestions regarding the timing, frequency and/or circumstances of a subsequent attestation.
We appreciate the commenter's request to address the subsequent attestation process in this final rule with comment period. We believe addressing the subsequent attestation requirement, including its timing, frequency, and applicable circumstances, in the 2028 rulemaking cycle will allow CMS to gain experience implementing the initial attestation requirement and to consider additional operational information before establishing the subsequent attestation process.
In response to our request, we also received comments on the subsequent attestation requirement process. We appreciate those suggestions and feedback and will take them into consideration for future rulemaking. As stated in the proposed rule (
91 FR 41982
), we anticipate addressing the subsequent attestation requirement in the 2028 rulemaking cycle.
In summary, after consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to codify, at § 419.23, the separate NPI and attestation requirements for payment under the OPPS for items and services furnished on or after January 1, 2028, with one technical edit in paragraph (a)(3) and the modification to address situations where CMS has not issued a provider-based status determination before the first date services are furnished. D. Documentation Requirements for Provider-Based Attestations
To support meaningful CMS oversight of provider compliance with the provider-based requirements of § 413.65, and consistent with the mandatory attestation requirement established by section 6225 of the CAA, 2026, in the proposed rule (
91 FR 41983
), we proposed that attestations submitted through the proposed standardized attestation process would include, or be supported by, documentation sufficient to demonstrate compliance with the applicable provisions of § 413.65(d), (e), (g), and (h). We described, as discussed later in this section, the categories of documentation that providers may be required to submit or retain in connection with their attestations. As discussed further, we stated that CMS anticipated that not all documentation described herein would be required at the time of initial attestation submission; rather, CMS and its contractors, including MACs, will employ risk-based screening and targeted documentation review processes to identify those attestations for which additional documentation is warranted. We stated the rationale behind using targeted documentation review is that any main provider typically manages its departments in a consistent manner. By drawing a sample from each main provider's universe of provider-based departments, we would be able to gain a reliable understanding of their universe. This approach would not only ensure adequate representation across all providers, regardless of their volume—it would also provide meaningful insight into whether compliance standards are being upheld across all departments. We invited public comment on the appropriate scope of documentation requirements, including whether any of the categories described should be modified, consolidated, or eliminated in order to reduce provider burden while preserving CMS' ability to evaluate compliance and protect the Medicare program. 91 FR 41983
through
41984
) we proposed the following documentation framework:
Attestation Form Completeness and Authorization:
++ We proposed that providers must submit a completed attestation using the CMS-standardized attestation form, signed and dated by an authorized official of the main provider as identified in PECOS. The attestation would be required to identify both the main provider and each off-campus outpatient department of the provider for which provider-based status is sought, including the applicable NPIs, provider numbers, addresses, and the date on which provider-based conditions were met or the date the department was acquired, as applicable. Where a provider designates a consultant or outside representative as the primary contact for the attestation, we proposed the provider must authorize the representative in writing.
Location:
++ We stated we anticipate the attestation system would have the ability to measure the distance requirement. However, if the distance is not systematically verified or exceeds 35-miles, we proposed providers would be required to submit supporting documentation in support of § 413.65(e)(3).
Licensure:
++ We proposed providers must be prepared to demonstrate that the off-campus outpatient department is operated under the same licensure as the main provider, consistent with § 413.65(d)(1), or to provide documentation that the applicable State does not require a separate license for the department.
Clinical Services Integration:
++ We proposed providers must be prepared to demonstrate that the off-campus outpatient department meets the clinical integration requirements of § 413.65(d)(2), including that professional staff at the department hold privileges at the main provider; that appropriate monitoring and oversight of the department by the main provider is in place; that inpatient and outpatient services of the department and the main provider are integrated; and that patients treated at the department who require further care have full access to all services of the main provider.
Financial Integration:
++ We proposed providers must be prepared to demonstrate that the revenues and expenses of the off-campus outpatient department are integrated with those of the main provider, consistent with § 413.65(d)(3), such that the department does not maintain a separate general ledger or trial balance independent of the main provider.
Public Awareness:
++ We proposed that providers must be prepared to demonstrate that the off-campus outpatient department is clearly identified to the public as part of the main provider, consistent with § 413.65(d)(4), and that patients entering the department are aware they are receiving services from the main provider.
Obligations of Hospital Outpatient Departments:
++ For off-campus outpatient departments that are departments of hospitals, we proposed that providers must be prepared to demonstrate compliance with the applicable obligations of hospital outpatient departments under § 413.65(g), including compliance with Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA) requirements, antidumping rules, site-of-service billing requirements, and the requirement to provide written notice to Medicare beneficiaries of their potential financial liability prior to the delivery of services at an off-campus location.
Ownership, Control, Administration, and Supervision (Off-Campus Departments):
++ We proposed providers must be prepared to demonstrate that the department operates under the ownership and control of the main provider consistent with § 413.65(e)(1), including that the department is 100 percent owned by the main provider and that the main provider retains final approval over administrative decisions, personnel policies, and medical staff appointments. We also proposed providers must also be prepared to demonstrate that the administrative functions of the department are integrated with those of the main provider consistent with § 413.65(e)(2), including through submission of an organizational chart reflecting the reporting relationship between the department and the main provider.

E. CMS Verification and Oversight Activities
Section 1833(t)(23)(B)(i) of the Act directs the Secretary to establish a process for determining, through site visits, remote audits, or other means as determined appropriate by the Secretary, whether each off-campus outpatient department of a provider is compliant with the applicable requirements. Consistent with this statutory direction, in the proposed rule (
91 FR 41984
), we proposed that CMS and its contractors, including MACs, employ a layered, risk-based approach to verification and oversight that would be designed to promote efficient processing of the significantly increased volume of attestations expected under the mandatory attestation requirement while preserving meaningful CMS oversight of provider compliance with § 413.65.
We proposed that, at the initial review stage, CMS and its contractors, including MACs, would conduct automated validation and screening of all submitted attestations to verify completeness, consistency with PECOS enrollment records, and the presence of required attestation elements. Attestations that pass automated validation would be processed for initial determination. Attestations that present indicators of incompleteness, inconsistency, or elevated compliance risk would be flagged for targeted documentation review, during which CMS or its contractors may request that the provider furnish supporting documentation from any or all of the categories described.
At the extended review stage, we proposed that CMS and its contractors, including MACs, would employ risk-based methodologies to select a subset of attestations for more extensive compliance review. Such methodologies may include remote audits of provider records and documentation, site visits conducted by CMS or its contractors to verify that the attested department meets the physical, financial, clinical, and administrative integration requirements of § 413.65, or investigations of potential non-compliance identified through data analysis, referral, or other sources. We stated the criteria and methodologies CMS would use to select attestations for extended review would be established through operational guidance and would be designed to focus oversight resources on providers and departments that present the highest risk of non-compliance with the provider-based requirements. We proposed that failure to submit requested documentation within the timeframe specified by CMS may result in a determination of non-compliance and recovery of payments as described in § 413.65(k).
We invited public comment on the appropriate scope and sequencing of documentation requirements, including whether the categories described should be further prioritized, consolidated, or phased in over time to facilitate provider compliance with the January 1, 2028 statutory deadline.

Providers will be asked to submit specific documentation to demonstrate compliance with each provider-based requirement at § 413.65. If a provider is found to be out of compliance for a specific requirement, we may extend the review of that requirement to departments not included in the sample. We will continue to develop policies and procedures, such as remote audits, data analysis, alternative data sourcing approaches and site visits, as we gain experience with the oversight of these off-campus provider-based requirements.

A. ICRs for the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting (OQR) Program
1. Background
In sections XIV. and XV. of this final rule with comment period, we discuss the finalized requirements for the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program. The Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program is generally aligned with the CMS quality reporting program for hospital inpatient services known as the Hospital Inpatient Quality Reporting Program. We refer readers to the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
90 FR 54029
through
54037

In this final rule with comment period, we are: (1) removing the Appropriate Follow-Up Interval for Normal Colonoscopy in Average Risk Patients measure beginning with the CY 2027 reporting period/CY 2029 payment determination; (2) including electronic clinical quality measures (eCQMs) into the existing validation process for chart-abstracted measures beginning with eCQM data from the CY 2027 reporting period affecting the CY 2030 payment determination; (3) reducing the validation selection pool from 500 to up to 400 HOPDs beginning with validation affecting the CY 2030 payment determination; and (4) removing the requirement for hospitals to resubmit medical documentation as part of their request for reconsideration of validation noncompliance, beginning with data from the CY 2026 reporting period affecting the CY 2028 payment determination.
As part of including eCQMs into the existing validation process for chart-abstracted measures beginning with CY 2027 eCQM data affecting the CY 2030 payment determination, we are: (1) modifying the number of chart-abstracted cases required for validation from 12 per quarter to a maximum of 7 per quarter per measure beginning with validation affecting the CY 2030 payment determination; (2) replacing the previously finalized 2-year validation cycle with a 3-year validation cycle, where hospitals selected for validation based on CY 2027 data affecting the CY 2029 payment determination will not be selected again for validation of the same data affecting the CY 2030 payment determination; (3) determining eCQM validation scores using the same methodology currently used to score chart-abstracted measure validation; (4) revising the policy to allow the results of educational reviews for all four quarters of chart-abstracted measure validation to be reflected in the final validation score prior to the calculation of the confidence interval; and (5) extending the educational review process established for chart-abstracted measure validation to eCQM validation.

D. ICRs for the Implementation of Section 6225 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 for the Requirements for Provider-Based Status (§ 413.65)
The requirements for a determination that a facility or an organization has provider-based status are in the regulations at § 413.65. Section 6225 of the CAA, 2026 added paragraph (23) to section 1833(t) of the Act, and prohibits Medicare payments for items and services furnished on or after January 1, 2028, unless off-campus outpatient departments of a provider meet certain conditions. New section 1833(t)(23)(A) of the Act requires, as a condition of receiving payment, that off-campus outpatient departments of a provider obtain and bill under separate NPIs and that main providers submit provider-based attestations in accordance with provisions at § 413.65. New section 1833(t)(23)(B)(i) of the Act requires the Secretary, through notice and comment rulemaking, to establish a process for each provider with an off-campus outpatient department to submit an initial and subsequent attestation, for the review of each such attestation and for the determination, through site visits, remote audits, or other means (as determined appropriate by the Secretary), whether each off-campus outpatient department is compliant with the requirements described in subparagraph (A). In addition, new section 1833(t)(23)(C) of the Act defines an “off-campus outpatient department of a provider” for purposes of paragraph (23) as a department of a provider (as defined in § 413.65) that is not located on the campus (also defined in § 413.65) of the main provider or is not within the distance described in such definition of campus from a remote location of a hospital (also defined in § 413.65).
As discussed in greater detail section XX. of this final rule with comment period, we finalized with certain modifications proposed changes to the provider-based regulations at § 413.65 to implement the new requirements of section 6225 of the CAA, 2026. Among those changes, we are revising § 413.65(b) to add a reference to the new mandatory attestation requirement for an off-campus outpatient department of a provider required by section 6225 of the CAA, 2026 and a maximum 5-year timeframe for any subsequent attestation(s), as proposed. In addition, as we proposed, we are establishing a standardized attestation form for provider-based determinations, in connection with the provisions of section 6225 of the CAA, 2026, that providers will submit through a centralized electronic system. The standardized form will replace the current MAC-specific templates. We are also finalizing our proposal to eliminate the mandatory requirement for off-campus provider-based facilities or organizations to supply supporting documentation at the time of attestation. Under our final policy, until the
(
printed page 70735)

Comment:
Some commenters stated that CMS' estimate understates the actual burden and fails to account for certain costs associated with the new requirements. Response:
We appreciate the additional information provided by commenters related to the time and costs associated with the attestation requirement. We believe that the best way to calculate the burden is to use an estimate of the number of hours associated with a typical provider's typical attestation. Although we recognize that the time taken to complete individual attestations may be shorter or longer than our estimate, and unique circumstances may contribute to this variation, it would not be feasible to include every possible situation into our estimate.
However, in response to the commenters' feedback that the burden estimate should account for additional factors and costs, including the need for multiple departments to be involved in the attestation process, and that the estimated time per attestation is not adequate, we are revising our estimate of the burden in this final rule with comment period. XXVII. Economic Analyses
A. Statement of Need
This final rule with comment period is necessary to make updates to the Medicare hospital OPPS rates. It is also necessary to make changes to the payment policies and rates for outpatient services furnished by hospitals and CMHCs in CY 2027. We are required under section 1833(t)(3)(C)(ii) of the Act to update annually the OPPS conversion factor used to determine the payment rates for APCs. We also are required under section 1833(t)(9)(A) of the Act to review, not less often than annually, and revise the groups, the relative payment weights, and the wage and other adjustments described in section 1833(t)(2) of the Act. We must review the clinical integrity of payment groups and relative payment weights at least annually. We are revising the APC relative payment weights using claims data for services furnished on and after January 1, 2025 through and including December 31, 2025, and processed through June 30, 2026, and updated HCRIS cost report information.
This final rule with comment period is also necessary to make updates to the ASC payment rates for CY 2027, enabling CMS to make changes to payment policies and payment rates for covered surgical procedures and covered ancillary services that are performed in ASCs in CY 2027. Because ASC payment rates are based on the OPPS relative payment weights for most of the procedures performed in ASCs, the ASC payment rates are updated annually to reflect annual changes to the OPPS relative payment weights. In addition, we are required under section 1833(i)(1) of the Act to review and update the list of surgical procedures that can be performed in an ASC, not less frequently than every 2 years.
In the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (
83 FR 59075
through
59079
), we finalized a policy to update the ASC payment system rates using the hospital market basket update instead of the CPI-U for CY 2019 through 2023. In the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we finalized a policy to extend the 5-year interim period by an additional 2 years, through CY 2024 and CY 2025, to enable us to more accurately analyze whether the application of the hospital market basket update to the ASC payment system resulted in a migration of services from the hospital setting to the ASC setting (
88 FR 81960
). In the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we finalized a policy to extend our utilization of the hospital market basket update as the update factor for the ASC payment system for one additional year, through CY 2026 (
90 FR 54058
). As discussed in section XIII. of this final rule with comment period, we are finalizing our proposal to extend our utilization of the hospital market basket update as the update factor for the ASC payment system for one additional year (through CY 2027). The ASC impacts discussed below reflect our application of the hospital market basket update for CY 2027.
In addition, this final rule with comment period is necessary to make policy changes for facilities reporting data under the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting and ASC Quality Reporting Programs. The primary objective of these quality reporting programs is to promote higher quality, more efficient health care for Medicare beneficiaries by collecting and reporting on quality-of-care metrics. This information is made available to consumers, both to empower Medicare beneficiaries and inform decision making, as well as to incentivize healthcare facilities to make continued improvements.
