Specifically, in this final rule with comment period, for CY 2027, for hospitals paid under the OPPS (other than those that are excepted for CY 2027), we are paying for separately payable drugs and biologicals that are obtained with a 340B discount, excluding those on pass-through payment status and vaccines, at ASP minus 28 percent instead of ASP+6 percent. For context, based on CY 2025 claims data, the total OPPS Part B drug payment is approximately $27.7 billion.
We note that in the CY 2025 claims available for OPPS ratesetting purposes that the modifier “TB” continued to be active, and identifies drugs and biologicals acquired through the 340B Drug Pricing program. Therefore, we used separately payable drug lines with prospective status indicator “K,” which would be subject to the 340B Payment policy, that also were billed with status indicator “TB” to identify lines that would be included for purposes of determining the budget neutrality adjustment. Under our final CY 2027 policy, rural SCHs, children's hospitals, and PPS-exempt cancer hospitals would be excepted from this payment policy and so they were similarly excepted from these calculations for budget neutrality and impact analysis purposes.
Using that claims data, we estimate that OPPS payments for separately payable drugs, including beneficiary copayments, will decrease by approximately $4.65 billion under this finalized policy, which reflects a $200 million decrease in the estimated reduction relative to the proposed rule estimate of $4.85 billion. This change is largely attributable to the changes made in the final CY 2027 340B Payment Policy and additional claims data available in the final rule. Because we are implementing this payment reduction in a budget neutral manner within the OPPS, the reduced payments for separately payable drugs purchased through the 340B Program will increase payment rates for other non-drug items and services paid under the OPPS by an offsetting aggregate amount.
In this final rule, we project that reducing payment for 340B drugs to ASP minus 28.0 percent will increase OPPS payment rates for non-drug items and services by approximately 7.5 percent in CY 2027. The estimated impacts of this policy are displayed in Table 112. We note that the payment rates included in Addendum A and Addendum B of this final rule with comment period do not reflect the reduced payments for drugs purchased under the 340B Program; however, they do include the increase to payments rates for non-drug items and services due to the corresponding increase in the conversion factor.
In summary, to maintain budget neutrality within the OPPS, the estimated $4.65 billion in reduced drug payments from adoption of this final 340B payment methodology will be redistributed in an equal offsetting amount to all hospitals paid under the OPPS through increasing the payment rates by 7.5 percent for nondrug items and services furnished by all hospitals paid under the OPPS for CY 2027.

h. Estimated Effects of OPPS Changes on the Medicare and Medicaid Programs
The effect of the update on the Medicare program is expected to be an increase of $1.78 billion in program payments for OPPS services furnished in CY 2027. The effect on the Medicaid program is expected to be limited to copayments that Medicaid may make on behalf of Medicaid recipients who are also Medicare beneficiaries. We estimate that the changes in this final rule would increase these Medicaid beneficiary payments by approximately $40 million in CY 2027. Currently, there are approximately 11.8 million dual-eligible beneficiaries, which represent approximately 40 percent of Medicare Part B fee-for-service beneficiaries. The impact on Medicaid was determined by taking 12 percent of the beneficiary cost-sharing impact. The national average split of Medicaid payments is 58 percent Federal payments and 42 percent State payments. Therefore, for the estimated $40 million Medicaid increase, approximately $25 million would be from the Federal Government and $15 million would be from State governments.

Comment:
A commenter requested that we incorporate site-of-service substitution effects into the impact analysis.
Response:
As noted earlier in this section, we do not attempt to predict behavioral responses to our policy changes to isolate the effects associated with specific policies or updates, but any policy that changes payment could have a behavioral response. In addition, we have not made any adjustments for future changes in variables, such as service volume, service-mix, or number of encounters.
Comment:

We appreciate the commenter's recommendation and will take it into consideration in the future.

2. Estimated Effects of CY 2027 ASC Payment System Changes
Most ASC payment rates are calculated by multiplying the ASC conversion factor by the ASC relative payment weight. As discussed fully in section XIII. of this final rule with comment period, we are setting the CY 2027 ASC relative payment weights by scaling the final CY 2027 OPPS relative payment weights by the final CY 2027 ASC scalar of 0.814. The estimated effects of the updated relative payment weights on payment rates are varied and are reflected in the estimated payments displayed in Tables 113 and 114.
Beginning in CY 2011, section 3401 of the Affordable Care Act requires that the annual update to the ASC payment system after application of any quality reporting reduction be reduced by a productivity adjustment. In CY 2019, we adopted a policy for the annual update to the ASC payment system to be the hospital market basket update for CY 2019 through CY 2023. In the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we extended this 5-year interim period an additional 2 years through CYs 2024 and 2025. In the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we extended the interim period an additional year through 2026. As discussed in further detail in section XIII. of this final rule with comment period, we proposed and are finalizing an extension of our utilization of the hospital market basket update as the update factor to the ASC payment system for 1 additional year (through CY 2027). Section 1886(b)(3)(B)(xi)(II) of the Act defines the productivity adjustment to be equal to the 10-year moving average of changes in annual economywide private nonfarm business multifactor productivity (as projected by the Secretary for the 10-year period, ending with the applicable fiscal year, year, cost reporting period, or other annual period). For ASCs that fail to meet their quality reporting requirements, the CY 2027 payment determinations would be based on the application of a 2.0 percentage point reduction to the hospital market basket update for CY 2027. We calculated the final CY 2027 ASC conversion factor by adjusting the CY 2026 ASC conversion factor ($56.322) by 1.0018 to account for changes in the pre-floor and pre-reclassified hospital wage indexes between CY 2026 and CY 2027, which includes our policy to limit wage index declines of greater than 5 percent, and by applying the CY 2027 hospital market basket update factor of 2.3 percent (which is equal to the final inpatient hospital market basket percentage increase of 3.2 percent reduced by a productivity adjustment of 0.9 percentage point). The final CY 2027 ASC conversion factor is $57.721 for ASCs that successfully meet the quality reporting requirements.

This contrasts with procedures performed in HOPDs under the OPPS, where the beneficiary is responsible for copayments that range from 20 percent to 40 percent of the procedure payment (other than for certain preventive services), although the majority of HOPD procedures have a 20-percent copayment. Second, in almost all cases, the ASC payment rates under the ASC payment system are lower than payment rates for the same procedures under the OPPS. Therefore, the beneficiary coinsurance amount under the ASC payment system will usually be less than the OPPS copayment amount for the same services. (The only exceptions will be if the ASC coinsurance amount exceeds the hospital inpatient deductible since the statute requires that OPPS copayment amounts not exceed the hospital inpatient deductible. Therefore, in limited circumstances, the ASC coinsurance amount may exceed the hospital inpatient deductible and, therefore, the OPPS copayment amount for similar services.) Beneficiary coinsurance for services migrating from physicians' offices to ASCs may decrease or increase under the ASC payment system, depending on the particular service and the relative payment amounts under the MPFS compared to the ASC. While the ASC payment system bases most of its payment rates on hospital cost data used to set OPPS relative payment weights, services that are performed a majority of the time in a physician office are generally paid the lesser of the ASC amount according to the standard ASC ratesetting methodology or at the nonfacility practice expense-based amount payable under the PFS. (4) Estimated Benefits
There will be quantifiable benefits for this final rule with comment period because we expect a reduction in the unnecessary utilization of the new Medicare OPD services subject to prior authorization. It is difficult to project the exact decrease in unnecessary utilization; however, based on a 25 percent savings percentage, we estimate an overall gross savings of $25 million. These savings represent a Medicare benefit from more efficient use of health care resources while still maintaining the same health outcomes for necessary services. We will closely monitor utilization and billing practices. The expected benefits would also include changed billing practices that would also enhance the coordination of care for the beneficiary. For example, requiring prior authorization for the additional OPD services would help ensure that the primary care practitioner recommending the service and the facility collaborate more closely to provide the most appropriate OPD services to meet the needs of the beneficiary. The practitioner recommending the service would evaluate the beneficiary to determine what services are medically necessary based on the beneficiary's condition. This would require the facility to collaborate closely with the practitioner early in the process to ensure the services are truly necessary and meet all requirements and that their supporting documentation is complete and correct. Improper payments made because the practitioner did not evaluate the patient, or the patient does not meet the Medicare requirements, would likely be reduced by requiring a provider to submit clinical documentation as part of its prior authorization request.

The Congressional Review Act (CRA) (

We believe that further notice and public procedure are unnecessary, and that it would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest to delay the effective date of the OPPS and ASC final rule with comment period for the following reasons.
If the effective date of this final rule with comment period is delayed by 60 days, the finalized OPPS and ASC payment system updated policies (including the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting (OQR) Program, the Ambulatory Surgical Center Quality Reporting (ASCQR) Program, prior authorization for additional Botulinum Toxin Injection services, implementation of certain Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 provisions for off-campus outpatient departments of a provider, Graduate Medical Education (GME) policies, and hospital accrediting organization policies concerning certain Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA) administrative requirements) will not be effective as of the beginning of the payment year, and CMS will be compelled to continue to use obsolete reimbursement rates which will disadvantage health care providers and suppliers.
In accordance with sections 1833(t)(9) and 1833(i)(2)(D) of the Act, the OPPS and the ASC payment systems are calendar year payment systems. We typically issue the OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period by November 1 of each year to both comply with the statutory requirement under section 1833(t)(9)(A) of the Act to annually review and update the OPPS on a calendar year basis and ensure 60 days' notice so that the payment policies for these systems are effective on January 1, the first day of the calendar year to which the policies are intended to apply. The Hospital OQR Program, REHQR Program, and the ASCQR Program are intended to align with the OPPS and the ASC payment systems, respectively.
In this final rule with comment period, we review and revise payment rates for specific services and adopt or revise other policies that relate to the OPPS/ASC payment system for CY 2027. Section 1833(t)(9)(A) of the Act requires that no less often than annually, the Secretary shall review and revise the groups, the relative payment weights, and the wage and other adjustments for outpatient services to take into account changes in medical practice, changes in technology, the addition of new services, new cost data, and other relevant information and factors. In addition, section 1833(i)(2)(D) of the Act states that the payment amount made for facility services furnished in connection with a surgical procedure furnished to an individual in an ambulatory surgical center should be reviewed and updated annually to take account of varying conditions in different areas. We find that, in order to comply with the statutory requirements to annually review and update these payment systems, to ensure that the payment policies for these systems are effective on an annual basis, and to promote an orderly transition to a new payment year, it is in the public interest to ensure that the rule is effective no later than 1 full year after the effective date of the previous year's update (that is, January 1 of each year). Moreover, it is in the public interest to waive the 60-day delay of the effective date, so that providers and suppliers are adequately reimbursed starting at the beginning of the calendar year. Therefore, we find good cause exists to waive the 60-day delay in the effective date for this final rule with comment period.

Department of Homeland Security
U.S. Customs and Border Protection
19 CFR Parts 110, 111, 141, 142 and 171
[USCBP-2026-1387; CBP Dec. 26-19]
RIN 1685-AA48
AGENCY:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Interim final rule; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
This document amends the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) regulations, consistent with Section 2 of
Executive Order 14411
, “Strengthening Customs Enforcement,” by establishing new requirements for foreign importers of record (IORs) when making entry, and corresponding responsibilities for licensed customs brokers with regard to their clients. The new regulations also set forth consequences for foreign IORs and customs brokers who fail to comply with the new requirements.
DATES:
This interim final rule is effective on January 5, 2027.  As explained in Section VII, licensed customs brokers may submit requests for delayed compliance with the changes in § 111.29 of
title 19 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(
19 CFR 111.29
) prior to January 5, 2027. All customs brokers are expected to be in full compliance with the requirements of this rule no later than May 6, 2027.
Comment date:
Comments on the rule must be received on or before January 5, 2027.

.

,

IX. Signing Authority
I. Public Participation
Interested persons are invited to participate in this rulemaking by submitting written data, views, or arguments on any aspect of this rulemaking. U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) also invites comments that relate to the economic or federalism effects that might result from this rule. If appropriate to a specific comment, the commenter should reference the specific portion of the rule, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include data, information, or authority that supports the recommended change.
II. Background
On June 3, 2026, the President signed Executive Order (E.O.) 14411 (Strengthening Customs Enforcement).
[
1
]
Section 1 of the E.O. emphasizes the importance of customs enforcement for purposes of national security, foreign policy, and the economy of the United States. It further states that effective customs enforcement prevents the importation of unlawful and dangerous goods, ensures importers of record (IORs) are correctly identified and held accountable for duties owed, and guarantees compliance with numerous Federal laws, including laws governing forced labor, rules of origin, origin marking, intellectual property, revenue collection, and product safety.
The E.O. calls for customs reform to remedy systemic inefficiencies, loopholes, insufficient enforcement mechanisms, and outdated processes that have created opportunities for malign actors to evade Federal law. IORs often use various arrangements and schemes to undervalue imports, withhold critical information about themselves and the goods being imported or its production process, and/or avoid payment of duties. These actions threaten national security, threaten product safety, undermine foreign relations, disadvantage domestic businesses, and harm Americans.
Sections 2(b) and (c) of
E.O. 14411
direct the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, through the issuance or modification of relevant regulations, policy or guidance, to prohibit foreign IORs from making informal entry pursuant to
19 U.S.C. 1498
and to require foreign IORs who want to make formal entry to either be a Customs Trade Partnership Against Terrorism (CTPAT) validated participant or use a licensed customs broker who is a CTPAT validated participant. Section 10 of the E.O. provides definitions for certain terms, such as “foreign IOR” and “U.S. IOR,” that are intended to assist in the enforcement of the E.O.'s directives.
One of CBP's many critical mission sets is to facilitate legitimate trade that supports economic growth while shielding the American public and businesses from illicit trade, including unsafe products, intellectual property theft, and unfair trade practices. In particular, with respect to foreign IORs, CBP faces challenges enforcing their financial obligations to the U.S. government arising from lost revenue, such as from unpaid duties and taxes. In addition, CBP cannot easily ensure that foreign IORs are complying with U.S. customs and trade laws to prevent the importation of dangerous and
(
printed page 69978)
unlawful goods. These challenges exist primarily because foreign IORs and their assets are primarily located outside the United States.
Consistent with the E.O. and governing statutes, this rulemaking addresses the challenges presented by foreign IORs. Section 2(b) of the E.O. instructs CBP to prohibit foreign IORs from filing informal entry because, among other reasons, such IORs are not similarly situated to U.S. IORs and may be less familiar with U.S. customs laws. Foreign IORs also present challenges when CBP pursues enforcement actions against them. Similarly, Section 2(c) of the E.O. instructs CBP to prohibit foreign IORs who have not been vetted by CBP through CTPAT validation from making formal entry, unless they rely on a CTPAT validated broker to file the entry. This is necessary to treat all IORs equally based on their individualized circumstances to protect the revenue and strengthen national security.
Through CTPAT validation of IORs, CBP is able to ensure proper vetting of foreign IORs that mitigates risks to revenue, domestic industry, American consumers, and national security—CTPAT validation allows CBP to pursue effective enforcement against foreign IORs and provides heightened visibility into their corporate structures and supply chains. Because CTPAT validation offers CBP stronger insight into foreign IORs, CBP is not prohibiting foreign IORs who are CTPAT validated from filing informal entry in this rulemaking. Similarly, CBP is not prohibiting foreign IORs from filing informal entry through a CTPAT validated broker in this rulemaking. However, as further detailed in section VI.G. below, CBP will be monitoring the informal entries filed by foreign IORs and their brokers following the effective date of the rule. If CBP determines that informal entries filed by foreign IORs present risks to the revenue, national security, or public health and safety, CBP will take action to fully prohibit foreign IORs from using informal entry to enter goods for consumption.
CBP will only allow a foreign IOR to enter goods for consumption
[
2
]
on its own behalf,
i.e.,
to serve as the IOR for the entry, whether an informal or formal entry,
[
3
]
if the foreign IOR is CTPAT validated. Further, consistent with Section (2)(c) of the E.O., the only way for a foreign IOR who is not CTPAT validated to secure the entry and release of goods is by designating a CTPAT validated and licensed customs broker to make entry on the foreign IOR's behalf.
This rulemaking implements these requirements for foreign IORs when filing entries pursuant to the authority in
19 U.S.C. 1484
and
1498
. This rule will assist CBP in preventing foreign parties from evading U.S. customs and trade laws and will level the playing field for U.S. IORs by holding foreign IORs to the same standards and enforcement mechanisms to which U.S. IORs are currently held. Heightened requirements for foreign IORs will further CBP's mission to protect the American public and ensure the collection of revenue owed to the United States. With this rule, foreign IORs are prohibited from making informal entry of merchandise for consumption for which a CBP Form 3461 or 7501 must be filed unless the foreign IOR is either a CTPAT validated participant or uses a CTPAT validated and licensed customs broker. To make formal entry, a foreign IOR must also either be a CTPAT validated participant or use a CTPAT validated and licensed customs broker to enter merchandise for consumption. Foreign parties who are not CTPAT validated IORs must designate a licensed customs broker who is a CTPAT validated participant to file entry on their behalf. A designated licensed customs broker who is a CTPAT validated participant must act as the importer of record for the entry if such foreign parties are not the owner or purchaser of the merchandise being entered.
CBP is leveraging the CTPAT program to increase transparency as to foreign IORs transacting customs business in the United States and to better identify the merchandise they are importing. CTPAT validated participants have been vetted by CBP, have demonstrated that they are meeting certain security requirements,
i.e.,
the minimum security criteria (MSC), and have a known history of compliance, resulting in a higher degree of accountability and visibility into the foreign IOR's supply chain and security. Where a customs broker is acting on behalf of a foreign party, CBP is utilizing the existence of CTPAT validated and licensed brokers in the transaction to ensure transparency and accountability for a segment of the trade that presents higher risk than others.
III. Authority
Under section 66 of title 19 of the United States Code (
19 U.S.C. 66
), the Secretary of the Treasury
[
4
]
is authorized to prescribe regulations to be used in carrying out the provisions of laws relating to raising revenue from imports or to duties on imports, or to warehousing, and give directions to CBP officers and prescribe such rules and forms to be observed by them as may be necessary for the proper execution of the law. Section 1624 of title 19 (
19 U.S.C. 1624
) authorizes the Secretary of the Treasury to make such rules and regulations as may be necessary to carry out the provisions of the Tariff Act of 1930, codified at
19 U.S.C. 1001
et seq.
Section 4320 of title 19 (
19 U.S.C. 4320
)
[
5
]
authorizes the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to establish, among other things, a program that ensures collection of sufficient information to allow CBP to verify the existence of an IOR (
19 U.S.C. 4320(b)(1)(A)
), sufficient information to allow CBP to identify linkages or other affiliations between importers (
19 U.S.C. 4320(b)(1)(B)
), and sufficient information to allow CBP to identify changes in address and corporate structure of an importer (
19 U.S.C. 4320(b)(1)(C)
). Section 4321 of title 19 (
19 U.S.C. 4321
) authorizes the Commissioner of CBP, as part of an importer risk assessment program, to develop risk assessment guidelines for
(
printed page 69979)
IORs, including nonresident importers,
[
6
]
and procedures to ensure increased oversight of products imported by new nonresident importers relating to the enforcement of priority trade issues.
[
7
]
See
19 U.S.C. 4321(a)
and
(b)
. Section 4321(c) excludes validated Tier 2 and Tier 3 CTPAT participants from the requirements of
19 U.S.C. 4321
.
[
8
]
Sections 1484 and 1498 of title 19 (
19 U.S.C. 1484
and
1498
) authorize the Secretary of the Treasury to prescribe regulations for the declaration and entry of merchandise. All merchandise imported into the customs territory of the United States is subject to entry and clearance procedures, unless excepted.
See
section 141.4(a) of
title 19 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(
19 CFR 141.4(a)
). These procedures ensure the proper appraisement, valuation, and tariff classification of the merchandise for the purpose of collecting the lawful amount of duties owed, as well as ensuring compliance with all laws and regulations administered and enforced by CBP. Sections 1484 and 1498 provide for different procedures for the entry and clearance of merchandise depending upon the aggregate value of the shipment. There are “formal entry” procedures established by
19 U.S.C. 1484
and
1485
, which are generally applicable to shipments of merchandise valued in excess of $2,500.
Title 19 CFR
part 142 implements
19 U.S.C. 1484
, as amended, and prescribes formal entry procedures.
Section 1498 of title 19 (
19 U.S.C. 1498
) authorizes special rules and regulations for the entry of certain merchandise, which includes section 1498(a)(1)(A) concerning shipments of merchandise valued at $2,500 or less (referred to as “informal entries”). Such entries may be, but are not required to be, subject to the requirements for formal entry prescribed at
19 U.S.C. 1484
and
1485
. Informal entry regulations are found at
19 CFR part 143, subpart C
. While informal entries are “excepted” from formal entry requirements, as noted, the Secretary of the Treasury may include any formal entry requirement in the rules and regulations governing informal entry.
19 U.S.C. 1498(b)
. The statutory framework of
19 U.S.C. 1498
authorizes, in effect, a less stringent entry process than under
19 U.S.C. 1484
, which has developed into a process with fewer forms and procedures as compared to the formal entry process. As a result, informal entry procedures are generally less burdensome and complex than the formal entry procedures. However, CBP may require formal entry for any merchandise if deemed necessary for purposes of admissibility, revenue protection, or the efficient conduct of customs business.
19 CFR 143.22
.
Section 1641 of title 19 (
19 U.S.C. 1641
) authorizes the Secretary of the Treasury to prescribe such regulations relating to the customs business of customs brokers as the Secretary considers necessary to protect importers and the revenue of the United States, including regulations relating to the furnishing of information to CBP, and to carry out the provisions of
19 U.S.C. 1641
.
Section 1592 of title 19 (
19 U.S.C. 1592
) authorizes CBP to assess civil penalties against any person who, by fraud, gross negligence or negligence, enters or introduces, or attempts to enter or introduce, merchandise into commerce of the United States by means of a material false statement or omission.
The Security and Accountability for Every (SAFE) Port Act of 2006 (
Pub. L. 109-347
, 120 Stat. 1884 (2006),
6 U.S.C. 961
et seq.
) authorizes the Secretary of DHS, acting through the Commissioner of CBP, to establish a voluntary government-business initiative to build cooperative relationships that strengthen and improve overall security of the international supply chain and U.S. border security, and facilitate the movement of secure cargo through the international supply chain, known as CTPAT.
See
6 U.S.C. 962
,
964
and
965
. The CTPAT program plays a crucial role in safeguarding the economic and national security of the United States by acting as a vital component of CBP's multi-layered, risk-based security strategy. By securing international supply chains, the program helps prevent the entry of terrorist weapons, narcotics, and other contraband, thereby mitigating threats to national security. The CTPAT program contributes to the nation's prosperity by ensuring the free and fair flow of legitimate trade, preventing costly disruptions, and fostering a secure trade environment. The program's commitment to customs and trade enforcement provides an essential platform to combat trade fraud and protect American consumers and industries.
CBP encourages participation in this program by providing benefits to participants meeting or exceeding the CTPAT program requirements. An individual or company
[
9
]
that wishes to participate in the CTPAT program must complete an application in the CTPAT Portal
[
10
]
demonstrating that it meets the MSC
[
11
]
to establish eligibility for the program. Once a company is accepted into the program and receives “certified” status, the CTPAT participant will undergo a validation to verify the participant's supply chain security processes.
6 U.S.C. 964
. At the conclusion of a successful validation, the participant will be granted “certified—validated” status.
6 U.S.C. 965
. Upon becoming a participant in the CTPAT program, an individual or company enjoys a variety of benefits, which are listed on CBP's website at
https://www.cbp.gov/​border-security/​ports-entry/​cargo-security/​ctpat
.
[
12
]
IV. Challenges Relating to Foreign Importers of Record
Unlike other countries that either do not allow foreign persons to act as an IOR or have strict processes for becoming a foreign IOR,
[
13
]
in the United
(
printed page 69980)
States, a foreign individual or entity may become an IOR and make entry in the United States solely by submitting CBP Form 5106 (Create/Update Importer Identity Form) to request a CBP-assigned number, or by using an Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Employer Identification Number (EIN), which provides only basic contact and business information to CBP. Many of the foreign individuals and entities who become IORs appear to be U.S.-based in the Automated Commercial Environment (ACE) because they list a U.S. address, which may be the address of an agent or post office box for mail. In reality, these foreign individuals or entities have no physical presence and no assets beyond a mailing address in the United States and are considered shell companies. These shell companies obscure the real identity and corporate structure of their owner,
[
14
]
as well as ownership of the entity's assets, enabling tax evasion, financial fraud and other financial crimes. Due to the anonymity of a shell company's identity and the identity of its owner(s), it is difficult to track and verify the company's financial transactions, including customs entries, and to prevent the importation of potentially unsafe merchandise, such as counterfeit goods and precursor chemicals for the purposes of manufacturing illicit substances, into the United States. Thus, these shell companies pose a significant threat to national security, economic security, and public safety.
These shell companies may also engage in misclassification, undervaluation, or other duty evasion schemes, knowing that CBP's options for enforcement are limited when assets and individuals are located outside of the United States and that it is more difficult for CBP to detect linkages and affiliations. In such cases, when detected by CBP, these shell company IORs may be placed on live entry pursuant to
19 CFR 142.13(a)(3)
, which mandates the filing of an entry summary and deposit of all estimated duties, taxes, and fees owed to obtain the merchandise's release from CBP custody, and may have their immediate delivery privileges discontinued pursuant to
19 CFR 142.25(a)
. However, the shell company IOR may export the shipment rather than pay the estimated duties, taxes, and fees at that time, making collection efforts fruitless, and later attempt to re-enter the goods under a different shell company. Enforcement actions against shell companies are challenging because the foreign entity may simply shut down an existing shell company and begin importing as a new shell company. When an IOR is registered with CBP by submitting CBP Form 5106, CBP is only aware that the entity is a foreign IOR if the IOR lists its foreign address.
[
15
]
Once the IOR has begun importing and becomes liable for the payment of duties, penalties, or liquidated damages, CBP may later learn through its investigations and enforcement actions that an IOR who listed a U.S. address was in reality a shell company set up on behalf of a foreign company to avoid paying CBP debts that become due or evade other enforcement consequences. By this point, the economic damage undercutting U.S. domestic industry has already been completed.
The United States faces substantial challenges when seeking to enforce U.S. customs and trade laws against foreign IORs. One of these challenges is the enforcement of financial obligations to the U.S. government, including duties. Pursuing the collection of duties, penalties, and liquidated damages is often ineffective because these entities' operations are outside U.S. jurisdiction, and their assets and key individuals are located outside U.S. jurisdiction. While CBP can use tools such as “live entry”
[
16
]
and discontinuance of immediate delivery privileges pursuant to
19 CFR 142.13
and
142.25
to secure future obligations, amounts already owed to CBP often go uncollected if the entity is unwilling to pay. Data collected from October 2020 through the beginning of February 2026 shows that the unpaid bill amount per entry is $29.16 for foreign IORs as compared to $22.57 for U.S. IORs, which is 29% lower for U.S. IORs.
[
17
]
As of February 6, 2026, the total principal bill amount (not including interest) owed by non-CTPAT foreign IORs for uncollected bills that were opened on or after October 1, 2020, and remained unpaid, was $1.01 billion. After CBP audits uncovered $1.16 billion in lost revenue from foreign IORs between January 1, 2020, and August 27, 2026, CBP was able to recoup only $35.7 million, implying a collection rate of 3.1% for the missed payments.
[
18
]
For U.S. IORs, that collection rate was 15.2%. Additionally, live entry and discontinuance of immediate delivery privileges are limited in their effectiveness where foreign IORs reconstitute their identities and create new fake companies. These new shell companies operate under a different name and exist solely to evade enforcement consequences for violations of U.S. law. While CBP's enforcement authority extends to any individual or entity importing merchandise into the United States, enforcement is often more effective against individuals and entities located within the United States. When an IOR's operations and the majority if not all of its financial assets are located outside the United States, CBP's ability to compel compliance with U.S. customs and trade laws, conduct investigations, collect owed revenue, identify linkages and affiliations, or enforce penalties is significantly reduced. Moreover, the government's ability to pursue legal action against, or collect duties from, these foreign entities is more complex because they are not subject to U.S. jurisdiction due to the revenue rule.
The revenue rule is a longstanding common law doctrine that permits the courts of one country to refuse to entertain lawsuits that are initiated by a foreign country to enforce the foreign country's revenue laws.
Her Majesty the Queen
v.
Gilbertson,
597 F.2d 1161, 1164-1165 (9th Cir. 1979);
see also Holman
v.
Johnson,
(1775) 98 Eng. Rep. 1120-1121 (K.B. 1775) (stating that “no country ever takes notice of the revenue laws of another”). The rationale behind the rule is threefold: first, the international principle of comity precludes the courts of one nation from scrutinizing (and potentially bringing embarrassment upon) the public laws of another nation; second, one nation's utilization of another nation's court system to enforce its own revenue laws is an extension of the former nation's sovereign power, and that assertion of sovereign power within the territory of another nation violates national sovereignty principles; and third, permitting the courts of one nation to interpret the complex revenue laws of a
(
printed page 69981)
foreign nation would result in great administrative difficulties at great expense to the interpreting nation.
Gilbertson,
597 F.2d at 1164 (quoting
Moore
v.
Mitchell,
30 F.2d 600, 604 (2nd Cir. 1929));
Gov't of India
v.
Taylor,
(1955) A.C. 491, 511-514 (H.L. 1955). Thus, the revenue rule protects the independent sovereignty of each nation and prevents the courts of one country from becoming an extension of the judicial branch of another. Lawsuits to recover U.S. customs duties, penalties, and liquidated damages are all within the jurisdiction of the federal courts.
See, e.g.,
28 U.S.C. 1331
,
1582
. However, enforcement of such a judgment from a federal court in a foreign jurisdiction would likely be precluded by that jurisdiction's observance of the revenue rule, or at least time-consuming and exceedingly difficult to pursue.
Verification of the accuracy of import and entry documentation, conducting audits, or performing site visits of a foreign IOR's premises are all considerably more difficult and resource intensive for foreign IORs. CBP also faces challenges in enforcing CBP recordkeeping requirements on foreign IORs. Although all importers, foreign and U.S., are subject to recordkeeping requirements under
19 U.S.C. 1508
, it is much easier and more straightforward for CBP to conduct document verification and examination of records for domestic entities. Communication barriers and lack of understanding of U.S. laws and regulations can further hamper CBP's enforcement ability and result in delays, difficulty in resolving issues, and a higher incidence of errors and non-compliance.
Generally speaking, it is inherently more complex for CBP to ensure compliance by foreign IORs, as compared to U.S. IORs. Foreign IORs may exploit U.S. customs and trade laws and refuse to pay their customs debts, knowing the challenges posed by international enforcement of domestic customs laws and regulations. Because of these challenges in holding foreign IORs accountable, there is decreased incentive for foreign IORs to comply with U.S. laws and regulations intended to ensure the safety of imported merchandise and to secure the revenue; foreign IORs avoid the consequences that U.S. IORs face, because their assets and key individuals may be beyond the reach of CBP and the U.S. courts. Principles such as the revenue rule reinforce why it is important for the United States to impose heightened requirements on foreign IORs, who can more easily evade payment of amounts owed and other consequences for noncompliance with U.S. customs and trade laws. These challenges are unique in the context of foreign IORs.
V. Addressing the Challenges Relating to Foreign Importers of Record
It is critical that CBP be able to counter the challenges discussed above through meaningful and effective enforcement actions. Thus, pursuant to the authorities set forth above, and consistent with
E.O. 14411
, CBP is implementing additional requirements for foreign IORs to make entry. This rule will require foreign IORs to be CTPAT validated, or to use a CTPAT validated and licensed customs broker to make entry. These new requirements will promote compliance and accountability. Licensed customs brokers will have new responsibilities corresponding with the new foreign IOR requirements to verify and declare that their client meets the qualifications to be considered a U.S. IOR before reporting as a U.S. IOR. Lastly, this rule will impose a new requirement on U.S. IORs to declare their qualification as a U.S. IOR.
To implement these new requirements, CBP is establishing a new part 110 (Importers of Record) in
title 19 of the CFR.
This new part contains two sections laying out the qualifications to be considered a “U.S. importer of record,” or “foreign importer of record,” as well as a new definitions section defining the terms “beneficial owner,” and “physical domestic assets.” This new part 110 provides predictability and standardization for trade members which previously did not exist.
First, CBP establishes the requirements that must be met to be considered a U.S. IOR in new
19 CFR 110.2(a)
, to allow CBP, IORs, and customs brokers to know who qualifies as a U.S. IOR and who does not. Pursuant to this new provision, a U.S. IOR is an individual who is a United States citizen or lawful permanent resident, or an entity that is organized under the laws of the United States, is located in the United States, and maintains at all times: (i) at least 51% of beneficial owner(s) who are United States citizens or lawful permanent residents and have control of the entity; or (ii) direct ownership of a significant amount of unencumbered real property in the United States. With respect to real property ownership, the property can be subject to some encumberment, but the net unencumbered value of the real property must be of a significant amount. Whether an individual or entity qualifies as a U.S. IOR is subject to verification by CBP as set forth in a new § 110.2(b). A foreign IOR is defined as an IOR who does not meet the criteria of a U.S. IOR, pursuant to § 110.3.
In the new § 110.2(b), CBP has set forth a verification process for confirming that a party meets the requirements to be considered a U.S. IOR. The determination of whether an entity qualifies as a U.S. IOR or a foreign IOR will vary depending upon the circumstances in each instance. To verify that an entity is located in the United States for qualification as a U.S. importer of record, CBP will take into account, among other considerations, the size and scale of the overall operations of the entity and whether it is an instrumentality of a foreign manufacturer without a substantial presence in the United States. Criteria which CBP may consider in its discretion and to the extent relevant, include, but are not limited to, whether: (1) the entity's principal place of business is in the United States; (2) the entity has a physical presence in the United States where substantial business transactions are conducted, such as paying employees, generating revenue, or operating retail locations; (3) the entity maintains sufficient unencumbered physical domestic assets, as defined in § 110.1; (4) the entity directly owns a sufficient amount of unencumbered real property in the United States; (5) the entity's gross sales generally exceed its cost of goods sold and the entity is structured in a manner that it is anticipated to generate its own profit; and (6) the entity is sufficiently capitalized. As good governance, CBP is providing this non-exhaustive list of criteria that CBP will consider when verifying the identity and status of an IOR. These criteria are flexible as CBP cannot predict all possible circumstances that may be relevant for verification purposes. Having the newly created criteria available will allow CBP to verify that an entity's declaration meets the requirements under § 110.2, which in turn increases supply chain security, revenue protection, and compliance with the customs law of the United States.
In its verification, CBP may review records, such as, proof of citizenship or lawful permanent residence, corporate charters, financial statements and records, purchase receipts, or documents of title, provided at the request of CBP. Pursuant to
19 U.S.C. 1508
, an IOR, or other party who imports merchandise into the customs territory of the United States, or an agent of an IOR or person whose activities require the filing of a declaration or entry, or both, must make, keep, and render for examination and inspection records which pertain to
(
printed page 69982)
any such activity and are normally kept in the ordinary course of business.

19

To ensure CBP can adequately verify the status of IORs, the IOR must, pursuant to
19 U.S.C. 1508
, comply with statutory recordkeeping and production requirements, and CBP retains the authority to request proof from the IOR as to its qualification as a U.S. IOR.
CBP is taking a comprehensive approach to distinguish the level of risk associated with foreign and U.S. IORs, to establish requirements commensurate with that risk, thus putting all importers (including nonresident importers as described in
19 U.S.C. 4321
) on equal footing. These new regulatory provisions require consideration of both substance (such as ownership, physical presence, and U.S.-based assets) and form (such as place of incorporation or organization and address) as indicators of whether an individual or entity is a U.S. or foreign IOR. The existing references to a “nonresident importer” in CBP regulations (found in subparts B and C of part 141) capture importers who are not U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents or not entities organized under the laws of the United States or its territories; that is, importers who have met a low threshold to qualify as nonresident importers. A nonresident importer could simply be an importer who is not incorporated within the customs territory of the United States (§ 141.18), whereas a foreign IOR is an individual or entity who has not satisfied a variety of specific criteria, such as at least 51% beneficial ownership or direct ownership of a significant amount of unencumbered real property in the United States. The existing references to a “nonresident importer” within CBP regulations are not in conflict with the new regulations for U.S. IORs and foreign IORs, as these new regulations create additional requirements for importers. The regulatory changes implemented by this rule that distinguish a U.S. IOR from a foreign IOR present a clearer framework for importers and a higher threshold to qualify as a U.S. IOR. Central to these new definitions is ensuring that physical assets of the importer are located in the United States, increasing the likelihood that CBP can collect revenue owed from all IORs and enabling CBP to better identify potential linkages and affiliations when an importer's assets are transferred.
In support of § 110.2(a)(2)(iii)(A) regarding U.S. IORs, CBP is defining the term “beneficial owner” in new § 110.1. CBP is including the “beneficial owner” condition in the requirements for a U.S. IOR because illicit actors often use corporate structures, such as shell companies, to conceal their identities, which undermines U.S. national security and threatens the domestic economy. Shell companies can shield identities of the beneficial owners, enabling them to transact business in the United States without facing legal consequences and evading enforcement mechanisms, creating an uneven playing field for U.S. businesses engaged in legitimate trade. Including a definition of “beneficial owner” enables CBP to identify the true individual or individuals exercising control over the entity responsible for the importation of goods. Also, by defining “beneficial owner,” CBP is providing clarity and transparency to trade members as to CBP's understanding of who qualifies as a beneficial owner. At the same time, CBP is facilitating compliance and revenue collection as a clear definition will reduce the ability of bad actors to use shell companies to evade duties and other customs and trade law requirements.
The term “beneficial owner” means, with respect to an entity, an individual who is a natural person, and directly or indirectly, through any contract, arrangement, understanding, relationship, or otherwise, either exercises substantial control over the entity, or owns or controls not less than 25 percent of the ownership interests of the entity. The “beneficial owner” definition includes circumstances where multiple layers of entity ownership exist between the natural person and the entity, such as a corporation that is owned by another corporation that is owned by a natural person, in which case the natural person is the beneficial owner despite the layers of entity ownership. The definition specifically excludes: (1) a minor child, as defined in the State in which the entity is formed, or in the case of an entity that was not formed in the United States an individual who has not yet attained the age of 18, if the parent or guardian of the minor child meets the definition of a beneficial owner; (2) an individual acting as a nominee, intermediary, custodian, or agent on behalf of another individual; (3) an individual acting solely as an employee of a corporation, limited liability company, or other similar entity and whose control over or economic benefits from such entity are derived solely from the employment status of the person, provided that such a person is not a senior officer; (4) an individual whose only interest in a corporation, limited liability company, or other similar entity is through a right of inheritance; or (5) a creditor of a corporation, limited liability company, or other similar entity, unless the creditor meets the requirements of an individual who, directly or indirectly, through any contract, arrangement, understanding, relationship or otherwise exercises substantial control over the entity or owns or controls not less than 25 percent of the ownership interests of the entity. For purposes of this definition, an individual might be a beneficial owner through substantial control, ownership interest, or both. Substantial control can be exercised by an individual who is either a senior officer (
e.g.,
the entity's president, or chief executive officer), has the authority to appoint or remove certain officers of the entity, or is an important decision-maker regarding the entity's business, finances and structure. Ownership interests that establish ownership rights in the entity include shares of equity, stock voting rights, or any other mechanism used to establish ownership. As all entities are substantially controlled by one or more individual(s), every entity must have at least one beneficial owner for purposes of determining as to whether an entity is a U.S. IOR. An entity may have multiple beneficial owners and there is no maximum number of beneficial owners.
To develop this definition, CBP reviewed a preexisting Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) definition (
31 CFR 1010.380(d)
), established by statute
[
20
]
to provide further consistency for the overall understanding of “beneficial owner” and expectations for trade members. This definition expands on the FinCEN definition by adding a paragraph to account for instances where an entity is incorporated/formed in the United States and is owned entirely by one or more other entities that are also incorporated/formed in the United States, but the natural persons who ultimately own the various layers of entities are not U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. This additional language is intended to clarify that natural persons must be identified as the beneficial owners, even where multiple layers of entity ownership exist
(
printed page 69983)
and that such multiple layers of entity ownership do not diminish the obligation to report the natural person beneficial owners. It is noteworthy that “beneficial owner” is defined in this document for the purpose of this rulemaking and CBP is not bound by FinCEN's interpretation of that term in other contexts, nor are these regulations impacted by whether FinCEN requires submission of beneficial ownership information.
Lastly, CBP is adding a definition of “physical domestic assets,” which becomes relevant when CBP verifies whether an IOR qualifies as a U.S. IOR pursuant to new § 110.2(b)(3). “Physical domestic assets” are defined as cash deposited in a U.S. bank account, U.S. Treasury bonds, and real property, inventory, machinery, and/or equipment that is physically located in the United States. It is important to note that CBP did not use the term “tangible” in this context as tangible assets may include accounts receivable which CBP purposefully excluded from this definition. Assets identified as physical domestic assets in CBP's definition are more readily capable of being traced and seized, which increases the likelihood of successful collection of customs debts. The physical nature of the assets is important for serving the purpose of these regulations. Valuation of intangible assets is often speculative and subject to manipulation, particularly in the context of IORs who may be structured as a separate entity from a retailer ultimately selling the product to the public. Additionally, receivables may be due from foreign parties, creating the potential for manipulation of their valuation and diminishing the likelihood of collection.
This definition of “physical domestic assets” covers a limited universe of assets that are relevant for the purpose of determining affiliations of entities. CBP needs to understand affiliations because foreign IORs can easily evade CBP requirements and verifications by creating new companies. By considering the types of assets covered under this definition, CBP is better able to identify shell companies that foreign actors use to evade U.S. customs laws. In addition, CBP's ability to pursue collection from successor companies, alter egos
[
21
]
or other parties when piercing the corporate veil
[
22
]
is increased, potentially reaching physical domestic assets improperly transferred to individuals tied to the shell company, such as corporate officers or shareholders.
CBP is adding two new sections to subpart B of part 141 (§ 141.21 and § 141.22), pertaining to the right to make entry and declarations on entry. Pursuant to paragraph (a) of new § 141.21, a foreign IOR, as defined in § 110.3, may not enter merchandise for consumption unless specific requirements are met. This restriction is applicable to merchandise entered for consumption (§ 141.0a(f)) for which a formal entry is required to be filed or, if an informal entry is filed, for which an informal entry is required to be filed on CBP Form 3461 and/or CBP Form 7501, or their electronic equivalents.

Pursuant to § 141.21(b)(1), if the foreign IOR is CTPAT validated and has the right to make entry pursuant to § 143.26 for informal entry or
19 U.S.C. 1484(a)(2)(B)
for formal entry, the foreign IOR may enter merchandise for consumption or designate a customs broker to make entry. A CTPAT validated foreign IOR choosing to hire a customs broker may elect to hire a CTPAT validated broker, or a non-CTPAT validated broker.
Pursuant to § 141.21(b)(2), a foreign IOR who is not CTPAT validated must designate a customs broker licensed under
19 U.S.C. 1641
who is validated through the CTPAT program to either make entry or to act as the importer of record on the entry.

If a customs broker acts as the importer of record for the entry on behalf of a principal on the power of attorney (§ 141.46) who is not an importer of record, and that principal would qualify as a foreign importer of record pursuant to § 110.3 of this chapter, the broker must also be validated through the CTPAT program. The designated customs broker who is validated through the CTPAT program must act as the IOR for the entry if the principal on the power of attorney (§ 141.46) is not the owner or purchaser of the merchandise.
It is important to note that, upon the effective date of this rule (January 5, 2027), being a licensed customs broker alone is not sufficient to file entry on behalf of a foreign IOR or a foreign principal on a broker's power of attorney, unless that foreign IOR is itself a CTPAT validated IOR. CBP has limited visibility into the information pertaining to a foreign party when a customs broker is filing the entries on behalf of the foreign party. A CTPAT validated broker has demonstrated to CBP that it has controls in place to give the broker insight into its client and the client's supply chain. As a result, CBP is requiring that a customs broker acting on behalf of a non-CTPAT validated foreign IOR be CTPAT validated, to ensure that a trusted party is filing the entry and entry summary. This places CBP in a better position to protect the revenue, ensure supply chain security, and guarantee the safety of the American public.
CTPAT is highly effective in securing international supply chains by requiring its participants to implement stringent security measures for their cargo, personnel, and facilities. This program encourages companies to proactively identify and mitigate risks such as terrorism, smuggling, and other illicit activities within their supply chains. By partnering with the private sector, CTPAT enables CBP to enhance cargo security and streamline legitimate trade, allowing enforcement resources to focus on higher-risk shipments. CTPAT's primary focus is on security and trade compliance, and its operational model inherently promotes transparency. The program requires participants to submit detailed security profiles and engage in a rigorous validation process with CBP to confirm compliance with established MSC, fostering a clear understanding of security practices between the government and the trade community. In addition, CBP is more likely to collect debt from CTPAT validated participants than from non-CTPAT participants. The analysis in section VIII.B. below shows that, on average, the uncollected bill amount per entry summary for CTPAT validated foreign IORs is much lower than for non-CTPAT foreign IORs, who more easily evade payment of outstanding bills, penalties, or claims for liquidated damages.

Current § 111.29(a) sets forth a customs broker's responsibility to exercise due diligence in making financial settlements and answering correspondence, among other responsibilities. CBP is adding a new § 111.29(a)(2) to include the responsibility of a customs broker to verify that a client meets the qualifications to be considered a U.S. IOR, after redesignating existing paragraph (a) as paragraph (a)(1). A customs broker, prior to filing a declaration on behalf of a client pursuant to § 141.22, must verify that the client qualifies as a U.S. IOR. As mentioned above, the client records may include, but are not limited to, proof of citizenship or lawful permanent residence, corporate charters, financial statements and records, purchase receipts, or documents of title. If a customs broker determines during the review of the client records that the client is not a U.S. IOR, the broker must cease filing entries on behalf of the client if the broker is not CTPAT validated. CBP has also updated § 111.21(a) and 111.23, to require that the broker maintain records related to the broker's verification for five years from the date of the verification.

19 U.S.C. 1641

19 U.S.C. 1592

19 U.S.C. 1592

19 U.S.C. 1641

Economic security is national security, and customs law enforcement is essential to protect the economy of the United States and the health and safety of the American people. Customs law enforcement requires the ability to assess stringent penalties to ensure an adequate deterrent effect on customs brokers that fail to comply with the law. Historically, CBP has penalized brokers pursuant to
19 U.S.C. 1641
, which sets a maximum monetary penalty amount of $30,000 for violations. Moreover, pursuant to existing paragraph (K) in Appendix B to part 171, CBP has assessed penalties against customs brokers pursuant to
19 U.S.C. 1592
only in those cases where the broker was involved in a violation with a culpability level of fraud or where the agency could demonstrate the broker benefited from the violation. Although penalties up to $30,000 are available under
19 U.S.C. 1641

19 U.S.C. 1592

VI. Explanation of Amendments to the CBP Regulations
A. Amendments to Part 110
CBP is creating a new part 110 in
title 19 of the CFR
, and adding subparts A and B. In new § 110.1, CBP has added new definitions for the terms “beneficial owner,” and “physical domestic assets.” In new § 110.2, CBP has laid out the requirements to be considered a U.S. importer of record, and the verification requirements associated with that status. In new § 110.3, CBP has explained that any IOR not qualified to be considered a U.S. IOR is considered a foreign IOR. Subpart B is reserved.
B. Amendments to Part 111
CBP is amending part 111, in accordance with the requirements discussed above. Specifically, CBP is amending §§ 111.21 and 111.23 by adding the requirement that brokers maintain records related to verifying that the client meets the threshold for a U.S. IOR under § 110.2. CBP is also amending § 111.29 by redesignating paragraph (a) as a new paragraph (a)(1) and adding a new paragraph (a)(2) to include a customs broker's responsibility for verifying a client's qualification as a U.S. IOR.
C. Amendments to Part 141
CBP is amending part 141, in accordance with the requirements discussed above. Specifically, CBP is adding two new sections (§ 141.21 and § 141.22). New § 141.21 states that a foreign IOR may not enter merchandise for consumption unless it is a CTPAT validated IOR or designates a customs broker who is CTPAT validated, and lays out associated requirements. New § 141.22 states that a U.S. IOR must submit a declaration as to its qualification as a U.S. IOR at the time of filing an entry and entry summary. CBP has also amended § 141.46 to clarify that a power of attorney is required even when the broker is acting as the IOR for an entry. In addition, the general authority citation for part 141 is revised to include
19 U.S.C. 4320
and
4321
.
D. Amendments to Part 142
CBP is amending part 142, in accordance with the requirements discussed above. Specifically, CBP is amending § 142.13 by adding a new paragraph (a)(5) that states that CBP may impose a live entry requirement if the importer inaccurately declares to CBP its qualification as U.S. IOR pursuant to § 141.22. CBP is also adding a new § 142.13(e) to clarify that CBP may impose a live entry requirement on formal and informal entries under the provisions of part 142 and part 143.
E. Amendments to Part 171
CBP is amending Appendix B to part 171, which sets forth guidelines for the imposition and mitigation of penalties for violations under
19 U.S.C. 1592
. Specifically, CBP is revising paragraph (K) in Appendix B, as discussed above.
F. Severability
CBP intends for the provisions contained in this rulemaking to be severable from each other and to be given effect to the maximum extent possible, such that if a court holds that any provision is invalid or unenforceable—whether in its entirety or as to a particular person or circumstance—the other provisions will remain in effect as to any other person or circumstance.

]
The various provisions in this IFR are designed to function sensibly without the others, and CBP intends for them to be severable so that each can operate independently.
G. Alternative and Request for Comments
As noted in Section II, above, although Section 2(b) of the E.O. directs CBP to prohibit foreign IORs from filing informal entry, CBP has not implemented that prohibition in this interim final rule. However, CBP will continue to monitor informal entries for consumption filed by CTPAT validated foreign IORs and CTPAT validated brokers on behalf of foreign IORs. If CBP determines that requiring that informal entries for foreign IORs be filed by a CTPAT validated party is insufficient to protect the revenue, national security, and the health and safety of the American people, CBP may prohibit informal entries for consumption filed by a foreign IOR or a broker acting on their behalf. CBP welcomes public comment on this alternative, in addition to the approach implemented by this interim final rule.

This interim final rule addresses challenges resulting from importations by foreign IORs. Securing America's borders, regulating and vetting foreign actors, and protecting its citizens from external threats is a foreign affairs function of the United States. Importations into the United States across America's borders can pose threats to U.S. citizens, including threats from contraband and harmful materials that can flow across the border, as well as narcotics trafficking and other destabilizing or unlawful activities, including the flow of dangerous drugs, weapons, and technology. Further, ensuring foreign parties abide by U.S. trade law is a core foreign affairs function. Unchecked importations by foreign actors into the United States can undermine domestic markets and supply chains—for instance, foreign government assistance and subsidies, such as tax breaks to foreign manufacturers, enable them to sell cheaper goods and disadvantage domestic companies. In response, the U.S. may establish antidumping and/or countervailing duties to counteract foreign government assistance and subsidies. Tracking and vetting foreign importers is critical to counteracting bad actors in the trade space, preventing evasion of U.S. trade law, and upholding the integrity of domestic markets and supply chains. If customs and trade laws cannot be adequately enforced against foreign importers of record, it leaves American citizens vulnerable to foreign actors and foreign governments. Accordingly, this rule is clearly and directly involved in a core foreign affairs function.

As discussed above, this interim final rule establishes new requirements for foreign IORs and U.S. IORs when making entry in the United States. Background
To fulfill its mission, CBP must ensure that importers of record (IORs) pay the applicable duties, taxes, and fees for their imports as well as any monetary penalties issued by CBP. Sometimes, CBP discovers that an IOR underpaid its duties through misrepresentations such as undervaluation, false country of origin, transshipment, misclassification, or false invoices. Other times, an IOR will simply refuse to pay any duties in the first place. Upon discovery of underpayment, CBP can issue a penalty to the IOR, but the IOR may not cooperate in paying. CBP can collect on the basic importation and entry bond, but sometimes the bond saturates, meaning that it does not cover the full amount owed. In that case, CBP can try to seize the IOR's assets. This option can be difficult when the IOR is foreign, as a foreign IOR may have few if any real assets in the United States, and whatever assets the foreign IOR has in its home country may be unreachable to the U.S. government. CBP can require the IOR to file live entry and suspend immediate delivery privileges for all future importations until that IOR makes any outstanding payments to CBP, but foreign IORs may be able to evade these requirements through creation of shell companies. When an IOR is based outside the United States, CBP has less visibility into the IOR's operations and assets than it does with U.S. IORs, making it easier for the foreign IOR to conceal its identity and harder for CBP to hold the IOR and its affiliates accountable. As a result, foreign IORs that receive or anticipate enforcement or collection actions by CBP will sometimes switch to a new name to evade consequences for past actions. Foreign IORs can therefore avoid payments to CBP and other consequences more easily than U.S. IORs can, giving the former an unfair advantage.
While CBP has limited visibility into many foreign IORs' operations, IORs that are CTPAT validated are generally more transparent and trustworthy in their transactions and dealings with CBP. The CTPAT program ensures that participants meet minimum security criteria and abide by best practices. It also creates more visibility into the participants' supply chain and operations because the CTPAT participant must be in communication with its contact in CBP to show that it is continuing to meet the requisite standards. The CTPAT participant must also have visibility into the operations of businesses that it interacts with to ensure the supply chain is secure, as represented to CBP upon validation. Hence, if an IOR is not CTPAT validated, but uses a CTPAT validated broker, that broker will have obtained more information about the IOR's business than a non-CTPAT validated broker would have, and CBP will be better able to obtain information regarding the IOR from the broker if necessary. Requiring foreign IORs to be CTPAT validated or use CTPAT validated brokers will therefore strengthen CBP's ability to enforce collections on foreign IORs by increasing transparency into the foreign IORs' business and supply chain practices.
Purpose of the Rule
CBP faces challenges in enforcing collection of duties, penalties, and liquidated damages against foreign IORs because these IORs often have few, if any, physical assets in the United States and their bond does not fully cover amounts lawfully owed to CBP. This rule requires foreign IORs to either be CTPAT validated or to use a CTPAT validated broker so that the foreign IORs meet stricter standards of security and transparency. CTPAT validated brokers have more information about their clients' supply chains, and this information could improve CBP's ability to collect payments from the foreign IOR and identify other non-compliance with U.S. customs and trade laws. Furthermore, foreign entities will have more incentive to avoid exporting prohibited goods to the United States or otherwise violate CBP requirements if they are trying to maintain their CTPAT validated status. U.S. IORs will also have to provide documentation proving that they are a U.S. IOR at CBP's request, which will help CBP to determine which IORs claiming to be U.S. IORs are in fact foreign shell companies.
Baseline for the Rule
In this regulatory impact assessment (RIA), CBP analyzes the effects of the rule by comparing a baseline and an alternative scenario. Currently, foreign IORs import shipments into the United States without being CTPAT validated or using a CTPAT validated broker. Under this rule, foreign IORs would have to be CTPAT validated or use CTPAT validated brokers to enter merchandise into the United States. The effects of the rule are therefore the differences between the world under the current baseline and the world under this rule.

Benefits
Under the rule, CBP will be better equipped to enforce payments for duties, penalties, and liquidated damages from foreign IORs, and CBP will have more knowledge of which IORs are foreign or domestic. One of CBP's many critical mission sets is to facilitate legitimate trade that supports economic growth while shielding the American public and businesses from illicit trade, including unsafe products, intellectual property theft, and unfair trade practices. However, CBP cannot easily ensure that foreign IORs are complying with U.S. customs and trade laws to prevent the importation of dangerous and unlawful goods, potentially unsafe merchandise, such as counterfeit goods and precursor chemicals for the purposes of manufacturing illicit substances, into the United States. This program encourages companies to proactively identify and mitigate these risks within their supply chains, and these new requirements will allow CBP to more effectively focus its efforts on higher risk importers to interdict illicit drugs, intellectual property violative goods, misclassified merchandise, and other goods that pose risks to public safety.

While the increased revenue collected by the U.S. government would come directly from foreign IORs, those foreign IORs could pass on some share of the burden to U.S. individuals through price adjustments. To the extent that the revenue ultimately comes from U.S. individuals, the revenue is a transfer, not a benefit of the rule, as the gain to the U.S. government would equal the loss to the individuals. To the extent that the foreign IORs themselves bear the burden of increased payments to CBP, that share of the increased revenue is a benefit of the rule, as it entails a transfer from foreign entities to the U.S. government. By requiring foreign IORs to either become CTPAT validated or use a CTPAT validated broker, the rule will increase transparency into foreign IORs' operations, making it more difficult for bad actors to export prohibited goods to the United States.
The rule will also help to keep the supply chain safer from terrorist threats. Under the rule, more brokers will choose to become CTPAT validated so that they can continue serving non-CTPAT validated foreign IORs, and some foreign IORs may choose to become CTPAT validated so that they are not required to hire a CTPAT validated broker, though only foreign IORs that are Canadian are currently eligible for CTPAT validation. The increase in CTPAT validated entities will make the supply chain safer because an entity seeking CTPAT validation must work with CBP to identify security gaps and implement specific security measures and best practices. If the entity does not meet the minimum security criteria, CBP will recommend that the company address specific weaknesses as a condition to obtain CTPAT validation. The entity must also develop an internal validation process that preserves the security measures documented in its supply chain security profile. Therefore, entities that become CTPAT validated will make their supply chains less vulnerable to intrusion by terrorists or terrorist organizations. Besides increasing the number of CTPAT validated entities, the rule will also make the supply chain more secure by causing more non-CTPAT foreign IORs to use CTPAT validated brokers. One of the minimum security criteria for CTPAT validated customs brokers is that personnel “must review the information included in import/export documents to identify or recognize suspicious cargo shipments.” CTPAT validated brokers are therefore more vigilant than non-CTPAT validated brokers with regard to the cargo that their clients are importing.
Costs
CBP
The increased participation in CTPAT under the rule will result in costs to CBP. When a company applies for CTPAT validation, CBP must review the company's application and security profile. If CBP certifies the company, CBP then conducts a validation to verify that the company's stated security measures are implemented. This process may include interviews, document review, and site visits to domestic or foreign locations. During a site visit, CBP supply chain security specialists (SCSS) review in detail the entity's import supply chain security procedures to determine whether the security procedures in place meet CTPAT standards. The SCSS later document their findings from the visit in a validation report. Even after a company receives CTPAT validation, CBP continues to incur costs from the company's CTPAT participation, such as the costs of revalidation. CBP estimates that the increase in CTPAT participation will result in costs to CBP totaling $10.9 million, including the costs of additional staffing, travel, equipment, and automation.
