Specific Taxonomic and Nomenclatural Changes
We provide below, in the same sequence as in table 1, a species-by-species discussion supporting the changes in scientific name, common name, or both in the Lists.
In certain instances, in the following discussions, we address changes to a species' scientific name. Per
50 CFR 17.11(c)
and
17.11(g)
for wildlife and
50 CFR 17.12(b)
and
17.12(g)
for plants, to determine a species' scientific name, we are to rely, to the extent practicable, on the Integrated Taxonomic Information System (ITIS) (
https://www.itis.gov/​
). ITIS is an online database used by the Service as a reference for Act-related taxonomic decisions. We have determined that, as a reviewer of current taxonomic literature, it maintains generally accepted lists of taxa that are both valid and verified (
81 FR 51550
at 51555, August 4, 2016). However, ITIS is not a taxonomic authority; it compiles information from other sources. In our experience, the taxonomic treatment it recognizes for some taxa is not always consistent with the best scientific data available. We are required by the Act to use the best scientific and commercial data available. When conflict exists, we rely on our own best professional judgment, the expertise of the scientific community, and current taxonomic literature (especially, but not limited to, primary sources) to determine the most appropriate taxonomic treatment (see
81 FR 51550
, August 4, 2016, citing
45 FR 13010
at 13012-13013, February 27, 1980).
Per section 3(16) of the Act (
16 U.S.C. 1532(16)
), the term “species” may include a taxon at the species rank, a taxon at the subspecies rank, or for vertebrates, a distinct population segment (DPS); a DPS is a non-taxonomic entity that is unique to the Act. In taxonomy, a species is indicated by the combination of two terms, the genus epithet and the species epithet, forming a binomial. A subspecies is a form of infraspecific taxon; that is, a taxon hierarchically below the species rank or level. In zoological nomenclature, a subspecies is indicated by the combination of three terms, the genus epithet, the species epithet, and the subspecies epithet, forming a trinomial. In botanical nomenclature, multiple forms of infraspecific taxa are used indicating various taxonomic ranks.
For our purposes implementing the Act with respect to plants, we focus on the infraspecific taxa of subspecies and variety. For the purposes of section 3(16) of the Act, we consider plant varieties to be equivalent to subspecies (
43 FR 17910
at 17912, April 26, 1978). Consistent with the International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants (ICN), we use abbreviations to distinguish between the two categories. The ICN is the set of internationally agreed upon rules and recommendations that botanical taxonomists use in the naming of algae, fungi, and plants. As such, we use the abbreviation “var.” (punctuation included) to indicate a variety. However, the abbreviation for indicating a subspecies has changed in botanical nomenclature; it had long been “ssp.” (punctuation included), but the ICN now recommends “subsp.” (punctuation included). We note that ITIS currently uses “ssp.” as the abbreviation to indicate botanical subspecies. This contrasts with the recommendation of the ICN, and we consider the ICN to provide the best scientific information on this matter. Therefore, in instances where we are addressing subspecies of plants, we are shifting the abbreviation we use from “ssp.” to “subsp.” We are doing this on
(
printed page 70018)
a case-by-case basis, when appropriate, and not en masse.
Additionally, in certain instances in the following discussions, we address species that include synonyms. Per
50 CFR 17.11(b)
for wildlife common names, 17.11(c) for wildlife scientific names, 17.12(b) for plant scientific names, or 17.12(c) for plant common names, we sometimes parenthetically include one or more synonyms as part of the common name or scientific name when confusion might arise from the use of different names for the same taxon. When there is little chance for confusion, we do not include synonyms.
San Bernardino Kangaroo Rat
We are changing “San Bernardino Merriam's kangaroo rat” to “San Bernardino kangaroo rat.” This is an editorial change, not a taxonomic change. The scientific name remains the same. We acknowledge that the listed entity is a subspecies of the associated species-level taxon, Merriam's kangaroo rat (
Dipodomys merriami
). We further acknowledge that by including “Merriam's” in the common name of the subspecies, it indicates a hierarchical taxonomic relationship with
Dipodomys merriami.
However, “San Bernardino kangaroo rat” is used much more widely in the scientific literature as the common name for
Dipodomys merriami parvus.
Because of this, we are changing the common name. This editorial change does not affect the range or the listing status of this subspecies; we continue to recognize the listed entity at the subspecies rank for the purposes of section 3(16) of the Act. Critical habitat has been designated for this species, but “San Bernardino kangaroo rat” is consistent with the common name we use in
50 CFR 17.95
. As such, no changes are needed in that section.
Stephens' Kangaroo Rat
We are changing “
Dipodomys stephensi
(incl.
D. cascus
)” to “
Dipodomys stephensi.”
This is an editorial change, not a taxonomic change. The common name remains the same. We are removing the parenthetical synonym. The current scientific literature recognizes
Dipodomys stephensi
as the most appropriate name for this taxon; the name
Dipodomys cascus
was established later in time and does not have nomenclatural precedence (that is, it is a junior synonym, in part) (ITIS 2024r, unpaginated); it has not been used for many years. At this point, there is little chance for confusion. Therefore, for simplicity, we are removing the synonym. ITIS (2024s, unpaginated) recognizes
Dipodomys stephensi
as the current (valid) scientific name for this taxon. This editorial change does not affect the range or the listing status of the species; we continue to recognize the listed entity at the species rank for the purposes of section 3(16) of the Act. A species-specific “4(d)” rule (a rule issued under the authority of section 4(d) of the Act) has been designated for this species, but it does not mention the parenthetical synonym; consequently, no changes are needed in
50 CFR 17.40(t)
. Critical habitat has not been designated for this species, and no changes are needed in
50 CFR 17.95
.
Inyo California Towhee
We are changing the scientific name from “
Melozone crissalis eremophilus”
to “
Melozone crissalis eremophila.”
This is an editorial change, not a taxonomic change. The common name remains the same. On July 31, 2023, we recognized the genus-level taxonomic realignment for this listed entity from
Pipilo
to
Melozone
(
88 FR 49310
). However,
Pipilo
is masculine, and
Melozone
is feminine (David and Gosselin 2002, p. 259). Consequently, the subspecific name or epithet (the third name in the trinomial) should be changed from
eremophilus
to
eremophila
to remain consistent with the grammatical gender of the newly recognized genus name (or genus epithet). Information in ITIS (2024ab, unpaginated) supports the feminine orthography; however, ITIS does not currently recognize the subspecies. As discussed in our 2024 5-year status review for the Inyo California towhee (Service 2024, pp. 5-7), we are continuing to recognize the subspecies at this time, contrary to ITIS. This nomenclatural revision does not affect the range or the listing status of this subspecies; we continue to recognize the listed entity at the subspecies rank for the purposes of section 3(16) of the Act. Critical habitat has been designated for this species, and we are making commensurate changes in the subspecies' scientific name in
50 CFR 17.95
.
Western Snowy Plover [Pacific Coast DPS]
We are changing the scientific name from “
Charadrius nivosus nivosus”
to “
Anarhynchus nivosus nivosus,”
we are changing the common name “western snowy plover [Pacific Coast population DPS]” to “western snowy plover [Pacific coast DPS],” and we are changing the DPS's entry in the “Where listed” column in
50 CFR 17.11
(h) from “Pacific Coast population DPS—U.S.A. (CA, OR, WA), Mexico (within 50 miles of Pacific coast)” to “U.S.A. (CA, OR, WA), Mexico (Baja California, Baja California Sur); within 50 miles of Pacific coast.” On April 21, 2006 (
71 FR 20607
at 20618), we determined that the listed entity qualified as a DPS under our DPS policy (
61 FR 4722
, February 7, 1996). This DPS is a population of the western snowy plover, a taxon at the subspecies rank. We are changing the entry for the scientific name of the listed DPS to reflect a taxonomic change of the subspecies.
Analyses of molecular data and other characteristics indicate that
Charadrius
(broadly speaking) is paraphyletic (Barth et al. 2013, figure 1 therein; Dos Remedios et al. 2015, figure 1 therein; Černý and Natale 2022, figure 6 therein); that is, the genus, as it has been traditionally recognized, comprises more than one evolutionary lineage. To better reflect the snowy plover's evolutionary lineage, most authorities have transferred it (along with several other
Charadrius
species) to the genus
Anarhynchus
in their recent treatments (Clements et al. 2023, unpaginated; Medler 2023, unpaginated; Gill et al. 2024, unpaginated; but see Handbook of the Birds of the World (HBW) and BirdLife International 2024, unpaginated). Additionally, the North American Classification Committee (NACC) of the American Ornithological Society (AOS) (formerly the Committee on Classification and Nomenclature of the American Ornithologists' Union) also recently accepted the genus-level change for the snowy plover, recognizing the species as
Anarhynchus nivosus
(Chesser et al. 2024, p. 2). The AOS NACC is widely accepted as the leading authority of avian taxonomy in North America. While the AOS NACC no longer explicitly addresses taxa at the subspecies rank, because of the hierarchical structure of zoological taxonomy, changes at the genus level are also reflected at the species- and subspecies-levels as well. Thus, the best scientific information available indicates that the scientific name for the DPS's underlying taxon is now
Anarhynchus nivosus nivosus.
The ITIS entry for the western snowy plover does not currently reflect the recent information in the scientific literature (ITIS 2024, unpaginated); the most recent references ITIS cites for this taxon are from 2022. We conclude that ITIS does not currently provide the best available scientific information for this subspecies. Based on our review of the scientific literature, we recognize
Anarhynchus nivosus nivosus
as the scientific name for the DPS. This taxonomic revision does not affect the range or the listing status of this DPS; we continue to recognize the listed
(
printed page 70019)
entity as a DPS of a vertebrate subspecies for the purposes of section 3(16) of the Act.
Additionally, as part of our review of the scientific name entry in
50 CFR 17.11
, we reviewed the common name entry. We are changing two aspects of the common name. First, we conclude that it is not necessary to capitalize the “c” in “coast.” The “Pacific Coast” is not a widely recognized proper noun, and when it is used, it is typically equivalent to the “West Coast,” referring to the Pacific coastal region of the conterminous United States. The range of the DPS also includes a portion of the Pacific coastal region of the Baja California Peninsula, Mexico, and therefore, “Pacific Coast” does not adequately describe the DPS's range. Second, we conclude that including the word “population” in the common name for the DPS is redundant; clarity is diminished by including the first use of the term in the entity's common name when the DPS initialism is written out: western snowy plover [Pacific coast
population
distinct population segment]. We are removing the first instance of that word in that phrase. As such, we are changing the entry for the common name to “western snowy plover [Pacific coast DPS].” This common name revision does not affect the range or the listing status of this DPS. Critical habitat has been designated for this DPS, and we are making commensurate changes in the DPS's scientific name and common name in
50 CFR 17.95
.
Moreover, as described in
50 CFR 17.11(d)
, the “Where listed” column in
50 CFR 17.11(h)
sets forth the geographic area where the species is listed for purposes of the Act. Currently, the entry in this column for the DPS reads “Pacific Coast population DPS—U.S.A. (CA, OR, WA), Mexico (within 50 miles of Pacific coast).” This is somewhat unclear. We are changing it to “U.S.A. (CA, OR, WA), Mexico (Baja California, Baja California Sur); within 50 miles of Pacific coast.” This change addresses three potential sources of confusion. First, the phrase “Pacific Coast population DPS—” at the beginning of the entry is unnecessary. When similar phrases are used in the List of Endangered and Threatened Wildlife, they are used to distinguish between or among different DPSs of the same species. For example, compare with the various entries for DPSs of the humpback whale (
Megaptera novaeangliae
) or steelhead (
Oncorhynchus mykiss
). Second, the new wording better indicates that the “within 50 miles of the Pacific coast” phrase applies to California, Oregon, and Washington as well as the DPS's range in Mexico, including the Mexican States of Baja California and Baja California Sur. This clarification is consistent with how we have long considered the range of the DPS. For example, our description of the DPS's range in the recovery plan (Service 2007, p. 1) states, “[t]he Pacific coast population [of the western snowy plover] is defined as those individuals that nest within 50 miles of the Pacific Ocean on the mainland coast, peninsulas, offshore islands, bays, estuaries, or rivers of the United States and Baja California, Mexico.” While this definition is more complete, it is still not entirely accurate as written; it does not include the Mexican State of Baja California Sur. This oversight is inconsistent with mapped or described ranges in our earlier publications (
71 FR 20607
at 20609, April 21, 2006; Service 2007, p. 2 (figure 1); Service 2019b, p. 2). Thus, to address the third potential source of confusion, we are also amending the “Where listed” column to explicitly include the Mexican States of Baja California and Baja California Sur. These editorial changes do not affect the range or the listing status of the DPS, and they have no bearing on
50 CFR 17.95
.
Arroyo Toad
We are changing the common name “arroyo (=arroyo southwestern) toad” to “arroyo toad.” This is an editorial change, not a taxonomic change. We are removing the synonym in the common name entry. The scientific name remains the same. When we listed this species in 1994, it was recognized as the arroyo southwestern toad (
Bufo microscaphus californicus
) (
59 FR 64859
, December 16, 1994). With subsequent taxonomic revisions, as described in
74 FR 52612
(October 13, 2009), we now recognize the listed entity as the arroyo toad (
Anaxyrus californicus
). This combination is widely used in the scientific literature. At this point, there is little chance for confusion. Therefore, for simplicity, we are removing the synonym in the common name. This editorial revision does not affect the range or the listing status of the species; we continue to recognize the listed entity at the species rank for the purposes of section 3(16) of the Act. Critical habitat has been designated for this species; however, the synonym is not included and “arroyo toad” is consistent with the common name we use in
50 CFR 17.95
. As such, no changes are needed in that section.
Desert Slender Salamander
We are changing the scientific name from “
Batrachoseps aridus”
to “
Batrachoseps major aridus.”
This reflects a taxonomic change. The common name remains the same. We provide the background for this change in our 2014 5-year review (Service 2014, pp. 5-6 and 14), which is updated in the following discussion. Southern California slender salamanders (genus
Batrachoseps
) show high genetic diversity and complex phylogenetic lineages, which results in taxonomic uncertainty in
Batrachoseps
taxa in this region, including the desert slender salamander (Jockusch et al. 2020, entire). Further, the extreme scarcity of desert slender salamanders has limited the extent to which the entity has been assessed by modern methods (Martínez-Solano et al. 2012, p. 147; Jockusch et al. 2015, p. 67). ITIS currently does not recognize the desert slender salamander as a taxon, either as a species or a subspecies (ITIS 2024g, unpaginated; 2024h, unpaginated); ITIS's treatment does not consider it distinguishable from the garden slender salamander (
B. major
) (ITIS 2024i, unpaginated). However, it is unclear how ITIS came to its conclusion because the references it cites are inconsistent. For example, one of its references, the Amphibian Species of the World online database (Frost 2024a, unpaginated; 2024b, unpaginated) currently notes that the distinguishability of the desert slender salamander is ambiguous, whether at the species level or subspecies level, but the Committee on Standard English and Scientific Names for Reptiles and Amphibians North of Mexico, another reference ITIS cites, has recognized
Batrachoseps major aridus
in the past three editions of its list, the first of which ITIS cites (Crother 2008, p. 15; Crother 2012, p. 25; Crother 2017, p. 27). We conclude that ITIS does not currently provide the best available scientific information for this taxon. In all, in our review of the scientific literature (primary sources and taxonomic authorities), we find no consensus in the taxonomic treatment. While few sources support recognizing the desert slender salamander at the species rank (
B. aridus
), some sources support recognizing it as a population of garden slender salamander (
B. major
) and not as distinguishable taxon, and other sources support recognizing it at the subspecies rank (
B. m. aridus
). Currently, we are recognizing the desert slender salamander as a subspecies,
B. m. aridus,
consistent with Crother et al. (2017, p. 27). This taxonomic revision does not affect the range or the listing
(
printed page 70020)
status of this entity; however, with this change, we now recognize the listed entity at the subspecies rank for the purposes of section 3(16) of the Act. Critical habitat has not been designated for this species, and no changes are needed in
50 CFR 17.95
.
El Segundo Blue Butterfly
We are changing the scientific name from “
Euphilotes battoides allyni”
to “
Euphilotes allyni.”
This reflects a taxonomic change. The common name remains the same. As we noted in our 2021 5-year review (Service 2021a, pp. 2-3), an analysis of genetic data determined that the population of
Euphilotes battoides
-type butterflies sampled from coastal Los Angeles County was the most distinct of several populations of
Euphilotes battoides
-type butterflies sampled from within Southern California (Dupuis et al. 2020, p. 1911). This subsequently prompted recognition of the El Segundo blue butterfly at the species rank,
Euphilotes allyni
(Rubinoff et al. 2021, pp. 161-162). The genetic evaluation confirmed that the range of the El Segundo blue butterfly is limited to the area from the northern portion of the Palos Verdes Peninsula to the area near Ballona Lagoon (Service 2021a, p. 7). The genetic data also indicated that other populations of similar-looking blue butterflies elsewhere that were suspected to be El Segundo blue butterflies, are not
E. allyni
(see discussion in Dupuis et al. 2020, pp. 1899, 1914-1915)
.
Currently, ITIS continues to recognize
Euphilotes battoides allyni
as the current (valid) scientific name for the El Segundo blue butterfly (ITIS 2024x, unpaginated). It appears that ITIS's entry for this taxon does not reflect the recent information in the scientific literature because the most recent reference it cites is from 2009. We conclude that ITIS does not currently provide the best available scientific information for this taxon.
We are recognizing the El Segundo blue butterfly as
Euphilotes allyni.
This taxonomic revision does not affect the range or the listing status of this entity; however, with this change, we now recognize the listed entity at the species rank for the purposes of section 3(16) of the Act. Critical habitat has not been designated for this species, and no changes are needed in
50 CFR 17.95
.
Acanthomintha duttonii (San Mateo thornmint)
We are changing the scientific name from “
Acanthomintha obovata
ssp.
duttonii”
to “
Acanthomintha duttonii.”
This reflects a taxonomic change. The common name remains the same. Based on a reevaluation of the species, Jokerst (1991, p. 278) elevated the taxon to species rank. This treatment was recognized and accepted in the Jepson eFlora (Miller and Jokerst 2012, unpaginated). The Jepson eFlora (Jepson Flora Project 2024, unpaginated) is the regularly updated online version of The Jepson Manual: Vascular Plants of California (Baldwin et al. 2012, entire). The Jepson Manual is the standard flora for California in which contributing authors provide systematic treatments of all the State's taxonomic groups; it is widely considered an authoritative source for botanical taxonomy in California. ITIS (2024a, unpaginated) also recognizes and accepts this combination. This taxonomic revision does not affect the range or the listing status of this entity; however, with this change, we now recognize the listed entity at the species rank for the purposes of section 3(16) of the Act. and that the Kneeland Prairie pennycress should be assigned as a subspecies under
Noccaea fendleri
(Koch and Al-Shehbaz 2004, p. 382). This treatment was recognized and accepted in the Jepson eFlora (Al-Shehbaz 2012b, unpaginated). ITIS (2024ad, unpaginated) also recognizes and accepts this combination. This taxonomic revision does not affect the range or the listing status of the taxon; however, with this change, we now recognize the listed entity at the subspecies rank for the purposes of section 3(16) of the Act. Critical habitat has been designated for this species, and
(
printed page 70025)
we are making commensurate changes in
50 CFR 17.96
.
Hesperocyparis goveniana (Gowen cypress)
We are changing the scientific name from “
Cupressus goveniana
ssp.
goveniana”
to “
Hesperocyparis goveniana.”
This reflects a taxonomic change. The common name remains the same. When we listed the entity in 1998 (
63 FR 43100
, August 12, 1998), we recognized it at the subspecies rank (Bartel 1993, p. 112). Its taxonomic rank was based on a sister infraspecific taxon,
C. g.
subsp.
pigmaea
(Bartel 1993, p. 112). Subsequent phylogenetic analyses indicated that
C. g.
subsp.
pigmaea
was not closely related to
C. g.
subsp.
goveniana
(Bartel et al. 2003, p. 699; Adams et al. 2009, p. 182), and the entity previously recognized as
C. g.
subsp.
pigmaea
became recognized as a separate taxon at the species rank. Without a sister infraspecific taxon, the infraspecific epithet no longer applied to the Gowan cypress, and the entity previously recognized as
C. g.
subsp.
goveniana
became recognized at the species rank,
C. goveniana.
Additionally, as discussed in our 2012 5-year review (Service 2012, p. 4), Adams et al. (2009, pp. 179, 181) also found that the New World
Cupressus
species were sufficiently differentiated from Old World taxa to be recognized under a new, separate genus,
Hesperocyparis,
including
H. goveniana.
This treatment was recognized and accepted in the Jepson eFlora (Bartel 2012, unpaginated). ITIS (2024aa, unpaginated) also recognizes and accepts this combination. This taxonomic revision does not affect the range or the listing status of the species; however, with this change, we now recognize the listed entity at the species rank for the purposes of section 3(16) of the Act. Critical habitat has not been designated for this species, and no changes are needed in
50 CFR 17.96
.
Required Determinations
Clarity of the Rule
We are required by Executive Orders 12866 and 12988 and by the Presidential Memorandum of June 1, 1998, to write all rules in plain language. This means that each rule we publish must:
(a) Be logically organized;
(b) Use the active voice to address readers directly;
(c) Use clear language rather than jargon;
(d) Be divided into short sections and sentences; and
(e) Use lists and tables wherever possible.
If you feel that we have not met these requirements, send us comments by one of the methods listed in
ADDRESSES
. To help us to revise this rule, your comments should be as specific as possible.
National Environmental Policy Act
We have determined that environmental assessments and environmental impact statements, as defined under the authority of the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (
42 U.S.C. 4321
et seq.
), need not be prepared in connection with regulations issued pursuant to section 4(a) of the Act. We published a notice outlining our reasons for this determination in the
Federal Register
on October 25, 1983 (
43 FR 49244
).
Government-To-Government Relationship With Tribes
In accordance with the President's memorandum of April 29, 1994, “Government-to-Government Relations with Native American Tribal Governments'” (
59 FR 22951
),
Executive Order 13175
, and the Department of the Interior's manual at 512 DM 2, we readily acknowledge our responsibility to communicate meaningfully with recognized Federal Tribes on a government-to-government basis. In accordance with Secretarial Order 3206 of June 5, 1997 (American Indian Tribal Rights, Federal-Tribal Trust Responsibilities, and the Endangered Species Act), we readily acknowledge our responsibilities to work directly with Tribes in developing programs for healthy ecosystems, to acknowledge that Tribal lands are not subject to the same controls as Federal public lands, to remain sensitive to Indian culture, and to make information available to Tribes. We have determined that this rule will not affect Tribes or Tribal lands.

AGENCY:
U.S. Integrated Ocean Observing System (IOOS®), National Ocean Service (NOS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Department of Commerce.
ACTION:
Notice of new member solicitation for the United States Integrated Ocean Observing System (U.S. IOOS) Advisory Committee.
SUMMARY:
NOAA is soliciting applications for membership on the United States Integrated Ocean Observing System Advisory Committee (the Committee), which is a Federal Advisory Committee. The Committee is mandated by the Integrated Coastal and Ocean Observation System Act of 2009 (the Act), part of the Omnibus Public Land Management Act of 2009 (
Pub. L. 111-11
), and the Coordinated Ocean Observations and Research Act of 2020 (
Pub. L. 116-271
) to provide advice to the NOAA Administrator and to the Interagency Ocean Observation Committee on the planning, integrated design, operation, maintenance, enhancement, and expansion of the United States Integrated Ocean Observing System (U.S. IOOS). NOAA is accepting applications for membership on the Committee to fill vacancies that will occur on September 14, 2027. NOAA encourages applications from individuals with expertise and/or experience in the following areas: coastal and ocean observing; data management and architecture; coastal and ocean modeling; Great Lakes; philanthropy; Non-Governmental Organization; scientific institutions (Academic); IOOS regional interests; State, local and tribal interests; blue economy; social science; public-private partnerships; marine technologies industries; ocean and coastal leadership; and other science-related fields.
DATES:
Applications should be submitted no later than January 5, 2027. Applications received after January 5, 2027 may not be considered during this membership application cycle, but may be considered for future membership cycles.
ADDRESSES:
Applications and questions about applications should be submitted via email
ioos.ac.staff@noaa.gov
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Krisa Arzayus, Designated Federal Official, U.S. IOOS Advisory Committee, U.S. IOOS Office,
krisa.arzayus@noaa.gov
or visit the U.S. IOOS Advisory Committee website at
https://ioos.noaa.gov/​community/​u-s-ioos-advisory-committee/​
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
U.S. IOOS (
https://ioos.noaa.gov
) is an integrated network of people and technology gathering coastal data and developing tracking and predictive tools to benefit the economy, the environment, and public safety at home, across the nation, and around the globe. U.S. IOOS promotes research to develop, test, and deploy innovations and improvements in coastal and ocean observation technologies and modeling systems, addresses regional and national needs for ocean information, gathers data on key coastal, ocean, and Great Lakes variables and ensures timely and sustained dissemination and availability of these data for societal benefits. U.S. IOOS benefits national safety, the economy, and the environment through support for national defense, marine commerce and forecasting, navigation safety, weather, economic development, ecosystem-based management of marine and coastal areas, conservation of ocean and coastal resources and public safety. This notice responds to the Act (
Pub. L. 111-11
, section 12304), which requires the Under Secretary of Commerce for Oceans and Atmosphere to solicit nominations for Committee membership. The Committee advises the NOAA Administrator and Interagency Ocean Observation Committee on matters related to the responsibilities and authorities set forth in section 12302 of the Act and other appropriate matters as the Under Secretary refers to the Committee for review and advice. The Committee has approximately fifteen voting members. For additional information about the Committee responsibilities, see
https://ioos.noaa.gov/​community/​u-s-ioos-advisory-committee/​
.
II. Eligibility and Criteria
Membership is open to individuals from academia; local, state or tribal government; industry; non-governmental not-for-profit, and other ocean-related institutions. Full-time officers or employees of the United States are not eligible. Race or sex shall not be considered in selection of Committee members. Members shall be qualified by education, training, and experience to evaluate scientific, technical, and programmatic information related to the design, operation, maintenance, or use of the U.S. IOOS, or use of data products provided through the U.S. IOOS.
III. Terms of Service
The NOAA Administrator shall appoint new Committee members for three-year terms, renewable once for an additional three-year term. The next term will begin on September 14, 2027.
IV. Expectations
The Committee will meet at least once each year in-person, with additional virtual meetings throughout the year. In a typical year, a committee member is expected to attend at least one in-person meeting (2-4 days including travel) and commit approximately 20-25 additional hours to attend virtual meetings and draft recommendation reports. Members of the Committee will not be compensated for service on the Committee, but they may be allowed travel expenses, including per diem in lieu of subsistence, in accordance with
subchapter I of chapter 57 of title 5, United States Code
.
V. Application
To apply for membership, applicants must submit the following items. The entire package should not exceed eight pages.
(1) A cover letter that serves as a statement of interest to serve on the Committee and provides the requested information listed below.
(a) Applicant's area(s) of expertise, as aligned with the expertise requested in the
SUMMARY
section above.
(b) The geographic region(s) of the country most closely associated with the applicant's area of expertise. This does not need to be the region the applicant currently resides in.
(c) Previous/current leadership or professional experience that may contribute to the effectiveness of the Committee.
(d) Familiarity and experience with U.S. IOOS data, products, and services.
(e) Breadth and scope of knowledge of stakeholders, users, or other groups who interact with NOAA or other U.S. IOOS agencies and whose views and input applicant believes they can share with the panel.
(2) A short biography of 300 to 400 words.
(3) A current resume.
(4) The nominee's full name, title, institutional affiliation, mailing address, email, and phone.
VI. Selection
Nominations will be reviewed and evaluated based on expertise, Committee needs, and balance considerations. Final appointments are made by the NOAA Administrator. Individuals selected for membership become a Special Government
(
printed page 70065)
Employee (SGE) of the United States Government. An SGE is an officer or employee of an agency who is retained, designated, appointed, or employed to perform temporary duties, with or without compensation, for not to exceed 130 days during any period of 365 consecutive days, either on a full- time or intermittent basis. Applicants who are selected to serve on the Committee must complete the following actions before they can serve as a committee member:
(1) Security Clearance (on-line Background Check and fingerprinting).
(2) Confidential Financial Disclosure Report—SGEs are required to file annually a Confidential Financial Disclosure Report to avoid involvement in a real or apparent conflict of interest.
(3) Attend annual ethics briefings to comply with government ethics standards.

Integrated Coastal and Ocean Observation System Act, part of the Omnibus Public Land Management Act of 2009 (
Public Law 111-11
), and the Coordinated Ocean Observations and Research Act of 2020 (
Public Law 116-271
).

Acting Director, U.S. IOOS Office, National Ocean Service, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

I. Executive Summary
This final rule,
Prohibiting Illegal Discrimination in Registered Apprenticeship Programs,
removes burdensome requirements for Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors contained in the regulation at
29 CFR part 30
, and replaces the part 30 regulation's complicated array of apprenticeship-specific nondiscrimination requirements with a more straightforward requirement that all Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors comply with all Federal and State laws and regulations prohibiting discrimination. In addition, the final rule provides clarity to apprenticeship stakeholders regarding the appropriate forums for advancing and remediating issues relating to alleged discrimination in Registered Apprenticeship programs.
Under this final rule, Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors will no longer be required to comply with the burdensome administrative requirements contained in the part 30 regulation, which included a general duty for all sponsors to engage in affirmative action and meet equal employment opportunity (EEO) obligations. The part 30 regulation's general duty to engage in affirmative action included mandates to designate an individual to manage the program's EEO policy, to conduct anti-harassment training, and to post an equal opportunity pledge, among other burdensome requirements. The final rule also removes the burdensome and legally questionable regulatory mandate that sponsors with five or more apprentices comply with more extensive affirmative action requirements, which included conducting utilization analyses and setting numerical goals for hiring apprentices based upon their race, sex, and ethnicity. The Department expects that removing these obligations will significantly reduce administrative burdens for sponsors and will also support the growth of Registered Apprenticeship programs, in alignment with the Department's and Administration's goals and priorities.
In their place, this final rule substitutes a streamlined requirement that all Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors comply fully with all applicable Federal and State laws and regulations prohibiting illegal
(
printed page 70165)
discrimination. This requirement, along with a revised regulatory framework for discrimination-related complaints, provides needed clarity to apprenticeship stakeholders on the most appropriate and effective course of action for apprentices to raise and seek remediation of discrimination-related issues. Finally, the final rule includes a requirement that any State seeking new or continued recognition from the Department's Office of Apprenticeship (OA) as a State Apprenticeship Agency (SAA) must establish State laws and regulations that conform to the revised part 30 regulation, so that Registered Apprenticeship programs throughout the National Apprenticeship System are subject to a consistent set of requirements related to nondiscrimination in apprenticeship.
II. Background and Purpose of the Revised Part 30 Regulation
A. Legal Authority To Promulgate Registered Apprenticeship Regulations
The National Apprenticeship Act (NAA) (also known as the Fitzgerald Act), 50 Stat. 664,
[
1
]
was enacted by Congress in 1937. Among other things, the NAA authorizes the Secretary of the Department of Labor to “formulate and promote the furtherance of labor standards necessary to safeguard the welfare of apprentices, to extend the application of such standards by inclusion thereof in contracts of apprenticeship, to bring together employers and labor for the formulation of programs of apprenticeship, [and] to cooperate with State agencies engaged in the formulation and promotion of standards of apprenticeship.” 50 Stat. 664.
[
2
]
The NAA forms the basis of the Department's legal authority to oversee the National Apprenticeship System and develop and advance labor standards, in conjunction with apprenticeship stakeholders throughout industry, labor, and State and local jurisdictions, for Registered Apprenticeship programs. Pursuant to this statutory authority, the Department has designated OA, within the Department's Employment and Training Administration (ETA), as the office responsible for conducting oversight, establishing rules and policies related to Registered Apprenticeship, and promoting the success and expansion of the Registered Apprenticeship model.
To implement the aims of the NAA, OA has promulgated regulations, found at
29 CFR parts 29
and
30
, to formalize labor standards that all Registered Apprenticeship programs must meet, and establish processes to conduct National Apprenticeship System oversight in coordination with State and local jurisdictions. The Department's legal authority to promulgate regulations related to Registered Apprenticeship, as well as the scope and content of such regulations, is rooted in the NAA. Under such authority, the Department must also periodically revisit the governing regulations at
29 CFR parts 29
and
30
in light of evolving economic conditions, changes impacting the labor market, or other developments impacting workforce development and apprenticeship.
The regulation at
29 CFR part 29
(part 29) implements the NAA's statutory directive to the Department to establish labor standards for Registered Apprenticeship programs and safeguard the welfare of apprentices. The first version of a regulation that set forth standards of apprenticeship was issued by the Department in 1977, and the last major revision to the part 29 regulations was issued in 2008. The part 29 regulation, and the labor standards that it established, serve as the primary regulatory framework for Registered Apprenticeship programs. The part 29 regulatory requirements for Registered Apprenticeship programs are intended to allow sponsors of such programs to tailor programs to meet their workforce needs while maintaining the high quality that has characterized Registered Apprenticeship for decades.
The regulation at part 30 requiring nondiscrimination and equality of opportunity in Registered Apprenticeship programs was first issued by the Department in 1963, and was subsequently updated by the Department in 1971, 1978, and 2016. Across these iterations, the part 30 regulation evolved from a prohibition against discrimination (also described as a requirement for sponsors to select apprentices “solely on the basis of their qualifications compared to those of other applicants”), to include various other requirements for sponsors and State agencies. For sponsors, additional requirements imposed by the part 30 regulation included: developing and posting a policy committing to equal opportunity; conducting anti-harassment training; providing a written notice to apprentices informing them of their right to file discrimination complaints and the process for doing so; and (for those Registered Apprenticeship programs enrolling five or more apprentices) conducting utilization analyses as part of their affirmative action plans and inviting apprentices to voluntarily disclose their disability status. The part 30 regulation also included a requirement for State agencies to develop a “State EEO plan” in order to seek or maintain recognition as an SAA, among other requirements.
Acting on the Department's authority to promulgate apprenticeship regulations under the NAA, the Department issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) entitled
Prohibiting Illegal Discrimination in Registered Apprenticeship Programs
in the
Federal Register
on July 2, 2025, (
90 FR 28947
) as the first step in a transparent process to update the part 30 regulation.
[
3
]
This first step of the rulemaking process for Federal agencies, which is governed by the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), as amended, at
5 U.S.C. 553
, supports transparent policymaking by allowing the Department to publish its proposed approach to updating the regulation and explain its rationale for the proposed changes, and by allowing the public to examine, assess, and provide public comments in response to the Department's proposal. In the NPRM, the Department proposed to update and significantly streamline the part 30 regulation to return to a more straightforward nondiscrimination requirement for Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors and clarify the most appropriate and effective processes and forums for raising and remediating issues related to alleged illegal discrimination in Registered Apprenticeship programs. The Department assessed public comments on its proposal and reexamined its rationale and goals for the rulemaking in light of the views, arguments, and data shared by public commenters, in developing this final rule in accordance with the APA.
B. Registered Apprenticeship: Opportunities for Expansion
For nearly a century, the Department has supported the administration of Registered Apprenticeship programs and overseen the National Apprenticeship System. Registered Apprenticeship is a proven workforce development strategy that combines paid on-the-job learning (OJL) and related instruction, providing tangible benefits to employers and career-seekers alike. Registered Apprenticeship enables employers to design training programs that meet their workforce development needs, empowers apprentices to advance their careers
(
printed page 70166)
through structured training that develops critical occupational skills and competencies and ultimately leads to an apprentice becoming proficient in an occupation. What began as a training strategy for the skilled trades has evolved and expanded to include a wider range of occupations across industries, including growth sectors such as information technology, health care, and financial services.
At the end of fiscal year (FY) 2025, according to OA data on Registered Apprenticeship programs nationwide, 26,628 active Registered Apprenticeship programs provided training to more than 700,000 apprentices.
[
4
]
These programs provide training in more than 1,000 occupations determined to be “apprenticeable”
[
5
]
across industries ranging from advanced manufacturing and construction to education, financial services, information technology, and health care. The number of apprentices has grown steadily over the past decade; the total number of active apprentices at the end of FY 2025 represented a 77% increase from the 395,764 active apprentices in FY 2016. Since 2016,
[
6
]
the Department has expanded its role in administering the National Apprenticeship System to include targeted investments to support Registered Apprenticeship growth. These investments have grown from around $90 million in FY 2016 to $185 million in FY 2021, $235 million in FY 2022,
[
7
]
and $285 million in FYs 2023, 2024, 2025, and 2026.
[
8
]
Despite the steady growth of the National Apprenticeship System, the Department recognizes that Registered Apprenticeship's impact on the U.S. economy, overall, remains limited. Registered Apprenticeship is underutilized as a workforce development solution in the United States when compared to the impact of apprenticeship in other developed nations. In the United States, apprentices comprise a significantly smaller share of the overall workforce than in other countries with strong and established apprenticeship systems (such as Australia, Canada, Germany, and the United Kingdom).
[
9
]
Given this underutilization of apprenticeship in the United States, the Department is determined to address factors that serve to limit the accelerated expansion and utilization of the model, including removing burdensome regulatory requirements like the complex and legally questionable set of requirements contained in the existing part 30 regulation.
While the Department is supportive of efforts to expand Registered Apprenticeship into new sectors and occupations where the training model is not currently widespread, the preponderance of Registered Apprenticeship programs remain within the skilled trades. In 2026, OA's data on apprenticeship participation by industry indicates there are nearly 270,000 apprentices in Registered Apprenticeship programs in the construction sector, a significant plurality compared to other industries.
[
10
]
This concentration of programs in the skilled trades limits Registered Apprenticeship's potential economy-wide impact and contributes to the false narrative that this training model is only suitable for that sector. Registered Apprenticeship's combination of structured OJL and related instruction is a proven training strategy that has consistently benefited both employers and career-seekers and can be adapted across industries (including growth sectors like information technology and healthcare).
The Registered Apprenticeship model has significant potential to meet the workforce development needs of more employers and provide more apprentices with opportunities to develop their careers, and as such, the Department views the expansion of the model as a pathway to greater economic prosperity in the United States. In a 2023 report (updated in February 2026), the U.S. Chamber of Commerce analyzed economic trends in job openings, labor force participation, and other labor market indicators.
[
11
]
This analysis showed that over the past two decades, job openings have increased, on average, while the number of unemployed workers has decreased, resulting in a persistent shortage of workers available to fill open positions. The analysis shows that while the gap between job openings and available workers has evened out following economic shocks and disruptions related to the COVID-19 pandemic (when unemployment spiked to 23 million unemployed workers in 2020), State-level economic data indicates that some States face significant challenges in filling job openings. South Dakota, for example, had 41 available workers for every 100 open jobs, and nationwide, only ten States report a surplus of available workers.
In general, labor force participation has been on the decline for the past two decades, due to a range of factors including retirements, an aging workforce, and reliance on means-tested public benefits. Further, employers increasingly point to a mismatch in the skills they need for their workforce and the skills possessed by job seekers when describing challenges in filling open positions. Surveys and analyses of hiring trends indicate that, while many employers have open positions and are seeking to hire employees, they struggle to fill these positions because they struggle to find candidates that possess the skills they need. One recent analysis estimates a potential shortage of approximately 5.25 million workers with education and training beyond high school through 2032, including projected shortages in several occupations that have historically relied on work-based training.
[
12
]
(
printed page 70167)
The Department sees Registered Apprenticeship as a critical strategy for increasing job seekers' skills and empowering employers to design training programs that develop in-demand skill sets. Registered Apprenticeship programs' training plans are based on industry training standards, meaning that industry leaders have input into the skills and competencies needed for an occupation. Sponsors of Registered Apprenticeship programs use these industry-derived inputs in designing programs that fit their specific needs (or the needs of employers who participate in the program). During the past two decades, the Registered Apprenticeship model has expanded into industries beyond the skilled trades, but still accounts for a small share of the overall labor force that lags far behind other advanced economies.
[
13
]
The Department views Registered Apprenticeship as a successful strategy for helping more employers meet their workforce development needs, a view that is more pronounced and relevant in the labor market of 2026, when job openings increasingly require higher levels of technical and specialized skills. As such, the Trump Administration has made the expansion of Registered Apprenticeship a top priority.
Registered Apprenticeship stakeholders, including those with established programs and those interested in starting programs, have pointed to the administrative burdens and direct costs of starting and operating a program as factors that limit the expansion and uptake of the model.
[
14
]
While Federal and State funds have helped mitigate these challenges, stakeholders still report impediments, including compliance with the administrative requirements found in Federal and State regulation. The Department has determined that substantially reducing the regulatory burdens that were imposed upon program sponsors by the part 30 regulation is an indispensable prerequisite for achieving the Department's ongoing goal of expanding Registered Apprenticeship to meet the needs of the labor market.
The Department's determination to update the part 30 regulation with this final rule also aligns with the Administration's priorities for the Department and Registered Apprenticeship. On January 31, 2025, in the first days of his Administration, President Trump signed
E.O. 14192
,
Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation,
which directed Federal agencies to identify opportunities to review and revise or rescind any regulations that impose undue burdens on Americans and American businesses, with the goal of increasing flexibility for businesses and accelerating economic prosperity.
[
15
]
The President also issued
E.O. 14278
,
Preparing Americans for High-Paying Skilled Trade Jobs of the Future,
which directed Federal agencies to prioritize investments and develop strategies to support workforce development, and specifically instructed the Departments of Labor, Education, and Commerce to develop a plan to achieve 1,000,000 active apprentices in Registered Apprenticeship programs.
[
16
]
The Department views this final rule rescinding the burdensome and legally questionable elements of the part 30 regulation as a critical step towards meeting the Administration's directives, growing Registered Apprenticeship's footprint in the broader economy, and supporting economic prosperity for employers and job seekers in the modern labor market.
C. Historical Background on Part 30 and on Prohibiting Illegal Discrimination in Apprenticeship
In issuing this final rule, the Department has determined that it can fulfill the NAA's statutory mandate to “safeguard the welfare of apprentices” by simply requiring that sponsors comply with already applicable Federal and State employment nondiscrimination laws. The importance of establishing clarity and consistency in the laws and policies governing nondiscrimination in Registered Apprenticeship programs is best understood by tracing the evolution of the part 30 regulation, the pertinent provisions of applicable Federal nondiscrimination laws, and relevant Supreme Court decisions relating to the constitutionality of group-based preferences generally.
The original version of the
29 CFR part 30
regulation
[
17
]
(issued by the Department in December 1963) barred Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors from engaging in discrimination against apprentices on the basis of race, color, creed, or national origin in all phases of apprenticeship, stipulated that the selection of apprentices by programs be made “solely on the basis of their qualifications compared to those of other applicants,” and provided for the deregistration of apprenticeship programs that failed to comply with those mandates.
[
18
]
In effect, the Department's issuance of the 1963 part 30 regulation prohibiting illegal discrimination by Registered Apprenticeship programs formulated a new minimum standard of apprenticeship designed to safeguard the welfare of apprentices, one that was later supplemented by the establishment of additional labor standards of apprenticeship (at
29 CFR part 29
) concerning, among other things, the payment of progressive wages and the provision of safe working environments to apprentices. However, it is important to note that neither the 1963 part 30 regulation nor its later iterations (in 1971, 1978, and 2016) provided apprentices with meaningful, individualized remedies (such as make-whole relief) to address instances of illegal discriminatory conduct against such persons by a program sponsor.
The absence of such individualized remedies for illegal discrimination against apprentices under the part 30 regulation, however, was addressed in the following year, when Congress enacted the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 78 Stat. 257 (the Act). Title VII of the Act (which applies to employers with 15 or more employees, among other covered
(
printed page 70168)
entities) prohibits employment discrimination against individuals on the basis of their race, color, religion, national origin, and sex. In particular, section 703(d) of the Act states that “[i]t shall be an unlawful employment practice for any employer, labor organization, or joint labor-management committee controlling apprenticeship or other training or retraining, including on-the-job training programs to discriminate against any individual because of his race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in admission to, or employment in, any program established to provide apprenticeship or other training.”
[
19
]
Section 706(g) of the Act further authorizes a wide range of remedies for employees (including apprentices) who have experienced discrimination at the hands of a covered entity based upon their race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.
[
20
]
The Act also established the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), a specialized Federal agency vested by Congress with the authority to receive and investigate complaints from job applicants and employees (including apprentices) alleging violations of Title VII (as well as alleged violations of other Federal employment discrimination statutes subsequently enacted by Congress).
Significantly, the text of Title VII contains no provision requiring employers or apprenticeship programs to adopt a compulsory, nonremedial scheme of group-based preferences (such as affirmative action arrangements) in hiring or employment that takes into consideration the race, color, religion, sex, or national origin of job applicants.
[
21
]
The absence of such a general mandate in Title VII is highlighted by the inclusion (at section 703(j) of the Act
[
22
]
) of a proscriptive rule of statutory construction specifically governing the provisions of Title VII. Section 703(j) stipulates, in relevant part, that nothing contained in Title VII shall be interpreted to require any employer, employment agency, labor organization, or joint labor-management committee subject to the title “to grant preferential treatment” to any individual or to any group based on the race, color, religion, sex, or national origin of such individual or group in order to address an imbalance which may exist in the demographic composition of an employer's or other covered entity's work force or membership, including those individuals “admitted to, or employed in, any apprenticeship or training program,” as compared to the demographic composition “in any community, State, section, or other area, or in the available work force in any community, State, section, or other area.”
In effect, the language of section 703(j) precludes governmental entities, such as Federal courts and relevant Federal administrative agencies, from interpreting Title VII's provisions in such a way as to require an employer or an apprenticeship program subject to the Act to grant preferential treatment to individuals or groups in hiring and employment based upon their race, color, religion, sex, or national origin for the purpose of achieving or maintaining demographic “balance” in that employer's or apprenticeship program's workforce. However, in those limited instances where a court finds that an employer or apprenticeship program has intentionally engaged in illegal, discriminatory employment practices under Title VII, the court has the discretion under section 706(g) of the Act to impose a narrowly tailored, time-limited affirmative action plan to remedy such discriminatory conduct.
See Loc. 28 of Sheet Metal Workers' Int'l Ass'n
v.
E.E.O.C.,
478 U.S. 421, 444-45 (1986) (plurality opinion);
id.
at 483 (Powell, J., concurring in part and concurring in judgment) (finding that the District Court had acted within the remedial authority under section 706(g) in establishing a numerical membership goal based on the percentage of nonwhites in the relevant labor pool where the union had repeatedly and egregiously violated Title VII and ignored prior judicial orders).
Taken together, the foregoing provisions of Title VII established a comprehensive statutory framework under which Congress outlawed all employment discrimination in apprenticeship and training programs covered by the Act based upon race, color, religion, sex, or national origin; provided effective remedies to individual apprentices who were subjected to such forms of illegal discrimination by covered employers and apprenticeship programs; precluded interpreting Title VII to require the utilization of nonremedial, group-based preferences by covered apprenticeship and training programs to address imbalances in the demographic composition of a program's workforce; and established a Federal agency (the EEOC) with the statutory authority and subject-matter expertise to investigate discrimination complaints by apprentices and to identify violations of Title VII by covered apprenticeship programs. The express inclusion of apprentices and apprenticeship and training programs within the scope of Title VII's statutory protections demonstrates that Congress was concerned about the prevalence of discrimination in these programs in the early 1960s, and was intentional in enacting legislation specifically prohibiting program sponsors from engaging in such egregious employment practices.
[
23
]
In 1971, subsequent to the enactment of Title VII, the Department modified the part 30 regulation by adding sex as a protected category with respect to nondiscrimination by program sponsors; this particular amendment effectively aligned the text of part 30 with the protected nondiscrimination categories that were established by Congress in Title VII. However, the 1971 version of the part 30 regulation also introduced and imposed upon apprenticeship programs enrolling five or more apprentices a compulsory, nonremedial affirmative action requirement of indefinite duration, and mandated the establishment of numerical hiring goals by such programs in the selection of apprentices from minority groups.
[
24
]
Clearly, the Department's 1971 issuance of a regulation mandating the establishment by such apprenticeship programs of a permanent system of nonremedial, nonvoluntary, group-based preferences in the selection of apprentices was fundamentally at odds with the unambiguous policy direction charted by Congress in sections 703(d) and (j) of Title VII regarding apprenticeship: namely, that
all
employment discrimination against
(
printed page 70169)
apprentices based upon their race, color, religion, sex, or national origin is illegal, and that the use of group-based preferences to adjust demographic imbalances which may exist in an apprenticeship program's workforce must never be required (unless such preferences are temporarily imposed by a court to remedy proven instances of manifest, intentional discriminatory conduct by a program). In a broader sense, however, the Department's regulatory imposition of affirmative action requirements for certain Registered Apprenticeship programs in the 1971 part 30 regulation—and the retention of these requirements in the 1978 and 2016 versions of the regulation—effectively substituted the policy preferences of an agency of the administrative state for the considered legislative judgments of the nation's elected representatives in delineating the appropriate scope and content of Federal employment nondiscrimination laws and policies relating to apprenticeship.
On June 29, 2023, the Supreme Court of the United States handed down a decision in a landmark case involving the use of race-based preferences in university admissions,
Students for Fair Admissions, Inc.
v.
President and Fellows of Harvard College,
600 U.S. 181 (2023) (
SFFA
). In
SFFA,
the Supreme Court held that the use of such racial preferences by Harvard and the University of North Carolina in their admissions processes violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution. Several NPRM commenters mischaracterized the extent to which the Department relied upon the decision in
SFFA
in proposing to rescind the race-, sex-, and ethnicity-based affirmative action provisions contained in part 30. To be clear, the Department did not and does not claim that
SFFA's
holding regarding race-based admissions in higher education
compels
the rescission of part 30's affirmative action provisions. Nevertheless, the Department considers the Supreme Court's decision in
SFFA
to be relevant to this rulemaking insofar as it signals the Court's apparent willingness to revisit the constitutionality of race-based selection and admissions procedures that it had previously upheld in earlier decisions. In his
SFFA
opinion striking down these types of preferences, Chief Justice Roberts opined that “[e]liminating racial discrimination means eliminating all of it,” 600 U.S. at 206, and further observed that the Court has “time and time again forcefully rejected the notion that governmental actors may intentionally allocate preferences to those `who may have little in common with each other but the color of their skin,' ”
id.
at 220 (quoting
Shaw
v.
Reno,
509 U.S. 630, 647 (1993)). These categorical and pointed expositions of nondiscrimination and equal protection principles by the Chief Justice in
SFFA
—as well as similar viewpoints expressed by other justices in their concurring opinions—certainly do not augur well for the Court's future sanctioning of mandatory, nonremedial race-, ethnic-, and sex-based affirmative action efforts in Registered Apprenticeship.
Recognizing that government-mandated, group-based affirmative action schemes such as those contained in the 1971, 1978, and 2016 versions of the part 30 regulation “violate the text and spirit of our longstanding Federal civil-rights laws,” President Trump issued
E.O. 14173
, “Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity,” on January 21, 2025.
[
25
]
Among other things, section 2 of
E.O. 14173
directed “all executive departments and agencies to terminate all discriminatory and illegal preferences, mandates, policies, programs, activities, guidance, regulations, enforcement actions, consent orders, and requirements.” Noting that longstanding Federal civil rights laws such as Title VII “protect individuals from discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin” and serve “as a bedrock supporting equality of opportunity for all Americans,”
E.O. 14173
affirmed that the President of the United States has “a solemn duty to ensure that these laws are enforced for the benefit of all Americans.” The issuance of this final rule by the Department prohibiting all illegal discrimination in Registered Apprenticeship programs fulfills President Trump's directive in
E.O. 14173
; moreover, it demonstrates appropriate respect for, and deference to, the nondiscrimination policies relating to apprenticeship that were enacted by Congress as part of Title VII of the Act.
In revising the content and scope of the part 30 regulation, the Department has determined that the affirmative action provisions described above are administratively burdensome and likely unlawful. Moreover, the Department is convinced that affirmative action schemes tend to promote the development of pernicious and divisive group-based preferences within our society, thereby undermining the goal of ensuring equality of opportunity for every American participating in the workforce. Accordingly, in issuing this final rule, the Department affirms that all applicants seeking admission to a Registered Apprenticeship program should be evaluated and selected strictly on the basis of individual merit and demonstrated potential, and that a person's race, color, religion, sex, or national origin must never be considered by a sponsor as a basis for either rejecting or granting preferential treatment to anyone seeking admission to a Registered Apprenticeship program.
D. Need for the Rulemaking: The Burdens and Challenges Imposed on Sponsors by the Part 30 Regulation
The Department has known for some time that, as its Task Force on Apprenticeship Expansion reported, “many employers choose to establish apprenticeship programs outside of the registered apprenticeship program, in part because of the paperwork and process involved in registering a program.” Apprenticeship Programs, Labor Standards for Registration, Amendment of Regulations,
85 FR 14294
,
14295
(Mar. 11, 2020). The Department has determined that this final rule updating the part 30 regulation is necessary to accomplish the Department's and Administration's goals of eliminating unnecessary and burdensome regulatory requirements and accelerating the expansion of Registered Apprenticeship. The part 30 regulation contains the type of onerous regulatory requirements targeted by the Administration's deregulatory directive contained in
E.O. 14192
; in particular, the Department has identified the affirmative action requirements of the part 30 regulation as illustrative of the complicated, burdensome, and ineffective regulations that Federal agencies are directed to rescind or revise under the E.O.
Accordingly, the Department has determined that revising the part 30 regulation is necessary to discontinue the regulatory imposition of a legally questionable, nonremedial, group-based preference scheme for certain Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors. Moreover, the Department has determined that this final rule is necessary to achieve cost savings for Registered Apprenticeship stakeholders and reduce the cost and administrative burden of establishing and maintaining Registered Apprenticeship programs. As outlined in the Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) accompanying this final rule, over a 10-year period, Registered Apprenticeship stakeholders stand to save more than $1 billion on costs related to compliance with the part 30
(
printed page 70170)
regulation, including developing and maintaining affirmative action programs and complying with other part 30 requirements. The E.O. directing Federal agencies to identify opportunities for increased regulatory flexibility established the potential for financial relief for the regulated community as a criterion for targeting burdensome regulations. Eliminating the costs of compliance with the part 30 regulation further informs the Department's determination that this final rule's significant revisions to the part 30 regulation are necessary.
E. Goals of the Revised Part 30 Regulation
The fundamental aims of this final rule are threefold: (1) to simplify sponsors' obligations with respect to nondiscrimination in apprenticeship by affirming the applicability and sufficiency of existing Federal and State laws governing nondiscrimination in the workplace; (2) to rescind the regulatory, nonremedial affirmative action mandate that the Department has imposed upon program sponsors since 1971—a mandate that the Department is concerned would not survive legal challenge and that was plainly inconsistent with the policies underlying the statutory, apprenticeship-related, nondiscrimination provisions of Title VII applicable to many of these same sponsors; and (3) to reduce the regulatory and administrative burdens on Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors—burdens that could inhibit the accelerated establishment and expansion of such vital workforce development programs—by removing all onerous, conflicting, duplicative, or unnecessary requirements found in the part 30 regulation.
The Legal and Practical Challenges Imposed Upon Program Sponsors by the Affirmative Action Provisions of the Part 30 Regulation
Alleviating the legal and practical challenges imposed on program sponsors by the affirmative action provisions of the part 30 regulation is a primary objective of the Department's final rule. As stated in the foregoing section, the part 30 regulation's affirmative action mandate for certain apprenticeship programs imposed an onerous administrative burden upon these program sponsors and is inconsistent with this Administration's efforts to enforce merit-based opportunity, as the requirements may induce these sponsors to engage in the unequal and illegal treatment of individual apprentices (as well as applicants for apprenticeship) based upon their race, sex, or ethnicity.
In the public comments submitted to the Department in response to the NPRM, several commenters discounted or glossed over the significant and self-evident administrative burdens that the affirmative action provisions of the part 30 regulation imposed upon certain program sponsors, particularly those that operate small- and medium-sized enterprises. These commenters opined that the affirmative action provisions of the part 30 regulation imposed no undue burdens, simply requiring certain sponsors (
i.e.,
those that employ five or more apprentices) to identify imbalances in the demographic composition of the sponsor's apprenticeship workforce, to set “aspirational” hiring goals based upon that analysis, and to make “good faith” efforts to address such imbalances, while simultaneously adhering to the general prohibition on making apprenticeship hiring decisions based upon an applicant's race, ethnicity, or sex. These commenters, however, failed to either recognize or acknowledge that the part 30 regulation's nondiscrimination and affirmative action provisions, taken together, imposed fundamentally contradictory and irreconcilable legal mandates upon apprenticeship programs.
The internally inconsistent regulatory requirements contained in the part 30 regulation are illustrated by examining the content of the affirmative action provisions of that regulation at § 30.4. While § 30.4(a)(5) states that the “commitments made in an affirmative action program are not intended and must not be used to discriminate against any qualified applicant or apprentice” on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, disability, age or national origin, § 30.4(a)(2) admonishes sponsors that “if women, individuals with disabilities, or individuals from a particular minority group . . . are not being admitted into apprenticeship at a rate to be expected given their availability in the relevant labor pool, the sponsor's affirmative action program must include specific, practical steps designed to address any barriers to equal opportunity that may be contributing to this underutilization.” Such “practical steps” will frequently involve the establishment of “utilization goals” based upon an individual's race, sex, and ethnicity to address such demographic imbalances in the apprenticeship program's workforce (see § 30.4(d)).
The fundamental policy premise underlying the affirmative action provisions contained in the part 30 regulation was that “absent discrimination, over time a sponsor's apprenticeship program, generally, will reflect the sex, race, ethnicity, and disability profile of the labor pools from which the [apprenticeship] sponsor recruits and selects.”
See
29 CFR 30.4(a)(2)
. This premise was and is constitutionally dubious, however, and the Department's concomitant regulatory requirement of setting utilization goals in the hiring of apprentices based upon the race, sex, and ethnicity of a program applicant had the effect of inducing program sponsors to meet such numerical targets. The mandating of such numerical hiring goals, combined with the prospect of apprenticeship program deregistration for failing to take “good faith efforts” to meet such goals, plainly incentivized employers to engage in legally questionable, group-based preferential hiring practices in order to prevent an administrative finding by the Department that they had failed to engage in such affirmative action efforts.
The part 30 regulation (at
29 CFR 30.5(b)
) further stipulated that sponsors with 5 or more apprentices enrolled in their programs conduct, at least once every 3 years, detailed demographic and utilization analyses to assess and address the existence of imbalances with respect to certain demographic groups enrolled in their programs. By requiring the permanent, ongoing conduct of such analyses by certain program sponsors—and potentially requiring the establishment of group-based numerical hiring goals based upon the results—this regulatory provision constituted a mandate that such sponsors not only strive to achieve, but also continuously maintain, a demographic “balance” in their apprenticeship programs based upon race, sex, and ethnicity. Such a regulatory purpose, however, was and is plainly contrary to the fundamental policy thrust of Title VII, as demonstrated by the text of section 703(j) of the Act (discussed
supra
) and by the following passage contained in an interpretative, joint memorandum drafted by Senators Joseph Clark of Pennsylvania and Clifford Case of New Jersey that was addressed to their Senate colleagues at the time of the floor debate on H.R. 7152 (the bill that was later enacted by Congress as the Act): “There is no requirement in Title VII that an employer maintain a racial balance in his work force. On the contrary, any deliberate attempt to maintain a racial balance, whatever such a balance may be, would involve a violation of Title VII because maintaining such a balance
(
printed page 70171)
would require an employer to hire or refuse to hire on the basis of race . . .” 110 Cong. Rec. 7213 (1964). This joint statement by Senators Clark and Case neatly encapsulates the inescapable legal and practical dilemmas faced by Title VII-covered Registered Apprenticeship programs that attempted to comply in good faith with the open-ended, compulsory, nonremedial, and legally questionable affirmative action requirements that were contained in the part 30 regulation.
Accordingly, by rescinding the affirmative action requirements contained in the part 30 regulation, this final rule relieves Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors from vexing legal and practical dilemmas, while ensuring that an individual's admission to a Registered Apprenticeship program is made on a nondiscriminatory basis and solely on the basis of their qualifications compared to those of other applicants. The Department is confident that the provision of such regulatory relief to a large segment of program sponsors will accelerate the establishment and expansion of Registered Apprenticeship programs, resulting in a more skilled and productive American workforce.
Alleviating Undue Regulatory Burdens for Registered Apprenticeship Stakeholders
The Department has determined that the changes to the part 30 regulation codified in this final rule serve the Department's ongoing policy goal of expanding the Registered Apprenticeship model and its imprint on the national economy, a goal which aligns with the Administration's directive to the Department to expand Registered Apprenticeship and to achieve and surpass 1 million active apprentices. The part 30 regulation included a wide range of requirements that imposed administrative and financial burdens on Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors, and the Department expects that the rescission of these requirements will have a significant impact on Registered Apprenticeship program expansion. In particular, the Department expects that the rescission of the general obligation to engage in affirmative action for all sponsors, and the affirmative action program requirement for programs with five or more apprentices, will attract new sponsors to the National Apprenticeship System and encourage existing sponsors to expand their programs by substantially reducing the administrative burden necessary to establish and maintain a Registered Apprenticeship program.
E.O. 14192
directed Federal agencies to identify and rescind regulations that impose significant administrative or financial burdens (including on American businesses). The burdensome administrative requirements of the part 30 regulation began impacting Registered Apprenticeship programs from their very inception, even before they are registered with a Registration Agency. Registration of a program depends on compliance with the requirements at parts 29 and 30, and sponsors must review both parts to understand what elements they need to develop or commit to at the program development stage. Under the part 30 regulation, all prospective program sponsors were required to identify their process for the selection of apprentices (per § 30.10); identify staff responsible for overseeing the program's commitment to equal opportunity (per § 30.3(b)(1)); develop and disseminate an equal opportunity policy, including posting the Equal Opportunity pledge in the program's standards and at sites where apprentices are trained (per § 30.3(b)(2)); and plan for and address various other requirements, all before their program was even registered. These requirements presented challenges for prospective sponsors new to the system in designing Registered Apprenticeship programs that satisfied all of the requirements contained in parts 29 and 30.
