In Registered Apprenticeship, compulsory affirmative action programs were the clearest example of regulatory requirements that imposed significant administrative and financial burdens on the regulated community, without providing tangible benefits to either the regulated entities, the individuals they serve, or the Federal Government. Under the part 30 regulation, all sponsors had a general duty to engage in affirmative action. In addition, sponsors with five or more apprentices were required to develop and adhere to affirmative action programs, including creating and updating a written document that memorializes the affirmative action program (per § 30.4(e)). The part 30 regulation required sponsors to include in their written affirmative action program, and adopt as an ongoing operational practice, a utilization analysis examining race, sex, and ethnicity, utilization goals for race, sex, and ethnicity; a utilization analysis and goal for individuals with disabilities; targeted outreach, recruitment, and retention policies; ongoing review of personnel policies; and annual reminders to apprentices to voluntarily disclose their disability status. These requirements were detailed at §§ 30.4 through 30.9 and 30.11 of the part 30 regulation.
Developing and maintaining an affirmative action program was a significant undertaking for Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors under the existing part 30 regulation, and OA provided significant technical assistance to both prospective and existing programs to explain these requirements. As affirmed by commenters in the public comments received in response to the Department's NPRM, some commenters reported investing significant administrative and financial resources in-house (or even externally, with consultants or outside legal assistance) to train staff, conduct the required analyses objectively and accurately, and address any legal issues related to apprentice recruitment, hiring, and retention policies. The development of an affirmative action program has been a resource-intensive undertaking for many sponsors (even with the 2-year timeframe from the point of program registration that new sponsors were allowed to develop the plan at § 30.4(e)(1)(ii)), a mandate which significantly complicated the efforts of sponsors in establishing and maintaining their apprenticeship programs. Many sponsors also faced ongoing and significant administrative burdens related to establishing and maintaining affirmative action programs, including conducting the required analyses, and updating their written plan every time the sponsor completes such analyses.
Aside from the foregoing administrative elements of developing and maintaining affirmative action programs, the part 30 regulation imposed regulatory burdens on Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors by dictating key aspects of their recruitment, hiring, and retention policies through utilization analyses that incentivized them to consider arbitrary aspects of applicants' backgrounds—namely, their group-based demographic characteristics. In the case of individuals with disabilities, the requirement even extended to setting a fixed percentage utilization goal that sponsors were charged with meeting, which created an even more prescriptive framework that infringed on a sponsor's freedom to make hiring decisions based purely on their business and workforce needs.
Several commenters advocated for the retention of the existing part 30 regulation, asserting that its requirements were instrumental in raising rates of participation in
(
printed page 70172)
Registered Apprenticeship programs by women and minority groups. However, as detailed later in this preamble, the Department maintains that the correlation posited by these commenters between post-2016 participation outcomes for certain demographic groups and the part 30 regulation's affirmative action requirements is inconclusive. Moreover, such statistical inferences do not alter the fundamental and inescapable reality that compulsory, nonremedial, group-based preferences and affirmative action schemes are inherently discriminatory—and therefore legally suspect—because they treat individuals differently based upon their race, sex, or ethnicity. Accordingly, any arguments advanced to justify affirmative action arrangements that are based upon the general notion of achieving and maintaining greater demographic “balance” or “diversity” in the apprenticeship workforce are not only contrary to the principle of hiring individuals solely on the basis of merit and without reference to their ancestry or group identity, but are also unlikely to withstand legal scrutiny by the courts. Even a noted proponent of affirmative action based upon race, Professor Randall Kennedy of the Harvard Law School, has candidly acknowledged that “[r]acial affirmative action
does
distinguish between people on a racial basis. It
does
discriminate. It
does
redistribute resources. It
does
favor preferred racial categories of candidates . . . It
does
generate stigma and resentment. These issues cannot be hidden for long behind verbal tricks (emphasis in original).”
[
26
]
Similarly, any system of group-based hiring preferences that makes distinctions among individuals based upon their sex or ethnicity is inherently discriminatory in its purpose and effect.
In issuing this final rule prohibiting illegal discrimination in Registered Apprenticeship programs, the Department seeks to ensure that a candidate's admission to such a training program is based solely upon their individual merit and their demonstrated potential for success. Accordingly, such an approach necessitates the rescission of all of the part 30 regulatory provisions that imposed affirmative action requirements on sponsors (such as those setting numerical, nonremedial hiring goals in the selection of apprentices based upon an individual's race, sex, ethnicity, religion, or national origin), as such mandates are contrary to the fundamental goal of guaranteeing genuine equality of opportunity for each and every American who participates in the workforce. At a time when the accelerated expansion of Registered Apprenticeship training is needed to equip American workers of all backgrounds with the occupational skills they need to succeed in a competitive global marketplace, it is essential that the Department rescind such burdensome and legally vulnerable regulatory provisions that could effectively inhibit the growth of this proven workforce development model.
III. Overview of the Revised Part 30 Regulation
A. Summary of the Final Rule's Provisions
This final rule rescinds or significantly revises the burdensome requirements of the part 30 regulation and replaces them with a more straightforward Federal standard for nondiscrimination in Registered Apprenticeship. The final rule explains how Registration Agencies will monitor and enforce program sponsors' compliance with the revised part 30 regulation. The final rule also changes requirements for SAAs related to the part 30 regulation and clarifies the Department's expectation that Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors must not be subject to inhibitive or contradictory nondiscrimination requirements in apprenticeship laws or regulations across States. With this final rule, the Department eliminates the apprenticeship-specific framework for EEO and nondiscrimination contained in the part 30 regulation. Under the part 30 regulation as revised by this final rule, program sponsors are still bound by a firm nondiscrimination requirement that clearly incorporates applicable Federal and State laws and regulations prohibiting illegal discrimination on the basis of race, color, religion, national origin, sex, age, genetic information, or disability. Under this final rule, Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors are no longer bound by a separate, apprenticeship-specific, and administratively burdensome nondiscrimination framework.
This final rule's purpose and applicability section, at
29 CFR 30.1
, lays out the Department's intent for the part 30 regulation going forward—to establish a “uniform Federal standard prohibiting illegal discrimination against apprentices (including applicants for apprenticeship)” and to clarify the scope of enforcement and compliance assistance by Registration Agencies (either OA or an SAA). Section 30.1 also clarifies that the part 30 regulation applies to all sponsors of Registered Apprenticeship programs, whether registered by OA or an SAA. It eliminates the prior part 30 regulation's § 30.1(c) on the regulation's “relationship to other laws,” which is covered under the revised § 30.3. The final rule also rescinds definitions specific to the part 30 regulation and instead clarifies that definitions contained in the part 29 regulation (at
29 CFR 29.2
) also apply to part 30. The prior part 30 regulation's definition section contained definitions already established in the part 29 regulation, or definitions specific to the prior part 30 regulation's requirements that are being rescinded in this final rule.
This final rule establishes the streamlined and clarified nondiscrimination requirement for all Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors at
29 CFR 30.3
. The updated § 30.3 language requires that Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors must comply with all applicable Federal and State laws prohibiting illegal discrimination on the basis of race, color, religion, national origin, sex, age (40 or older), genetic information, or disability. The Department notes that these protected characteristics align with the Federal nondiscrimination protections contained in Title VII of the Act and subsequent nondiscrimination statutes enacted by Congress, including the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA),
[
27
]
the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA),
[
28
]
and title II of the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008.
[
29
]
This section also lays out, at a high level, the consequences of a failure to comply with this nondiscrimination requirement, which include enforcement actions up to and including deregistration of the Registered Apprenticeship program. Under § 30.3, apprentices and applicants for apprenticeship are protected from discrimination “with respect to any benefit, term, or condition of employment associated with an apprenticeship.”
This final rule eliminates the EEO requirements applicable to all sponsors contained in part 30 regulation at § 30.3, as well as the regulation's affirmative action program requirements which are referenced at § 30.3 and elaborated on at §§ 30.4 through 30.9 and 30.11. These sections included a description of the
(
printed page 70173)
rule's prohibition on discrimination and discrimination standards and defenses; the general duty to engage in affirmative action applicable to all sponsors; the requirement to develop and disseminate an equal opportunity policy and post an Equal Opportunity pledge; universal outreach and recruitment requirements applicable to all sponsors; a prohibition on harassment, intimidation, and retaliation specific to apprenticeship; and the requirement for sponsors with five or more apprentices to establish demographic utilization goals (when appropriate) and maintain an affirmative action program.
This final rule eliminates the part 30 regulation's requirement (at § 30.11) that sponsors invite apprentices to voluntarily disclose their disability status upon enrollment in the program and annually thereafter. Under this final rule, however, apprentices are not precluded from voluntarily disclosing their disability status to Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors and are encouraged to do so, especially if they need to request reasonable accommodation related to their disability. In rescinding the part 30 regulation's affirmative action program requirements, the Department also eliminates the requirement that Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors conduct utilization analyses for individuals with disabilities and pursue a utilization goal for such persons established by the Administrator. The final rule also rescinds the part 30 regulation's requirements for sponsors related to the procedure for the selection of apprentices (at § 30.10), the recordkeeping requirements related to the part 30 regulation (at § 30.12), and the apprenticeship-specific prohibition against intimidation and retaliation (at § 30.17).
The final rule updates the part 30 regulation's section on complaints to clarify that complaints alleging illegal discrimination against apprentices should be referred to the EEOC or another relevant enforcement agency with the jurisdiction and expertise to adequately investigate and potentially remedy the issue. Under current practice, apprentices may submit complaints alleging instances of discrimination or other violations of part 30 requirements through ETA Form 9039 to the Registration Agency. In practice, Registration Agencies then forward complaints to the most relevant nondiscrimination enforcement agency, including the EEOC, the U.S. Attorney General, or a State-level Fair Employment Practices Agency (FEPA). The part 30 regulation contained a requirement for Registration Agencies to conduct investigations and provide written notice of findings to the respondent and the complainant, along with other regulatory requirements outlining who can file complaints, what information must be included in the complaint, a requirement for sponsors to provide written notice to apprentices of their right to file complaints, and a requirement for the Registration Agency to “attempt to resolve the matter quickly . . . whenever appropriate” (at § 30.14(c)(2)).
The revised part 30 regulation's section on complaints, at § 30.4 of this final rule, removes the investigative requirements for Registration Agencies and the notice requirement for program sponsors. The final rule establishes a simpler and less duplicative process that recognizes that the investigation and adjudication of complaints alleging illegal discrimination should be conducted by the appropriate investigative and enforcement agency. The revised section on complaints at § 30.4 of this final rule states that Registration Agencies in receipt of complaints alleging illegal discrimination against apprentices will “immediately” refer the complainant to the EEOC, the U.S. Attorney General, a State FEPA, or another appropriate enforcement entity. In accordance with this change to the part 30 regulation, the Department is also rescinding ETA Form 9039.
The part 30 regulation, as finalized in this rulemaking, also revises the process for Registration Agencies to assess compliance with part 30 requirements. The section on nondiscrimination compliance reviews and enforcement, at § 30.5 of this final rule, revises the current part 30 regulation's section on EEO compliance reviews (at § 30.13) to align with the content of the updated part 30 regulation and its streamlined nondiscrimination in apprenticeship requirement for program sponsors. Section 30.5 of this final rule clarifies that Registration Agency reviews for part 30 compliance will occur when a program is assessed for compliance with the part 29 regulation. The final rule's revised compliance review and enforcement section stipulates that a Registration Agency may initiate enforcement actions against a sponsor for failing to comply with the final rule's nondiscrimination requirement at § 30.3 when a final determination of a violation of an applicable nondiscrimination law (without any remaining right to appeal) has been made by an enforcement agency or court with jurisdiction over the matter and the authority to issue such final determinations.
This revision aligns with the change in the complaints section that eliminates the Registration Agency's duplicative role in investigating and adjudicating instances of alleged illegal discrimination against apprentices. Registration Agency staff, whether employed by OA or an SAA, lack the subject-matter background, expertise, and jurisdictional authority to investigate or adjudicate potential violations of Federal or State nondiscrimination law that FEPAs or courts possess. This final rule therefore returns this function and responsibility to the agencies and courts that do possess such authority. To provide additional clarity on the compliance framework for the part 30 regulation, the Department has added a provision in this final rule that requires sponsors to disclose to the Registration Agency any instances when a relevant enforcement entity or court has made a final determination that an applicable nondiscrimination violation has occurred with respect to an apprentice or applicant for apprenticeship in their Registered Apprenticeship program. This addition in the final rule is responsive to public comments that requested additional clarity on the compliance framework and will promote transparency and accountability regarding Registered Apprenticeship programs' adherence to applicable nondiscrimination laws.
Section 30.5(c) of this final rule stipulates that the Registration Agency may work with a sponsor who is the subject of a final determination from an enforcement entity or court to develop a compliance action plan, in alignment with any remedies prescribed by the enforcement entity or court. A sponsor's failure to adhere to such compliance action plans may lead to additional enforcement actions, including the suspension of the sponsor's right to register new apprentices or the initiation of full deregistration proceedings (as described in the part 29 regulation at § 29.8). In addition to requiring sponsors to disclose any final determinations to the Registration Agency, the Department has added a provision requiring sponsors to disclose to the Registration Agency any remedies prescribed by the enforcement entity or court that issued the final determination.
Section 30.6 of this final rule carries forward the reinstatement of the program registration section of the part 30 regulation (at § 30.16). This section allows programs that have been deregistered pursuant to a violation of
(
printed page 70174)
the part 30 nondiscrimination requirement to present evidence in support of reinstatement and permits Registration Agencies to reinstate programs in instances where such evidence is determined to be adequate.
This final rule also includes significant revisions to the part 30 regulation's requirements for SAAs, which are contained in § 30.7 of this final rule. This section stipulates that, within 1 year of the effective date of this final rule, State agencies seeking to obtain or maintain recognition as an SAA must submit a State plan for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship that demonstrates that the State's laws, regulations, policies, and operational procedures specific to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship conform to the requirements of the part 30 regulation. In this final rule, the Department updated the language at § 30.7 based, in part, on public comments received on the NPRM, which proposed that States' laws and regulations conform only to the part 30 regulation. To better align with the Department's intention to create a more uniform set of requirements for all Registered Apprenticeship programs as set forth in the NPRM, this final rule clarifies that State laws and regulations must conform to the part 30 Federal standard, and that the Department will only assess State laws and regulations specific to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship for conformity with part 30.
A primary goal motivating the Department's determination to update the part 30 regulation is the establishment of a uniform Federal standard for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship. Registered Apprenticeship stakeholders, particularly those with a national or multi-regional interest and operational imprint, have long requested that the Department promote a more coherent National Apprenticeship System, where Registered Apprenticeship stakeholders are not faced with conflicting or contradictory requirements depending on where their program operates. The Department has determined that establishing a uniform Federal standard for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship serves this goal and will work with States to identify discrepancies in nondiscrimination requirements for apprenticeship stakeholders that must be resolved under this final rule's requirement that State laws and regulations conform to the Federal standard in the part 30 regulation.
Section 30.7 of this final rule requires States seeking new or continued recognition as a SAA to submit their State laws and regulations in a State plan for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship and lays out the required elements and the Department's process for reviewing State plans. To determine whether the State plan conforms to the part 30 regulation, the Department will consider whether the State's laws and regulations include nondiscrimination or equal opportunity elements that constitute a separate, State-level legal or regulatory compliance framework specific to apprenticeship, and whether such laws and regulations would serve to restrict the growth and impact of Registered Apprenticeship in the State by imposing administrative barriers, excessive costs, or requirements that conflict with Federal or State nondiscrimination laws. OA will review State laws and regulations on a case-by-case basis and will provide technical assistance to States as needed to identify which elements of State laws and regulations do or do not conform to the Federal part 30 regulation.
The Department's decision to modify the regulatory language proposed in the NPRM to require that State laws and regulations “conform to” (rather than “conform only to”) the part 30 regulation aligns with the existing regulatory language found in the part 29 regulation governing labor standards for Registered Apprenticeship programs and the recognition of SAAs. Specifically, this change aligns with the regulatory language at
29 CFR 29.13(a)(1)
, which provides that States' apprenticeship laws and regulations “conform to” the requirements of the part 29 regulation. At § 29.13(a)(5), the part 29 regulation requires that States submit “a description of policies and operating procedures which depart from or impose requirements in addition to those prescribed in [the part 29 regulation].” The Department will apply this same approach in determining whether State laws and regulations pertaining specifically to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship conform to the Federal nondiscrimination in apprenticeship standard in this final rule. State plans for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship must conform to the revised part 30 regulation's prohibition on illegal discrimination stated at § 30.3, and must also describe any laws, regulations, or policies that depart from or impose additional requirements on Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors, including any apprenticeship-specific equal employment laws or regulations. Examples of nonconforming State laws or regulations include any laws or regulations that establish unlawful compulsory, nonremedial group-based preference schemes for sponsors, such as affirmative action programs, or laws or regulations that establish burdensome restrictions or administrative requirements specific to apprenticeship that could restrict or inhibit the growth of Registered Apprenticeship programs or that may conflict with the nondiscrimination requirements contained in this final rule and in applicable Federal laws.
This final rule retains the exemptions provision from the part 30 regulation, redesignating the provision as § 30.8 of this final rule. This provision allows sponsors to request exemptions from the part 30 regulation, “or any part thereof,” in writing, to the Registration Agency, which may grant exemptions for good cause. The provision also stipulates that SAAs must receive approval from the Department before granting any exemptions to program sponsors in their State. Finally, the final rule adds a severability provision (at § 30.9). This provision stipulates that, should a court of competent jurisdiction find that any provision of the revised part 30 regulation is invalid, the finding will not impact any other provision of the regulation.
B. The Role of Registration Agencies Under the Final Rule
The Department expects that this final rule will significantly reduce administrative burdens for both Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors and Registration Agency staff. The Department recognizes that Registration Agency staff expertise is rooted in analyzing labor standards for Registered Apprenticeship programs and providing technical assistance to program sponsors. The prior requirements of the 2016 version of the part 30 regulation introduced an entirely separate set of issues that required a distinct expertise—namely, the ability to provide technical assistance and oversight on affirmative action programs and nondiscrimination and EEO matters. The removal of these requirements in this final rule allows Registration Agency staff to focus on the issues they know best—supporting quality across all Registered Apprenticeship programs—and leaves the investigation and adjudication of issues pertaining to nondiscrimination and EEO to the agencies and courts that do possess the appropriate expertise and jurisdiction.
The revised part 30 regulation requires that all sponsors of Registered Apprenticeship programs adhere to applicable Federal and State laws and
(
printed page 70175)
regulations prohibiting illegal discrimination. This streamlined nondiscrimination requirement applies with respect to both apprentices and applicants to an apprenticeship program, and covers any benefit, term, or condition of employment associated with an apprenticeship. Registration Agencies must begin enforcing this requirement on the effective date of this final rule. Such enforcement will primarily occur through program reviews, and a review for compliance with the revised part 30 regulation will occur when the Registration Agency conducts program reviews for compliance with the part 29 regulation. Registered Apprenticeship programs will be deemed out of compliance with the revised part 30 regulation only if a final determination of a violation of an applicable nondiscrimination law against an apprentice or an applicant to an apprenticeship program, without any remaining right to appeal, is made by an enforcement agency or court with jurisdiction over the matter.
To support accountability and transparency, the Department added a provision to this final rule requiring sponsors to disclose any final determinations from a relevant enforcement entity or court regarding violations of applicable nondiscrimination law with respect to an apprentice or applicant for apprenticeship to the Registration Agency, as well as any remedies provided by such entities. To further support awareness of any such final determinations regarding Registered Apprenticeship programs, the Department recommends that Registration Agencies consider establishing Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) or other arrangements with these governmental enforcement agencies to maintain awareness of any final determinations concerning nondiscrimination violations against apprentices or applicants to an apprenticeship program by Registered Apprenticeship programs in their State. Registration Agencies may also consider contacting such enforcement agencies when a program comes up for review to identify any instances of final determinations concerning nondiscrimination violations.
When such a final determination has been issued, the Registration Agency may work with the program sponsor in question to develop a compliance action plan to address and remedy the issue. Any such plans must align with any remedies prescribed by the enforcement entity or court that issued the final determination. The Department's addition of a disclosure requirement in this final rule is intended to facilitate alignment of compliance action plans with the remedies for nondiscrimination violations prescribed by relevant enforcement entities. Under this final rule, the Registration Agency must monitor the sponsor's progress in implementing the compliance action plan and remediating the issue. If the Registration Agency determines that the sponsor is not following or implementing the compliance action plan, the Registration Agency may initiate enforcement actions, including suspension of the right to register new apprentices or the initiation of deregistration proceedings. This framework ultimately reflects a more efficient and fair approach to addressing instances of illegal discrimination in Registered Apprenticeship that incorporates the expertise, transparency, and due process protocols associated with enforcement entities or courts with jurisdiction over such matters.
Under this final rule, Registration Agencies will no longer investigate complaints alleging instances of illegal discrimination in Registered Apprenticeship programs and will instead forward any such complaints they receive to the relevant enforcement agency or court. These entities include the EEOC, State-level FEPAs or their equivalents, the U.S. Attorney General, or another appropriate enforcement entity. Registration Agency staff are not equipped to conduct such investigations, which require legal interpretations of both the substance of the alleged complaint as well as any relevant nondiscrimination laws or regulations.
Finally, SAAs, the State agencies recognized to perform the functions of Registration Agencies under
29 CFR 29.13
, must submit State plans for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship that show their State's laws, regulations, and policies pertaining specifically to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship conform to the revised Federal part 30 regulation. With this final rule, the Department requires any State seeking new or continued recognition as an SAA to revise any aspects of State law, regulation, or policy pertaining specifically to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship that do not conform to the Federal part 30 regulation. This includes repealing, rescinding, or revising any such laws, regulations, or policies that undermine the goals of this rulemaking, such as overly burdensome requirements that may impede Registered Apprenticeship expansion or requirements specific to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship that are inconsistent with existing Federal or State nondiscrimination laws. The Department expects that the Federal standard established in this final rule will promote the expansion and success of Registered Apprenticeship programs nationwide, and the Department will examine State laws and regulations pertaining specifically to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship to verify that any additional State-level requirements do not impose undue burdens on sponsors and do not adversely impact efforts to expand Registered Apprenticeship.
C. Transition Timelines
This final rule is effective on January 5, 2027, 60 days from its publication in the
Federal Register
. Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors must comply with the final rule's streamlined nondiscrimination requirement by this date, and Registration Agencies must assess programs' compliance with this final rule starting on the final rule's effective date. The Department determined that this compliance timeline would be feasible because sponsors were already required to comply with applicable Federal and State nondiscrimination requirements, which is retained as the core nondiscrimination requirement at § 30.3 of this final rule. State agencies seeking new or continued recognition as an SAA must submit State plans for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship that conform to the final rule within 1 year of the final rule's effective date. The Department will provide technical assistance to all Registered Apprenticeship stakeholders, including program sponsors and SAAs, on all aspects of this final rule, including its transition timelines and the process for requesting extension for good cause.
IV. Public Comments Received on the Proposed Rule
A. General Description of Comments
The Department received 372 public comment submissions, which included a form letter campaign that accounted for 311 comments, and 56 unique comments. Additionally, five comments were duplicates or not related to the subject of this rulemaking. The commenters represented a range of stakeholders from the public, non-profit, and private sectors. Public sector commenters included State and local government agencies and elected officials. Non-profit sector commenters included think tanks, advocacy groups, national and local labor unions,
(
printed page 70176)
professional associations, and trade associations. Private sector commenters included employers, employer associations, and program sponsors. The Department also received comments from individuals and anonymous commenters. Below, the Department addresses general comments on the proposed rule and the rulemaking process, and the section-by-section discussion of this final rule (sections V and VI) addresses comments about the specific regulatory changes the Department proposed in the NPRM.
B. Requests To Extend the Comment Period and Comments on Public Participation
Requests for Comment Period Extension
Comments:
A commenter requested that the Department extend the comment period for the proposed rule by 30 days to ensure that interested parties have a meaningful opportunity to participate in the rulemaking process. Another commenter requested a 45-day extension of the comment period to allow them to develop more comprehensive and well-supported commentary in support of the proposed rule.
Department Response:
The Department maintains that the 60-day comment period for public comments on the NPRM afforded stakeholders and any interested members of the public with sufficient time and opportunity to review the Department's proposal and rationale and develop critical public comments. The Department notes that the 60-day comment period aligns with the length of the comment period established for its previous NPRM,
National Apprenticeship System Enhancements
(
89 FR 3118
, Jan. 17, 2024), which was a longer and more complex rule that proposed additional regulatory requirements alongside rationale for such additions. The Department further notes that a 30-day comment period is generally considered to be the minimum period sufficient to provide the public with a meaningful opportunity to comment on a Federal agency rulemaking, and that Federal agencies often adhere to this minimum timeframe. The Department's 60-day comment period for this rulemaking is twice the length of this generally adhered to minimum timeframe under the APA. Accordingly, the Department rejected requests to extend the comment period and communicated this decision to public commenters by posting a response letter to the public docket for the NPRM indicating that the Department had received, and was rejecting, requests to extend the comment period. This response provided stakeholders with notice on the Department's decision with respect to the comment period early in the comment period and affirmed that commenters must submit their comments by September 2, 2025, as communicated in the NPRM.
Comments on Public Participation and Other Concerns
Comments:
A commenter expressed concern that the Department is issuing overlapping regulations at an aggressive pace, and that this makes it difficult for the public to provide meaningful assessments of the proposals. The commenter recommended pausing the current suite of regulatory efforts and taking time to assess their collective impact if implemented, including by conducting a community impact assessment. Similarly, another commenter expressed concern about the cumulative impact of these rulemakings on women.
A commenter requested that the Department extend the comment period for the proposed rule, particularly because the Department issued six proposed rules on July 1 and 2, and stakeholders for those rules significantly overlap; the commenter reasoned that this timing undermines stakeholders' ability to assess and respond to the proposals. The commenter recommended that the Department double the length of the comment periods for each rule, or stagger their deadlines to be no less than 21 days apart.
A commenter opposed the Department's statement that it “reserves the right to redact or refrain from posting sensitive information, libelous, or otherwise inappropriate comments, including those that contain obscene, indecent, or profane language; that contain threats or defamatory statements; or that contain hate speech.” The commenter reasoned that terms like “hate speech” and “inappropriate comments” are vague and provide officials with too much discretion over what commentary to publish, and that the First Amendment protects such expression anyway.
Department Response:
The Department maintains that the 60-day comment period provided Registered Apprenticeship stakeholders with ample time and opportunity to provide comprehensive reactions and criticisms to its proposal to revise the part 30 regulation, and is in keeping with the Department's practice of providing 60 days to comment on apprenticeship NPRMs. The Department does not consider the issuance of other NPRMs unrelated to the Registered Apprenticeship regulations as sufficient rationale for extending the comment period for this rulemaking, and rejected requests to extend the comment period beyond the 60 days communicated in the NPRM early in the comment period for this rulemaking.
The Department's statement that it reserves the right to redact certain sensitive, libelous, or inappropriate information in posting public comments reflects longstanding practice that is motivated by several factors, including the need to redact personally identifiable information or other sensitive personal information. In addition, while commenters are free to submit comments that include profane or indecent language, the Department is not obligated to post any such language publicly. While the Department favors transparency in the rulemaking process and has sought to establish transparency, as appropriate, throughout the process, such comments are not suitable for public posting and do not advance the public discourse on the proposal.
C. General Comments on the Proposed Rule
General Support
Comments:
The Department received several general comments in support of the proposed rule from public commenters, with some commenters agreeing with the Department's assertions in the NPRM that revising the part 30 regulation would reduce administrative burdens on Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors and stimulate growth throughout the National Apprenticeship System. Supportive commenters argued that eliminating the part 30 regulation's affirmative action requirements would make Registered Apprenticeship more attractive for prospective program sponsors, especially for smaller businesses and other stakeholders who view the extensive and complicated part 30 regulation as a barrier to entry into the National Apprenticeship System.
Some supportive commenters remarked that the part 30 regulation may have fostered discriminatory race-and sex-based preferences in Registered Apprenticeship programs and expressed appreciation for the Department's proposal to move to a merit-based system. Some commenters characterized the proposal as a needed step towards achieving equal opportunity in Registered Apprenticeship by removing what they referred to as race-and sex-based mandates, with one commenter suggesting that employers in their
(
printed page 70177)
industry were already incentivized to recruit inclusively due to business needs or economic factors like labor shortages. Some commenters supportive of the proposal also appreciated that, under the Department's proposal to remove documentation and reporting requirements related to affirmative action programs, sponsors would be free to focus on developing quality training programs that serve the needs of both employers and apprentices.
Department Response:
The Department appreciates the comments received in support of the proposed rule and the Department's objective to streamline and align part 30 with existing Federal nondiscrimination laws. The Department agrees with commenters who asserted that the proposed rule would reduce unnecessary administrative burdens on program sponsors, and with commenters who supported the Department's goal of establishing a robust, merit-based framework for all qualified Americans to enroll in an apprenticeship program.
The Department is committed to reducing duplicative or overlapping requirements that fail to directly serve the National Apprenticeship System. The Department agrees with commenters who agreed that apprenticeship stakeholders should focus on the development of strong, skills-based apprenticeship programs that effectively serve both employers and apprentices. The Department further agrees with the observation made by one commenter that competitive labor market conditions found in a number of industries, including construction, already necessitate broad recruitment from the available talent pool, independent of regulatory reporting mandates. The Department concurs that a streamlined regulatory framework that eliminates the requirement to establish affirmative action plans, among other things, will allow sponsors to focus on program quality.
General Opposition
Comments:
The Department received comments opposing the proposed rule, including some commenters who urged the Department to withdraw the proposed rule. Some commenters generally argued that the Department's proposal would undermine progress in expanding access to Registered Apprenticeship for underrepresented groups. Some commenters who opposed the proposed rule urged the Department to maintain the EEO, affirmative action, or other requirements contained in the part 30 regulation, asserting that these requirements have made a difference in increasing access to Registered Apprenticeship for underrepresented groups. Some commenters urged the Department to focus more of its efforts on implementing and enforcing the requirements contained in the part 30 regulation to maximize their impact.
Department Response:
The Department considered all public comments received in response to the NPRM and acknowledges that some commenters opposed the proposal and urged the Department to retain or strengthen the part 30 regulation. As explained later in this final rule's section-by-section discussion, the Department maintains that data on demographic trends in Registered Apprenticeship is inconclusive with respect to the correlation between the extensive EEO and affirmative action requirements contained in the part 30 regulation and any increases in participation by certain demographic groups. More fundamentally, however, the Department maintains that any arguments advanced to justify the retention of requirements intended to increase diversity in Registered Apprenticeship are contrary to the underlying purpose of this rulemaking, which is to ensure that apprentices are hired and retained based solely on the basis of individual merit without consideration of their race, sex, or ethnic origin. This final rule also reflects the Department's position that establishing a clear, consistent nondiscrimination standard for Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors provides a more legally sound and practical framework to support equal access to apprenticeship opportunities for all qualified individuals.
General Comments on the Department's Rationale
Comments:
Commenters provided general reactions to the Department's rationale for the proposal, with some commenters arguing that the Department had overstated or exaggerated the administrative burdens associated with the part 30 regulation. Other commenters asserted that the proposal would increase the prevalence of illegal discrimination in Registered Apprenticeship, and that the Department was incorrect in asserting that the proposal would clarify and strengthen nondiscrimination requirements in Registered Apprenticeship. Some commenters asserted that the proposal would restrict growth in Registered Apprenticeship by removing affirmative action requirements contained in the part 30 regulation, which the commenters described as a necessary tool for establishing widespread and equitable access to Registered Apprenticeship. One commenter critical of the proposal argued that the Department sought to return to a “bygone era” when discrimination was permissible and prevalent in Registered Apprenticeship.
Department Response:
The Department does not agree with commenters who asserted that the NPRM overstated the administrative burden associated with the part 30 regulation. The Department's conclusion that the current regulatory framework imposes significant compliance costs on program sponsors, as communicated in the NPRM and reinforced in this final rule, is supported by ongoing analysis of empirical data, including the economic analysis required under the rulemaking process. The Department's conclusion that the part 30 regulation imposes excessive administrative burdens on program sponsors is also supported by OA's experience overseeing the administration of Registered Apprenticeship programs. The Department has received consistent feedback from sponsors and other apprenticeship stakeholders on the administrative burden imposed by the part 30 regulation, including in the public comments received in response to the NPRM. Registered Apprenticeship stakeholders have consistently noted that program sponsors must dedicate substantial staff time and resources to meet the extensive requirements of the part 30 regulation.
Further, the Department maintains that some requirements contained in the part 30 regulation may have improperly induced sponsors to hire an apprentice based solely on their race, sex, or other demographic characteristics. The Department has determined that establishing a clearer and more concise nondiscrimination requirement for all Registered Apprenticeship programs aligns the apprenticeship regulations more closely with Federal nondiscrimination laws, and that clarifying and simplifying regulatory compliance requirements for program sponsors will support the expedited growth of Registered Apprenticeship programs.
The Department firmly rejects some commenters' characterizations of the proposal as a return to a “bygone era” that permitted discrimination and maintains that this final rule does not weaken the prohibition on illegal discrimination for all Registered Apprenticeship programs. It is the Department's position that this final
(
printed page 70178)
rule reaffirms and reinforces a prohibition on illegal discrimination by aligning the final part 30 regulation with established Federal nondiscrimination law.
General Impacts on Registered Apprenticeship Programs
Comments:
Several commenters expressed concern that the proposed rule would undermine Registered Apprenticeship programs' efforts to diversify programs and extend equal opportunities for all demographic groups. One of these commenters argued that Registered Apprenticeship programs can be a powerful tool for promoting economic mobility and establishing greater equity in the workplace, and warned that removing requirements to establish affirmative action plans would undo decades of progress in remediating discrimination and improved labor market outcomes for diverse groups. One commenter expressed concern that the Department's proposal would eliminate their ability to market their program to demographic groups that are underrepresented in their program, which would shrink the available talent pool and restrict apprenticeship growth.
Other commenters expressed concern about the impact of the proposed rule on their specific programs, including one commenter who discussed the proposal's potential impact on educator apprenticeship programs. The commenter stated that all students should have access to teachers who they relate to, who affirm their identities, and who teach with an understanding of the cultural context of their lives. The commenter added that when the teaching workforce is homogenous, students may feel invisible, which harms their learning outcomes. Another commenter asserted that the proposed rule would restrict active and expansive recruitment efforts that address gaps in the educator workforce.
Department Response:
The Department considered commenters' feedback on the potential impact of the proposed rule on existing Registered Apprenticeship programs and appreciates the opportunity to respond to such comments in this final rule. The Department agrees with commenters who asserted that Registered Apprenticeship is a pathway to greater economic mobility and career development for all qualified individuals. The Department does not agree that updating the part 30 regulation to remove burdensome requirements for program sponsors will undermine Registered Apprenticeship's efficacy or success as a strategy for career development and improved economic mobility. The Department emphasizes that Registered Apprenticeship opportunities will remain an attractive and comprehensive professional development solution and career path for all qualified individuals under this final rule. Further, the Department expects that reducing regulatory burdens for program sponsors will facilitate the expansion of the Registered Apprenticeship model and increased opportunities for career seekers. This final rule does not preclude Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors from engaging in recruitment efforts that fit their business needs, so long as such efforts do not constitute illegal discrimination in violation of Federal or State nondiscrimination laws and the streamlined nondiscrimination requirement for all sponsors at § 30.3 of this final rule.
The Department acknowledges the important role that educator apprenticeship programs can play in fortifying the teaching workforce. The Department's final rule does not prohibit sponsors from engaging in lawful recruitment efforts. Program sponsors, including those operating educator apprenticeship programs, should retain significant flexibility to design lawful outreach and recruitment strategies. The Department maintains that reducing prescriptive Federal mandates for all Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors, including those in the education sector, will provide program sponsors with greater flexibility in the design of their programs, including the structuring of outreach and recruitment strategies that best serve a sponsor's workforce needs.
General Comments on Economic Impacts
Comments:
Some commenters cautioned that the proposed rule could undermine participation in Registered Apprenticeship programs and obstruct progress towards achieving the Trump administration's goal of reaching 1 million active apprentices. One commenter added that the proposed rule would derail innovative recruitment strategies in apprenticeship and worsen the labor shortage in the construction industry. Another commenter maintained that research shows that workforce diversity, inclusion, and emotional intelligence are essential for innovation, and warned that the proposed rule could exacerbate labor shortages, especially in the construction industry, and undermine U.S. global competitiveness. Similarly, another commenter expressed concern that the proposed changes would create a less robust pipeline to fill broadband jobs during a period of major expansion of fiber-optic infrastructure.
Department Response:
The Department does not agree with commenters who asserted that updating the part 30 regulation to remove affirmative action and other requirements will reduce participation in Registered Apprenticeship programs. The Department expects that this final rule will have the opposite effect, and that significantly revising the part 30 regulation by removing burdensome requirements for program sponsors will drive expansion of the system. As such, this final rule aligns with and supports the Administration's ambitious goals to expand Registered Apprenticeship, along with other Administration directives (such as the directive to reduce regulatory burdens contained in
E.O. 14192
,
Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation
).
The Department also disagrees with the concern expressed by some commenters that the rule will exacerbate labor shortages, including in the construction industry. To the contrary, the Department expects that this final rule will support the expansion of both existing and new Registered Apprenticeship programs, including those in the construction sector, by eliminating administrative burdens that serve as a barrier to entry and an ongoing drain on administrative resources for program sponsors. As such, the Department does not agree with the commenter who suggested that the Department's proposal would undermine U.S. global competitiveness. It is the Department's position that this final rule will strengthen Registered Apprenticeship by replacing ineffective, administratively burdensome, and likely unlawful affirmative action requirements with a clearer and more concise nondiscrimination requirement. The Department expects that eliminating these requirements in favor of a system that prioritizes merit and employer needs will strengthen U.S. businesses and bolster U.S. global competitiveness.
General Comments on Recommended Alternatives
Comments:
Some commenters provided alternative suggestions to the changes proposed in the NPRM, including simplifying the regulations and compliance requirements or establishing a more concise set of EEO requirements. One commenter supportive of the Department's proposal to streamline nondiscrimination requirements suggested that the
(
printed page 70179)
Department consider funding incentives for sponsors who hire apprentices from underrepresented groups, stating that this approach would expand access to talent pools and maintain regulatory compliance.
Department Response:
The Department appreciates that commenters suggested alternative approaches to streamline the part 30 regulation, and notes that this final rule aligns with commenters who generally suggested that the Department should simplify nondiscrimination requirements in the Federal regulations governing Registered Apprenticeship. The Department further notes that establishing financial incentives for sponsors to hire apprentices from underrepresented groups is outside the scope of this final rule, fundamentally at odds with the policy priorities of the Administration and the Department, and potentially violates Federal law by incentivizing race-based selections.
D. Comments on Regulatory History and the Background of the Proposed Rule
Comments Regarding General History of Apprenticeship EEO Regulations
Comments:
Several commenters provided remarks on the Department's discussion of the history of the Registered Apprenticeship regulations, including the part 30 regulation. Some commenters said that since 1937, when the NAA was passed into law, the Department's apprenticeship regulations have evolved, with a consistent focus on implementing the NAA's directive to safeguard apprentice welfare. These commenters argued that the proposed rule threatens to undermine this core objective for the Department. The commenters added that EEO efforts became a major component of the Department's role in protecting apprentices' welfare due to a long history of racial and sex discrimination. The commenters stated that the Department's oversight and enforcement of regulatory requirements was central to the Department's success in protecting apprentice welfare, citing research that the commenter described as finding that weak oversight in the 1960s led to discrimination against Black apprentices with limited consequences. The commenters added that the existing regulations provide the Department with important regulatory tools for safeguarding the welfare of apprentices, ensuring that apprentices are positioned to succeed, and supporting an apprenticeship system that reflects the breadth of workers and communities across the United States.
Another commenter added that early activism and executive actions, specifically President Kennedy's 1963 E.O. 1114, was a “directive for the Federal government to require nondiscrimination in apprenticeships.” The commenter asserted that affirmative action in apprenticeship programs has been key to addressing exclusion in the trades, especially for young adults and youth with disabilities. A commenter criticized the Department's goal of restoring the original focus and purpose of the 1963 version of the regulation, reasoning that the 1963 version did not prohibit discrimination based on sex, including pregnancy, childbirth, and related medical conditions, which the commenter stated was both rampant and lawful at that time. A different commenter stated that the most recent update to the part 30 regulation, finalized in 2016, expanded protected categories to align with current employment discrimination law and employed a graduated enforcement approach.
Another commenter also described the historical development of
29 CFR parts 29
and
30
, agreeing with others that part 30 was initially established in 1963 in response to E.O.s 10925 and 11114. However, the commenter stated that since that time, employment law has matured with the passage of Title VII of the Act, the ADEA, and the ADA, among other laws. The commenter reasoned that, given these significant changes, it is appropriate to revisit whether the standards imposed by part 30 are necessary and whether they create unnecessary barriers to participation in Registered Apprenticeship.
Department Response:
The Department agrees with commenters who noted that employment law has matured since the part 30 regulation was initially promulgated in 1963, and that subsequent developments in the legal framework for prohibiting discrimination in employment justify the Department's proposal to revisit elements of the part 30 regulation that may be duplicative or that may conflict with the existing set of such laws. The Department notes that President Kennedy's memorandum directive to the Secretary of Labor on June 4, 1963, (Statement on Equal Employment Opportunity in Federal Apprenticeship and Construction Programs) was implemented by the issuance of the first iteration of the part 30 regulation (Nondiscrimination in Employment and Training) on December 18, 1963 (
28 FR 13775
). However, the 1963 version of the part 30 regulation did not mandate that Registered Apprenticeship programs establish nonremedial, compulsory affirmative action plans. As described earlier in the preamble to this final rule, the Department takes the position that affirmative action programs in apprenticeship are inherently discriminatory, and therefore likely unlawful.
The Department disagrees with the commenter that characterized the Department's proposal as an effort to restore the 1963 version of the part 30 regulation, which did not protect against discrimination based on sex, pregnancy, or childbirth. Under this final rule, the part 30 regulation does prohibit discrimination on such bases because it requires compliance with all Federal nondiscrimination laws, including Title VII. Further, the Department's role in providing technical assistance, which one commenter characterized as an important tool for protecting apprentice welfare, will continue under the final rule.
General Comments on the Department's Implementation of the Part 30 Regulation
Comments:
A commenter asserted that the current regulations have not been more effective because the Department adopted a prolonged, phased approach to implementing the regulation's requirements. The commenter asserted that the Department failed to fully phase in such requirements, noting that sponsors were not required to fully implement the changes finalized in the 2016 version of the part 30 regulation until their first compliance reviews, with the first compliance reviews reflecting updated part 30 requirements occurring after January 18, 2019. The commenter stated that, because those reviews occur on a 5-year cycle, some sponsors may not have had their first review until 2024 (and further noting that in some SAA States, compliance was delayed even further.)
The same commenter argued that the Department's implementation efforts were inadequate for numerous reasons, including what the commenter described as insufficient funding to implement the regulation and OA's consistent failure to request adequate funding from Congress. The commenter asserted that training for the Department's staff was limited, and updates to OA's staff manual were slow, as were the Department's efforts to make a data analysis tool available for the utilization analyses required under the regulation. The commenter asserted that OA's staff's efforts to implement the part 30 regulation were diverted due to the Department's pursuit of an alternative
(
printed page 70180)
apprenticeship model during the first Trump Administration. The commenter further noted that Circulars and Bulletins that conflicted with the part 30 regulation remained published for years, and that the Department failed to provide conforming templates for elements like selection procedures to clarify the regulation's requirements for program sponsors. The commenter also asserted that the Department was slow to review States' required EEO plans, remarking that even now, some States have failed to adopt conforming EEO plans.
Another commenter supportive of the existing part 30 regulation's requirements agreed that stakeholder education regarding the part 30 regulation's requirements only began recently, and suggested that increases in the number of females and African Americans in the trades, while promising, may have been more substantial had there been greater investment in oversight and enforcement of the current regulations.
A different commenter said that their Registered Apprenticeship program had diligently implemented the requirements of the part 30 regulation, and that the regulation's requirements were helpful in identifying a wider talent pool for recruitment. However, the commenter added that they understand the Department's decision to revisit the regulations due to the changing landscape in nondiscrimination law, and acknowledged the Department's efforts to reduce regulatory complexity and streamline the program registration process.
Department Response:
The Department disagrees with commenters' assertions that OA had failed to fully implement the part 30 regulation in a timely or practical manner. The Department's 2016 final rule establishing the most recent version of the part 30 regulation contained different compliance timelines for distinct provisions of the final rule, and the Department clearly communicated such timelines to program sponsors in the final rule and in technical assistance provided to sponsors and SAAs. OA staff did receive extensive training on the part 30 regulation, and OA developed several resources to support sponsor awareness and compliance with the regulation's numerous and complex requirements.
Ultimately, the Department strongly disagrees with commenters' assertions that implementation failures undermined the effectiveness of the part 30 regulation. As one commenter conceded, sufficient time has passed since the rule became effective for every sponsor to have undergone at least one compliance review. The Department does agree that sponsors and SAAs have experienced significant challenges in complying with the part 30 regulation, and it attributes such challenges to the complex and burdensome nature of the regulation. Moreover, the requirement that sponsors adopt a form of affirmative action predated the 2016 version of the part 30 regulation. In the Department's view, there is no empirical evidence to suggest that the effectiveness of the affirmative action requirements contained in any version of the part 30 regulation has been adversely impacted by the Department's implementation of such regulations.
E. Comments on Legal Authority
1. General Comments on the Department's Legal Authority
Comments:
A few commenters argued that the proposed rule would not satisfy the NAA's requirement that the Department promote labor standards necessary to safeguard the welfare of apprentices. These commenters asserted that the NAA charges the Department with establishing standards stricter than those applicable to the general workforce and that the proposed rule's limitations on Registration Agencies' investigative and enforcement authority would reduce apprentices' access to timely remedies. One commenter further argued that the NAA requires the Department to balance employer burden against apprentice protections, and that the proposed rule would deter sponsors from maintaining such protections. The same commenter added that the proposed rule would undermine the extensive network of labor-management programs designed to increase apprenticeship participation.
Department Response:
The Department has determined that it has the authority under the NAA to promulgate this regulation. The NAA “is written in very broad terms” and “contains a wide grant of authority to the Secretary of Labor.”
Gregory Elec. Co.
v.
U.S. Dep't of Labor,
268 F. Supp. 987, 991 (D.S.C. 1967). The NAA, in relevant part, requires that the Department formulate and promote the furtherance of labor standards necessary to safeguard the welfare of apprentices. The NAA does not dictate that the Department follow a specific approach and does not prescribe specific steps to safeguard the welfare of apprentices.
The Department maintains that requiring program sponsors to establish race-, ethnicity-, sex-, or disability-based utilization goals, engage in affirmative action based upon protected characteristics, or conduct employer-initiated inquiries into disability status does not safeguard the welfare of apprentices. Pursuing demographic balancing or proportional representation within apprenticeship programs, in fact, threatens the welfare of apprentices in that it undermines equal opportunity for all apprentices and applicants.
As discussed elsewhere in this preamble, the race- and sex-based affirmative action provisions of the prior regulation raise serious constitutional concerns. Those provisions required covered sponsors to conduct utilization analyses based on race, ethnicity, and sex, establish utilization goals when underutilization was identified, and undertake affirmative measures designed to address demographic disparities. At the very least, these provisions trigger heightened scrutiny under the Constitution's equal-protection principles. The Department declines to exercise its authority in a way that incentivizes sponsors to impermissibly consider protected characteristics when making employment decisions.
The Department exercises its authority in line with the policy choices expressed by Congress in other Federal civil rights statutes. Congress has enacted comprehensive nondiscrimination laws governing employment, including Title VII, and has expressly limited the reach of some of those statutes to employers meeting specified coverage thresholds. For example, Title VII generally applies only to employers with fifteen or more employees. The Department is reluctant to construe the NAA's vague and open-ended delegation as authorizing the Department to impose obligations on small employers that Congress expressly chose to exempt from nondiscrimination statutes. Furthermore, when Congress intends to authorize or require affirmative action based on protected characteristics, it generally does so expressly.
See, e.g.,
section 503 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973.
[
30
]
Even assuming the NAA could be construed to authorize such requirements, the Department declines to exercise that authority and instead respects Congress's policy judgment regarding the scope and applicability of Federal employment-discrimination obligations.
The Department has also explained below in this preamble that part 30's affirmative action requirements create significant tension with Title VII's substantive protections. Such
(
printed page 70181)
requirements encouraged race- and sex-based employment practices that conflict with Title VII's plain text prohibiting employment decisions motivated by race, color, religion, sex, or national origin and that do not fit comfortably within the narrow, judicially created exemption for affirmative action. The Department is reluctant to exercise the NAA's general grant of authority to maintain a regulatory scheme that creates substantial tension with Title VII.
Similarly, the disability-related provisions of the prior regulation created tension with the ADA. The prior regulation required sponsors to invite applicants and apprentices to disclose disability status upon enrollment and annually thereafter and required covered sponsors to pursue a nationwide disability utilization goal established by the Department. Section 102(d) of the ADA, however, prohibits employer-initiated inquiries concerning disability status of applicants and permits such inquiries of employees only in narrow, specified circumstances.
[
31
]
The Department is reluctant to exercise the NAA's general grant of authority to broadly require employer-initiated disability inquiries that are restricted under the ADA.
At bottom, the Department should exercise its authority under the NAA to formulate and promote only labor standards that are consistent with Federal statutes. That means the Department should not impose nondiscrimination obligations on small businesses that Congress expressly exempted, require sponsors to take action to meet race- and sex-based goals that would be unlawful under Title VII, or mandate employer-initiated inquiries of disability status that would run afoul of the ADA's restrictions on such inquiries.
The Department also disagrees with commenters who claim the NAA requires that the Department prescribe a heightened standard that is different from existing laws that are applicable to the general public. Rather, the Department has a wide grant of authority to determine the approach necessary to safeguard the welfare of apprentices. As set forth in the preamble to this final rule and in the section-by-section discussion of the changes to specific provisions, the Department determined that the revisions to the current part 30 will safeguard the welfare of apprentices by aligning with existing legal authorities in Federal and State law, ensuring that apprenticeship programs remain aligned with the full scope of civil rights protections. Enforcement agencies such as the EEOC and State FEPAs possess greater expertise in discrimination law and broader authority to provide individualized relief, including make-whole relief, than Registration Agencies. Accordingly, relying on those enforcement mechanisms, rather than a duplicative apprenticeship-specific process, will better protect apprentices who experience unlawful discrimination.
The Department also disagrees with the commenter that asserted that the proposed rule contradicts the labor-management provisions of the NAA. The NAA, in relevant part, directs the Department to bring together employers and labor for the formulation of programs of apprenticeship. As set forth in the preamble of this final rule and in the section-by-section analysis of the revisions to the current part 30, the Department has determined that the elimination of redundant, and likely illegal, requirements and the reduction of administrative burden will further the expansion and growth of the National Apprenticeship System. Specifically, this final rule, contrary to the commenter's assertion, promotes, rather than inhibits, the convening of employers and labor to establish apprenticeship programs by lowering barriers and associated burdens, consistent with the NAA.
2. Administrative Procedure Act
Comments:
One commenter argued that the NPRM is unlawful or violates the APA. Another commenter argued that the NPRM relies on unsubstantiated problems, such as concerns about “reverse discrimination” or pressures for sponsors to discriminate under the 2016 regulations. A commenter stated that, in contrast to the prior rulemaking in 2016—which they said did review apprenticeship data and analyze national labor force data to justify changes to the regulation—the Department did not include any examples, a quantitative analysis, or a factual record to support its claims under the NPRM. For example, one commenter stated they were unable to find any examples of recent EEOC charges brought against employers for discriminating against White males in apprenticeship programs, construction jobs, or trades jobs, while there are numerous examples of such cases concerning discrimination against racial minorities. Another commenter asserted that data demonstrates that discrimination against women and racial minorities is still a real concern. This commenter further stated that the Department ignored relevant available data and case law that did not align with the arguments presented under the proposed rule.
Given these perceived issues, a commenter argued that the NPRM failed to meet the APA standard that regulatory actions must examine the relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation for the action, including a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made. Another commenter asserted that the NPRM lacks sufficient data or a factual record, and therefore violates the APA's arbitrary and capricious standard, and does not satisfy the APA requirements for notice-and-comment rulemaking designed to ensure that the Department has made an informed decision.
Department Response:
As emphasized earlier in this preamble, the Department takes the position that while program sponsors should be held accountable for findings of illegal discrimination against apprentices, the affirmative action provisions contained in the part 30 regulation do not prevent such discrimination, and, in fact, may induce such discriminatory conduct by sponsors. The Department did not refer to the concept of “reverse discrimination” in the preamble to the NPRM; moreover, the Department's position, consistent with that of the EEOC, is that there is no such thing as “reverse” discrimination; there is only discrimination and workers are protected from such discrimination under the Constitution and nondiscrimination laws regardless of their race, ethnicity, or sex.
[
32
]
As some commenters noted, when the Department issued the 2016 version of part 30, the preamble to the rule that appeared in the
Federal Register
stated that Department had “analyzed participant demographics in apprenticeship programs . . . and the demographics of the national labor force” and had determined that “notable disparities exist in apprenticeship participation and completion.”
81 FR 92028
(Dec. 19, 2016). However, those comparative analyses of the prevalence of certain demographic groups in the national apprenticeship workforce and in the broader national labor force were incapable of establishing that such demographic “disparities” were caused by, or were proof of, discriminatory conduct by particular program sponsors. Rather, these analyses were undertaken to support the Department's stated
(
printed page 70182)
policy goals at the time of “[i]ncreasing diversity” in Registered Apprenticeship programs generally (
81 FR 92027
, Dec. 19, 2016) and of addressing the “underutilization of historically disadvantaged worker groups in apprenticeship.”
81 FR 92035
(Dec. 19, 2016).
However, in issuing this final rule, the Department has determined that the prior regulatory effort in part 30 to increase overall demographic diversity in Registered Apprenticeship programs through the establishment by certain apprenticeship programs of compulsory, group-based numerical hiring goals—while also seeking to protect individual apprentices in those programs against illegal employment discrimination on the basis of race, sex, and ethnicity—imposed distinct and fundamentally irreconcilable mandates on certain sponsors. Moreover, the Department maintains that the obligation to set such apprenticeship hiring goals in the existing and previous versions of part 30 were inherently discriminatory and legally questionable because they induced program sponsors to treat individuals differently based upon their group-based demographic identities. Therefore, the Department's prior analysis as to the prevalence of overall, global demographic disparities among certain groups enrolled in Registered Apprenticeship programs ought not be used to justify the retention of the compulsory, burdensome, and legally questionable affirmative action requirements contained in the existing part 30 regulation.
As some commenters noted, maintaining utilization goals that classify apprentices on the basis of race, ethnicity, and sex may induce sponsors to consider these protected bases as factors in their employment decisions. The Department's concern about discrimination is not unsubstantiated, as a commenter asserted. Rather, it is substantiated by the text of the regulations. The absence of formal complaints against sponsors for engaging in unlawful preferential treatment neither disproves the existence of such treatment nor undermines the Department's position that the part 30 affirmative action provisions incentivize sponsors to use improper governmental racial classifications in their selection decisions.
See Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod
v.
F.C.C.,
154 F.3d 487, 492 (D.C. Cir. 1998) (rejecting the Federal Communications Commission (FCC)'s argument that strict scrutiny should not apply to its EEO regulations because there was no evidence that a regulated entity had engaged in racial hiring, stating that “such an evidentiary obligation would turn equal protection analysis inside out.”). The developing case law regarding affirmative action also makes such classifications more vulnerable to challenge than they have been in the past.
See, e.g., Vitolo
v.
Guzman,
999 F. 3d 353 (6th Cir. 2021) (invalidating a program under the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 that disbursed funding to restaurant owners on the basis of the applicants' race and sex);
Mid-Am. Milling Co., LLC
v.
United States Dep't of Transportation,
No. 3:23-CV-00072-GFVT, 2024 WL 4267183, at *7 (E.D. Ky. Sept. 23, 2024) (citing to
SFFA
and finding that Plaintiffs were likely to succeed in their claim that the Department of Transportation's use of race and sex-based presumptions in the preferential award of Federal highway and transit funds violated the Constitution's guarantee of Equal Protection),
opinion clarified,
No. 3:23-CV-00072-GFVT, 2024 WL 4635430 (E.D. Ky. Oct. 31, 2024);
Ultima Servs. Corp.
v.
U.S. Dep't of Agric.,
683 F. Supp. 3d 745, 764 (E.D. Tenn. 2023).
Regarding the Department's decision to rely on external enforcement agencies to investigate allegations of illegal discrimination against apprentices, the Department maintains that this will result in more thorough investigations and more tailored, individualized remedies for apprentices who experience illegal discrimination.
