In the nearly 10 years since part 30 was last updated, the Department has determined that OA's limited expertise in nondiscrimination law and its inability to provide individual remedies prevents it from effectively remedying unlawful discrimination. The Department's reference in the NPRM to a lack of complaints and enforcement actions under the existing part 30 was not meant to convey that there is no discrimination. Instead, in the Department's view, the scarcity of complaints and enforcement actions related to part 30 suggests that the apprentice-specific enforcement scheme administered by the Department has provided little relief to apprentices outside of what is otherwise available through FEPAs, especially since the Department's usual practice has been to refer any complaints alleging illegal discrimination to the EEOC.
Because of the lack of effective enforcement, growing legal risks, and sponsor compliance costs under the current part 30, the Department has concluded that it is inappropriate to maintain this race- and sex-based approach to nondiscrimination in apprenticeship. Instead, the Department contends that a more streamlined approach will help expand apprenticeships for all workers and return the enforcement of nondiscrimination laws to the agencies properly equipped for the task. By accounting for these considerations in its determination that the current part 30 regulation is no longer “necessary to safeguard the welfare of apprentices,”
[
33
]
the Department has clearly provided a “reasoned explanation for the change,” satisfying the APA's requirements.
Cboe Glob. Markets, Inc.
v.
Sec. & Exch. Comm'n,
155 F.4th 704, 716 (D.C. Cir. 2025) (quoting
Encino Motorcars, LLC
v.
Navarro,
579 U.S. 211, 221 (2016));
see also Mozilla Corp.
v.
Fed. Commc'ns Comm'n,
940 F.3d 1, 55-56 (D.C. Cir. 2019) (upholding the FCC's adoption of a “light-touch” policy for governing internet rather than maintaining a utility-style regulation where the FCC determined that the harms the prior Order “was designed to prevent did not require the prior Order's regulatory measures but could instead be mitigated—at a lower cost—with transparency requirements, consumer protection, and antitrust enforcement measures”).
F. Comments on the Department's Goals for the Rulemaking
1. Ensuring Apprenticeship Regulations Comply With Nondiscrimination Law

in justifying the rescission of the current part 30 regulations. These commenters reasoned that

because part 30 expressly prohibits selection preferences and also prohibits using quotas in the context of apprenticeship programs, requiring only the establishment of aspirational goals. (
printed page 70183)
couple of commenters also maintained that the Department did not offer evidence that program sponsors were using protected characteristics in hiring decisions.

decision, in that there are frequent occasions when employer-demand outpaces the number of applicants requiring outreach, and nothing in the

to support this rulemaking, other commenters who favored the revision and streamlining of part 30 agreed with the Department's position that

is relevant, noting that the Constitution prohibits actions that discriminate on the basis of race unless such measures are narrowly tailored to serve a compelling state interest. These commenters cited several Supreme Court decisions, including the
SFFA
ruling, which they said clarified that race-preferential educational programs are illegal unless they satisfy the “twin protections” of the Equal Protection Clause. Another commenter noted that in the
SFFA
decision the court held that race-conscious admissions policies violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, and that existing regulations that establish a race-conscious preference would not survive legal challenge. Yet another commenter stated that the existing part 30 regulations require “arbitrary line drawings” related to “race” and “national origin” designations which have been rejected by the Supreme Court.
Department Response:
Commenters who suggested
SFFA'
s reasoning is cabined to the higher education context are mistaken. While
SFFA
was decided in the context of university admissions, the decision rests on longstanding and enduring equal-protection principles that predate and extend well beyond that context, and it reaffirmed that race-based governmental decision-making is presumptively invalid absent an exceedingly narrow justification. The Department cited
SFFA
in the NPRM precisely because it reaffirmed these bedrock equal-protection principles.
90 FR 28950
,
28955
(July 2, 2025). Indeed, the Supreme Court recently relied upon
SFFA
outside the higher education context to reiterate that “the general rule [is] that the Constitution almost never permits the Federal Government or a State to discriminate on the basis of race. Such discrimination triggers strict scrutiny” under the Constitution's equal-protection guarantee.
Louisiana
v.
Callais,
146 S. Ct. 1131, 1152 (2026) (quoting
SFFA,
600 U.S. at 207).
Lower courts have likewise relied on equal-protection principles articulated in
SFFA
to halt or strike down race-based governmental programs in a variety of contexts.
See, e.g., Mid-Am. Milling Co., LLC
v.
United States Dep't of Transportation,
No. 3:23-CV-00072-GFVT, 2024 WL 4267183, at *7 (E.D. Ky. Sept. 23, 2024) (citing to
SFFA
and finding that Plaintiffs were likely to succeed in their claim that the Department of Transportation's use of race and sex-based presumptions in the preferential award of Federal highway and transit funds violated the Constitution's guarantee of Equal Protection),
opinion clarified,
No. 3:23-CV-00072-GFVT, 2024 WL 4635430 (E.D. Ky. Oct. 31, 2024);
Ultima Servs. Corp.
v.
U.S. Dep't of Agric.,
683 F. Supp. 3d 745, 764 (E.D. Tenn. 2023) (citing
SFFA
and finding that the race-based presumption used by the Small Business Administration (SBA) and the Department of Agriculture in determining eligibility for preferencing in Federal contract awards failed strict scrutiny).
Contrary to some commenters' assertions, the constitutional relevance of
SFFA
does not depend upon whether apprenticeship programs are analogous to university admissions programs. The question is whether the government has employed racial classifications or induced race-based decision-making. The affirmative action provisions of the current part 30 regulation do exactly that. The regulation requires covered sponsors to conduct utilization analyses based on race and ethnicity, determine whether particular racial or ethnic groups are “underutilized,” establish race- and ethnicity-based utilization goals, and undertake affirmative measures designed to address such underutilization.
Although provisions in part 30 prohibit discrimination on the basis of race, sex, and ethnicity, the regulation's race-based provisions conflict with that legitimate mandate. Long before
SFFA,
courts repeatedly held that governmental policies pressuring or encouraging regulated entities to consider race in hiring, promotion, assignment, or other employment decisions constitute racial classifications attributable to the government.
See, e.g., Monterey Mechanical Co.
v.
Wilson,
125 F.3d 702, 710-13 (9th Cir. 1997);
Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod
v.
FCC,
141 F.3d 344, 351-54 (D.C. Cir. 1998);
MD/DC/DE Broadcasters Ass'n
v.
FCC,
236 F.3d 13, 19-20 (D.C. Cir. 2001). A racial classification must survive strict scrutiny, meaning it must be narrowly tailored to achieve a compelling governmental interest.
SFFA,
600 U.S. at 206. Sex-based classifications may be sustained only if they satisfy intermediate scrutiny—they must serve an important governmental objective and are substantially related to the achievement of that objective.
Vitolo,
999 F.3d at 364 (citation modified).
As stated in the NPRM, the affirmative action provisions currently found at
29 CFR 30.5(d)
require covered sponsors to establish specific numerical goals exclusively for the inclusion of women and racial and ethnic minorities in the program. Contrary to the commenters' assertion, the fact that part 30 requires setting “utilization goals” instead of “quotas” does not render these provisions race-neutral. It simply does not matter “whether a government hiring program imposes hard quotas, soft quotas, or goals. Any one of these techniques induces an employer to hire with an eye toward meeting the numerical target. As such, they can and surely will result in individuals being granted a preference because of their race.”
Lutheran Church,
141 F.3d at 354. Nor does it matter that § 30.4(a)(2) suggests that the race-based regulations are needed to achieve a demographic balance that would exist “absent discrimination.”
29 CFR 30.4(a)(2)
. As Chief Justice Roberts explained nearly twenty years ago: “The way to stop discrimination on the basis of race is to stop discriminating on the basis of race.”
Parents Involved in Cmty. Schs.
v.
Seattle Sch. Dist. No. 1,
551 U.S. 701, 748 (2007). That is because governmental actions that create “ `[d]istinctions between citizens solely because of their ancestry, are by their very nature odious to a free people whose institutions are founded upon the doctrine of equality.' ”
Callais,
146 S. Ct.
(
printed page 70184)
1131, 1152 (quoting
SFFA,
600 U.S. at 208).
Under the existing part 30, sponsors are also required to engage in outreach targeted to specific groups, as well as other burdensome activities when women or racial or ethnic minorities are underrepresented. Thais targeted outreach based on race, ethnicity, and sex, however, is legally vulnerable.
See MD/DC/DE Broadcasters Ass'n
v.
F.C.C.,
236 F.3d 13, 20 (D.C. Cir. 2001) (disagreeing with the premise that “preferential recruiting `disadvantag[es] no one' ” and subjecting the affirmative recruiting requirement to strict scrutiny). This focus on “utilization” and race- or sex-based responses to such underutilization undermines the justification that these goals and targeted efforts are meant to achieve EEO for
all
apprentices.
Cf. Monterey Mech. Co.
v.
Wilson,
125 F.3d 702, 711 (9th Cir. 1997) (system where contractors must subcontract percentages of work to minority or female owned subcontractors or show good faith effort to comply with the non-rigid “goals” is a racial classification under the Equal Protection Clause).
The premise underlying part 30's affirmative action provisions was that “absent discrimination, over time a sponsor's apprenticeship program, generally, will reflect the sex, race, ethnicity, and disability profile of the labor pools from which the sponsor recruits and selects.”
29 CFR 30.4(a)(2)
. This premise, however, is flawed because “[i]t is completely unrealistic to assume that unlawful discrimination is the sole cause of people's failing to gravitate to jobs and employers in accord with the laws of chance.”
See Watson
v.
Fort Worth Bank & Trust,
487 U.S. 977, 992 (1988). Section 30.4(a)(2)'s “completely unrealistic” premise also places unconstitutional pressure on sponsors to reach these goals. “The very term `underrepresentation' necessarily implies that, if such a situation exists, the [employer] is behaving in a manner that falls short of the desired outcome. The regulations pressure [employers] to maintain a workforce that mirrors the racial breakdown of their `metropolitan statistical area.' ”
Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod
v.
F.C.C.,
141 F.3d 344, 352 (D.C. Cir. 1998). The presence of a numerical goal, combined with the threat of deregistration for failing to take “good faith efforts” to meet those goals, incentivizes sponsors to engage in preferential hiring to avoid a finding that they have not engaged in such efforts.
Cf. Sussman
v.
Tanoue,
39 F. Supp. 2d 13, 26 (D.D.C. 1999) (finding that the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's affirmative action program need not be reviewed under strict scrutiny because the office administering the affirmative action program “had no authority comparable to the threat of extended government audit, license denial, and forfeiture which the Court of Appeals found would inevitably convert a potential concern about under-representation on the part of the FCC and the licensee into a hiring preference”).
To survive strict scrutiny, the Department would need to show that the race-based provisions of part 30 serve a compelling state interest. The Supreme Court's “precedents have identified only two compelling interests that can satisfy that standard.”
Callais,
146 S. Ct. at 1152 (quoting
SFFA,
600 U.S. at 207). The first is “avoiding imminent and serious risks to human safety in prisons,”
Id.,
which plainly has no application here. The second is “remediating specific, identified instances of past discrimination that violated the Constitution or a statute.”
Id.; see also City of Richmond
v.
J.A. Croson Co.,
488 U.S. 469, 497 (1989). Generalized assertions of societal or industrywide discrimination are insufficient to meet this standard, however; there must be specific instances of past intentional discrimination in which the Federal Government itself was an active or passive participant.
Id.
at 498-500;
see also Vitolo
v.
Guzman,
999 F.3d 353, 361 (6th Cir. 2021).
For the Department to impose the requirement to adopt race- and ethnicity-based utilization goals on all sponsors, the Department would need to show specific instances of its own participation in the discrimination, rather than that it is seeking to rectify general societal inequities.
See Wygant
v.
Jackson Bd. of Educ.,
476 U.S. 267, 275 (1986) (citing
Hazelwood School District
v.
United States,
433 U.S. 299, 308 (1977) for the proposition that the Court focuses “on prior discrimination as the justification for, and the limitation on, a State's adoption of race-based remedies”). The Department cannot meet this standard as the past rulemaking record for part 30 has not identified any such instances of past discrimination.
Furthermore, the utilization goals required by existing § 30.6 lack narrow tailoring, as their application has no clear end, applies regardless of occupation or industry, and the default data used to set the goal is the respective group's representation in the civilian labor force, a statistic that bears little relationship to any individual's interest in and qualifications for an apprenticeship.
See Rothe Dev. Corp.
v.
Dep't of Def.,
545 F.3d 1023, 1036 (Fed. Cir. 2008) (identifying the “relationship of the stated numerical goals to the relevant labor market” as a factor in determining narrow tailoring). Similarly, the existing part 30 sex-based goals and related affirmative action requirements are likely to trigger intermediate scrutiny, which they are unlikely to survive. The government must show that the favored sex “actually suffer[ed] a disadvantage” caused by discrimination in a particular field or context that the policy is designed to remedy to establish an important interest.
Mississippi Univ. for Women
v.
Hogan,
458 U.S. 718, 727-29 (1982). Statistical disparities between workforce composition and labor-market availability, standing alone, are insufficient to demonstrate an important governmental objective to remedy discrimination.
See Vitolo,
999 F.3d at 364 (citing
Craig
v.
Boren,
429 U.S. 190, 200-04 (1976)). Absent evidence that women suffered intentional discrimination in each of the specific trades or occupations subject to regulation, sex-based classifications in the form of goals cannot be justified as remedial measures.
Id.
at 365. For the same reasons that the race- and ethnicity-based goals are unlikely to demonstrate narrow tailoring, the sex-based goals are also unlikely to be found to be substantially related to the goal of remedying discrimination.
Given the constitutional infirmities created by the affirmative action provisions, the Department chooses to devote its resources to more supportable methods of expanding Registered Apprenticeship opportunities. If sponsors found certain elements of their affirmative action programs, such as their outreach or recruitment activities, to be helpful, they are free to continue those practices to the extent they are lawful. The Department is choosing, however, to no longer require such practices of sponsors. As discussed below, there are more effective and legally sound methods for protecting the welfare of apprentices.
Comments on Part 30's Conflict With Title VII
Comments:
A couple of commenters stated that, in the NPRM, the Department incorrectly argued that the part 30 regulations violate Title VII, and critiqued the Department's citation of the
Ames
v.
Ohio Department of Youth Services
as an inaccurate basis for some of the claims made by the Department in the NPRM. The commenters argued that existing regulations do not alter terms or conditions of employment
(
printed page 70185)
based on race, ethnicity, or sex, and simply require organizations to set aspirational goals which courts have permitted while prohibiting programs from making discriminatory employment decisions. The commenters maintained that the
Ames
decision determined that the standard for all plaintiffs bringing suits under Title VII should be the same regardless of whether they are a member of a historically disadvantaged group, and did not address the legality of race and sex neutral measures such as those required by part 30. One of these commenters stated that DOL also claims that affirmative action requirements in existing regulations cause employers to engage in disparate treatment based on race, sex, and ethnicity, but does not provide any evidence to support this claim. One commenter stated that multiple court rulings have found that affirmative action plans similar to the regulations in part 30 are permissible under Title VII. Another commenter also argued that the Department's reliance on
Ames
is inappropriate, reasoning that the decision focused on burden-shifting standards in individual employment disputes, and adding that the Court did not rule on the legality of proactive outreach, nonbinding affirmative action plans, or utilization goals in federally administered training programs.
A different commenter maintained that the existing regulations are in tension with Title VII because they require non-exempt program sponsors to take actions that Title VII prohibits. The commenter urged DOL to incorporate these rationales in the final rule.
A couple of commenters remarked that the proposed rule would align with several Administration E.O.s. One commenter stated that the proposed rules logically follows from President Trump's January 21, 2025,
E.O. 14173
, “Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity,” and the reasoning underlying it.
Department Response:
The Department maintains that the part 30 race-, ethnicity-, and sex-based affirmative action provisions are vulnerable to challenge under both the Constitution, for the reasons discussed above, and under Title VII. As
E.O. 14173
makes clear, Federal civil rights laws, including Title VII, “serve as a bedrock supporting equality of opportunity for all Americans” and illegal race- and sex-based preferences violate these laws. The Department agrees with the commenter that its rescission of the 2016 version's race-, ethnicity-, and sex-based utilization goals is consistent with Title VII and the principles articulated in
E.O. 14173
.
Commenters, however, have mischaracterized the Department's reliance on
Ames
v.
Ohio Department of Youth.
The Department does not claim that the
Ames
decision invalidates the existing part 30 affirmative action provisions as violative of Title VII. The Department cited
Ames
for the general proposition that, under both Title VII and the Equal Protection Clause, equal opportunity must extend to all apprentices, not just historically disadvantaged groups.
Ames
held that Title VII's disparate-treatment provision prohibits discrimination against
any individual,
thus “establishing the same protections for every `individual'—without regard to that individual's membership in a minority or majority group.” 605 U.S. at 309-10 (2025);
see also McDonald
v.
Santa Fe Trail Transp. Co.,
427 U.S. 273, 280 (1976) (holding that Title VII prohibits discrimination against non-minority individuals “upon the same standards” as minority individuals).
However, part 30's affirmative action requirements encourage preferential treatment of certain groups, specifically racial minorities and women.
29 CFR 30.4(a)
,
30.5(d)
.
Cf. Lutheran Church,
141 F.3d at 354 (race-based employment goals induce preferential treatment based on race). The holding in
Ames
increases the likelihood that a non-minority or male plaintiff could successfully sue a sponsor claiming that the sponsor improperly took race, ethnicity, or sex into account in making employment decisions pursuant to the part 30 affirmative action provisions.
Ames
v.
Ohio Dep't of Youth Servs.,
605 U.S. 303, 310 (2025) (“Our case law thus makes clear that the standard for proving disparate treatment under Title VII does not vary based on whether or not the plaintiff is a member of a majority group.”).
Even without the
Ames
holding, a lawsuit by a non-minority litigants alleging disparate treatment may be meritorious. Part 30's requirement for program sponsors to establish and take action to meet race- and sex-based goals conflicts with the plain text of section 703(a)(2) of the Act,
[
34
]
which makes it an unlawful employment practice to “classify” employees or applicants in a manner that deprives or tends to deprive individuals of employment opportunities because of race, color, sex, or national origin. The Civil Rights Act of 1991 amended Title VII (at section 703(m)
[
35
]
) to broaden this prohibition by providing that an unlawful employment practice is established when race, color, religion, sex, or national origin was even “a motivating factor” for an employment practice, even if other factors also motivated, or even drove, the decision. Title VII thus adopts a broad prohibition on race- and sex-based employment practices that, on its face, bars affirmative action measures to meet numeric goals based on those characteristics.
Notwithstanding the plain statutory text, the Supreme Court has construed Title VII to permit race- or sex-based affirmative action only in extremely narrow circumstances.
See United Steelworkers
v.
Weber,
443 U.S. 193 (1979);
Johnson
v.
Transp. Agency, Santa Clara Cnty, Cal.,
480 U.S. 616 (1987). Subsequent Supreme Court decisions call into question the continued viability of the
Weber-Johnson
framework.
See, e.g., Louisiana
v.
Callais,
146 S. Ct. 1131 (2026);
Ames
v.
Ohio Dep't of Youth Servs.,
605 U.S. 303 (2025);
SFFA,
600 U.S. 181 (2023
); and Ricci
v.
DeStefano,
557 U.S. 557, 579 (2009). While the framework is a judge-made doctrine that interprets Title VII atextually “to permit what its language read literally would prohibit,”
Johnson,
480 U.S. at 647 (O'Connor., J. concurring), the Department nonetheless assumes that
Weber-Johnson
remains controlling precedent.
Under the
Weber-Johnson
framework, an employer may voluntarily adopt a race- or sex-based measure to address a manifest imbalance in traditionally segregated job categories, provided that the measure is remedial in purpose, temporary in duration, and does not employ quotas or inflexible goals or unnecessarily trammel the interests of non-beneficiaries.
Weber,
443 U.S. at 208;
Johnson,
480 U.S. at 638. Such programs must be designed to eliminate the effects of past discrimination or segregation, not to maintain racial or sex balance for its own sake.
Johnson,
480 U.S. at 639-40. As the Eighth Circuit explained: “An affirmative action policy is valid [under Title VII] if the policy is remedial and narrowly tailored to meet the goal of remedying the effects of past discrimination.”
Humphries
v.
Pulaski Cnty. Special Sch. Dist.,
580 F.3d 688, 695 (8th Cir. 2009). It is often difficult for an employer to establish compliance with the strict limitations of
Weber
and
Johnson;
those who attempt such a path and fail necessarily violate Title VII with the practice in question.
To comply with the current part 30's affirmative action regulations, a covered sponsor must establish race- and sex-based employment goals and undertake related affirmative measures. The
(
printed page 70186)
Department is concerned that such practices do not fit within the
Weber-Johnson
framework—and certainly not generally across sponsors nationwide. As explained above, part 30's race- and sex-based requirements are not remedial: sponsors must undertake good faith efforts to meet, achieve, or approach proportional representation in terms of race and sex, not to specifically remedy manifest imbalances in a traditionally segregated job category. Nor are the requirements temporary: they have existed for decades, and unless rescinded, sponsors would continue to be subject to these regulations on an indefinite basis.
“[T]he existence of an affirmative action plan . . . when combined with evidence that the plan was followed in an employment decision is sufficient to constitute direct evidence of unlawful discrimination unless the plan is valid” under
Weber-Johnson. Frank
v.
Xerox Corp.,
347 F.3d 130, 137 (5th Cir. 2003) (quoting
Bass
v.
Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs,
256 F.3d 1095, 1110 (11th Cir. 2001)). Many sponsors' actions taken to comply with part 30's affirmative action regulations would not consistently satisfy the demanding
Weber-Johnson
framework and could therefore constitute direct evidence of unlawful discrimination in violation of Title VII. Part 30's utilization goals and related requirements thus compel regulated sponsors to adopt race- and sex-based employment practices that would be, in many cases, unlawful under Title VII. The Department should exercise its authority under the NAA to formulate and promote labor standards that are consistent with Federal law, rather than standards that create tension with Federal law.
Comments on the Application of
Executive Order 14168
Comments:
A commenter stated that the DOL fails to acknowledge that
E.O. 14168
defies settled Title VII case law. The commenter asserted that in
Bostock
v.
Clayton County, Georgia,
590 U.S. 644 (2020), the Supreme Court held that discrimination based on gender identity is a form of sex discrimination protected by Title VII, and as Executive Orders cannot override Supreme Court case law,
Bostock
remains the law of the land. A group of commenters stated that DOL inaccurately describes prevailing Title VII legal standards by claiming that the proposed elimination of sexual orientation as a category of prohibited discrimination is required to reflect “existing legal authorities” or “the current statutory language and legal standards governing nondiscrimination.” The group of commenters asserted that, in the
Bostock
ruling, the Supreme Court recognized that Title VII's prohibitions on discrimination on the basis of sex also bars discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.
One commenter expressed different interpretations of the
Bostock
ruling and its implications. This commenter asserted that while some claim that the
Bostock
decision prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, it does not. The commenter argued that in
Bostock,
the Court did not adopt a new protected basis of sexual orientation, transgender status, or gender identity in Title VII, but rather its holding and analysis was tied to what it viewed as a form of sex discrimination. The commenter further stated that the Court did not address the broad scope of conduct associated with sexual orientation or gender identify, and therefore it is inappropriate for DOL to impose nondiscrimination requirements based on these characteristics. The commenter concluded that, accordingly, the proposed rule would bring regulations into compliance with Federal nondiscrimination laws. Another commenter stated that rescinding the reference to “gender identity” that appears at
29 CFR 30.3(b)(5)
and
(c)
of the current regulations comports with President Trump's
E.O. 14168
“Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government,” which directed Federal agencies to modify regulations or policies that use the terms “gender” and “gender identity.”
Department Response:
The Department is removing all apprenticeship-specific nondiscrimination requirements, including references to sexual orientation and gender identity as specified protected bases under part 30, as mandated by
E.O. 14168
.
E.O. 14168
directs agencies to “enforce laws governing sex-based rights, protections, opportunities, and accommodations to protect men and women as biologically distinct sexes” and to “remove all statements, policies, regulations, forms, communications, or other internal and external messages that promote or otherwise inculcate gender ideology[.]” The Department therefore proposed to remove references to gender identity.
The Department disagrees with commenters who contend that these revisions improperly narrow the protections afforded by Federal nondiscrimination law. Commenters' objections rest on a misunderstanding of both the purpose and effect of this rulemaking. This final rule does not amend or limit the substantive protections afforded by Title VII or any other Federal or State nondiscrimination law. Rather, it rescinds the apprenticeship-specific nondiscrimination framework previously contained in part 30 and replaces it with a straightforward requirement that program sponsors comply with all applicable Federal and State laws prohibiting illegal discrimination. Under revised § 30.3, sponsors remain fully subject to all applicable nondiscrimination requirements imposed by Federal and State law, and apprentices retain whatever protections those laws provide.
The Department acknowledges commenters' reliance on
Bostock.
Nothing in this final rule purports to alter the legal effect of
Bostock
or to resolve questions concerning the scope of Title VII. The Department is not revising Title VII, nor is it exercising authority to define the substantive reach of that statute. Those questions remain governed by applicable law and are properly resolved by the other agencies and Federal courts charged with enforcing and interpreting Federal nondiscrimination statutes.
Accordingly, the Department has determined that it is unnecessary to maintain apprenticeship-specific regulatory provisions that separately enumerate particular protected categories or otherwise establish an independent nondiscrimination regime for Registered Apprenticeship programs. Instead, the final rule adopts a uniform standard requiring compliance with all applicable Federal and State nondiscrimination laws. To the extent those laws prohibit particular forms of discrimination, program sponsors remain bound by those requirements. To the extent those laws are interpreted, amended, or otherwise modified in the future, sponsors' obligations will change accordingly without requiring further amendments to part 30.
The Department therefore disagrees that the removal of apprenticeship-specific references to particular protected categories narrows the substantive protections available to apprentices. The final rule neither expands nor contracts the protections afforded under Federal and State nondiscrimination laws. Rather, it eliminates a duplicative apprenticeship-specific regulatory framework and returns responsibility for interpreting and enforcing those laws to other agencies and courts that possess the relevant statutory authority and expertise.
(
printed page 70187)
2. Streamlining Enforcement, Eliminating Duplicative Frameworks, and Aligning Apprenticeship Requirements with Federal Laws
General Comments About Streamlining Requirements
Comments:
Some commenters expressed support for the Department's proposal to streamline EEO requirements for Registered Apprenticeship programs. These commenters stated that the current regulations at
29 CFR part 30
impose unique EEO obligations on Registered Apprenticeship programs that have resulted in significant confusion, operational challenges, and compliance costs, potentially deterring the establishment of new apprenticeship programs and the growth of existing ones. One commenter concluded that compliance with existing nondiscrimination laws is sufficient.
Another commenter expressed support for DOL's efforts to harmonize the Department's rules for Registered Apprenticeship programs with nondiscrimination laws, arguing that the Department's proposed revisions are necessary to resolve the consequences of overlapping or unclear jurisdictional mandates.
However, one commenter asserted that the proposed rule risks increasing employer burden by shifting responsibility for EEO requirements to the “already overburdened” EEOC and other State agencies. The commenter maintained that employers consistently report that navigating multiple State-specific rules is more onerous than following a single Federal standard.
Department Response:
The Department appreciates the various commenters' support for the rule's streamlined and uniform approach to EEO and nondiscrimination requirements. The Department agrees that the requirements imposed under the existing rule were onerous, excessive, and impeded the goal of apprenticeship expansion. Accordingly, the Department maintains that this final rule fulfills the Administration's directive in
E.O. 14192
to eliminate regulations that impose costs, create confusion, hamper innovation, or otherwise restrain economic growth and opportunities for Americans.
The Department disagrees that the final rule increases compliance burdens by shifting responsibility to the EEOC or State agencies. Those agencies and the laws they administer govern sponsors regardless of whether part 30 exists. This rule does not create any new obligations under Federal or State nondiscrimination laws, nor does it create any new enforcement mechanisms. Rather, it eliminates a separate apprenticeship-specific compliance and enforcement regime that operated alongside existing Federal and State civil-rights laws. To the extent the commenter is concerned about multiple layers of regulation and bureaucracy, the final rule reduces, rather than increases, those layers by removing an additional apprenticeship-specific framework while leaving in place the generally applicable nondiscrimination laws that already govern sponsors.
3.
E.O. 14192
, Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation
Comments:
A commenter supported the proposed rule changes, arguing that the changes would provide numerous benefits, including reducing regulatory burdens, decreasing stakeholder confusion, providing clarity, and encouraging more apprenticeship program participation, and aligning with President Trump's executive orders on deregulation, merit-based opportunity, and preparing Americans for skilled trade jobs. Another commenter expressed support for the proposed rule's revisions to
29 CFR parts 29
and
30
, stating that these changes would remove a duplicative set of regulations on program sponsors and employers, and eliminate requirements for an unnecessarily complex array of goals, analyses, outreach, and annual reviews. A separate commenter concurred with the proposed removal of duplicative and outdated requirements.
A commenter maintained that it is essential to ensure that participating employers are not overburdened by reporting requirements and that employers can protect proprietary information, including trade secrets, program outlines, and other sensitive materials. The commenter urged the Department to consider broader improvements to the apprenticeship registration process and remove unnecessary administrative barriers and simplify the bureaucratic requirements for small and midsize employers. Specifically, the commenter recommended avoiding “government-centric language” that is not aligned with workplace operations, as well as delivering technical assistance through experienced practitioners, rather than static manuals and checklists.
Other commenters, however, disagreed with the Department's assertion that the part 30 regulation should be revised and streamlined to reduce undue regulatory burdens for Registered Apprenticeship stakeholders. One commenter asserted that the part 30 regulations are not burdensome on sponsors because States and other organizations have consistently created tools and templates for sponsors that have helped sponsors easily create affirmative action plans that support equal opportunity for Registered Apprenticeship program applicants. This commenter added that sponsors have been complying with these requirements for decades, and many sponsors already have policies and practices set up to effectively complete affirmative action plans, as well as internal auditing and reporting systems.
Department Response:
The Department appreciates comments that acknowledged the challenges that Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors face in complying with the existing part 30 regulation and the need for a clearer and less complex regulatory framework. The Department agrees with those commenters who opined that the existing part 30 regulation's requirements were expansive, duplicative, and unclear, and that they imposed a complex regulatory framework that did not serve sponsors' business needs. The Department further agrees that such regulatory complexity may have impeded the growth of the Registered Apprenticeship model by discouraging program uptake or expansion, and that revising and simplifying the part 30 regulation will lead to expansion of the model. As such, the Department's final rule streamlining the part 30 regulation serves the shared goals of the Department and this Administration to reduce regulatory burdens and expand Registered Apprenticeship. The Department also appreciates those commenters who acknowledged the alignment between this rulemaking and the Administration's deregulatory directive to Federal agencies (as outlined in
E.O. 14192
and cited in the NPRM as a motivation for this rulemaking).
The Department disagrees with commenters who asserted that the existing part 30 regulation did not impose meaningful burdens on program sponsors. Several commenters pointed to the availability of templates, technical assistance, internal auditing systems, and established compliance practices as evidence that sponsors could readily comply with the regulation. The Department does not find these observations persuasive. The existence of specialized templates, extensive technical assistance, compliance personnel, internal auditing systems, and recurring reporting processes demonstrates that sponsors and Registration Agencies devoted substantial time and resources to
(
printed page 70188)
satisfying the regulation's requirements. The fact that sponsors may have developed systems to facilitate compliance over time does not establish that the underlying requirements were simple, costless, or necessary.
Moreover, the Department is concerned not only with the burden imposed on existing sponsors that have already invested in compliance systems, but also with the effect of these requirements on employers considering whether to establish a Registered Apprenticeship program in the first instance. The Department concludes that reducing apprenticeship-specific compliance obligations will lower barriers to entry and facilitate broader adoption of the Registered Apprenticeship model.
The Department also received comments from employers describing the time, administrative effort, and resources devoted to compliance with affirmative action plans, utilization analyses, reporting obligations, and related requirements under part 30. After considering these comments and the record as a whole, the Department has determined that these apprenticeship-specific requirements imposed significant compliance costs while providing limited benefits beyond those already afforded by generally applicable Federal and State nondiscrimination laws. The Department therefore concludes that rescinding these requirements is an appropriate means of reducing unnecessary regulatory burden while continuing to protect apprentices through existing nondiscrimination protections.
5. Growing Registered Apprenticeship

Comments:
A commenter maintained that the proposed rule lacks compelling evidence that it would lead to apprenticeship growth. Another commenter opposed the proposed rule's description that the current regulations have limited adoption or participation, particularly among small businesses, citing personal site visits over the last 15 years showing no instances in which EEO or affirmative action requirements were reported as barriers, and over the last 3 years, the commenter said they have registered 12 new apprenticeship programs with over 200 apprentices without EEO being raised as a concern.
In contrast, a commenter supported the NPRM's statement that the costs and disincentives created by the current part 30 regulations may be greater in new and emerging industries, citing personal experience in the education sector where funding is limited (or not yet apportioned as part of existing budgets) to develop or register an existing apprenticeship program.
Additionally, a commenter expressed support for simplifying

Several commenters commented in support of further growing Registered Apprenticeship and modernizing the system, citing research that employers receive a positive return on investment, that apprentices receive higher wage increases than comparable workers, and that employers report apprenticeships are effective at addressing talent shortages. Department Response:
The Department agrees with the commenters that Registered Apprenticeship should continue to be expanded and that it is crucial in helping address workforce shortages. The Department anticipates that the removal of onerous and burdensome requirements, such as those that are rescinded under this final rule, should facilitate increases in system participation through burden reduction and lower barriers to entry.
The Department disagrees with commenters who asserted that this final rule's rescission of provisions of the existing regulation will harm the growth of the National Apprenticeship System and that these provisions were not onerous for small businesses. As discussed throughout this preamble and in greater depth within the sections on the rescission of the existing regulation, there is no robust causal evidence that the existing regulations led to the growth of the National Apprenticeship System. Based on its delivery of technical assistance to sponsors of various sizes (including small businesses), the Department expects that the reduction of compliance burdens associated with these rescissions will facilitate program creation and expansion.
Additionally, in response to the anecdote from a commenter that the sponsors the commenter worked with did not mention part 30 and EEO requirements as burdensome, other commenters who were sponsors themselves or represented sponsors responding to the NPRM did express that part 30 is burdensome. As a result, the Department concludes, and several commenters representing industry concurred, that the existing part 30 regulations are overly burdensome and thereby suppress, not expand, potential entities' participation in the National Apprenticeship System.
Regarding comments that suggested increased funding and the codification of the National Apprenticeship System as avenues to expand the model, the Department notes that Congress, not the Department, has the authority to pursue these activities. The Department also appreciates the suggestions to further streamline registration, such as improving reciprocity, and will consider these options if there are future rulemakings on part 29.

G. Comments on the Proposal's Impacts on Women, Racial and Ethnic Minorities, and Individuals With Disabilities
1. Data and Research on Demographic Representation and Economic Factors in Apprenticeship
Comments:
A couple of commenters suggested that empirical evidence shows that the part 30 regulation improved diversity within the apprenticeship system. For example, some commenters stated that women's participation in apprenticeship grew threefold over the last decade or so. One commenter noted that this increase in women's participation occurred after the Department implemented intentional investments to increase the number of women in apprenticeships. Several commenters provided evidence that showed, in their view, that this growth occurred in smaller sub-groups of apprentices as well. One commenter reasoned that these increases in representation demonstrate the success of current Federal regulations and feared the proposed rule's rescissions would reverse increases in diversity within the National Apprenticeship System. However, one commenter acknowledged that, while the National Apprenticeship System has diversified over the last decade, there is no clear evidence of a causal relationship between the issuance of the 2016 regulation and increases in participation rates among certain demographic groups.

A commenter said that despite progress, women remain significantly underrepresented in apprenticeship programs, making up just 14.3 percent of apprentices according to the OA data, while comprising nearly half (47.1 percent) of the labor workforce. These commenters asserted that removing the existing part 30 regulations would further exacerbate current demographic imbalances in the representation of certain demographic groups in apprenticeship. One commenter further argued that reducing these disparities could expand the talent pool available to employers, and that apprenticeship programs would need to reflect the full diversity of the U.S. population to effectively meet employer needs. Another commenter argued that if equal access were ensured for women, people of color, and other historically excluded groups, apprenticeship programs would better fulfill the goal of providing opportunity for all workers.
However, a commenter that expressed support for the Department's proposed revisions to part 30 argued that demographic disparities between apprenticeship programs and the broader workforce should not justify race-preferential programs. This commenter argued that history and culture can explain why certain groups are more common in some jobs, rather than discrimination. The commenter also observed that national and ethnic groups are not evenly distributed across most occupations, including apprenticeship programs.
Several commenters also discussed lower wages and occupational segregation among women who are apprentices and within the broader economy and, said that rescinding elements of part 30 would harm economic gains by women within apprenticeship. For example, one commenter stated that when you compare the full-time annualized salary of female versus male apprentices based on median hourly wage rates, female apprentices only earn 63.4 percent of their male counterparts earnings. The commenter added that women's median hourly earnings were significantly lower than men's across all races and ethnicities and were lowest for Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islanders and Black women who completed an apprenticeship. Commenters also stated that there is ongoing discrimination within the broader economy and the National Apprenticeship System, citing research, documented instances of discrimination, and surveys regarding discrimination and harassment. For example, a commenter said that, contrary to the Department's position, racial disparities in employment and positions are the result of discriminatory practices rather than lack of skills or personal preferences, citing research showing that equally qualified Black workers remain at a disadvantage compared to White workers when trying to enter certain industries, and referencing a 2023 National Bureau of Economic Research study concluding that occupational segregation in the United States today is substantially higher than what would be expected in a race-neutral environment. The commenter added that other studies show that resumes with White-sounding names were 10 percent more likely to get chosen for an interview than resumes with Black-sounding names. Another commenter suggested that the
(
printed page 70190)
recent charges brought by the EEOC against apprenticeship programs and construction companies for sex and race discrimination is evidence that discrimination continues to be a rampant problem.
One commenter, who identified herself as a Black woman, described her experience as a second-year apprentice; she discussed being passed over for training in favor of a White, male, first-year apprentice, despite being told by their foreman and general foreman that they would receive training on the next stage of the project. Another commenter cited their own 2021 national survey of tradeswomen, which found that one in four female apprentices reported never or rarely being treated equally when it came to lay-offs and about one out of five reported never or rarely being treated equally in work assignments, OJL, or in hiring.
Additionally, some commenters discussed how discrimination can impact apprentices after they are enrolled in the program as well. For example, one commenter reasoned that discrimination in hiring and access to hours of work means it will take longer to reach the hours required for apprenticeship progression and completion, delaying access to higher rates of hourly pay. The commenter also said that discrimination in access to work assignments, tools, and OJL means that women may have acquired fewer skills during their apprenticeship, making it harder for them to compete for skilled trades opportunities after completion.
Finally, several commenters maintained that diversity benefits more than just minority groups, citing research stating that more diverse companies have higher average profits, higher rates of innovation, and report higher revenues from launching new products, and also record higher worker satisfaction and worker longevity rates. A commenter suggested diversity could therefore help reduce turnover and help address existing skills gaps within the construction industry. Another commenter cited reports emphasizing the importance of human capital development (including critical thinking, emotional intelligence, and cross-cultural competencies) and diversity, rather than technical efficiency, in national economic and individual corporate performance. Similarly, a commenter remarked that actively encouraging individuals of color to consider jobs in teaching is important because research has consistently shown that a diverse educator workforce results in improved academic performance for all students, and especially for students of color.
Department Response:
The Department acknowledges certain commenters' use of demographic and economic data purporting to show the beneficial impact of diversity initiatives pertaining to apprenticeship. However, the Department fundamentally disagrees with the underlying premise advanced by several of these commenters: namely, that a central policy goal of the part 30 regulation should be to achieve and maintain a level of representation of certain groups in Registered Apprenticeship that mirrors the demographic prevalence of such groups in the broader labor force. Instead, in this final rule, the Department maintains that the central goal of the part 30 regulation must be the prohibition of all forms of illegal discrimination in Registered Apprenticeship.
As stated earlier in the preamble of this final rule, the Department asserts that compulsory, nonremedial, group-based preferences and affirmative action schemes are inherently discriminatory because they treat individuals differently based upon their race, sex, or ethnicity. Therefore, the use of data on the existence of demographic imbalances in the overall apprenticeship workforce to justify the indefinite continuation of affirmative action requirements runs counter to the Department's paramount goal of prohibiting all forms of illegal discrimination in Registered Apprenticeship. The Department reiterates its conviction that apprenticeship programs should be free to recruit, hire, and retain apprentices solely on the basis of merit, and without reference to an applicant's group identity, ancestry, or demographic characteristics.
The Department notes that commenters failed to provide any authoritative, persuasive, or conclusive evidence to support their assertions that the part 30 regulation has been effective in improving participation rates and outcomes for apprentices in certain demographic groups, or that the removal of part 30 requirements would lead to adverse impacts on apprentices or apprenticeship programs. While some commenters asserted that there have been meaningful gains in representation of certain groups in apprenticeship, other commenters maintained that demographic imbalances and issues of underrepresentation have persisted over the past decade. Some commenters also acknowledged that increases in representation of certain demographic groups could be tied to other factors unrelated to the part 30 regulations, including investments to expand apprenticeship, or broader labor market or economic trends. One commenter opposed to the elimination of the affirmative requirements acknowledged that there was no proof of a “robust causal link” between the part 30 regulation and any improvements in demographic representation in apprenticeship. As noted previously, the Department disagrees with the premise that a central policy goal of the part 30 regulation should be to achieve and maintain a level of representation of certain groups in Registered Apprenticeship that mirrors the demographic prevalence of such groups in the broader labor force. However, in order to be responsive to commenters, the Department reviewed its own apprenticeship data, labor market and economic data, and other resources to ascertain the impact of its proposal, and similarly did not identify any direct causal link between the part 30 regulation's requirements and increased representation of certain demographic groups in apprenticeship.
The Department has reviewed data on active apprentices across the prior two decades to assess changes in demographic representation in the National Apprenticeship System in developing this final rule.
[

]
An analysis of this data fails to demonstrate a direct correlation nor causal link between the updated affirmative action and EEO requirements in the 2016 version of the part 30 regulation and significant increases in representation of demographic groups in Registered Apprenticeship programs nationwide. From FY 2006 through FY 2015, the average annual growth rate in the total number of active apprentices was 2.3%, and from FY 2016 through FY 2025, the average annual growth rate in the total number of active apprentices was 7%. The average annual growth rate for women in Registered Apprenticeship from FY 2006 through-FY 2015 was 3.1%, and the average annual growth rate for women from FY 2016-FY 2025 was 12.3%. For Hispanic and Latino apprentices, average annual growth rates were 7.1% from FY 2006 through-FY 2015, and 11.1% from FY 2016 through-FY 2026. For African Americans, average annual growth rates were 3.7% from FY 2006-FY 2015 and 7.6% from FY 2016 through FY 2025. As discussed further below, increases in the representation of certain
(
printed page 70191)
demographic groups in Registered Apprenticeship programs may be attributable to increases in demographic representation in certain occupations or industries outside of the Registered Apprenticeship context, increases in Federal funding to support apprenticeship expansion, or other labor markets factors and trends. The Department does not agree with commenters who posited that the part 30 regulation's requirements, such as the affirmative action program or EEO requirements established in the 2016 regulation, directly caused increases seen in representation of certain demographic groups in Registered Apprenticeship programs.
It is important to consider a comprehensive analysis of labor market trends, both within and outside Registered Apprenticeship, in assessing the impact of the part 30 regulation on representation of certain demographic groups in Registered Apprenticeship programs over the past two decades. As mentioned earlier, across this time frame, Registered Apprenticeship has expanded and evolved from a training model primarily used in the skilled trades to include more occupations, industries, and economic sectors. Two key growth areas for Registered Apprenticeship are the information technology and healthcare sectors; Registered Apprenticeship programs in the information technology sector grew from 20 programs in FY 2016 to 132 programs in 2025, while programs in healthcare grew from 533 programs in FY 2016 to 1,170 programs in 2025. Meanwhile, women's overall representation in the workforce in those two sectors has increased substantially in recent decades. The share of women in the information technology workforce has grown from a baseline of around 9% in the early 2000s to around 23% of today's information technology workforce in the United States.
[
37
]
The growth of women's participation in the healthcare workforce is even more striking. Based on data from the American Community Survey, a study from the U.S. Census Bureau reported that women have driven 80% of labor force growth in the healthcare sector since the early 2000s, with the number of full-time women in health care occupations nearly doubling from around 5 million employees in 2000 to around 9 million employees in 2019.
[
38
]
These examples of broader demographic trends in the labor market demonstrate that it is not possible to conclusively attribute any growth in the representation of certain demographic groups in Registered Apprenticeship to the affirmative action provisions of the part 30 regulation. The slight increases in representation of certain demographic groups over the prior two decades corresponds with an overall increase in the average annual growth rate for all apprentices, and also could be attributable, in part, to the expansion of the model into new industries (outside of construction and the skilled trades), such as information technology and healthcare. In addition, overall increases in apprenticeship numbers and the slight increases in representation of certain demographic groups coincides with the introduction of increased, sustained Federal funding to support Registered Apprenticeship growth.
In summary, several of the commenters who supported the retention of the affirmative action provisions found in the 2016 version of the part 30 posited or inferred a correlation between the compulsory regime of group-based preferences contained in the regulation and increases in the demographic representation of certain groups (particularly women and Latinos) in Registered Apprenticeship programs that occurred after the issuance of that rule. In addressing such comments, the Department reiterates its firm commitment to the principle that individuals from all backgrounds—regardless of their race, ethnicity, sex, religion, or national origin—must be afforded the opportunity to compete on an equal, nondiscriminatory basis for admission into a Registered Apprenticeship program, and that apprentices must be selected and hired by program sponsors on the basis of their qualifications alone. Furthermore, as one commenter acknowledged, the available demographic data does not provide sufficient evidence of a “robust causal link” between the affirmative action requirements of the part 30 regulation and the subsequent increase in the representation of discrete groups in Registered Apprenticeship programs.
Some commenters offered assertions positing a direct correlation between certain economic outcomes and benefits and the increased participation of underrepresented groups in apprenticeship, such as improved profits, greater innovation, higher wages, and improved worker satisfaction and longevity. The Department maintains that not only are these supposed correlations unsubstantiated, they do not alter the Department's conviction that affirmative action requirements induce sponsors to treat individuals differently based on demographic characteristics and are therefore inherently discriminatory.
The Department acknowledges the concerns raised by commenters that, over time, illegal discrimination has persisted in both the broader labor market and in Registered Apprenticeship. As stated earlier, the Department's primary focus with this final rule is to clarify and strengthen the nondiscrimination requirement for Registered Apprenticeship in the part 30 regulation. In eliminating a duplicative, apprenticeship-specific regulatory framework for resolving issues related to discrimination, apprentices will better understand how to obtain individualized relief (which the existing part 30 regulation fails to provide). The Department maintains that establishing a stronger and more streamlined nondiscrimination framework in the revised part 30 regulation better aligns with the Department's mandate to protect apprentice welfare under the NAA.

V. Section-by-Section Analysis of the Final Rule—Rescissions of Current Part 30
A. Rescission of Equal Opportunity Standards for All Sponsors
In the NPRM, the Department proposed to remove a number of requirements that the 2016 version of the part 30 regulation had applied to all program sponsors, regardless of size; these mandates included, among other things, the internal dissemination of a sponsor's equal opportunity policy, the sponsor's ongoing maintenance of a list of current recruitment sources for apprentices, the sponsor's provision of anti-harassment training to apprentices and journeyworkers who work with apprentices, and the sponsor's establishment of a procedure for handling and resolving complaints involving such harassment. After due consideration of the comments received concerning the proposed removal of these requirements, the Department has determined to rescind these previous part 30 mandates in this final rule.
Comments:
A commenter said that by revising
29 CFR 30.3
to direct program sponsors to comply with all applicable Federal and State laws and regulations prohibiting illegal discrimination, the proposed rule would relieve sponsors from establishing or undertaking a complex array of goals, analyses, outreach, and annual reviews. More specifically, the commenter also expressed support for removing the requirement to establish an EEO coordinator.
A commenter supported the simplification and streamlining of the existing nondiscrimination regulations into one standard, stating that the protected bases in proposed § 30.3 mirror the bases protected by civil rights laws passed by Congress and enforced by the EEOC—Title VII of the Act, the ADEA, the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008, and the ADA. The commenter added that, unlike the revised version of part 30 contained in this final rule, the content of § 30.3 overreaches by imposing nondiscrimination requirements not found in the text of statutes passed by Congress, such as requiring nondiscrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity.
However, several other commenters expressed strong opposition to the rescission of the foregoing provisions of § 30.3. One commenter opposing the rescission maintained that the equal opportunity pledge, the assignment of a person responsible for EEO, and information sessions on EEO requirements remain necessary due to continued prevalence of harassment in Registered Apprenticeship programs, as well as the need to reiterate sponsors' commitment to EEO and communicate that commitment internally to all affected parties. Another commenter asserted that the proposed rule's rationale for rescinding these requirements does not consider the end goal of Registered Apprenticeship programs, which is to ensure that sponsors receive a return on investment, adding that where appropriate accommodations and support are not provided, programs see premature apprentice dropouts. A commenter remarked that Federal standards still matter because many sponsors operate in multiple States, and without a consistent Federal framework, employers may lower compliance across the board. Another commenter expressed concern that removing EEO requirements would make it difficult for programs to demonstrate compliance with civil rights laws and protect themselves from legal risk.
Department Response:
The Department agrees with the commenter that characterized the requirements under existing § 30.3 as unnecessary and complex. Accordingly, the Department notes that it is maintaining a simpler and more streamlined Federal standard under this final rule through the new nondiscrimination standard contained in § 30.3 of this final rule. Additionally, and as described in greater detail below, sponsors covered by Federal nondiscrimination laws are already obligated to post a notice describing the protections afforded under Federal laws that prohibit job discrimination based on race, color, sex, national origin, religion, age (40 and older), equal pay, disability, or genetic information, and retaliation.
The Department recognizes that many sponsors may find EEO coordinators, anti-harassment training, internal complaint procedures, and similar practices useful. Nothing in this final rule prohibits sponsors from maintaining such programs. The Department has concluded, however, that these practices need not be mandated through a separate apprenticeship-specific regulatory regime because sponsors are already subject to Federal and State nondiscrimination laws and possess strong incentives to maintain workplaces free from unlawful discrimination and harassment. Sponsors remain free to adopt compliance structures they determine are appropriate for their workforce, operations, and legal obligations. To the extent commenters assert that such practices help sponsors demonstrate compliance with applicable civil-rights laws or reduce litigation risk, sponsors remain free to retain those practices under this final rule.
1. Assertions Made About Reduced EEO Protections
Comments:
A commenter expressed concern that the practical effect of rolling back comprehensive EEO protections could be to limit remedies to address discrimination in apprenticeship programs. This commenter stated that the proposed rule incorrectly asserts that “the protected characteristics contained in § 30.3(a) of the current part 30 are duplicative of the nondiscrimination requirements contained in a number of Federal civil rights statutes.” The commenter argued that, consequently, the proposed rule fails to account for potential harms to apprentices, as well as resultant limitations to DOL's authority to remedy discrimination in apprenticeship programs because of this change. The commenter stated that “by eliminating the longstanding prohibition on discrimination against apprentices based on certain protected characteristics . . . and instead aligning the regulation with existing civil rights laws applicable in the private sector, the Proposed Rule adopts the small employer carveouts of these civil rights laws.” The commenter asserted this would limit the coverage of nondiscrimination requirements and
(
printed page 70193)
eliminate the authority of the Department to take enforcement action against small employer sponsors who engage in discrimination.
A commenter opined that, contrary to the Department's assertion in the NPRM, the current part 30 regulations do not duplicate Title VII, and instead go well beyond Title VII in providing substantive protections from discrimination and mechanisms for preventing discrimination. Specifically, unlike
29 CFR part 30
, this commenter asserted that Title VII likely does not apply to all program sponsors, or to all of the apprenticeship activities of sponsors. The commenter noted that Title VII applies to employment discrimination by “employers, labor unions, and joint labor-management committees controlling apprenticeship or other training or retraining, including on-the-job training programs,” and makes it unlawful for such entities “to discriminate against any individual because of his race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in admission to, or employment in, any program established to provide apprenticeship or other training.” In contrast, the commenter said
29 CFR part 30
applies to “sponsors of apprenticeship programs registered with either DOL or a recognized SAA.” The commenter noted that sponsors are responsible for not only for overseeing admission to and employment in training programs, but also a wide range of other activities, and it is unclear whether Title VII would cover the full scope of activities that sponsors engage in. Another commenter expressed concern that removing these EEO requirements would make it difficult for programs to demonstrate compliance with civil rights laws and protect themselves from legal risk.
Department Response:
In response to some commenters' concerns surrounding protected characteristics, the Department notes that covered apprentices are protected from discrimination on the bases of all the same protected characteristics as under existing § 30.3(a) through the following Federal statutes or precedent set by Supreme Court cases interpreting them: Title VII of the Act, the ADEA, the ADA, and the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008.
In response to concerns raised by certain commenters about the statutory thresholds excluding small employers from coverage under Title VII and other Federal nondiscrimination laws, the Department notes that Congress purposefully excluded small employers from these statutory nondiscrimination requirements. The application of nondiscrimination requirements to private employers is fundamentally a matter of legislative judgment. In statutes ranging from Title VII to the ADA and ADEA, Congress made explicit policy determinations regarding which employers should be subject to Federal nondiscrimination requirements and which should be exempt. Congress repeatedly chose not to extend those statutory obligations to certain smaller employers, reflecting a legislative balancing of the benefits of nondiscrimination regulation against the burdens such requirements impose on small businesses.
The Department declines to exercise its authority under the NAA in a manner that effectively subjects small employers to regulatory obligations that Congress expressly determined should not apply to them. The Department believes that the better exercise of its authority is to respect the coverage determinations embodied in Federal civil-rights statutes and to align apprenticeship requirements with the scope of those statutes rather than creating a separate apprenticeship-specific regime that expands their reach to small employers. Congress remains free to revise the coverage thresholds contained in those laws should it determine that broader coverage is warranted.
Moreover, the alignment of part 30 with the employee size-based exclusions contained in existing Federal nondiscrimination laws or relevant State nondiscrimination laws will reduce administrative burdens on certain program sponsors—particularly small- and medium-sized enterprises—that could inhibit the accelerated establishment and expansion of programs. As certain small entities that sponsor apprenticeship programs have been excluded from coverage by applicable Federal nondiscrimination laws such as Title VII, the Department should refrain from extending apprentice nondiscrimination protections on a broader basis than Congress expressly authorized under those statutes.
The Department defers to the EEOC or other relevant enforcement agencies in determining which employment practices of sponsors are covered under the various civil rights statutes. The Department notes, however, that courts have interpreted Title VII's training program provision at section 703(d) to cover more than mere “admission to” such programs, contrary to the commenter's assertion.
See, e.g., Langford
v.
Int'l Union of Operating Eng'rs, Loc. 30,
765 F. Supp. 2d 486, 499 n.6 (S.D.N.Y. 2011) (acknowledging that section 703(d) of Title VII provides a valid basis for a hostile work environment claim);
Herrera
v.
Int'l Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, Local No. 68,
228 F. Supp. 2d 1233, 1242 (D.Colo. 2002) (stating that “[t]he plain language of [section 703(d)] prohibits sex discrimination against an individual who is `employed in' an apprenticeship training program” and citing to
29 CFR 30.1
as providing similar protections).
The Department maintains that, under the final rule, the Department retains the authority to deregister an apprenticeship program in instances where there has been a finding of discrimination by a governmental agency or a court made pursuant to applicable statutory standards. In response to those commenters that expressed concern about the Department losing authority to issue individual remedies under the final rule, the Department notes that the existing part 30 does not offer individualized remedies for apprentices who suffer employment discrimination based upon their race, sex, or ethnicity, but only provides for the issuance of program-level sanctions such as deregistration. Under existing part 30, individual apprentices seeking make-whole remedies are free to pursue rights of action under other statutes such as Title VII. With respect to the steps that existing part 30 prescribes to prevent discrimination, the Department acknowledges that these steps are not required under Title VII. Removing these excessive requirements is, again, in line with the goals of this Administration and with Congressional intent in enacting Title VII. Sponsors are, however, encouraged to continue adopting any lawful preventative measures that they find effective. The Department will simply not dictate the specific measures a program must take to do so.
