The commenter also recommended that sponsors conduct universal outreach and employ facially neutral selection procedures to the extent possible. The commenter further recommended that the Department take certain actions to clarify compliance requirements, including integrating a review of nondiscrimination compliance into a sponsor's basic program oversight, and clarifying that youth apprenticeship programs do not violate nondiscrimination laws.
Another commenter recommended that the Department continue to consider measures to lower administrative burdens and provide incentives to participate in apprenticeship, including creating a system that promotes flexible program models that contain the most essential components of apprenticeship, and incentivizing organizations, like local industry associations, to serve as intermediaries. The commenter also recommended expanding financial incentives, such as apprentice wage reimbursement, and allowing more efficient and effective delivery of programming, including by removing the apprenticeable occupations framework.
Department Response:
In response to questions posed by a commenter, and as described in § 30.5 of this final rule, a Registered Apprenticeship program only will be deregistered if there is a final determination made by an enforcement entity or court that the program has violated an applicable nondiscrimination law and the Registration Agency determines that a compliance action plan is not being implemented in accordance with the remedy prescribed by the enforcement entity or court. Accordingly, programs will not be deregistered for continuing to conduct their current activities or if their program experiences increased diversity so long as the program has not violated any applicable Federal or State nondiscrimination laws.
With respect to the commenter that suggested the inclusion of a provision in this final rule that a sponsor affirm in writing that they are in compliance with all applicable Federal and State employment nondiscrimination laws and will utilize facially neutral selection procedures, the Department takes the position that such written affirmations are unnecessary and would not necessarily enhance program accountability, as such obligations are already mandated under applicable Federal nondiscrimination laws. Nothing in this final rule prohibits sponsors from voluntarily providing written notices regarding apprentice rights, obtaining written acknowledgments or certifications from program participants, or adopting other compliance measures that sponsors determine are appropriate for their operations. Although the Department declines to mandate such practices through part 30, sponsors remain free to maintain them if they believe they assist with compliance, workforce management, apprentice retention, or risk mitigation.
Similarly, this commenter's recommendation that sponsors inform apprentices of their part 30 rights in writing is redundant, as employers with 15 or more employees that sponsor Registered Apprenticeship programs are already obligated to post a notice describing the Federal laws prohibiting job discrimination based on race, color, sex, national origin, religion, age (40 and older), equal pay, disability or genetic information, and retaliation. Title VII of the Act imposes a monetary penalty for covered employers who fail to post these notices. The “Know Your Rights: Workplace Discrimination is Illegal” poster, prepared by the EEOC, summarizes these laws and explains how employees or applicants can file a complaint if they believe that they have experienced discrimination.
The Department also declines to adopt this commenter's suggestion that the part 30 regulation should clarify that youth apprenticeship programs do not violate nondiscrimination laws, as such a determination should be made by the EEOC. In response to the other comments summarized above, the Department notes that the thoughtful suggestions advanced by these commenters for taking non-regulatory measures to reduce administrative burdens on program sponsors and to provide financial incentives to apprenticeship stakeholders fall outside of the scope of the part 30 rulemaking initiative; accordingly, as this final rule does not constitute a suitable regulatory or policy vehicle for addressing such suggestions, the Department refrains from providing a response to these commenters.
B. Rescission of Affirmative Action Requirements
1. Affirmative Action Programs (§ 30.4)
In the NPRM, the Department explained that existing § 30.4 required non-exempt sponsors to establish affirmative action programs, document them in a written plan, and implement components specified in §§ 30.4 through 30.9 and 30.11. These compulsory, nonremedial, and ongoing sponsor requirements included conducting demographic utilization analyses, and setting numerical hiring goals and undertaking targeted outreach, recruitment, and retention activities where apprenticeship workforce underutilization based on race, sex, and ethnicity was determined to exist. These sponsor requirements also included annually reviewing personnel processes, as well as disability-related obligations, such as tracking progress toward an OA established utilization goal and inviting apprenticeship applicants to self-identify as individuals with disabilities. The NPRM articulated the Department's position that, taken together, these affirmative action program requirements across §§ 30.4 through 30.9 and 30.11 are unduly burdensome and legally questionable. In the NPRM, the Department also solicited comments from all interested parties, including Registered Apprenticeship stakeholders, on its proposal to remove the affirmative action requirements from part 30, and invited public input on how the administrative burdens associated with these regulatory mandates affected program operations or decisions to participate in Registered Apprenticeship.
After due consideration of the comments discussed below, the Department has determined, as proposed in the NPRM, to rescind the requirements set forth in §§ 30.4 through 30.9 and 30.11 in this final rule.

A commenter expressed its appreciation for the Department's observation in the NPRM that the current part 30 requirements have limited, rather than promoted, apprenticeship opportunities without corresponding gains in program effectiveness or integrity. The commenter asserted that simplifying sponsors' EEO obligations would better achieve the Secretary of Labor's obligations under the NAA and promote expansion of Registered Apprenticeship programs, which the commenter asserted would expand opportunities for women, minorities, and underrepresented groups to enter and succeed in the construction trades. The commenter specifically supported
(

rescinding the affirmative action program requirements, which the commenter described as burdensome. The commenter stated that currently, these plans must be updated annually, even when there are no material changes in workforce composition or recruitment practices, and that sponsors must maintain detailed records related to these affirmative action programs because they are subject to records requests and audits. Another commenter reiterated its previous objections (expressed at the time of the 2016 part 30 rulemaking) to the affirmative action program requirements that were imposed on small programs under § 30.4, and generally supported eliminating such requirements. In particular, the commenter asserted that affirmative action program requirements were difficult for nonunion program sponsors to implement.
Another commenter critiqued the existing part 30 regulation's affirmative action requirements, stating such requirements are based on the fundamentally flawed and abstract premise that any demographic disparities in a sponsor's or employer's workforce constitute
per se
discrimination. This commenter argued that there could be nondiscriminatory reasons why the demographic makeup of a given workforce may not mirror the demographic makeup of the local labor market, and that disparities alone without evidence of actual disparate treatment should not be used as a proxy for unlawful discrimination. The commenter further asserted that the part 30 regulation simultaneously prohibits discrimination while incentivizing and inducing disparate treatment of applicants through utilization analysis, utilization goals, and targeted outreach. According to the commenter, such disparate treatment is not supported by the text of neither the NAA nor Federal nondiscrimination laws, and that in

However, the Department also received some comments opposing the proposed rescission of the affirmative action provisions contained in part 30. A commenter maintained that the nondiscrimination protections contained in Title VII are not an adequate substitute for the affirmative action measures required by part 30, and supported the Department's prior analysis (contained in the preamble to the 2016 version of the part 30 final rule) that such measures are necessary because of the “residual impact of longstanding discrimination.” The commenter asserted that such active measures can be successful, as illustrated by another statement from the Department in the preamble to the 2016 part 30 final rule that “women do participate and succeed in apprenticeship programs at higher levels when provided equal opportunity and support.” The commenter discussed a survey which, according to the commenter, illustrates that diversity goals are key contributors to tradeswomen's success in their occupations. The commenter concluded that the Department could make these active requirements less burdensome without eliminating them entirely.
Similarly, another commenter cited surveys showing that only a small percentage of apprentices and females working in manufacturing trades were directed toward their career by a school counselor or an American Job Center. The commenter concluded that in the absence of systematic outreach, many women may miss out on the opportunities presented by apprenticeships in high-paying fields, and employers would lose out because they only would access a very incomplete talent pool.
A commenter criticized the Department's assertion in the NPRM that the current regulation “has not demonstrated clear benefits in terms of improved protections against unlawful discrimination for apprentices.” This commenter maintained that the outreach and affirmative action tools and mandates contained in part 30 have added value for program sponsors seeking new talent. The commenter said that 36.5 percent of States identify the “challenge of recruiting qualified applicants” as a barrier to apprenticeship expansion. The commenter added that firms have indicated that some of the best practices for meeting labor shortages include setting realistic goals for inclusion and diversity, regularly evaluating the status of those goals, and adjusting appropriately to meet them, arguing that these are all tenets of affirmative action plans. The commenter also provided examples of successful efforts to expand diversity in apprenticeships, including a program in Massachusetts where the proportion of women in construction apprenticeships grew by over 200 percent across a 5-year period thanks to partnerships among job training providers, firms, developers, community organizations, and local government. The commenter further asserted that affirmative action practices can be valuable to new apprenticeship industries, citing that 90 percent of hiring managers in information technologies consistently report difficulties in finding and hiring talent, and 83 percent report that this worker shortage is slowing company revenue growth.
Department Response:
After considering these comments, the Department remains convinced that the affirmative action requirements contained in the existing part 30 regulation effectively undermined genuine equality of opportunity for apprentices and candidates for apprenticeship, imposed excessive administrative burdens on program sponsors, and may effectively induce such program sponsors to engage in discriminatory and illegal employment practices. The existing part 30 regulation requires outreach initiatives and incentivizes hiring decisions based not upon the merits or qualifications of individual candidates, but rather upon a candidate's race, sex, and ethnicity. By abandoning this divisive and pernicious framework in this final rule, the Department is seeking to maximize apprenticeship opportunities for qualified individuals from all backgrounds, irrespective of a person's race, sex, ethnicity, national origin, disability status, or religion.
The Department also asserts that this final rule will ease the administrative burden on sponsors generally, and particularly on those smaller sponsors that have five or more apprentices but that may not possess the resources or personnel needed to conduct the complex workforce demographic analyses required under the current part 30. Similarly, the Department acknowledges one commenter's assertion that these requirements posed particular implementation challenges for non-joint group programs that do not exert close control over the hiring process for employers participating in the program. (See
Associated Builders & Contractors, Inc. Baltimore Metro.
(
printed page 70196)
Chapter
v.
O'Connor,
75 F. Supp. 2d 440, 441 n.3 (D. Md. 1999) (“[N]onjoint' refers to apprenticeship programs without any participation by labor interests.”)). The Department asserts that all programs will benefit from the removal of these burdensome affirmative action requirements and this final rule's emphasis on alignment with existing, congressionally enacted nondiscrimination law.
To the extent certain outreach efforts have been helpful to sponsors, sponsors may continue to engage in such efforts as part of a broad, nondiscriminatory outreach program to all qualified individuals (regardless of their race, sex, or ethnicity). Eliminating specific, inflexible targeted outreach requirements that go beyond complying with nondiscrimination law, and that focused on recruiting from only a limited, “underutilized” applicant pool, will reduce burdens on sponsors by enabling them to conduct outreach and recruitment in whatever lawful way they deem makes the most sense for their program. The Department is simply rescinding the one-size-fits-all approach that was imposed upon sponsors in the 2016 version of the part 30 rule. Additionally, eliminating the requirement for covered sponsors to maintain race-, sex-, and ethnicity-based affirmative action programs removes unlawful pressure on sponsors to recruit and hire apprentices from specific demographic groups, and also eliminates potential confusion and conflict with operating under various State law interpretations of nondiscrimination requirements.
See, e.g.,
Tex. Att'y Gen. Op. No. KP-0505 (2026) (re: “Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion” in Texas); Op. Att'y Gen. Fla.2026-02 (2026) (“Attorney General Opinion: State Laws Requiring Racial Discrimination are Unconstitutional”).
In summary, the Department encourages program sponsors to promote genuine equality of opportunity for all apprentices and applicants for apprenticeship in any lawful manner and, under this final rule, will hold accountable those programs found to have engaged in unlawful discrimination.
2. Utilization Analysis for Race, Sex, and Ethnicity (§ 30.5) and Establishment of Utilization Goals for Race, Sex, and Ethnicity (§ 30.6)
Existing § 30.5 requires those sponsors maintaining affirmative action programs to evaluate and analyze the demographic composition of their apprenticeship workforce by race, sex, and ethnicity, and to compare the representation of those groups in their workforce with the availability of those populations within the sponsor's relevant recruitment area. After conducting this analysis, if the sponsor determines that the representation of women, Hispanics or Latinos, or a specific racial minority group in their apprenticeship workforce is significantly lower than what would be reasonably anticipated, the sponsor is obligated to establish a utilization goal for the underrepresented group in accordance with § 30.6. Pursuant to § 30.6, that utilization goal must be “at least equal to the availability” of the underutilized group in the relevant recruitment area.
As previously discussed, the Department remains convinced that the foregoing part 30 provisions, which have required programs to analyze and to calibrate the racial, sex, and ethnic composition of their apprenticeship workforces, effectively conflict with the express Congressional prohibition on the mandatory conduct of such utilization analyses contained in section 703(j) of the Act, and also confront the sponsors of apprenticeship programs with insoluble practical and legal dilemmas. Despite the admonitory language at § 30.6(d)(2) of the part 30 regulation stipulating that the establishment of utilization goals “may not provide a sponsor with a justification to extend a preference to any individual, select an individual, or adversely affect an individual's status as an apprentice, on the basis of that person's race, sex, or ethnicity,” the regulation's compulsory imposition of such goal-setting upon certain sponsors may nevertheless induce those sponsors to engage in unlawful race- and sex-based apprenticeship hiring decisions in order to avoid the prospect of adverse administrative actions or sanctions by the Department (including program deregistration). As discussed earlier in the preamble, the contradictory and incoherent regulatory mandates in part 30 that simultaneously impose nondiscrimination and affirmative action requirements upon Registered Apprenticeship programs are plainly irreconcilable, contravene the fundamental policy objectives expressed in landmark Federal employment nondiscrimination statutes enacted by Congress (such as Title VII), and effectively induce sponsors to engage in impermissible group-based discrimination in the hiring and employment of apprentices based upon their race, sex, and ethnicity.
From a constitutional standpoint, the Supreme Court's recent decision in
SFFA
makes clear that race-based selection decisions would be subject to exacting scrutiny; a system of apprenticeship that codifies and incentivizes such improper preferences would likely not withstand legal scrutiny. The relevant inquiry is whether the regulatory scheme encourages, induces, or effectively requires employment decisions because of race.
See Anderson
v.
Martin,
375 U.S. 399, 402 (1964). Where such pressure exists, courts treat the regulatory framework itself as a racial classification subject to strict scrutiny.
Lutheran Church,
141 F.3d at 352-53;
MD/DC/DE Broadcasters Ass'n,
236 F.3d at 19-20. And that is precisely what the regulatory framework does. Similarly, while intermediate scrutiny is less demanding than strict scrutiny, the Department also concludes that the sex-based affirmative action requirements of the existing part 30 raise serious constitutional concerns and are unlikely to survive constitutional scrutiny.
Additionally, the Supreme Court's recent decisions in
Ames
v.
Ohio,
605 U.S. 303 (2025), and
Muldrow
v.
St. Louis,
601 U.S. 346 (2024) increase the likelihood that such affirmative action policies could be challenged by clarifying that the standard for proving disparate treatment under Title VII does not vary based on whether or not the plaintiff is a member of a majority group and that plaintiffs need only demonstrate that they suffered “some harm” in relation to an allegation of unlawful discrimination in employment (such as being adversely impacted by an employer's affirmative action policy).
After due consideration of the comments received concerning these part 30 provisions, as well as the administrative burden and legal vulnerability concerns identified above, the Department has decided to rescind, in this final rule, the foregoing part 30 affirmative action-related provisions that required sponsors to conduct a utilization analysis that takes into account the race, sex, and ethnicity of the apprentices enrolled in their programs, and to set utilization goals to address and rectify any group-based demographic imbalances revealed by such an analysis.
Comments:
Several commenters expressed support for the Department's proposal to rescind the requirement that sponsors with five or more apprentices conduct utilization analyses of their apprenticeship workforces. One commenter stated that their organization's members characterized these utilization analysis requirements as “confusing,” “very expensive,” and “onerous.” Another commenter stated that the Department's proposed revision of part 30 would appropriately
(
printed page 70197)
eliminate the mandate for program sponsors to adopt separate affirmative action programs in favor of aligning compliance requirements with existing Federal and State laws prohibiting discrimination. This commenter reasoned that by focusing on compliance with established nondiscrimination laws, the proposed revisions eliminate costly and duplicative requirements. The commenter added that sponsors would be able to apply existing equal employment frameworks—already in place for their broader workforce—to apprenticeship programs. The commenter concluded that this would lead to an increase in sponsorship opportunities.
However, several other commenters expressed their opposition to the Department's proposed rescission of the utilization analysis requirement. One commenter claimed that eliminating the utilization analyses would make it more difficult for sponsors to identify disparities in their workforces and determine if they are complying with nondiscrimination law. The commenter maintained that the § 30.5 analysis should be retained to help sponsors avoid litigation risks because it is a proactive version of the burden of proof required by the courts in disparate impact cases; the commenter conceded, however, that part 30's utilization analysis does not require sponsors to identify the cause of any disparity as would be required in a disparate impact case. Finally, this commenter opined that existing legal remedies under nondiscrimination law “are merely reactionary to incidents of discrimination” and therefore a framework of “proactive” affirmative action policies, such as those outlined in §§ 30.5 through 30.10 of the 2016 part 30 regulation, are necessary to sustain “the increased diversity of the apprenticeship workforce.”
A commenter stated that, in the NPRM, the Department misconstrued the utilization analysis provision, arguing that it is only intended to establish a benchmark to determine whether barriers to equal opportunity may exist, not to establish discrimination. The commenter added that a sponsor's determination that a utilization goal is required does not constitute a finding or admission of discrimination, and that the current regulation is carefully tailored to ensure that the availability analysis excludes nondiscriminatory factors that may explain differences between the two. The commenter further noted that sponsors are only required to establish goals when there is a “significant disparity” in a “Major Occupation” and that only 25 percent of programs are large enough to be subject to the utilization goal-setting requirement.
A group of commenters similarly stated that the Department's proposal to rescind the existing utilization goals for race, sex, and ethnicity is problematic because the proposed rule rests largely on speculation that the program provisions “may induce” or “incentivize” sponsors to engage in illegal race- or sex-based decision-making in selection decisions, even though making selection decisions based on race and sex violates existing regulations.
Department Response:
The Department agrees with the comment describing the utilization analyses as confusing and onerous. Indeed, in the 2016 final rule, the Department received some comments from sponsors expressing confusion over how to complete the analyses. In response, the Department committed to working “closely with each sponsor at its regular compliance reviews to develop and conduct an availability analysis and to set or reassess utilization goals for race, sex, and ethnicity, if necessary.”
81 FR 92057
(Dec. 19, 2016). The Department has determined that conducting these analyses has been overly time-consuming for both sponsors and Registration Agency staff and therefore it will now devote its limited resources to more effective solutions. Maintaining §§ 30.5 and 30.6 without devoting substantial staff support only would increase the burden on sponsors in completing the analyses—a burden that the Department concludes is no longer justified or supportable.
In response to the commenter expressing concern that sponsors will not have the ability to monitor their compliance with nondiscrimination laws in the absence of the current requirements of § 30.5, the Department echoes the point made by another commenter that the utilization analyses were never intended to serve as indicators of unlawful discrimination. In fact, § 30.6(b) made clear that “[a] sponsor's determination under § 30.5 that a utilization goal is required constitutes neither a finding nor an admission of discrimination.” The Department therefore rejects the commenter's contention that “[i]t is exactly the means to prove such a claim of discrimination that the Proposed Rule seeks to end.”
While the goal-setting process required by current § 30.6 and a claim of disparate-impact discrimination both rely on statistical disparities, the analyses are not identical and cannot be used interchangeably. A determination as to whether discrimination exists requires an examination of personnel activity data such as hires, promotions, or terminations, and an analysis of the affected selection process, qualification requirements, positions at issue and the reasons for the sponsor's actions. Thus, the requirement that sponsors then set a race-, ethnicity-, or sex-based utilization goal is unrelated to the detection of discrimination. Furthermore, the Department never looked to the utilization analyses in assessing whether a sponsor had engaged in unlawful discrimination or harassment. Finally, such quota-like measures are illegal under section 703(a) of Title VII.

39
]
However, sponsors are encouraged to continue taking any legal steps that they find helpful in assessing their programs to prevent unlawful discrimination. And, pursuant to proposed § 30.5, the Department will continue to have the authority to deregister programs for conducting illegal discrimination against apprentices, as determined by a relevant court or agency, and thereby safeguard the welfare of apprentices in Registered Apprenticeship programs. The Department maintains that, by eliminating confusing requirements regarding utilization analyses, Registered Apprenticeship will grow and create more opportunities for all workers.
In response to this commenter's concern that the remedies available to apprentices under current Federal civil rights statutes are essentially “reactive” and do not address workplace cultures that create “barriers to entry” for apprentices from certain groups, the Department again notes that these civil rights statutes provide apprentices with additional potential remedies, such as forms of individualized relief that are not available under part 30. As one commenter noted, only about 25 percent of sponsors are currently required to comply with the current affirmative action program provisions, thereby limiting any utility claimed by the commenters. Furthermore, sponsors may choose to employ lawful, race-neutral proactive means to remove barriers to entry in their programs, rather a compulsory, nonremedial regulatory regime of hiring preferences.

The Department completely rejects the notion advanced by these commenters that the rescission of the provisions of the 2016 version of the part 30 regulation that mandated that certain program sponsors adopt preferential utilization goals based upon the race, sex, and ethnicity of apprentices will hinder individuals from these groups “from accessing opportunities on an equal basis.” The Department reiterates that this final rule's removal of the pernicious, group-based demographic analyses and affirmative action mandates that were contained in the previous version of part 30 is intended to reaffirm that
all
employment discrimination against apprentices based upon their race, color, religion, sex, or national origin is illegal, and that the use of group-based preferences to promote “equity efforts” for select populations is legally questionable and completely contrary to the policy thrust of Title VII. The Department also challenges the assertion made by one of these commenters that the rescission of these utilization goals would result in “devastating consequences on women's participation in apprenticeships, particularly in higher paying fields where women are a small minority of apprentices.” The Department fundamentally rejects the abstract and invidious notion that group-based outcomes, rather than demonstrated individual merit, should influence or determine whether a person should be admitted to a Registered Apprenticeship program.
Costs Associated With Rescinding Utilization Analysis and Goals for Race, Sex, and Ethnicity
Comments:
A commenter opined that rescinding the utilization analysis requirements under § 30.5 would render the Department incapable of reviewing the rule's efficacy with respect to claims of harassment and discrimination. The commenter questioned how the Department would know if its claims of more effective relief for victims would come to fruition without tracking demographic data. The commenter stated that by failing to offer any solution to collect relevant demographic data or enforcement outcomes, the Department is skirting its responsibility to ensure the welfare of apprentices as mandated by Congress.
Department Response:
The Department disagrees with this commenter's assertion that the final rule's removal of the demographic data collection requirements contained in the 2016 version of the part 30 regulation will harm the welfare of apprentices. If an individual apprentice believes that they have been harmed by an employer's or program sponsor's discriminatory or harassing conduct, that person may still have recourse under Title VII and other Federal and State nondiscrimination laws to file a complaint with the EEOC or a State's FEPA. As noted earlier in this preamble,
29 CFR part 30
has never provided individualized, make-whole remedies to apprentices or applicants who have been injured by such illegal conduct, while Title VII and other employment nondiscrimination laws do provide such potential individual relief. Contrary to the commenter's assertion, the Department maintains that the removal of these burdensome and cumbersome demographic data collection requirements—requirements that were imposed on sponsors primarily to support the onerous group-based preferences and affirmative action mandates contained in the 2016 version of part 30—will serve to accelerate apprenticeship growth and will enhance the welfare of apprentices by promoting the hiring of apprentices solely on the basis of individual merit. The Department also wishes to note that, pursuant to a technical amendment to
29 CFR 29.7(l)
made by this final rule with respect to the required content of apprenticeship agreements, the Department will nevertheless retain the right to request demographic data regarding individual apprentices.
Alternative Approaches
Comments:
A commenter stated that while the revision and elimination of numerical goals and requirements may simplify the registration process for new and existing program sponsors, the Department should replace these eliminated regulations with a focus on and investment in activities that support veterans, individuals with disabilities, and discouraged workers in accessing Registered Apprenticeship programs.
This commenter argued these requirements help programs reach diverse candidates, especially as apprenticeships expand beyond traditionally White and male-dominated trades. The commenter suggested an alternative approach that would maintain workforce analysis requirements without specific targets, which would help modernize the apprenticeship system while ensuring diverse representation.
Department Response:
The Department notes that nothing in §§ 30.5 and 30.6 specifically addressed the employment of veterans or discouraged workers. Sponsors will remain free to engage in any lawful recruitment and retention efforts focused on these groups, particularly as targeted outreach to veterans and workers with disabilities does not raise the same legal concerns as doing so on the basis of race, ethnicity, or sex. And, as stated above, removing only the goals themselves, while still requiring a race-, ethnicity-, and sex-based utilization analysis would not fully address the Equal Protection concerns identified by the Department.
No alternative option would satisfy the Department's goals of aligning the regulations with recent court decisions regarding affirmative action if the regulation continued to improperly require that sponsors take race, sex, and ethnicity into account in evaluating their program's employment processes. Additionally, removing only the requirement to set goals themselves, while still requiring the collection of demographic data, the review of personnel processes, targeted outreach, and the invitation to identify as an individual with a disability would do very little to address the associated burden identified by several commenters.
3. Utilization Goals for Individuals With Disabilities (§ 30.7) and Invitation To Self-Identify as an Individual With a Disability (§ 30.11)
As emphasized throughout this final rule preamble, the Department contends that the central goal of a program
(
printed page 70199)
sponsor's hiring process should be to attract, admit, and retain those individuals—regardless of their group identity—who possess the right mix of the relevant skills and capabilities that are required for the successful completion of an apprenticeship program. Accordingly, ensuring that all qualified candidates, including people with disabilities, are eligible for consideration in the hiring and promotion process on an equal, nondiscriminatory basis is critically important to realizing this goal. Similarly, in keeping with the workplace protections for individuals with disabilities that were enacted by Congress in the ADA, the Department is committed to facilitating the hiring and retention of skilled and capable workers through the provision of effective job accommodation for apprentices and other employees with disabilities. While this final rule rescinds the burdensome and problematic regulatory mandates imposed on program sponsors by §§ 30.7 and 30.11 of existing part 30, the Department nevertheless continues to encourage program sponsors to establish supportive workplace policies and practices for individuals with disabilities. The voluntary implementation of such initiatives on behalf of these workers can be instrumental in advancing the broader goal of ensuring genuine equality of opportunity for all qualified individuals who seek to participate in the American workforce.
In the NPRM, the Department noted that the current regulation, at § 30.7, requires sponsors to conduct a utilization analysis of the participation of individuals with disabilities in their program, and establishes a specific utilization goal of 7% that sponsors must aim to achieve. Under the current regulation, if the share of apprentices with disabilities in a program are found to be below this threshold, sponsors are required to identify barriers to equal opportunity and to implement targeted measures to mitigate such barriers. The Department proposed eliminating this requirement in the NPRM, as well as the requirement that sponsors invite apprentices (or applicants for apprenticeship) to self-identify as having a disability. The Department maintained that these obligations were burdensome, and that sponsors faced practical and legal challenges in meeting these requirements.
The Department also noted in the NPRM that sponsors with 15 or more employees are already subject to title I of ADA, which affords important protections against discrimination to individuals with disabilities. The apprenticeship-specific nondiscrimination requirements in part 30, including the 7% utilization goal for sponsors, do not afford apprentices with meaningful access to remedies for alleged workplace discrimination. Instead, this goal requires sponsors to consider factors other than merit and qualifications in making decisions about outreach, recruitment, and hiring for their program. Therefore, the Department proposed eliminating the requirement to conduct a disability-focused utilization analysis and the regulation's specific 7% utilization goal, in line with the Department's broader objectives to emphasize merit-based hiring and expand employment and training opportunities for all American workers, including individuals with disabilities.
The Department also proposed rescinding § 30.11, which requires sponsors maintaining an affirmative action program to invite applicants and current apprentices to self-identify as an individual with a disability. In the NPRM, the Department asserted that this requirement creates confusion among sponsors and other apprenticeship stakeholders, and that the requirement has resulted in a high level of administrative burden for program sponsors. Additionally, the Department maintained that compliance with this requirement presents practical and legal challenges for program sponsors, who must protect apprentice confidentiality and privacy while simultaneously taking actions to meet a specific 7 percent utilization goal for individuals with disabilities. Sponsors' invitations to applicants and apprentices to disclose disabilities under § 30.11 constitute “inquiries” prohibited by section 102(d)(2)(A) and (d)(4)(A) of the ADA.

Accordingly, for the reasons discussed in the NPRM and in response to the comments summarized below, the Department is finalizing the rescission of these disability-related provisions in this final rule.

For example, one commenter referenced research that the commenter described as showing that employers of apprentices do not perceive the collection of demographic apprenticeship data as a major cost or inhibitor to the growth of apprenticeship programs. Another commenter asserted that if the requirement was onerous there would be limited voluntary compliance for sponsors with fewer than five apprentices—which the commenter said is not true. Department Response:
The Department agrees with the commenters expressing concerns over the administrative burden imposed on programs by the disability utilization analysis, as well as concerns with potential ADA conflicts resulting from the requirement to invite applicants and apprentices to identify as individuals with disabilities.
In response to commenters who discussed the benefits and value of collecting information on individuals with disabilities participation in workforce training programs and pursuing increased representation of such individuals in the workforce, the Department notes that nothing in this final rule prohibits sponsors from exercising their own judgment in making inquiries or proactive efforts to employ qualified individuals with disabilities, so long as any such actions are consistent with the ADA and its implementing regulations. With this final rule, sponsors will no longer be subject to the current part 30 regulation's mandates concerning the collection of information on individuals with disabilities, nor its requirements concerning the employment of individuals with disabilities.
In response to the commenter who suggested changing the nature of the inquiry to a “declaration,” the Department is not persuaded that such a recharacterization would eliminate the Department's concerns with improperly requesting disability information under the ADA, which were echoed by other commenters in response to the NPRM. In addition, the Department takes the position that such an adjustment would neither eliminate, nor meaningfully reduce, the administrative burden associated with storing responses to disability inquires in a secure and confidential manner. The Department also agrees with the commenter who suggested that the existing part 30 regulation specifies that the utilization goals should not be construed as rigid quotas.
[
42
]
However, the Department has determined that these utilization goal requirements, along with other affirmative program requirements in the existing regulation, have had the practical effect of inducing sponsors to make preferential hiring decisions based on demographic characteristics. Accordingly, the Department has decided to remove the legally questionable affirmative action requirements from the revised part 30 regulation.
The rescission of the disability utilization analysis within part 30 is consistent with the Department's decision to rescind the similar utilization analysis and goal as a form of required affirmative action under the implementing regulations for section 503 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973.
90 FR 28494
(July 1, 2025). While the utilization goal required by existing § 30.7 was not issued pursuant to section 503, the part 30 disability utilization goal was designed to mirror the one issued by OFCCP under section 503 and the reasons for removing both goals are related. In both cases, the Department contends that the analyses and goals are unnecessarily burdensome, rely on ambiguous statutory authority, create the possibility of conflicts with the ADA, and put pressure on sponsors to use hiring quotas despite regulatory prohibitions on doing so.
The Department recognizes that the disability goal and utilization analysis would not be subject to strict scrutiny review under equal protection principles in the same way that the race- and ethnicity-based utilization goals and Canalyses would be pursuant to
SFFA.
The Department did not rely on
SFFA
in proposing to rescind existing § 30.7. However, the regulatory mandate
(
printed page 70201)
that sponsors not treat the disability goal as a quota is inherently at odds with the expectation that sponsors undertake good faith efforts to attain a workforce that meets the 7 percent utilization goal. This tension creates confusion among sponsors regarding their obligations with respect to ensuring equal opportunity for individuals with disabilities.
The Department emphasizes that, while it is no longer requiring covered sponsors to conduct these utilization analyses, sponsors remain free to assess their programs and encourage the participation of qualified apprentices with disabilities in any lawful way. As is the case for Federal contractors under section 503, the Department encourages sponsors to continue supporting the employment and advancement of qualified apprentices with disabilities in ways that do not involve the setting of a numerical goal or that depend on the sponsor's knowledge of a particular applicant's or apprentice's disability status.

Legal Interpretation of ADA and Self-Identification
Comments:
A commenter stated that asking applicants to voluntarily disclose a disability is not a violation of the ADA's prohibition on disability-related pre-employment inquiries. This commenter opined that the affirmative action requirements in section 503 were in place when the ADA was passed in 1990, although the utilization goal would come later in regulations. The commenter added that implementing an affirmative action plan and reporting on its success required employers to know whether they are hiring individuals with disabilities but did not end either the prohibition on pre-employment inquiries or affirmative action for people with disabilities. The commenter also cited a 2018 EEOC declaration which stated that for more than 20 years it had been recognized that “the ADA permits affirmative action on behalf of individuals with disabilities, whether legally required or voluntarily undertaken,” and also reaffirmed enforcement guidance from 1995 on “Preemployment Disability-Related Questions and Medical Examinations Under the ADA,” which explained that employers may ask job applicants to voluntarily self-identify as individuals with disabilities for affirmative action purposes under certain conditions. Similarly, another commenter stated that the EEOC has consistently upheld voluntary self-disclosure of disability at the applicant stage as permissible under the ADA.
Another commenter noted that a 2013 letter from the EEOC legal counsel indicated that such inquiries are permissible under the ADA but argued that this letter should not be relied on by DOL. The commenter said that the letter is from a single attorney at the EEOC and does not represent the Commission, does not make a statutory argument, and its conclusion contradicts the best reading of the ADA. The commenter added that, even assuming the ADA is ambiguous, whatever deference the EEOC had to interpret ambiguous provisions of the ADA is gone following
Loper Bright Enterprises
v.
Raimondo,
which directs agencies and courts to determine the best reading of a statute.
Department Response:
The Department maintains that requiring covered sponsors to invite applicants and apprentices to self-identify as individuals with disabilities is in tension with the best reading of the ADA's text. With respect to job applicants, section 102(d)(2)(A) of the ADA states that an employer “shall not . . . make inquiries of a job applicant as to whether such applicant is an individual with a disability.”
[
44
]
But this inquiry is what § 30.11(a)(1) currently requires. (“A sponsor adopting an affirmative action program pursuant to § 30.4 must invite applicants for apprenticeship to inform the sponsor whether the applicant believes that he or she is an individual with a disability as defined in § 30.2.”) Although the disability inquiry requirement is framed as an “invitation” for applicants to “self-identify” disability status, this is a requirement imposed on the sponsor. And while congressional committee reports may have suggested that the ADA's ban on preemployment inquiries would not apply to data collected for certain affirmative action purposes,
see, e.g., Associated Builders & Contractors
v.
Shiu,
30 F.Supp.3d 25, 37-38 (D.D.C. 2014), legislative history cannot overcome the statute's plain meaning because “legislative history is not the law.”
Epic Sys. Corp.
v.
Lewis,
584 U.S. 497, 523 (2018). DOL must interpret the statute based on “what the statute means,” not “what the legislature meant.”
Id.
(quoting
Schwegmann Bros.
v.
Calvert Distillers Corp.,
341 U.S. 384, 397 (1951) (Jackson, J., concurring)). Therefore, legislative history cannot change what section 102(d)(2)(A) and (B) of the ADA commands: a covered entity “shall not” make preemployment “inquiries” as to an applicant's disability status, except in only a few situations expressly enumerated in the ADA.
45
See Milner
v.
Dep't of Navy,
562 U.S. 562, 574 (2011). (“Legislative history, for those who take it into account, is meant to clear up ambiguity, not create it.”).
With respect to current apprentices/employees, section 102(d)(4)(A) of the ADA states that an employer “shall not make inquiries of an employee as to whether such employee is an individual with a disability . . . unless such . . . inquiry is shown to be job-related and consistent with business necessity.”
[
46
]
Current § 30.11(c), which requires all covered sponsors to annually remind apprentices that they may voluntarily update their disability status, does not limit this requirement to situations where the sponsor determines that such an inquiry is job-related and consistent with business necessity. Current § 30.11 therefore requires sponsors to make disability inquiries that likely run afoul of the ADA and the rescission of this requirement ensures that part 30 does not compel conduct that the ADA either prohibits or permits only in limited circumstances not reflected in current § 30.11.
As some commenters noted, the EEOC has issued subregulatory guidance indicating that otherwise-prohibited disability-related inquiries are lawful when made in order to benefit individuals with disabilities. Most notably, this guidance has been captured in the 1995 Enforcement Guidance and in the 2013 letter from the EEOC's Office of Legal Counsel.
See
78 FR 58682
,
58691
(Sept. 24, 2013). Upon consideration, DOL concludes that this guidance is inconsistent with the best reading of the statute and will not defer to it.
The Department first notes that it agrees with the commenter regarding the reliability and authority of the 2013 EEOC Office of Legal Counsel Letter in that it does not reflect the views of the entire Commission but only those of single attorney. Second, the substance of the letter is not clearly in line with the statutory text of the ADA. Recent Supreme Court precedent reinforces the need to adhere to the statute's best
(
printed page 70202)
reading. In
Loper Bright Enterprises
v.
Raimondo,
603 U.S. 369 (2023), the Court emphasized that “`statutes . . . have a single, best meaning'” that is “`fixed at the time of enactment.'” 603 U.S. at 400 (quoting
Wisconsin Central Ltd.
v.
United States,
585 U.S. 274, 284 (2018)). Applying that principle here, the Department concludes that the best reading of section 102(d)(2)(A) of the ADA
[
47
]
is that employers may not make disability-related inquiries of job applicants prior to an offer of employment, regardless of the employer's intent or the framing of the question.
Although sponsors are required to keep disability disclosures confidential and not use them in employment decisions, confidentiality requirements do not eliminate the practical pressures or risk of distress that individuals may experience when presented with an employer-initiated request to disclose disability status. Additionally, sponsors have indicated confusion over how best to keep such data confidential while integrating their program data with RAPIDS. This practical confusion, along with the questionable legality of the invitation itself, places sponsors in a challenging position. Through this final rule, the Department aims to ease any confusion sponsors may have experienced resulting from the requirement to invite disability self-identification.
Alternative Approaches and Recommendations
Comments:
A commenter recommended that, while the revision and elimination of numerical goals and requirements may simplify the registration process for new and existing Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors, DOL should replace these eliminated regulations with a focus on and investment in activities that, among other groups, assist individuals with disabilities in accessing Registered Apprenticeship programs.
Department Response:
The Department is committed to the expansion of Registered Apprenticeship programs for all qualified workers and encourages the full participation of individuals with disabilities in those programs. At the same time, the Department contends that mandating the use of burdensome and prescriptive analyses that fail to respect the privacy of individuals with disabilities is not the best means of accomplishing these objectives. As discussed previously, the Department maintains various resources that can assist sponsors in making their Registered Apprenticeship programs more accessible to individuals with disabilities. For example, the Department's Office of Disability Employment Policy has created an Apprenticeship Toolkit, which is designed to provide information on a series of topical areas focused on Registered Apprenticeship and how it can be used to provide employment opportunities for people with disabilities. The Department encourages sponsors to take advantage of these, and other resources, to support apprentices with disabilities.
4. Targeted Outreach, Recruitment, and Retention (§ 30.8)
Existing § 30.8 mandates that sponsors who identify instances of underutilization engage in focused outreach, recruitment, and retention strategies designed to enhance the number of applications from, and improve the retention of, apprentices belonging to the targeted group(s) or individuals with disabilities, as applicable. However, given that these requirements involve race- and sex-based data that could impact final recruitment decisions, the Department has determined that they carry similar legal risks as those associated with the utilization goals based on race, sex, and ethnicity.
These regulatory requirements may exert pressure on sponsors to prioritize recruiting candidates from specific racial, sex-based, or ethnic backgrounds, potentially resulting in unequal treatment of individuals in different demographic categories. This pressure could lead sponsors to allocate their limited recruitment resources disproportionately to benefit certain minority groups.
MD/DC/DE Broadcasters Ass'n
v.
FCC,
236 F.3d 13, 15, 20-21 (D.C. Cir. 2001),
cert. denied,
534 U.S. 1113 (2002). Thus, for the same reasons discussed in § 30.5, the Department is rescinding these requirements.
Additionally, the Department's rescission of existing §§ 30.5 and 30.7 removes the circumstances under which findings to engage in such activities might occur. Accordingly, the “targeted” activities in current § 30.8 are no longer required and the Department will proceed with rescission.

In contrast, several commenters opposed rescinding outreach requirements. Another commenter asserted that removing the regulatory basis for sponsors' existing outreach, recruitment and retention programs would limit the pool of apprentices available for selection. Another commenter agreed and stated growth is needed in the construction industry (which has faced an ever-increasing shortage since the mid-2000s) and that part 30's approach aligns with the measures in President Trump's plan for “engaging and supporting the disconnected workforce.” Several commenters stated that requiring program sponsors to consider the diversity of their apprentices in their recruitment process positively impacts Registered Apprenticeship expansion to underrepresented groups in their industry, and described successful programs that have implemented recruitment and outreach goals, especially within the construction industry. For example, one commenter said there has been a notable uptick in Registered Apprenticeship programs conducting affirmative outreach to populations underrepresented in the construction trades, and cited that in the last 4 years, there have been two new direct-entry pathways formally created in the Chicago area between local trade union apprenticeship programs and local pre-apprenticeship programs. The commenter also described a July 2024 roundtable hosted by Chicago Women in Trades with the EEOC Vice Chair where industry leaders shared the efforts they were making through the framework of
29 CFR parts 29
and
30

Similarly, a commenter expressed that several Registered Apprenticeship programs have identified recruitment strategies targeting certain protected classes which have proved fruitful in building and maintaining robust
(

The commenter requested guidance regarding the extent to which such recruitment strategies are not compliant and specific examples of types of recruitment strategies that would not be deemed compliant under the proposed rule. Another commenter asserted that the part 30 regulation gives non-White and nonmale individuals a chance to enroll in apprenticeship without them having to “know someone on the inside,” or other historical practices that have resulted in denied equal opportunities for women and people of color.
A commenter stated that removing outreach requirements risks employers misinterpreting this as a reason to reduce deliberate recruitment of veterans, who often face barriers transitioning to civilian careers, and recommended that DOL explicitly clarify that nothing in the rule prevents or discourages sponsors from prioritizing veteran recruitment through engagement with veteran-serving organizations and workforce partners.
Department Response:
The Department appreciates the comments discussing the recruitment challenges faced by sponsors. The Department maintains that this final rule gives sponsors more flexibility to lawfully recruit apprentices. By rescinding the overly prescriptive provisions in existing § 30.8, sponsors will no longer be required to expend resources on recruitment and retention activities that may not have benefited their programs. To the extent sponsors have found any partnerships or recruitment strategies to be useful, sponsors remain free to continue using those methods on a nondiscriminatory basis. The Department defers to the respective EEO enforcement agencies in determining whether specific recruitment methods are consistent with applicable nondiscrimination laws. Ultimately, the Department is confident that the removal of the onerous requirements under the existing part 30 regulation will spur expansion of the National Apprenticeship System generally, creating more opportunities for women, Americans of color, and all Americans across all demographic groups to access the training model.
In response to those commenters raising concerns about recruitment targeted towards veterans, the Department notes that targeted outreach on this basis does not raise the same constitutional concerns as outreach targeted to members of a specific race or sex. Sponsors are encouraged to continue engaging in efforts to recruit veterans. Existing § 30.8 did not contain any requirements specific to the recruitment of veterans; the rescission of this section, therefore, will not impact the ability of sponsors to continue engaging in such efforts. The same is true of other recruitment strategies relying on non-protected bases, such as geography and income status. The Department supports programs that seek to reach all potential applicants, and the rescission of existing § 30.8 enables sponsors to conduct outreach and recruitment in line with their business needs and in a lawful manner.

Impact on Women and Other Groups
Comments:
A commenter stated that the Department's proposed changes to targeted outreach requirements would threaten participation for women in apprenticeships, particularly in high-paying fields where women are a small minority of apprentices. The commenter described research they said shows apprentices are often provided with limited information on career opportunities, particularly among women. (

Department Response:
As stated elsewhere in this preamble, a fundamental purpose of this final rule is to rescind all provisions of the part 30 regulation that aimed to impose legally problematic “equitable” outcomes on the demographic composition of apprenticeship programs through a systematic regime of group-based preferences that are tied to an individual's race, sex, or ethnicity. Accordingly, any arguments advanced by commenters to justify retaining the targeted recruitment provisions found at existing § 30.8 and that are grounded upon the general notion of achieving or maintaining greater demographic “balance” or “diversity” in a sponsor's apprenticeship workforce through targeted recruitment efforts are contrary to the fundamental principle of hiring individuals solely on the basis of merit and without considering demographic characteristics. Additionally, nothing in the final rule precludes individual sponsors from voluntarily conducting lawful outreach or recruitment activities to attract qualified apprenticeship candidates from all backgrounds or from engaging in hiring practices they believe to be in their business interest, provided that such activities and practices conform with applicable nondiscrimination laws.
Reliance Interests and Existing Investments in Outreach Programs
Comments:
A commenter stated that the rescission of outreach and recruitment requirements would strongly impact the reliance interest of their training network. The commenter stated that existing § 30.8 currently requires programs that identify underutilization to engage in neutral outreach activities (that are not race- or sex-based) but that are designed to reach underrepresented communities. The commenter stated that, relying upon these part 30 regulatory provisions, sponsors affiliated with the commenter's organization have invested significant funds and human resources to build a variety of strategies and programs that support growth. The commenter stated that the rescission of these regulations would seriously undermine these programs and imperil the years of investments which have gone into their creation, particularly by the labor-management organizations that are responsible for JATCs. The commenter also asserted that outreach and recruitment activities under § 30.8 are legal under Federal and State nondiscrimination laws.
Another commenter stated that the Department's proposed rescission of § 30.8 would adversely impact the significant reliance interests of Registered Apprenticeship programs that have adapted outreach and recruitment to comply with the part 30 regulation. The commenter stated that, under the regulation, sponsors have been required to develop a list of recruitment sources that generate referrals of women, minorities, and persons with disabilities, with contact information for each source, and to notify these sources in advance of any apprenticeship opportunities. The commenter continued that the broad rescission of this provision would disrupt past success by JATCs in developing recruitment sources and partnerships particularly in blue collar professions due to vocational training and careers becoming less popular. The commenter asserted that its recruitment efforts in schools, community colleges, and community-based organizations have been successful, but expressed concern that, under the Department's proposal, such efforts would cause a Registered Apprenticeship program to risk deregistration.
Department Response:
The part 30 regulation mandated that sponsors subject to utilization goals under § 30.8 of that regulation conduct “targeted outreach, recruitment, and retention activities that are likely to generate an increase in applications for apprenticeship and improve retention of apprentices” from “underutilized groups” based upon race, sex, and ethnicity. The Department has determined that preferential treatment in the recruitment of apprentices is inherently discriminatory in nature, and thus legally suspect. The Department takes the position that the deliberate targeting of individuals from “underutilized” groups in apprenticeship outreach and recruitment based upon shared characteristics of race, sex, or ethnicity necessarily disadvantages the recruitment of individuals who do not belong to such groups.
In rescinding this preferential and discriminatory recruitment provision, the Department reaffirms the view that individuals from all backgrounds—regardless of their race, ethnicity, sex, religion, or national origin—must be afforded the opportunity to compete on an equal, nondiscriminatory basis for admission into a Registered Apprenticeship program. The Department takes the position that every apprentice should be recruited without regard to their race, sex, or ethnicity, and that every apprentice should be hired or retained by a program sponsor on the basis of their qualifications and performance alone.
While the Department acknowledges that certain program sponsors have made significant investments to satisfy the requirements that were contained in § 30.8 of the 2016 regulation, the Department nevertheless takes the position that a sponsor's recruitment activities must be nondiscriminatory in their operation. Accordingly, in accordance with this final rule and governing nondiscrimination law, program sponsors that have made significant investments in apprenticeship recruitment and outreach activities are free to continue such initiatives, provided that these efforts are designed to attract and retain qualified candidates from all backgrounds, and do not constitute preferential, discriminatory conduct based upon an individual's race, sex, and ethnicity.
Some commenters implicitly acknowledged the burden associated with the part 30 regulation's outreach and recruitment requirements in stating they have invested significant resources into complying with the existing § 30.8. By rescinding these provisions, the Department is reducing the administrative and regulatory burden placed on sponsors to comply with part 30 requirements. Finally, because the Department is not infringing on sponsors' ability to voluntarily maintain legally compliant outreach activities, the Department maintains that removing part 30 requirements will not adversely impact sponsors' reliance interests associated with part 30 regulatory requirements that are being rescinded with this final rule.

The Department has concluded that this requirement is both confusing and burdensome, as sponsors are already subject to Federal and State nondiscrimination laws and have established procedures to maintain compliance, rendering this additional regulatory obligation unnecessary.
Moreover, the Department expressed the view in the preamble to the NPRM that eliminating this requirement would
(
printed page 70205)
enable sponsors to explore innovative strategies, reduce redundancy in compliance efforts, and align with the Administration's commitment to promoting efficiency and effectiveness in apprenticeship programs. The Department also opined that rescinding this mandate would allow sponsors to pursue innovative approaches, reduce duplication, and align with the Administration's stated policy to “significantly reduce the private expenditures required to comply with Federal regulations to secure America's economic prosperity . . .” as established by
E.O. 14192
, Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation.
The Department did not receive public comments specifically related to its proposed rescission of § 30.9. Therefore, for the reasons discussed in the NPRM and reiterated in this final rule, the Department is finalizing the rescission of this provision.
C. Rescission of the Anti-Harassment Training Requirement and the Provision Relating to Retaliation Against Apprentices
In the NPRM, the Department proposed rescinding the existing regulatory mandate contained in § 30.3(b)(4), which requires all Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors to conduct anti-harassment training. The Department also proposed rescinding existing § 30.17, which prohibits intimidation, retaliation, discrimination, and coercion against apprentices for filing a complaint, opposing a prohibited practice, assisting investigations, or exercising rights or privileges provided under part 30. The Department proposed eliminating these provisions in the NPRM to remove unnecessary administrative burdens or duplicative regulatory requirements on program sponsors, and to align the content of part 30 with governing Federal nondiscrimination laws prohibiting harassment in the workplace. After consideration of the comments received concerning the proposed rescission of these regulatory provisions, which are summarized and addressed below, the Department has determined to finalize these proposed changes in this final rule.
As a general matter, the Department has consistently maintained that harassing conduct in the workplace is plainly unacceptable. Depending on the facts, the harassment of an apprentice on the basis of their race, sex, or other protected characteristics may give rise to a hostile work environment allegation under Title VII of the Act or other applicable employment nondiscrimination laws, a claim which may be appropriate for further investigation by the EEOC or a State FEPA. From a labor standards perspective, the Department recognizes that the prevalence of such conduct in the workplace, including in Registered Apprenticeship programs, could undermine the dignity of individual employees and diminish worker productivity and morale.
Accordingly, while this final rule removes the overbroad and administratively burdensome requirement that all Registered Apprenticeship programs, regardless of their size, must conduct comprehensive anti-harassment training for those individuals connected with the program, the Department does not seek to discourage sponsors from voluntarily adopting lawful strategies and measures that are carefully tailored to minimize the occurrence or mitigate the impact of such impermissible conduct in their respective programs. However, the Department cautions sponsors that, to avoid giving rise to potential hostile work environment claims under Title VII or other nondiscrimination laws, any anti-harassment strategies or measures that are voluntarily instituted by a program must avoid unlawfully stereotyping or demeaning any group of employees or apprentices based upon their sex, race, or other protected characteristics.
Comments:
One commenter expressed support for rescinding the part 30 anti-harassment training requirements because it would provide regulatory relief to employers while preserving nondiscrimination protections. However, another commenter opposed these rescissions, asserting that the removal of the anti-harassment training requirements would remove essential apprentice safeguards, would undermine the standard and value of Registered Apprenticeship, and would likely worsen the work environment for many apprentices, particularly those who are in occupations where they are the minority of workers. Several commenters also cited data purporting to demonstrate that the compulsory provision of anti-harassment training by sponsors has resulted in tangible benefits that have outweighed the costs of these trainings, such as higher apprenticeship completion rates, reduced levels of harassment in the workplace, and a lower risk of potential sponsor liability.
Several commenters also maintained that the anti-harassment training requirement contained in the existing part 30 remains necessary because of the ongoing prevalence of sex- and race-based harassment, intimidation, bullying, and retaliation, both generally and within the construction trades, and particularly against women. For example, one commenter cited a report stating that the majority of apprentices who failed to complete their programs identified harassment and discrimination as the reason they resigned from their apprenticeship or as one of the biggest challenges they faced during their apprenticeship, and that more than half of the apprentices who left or seriously considered leaving the trades cited harassment or lack of respect as the reason. Another commenter stated that 57.9 percent of tradeswomen who made the decision to speak up about discrimination or harassment to someone in authority felt their concerns were not addressed satisfactorily. Other commenters cited other surveys, research, and apprentice testimony as well to illustrate the prevalence of harassment.
Several commenters asserted that, in contrast to the data and research they provided purporting to show the need for retaining the compulsory anti-harassment training provisions of part 30, the Department did not offer any compelling rationales in the NPRM to support its proposed removal of the anti-harassment training requirement. One commenter asserted that, in the preamble to the proposed rule, the Department had argued that the anti-sexual harassment training regulations in part 30 conflicted with merit principles, and that the only legal standard cited for this proposition was the
SFFA
decision, which did not address the issue. The commenter stated that the proposed rule's suggestion that anti-harassment training is potentially unlawful is unfounded and likely to have a chilling effect on Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors. This commenter stated that they were not aware of an instance in which a court held that a training aimed at preventing sexual harassment was unlawful, and that numerous courts have upheld the lawfulness of trainings to encourage diversity and respect. Lastly, the commenter suggested there are other ways to reduce the burdens related to the mandatory provision of anti-harassment training without eliminating the requirement.
One commenter stated that pointing to Title VII as adequate protection for apprentices from discrimination and harassment is not accurate, considering the special contexts of the apprenticeship model and the limitations of an enforcement mechanism almost solely dependent on worker complaints. Similarly, another commenter urged the Department to
(
printed page 70206)
retain all provisions expressly stipulating that harassment will not be tolerated, such as the anti-intimidation and anti-retaliation provisions; this commenter maintained that removing these regulatory provisions would deprive apprentices of a viable means of redress for intimidation and retaliation.
A commenter recommended that, rather than eliminating the anti-harassment training requirement, the Department should instead require stronger diversity training for employers and mentors, covering topics including but not limited to cultural competency, inclusivity, bias awareness, and nondiscrimination law. Another commenter added that the Department should continue to provide free online trainings.
Several commenters also expressed opposition to the proposed rescission of the regulatory prohibition on intimidation and retaliation found at § 30.17, contending that the removal of this provision would reduce awareness of such protections, create delays in the resolution of complaints, and create barriers for apprentices to assert their rights if they are experiencing intimidation or retaliation. One commenter urged the Department not to rescind this provision because it would burden youth apprentices with navigating complex Federal court systems. Some commenters also stated that the elimination of this provision could discourage apprentices from speaking up about discrimination, unsafe, or unfair practices and may result in higher attrition and lower completion rates among the most vulnerable apprentices. A commenter expressed particular concern about the proposed change in combination with the other changes that require Registration Agencies to await final determinations of discrimination, reasoning that apprentices who are retaliated against for having witnessed discrimination would have to undergo lengthy processes before receiving any remedy.
Department Response:
The Department agrees with those commenters who asserted that the rescission of these regulatory provisions would remove burdensome or duplicative mandates from part 30, thereby providing meaningful regulatory relief to program sponsors. Importantly, the Department notes that, by dispensing with such mandates, the final rule will enable sponsors to align their compliance obligations with the requirements of applicable nondiscrimination laws and protections with which they may be most familiar.
While the Department acknowledges the existence of reports that illustrate the harmful effects of workplace harassment on apprentice retention, the Department also notes the absence of data demonstrating the efficacy of compulsory anti-harassment training in counteracting such outcomes. As such, it disagrees with the conclusion reached by some commenters that the rescission of the existing part 30 training requirement removes an integral tool for protecting apprentices from harassing conduct. Rather, the Department maintains that existing legal protections against harassment or retaliation that are afforded under existing Federal and State nondiscrimination laws are sufficiently robust.
Title VII prohibits workplace harassment, which may occur when an employee is subjected to unwelcome remarks or conduct based on protected characteristics. As noted earlier, harassment based on a protected characteristic is illegal when it results in an adverse change to a term, condition, or privilege of employment,
Muldrow
v.
City of St. Louis,
144 S. Ct. 967 (2024), or it is so frequent or severe that a reasonable person would consider it intimidating, hostile, or abusive.
See
Title VII of the Act, section 703(a)(1).
[
48
]
Title VII also prohibits retaliation by an employer because an individual has engaged in protected activity under the statute.
Id.
at section 704.
[
49
]
Because of the foregoing Title VII prohibitions against harassment and retaliation, which are grounded in the language of the statute and elaborated under subsequent case law, the Department considers the existing regulatory provision at § 30.3(b)(4) mandating the provision of anti-harassment training by all Registered Apprenticeship programs to be unduly burdensome, and the existing regulatory provision at § 30.17 prohibiting retaliation for engaging in a protected activity to be largely redundant of existing Federal protections and therefore unnecessary. Moreover, under the foregoing Title VII provisions, individual apprentices who allege that they have been subjected to such impermissible employer conduct or work environments may file a complaint with, and request relief from, the EEOC or a State FEPA—and a final agency or court determination that a program sponsor has engaged in such behavior could potentially result in the Department's deregistration of that program. Given these existing protections under nondiscrimination law, the removal of these burdensome or duplicative requirements from part 30 aligns with
E.O. 14278
's mandate that the Department seek to expand Registered Apprenticeship and improve efficiency.
The Department does not dispute that anti-harassment training may be beneficial in some workplaces. Rather, the Department has concluded that the decision whether, how, and how often to provide such training should be left to sponsors rather than prescribed through a uniform Federal apprenticeship-specific mandate. The Department's decision to rescind the mandatory anti-harassment training requirement should not be construed as prohibiting such training. Sponsors remain free to provide anti-harassment training, establish workplace-conduct policies, and undertake other measures they determine are appropriate for their workplaces and apprenticeship programs. The final rule merely eliminates the Federal regulatory mandate that all program sponsors conduct such training regardless of their size, circumstances, and need for such training. Some sponsors may find anti-harassment training beneficial and may voluntarily choose to provide such training. The Department's conclusion is simply that Federal law does not require a separate apprenticeship-specific mandate in light of existing statutory protections against harassment and retaliation.
D. Rescission of Apprenticeship Selection Procedure Requirements
Under the NPRM, the Department suggested rescinding § 30.10, which outlined the permissible methods for sponsors to select apprentices. This provision allowed sponsors to utilize any selection method or combination of methods, so long as those methods adhered to the criteria established in the regulation.
