The Department concluded that these provisions were unnecessary, as they either duplicated the prohibitions against discrimination in selection and related employment practices already established under Title VII or imposed additional regulatory burdens on sponsors beyond those mandated by Title VII.
For the reasons discussed in the NPRM and in response to comments discussed below, the Department has determined to finalize the rescission of this regulatory provision as originally proposed.
Comments:
Several commenters opposed rescinding the apprenticeship selection procedure requirement. For example, one commenter opposed the rescission because it enables
(
printed page 70207)
Registration Agencies to know the minimum requirements for entry into a Registered Apprenticeship program, thus helping to ensure nondiscrimination in such a program. Several commenters also said that the apprenticeship selection procedure recruitment was intended to expand access and representation in apprenticeship programs. These commenter suggested retaining this requirement is important for building pipelines for individuals into the system and to ensure the apprenticeship system is accessible to all workers. One commenter stated that this apprenticeship selection requirement helps support the success of quality pre-apprenticeship and apprenticeship readiness programs in their State, as sponsors may specify in their selection procedures that completers of these preparatory programs can receive advanced standing, direct interviews, or direct entry into their Registered Apprenticeship program.
However, another commenter disagreed and supported the rescission because they said that the current apprentice selection procedure requirement is burdensome and complicates the process to recruit apprentices, particularly for industries facing shortages like construction.
Department Response:
In response to these comments, the Department takes the position that the inclusion of a sponsor's procedures for the selection of apprentices in the program's standards of apprenticeship (as was required in § 30.10(b)(1) of the 2016 part 30 regulation and in § 29.5(b)(21) of the 2008 part 29 regulation) was unnecessary and unduly burdensome, and that the rescission of this requirement in this final rule is therefore appropriate.
Requiring sponsors to include selection procedures in their apprenticeship standards is not necessary to ensure compliance with applicable nondiscrimination laws or to safeguard apprentice welfare. Questions concerning the legality of selection practices are appropriately addressed under generally applicable Federal and State nondiscrimination laws and by the agencies charged with enforcing those laws. Accordingly, the Department concludes that mandatory inclusion of selection procedures in apprenticeship standards is not necessary to ensure equal opportunity within Registered Apprenticeship programs. Sponsors remain free to include selection procedures in their standards or other program materials if they determine that doing so promotes transparency, consistency, or effective program administration.
The Department also reiterates that § 30.10(b)(1) of the part 30 regulation imposed obligations on program sponsors beyond those mandated under Title VII by requiring compliance with the Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures (UGESP), which provides discretionary guidance to the EEOC and employers regarding validation of selection procedures rather than binding substantive standards.
See
29 CFR 1607.1
. Accordingly, the rescission of that regulatory provision was appropriate in order to align part 30 with the scope of Title VII's requirements and to reduce regulatory burden upon program sponsors. Furthermore, the Department has proposed in a separate rulemaking to rescind its codification of UGESP at
41 CFR part 60-3
as applied to covered contractors because of the revocation of
E.O. 11246
, which provided the underlying authority for that rule. Finally, the Department of Justice's Office of Legal Counsel recently issued an opinion concluding that the EEOC's existing interpretations of the disparate impact provisions in Title VII, including as reflected in UGESP, “embrace an unconstitutional reading of Title VII.”
See Constitutionality of Disparate-Impact Liability Under Title VII,
50 Op. O.L.C. __, at *2 (June 9, 2026) (“Disparate-Impact Liability”).
Similarly, the requirements contained in § 30.10(b)(3) of the part 30 regulation were redundant of the obligations already imposed upon certain program sponsors by the ADA and the EEOC's implementing regulations at
29 CFR part 1630
. However, the Department notes that nothing in this final rule precludes program sponsors from voluntarily including selection procedures in their standards. This rescission simply removes a description of the program's selection procedures as a mandatory requirement. Overall, the Department maintains that the rescission of § 30.10 of the existing part 30 regulation in this final rule will significantly reduce compliance burdens on program sponsors, thereby facilitating the accelerated establishment and expansion of Registered Apprenticeship programs, particularly in those sectors and occupations that are currently facing acute labor shortages.
In response to one commenter, the Department is clarifying that nothing in this final rule prohibits sponsors from providing advanced standing, direct interviews or direct entry into their Registered Apprenticeship program for individuals that complete a pre-apprenticeship or other preparatory program. Sponsors should record their policy for granting advanced standing to preparatory program completers and must ensure this policy allows all applicants to be equally granted such standing as required by
29 CFR 29.5(b)(12)
.
E. Rescission of Sponsor Recordkeeping Requirements
The Department proposed to rescind § 30.12, which imposed certain recordkeeping requirements on program sponsors.
Comments:
A commenter expressed concern that by eliminating recordkeeping requirements, data from sponsors about the availability of apprenticeship opportunities across demographic categories would become inconsistent and impossible to assess, significantly weakening the effectiveness of
29 CFR part 30
. However, another commenter stated that it would rescind burdensome recordkeeping requirements including the obligation of retaining detailed demographic information about each apprentice and applicant for multiple years.
Department Response:
The Department disagrees with commenters who suggest that the rescission of § 30.12 will prevent meaningful oversight. As discussed elsewhere in this preamble, the Department does not view the assessment of demographic proportionality as an appropriate purpose of part 30. Rather, the purpose of part 30 is to prohibit unlawful discrimination and ensure that apprenticeship opportunities are made available on an equal basis to all individuals. Therefore, the continued maintenance of extensive sponsor-level demographic records is not necessary to safeguard apprentice welfare or enforce applicable nondiscrimination laws. In the NPRM, the Department clarified that apprenticeship agreements must still include “a request for demographic data about the apprentice.” The elimination of sponsors' recordkeeping obligations for part 30 requirements does not eliminate part 29's requirements to collect and maintain demographic data on apprentices through the apprenticeship agreement requirements at
29 CFR 29.7(l)
and recordkeeping requirements at
29 CFR 29.5(b)(23)
.
VI. Section-by-Section Analysis—Revised Part 30 Under the Final Rule
A. Section 30.1—Purpose and Applicability
The proposed introductory “Purpose and Applicability” section would have significantly updated and condensed
(
printed page 70208)
the previous “Purpose, applicability, and relationship to other laws” provision in part 30. In alignment with the policy approach described above, proposed § 30.1 eliminated references to affirmative action and removed redundant language concerning protected bases and complaint processes, which are addressed elsewhere in the regulation.
Proposed § 30.1 of this final rule explicitly stated that the part 30 regulation establishes a uniform Federal standard that prohibits unlawful discrimination against apprentices and applicants in Registered Apprenticeship programs. It also reaffirmed that these nondiscrimination requirements apply to program sponsors and must be enforced by SAAs. Furthermore, it clarified the scope of compliance reviews, compliance assistance, and enforcement actions to be conducted by the Registration Agency. For the reasons discussed in the NPRM and in response to comments discussed below, the Department is finalizing this provision as proposed.
Comments:
A commenter asked if the Department considered applying the proposed changes only to employers greater than a certain size (
e.g.,
500 or more employees).
Department Response:
As stated in the final regulatory language at § 30.1, this final rule creates a uniform, non-burdensome Federal standard for all Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors to follow applicable Federal and State nondiscrimination laws. The Department considered applying the changes to the part 30 regulation only to employers greater than a certain size, but it determined that doing so would not serve the interest of establishing a uniform rule. The Department has determined that uniformity promotes greater clarity for Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors on their obligation to prevent and address illegal discrimination against apprentices, as well as part 30's applicability to all programs.
B. Section 30.2—Definitions
Under the NPRM, the Department proposed to eliminate all definitions in the current part 30 regulation and to adopt by reference the applicable existing definitions from the labor standards of apprenticeship regulation at
29 CFR part 29
. In the NPRM, the Department maintained that the definitions found in existing § 30.2 are either duplicative of those in
29 CFR 29.2
or would no longer be relevant due to the significant revisions proposed to the substantive provisions of part 30.
The Department asserts that consolidating all apprenticeship-related definitions within the existing regulatory framework of
29 CFR part 29
will reduce administrative burdens on sponsors of Registered Apprenticeship programs and other stakeholders by providing a single point of reference for definitions within the Federal apprenticeship regulations. For the reasons discussed in the NPRM and in response to comments discussed below, the Department is finalizing the provision as proposed.
Comments:
A commenter agreed with the proposed revision to remove definitions in
29 CFR 30.2
and adopt by reference the existing definitions found in
29 CFR 29.2
, stating that the definitions in both parts should be aligned and that doing so would “reduce confusion for the regulated community” and simplify compliance for sponsors and employers.
This commenter recommended retaining certain definitions proposed for removal, such as “pre-apprenticeship program,” which is not currently defined in
29 CFR 29.2
. The commenter opposed removing this as a defined term in the apprenticeship regulations, asserting that defining key terms provides clarity for apprenticeship stakeholders. Alternatively, if the Department does not retain the definition in regulation, the commenter recommended that the Department update Training and Employment Notice No. 23-23 to align with recent E.O.s, or with the definition of “pre-apprenticeship program” under the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA) regulations at
20 CFR 681.480
. The commenter also urged the Department to preserve the definition of “selection procedure” in a revised
29 CFR 29.2
to ensure Registration Agencies understand program entry requirements and to help prevent discrimination. Lastly, the commenter recommended preserving definitions for “race,” “ethnicity,” and “disability,” either in revised § 29.2 or by citing other Federal definitions, to facilitate effective data collection.
Department Response:
The Department appreciates the comments regarding the consolidation of definitions within part 29 as proposed by the NPRM. Regarding a commenter's concerns about eliminating the definition for “pre-apprenticeship,” the Department notes that pre-apprenticeship programs are not registered by the Department pursuant to the NAA. As such, the Department does not regulate such programs. The Department maintains that this rulemaking updating part 30 requirements is not an appropriate vehicle for establishing any regulatory definitions or other regulations for pre-apprenticeship programs. The Department agrees with the commenter's suggestion to align any future guidance on pre-apprenticeship with the Administration's E.O.'s, as well as the definition for pre-apprenticeship from the WIOA regulation at
20 CFR 681.480
, to support alignment among workforce development programs overseen by the Department.
In response to comments on the removal of the definition of “selection procedures,” the Department asserts that a definition of this term is not necessary in this final rule due to the substantial revisions to part 30 and the conforming edits to
29 CFR 29.5(b)(21)
, which remove all references to the term “selection procedure” from parts 29 and 30. Furthermore, the Department notes that the definition of “selection procedure” was drawn from the UGESP. As noted earlier in the preamble, the Department has proposed in a separate rulemaking to rescind its codification of UGESP at
41 CFR part 60-3
.
Regarding maintaining definitions for race, ethnicity, and disability, the final rule's conforming edits to existing § 29.7(l) eliminate the requirement that a sponsor must specifically request information from apprentices on their race, sex, ethnicity, and disability status. Instead, under this final rule, sponsors only are required to include “a request for demographic data about the apprentice” within apprenticeship agreements. Accordingly, the Department has determined it is not necessary to include a regulatory definition for these terms to assist with data collection.
C. Section 30.3—Nondiscrimination Standards Applicable to All Sponsors
Under the NPRM, the Department proposed obligating all sponsors of a Registered Apprenticeship program to comply with all applicable Federal and State laws and regulations prohibiting illegal discrimination on the basis of race, color, religion, national origin, sex, age (40 or older), genetic information, or disability. The Department explained in the NPRM that this list of protected bases is fully consistent with the content and scope of currently applicable Federal civil rights statutes, including Title VII of the Act and its subsequent amendments, the ADEA, as amended, the ADA, as amended, and the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008.
The proposed regulatory provision additionally specified that non-compliance by a Registered
(
printed page 70209)
Apprenticeship program sponsor with relevant Federal and State nondiscrimination laws may lead to enforcement actions or deregistration proceedings by a Registration Agency, in accordance with § 30.5 of the proposed rule, if the non-compliance pertains to illegal discrimination against an apprentice or an apprenticeship applicant regarding any aspect of employment benefits, terms, or conditions related to the apprenticeship. The Department's intent is to confer the benefits of registration upon those sponsors that conduct their programs in a manner consistent with applicable Federal and State nondiscrimination laws. Further, the Department has an interest in carrying out the Administration's directive to undertake deregulatory actions where existing regulations impose unnecessary and burdensome requirements on businesses.
Accordingly, for the reasons discussed in the NPRM and in response to comments discussed below, the Department is finalizing the provision as proposed.
1. General Comments on the Proposed Nondiscrimination Standards Provision
Comments:
A couple of commenters expressed support for revising § 30.3 to direct Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors to comply with all applicable Federal and State laws and regulations prohibiting illegal discrimination to eliminate unnecessarily complex requirements.
However, other commenters opposing the change stated that the proposed rule would replace § 30.3's robust protections with a generic requirement to comply with “applicable Federal and State laws” governing discrimination, which would weaken safeguards, reduce accountability, and would leave certain apprentices unprotected. One of these commenters concluded that, under the proposed rule, sponsors that are not joint labor-management committees or do not have at least 15 employees or members would not be covered by any nondiscrimination law. Other commenters noted that, while Title VII of the Act provides that it is unlawful for employers, labor organizations, or joint labor-management committees controlling apprenticeship to discriminate, there are apprenticeship programs run by other entities (such as non-profit trade associations) that do not fall under any of these categories. These commenters asserted that current § 30.3 helps bridge this gap and provide protections to apprentices in programs not covered by Title VII. Some of these commenters cited the case of
Salas
v.
Independent Electrical Contractors Inc.
(W.D. Wash. May 6, 2013), where an apprentice sued his non-joint apprenticeship program alleging discrimination, but the Federal district court held that because the apprentice was not an employee of the apprenticeship program and the program had only five employees, the program did not constitute an “employer” under Title VII. Moreover, the court noted that because the program was not associated with a union, it did not constitute a “joint labor-management committee,” thus leaving the apprentice without legal recourse. One of these commenters further remarked that several States' nondiscrimination laws do not seem to cover non-joint apprenticeship programs, including Kentucky, New York, Louisiana, Utah, Virginia, and Montana, and provided language from those States' nondiscrimination laws to support their position.
Department Response:
The final rule adopts this provision as proposed. The Department agrees with the commenters that the revisions to § 30.3 will eliminate unnecessarily complex requirements, focusing instead on compliance with laws with which employers are already familiar.
The Department disagrees with the commenters that the proposed protections are not sufficiently robust and reiterates that apprentices retain safeguards available under Federal and State nondiscrimination laws. To the extent that certain apprentices are not covered by those existing laws, Congress and State legislatures have chosen the relevant jurisdictional thresholds, and they could seek to amend them in the future. For example, Congress specifically contemplated coverage of apprentices in Title VII, including in sections 703(d) and 704(a) and (b),
[
50
]
while also setting in section 701(b) a statutory minimum of 15 employees for covered employers.
[
51
]
In response to comments citing the
Salas
case—which dealt with the definition of “employee” under Title VII, the ADEA, and Washington State law—the Department recognizes that there are some entities with apprentices that are not covered by Federal or State nondiscrimination laws, including those that have fewer employees than statutory minimums. Congress and some State legislatures likewise determined that nondiscrimination laws apply to employers, labor organizations, and joint labor-management committees.
As indicated earlier in this preamble, the Department is convinced that it would be manifestly improper to retain any of the regulatory provisions contained in part 30 (such as the regulatory language delineating the scope of coverage of the nondiscrimination provision available under existing § 30.3) that may have operated to either circumvent or contravene the foregoing coverage provisions of Title VII or of other applicable Federal or State employment nondiscrimination statutes. Were the Department to retain such broadly encompassing regulatory coverage language in this final rule—as it was urged to do by several commenters—the Department would be essentially subverting the legislative intent of Congress and of State legislatures via an agency regulation, which is a plainly inadmissible course of action. The Department does not wish to exercise its authority under the NAA in a manner that contravenes clear Congressional instruction. Accordingly, as Congress did not include non-joint committees as entities falling under Title VII's definition of “employer” or “labor organization,” the Department defers to the apparent legislative intent of the Nation's elected representatives and declines to adopt these commenters' recommendations.
In this connection, the Department has consistently maintained that the sponsor of a Registered Apprenticeship program is the entity that bears responsibility for ensuring that the program is conducted and operated in a manner consistent with all governing apprenticeship-related statutes and regulations, including compliance with the nondiscrimination requirements contained in this final rule. This broad compliance obligation applies to all models of program sponsorship, regardless of whether the sponsor directly employs each of the apprentices enrolled in their program, or instead operates a “group” program (administered on either a joint or a non-joint basis) in which one or more participating employers have agreed, in writing, to adopt the sponsor's apprenticeship standards for the training of their respective apprenticeship cohorts. There may be instances where the sponsor of a group program receives information—either through their own monitoring or as a result of a program review by the Registration Agency—that a participating employer has not met their contractual obligation to follow the program's standards of apprenticeship, or has failed to comply with governing
(
printed page 70210)
apprenticeship-related laws (such as applicable Federal employment nondiscrimination statutes or the part 30 requirements contained in this final rule). In such cases, the group sponsor should promptly implement effective corrective measures to ensure participating employers' ongoing compliance with their program standards, which includes the requirement to comply with part 30.
Further, the Department notes that the current part 30 enforcement structure was largely duplicative of other Federal and State law protections, and that these revisions will remove this duplication, thereby reducing burden and confusion among sponsors, who should already be familiar with Federal and State nondiscrimination laws. This aligns with
E.O. 14278
's mandate that the Department seek to expand Registered Apprenticeship and improve efficiency.
2. State Law Requirements
Comments:
A commenter expressed concern about the proposed regulatory provision at § 30.3, which would require compliance with “all applicable” Federal and State laws and regulations prohibiting discrimination. The commenter interpreted this as requiring compliance with all nondiscrimination laws that apply to a program sponsor but reasoned that “applicable” State laws and regulations could be read more narrowly to refer only to those that pertain exclusively to nondiscrimination in apprenticeship, as in proposed § 30.7(b)(1)(i). Therefore, the commenter asked the Department to clarify its intent and the scope of laws covered by § 30.3. Regardless, the commenter urged DOL to drop the requirement to comply with State nondiscrimination laws and regulations, expressing concern that requiring compliance with State laws would undermine the Trump administration's goals and executive orders on “restoring biological truth, protecting women and girls, and eradicating gender ideology.” Furthermore, the commenter cautioned that State nondiscrimination laws and regulations may not be as solicitous as Federal laws and regulations, citing
Union Gospel Mission
v.
Ferguson,
No. 23-2606, 2024 WL 3755954 (9th Cir. Aug. 12, 2024), regarding protections for religious organizations to run their organizations in accordance with their religious beliefs. Citing
World Vision
v.
McMahon,
the commenter argued, that while the First Amendment applies to State nondiscrimination laws, Federal statutory protections for religious liberty do not. The commenter proposed specific alternative regulatory text for § 30.3 to address these concerns.
Similarly, another commenter supported retaining the prohibition on religious discrimination but remarked that religious employers should have the ability to apply religious criteria when making workforce decisions. However, the commenter expressed concern that removing the language referring to legal standards and defenses applied under Title VII could prevent religious employers from invoking Title VII's exemptions in the apprenticeship context.
A commenter expressed concern that removing the detailed language currently in § 30.3 would leave SAAs with fewer tools to train sponsors and employers on compliance and to prevent discriminatory practices before they escalate to legal action. The commenter recommended that if finalized, the Department should offer guidance, training, and tools to address this concern.
A commenter recommended that the Department issue subregulatory guidance outlining when OA would exercise its authority to register apprenticeship programs in SAA States, as permitted under § 29.13(j)(2), in the context of SAAs found to be out of compliance with the proposed rule because of nondiscrimination policies that do not “conform only” to the rule. Refer to section V.F.7.a for additional commentary on State nondiscrimination laws and their conformity to the requirements of part 30.
Department Response:
The Department agrees with the commenters' interpretation that § 30.3 requires program sponsors to comply with all applicable State laws that prohibit illegal discrimination on the delineated bases. The Department notes that there is a distinction between the language set out in § 30.3 and § 30.7. Under the final rule's revised language, § 30.7 clarifies that its provisions cover State laws, regulations, policies, and operational procedures specific to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship. In this way, the Department intends for the scope of laws subject to § 30.7 to be narrower than § 30.3, as § 30.3 requires compliance with all applicable Federal and State laws prohibiting illegal discrimination on the listed bases. In response to the commenter's concern about undermining the Administration's goals if State law compliance is required, the Department notes that, absent the language in § 30.3, entities that serve as program sponsors will still be required to comply with applicable State laws as long as such laws have not been held to conflict with Federal law, regardless of whether the entity chose to become a program sponsor. Additionally, the language in § 30.5 directs Registration Agencies to assess compliance based on any final determinations of a sponsor's violation of an applicable nondiscrimination law made by an enforcement entity or court—a determination that would have been made regardless of the language in § 30.3. Thus, the final rule does not place any additional regulatory burdens or coverage requirements onto sponsors.
The Department appreciates commenters' concerns surrounding religious liberty and the availability of religious exemptions for program sponsors. The Department acknowledges that, under the United States' system of federalism, religious liberty protections are dependent on whether State or Federal law applies. The Department points out that, federally, Title VII of the Act and the ADA, provide exemptions for religious organizations, which would apply to all employers covered by those laws, including in the apprenticeship context. While Federal statutory protections for religious liberty do not apply to State nondiscrimination laws, many States have chosen to enact their own statutory and regulatory schemes to protect religious liberty and provide religious exemptions. For example, several States have enacted their own religious freedom laws that are modeled after the Religious Freedom Restoration Act.
[
52
]
The Department asserts that agencies including the EEOC and State FEPAs are better positioned to further address the applicability of religious exemptions as they enforce the applicable statutes.
Additionally, the Department notes that the provisions of part 30 have no bearing on the availability of religious exemptions under Title VII (or other nondiscrimination statutes), and that the Department will respect a court's determination that a sponsor has properly invoked an exemption when considering the sponsor's compliance with the standard in § 30.3. As such, in response to commenters requesting that the Department change the proposed text at § 30.3 to remove the requirement that sponsors must comply with State nondiscrimination laws, the Department declines to adopt the suggestion, but notes that the existing part 30 exemption provision is being retained in this final rule. This provision allows sponsors to request exemptions from part 30 requirements in writing, supported by an explanation of the
(
printed page 70211)
reasons for the request. Where a sponsor has been found to be in violation of a State law that the sponsor views as infringing on its religious liberties, the sponsor may request an exemption pursuant to § 30.8 from the Registration Agency and the Registration Agency will consider whether the sponsor has presented good cause sufficient to avoid deregistration on the grounds of such violation.
In response to the comment expressing concern that SAAs will have less compliance assistance and resources to help prevent illegal discrimination, the Department provides that it will engage in technical assistance as requested. Additionally, the Department notes that the relevant Federal and State enforcement agencies can engage in compliance assistance and may have guidance, training, and other resources available that covered entities can utilize in their compliance efforts.
3. Youth Apprenticeship
Comments:
A commenter requested clarification or subregulatory guidance from the Department on how the proposed § 30.3's prohibition of discrimination based on age (40 or older) can be navigated when developing youth apprenticeship programs. The commenter said that while they are supportive of this provision to ensure no age discrimination is allowed, dedicated youth apprenticeship programs with upper age requirements at 24 may be considered discriminatory based on age. The commenter remarked that this is further challenging for instances where high school Career and Technical Education programs may seek to be sponsors of Registered Apprenticeship programs, but in most instances, a student cannot be in high school after age 21. The commenter elaborated that this tension is compounded by the fact that on April 2, 1996, the EEOC adopted a rule that ended the longstanding policy exemption for apprenticeship programs from coverage under the ADEA. The commenter noted that OA issued a policy in Circular 96-01 on May 30, 1996, which communicated that upper age limits on programs were no longer allowed, but this circular was rescinded on June 4, 2020, by Circular 2020-01.
Department Response:
The Department appreciates the commenter's interest in expanding Registered Apprenticeship opportunities for youth. Under the final rule, what activity constitutes illegal discrimination on the basis of age is a matter for the EEOC to determine in their enforcement of the ADEA. Furthermore, the Department maintains that this part 30 rulemaking is not a suitable regulatory vehicle for addressing the topic of Federal registration of youth apprenticeship programs.
D. Section 30.4—Complaints
In the NPRM, the Department proposed to remove the complaint provision in the current part 30 regulation and to replace it with a substantially simplified complaint process set forth at proposed § 30.4. Under that proposal, the Registration Agency would direct individuals alleging unlawful discrimination to an enforcement authority with the appropriate jurisdiction and expertise to investigate compliance with Federal or State nondiscrimination statutes or regulations. Examples of such authorities include the EEOC, the U.S. Attorney General or a State Attorney General, and relevant State enforcement agencies (such as FEPAs). The Department proposed this change after determining that the existing part 30 complaint procedures are burdensome, difficult to navigate, and ineffective, and that Registration Agencies are less well-suited to investigating or resolving apprentice discrimination complaints than the enforcement entities identified in proposed § 30.4.
As explained in the NPRM, replacing a duplicative, apprenticeship-specific complaint mechanism with a straightforward referral process advances the Administration's deregulatory objective to eliminate unnecessary regulatory burdens, ensures that complaints are handled by agencies with the requisite expertise, and serves apprentices' interests by providing a single, clear avenue for filing complaints. Accordingly, for the reasons discussed in the NPRM and in response to comments discussed below, the Department is finalizing the provision with minimal edits. In response to comments discussed below, the Department is revising the proposed language to eliminates language in § 30.4(c) that could have been interpreted as only allowing SAAs to refer complaints to State FEPAs. The Department is also adding that a Registration Agency may refer complaints to any Federal or State enforcement entity with jurisdiction over discrimination issues. Under the revised language as adopted by this final rule, the Department is clarifying that complaints can be referred by any Registration Agency to the EEOC, the U.S. Attorney General, a State FEPA, or another Federal or State enforcement agency with jurisdiction over discrimination issues as appropriate. Furthermore, a complaint may be referred to several of these entities as appropriate.
1. Support for the Proposed Provision
Comments:
A commenter expressed support for proposed § 30.4 and shifting enforcement of nondiscrimination laws and regulations to the EEOC, the U.S. Attorney General, and for an SAA, to its FEPA. The commenter stated that this change would eliminate duplicative oversight and enforcement by DOL without sacrificing necessary oversight and enforcement and still retaining the possibility of deregistration by DOL after a final determination of unlawful discrimination. The commenter also stated that nothing in the proposal would prohibit an apprentice from filing a charge of discrimination with the EEOC or State agencies directly.
Department Response:
The Department appreciates the commenter's support for the proposed changes and agrees with the commenter that these changes would eliminate duplicative oversight and enforcement measures.
2. Concerns About Removing Registration Agency Authority
Comments:
Several commenters expressed opposition to the proposal to eliminate the authority of Registration Agencies to investigate discrimination complaints. These commenters expressed concern that the proposal would eliminate the existing compliance review framework and restrict enforcement actions to cases where a final determination of discrimination had already been made by a court or enforcement entity, which would limit the ability of Registration Agencies to address discrimination effectively.
Several commenters further reasoned that referral-only enforcement would delay remedies, reduce the deterrent effect on noncompliant sponsors, leave apprentices unprotected during lengthy Federal investigations, severely restrict Registration Agencies' options for timely interventions, and erode the cooperative Federal-State framework that has long underpinned the success of the National Apprenticeship System. For example, one commenter said that requiring complaints to be referred to other agencies would mean that sponsors that discriminate would virtually never face deregistration because of how long final determinations will take to reach Registration Agencies. The commenter remarked that under Title VII, a party
(
printed page 70212)
alleging illegal discrimination can file a lawsuit in Federal court after completing the prerequisite administrative requirements, but the percentage of Federal EEOC or State FEPA investigations that result in a Federal court lawsuit is very small. Of these, only a small proportion become final through a court decision where an appeal is not filed, because most cases are settled. The commenter also said that the EEOC itself does not issue final determinations, but complainants must pursue their complaints in court after the EEOC makes a preliminary determination.
A commenter expressed concern that the proposal would render Registration Agencies as passive intermediaries and said that research suggests OA and SAAs are often able to resolve discrimination complaints with technical advice and by intervening informally. The commenter warned that such interventions, which the commenter described as timely and cost effective, may be lost under the proposed changes. The commenter further stated that under the proposed rule, if implemented, apprenticeship agencies may be less likely to become aware of potential misconduct because they would no longer be the primary recipient of complaints, thus they may be less likely to help resolve and address complaints. Another commenter stated that eliminating program complaint investigation authority without analysis of its impact on apprentices' ability to seek relief is inconsistent with the NAA's mandate, particularly in terms of how its impact on the timeline for relief for apprentices would affect the welfare of apprentices.
As a result of these concerns, several comments recommended that Registration Agencies should retain their authority to investigate and pursue remediation of discrimination complaints under the existing regulation. One commenter said the retention of this authority is particularly important for issues that implicate both nondiscrimination and broader part 29 compliance. Similarly, another commenter recommended that to align with the NAA's directive to safeguard apprentice welfare, the final rule should consider: (1) retaining investigative and enforcement authority for Registration Agencies to address complaints of discrimination, harassment, or intimidation; (2) enhancing agencies' capability to provide technical assistance in resolving issues with employers collaboratively before they escalate; and (3) clarifying referral protocols to ensure coordination with EEOC or State FEPAs.
Department Response:
The Department disagrees with the concerns raised by these commenters. The Department has determined that investigation of discrimination complaints and related tasks are better left with the EEOC or State-level FEPAs because such agencies have the appropriate subject matter expertise and jurisdiction over such matters. For example, the EEOC is the most appropriate enforcement agency for making a determination that a program sponsor violated an applicable Federal nondiscrimination law. Registration Agencies, by contrast, are apprenticeship administrators whose primary responsibility is the registration, oversight, and promotion of Registered Apprenticeship programs. The Department therefore concludes that the investigation and adjudication of discrimination complaints should be conducted by entities specifically established for that purpose rather than by Registration Agencies operating under the NAA.
Under this final rule, once the Registration Agency is made aware of such a determination concerning a Registered Apprenticeship program sponsor, it may initiate appropriate administrative actions, including establishing a compliance action plan or initiating deregistration proceedings, as described in the section-by-section discussion of the nondiscrimination compliance and enforcement section at § 30.5 of this final rule.
The Department is unpersuaded that a referral-based framework will undermine apprentice welfare. To the contrary, the Department maintains that apprentice welfare is best served when allegations of unlawful discrimination are investigated by agencies with the expertise, procedural safeguards, and remedial authority necessary to resolve such claims. The EEOC, State FEPAs, the Department of Justice, and similar entities possess the expertise, jurisdiction, procedural safeguards, and remedial authority necessary to investigate discrimination claims and adjudicate alleged violations of Federal and State civil-rights laws. Registration Agencies, by contrast, lack these key capabilities. The Department is convinced that directing complainants to the appropriate enforcement authority better aligns discrimination enforcement responsibilities with the institutions specifically established to carry out those functions, rather than maintaining a parallel apprenticeship-specific process.
The Department also disagrees with some commenters' suggestion that the ability of Registration Agencies to provide informal technical assistance or facilitate voluntary resolutions justifies retaining investigative authority over discrimination complaints. While the Department recognizes that Registration Agencies have occasionally assisted sponsors and apprentices in resolving workplace disputes, the commenters' observations merely demonstrate that Registration Agencies have historically referred many discrimination complaints to appropriate Federal or State enforcement agencies while providing ancillary assistance where appropriate. Indeed, the report cited by one commenter noted that SAAs frequently refer discrimination complaints to State or Federal FEPAs, particularly where the SAA lacks the means or expertise to investigate the allegations independently.
[
53
]
This report thus confirms that the referral-based approach proposed in the NPRM is already common practice for both OA and SAAs. The final rule formalizes and clarifies this practice by directing discrimination complaints to the agencies specifically charged with enforcing nondiscrimination laws.
The Department further maintains that significant administrative consequences, including the development of compliance action plans, suspension of the right to register new apprentices, or deregistration, should be predicated upon findings made by entities possessing legal authority to investigate and adjudicate claims of unlawful discrimination. Registration Agencies should not independently make de facto determinations regarding violations of Federal or State nondiscrimination laws, which risks inconsistent enforcement and conflicting interpretations of nondiscrimination requirements.
Similarly, the Department disagrees with some commenters' assertions that a referral-based approach undermines the NAA's directive to safeguard the welfare of apprentices. The Department has determined that referring complaints alleging illegal discrimination to appropriate enforcement agencies will better safeguard the welfare of apprentices by ensuring that the substance of the complaint will be investigated by entities with the appropriate expertise
(
printed page 70213)
and providing apprentices with a legitimate opportunity to receive individualized relief in response to the alleged illegal conduct. The Department notes that such individualized forms of relief are available under Title VII and other Federal statutes, but have never been included in the part 30 regulation.
Separately, in response to one commenter who asserted that the EEOC does not issue final determinations and that complainants must pursue complaints in court after a preliminary determination by the EEOC, the Department maintains that this and other similar enforcement agencies are the most appropriate venues for apprentices to raise allegations of discriminatory conduct by an apprenticeship program. In response to the commenter raising concerns about delayed enforcement, while the Department acknowledges that it is possible that the referral of complaints to other agencies may take additional time, such referrals nevertheless ensure that such complaints are investigated and handled appropriately, and that determinations are made accurately by entities with the relevant expertise.
3. Concerns About Reliance on Complaints
Comments:
Some commenters expressed concern about the proposal's reliance on complaints to address discrimination. These commenters stated that most individuals who experience discrimination do not file formal complaints due to, among other reasons, fear of retaliation, a lack of resources, or concerns that final determinations are rare and often take years to resolve. One commenter cited research which it found that only between 6 and 13 percent of harassment incidents are formally reported in the construction trades, in part due to fears of retaliation or that their compliant will not be acted upon. Some commenters also asserted that relying on a complaints-driven civil rights compliance system would place the burden of preventing discrimination on apprentices, and maintained that such a system would be ineffective and unfair.
54
Another commenter added that the EEOC recommends that multiple people in an organization should be authorized to receive complaints, so that complainants have more reporting options.
Department Response:
The Department understands commenters' concerns that some apprentices who experience discrimination may choose not to file formal complaints. The Department is not persuaded, however, that retaining apprenticeship-specific compliance reviews would meaningfully uncover instances of unlawful discrimination.
The compliance reviews conducted under the prior regulation were principally designed to assess compliance with the affirmative action requirements contained in part 30, including utilization analyses, utilization goals, action taken to meet such goals, and related recordkeeping requirements. As discussed elsewhere in this preamble, the Department has determined that these requirements were burdensome and, in many cases, likely unlawful. While there is no longer a need to conduct compliance reviews that assess compliance with the rescinded provisions of part 30, the final rule at § 30.5 does preserve a mechanism for monitoring compliance with the revised part 30 requirements pursuant to the program review provision under
29 CFR 29.6
.
While affirmative action requirements can be assessed through the review of records and other objective indicators, individual allegations of intentional discrimination frequently involve fact-specific disputes concerning motive, intent, harassment, or other conduct directed at particular individuals. Such matters are frequently identified only through complaints, witness testimony, and investigative procedures conducted by agencies and courts with expertise in enforcing nondiscrimination laws. It is unsurprising that Congress and State legislatures have generally relied on complaint-driven processes to enforce nondiscrimination laws. Therefore, allegations of unlawful discrimination are more appropriately addressed through the established Federal and State nondiscrimination enforcement framework than through apprenticeship-specific compliance reviews.
Commenters' concern over the chilling effect on employees who file complaints is addressed by Federal and State nondiscrimination laws that prohibit retaliation against individuals who file complaints or otherwise participate in protected activities. If a sponsor is found to have engaged in unlawful retaliation under one of these laws or any other applicable nondiscrimination law, the EEO agency and the Department can hold the sponsor accountable pursuant to revised § 30.5. Finally, in response to one commenter's concern, the Department also clarifies that nothing in the rule prohibits sponsors from designating multiple people within their organizations as being responsible for receiving complaints related to nondiscrimination law.
4. Comments Alleging Certain Harmful Impacts That Would Result From the Department's Proposed Streamlining of Enforcement and Oversight Activities
Comments:
A commenter asserted that the proposed rule would reduce Registration Agency oversight and intervention in cases of discrimination and harassment and would therefore likely increase non-completion of apprenticeship programs, preventing employers and labor markets overall from the benefits of investments in apprenticeship. The commenter also cited research finding that the lifetime costs of workplace sexual harassment and retaliation were particularly high for those pushed out of well-paid occupations, reaching $1.3 million for an apprentice in the construction trades.
Another commenter also raised questions on how Registration Agencies would become aware of final determinations. One commenter recommended that the Department consider data sharing practices or subregulatory guidance on how it will receive final judgments and pursue enforcement actions for consistency.
Department Response:
While these commenters raised concerns regarding the proposed rule's adverse impacts upon apprenticeship completion rates and the lifelong costs of discrimination and harassment, they did not provide persuasive evidence that the compliance review provisions in the existing part 30 regulation have been effective in mitigating the prevalence of discrimination and other forms of egregious conduct in the apprenticeship workplace. As with discrimination, it is unclear how, for instance, compliance review can detect unreported harassment allegations. Since apprentices will retain the opportunity to file complaints in response to such conduct, and will have a more streamlined and clear approach to filing such complaints, the Department does not agree that the proposed regulatory revisions will harm completion rates or will result in an increase in the prevalence of discrimination or harassment in apprenticeship programs.
The Department received comments requesting clarity regarding how Registration Agencies will be made aware when a final determination from an enforcement entity or court regarding a violation of applicable nondiscrimination against a program's apprentice or applicant for apprenticeship. The Department appreciates these comments and has included a provision in the “Nondiscrimination Compliance and Enforcement” section of this final rule,
(
printed page 70214)
at § 30.5(b)(1) and (2), that requires sponsors to report any final determinations that an applicable nondiscrimination law has been violated with respect to an apprentice or applicant for apprenticeship to the Registration Agency within 60 days. The Department asserts that this requirement will strengthen transparency and accountability regarding sponsors' compliance with applicable nondiscrimination laws.
Further, the Department maintains that there are several ways Registration Agencies can work with the EEOC or State FEPAs and the court system to be informed of final determinations of illegal discrimination against apprentices or applicants to an apprenticeship program. For example, Registration Agencies could review court filings or could send inquiry letters to the relevant Federal and State FEPAs as part of the program review process. To the extent possible and appropriate, Registration Agencies are also encouraged to develop MOUs and other partnerships with Federal and State FEPAs to receive notifications of final determinations concerning nondiscrimination violations against apprentices or applicants to an apprenticeship program by Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors from such governmental entities or establish a mechanism by which Registration Agencies can make inquiries. The Department maintains that the addition of a self-disclosure requirement for sponsors whose program is the subject of a final determination will facilitate Registration Agencies' awareness of any relevant nondiscrimination law violations among the Registered Apprenticeship programs they oversee and declines to add any specific requirements for Registration Agencies to establish information-sharing agreements to verify such violations. Given that different options may be suitable based on different administrative structures across States, the Department maintains that imposing a uniform approach for Registration Agencies to conduct any additional verification of such information through regulatory text is not appropriate.
5. Other Administrative Concerns Related to Complaints
Comments:
A commenter remarked that, among other issues, one concern with requiring complaints to be referred to State FEPAs is that in two SAA States, Alabama and Arkansas, there is no such State agency, and that in some other SAA States, there may be multiple applicable agencies, but the proposed rule does not provide clarity on identifying the correct agency. The commenter also expressed concern about the lack of discretion for Registration Agencies allowed under the proposed rule, specifically posing a hypothetical where the EEOC's budget were to shrink to the point where it could not accept additional complaints from OA. Additionally, another commenter expressed concern that the proposed changes would place investigative and resource strains on already under-resourced agencies.
A commenter warned that the proposed rule's reliance on complaints would largely inhibit Registration Agencies' ability to perform compliance reviews. The commenter stated that while the rule nominally retains the compliance review provision, the Registration Agency would not be able to initiate any enforcement action against a sponsor unless there was a final determination of wrongdoing, which would rely on the filing of complaints by apprentices. As a result, the commenter warned that the proposed reliance on complaints would mean that Registration Agencies would have no authority to take any action if they observe blatant discrimination that violates part 30 while they are conducting a part 29 review unless and until there is a final determination.
Department Response:
Regarding the concern that some States do not have a State FEPA, as the preamble above clarifies, this final rule does not limit SAA States to referring complaints to their State FEPA. Under the final rule, SAA states may refer the complaint to any Federal or State agency with appropriate subject matter expertise and jurisdiction over matters concerning illegal discrimination. In response to this concern, and as noted above, the Department has changed the regulatory text at § 30.4 in this final rule to clarify that the list of enforcement entities is not limited to the EEOC, U.S. Attorney General, or State FEP, and that Registration Agencies may refer the complaint to any other appropriate enforcement entities with appropriate subject matter expertise and jurisdiction. In addition, the Department changed the regulatory text at § 30.4 to clarify that Registration Agencies are not limited to referring complaints to one enforcement entity, and may refer complaints to multiple entities as appropriate.
In response to commenters' concerns that the EEOC is facing restraints on its resources that could impact its capacity to handle complaints effectively, the Department notes that the budgetary resources and staffing capacity of the EEOC are determined by Congress and not the Department. Additionally, the Department has received only a small number of discrimination complaints from apprentices under the existing regulation, and notes that its longstanding practice has been to refer such complaints to the EEOC as the appropriate Federal agency for determining whether an allegation of discriminatory conduct has merit. EEOC data indicates that the agency received over 88,000 charges of workplace discrimination in FY 2024 alone, whereas the Department has received fewer than 60 complaints of discrimination under part 30 from apprentices since the beginning of FY 2021.
[
55
]
Finally, the Department does not share commenters' concerns that the proposed rule would limit the ability of Registration Agencies to initiate any enforcement actions against a sponsor unless there was a final determination of illegal discrimination. The Department maintains that it is appropriate to defer adverse administrative actions under part 30 against a program sponsor until the Department has received confirmation that a violation of an applicable nondiscrimination law has occurred from an enforcement agency with the appropriate subject matter expertise and jurisdiction to make such determinations.
E. Section 30.5—Nondiscrimination Compliance Reviews and Enforcement
In the NPRM, the Department proposed eliminating the extensive EEO and affirmative action requirements in the current part 30 regulation and revising the existing compliance and enforcement framework in §§ 30.13 and 30.15 by consolidating and simplifying those provisions into a new § 30.5. Under the current rule, the Department conducts routine “EEO compliance reviews” to evaluate sponsors' adherence to the comprehensive set of requirements across part 30, with particular attention to the development and implementation of an affirmative action program required for programs with five or more apprentices under current § 30.4, the contents of which are detailed in §§ 30.5 through 30.9 and 30.11. Accordingly, the Department proposed to merge the compliance review and enforcement components of the regulation into a single section—“Nondiscrimination compliance reviews and enforcement”—at proposed § 30.5.
(
printed page 70215)
This proposal was designed to focus Departmental resources—principally OA staff's expertise in apprenticeship program quality—on labor standards rather than on making legal determinations regarding compliance with the extensive EEO and affirmative action obligations in the existing part 30 regulation. Consistent with this approach, the Department proposed to rely solely on final determinations issued by an enforcement entity or court with jurisdiction over the matter. The Department anticipated that deferring to the authority and expertise of these entities to decide whether sponsors or other apprenticeship stakeholders (such as employers participating in Registered Apprenticeship programs) have engaged in unlawful discrimination under applicable Federal or State statutes or regulations would yield a more efficient oversight system, strengthen accountability, provide clearer expectations for stakeholders, and result in more appropriate and effective remedies for individuals subjected to discrimination, harassment, or other unlawful treatment in Registered Apprenticeship.
The Department also proposed that compliance reviews related to the streamlined part 30 nondiscrimination requirement occur alongside the program's routine review for compliance with part 29, and that Registration Agencies initiate enforcement actions for violations of the part 30 nondiscrimination requirement only after a court with jurisdiction over employment discrimination (including alleged discrimination involving apprentices or applicants to apprenticeship programs) issues a final, non-appealable determination finding a violation of applicable nondiscrimination laws or regulations. This sequencing was intended to ensure that Registration Agencies do not act while related matters are pending adjudication, consistent with due process principles. Proposed § 30.5(c) outlined the enforcement initiation process, including collaborating with the sponsor to develop a compliance action plan that aligns with the remedy prescribed by the enforcement entity or court. Under proposed § 30.5(c), if a Registration Agency determines that a sponsor is not carrying out the compliance action plan in accordance with the enforcement entity's or court's remedy, the Agency may take additional enforcement steps, including suspending the sponsor's authority to register new apprentices or commencing formal deregistration proceedings under
29 CFR 29.8
.
The Department concluded that this streamlined compliance and enforcement framework preserves Registration Agencies' essential role in conferring the benefits of registration and, when necessary, rescinding registration. The Department received several comments requesting clarity on how the proposed compliance framework would work in practice; specifically, how Registration Agencies would be made aware when an enforcement entity or court makes a final determination that an applicable nondiscrimination law was violated with respect to an apprentice or an applicant for apprenticeship. The Department appreciates these comments and agrees that additional clarity on the enforcement framework will benefit stakeholders and support transparency and accountability regarding Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors' compliance with applicable nondiscrimination laws. Accordingly, in this final rule, the Department has added a requirement that sponsors notify the Registration Agency of any final determinations regarding a violation of an applicable nondiscrimination law with respect to an apprentice or applicant for apprenticeship made by a relevant enforcement entity or court within 60 days at § 30.5(b)(1). In addition, at § 30.5(b)(2) of this final rule, the Department has added a requirement for sponsors to disclose the details of any remedies prescribed by the enforcement entity or court to the Registration Agency. The Department has determined that this additional disclosure requirement will facilitate the requirement that the Registration Agency work with the sponsor to develop a compliance action plan that aligns with any such remedy set forth in § 30.5(c) of this final rule. Aside from these additions to the final rule, the Department is adopting § 30.5 as proposed.
Support for the Proposed Compliance Review and Enforcement Provision
Comments:
A commenter expressed support for the proposed review and enforcement provision. This commenter reasoned that empowering sponsors to tailor compliance plans to their unique operations, rather than imposing a rigid, one-size-fits-all model, would more effectively promote adherence to Title VII and other nondiscrimination laws in apprenticeship programs. This commenter expressed further support for the proposed enforcement regime, stating that the proposed rule appropriately recognizes that Congress established particular enforcement regimes for nondiscrimination laws and established specific remedies, and that it does not seek to add new enforcement regimes or sanctions on top of those established by Congress. However, the commenter expressed concern about the discretion that would be granted to Registration Agencies to assess whether a compliance plan is being followed and when a violation is resolved, stating that these determinations should remain the purview of the court or agency that issued the original order.
While expressing general support for the provision, a commenter recommended that the Department consider establishing a new regulatory provision that creates a “rebuttable presumption of compliance” for programs that demonstrate adherence to key voluntary practices in nondiscrimination and equal opportunity. This commenter remarked that this approach is used successfully by other agencies, and suggested that this approach could assist in addressing reliance interests of existing sponsors who are already complying with the 2016 final rule and reduce the overall regulatory burden while still providing regulatory incentives for programs to exceed the minimum nondiscrimination requirements with good practices and behaviors. The commenter provided alternative regulatory text to effect this suggestion.
Department Response:
The Department appreciates these supportive comments. The Department understands the concern regarding the wide degree of discretion available to Registration Agencies under the proposed rule. The Department agrees that it is crucial that there be consistency across Registration Agencies in determining if compliance plans are being followed and that Registration Agencies defer to the remedial actions that enforcement agencies direct sponsors who have been found to have engaged in discriminatory conduct to undertake. In response to comments discussing the need for compliance action plans to adhere to the remedies to nondiscrimination violations provided by enforcement entities or courts, the Department has added a disclosure requirement for sponsors whose programs are the subject of such final determinations. This disclosure requirement will ensure that Registration Agencies are aware of the remedy provided by the enforcement entity or court, and that any compliance action plans established to address violations of nondiscrimination laws are suitably aligned with any such remedies. The Department confirms that the
(
printed page 70216)
enforcement framework established in this final rule does not add any new enforcement mechanisms beyond those established by Congress.
In response to a commenter's suggestion to create a “rebuttable presumption of compliance,” the Department maintains that the proposed enforcement framework would effectively establish such a presumption of compliance, as a program only would be found noncompliant if there is a final determination that the program violated an applicable nondiscrimination law.
1. Comments on the Status Quo and the Department's Reasoning
Comments:
One commenter stated that compliance reviews serve important functions in an enforcement scheme that are not and cannot be served by relying solely on complaints. The commenter remarked that apprentices and applicants are not always aware of discriminatory practices, especially with regard to recruitment and hiring decisions, and that compliance reviews can uncover such practices. The commenter further argued that the Department's reasoning for the proposed change, that Registration Agency staff do not have the required expertise to enforce nondiscrimination requirements, does not stand up to scrutiny. The commenter said that the Department underestimates staff abilities and knowledge; that the Department has substantial resources it can provide to Registration Agency staff to train and support them in their enforcement of nondiscrimination requirements; and that while other enforcement authorities may have more expertise in nondiscrimination law, they are unlikely to have expertise in apprenticeship, which may be necessary to understand forms of discrimination unique to the apprenticeship setting. The commenter also stated that the Department has extensive resources in other departments, mainly the Solicitor's Office, that could provide training, back-up, assistance, and legal analysis to Registration Agency staff and that the Department did not evaluate utilizing the Solicitor's or other existing resources as an alternative to the proposed rule.
Another commenter stated that the proposed rule is correct in arguing that OA lacks the capacity to properly enforce the EEO regulations under
29 CFR part 30
, and there are not enough career staff to perform compliance reviews, as required under § 30.13. However, the commenter did not agree that Registration Agency staff lack the knowledge and experience to ensure compliance with the affirmative action requirements. The commenter concluded that any challenges with enforcing the existing framework could be solved by hiring additional staff to perform compliance reviews of affirmative action requirements or utilizing SAAs to perform compliance reviews.
Department Response:
In response to these comments, the Department reiterates that, as a general matter, FEPAs are better suited than Registration Agencies to make authoritative administrative determinations regarding whether a program sponsor's hiring practices or other workplace practices constitute illegal discrimination against apprentices or applicants. One commenter acknowledged this reality, agreeing with the Department that FEPAs possess more subject-matter expertise in assessing and identifying discriminatory conduct by employers. Accordingly, the Department has determined that it is wasteful and duplicative for a Registration Agency to conduct investigations into allegations of illegal discrimination, to attempt to resolve issues locally, or to make determinations with respect to discriminatory workplace practices when a referral to the EEOC or other FEPA with subject-matter expertise may be the most appropriate course of action. The Department maintains that providing additional training on nondiscrimination law for Registration Agency staff would be an inefficient use of limited agency resources, particularly since there are other enforcement agencies, such as the EEOC and State FEPAs, that have been directed by Federal and State laws to evaluate allegations of illegal discrimination.
In response to the commenter who suggested Registration Agencies' expertise in apprenticeship matters is useful in determining whether discrimination has occurred in a Registered Apprenticeship program, the Department notes that nothing in this final rule prevents Registration Agency staff from responding to inquiries from enforcement agencies during their investigation. The commenter did not provide any concrete examples of how the expertise of Registration Agencies regarding apprenticeship matters is specifically beneficial in investigating discrimination complaints. The Department maintains that investigating complaints alleging discrimination against apprentices should not differ from the investigation of complaints in other employment settings.
F. Section 30.6—Reinstatement of Program Registration
The Department proposed to retain the “Reinstatement of program registration” provision at current § 30.16. As part of the streamlined part 30 framework under the NPRM, sponsors would retain the right to request reinstatement of registration by demonstrating—to the Registration Agency and to the court that issued the final determination of a violation of applicable nondiscrimination law or regulation—that the program was being operated in compliance with nondiscrimination law and this part. The proposal preserved the existing requirement that sponsors present “adequate evidence” of compliance with part 30. Because violations under part 30 would have been confirmed by a court of competent jurisdiction, sponsors would have been required to provide evidence satisfactory to that court that they had addressed the issues underlying the nondiscrimination complaint, including implementing any ordered remedies. Retaining a reinstatement provision was consistent with the proposed compliance approach and supported the Department's objective, in streamlining the regulation, to enhance regulatory flexibility for Registered Apprenticeship stakeholders.
The Department did not receive public comments related to proposed § 30.6. Accordingly, for the reasons discussed in the NPRM, the Department finalizes the provision as proposed.
G. Section 30.7—State Apprenticeship Agencies
In the NPRM, the Department proposed to rescind parts of current § 30.18, the provision covering SAAs, in the existing part 30 regulation. The Department explained that the current part 30 regulation, and the existing regulatory requirements for SAAs under part 30, have not been fully successful in achieving a uniform national standard for nondiscrimination and equality of opportunity in Registered Apprenticeship, as evidenced by the variations in content and requirements in the State EEO plans required by existing § 30.18. Given the inconsistencies the existing part 30 regulation has created across SAAs, the Department proposed a new section for SAA requirements related to the part 30 regulation, at proposed § 30.7, that reflects the Department's determination that sponsors operating Registered Apprenticeship programs should not be required to comply with excessive and legally suspect requirements that only apply to Registered Apprenticeship and
(
printed page 70217)
not their general workforce. In the NPRM, the Department argued that proposed § 30.7 would facilitate the establishment of a uniform Federal standard governing nondiscrimination in Registered Apprenticeship and reduce administrative burdens for SAAs by stipulating that compliance with applicable Federal and State nondiscrimination laws is sufficient to conform with the requirements of an updated part 30 regulation.
As proposed, § 30.7(a) would have required that, within 1 year of the effective date of the final rule, all SAAs seeking to obtain or maintain recognition under current § 29.13 must ensure that their State's apprenticeship laws, regulations, policies, and procedures specifically pertaining to nondiscrimination for apprentices “conform only to the requirements of this part [30].” This provision was proposed to relieve SAA States from having to impose the complex, burdensome, and legally suspect set of regulatory obligations that are found in current version of part 30 and would substitute a straightforward requirement that such states conform to the nondiscrimination requirements found in applicable Federal and State laws. The Department explained that the purpose of this proposed provision was to establish a nationally uniform standard for nondiscrimination protections across all States participating in the National Apprenticeship System.
In proposing to establish a uniform Federal standard at proposed § 30.7(a), the Department sought to ensure that State laws and regulations concerning nondiscrimination or equality of opportunity in Registered Apprenticeship were coextensive in their substance and scope with the requirements of the proposed revision to part 30 and consistent with Federal and State nondiscrimination laws. The Department explained that attaining a uniform standard across all States would be particularly helpful for sponsors that register and operate their programs in multiple States, and would foster an environment that is conducive to accelerating the expansion of Registered Apprenticeship programs. In addition, proposed § 30.7(a) would have allowed States to seek an extension for “good cause” to provide needed flexibility for States with differing legislative or regulatory processes to enact and implement laws that conform only to the requirements stipulated at proposed § 30.7.
Proposed § 30.7(b) and its subordinate paragraphs set forth the elements of State plans for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship for States seeking new or continued SAA recognition. Proposed § 30.7(b)(1)(i) stipulated that State plans include all of a State's statutes, regulations, and policies pertaining specifically to nondiscrimination in apprenticeship, and that such statutes, regulations, and policies conform only to the requirements of the proposed part 30. The Department explained that this language would help to prevent operational fragmentation among State-registered programs and would ensure consistent application of nondiscrimination standards. Proposed § 30.7(b)(1)(ii) further stipulated that all State-registered programs comply with a State's Department-approved State plan within 180 days from the date that the Department approved the State plan submitted under proposed § 30.7(a). The Department determined that a 180-day compliance window would allow for an orderly and timely transition to full implementation at the program level, particularly since sponsors must already be operating their apprenticeship program in compliance with the applicable Federal and State nondiscrimination laws.
Proposed § 30.7(b)(2) mirrored the purpose of existing § 30.18(a)(2)(i-iii) in outlining the review process that OA will undertake upon receipt of the State plan, including providing technical assistance to support conformity with Federal regulations. Similarly, proposed § 30.7(b)(3) stipulated that if an SAA State did not submit a revised State plan that adequately responded to OA's provision of technical assistance on nonconformity issues within 90 days, OA may initiate derecognition proceedings set forth in § 29.14 and proposed § 30.7(e) to formally derecognize the SAA. The Department explained that this provision was intended to provide both due process and accountability for the State. Proposed § 30.7(b)(4) reaffirmed the requirement at existing § 30.18(a)(4) that any subsequent amendments to the State plan for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship must be submitted to the OA Administrator for review and approval prior to implementation to promote alignment between State plans and the Federal nondiscrimination framework described herein.
The recordkeeping requirements stipulated by proposed § 30.7(c) largely replicated the SAA recordkeeping obligations currently found in § 30.18(b), which require a recognized SAA to keep records pertaining to program compliance reviews, complaint investigations, and any other records pertinent to a determination of compliance with the part 30 regulation. These records must be maintained for five years from the date of their creation. The proposed recordkeeping provision was intended to reinforce OA's ability to continue overseeing and auditing compliance over time, including by requiring SAAs to maintain adequate documentation to enable OA to make informed decisions about SAAs' recognition status.
Proposed § 30.7(d)(1) stated that OA would retain full authority to conduct compliance reviews of all registered programs for Federal purposes, even programs registered by an SAA. Similarly, proposed § 30.7(d)(2) reiterated that any SAA that fails to comply with the requirements of this proposed rulemaking would be subject to deregistration proceedings as provided in the part 29 regulation at §§ 29.8(b) and 29.10. The Department explained that the rescission of existing § 30.18(c)(2) and (4)(i) through (iii) was intended to align with proposed § 30.4, which proposed a significantly streamlined complaints framework for complaints alleging illegal discrimination against apprentices. The Department determined that these revisions would more efficiently deploy agency resources and would prevent duplication of investigatory efforts with those civil rights enforcement agencies that possess the statutory authority and expertise to conduct such inquiries. Under this approach, the Department would no longer independently investigate or resolve complaints of discrimination in Registered Apprenticeship. However, OA would retain the authority to refer complaints to appropriate civil rights enforcement agencies (under proposed § 30.4), and to take appropriate enforcement action (under proposed § 30.5) based on another agency's findings regarding discriminatory conduct by program sponsors.
Proposed § 30.7(e) replicated the content of current § 30.18(d). This derecognition provision may be utilized by the Department in appropriate circumstances to assure full conformity by SAA states with Federal nondiscrimination obligations contained in this part.
