The Department received some public comments on proposed § 30.7, with some focused on the proposed standard that State laws, regulations, and policies on nondiscrimination in apprenticeship conform only to the revised part 30 regulation. The Department considered all public comments, including comments discussing the proposed “conform only to” standard for SAAs, in developing this final rule. In response to concerns raised by public commenters,
(
printed page 70218)
the Department has made adjustments to the final regulatory text at § 30.7, including changing the standard to require that SAAs' State laws and regulations “conform to” the revised part 30 regulation, and specifying in the regulatory text throughout § 30.7 that such standard applies to State laws and regulations that pertain specifically to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship. The Department also clarified its requirements for the content of State plans for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship necessary for recognition or continued recognition. These changes to the final rule regulatory text are described below in the Department's responses to public comments on this proposed provision, as are instances where the Department is adopting the regulatory text proposed in the NPRM.
1. Comments on the Proposed Requirement That State Laws Relating to Nondiscrimination in Apprenticeship Must “Conform Only to the Requirements of [Part 30]” (§ 30.7(a))
Clarification of the “Conform Only to” Requirement
Comments:
A commenter expressed concern that the proposed rule did not describe how SAAs' autonomy would be maintained or clarify the extent to which it would supersede SAAs' prerogatives for addressing specific needs within their jurisdictions. Another commenter criticized the proposed provision as contradicting the cooperative federalist model of the NAA. These commenters recommended allowing SAAs to continue exercising their current level of apprenticeship system oversight to preserve innovation and local regulatory responsiveness. A group of commenters opined that the NPRM contains contradictory statements about States' ability to establish their own nondiscrimination laws (
e.g.,
that States have the ability to establish nondiscrimination laws but that States must “conform only” to part 30) and expressed concern that, as written, the proposed rule would create confusion about the interaction of State and Federal laws, thereby undercutting States' rights. One commenter requested that the Department clarify whether SAAs are prohibited from retaining or enforcing additional EEO-related provisions, how the Department would treat enforcement of requirements that are “in addition to” but not inconsistent with part 30, and what options would be available to sponsors in SAA States where such additional EEO-related provisions are being enforced.
One commenter requested that the Department provide guidance on situations where apprenticeship programs may be subject to conflicting State and Federal requirements, such as if a State maintains nondiscrimination provisions that go beyond the streamlined Federal requirements. This commenter recommended that the Department establish clear procedures for resolving such conflicts, adding that failure to do so could burden sponsors and deter prospective sponsors from registering their programs. This commenter also requested that the Department clarify that the requirement for regulatory uniformity would be confined to part 30 nondiscrimination requirements, and not expand to apprenticeship registration requirements under part 29. The commenter reasoned that the flexibility of the existing OA-SAA system is important for allowing programs to reflect local- and State-level labor market conditions, trade-specific considerations, and collective bargaining agreements, such as setting wages appropriate to local cost of living and journeyworker-to-apprentice ratios and training curricula appropriate for an occupation's safety and training requirements. The commenter also requested that the Department affirm that the proposed rule would not override State laws or policies governing apprenticeship program standards outside the scope of EEO requirements.
One commenter expressed support for the Department taking steps to ensure that SAAs conform to Federal standards and do not discriminate against merit-based apprenticeship programs. Another commenter, which expressed support for this provision and recommended removing the State law requirement from the § 30.3 nondiscrimination standard, opined that the Department may need to modify the provision to clarify that sponsors are not obligated to comply with State nondiscrimination requirements where they go beyond or conflict with Federal requirements.
Some commenters opposed the provision at proposed § 30.7(a), arguing that it would improperly impede States' constitutional authority to implement their own State laws and programs that meet local needs. Some commenters asserted that this change would set a “concerning” precedent for undermining States' rights. One commenter expressed opposition to what it characterized as the Department's effort to reduce proactive and innovative policymaking at the State level. This commenter opined that women's participation rate in apprenticeships varies widely across States, but that women have made significant strides in high-paying fields in SAA States due to proactive policies, such as data analysis and reporting, research, funding, and cooperation among industry stakeholders; the commenter concluded that limiting States' ability to innovate and take initiative would stifle these gains.
A commenter expressed opposition to limiting States' authority to promote EEO and advance civil rights beyond Federal requirements. The commenter reasoned that the NAA contemplates shared authority between the Federal Government and the States. This commenter asserted that the NAA's language on shared authority means that States can meet or exceed the minimum requirements set by OA, adding that States have implemented additional protections, such as for marital status and gender identity. The commenter characterized the proposed conformity requirement as improper overreach.
Another commenter expanded on these sentiments, arguing that the NPRM exceeds the Department's authority under the NAA by restricting the ability of States to go above and beyond the Federal rules for preventing discrimination, and reasoning that, while Congress may preempt State laws, it declined to do so with respect to apprenticeship standards. This commenter opined that the plain meaning of the statute is that States have their own authority to effectuate standards of apprenticeship, and that Federal requirements are a floor that States must meet, not a ceiling they cannot exceed. The commenter further asserted that the rule would force many SAAs to abandon their unique protective nondiscrimination and affirmative action requirements.
While similarly arguing that the Congress did not intend for the NAA to have a preemptory effect, a group of commenters asserted that Title VII expressly disavows preemption of State nondiscrimination laws, adding that a State law exceeding the proposed rule's narrow standards does not mean that there is a conflict with Federal law warranting preemption.
Department Response:
The Department appreciates commenters' concerns and requests for clarity as to the scope of this rule's nondiscrimination standard and SAA conformity. Upon review and analysis of the comments, the Department views it as necessary to clarify its intent regarding the applicability of the conformity analysis to State laws, regulations, or policies that specifically pertain to nondiscrimination in Registered Apprenticeship. The Department intends to focus solely on
(
printed page 70219)
any additional nondiscrimination or equal opportunity requirements imposed upon sponsors that are specific to Registered Apprenticeship. Because SAAs are recognized by the Department to register apprenticeship programs for Federal purposes, the Department is exercising its authority under the NAA to review State requirements that are specific to Registered Apprenticeship to determine conformity with Federal requirements. In other words, the Department is not purporting to regulate generally applicable State nondiscrimination laws and requirements but rather to ensure that, in exercising the Department's delegation of authority to register apprenticeship programs for Federal purposes to SAAs, such delegated authority is not provided to States with nondiscrimination or equal opportunity laws and requirements that apply specifically to Registered Apprenticeship that conflict with Federal nondiscrimination law or the overall purpose of the NAA. This is in furtherance of the Department's interest in uniformity within the Registered Apprenticeship system, reduced burden on sponsors, and facilitation of the growth of Registered Apprenticeship. Thus, the Department only will consider State laws and requirements specifically pertaining to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship when determining whether to confer initial or continued recognition to an SAA under the revised part 30 regulation.
To that end, and to address commenters' concerns about the interaction of Federal and State nondiscrimination requirements, the final rule modifies § 30.7(a) to clarify that § 30.7 of this final rule only applies to State statutes, regulations, policies, and operational procedures that specifically pertain to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship. This refers to those nondiscrimination or equal employment requirements that apply to sponsors by virtue of their participation in the Registered Apprenticeship system; it does not refer to laws that specifically include program sponsors among the covered entities but that do not impose obligations that are unique to such sponsors. This modification is responsive to commenters' concerns that the Department's proposed language sought to infringe upon States' authority to regulate nondiscrimination requirements in their States, which may exceed Federal nondiscrimination laws, and clarifies the Department's intent to analyze any additional nondiscrimination or equal opportunity requirements that are specific to Registered Apprenticeship. As stated throughout the preamble, with this final rule, the Department intends to remove burdensome, duplicative, and legally questionable requirements for Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors that discourage or disincentivize sponsors from participating in Registered Apprenticeship.
This change to the final rule at § 30.7 clarifies that the Department will review State-level laws, regulations, and policies specific to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship when assessing a State's request to obtain or retain recognition as an SAA. SAAs must include any State laws, regulations, or policies that contain nondiscrimination or equal opportunity requirements specific to Registered Apprenticeship in their State plans for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship so that the Department can assess whether any apprenticeship-specific requirements are unduly burdensome, unlawful, or detrimental to the expansion of Registered Apprenticeship opportunities for all qualified individuals. The Department does not intend to preempt State nondiscrimination laws; however, it does intend to create a uniform Federal standard for nondiscrimination and equal opportunity in Registered Apprenticeship that applies to SAAs seeking to register apprenticeships for Federal purposes.
In conjunction with this modified language in the final rule, the Department has also modified the conformity language from “conform only to” to “conform to” in § 30.7(a) and (b). The Department acknowledges the concerns raised by the commenters regarding federalism, States' authority to regulate nondiscrimination laws in their states, and the various questions raised about the impact of a “conform only to” analysis on the recognition of SAAs. The Department has determined that using the “conform to” language in part 30 provides consistency across the apprenticeship regulations, meets the Department's goals of streamlining nondiscrimination requirements, and provides sufficient basis for review, technical assistance, and SAA derecognition, if necessary. The Department has also determined that this change addresses concerns about Federalism and the balance between State and Federal authority in regulating nondiscrimination within each State. As described below, the Department views this change from “conform only to” to “conform to” as addressing commenters' concerns by: (1) providing consistency in the review of SAAs across parts 29 and 30; (2) mitigating concerns about preemption of State nondiscrimination laws; and (3) allowing the Department to review SAA recognition under the revised part 30 with an individualized analysis of whether each SAA conforms to the revised regulations.
In addition, in this final rule, the Department has added “equal opportunity” to the regulatory text at § 30.7(a), and at § 30.7(b)(1)(i) and (ii), to clarify that the Department intends to review any State-level laws, regulations, and policies on equal opportunity that are specific to Registered Apprenticeship in determining whether a State's laws, regulations, and policies conform to the requirements of this part. The Department's decision to add “equal opportunity” to the apprenticeship-specific State laws, regulations, and policies that it will review in determining whether a State's laws, regulations, and policies conform to the requirements of this part provides clarity to Registered Apprenticeship stakeholders on the scope of the Department's part 30 analysis for SAA recognition. The Department recognizes that States have established apprenticeship-specific equal opportunity requirements based on the existing part 30 requirements that are being revised, including the requirements for the State EEO plan contained in § 30.18 of the existing regulation. The Department is concerned that such requirements may have restricted growth of the Registered Apprenticeship system by discouraging employers from becoming sponsors, and that some of those requirements may induce disparate treatment of applicants for apprenticeship programs based on their race or sex. Both of these impacts run counter to the Department's goals with this rulemaking, which include removing barriers to participation in Registered Apprenticeship, aligning the Department's apprenticeship regulations with applicable Federal and State nondiscrimination laws, and safeguarding apprentice welfare by removing requirements for sponsors to consider factors other than an applicant's merit in recruiting and hiring apprentices.
Consistency in the Review of SAAs
The Department has long applied the “conform to” analysis when recognizing SAAs. This is the standard articulated in part 29 under which the Department reviews State applications for recognition as SAAs and under which the Department has successfully
(
printed page 70220)
derecognized an SAA due to its failure to conform to part 29 regulations. The “conform to” analysis is familiar to SAAs and ensures consistency in SAA review across both parts 29 and the revised part 30. This more uniform approach across the regulations allows for consistency in review and recognition of SAAs and avoids differing approaches to monitoring conformity with both parts 29 and 30. This approach is also responsive to commenters' concerns that SAAs continue exercising their current level of apprenticeship system oversight, innovation, and responsiveness to local conditions—indeed, this uniformity across both parts 29 and 30 will allow for a continuation of this same level of SAA autonomy within the requirements of the revised part 30. This change relaxes the rigidity of the “conform only” language, allows flexibility to the States to consider their own unique circumstances so long as they conform to the revised part 30, and ensures that the Department maintains the ability to recognize or derecognize SAAs based on their conformity to the revised part 30 regulations.
Federalism and State Nondiscrimination and Equal Opportunity Laws
The Department intends to review State plans for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship to ensure that State laws, regulations, policies, or operational procedures specific to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship conform to the nondiscrimination standard in § 30.3. This does not mean that State laws must mirror exactly the language of the regulations, nor does it mean that any deviation will result in a finding of nonconformity. The Department does, however, expect that the part 30 revisions will create greater uniformity in the application of nondiscrimination in Registered Apprenticeship across the Registered Apprenticeship system as a whole and expects SAAs to adopt their laws, regulations, policies, or operational procedures in accordance with the revised part 30 requirements in order to obtain or maintain recognition as SAAs. With respect to commenters' concerns about State nondiscrimination laws that may be in addition to those in part 30, the Department views its clarification regarding the scope of its review of SAAs and the adjustment of the conformity language to be responsive to these concerns. Indeed, the Department envisions review of SAAs to largely follow the review process in part 29, whereby the Department reviews for conformity, provides technical assistance as needed, and works cooperatively with the State to ensure conformity with the revised part 30 regulations. The Department does not view its interest in uniformity and clarity in nondiscrimination requirements specific to Registered Apprenticeship across the National Apprenticeship System to be a barrier to State innovation as the nondiscrimination standard is firmly rooted in Federal nondiscrimination law that is applicable across the National Apprenticeship System. Further, the nondiscrimination standard in § 30.3 does not serve to supplant State nondiscrimination law (instead, the standard incorporates such laws), and States laws regarding nondiscrimination are not preempted by this rule; rather, States must conform to the revised part 30 regulations should they include or wish to include additional nondiscrimination or equal opportunity requirements, beyond any broadly applicable State nondiscrimination requirements, that are specific to registering apprenticeship programs for Federal purposes. In this vein, the Department is acting well within its authority to promote standards of apprenticeship applicable across the National Apprenticeship System as a whole; ease the regulatory burden upon sponsors, employers, and SAAs alike; and further its goal of expanding Registered Apprenticeship.
Additionally, with respect to concerns about the Department's review of affirmative action requirements, as discussed more fully below, it is indeed the Department's intent to eliminate illegal consideration of protected characteristics in Registered Apprenticeship, and it will consider any SAA affirmative action provisions—in addition to other nondiscrimination requirements—that require consideration of protected characteristics that may induce race-based decision-making in Registered Apprenticeship, as determined by an enforcement authority or court with jurisdiction over such claims. Furthermore, the Department will review an SAA's additional nondiscrimination requirements, affirmative action or otherwise, to assess whether they infringe upon the Department's authority under the NAA and its core duties of overseeing and expanding the Registered Apprenticeship system.
Individualized Assessments of Conformity
The Department intends to analyze SAA plans to ensure that they do not interfere with the Department's goals of expanding the National Apprenticeship System and establishing a more uniform set of requirements for Registered Apprenticeship programs across all States. The Department's review for conformity under the well-established “conform to” standard will allow for the flexibility necessary to make an individualized determination as to each SAA's conformity to revised part 30 requirements. The Department also intends to take any such action that it deems necessary under the authority of the NAA and the regulations at parts 29 and 30 to deny recognition to SAAs that fail to conform to the revised part 30 requirements. In reviewing for conformance, the Department will analyze whether a State's statutes, regulations, policies, and operational procedures specific to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship comply with this part and with the Department's responsibilities under the NAA, including whether they limit the expansion of apprenticeship opportunities.
With respect to the concerns and requests for clarity about sponsors' rights if there are additional EEO protections within a State with a recognized SAA, the Department expects sponsors to follow State laws regarding nondiscrimination so long as the SAA continues to be recognized by the Department. Should sponsors have concerns about an SAA's compliance with the revised part 30 regulations, they may submit complaints to the Department through the established complaint process in part 29. Further, should sponsors encounter barriers to registration with an SAA for any reason, they may seek to register directly with OA. The Department emphasizes that sponsors must continue to follow State nondiscrimination laws that are applicable to them as sponsors of Registered Apprenticeship programs or employers of apprentices and that the Department's recognition of an SAA should provide the necessary assurance to the sponsors of their obligations under nondiscrimination laws as applicable to Registered Apprenticeship. Conversely, with respect to concerns about the Department's impeding of progress made in increasing women's participation rate in Registered Apprenticeship, the Department's analysis of SAA nondiscrimination requirements will not prohibit SAAs from taking merit-based actions to increase participation in Registered Apprenticeship; rather, the Department will consider whether SAAs have requirements that limit or inhibit the
(
printed page 70221)
growth of Registered Apprenticeship or that permit unlawful discrimination, such as affirmative action requirements that may induce Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors to treat applicants for apprenticeship programs differently based on their race or sex.
2. State Plan for Nondiscrimination in Apprenticeship (§ 30.7(b))
Comments:
A commenter requested that the Department clarify the meaning and scope of its reference to the “policies and operational procedures related to nondiscrimination” that would be required to conform only to the revised part 30 and to provide examples of what is meant by those terms. Another commenter requested that SAAs be permitted to continue to impose requirements contained in the existing part 30 regulation, such as its universal outreach, anti-harassment, and selection procedure requirements. The commenter described these requirements as important elements of a comprehensive approach to increasing participation in Registered Apprenticeship.
Department Response:
As discussed above, the Department has adjusted the “conform only to” requirement to “conform to” and has also specified that the State laws, regulations, or policies affected by this rule are those that specifically pertain to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship. For example, if a State has a law that extends certain protections specifically for apprentices in Registered Apprenticeship programs, then it would be required to include that law in its State plan. Similarly, if the State has requirements for outreach policies and procedures that involve outreach to certain demographic groups for the purpose of increasing Registered Apprenticeship participation, the SAA would be required to include such policies in its State plan.
With respect to the suggestions to include additional requirements for SAAs and their State plans, including universal outreach or other requirements from the part 30 regulation that the Department is rescinding with this final rule, the Department appreciates these suggestions but declines to add additional requirements in the State plan beyond those discussed below. This final rule streamlines nondiscrimination requirements in the part 30 regulation, and the Department's requirements for State plans follow a similar streamlining. As such, the Department declines to impose additional affirmative requirements in State plans that would include policies and procedures not required by the final rule.
Based on the Department's review and analysis of the NPRM and the public comments submitted in response to the NPRM, however, the Department has added additional provisions to the State plan requirements to clarify the contents of the State plan necessary for the Department's review of conformity. These additions further clarify the final part 30 regulatory text to explain how the Department will conduct analyses of State plans to determine whether they conform to the regulation, as requested by public commenters. The Department expects that these additions will provide additional clarity for States on what to include in State plans such that they include all relevant information regarding State nondiscrimination requirements specific to Registered Apprenticeship. The Department's review for conformity will include an assessment of whether any additional requirements frustrate or impede the Department's authority under the NAA to expand Registered Apprenticeship, including whether they impose additional unnecessary burden or cost upon sponsors, disincentivize the establishment of new Registered Apprenticeship programs or growth of existing programs, or create unnecessary bifurcation within the National Apprenticeship System. The Department additionally expects SAAs to adhere to their responsibility to prohibit illegal discrimination in Registered Apprenticeship by removing requirements that promote illegal discrimination, such as requirements that may induce sponsors to make apprentice employment decisions based on their race or sex rather than their merit and qualifications, as determined by enforcement entities or courts with jurisdiction over such claims. As the Department discussed at length above regarding affirmative action programs, whether a particular law or policy constitutes illegal discrimination is a final determination made by an enforcement entity or court. The Department emphasizes that its focus is on eliminating unnecessary barriers for the growth of Registered Apprenticeship and removing legally questionable requirements imposed upon sponsors of Registered Apprenticeship programs. SAAs are recognized by the Department to carry out the responsibilities of a Registration Agency. As such, in order to obtain or maintain recognition as an SAA, States have the responsibility to change any State laws or regulations specific to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship that create such unnecessary barriers. In developing State plans for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship, the Department expects States seeking to obtain or maintain recognition as an SAA to adjust any such laws or regulations.
The Department modified § 30.7(b)(1)(i) in this final rule to remove the word “only” so that the provision adheres to the “conform to” standard that the Department has adopted in the final rule. This is consistent with the change in § 30.7(a) of this final rule and the rationale described above for using a “conform to” standard rather than “conform only to” when evaluating State plans. The Department also included a provision at § 30.7(b)(1)(ii) in this final rule to clarify that State plans must “[i]nclude a description of any State statutes, regulations, policies, and operational procedures pertaining specifically to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship which impose requirements in addition to those prescribed in this part” to provide increased clarity for on what laws, regulations, and policies the Department will review when evaluating State plans. This is necessary to confirm that the SAA is submitting all State statutes, regulations, policies, and operational procedures relevant to the analysis of the State plan. This provision complements § 30.7(b)(1)(i) in the final rule because it serves to ensure that any State-level requirements specific to nondiscrimination in Registered Apprenticeship that go beyond the requirements of this final rule are assessed and evaluated by the Department for conformity. The Department will assess any additional requirements to determine whether they conflict with, contradict, or undermine the Department's authority under the NAA and its goal of expanding Registered Apprenticeship.
The Department also added a new § 30.7(b)(1)(iii) to this section outlining requirements for State plans for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship, which provides that States must “Not require any sponsor seeking to register a program with the State for Federal purposes, through any State statutes, regulations, policies, or operational procedures, to engage in any activity that is unlawful under Federal or State nondiscrimination law.” This directly addresses the Department's concerns articulated throughout this rulemaking about illegal discrimination in Registered Apprenticeship and explicitly prohibits States seeking to obtain or maintain recognition as an SAA from retaining laws or regulations
(
printed page 70222)
specific to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship that incorporate such illegal preferences. The provision also provides clarity, as requested by commenters, on legal or regulatory requirements specific to apprenticeship that do not conform to this part. The Department is particularly concerned about legally questionable affirmative action plans that may run afoul of nondiscrimination law and will be paying particular attention to this issue as it evaluates State plans for conformity. SAAs are expected to update their statutes, regulations, policies, and operational procedures pertaining to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship to remove any requirements for Registered Apprenticeship programs to engage in practices that would constitute illegal discrimination under Federal and State law.
As discussed in sections pertaining to the revised procedures for complaints and compliance reviews above, the Department will not make an independent determination about the legality of any preferential program but will rely on decisions by agencies or courts with competent jurisdiction. The Department did not receive any comments on proposed § 30.7(b)(2) through (4) regarding OA's review of the State plan for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship and adopts the provision as proposed. Similarly, because the Department did not receive any comments on proposed § 30.7(c) (Recordkeeping requirements) nor on proposed § 30.7(d) (Retention of authority), the Department adopts the provisions as proposed.
3. Program Compliance Timelines for Programs and SAAs
Comments:
A commenter expressed concern about the proposed 1-year compliance timeline for States to update their laws and regulations to conform with the proposed rule, reasoning that in their State, the legislature would likely only have one session in which to complete the revisions, and that the SAA only can request that the legislature make the necessary changes, not demand it. Another commenter expressed a similar concern about the length of time necessary for the administrative rulemaking process and legislative process. A commenter criticized the proposed rule for not acknowledging the burden that States would face in updating their laws and policies. These commenters therefore recommended extending the compliance timeline to at least 2 years. Similarly, a commenter disagreed with the Department's estimate of the burden on SAAs, State legislatures, and OA staff, and commented that the time and effort involved would detract from other work necessary to support and expand Registered Apprenticeship.
Department Response:
The Department appreciates commenters' concerns regarding the timeline for SAA compliance to conform with the proposed rule. The Department is well aware that State legislative timelines and processes dictate the speed with which a State can update its laws to conform with the revised part 30. The Department anticipates that its adjustments to § 30.7(a) and (b) in the final rule provide additional clarity of the Department's review of SAA State plans for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship that conform to the requirements of this part and anticipates that this will ease the burden on SAAs.
The Department has also accounted for delays and internal processes by allowing an extension for good cause to be sought by the SAA and granted by the Administrator. This balances the Department's goals of effectuating this rule in a timely manner with the understanding that States may need to seek an extension of time from the Administrator should there be barriers to achieving compliance within 1 year of the effective date of this rule. The Department has determined that the SAAs' ability to seek and be granted an extension sufficiently addresses these concerns.
Finally, the Department appreciates that this change will require effort by SAAs and the Department alike. SAAs will be required to update their laws and policies to conform to this part, and OA will be required to devote time and effort to review SAA plans. The Department disagrees, however, that this will detract from its goal of expanding Registered Apprenticeship. On the contrary, the Department has determined the revised part 30 will result in efficiencies and reduced requirements that are well worth any time and effort spent on effectuating this rule and are fully consistent with the goal of expanding Registered Apprenticeship.
Comments:
A commenter expressed concern that it would be challenging for SAAs to ensure program compliance with the proposed rule within 180 days of a State plan being approved, based on their past experiences with seeking statewide changes to apprenticeship programs. The commenter recommended extending the program compliance timeline to 1 year.
Department Response:
The Department appreciates commenters' concern about the ability of sponsors to comply with the new requirements of the State plan within 180 days. Nonetheless, given that the State plan requirements in this final rule are fewer and less burdensome on sponsors than the existing part 30 requirements and that entities are already subject to and required to comply with applicable State and Federal nondiscrimination laws, the Department does not anticipate that there will be a need for additional time. This rule requires that sponsors comply with the nondiscrimination standard in § 30.3. To the extent that the State plan includes any additional requirements specific to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship, such requirements must conform to the requirements of the revised part 30; therefore, the Department anticipates that requirements on sponsors will decrease, and compliance with the State plan will not result in additional burden on sponsors. As such, the Department is finalizing the compliance timeline for programs registered in SAA States at 180 days in this final rule at § 30.7(b)(iv).
4. Comments on Changes to SAA Compliance and Review Requirements in Part 30
Comments:
A commenter expressed concern about changes to provisions related to reviews of SAAs, warning that they would result in regulatory uncertainty for SAAs and adversely impact Registered Apprenticeship programs and apprentices. The commenter recommended DOL establish clear guidelines and process descriptions that would ensure system stability and program continuity, including a description of review metrics, how reviews would be conducted, and available remedies for improvement. The commenter also recommended a description of enforcement mechanisms that include whether penalties would extend beyond loss of recognition and include other impacts such as funding. The commenter further recommended regulatory guidance framing how existing programs and apprentices would be impacted if a State were found to be noncompliant, whether options would be available to programs and apprentices, and the role of OA in that process.
A commenter recommended that the Department clarify a compliance review schedule for SAAs, including frequent program reviews or audits and the provision of actionable technical assistance. The commenter further recommended that the Department include other requirements for SAAs,
(
printed page 70223)
including requiring that SAAs measure program success through equity indices that show the representation of apprentices from underserved demographic groups, publish disaggregated data and center data in determining priorities, making investment decisions, and developing staff trainings and technical assistance programs. The commenter further recommended that the Department require SAAs to conduct regular, anonymized surveys of apprentices to gauge their experiences in Registered Apprenticeship programs, and to address issues that interfere with apprentices' entry into and completion of Registered Apprenticeship programs (citing aptitude tests that, according to the commenter, tend to screen out applicants from underserved groups).
Another commenter expressed support for the potential to ease the burden for small and medium size business sponsors but anticipated an added burden on SAAs to comply with the regulatory changes and a need for technical assistance regarding outreach to populations not traditionally served by Registered Apprenticeship in order to meet the Administration's goal of one million new apprentices.
Department Response:
The Department appreciates that there may be a need for subregulatory guidance, technical assistance, and other cooperation with SAAs to ensure successful implementation of this final rule. The Department notes that OA already conducts SAA reviews for compliance with parts 29 and 30, and such compliance reviews will continue under the revised part 30 requirements. The Department further notes that mechanisms for accountability, review, the processing of complaints, SAA derecognition and associated impacts are addressed by part 29's conforming edits that incorporate an SAA's State plan for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship and other sections of part 30. These mechanisms are reinforced in proposed § 30.7(d) (Retention of authority), which cites to OA's authority in § 29.13 to conduct compliance reviews of all Registered Apprenticeship programs and in §§ 29.8(b) and 29.10 to deregister for Federal purposes an apprenticeship program registered with an SAA, and § 30.7(e) (Derecognition), which cites to § 29.14's derecognition proceedings for SAAs that fail to comply with the requirements of § 30.7. Given the integration into part 29 of the review of SAAs and their State plans for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship, the Department declines to create additional unnecessary and duplicative processes and procedures for review of SAA compliance with part 30 and adopts § 30.7(d) and (e) as proposed.
Finally, with respect to concerns about SAA outreach to populations less familiar with Registered Apprenticeship, the Department is eager to work with States on recruitment of apprentices and remains committed to working with SAAs to reach the goal of 1 million active apprentices in a manner that is merit-based and consistent with Federal law.
H. Section 30.8—Exemptions
The Department proposed to maintain the “Exemptions” provision from the current part 30 at § 30.19. The proposed revisions were intended to reduce burdens on Registered Apprenticeship stakeholders, and the Department determined that preserving the part 30 exemptions supports this objective and maintains the regulatory flexibility embedded in the existing rule. Under the existing provision, which the Department proposed to keep, sponsors were required to submit written requests for exemptions from part 30 requirements to the Registration Agency, which could grant exemptions for good cause. The Department also proposed to retain the requirement that SAAs receiving exemption requests from sponsors in their State obtain OA approval before issuing an exemption. Therefore, proposed § 30.8 reflected the same regulatory text as § 30.19.
Accordingly, for the reasons discussed in the NPRM and in response to comments discussed below, the Department is finalizing the provision as proposed.
1. Religious Exemptions
Comments:
A commenter expressed support for adding a specific religious exemption to the regulations, arguing that religious organizations have protections under the First Amendment, the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, and Title VII, proposing specific regulatory text stating that regulations “do not apply to a religious organization to the extent that application of these regulations would be inconsistent with the religious tenets of the organization,” similar to title IX exemption language.
Another commenter expressed support for religious employer exemptions on the basis of “sex,” “disability,” and “religion” as protected characteristics, and stated that religious employers should be able to invoke the ADA's religious exemption in the apprenticeship context. The commenter maintained that some courts have held that “gender dysphoria” is a disability, despite the exclusion in the ADA and section 7(20)(F) of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973

56

of “gender identity disorders” from the definition of “disability,” and that religious program sponsors would not be able to invoke the ADA's religious exemption, and that program sponsors would be required to accommodate the “disability” of gender dysphoria. Additionally, because of the proposal to remove the language at § 30.3 referring to legal standards and defenses applied under Title VII, the commenter recommended that the Department include an explicit exemption for religious employers from applications of the nondiscrimination rule that conflict with their religious tenets and suggested incorporating language, with necessary revisions, from the religious exemption in title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 and its implementing regulations.

E.O. 14168

Department Response:
The Department appreciates the comments raising concerns about the need for religious exemptions. The Department will take seriously any request for an exemption from this regulation under proposed § 30.8, including those citing religious freedom as the reason supporting the request. Because the Department will, pursuant to this final rule, defer to other enforcement agencies in determining compliance with applicable nondiscrimination laws, it no longer needs to incorporate into part 30 the standards and exemptions from external statutes, such as Title VII and the ADA. As noted earlier in the preamble, the Department will respect the application of religious exemptions as determined by the relevant enforcement agency in determining a sponsor's compliance with proposed § 30.3. As such, the Department does not think a specific exemption for religious sponsors is necessary, particularly as such an exemption would not relieve the sponsor from complying with the applicable
(

In response to some commenters' preference for different terminology, including using “sex” instead of “gender,” the Department agrees that the terminology the Department uses should align with the terminology used in relevant Federal nondiscrimination statutes, such as Title VII. The Department concurs that aligning its language with existing nondiscrimination laws promotes clarity for the regulated community.
2. Other Exemption Comments
Comments:
A commenter urged the Department to clarify the exemption process by providing examples and guidance on when exemptions may be granted, expressing concern that exemptions in industries with prevailing wage projects could create unfair competitive advantages, particularly in high-hazard industries like construction and energy. The commenter recommended developing guidance detailing the exemption process and evaluation criteria.
Department Response:
Under the text of proposed § 30.8, which mirrors the existing exemption provision at § 30.19, exemption requests must be in writing and must identify the provision(s) of part 30 from which the applicant is seeking exemptive relief. The provision further clarifies that all exemption requests to the Registration Agency must demonstrate “good cause” to support the applicant's exemption request.
The Department declines to provide specific examples of permissible exemptions in this final rule, as the exemption provision is meant to provide flexibility to sponsors on a case-by-case basis. The Department notes, however, that an exemption issued pursuant to § 30.8 of this final rule only would extend to requirements covered by part 30 (as has been the case under existing § 30.19). This final rule's exemption provision does not authorize a Registration Agency to grant an exemption from the part 29 requirements, or any other applicable law, including those related to prevailing wages.
I. Section 30.9—Severability
As a prudential measure, the Department has decided to add (at § 30.9) a severability provision to the text of this revised and streamlined part 30. This new provision states that, to the extent that any provision of part 30 is declared invalid by a court of competent jurisdiction, the Department intends for all other provisions of part 30 that are capable of operating in the absence of the specific provision that has been invalidated to remain in effect. The Supreme Court has previously held that a statute or regulation is severable if its separate provisions are “wholly independent of each other” and can operate independently.
Brockett
v.
Spokane Arcades, Inc.,
472 U.S. 491, 502 (1985). In the case of this final rule, the Department takes the position that no other provisions of the revised part 30 would be affected if a particular provision of the regulation is found to be unlawful or invalid. Moreover, the Department expects that courts and regulated parties would be able to apply the remaining provisions of this final rule if one of its provisions was held to be invalid. See
Department of Education et al
v.
Louisiana,
603 U.S. 866, 868 (2024) (
per curiam
) (denying the government's request to stay a preliminary injunction against an entire rule where only parts of the rule were found to be invalid).
J. Technical and Conforming Edits to Part 29
The Department proposed limited technical and conforming amendments to
29 CFR part 29
to align that part with the proposed revisions to
29 CFR part 30
. The Department proposed updating cross-references and terminology in part 29 to reflect the revised nondiscrimination framework in part 30. For example, the Department proposed to amend part 29 at §§ 29.3(b)(2) and 29.5(b)(21) to align with the streamlined nondiscrimination requirements in revised part 30, including referencing the proposed “State plan for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship” in § 29.5(b)(21) and removing other references to requirements from the existing part 30 regulation (such as the equal opportunity pledge and affirmative action requirements) in the part 29 section covering standards of apprenticeship.
The Department proposed revising part 29 at § 29.12 (Complaints) to clarify that allegations of unlawful discrimination—based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, age, disability, genetic information, or other protected characteristics—would be referred by the Registration Agency to the appropriate enforcement authority, consistent with proposed § 30.4. This revision conformed to the proposed structure under which enforcement for discrimination would be handled by agencies with jurisdiction to administer applicable nondiscrimination laws, such as the EEOC, the U.S. Department of Justice, State FEPAs, or other enforcement agencies as appropriate.
The Department proposed amendments to § 29.7 (Apprenticeship Agreement) to reflect the protected characteristics specifically covered by applicable Federal nondiscrimination statutes. As proposed, § 29.7(j) would prohibit discrimination in apprenticeship on the bases of race, color, religion, national origin, sex, age (40 or older), genetic information, and disability, thereby ensuring consistency with the statutory text of Title VII of the Act, the ADEA, the ADA, and the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act.
The Department also proposed modifying § 29.7(l) by removing explicit references to an apprentice's race, sex, ethnicity, and disability status and replacing them with a general request for demographic information. The Department determined that a broad authorization to request “demographic information” would provide greater flexibility for apprenticeship stakeholders and Registration Agencies regarding the collection of demographic information in Registered Apprenticeship.
In addition, the Department proposed edits to the provisions governing SAA recognition and operation. The Department proposed revising §§ 29.13 and 29.14 to require State apprenticeship statutes, nondiscrimination plans, and enforcement procedures to conform to the streamlined Federal requirements in revised part 30. These changes were intended to reduce divergence between OA and SAA jurisdictions, eliminate inconsistent nondiscrimination standards across States, and promote uniform application and enforcement nationwide.
Finally, the Department proposed conforming updates throughout part 29 to replace outdated references and to clarify that nondiscrimination enforcement responsibilities rest with the appropriate governmental entities with jurisdiction to administer Federal or State nondiscrimination laws. These included proposed revisions to § 29.11 (Limitations) to reflect applicable law and Executive Orders, and updates to recordkeeping provisions in §§ 29.13 and 29.14 to align with the proposed updates to the part 30 regulation and the recordkeeping requirements for SAAs that would be necessary under the revised part 30 regulation and its updated requirements for SAAs.

One commenter asked the Department to clarify what demographic information it intends to collect, and recommended collecting information pertaining to veteran status, as it applies to the Post 9-11 Veterans Educational Assistance Act of 2008 (title V of
Pub. L. 110-252
), the Veterans Apprenticeship and Labor Opportunity Reform Act (VALOR Act) (
Pub. L. 115-89
), and the Support for Veterans in Effective Apprenticeships Act (
Pub. L. 116-134
). Another commenter recommended that the Department utilize tools, such as artificial intelligence, to minimize reporting burden, create public dashboards to track this data, and use that data to evaluate the impact of the final rule within 3 years of its implementation and every 5 years thereafter.
Department Response:
The Department understands the comments raised by commenters but disagrees that the conforming edits raise concern for data collection. The Department maintains that a general request for demographic information is consistent with existing practice, and that removing reference to specific categories of demographic information would not adversely affect data quality nor stakeholders' ability to aggregate, analyze, and identify trends, outcomes, and other data-drive insights related to Registered Apprenticeship. The Department expects a general request for apprentices' demographic information will still yield valuable data on apprentices' race, sex, and ethnicity, along with other demographic characteristics that apprentices may report about themselves. In response to one commenter specifically, the Department confirms that it intends to continue to collect information on veteran status. Veteran status is not listed in the description of demographic characteristics at existing § 29.7(l), and as such, the Department's conforming edit to that provision does not alter the section of ETA Form 671, Section II (the apprenticeship agreement form), that provides for the collection of information on apprentices' veteran status, which supports compliance with the VALOR Act and the other laws cited by the commenter.
The Department notes that the collection of additional demographic data at the SAA level is not necessarily precluded under this final rule. However, the Department encourages SAAs to align demographic data collections with the Department's approach and afford stakeholders with flexibility in the collection of demographic data to reduce burdens and challenges associated with requiring that sponsors solicit particular demographic information in apprenticeship agreements.
In response to one commenter's request that the Department review and make accessible data to evaluate the impacts of the rule in the years following publication, the Department notes it will continue to monitor and evaluate the impacts of this rule (and other policies implemented throughout the National Apprenticeship System) using relevant apprenticeship data.

K. Final Rule Implementation
Under the NPRM, the Department proposed requiring SAAs to submit a State plan for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship that demonstrates that the State's apprenticeship laws, regulations, policies, and operational procedures related to the nondiscrimination obligation conform only to the requirements of this part. The NPRM required the plan's submission within 1 year of the effective date of the final rule and provided that extensions may be granted for good cause by the OA Administrator. The proposed rule further stipulated that SAAs must require all apprenticeship programs registered with the State for Federal purposes to comply with the requirements of the State's plan within 180 days from the date that OA provides written approval of the State plan for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship.
The NPRM did not include a specific transition date for sponsors registered with OA directly to comply with the new rule. In this final rule, the Department clarifies that these sponsors are expected to comply with the final rule when it becomes effective 60 days after its publication in the

. In addition, the Department reiterates that it has changed the provision at § 30.7 of this final rule to require that SAAs' laws, regulations, and policies specific to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship conform to the requirements of this part.

1. Effective Date and Timeline for Implementation
Comments:
A few commenters expressed concern that the 1-year implementation timeline for SAAs to submit State plans for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship that reflect the proposed rule's requirements would not be sufficient. The commenters remarked that State processes that would be required for full implementation of the final rule include public comment and public hearings by legislative bodies and enacting legislation to revise statutory provisions that conflict with the rule, a process that can vary by State and may require longer than 1 year. The commenters provided several suggestions for extending the implementation timeline, including extending to 2 years or allowing for two legislative sessions.
Department Response:
The Department maintains that 1 year is sufficient for SAAs to comply with the final regulation, especially given the final rule adopts a “conform to” instead of a “conform only to” standard for State plans for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship. Additionally, through a review of relevant State laws, regulations, and policies, the Department determined that many SAAs are presently complying with the requirements of current part 30 because they incorporate the Federal part 30 regulation by reference in their State laws, regulations, or policies. Therefore, these States will not need to undertake State legislative or administrative rulemaking, or other processes, to comply with and implement the final rule.
For States that will require updates to State laws, regulations, or other policies to implement this final rule, the Department has determined that the 1-year implementation timeline is sufficient for States to make any such changes. Because of the nature of the revisions to part 30, any updates to State laws, regulations, or policies would primarily involve the removal of elements that are no longer required by part 30. The Department acknowledges that changes to State laws or regulations may require additional time, and the final rule accounts for this possibility by providing the OA Administrator with the authority to grant extensions of the implementation timeline for good cause. The Department intends to provide extensions for good cause to any State that needs an extension of the implementation timeline to make updates to State laws, regulations, and policies if the State is making good faith efforts to comply with this final rule.

29 CFR 29.14(e)
provides such a process and is appropriate to address this potential scenario. The Department maintains that the 30 days provided under § 29.14(e) is sufficient for sponsors to request registration with OA. Finally, the Department confirms that it will not pursue any enforcement or punitive actions not currently contemplated under the existing apprenticeship regulations against program sponsors or SAAs.

Comments:

29 CFR part 30
accounts for only 0.13 percent of total sponsor costs and noted that sponsors generally do not identify regulatory compliance as a major barrier to program operation. Some of the commenters further stated that, based on their estimate of an average annual total cost of program delivery of $80,768 per apprentice, compliance with part 30 amounts to approximately $102 per apprentice annually. The commenters also referenced an analysis indicating that the NPRM's estimate of regulatory compliance at registration is 1.88 times the total median registration costs reported by employers and more than 37 percent of total mean registration costs, concluding that the NPRM's characterization of part 30 as a “substantial barrier to employer entry and program sustainability” is incorrect.
Department Response:
In response to these comments, the Department acknowledges the data and comparisons submitted but disagrees with the conclusion that existing part 30 requirements are not burdensome. In the Department's view, the 2016 final rule imposed excessive administrative requirements, as well as affirmative action obligations that are legally vulnerable, and that impede the goal of apprenticeship expansion. Revisions to part 30 are necessary to eliminate a duplicative EEO framework that applies only to Registered Apprenticeship. This final rule therefore adopts a streamlined approach consistent with the Administration's directive to reduce regulatory burdens. Recent U.S. Supreme Court decisions have clarified the legal limitations on race- and sex-based measures under the Equal Protection Clause and Federal nondiscrimination laws. These developments raise serious questions about the validity of certain affirmative-action-related provisions in part 30, particularly those that incentivize or induce sponsors to make decisions based on protected characteristics. In light of recent court decisions, the Department has determined that revising part 30 is necessary to ensure the regulatory framework for Registered Apprenticeship is fully aligned with nondiscrimination standards and legal precedent.
The Department also notes that comparisons expressing part 30 compliance costs as a share of total apprenticeship program costs are of limited value. The majority of program costs identified in the analyses cited by commenters consist of apprentice wages, which are associated with well-documented benefits to sponsors. These wages lead to increased productivity and improve long-term workforce development, which are the benefit returns that are under study in the source provided by the commentor. By contrast, the administrative and affirmative action obligations imposed by part 30 represent non-productive overhead costs that do not generate operational benefits. Accordingly, even when expressed as a relatively small share of total program expenditures, compliance costs may nonetheless constitute a meaningful barrier to employer entry and program sustainability, particularly for small or first-time sponsors, because these costs are not an investment with meaningful returns to the sponsor. The Department therefore does not agree that a per-apprentice compliance cost of approximately $102 annually is inconsequential, or that such figures undermine the NPRM's conclusion that existing part 30 requirements impose a substantial and disproportionate administrative burden. The Department maintains that the NPRM's estimates reflect the best available data on the administrative activities required of sponsors under part 30 and that the projected cost savings from removing these requirements remain appropriate.

The commenter also suggested that routine updates to anti-discrimination training, under the current regulation, do not require extensive time or the senior-level involvement assumed in the Department's calculations.

Additionally, the Department acknowledges the cyclical administrative burden related to the preparation, review, and implementation of updated materials. Accordingly, the Department has not adjusted the cost estimates in response to this comment.

Comments:
Commenters expressed concern that the proposed requirement that SAA nondiscrimination laws “conform only to” part 30 could undermine State autonomy, conflict with the cooperative federalism framework, and create uncertainty regarding the interaction between Federal and State requirements, including whether States could maintain or enforce additional EEO provisions and how potential conflicts would be resolved. Several commenters requested clarification on the scope of the requirement and its application to State policies and procedures, while others emphasized the importance of preserving flexibility for States to address local labor market conditions and maintain broader apprenticeship program authorities.
Department Response:
As discussed earlier in the preamble, the Department revised the regulatory text to require that State laws “conform to” part 30. Retaining a “conform to” standard preserves State flexibility by allowing SAAs to maintain or adopt requirements that are compatible with, but not limited to, Federal rules. This approach avoids Federal preemption of State policies while maintaining Departmental oversight to ensure consistency with baseline Federal standards. Because the existing CFR framework already requires State plans and programs to “conform to” Federal requirements, this provision does not introduce new compliance obligations. As a result, the final rule is not expected to impose incremental costs or generate additional regulatory impacts relative to the current baseline.

5. Cost Savings
The Department first presents the cost savings that will accrue under the final rule. Most of these cost savings accrue to the sponsors of Registered Apprenticeship programs because the final rule eliminates several requirements for sponsors under the current part 30 regulations. The savings from eliminating these requirements are discussed in greater detail below.
Eliminating One-Time Costs for Sponsors of New Registered Apprenticeship Programs
Under the current part 30 regulation, sponsors must post their equal opportunity pledge on bulletin boards and through electronic media, such that it is accessible to all apprentices and applicants to apprenticeship programs. This requirement imposes costs on sponsors operating a Registered Apprenticeship program for the first time, as they are required to take staff time to post this pledge. Under Title VII
[
63
]
and the ADA,
[
64
]
employers are already required to post a notice summarizing Federal laws prohibiting discrimination in employment. Removing this comparable requirement from part 30 would therefore lead to savings for new sponsors of Registered Apprenticeship programs without depriving apprentices of crucial information about their employment rights.
The Department assumed that new sponsors would choose to put up a physical copy of the pledge and also post it on their website. The Department assumed it takes a sponsor 5 minutes (0.08 hours) to post the pledge and that this task is performed by an administrative assistant. To calculate the hourly compensation rate, the Department used the median hourly wage rate for Secretaries and Administrative Assistants, Except Legal, Medical, and Executive (Standard Occupational Classification code 43-6014) of $22.70,

[

We multiplied the time estimate for this provision by the hourly compensation rate to obtain a total labor cost per sponsor of $2.89 ($36.10 × 0.08). To estimate the materials cost, the Department assumed that the pledge is one page, and that the cost per page for photocopying is $0.10, resulting in a materials cost of $0.10 ($0.10 × 1) per sponsor. The total cost of putting up a physical copy of the pledge per sponsor is therefore $2.99 ($2.89+$0.10). Additionally, the Department also assumed it takes a sponsor 10 minutes (0.17 hours) to post the pledge on its website and that this task is performed by a web developer at an hourly compensation rate of $72.57.

Eliminating Ongoing Costs for All Sponsors
The current part 30 regulations also require that each sponsor conduct orientation and periodic information sessions for apprentices, journeyworkers who directly supervise apprentices, and other individuals connected with the administration or operation of the sponsor's apprenticeship program to inform and remind such individuals of the sponsor's EEO policy with regard to apprenticeship (current § 30.3(b)(2)(iii)). Under current § 30.3(b)(4)(i), sponsors are also required to provide anti-harassment training, which we assume is incorporated into periodic orientation and information sessions. This training must include active participation by trainees, such as attending a training session in person or completing an interactive training online and includes, at a minimum, communications to apprentices and journeyworkers who directly supervise apprentices that harassing conduct will not be tolerated, the definition of harassment and types of conduct that constitute harassment, and the right to file a harassment complaint.
Using data from RAPIDS, the Department calculated that there are on average 25.4 apprentices per sponsor, rounded down to 25 apprentices per program.

Additionally, under the current part 30, all sponsors are required to reach out to a variety of recruitment sources, including organizations that serve individuals with disabilities, to ensure universal recruitment (current § 30.3(b)(3)). Sponsors are required to develop a list of recruitment sources that generate referrals of women, minorities, and persons with disabilities with contact information for each source. Further, sponsors are required to notify these sources in advance of any apprenticeship opportunities and while a firm deadline is not set, the part 30 regulations suggest 30 days' notice if possible. This current outreach protocol may lead employers to incur costs due to the additional delay it introduces into the hiring process. The Department, however, does not have enough information to estimate the potential costs sponsors currently incur from these delays.
The kinds of activities sponsors engage in to satisfy this outreach requirement include distributing announcements and flyers detailing job prospects, holding seminars, and visiting some of the sources who are likely able to provide access to designated groups. The Department assumed that the cost to sponsors to distribute information to designated groups will be the labor cost to comply with this provision. We also assumed that the activity to satisfy this provision will be performed by a human resources manager and an administrative assistant with hourly compensation rates of $113.78 and $36.10, respectively. We assumed this task takes 30 minutes (0.5 hour) of a human resources manager's time and 30 minutes (0.5 hour) of an administrative assistant's time per targeted source. We calculated the cost of this provision per affected sponsor by multiplying the time each staff member devotes to this task by their associated hourly compensation rates. We then multiplied the total labor cost by the assumed number of outreach sources (5) and by the total number of sponsors. All sponsors are assumed to conduct this outreach in all years. We estimated the cost savings from eliminating this outreach provision at $10.05 million in the first year, with an annualized savings from the elimination of this cost for sponsors at $10.62 million with 3 percent discounting and $10.58 million with 7 percent discounting.
Savings From Eliminating Costs of Performing Utilization and Workforce Analysis Costs for Sponsors With Five or More Apprentices
The current part 30 regulations require sponsors with five or more apprentices to establish utilization goals for women and minorities (current §§ 30.5 through 30.7). First, sponsors conduct a workforce analysis to identify the racial, sex, and ethnic composition of their apprentices. Second, an availability analysis will establish a benchmark against which the existing composition of apprentices will be compared. Sponsors establish utilization goals and engage in targeted outreach, recruitment, and retention efforts when the sponsor's utilization of women, Hispanics or Latinos, or individuals in racial minority groups are “significantly less than would be reasonably expected given the availability of such individuals for apprenticeship.” Registration Agencies work closely with sponsors during compliance reviews to assist in the development of an availability analysis and setting or reassessing utilization goals for race, sex, and ethnicity. The Department also provides a data tool to assist in the collection and analysis of relevant demographic data for the purposes of goal setting.
The Department determined that eliminating the utilization goal requirement will create three types of cost savings: Savings from the elimination of costs associated with the familiarization with the data tool for new sponsors, savings from the elimination of costs associated with the workforce analysis, and savings from
(
printed page 70233)
the elimination of costs associated with the utilization analysis.
To quantify the savings from the elimination of costs associated with new sponsors' familiarization with the data tool, the Department assumed that new sponsors with five or more apprentices (384 in 2026) will incur one hour of human resources manager labor ($113.78 per hour) to familiarize the organization with the tool. We estimated this will create $43,700 in cost savings from the elimination of these tool familiarization costs in the first year of 2026. We repeated this calculation for the following years. We estimated that removing the utilization goal requirement from part 30 therefore creates an annualized savings of $54,729 with 3 percent discounting and $53,872 with 7 percent discounting from the elimination of new sponsors' tool familiarization costs.
To calculate the savings from removing the workforce analysis requirements from part 30, the Department determined that the methodology for conducting workforce analyses under the current part 30 results in 2 hours of human resources manager labor ($113.78 per hour) for all sponsors with five or more apprentices (7,813 in 2026). Under the current part 30 regulations, all sponsors with five or more apprentices must conduct workforce analysis every 2.5 years. In calculating the savings for each year, the Department divided the number of applicable sponsors in each year by 2.5 to reflect the assumption that sponsors would have conducted the analysis once per the 2.5-year timeline. This means that in any given year 40 percent of sponsors with five or more apprentices would have conducted the workforce analysis, or that it would have taken 2.5 years to have these sponsors conduct new workforce analyses. We estimated the cost savings from eliminating the requirement to conduct workforce analyses in the first year at $711,149 (7,813 × 0.4 × $113.78 × 2 hours). We repeated this calculation for the following years using the appropriate number of sponsors in any given year, resulting in an annualized savings from the removal of the workforce analysis requirement of $890,620 with 3 percent discounting and $876,680 with 7 percent discounting for sponsors.
To calculate the savings from the removal of the utilization analysis requirement, the Department determined that the utilization analysis resulted in 0.5 hour of human resources manager time ($113.78 per hour) for all sponsors with five or more apprentices (7,813 in 2026) every 5 years (because the utilization analysis is completed in support of the compliance review process, which has typically been performed at 5-year intervals for programs in OA States). The cost savings from removing the requirement to conduct utilization analyses in the first year is $88,894 (0.5 hour × $113.78 × (7,813/5 years)). We repeated this calculation for the following years, and the savings to sponsors from not having to conduct utilization analyses results in an annualized cost savings of $111,327 with 3 percent discounting and $109,585 with 7 percent discounting for sponsors.
In addition to the normal outreach, recruitment, and retention activities required of all sponsors under current part § 30.3(b), current § 30.8 requires a sponsor of an apprenticeship program to engage in targeted outreach, recruitment, and retention, if: (1) the sponsor's utilization analyses revealed underutilization of a particular designated group or groups of individuals pursuant to current § 30.6; or (2) the sponsor has determined pursuant to current § 30.7(e) that there are impediments to EEO for individuals with disabilities. We assumed that this additional outreach happens in the same manner as the universal outreach discussed above.
We assumed that the current cost to sponsors to distribute information about apprenticeship opportunities to organizations serving individuals with disabilities is the labor cost. We also assumed that the labor for this provision will be performed by a human resources manager and an administrative assistant with hourly compensation rates of $113.78 and $36.10, respectively. The Department estimated that this dissemination task takes 30 minutes (0.5 hour) of a human resources manager's time and 30 minutes (0.5 hour) of an administrative assistant's time per targeted source. We estimated the cost of the current provision per affected sponsor is the time each staff member devotes to this task multiplied by their associated hourly compensation rates. Based on this calculation we estimated a labor cost of $74.94 (($113.78 × 0.5) + ($36.10 × 0.5)) per source.
We estimated that the number of sponsors who need to engage in targeted outreach and recruitment for at least one relevant demographic group is 95 percent of the total sponsors with five or more apprentices. We understand this is likely an over-estimate of the number of sponsors that must conduct this outreach, as more than 5 percent of sponsors may meet their utilization goal for all demographic groups and may not have to conduct outreach; however, the Department does not have complete or reliable data to produce an alternative estimate. We then multiplied this total labor cost by the number of sponsors with five or more apprentices (7,813 in 2026), the share of sponsors that undertake a utilization analysis in any given year (20 percent), and the share of sponsors that are estimated to identify underutilization or problem areas in one or more of the relevant demographic groups (95 percent).

The cost savings from eliminating this requirement is equal to these estimated costs since sponsors will no longer need to conduct this outreach. We repeated this calculation for the following years using the appropriate number of sponsors in any given year.
