Non-Quantified Cost Savings
In addition to the cost savings discussed above, there are several other cost savings from streamlining the nondiscrimination requirements under part 30 that are not included in the Department's quantitative analysis. Under the final rule, sponsors will benefit from a more streamlined and less complex part 30 regulation, reducing confusion and the time required to answer questions or address confusion regarding compliance requirements. The final rule will also benefit sponsors by removing the legally questionable components of the current part 30 regulations, thereby eliminating legal risk that sponsors could be sued or legally challenged for actions taken to comply with part 30, such as setting utilization goals regarding the race or sex of program participants. Additionally, the final rule will eliminate the costs associated with discrimination complaint investigations involving obtaining full complaint information, gathering relevant materials (
e.g.,
interview statements, transcripts, pertinent documents), and developing a narrative report of the allegations and investigation findings.
[
78
]
Since the final rule reduces the barriers for sponsors to create and operate Registered Apprenticeship programs, it may also lead to the registration of additional apprenticeship programs. The enhanced growth of Registered Apprenticeship programs could improve access for individuals to enroll in apprenticeships and receive high-quality job training—boosting their long-term earnings and having spill-over effects in the local economy. The proliferation of Registered Apprenticeship programs also could benefit local employers, as the training of additional skilled apprentices could expand local talent pools and allow employers to more easily fill positions for in-demand occupations.
(
printed page 70235)
Finally, chief among these cost savings is the elimination of regulatory provisions that have the effect of encouraging the use of race- and sex-based preferences in apprenticeship selection and advancement decisions. By removing these requirements, the final rule promotes a return to individual, merit-based evaluation, consistent with the principle that all Americans should be treated as individuals rather than as members of demographic groups. This shift will strengthen public confidence in the fairness of the apprenticeship system, reduce legal uncertainty, and encourage broader participation by sponsors who may have been deterred by the prior rule's prescriptive and group-based mandates.
While these cost savings could be substantial, the Department did not estimate these cost savings because of data limitations that impede our ability to accurately quantify these cost savings. Collectively, however, these cost savings reinforce the Department's conclusion that the advantages of this proposal outweigh any potential costs.
6. Costs
Below, the Department presents the costs estimated to be incurred by relevant stakeholders, mainly program sponsors and SAAs, from this final rule. These costs are broken into three major categories: costs to sponsors and SAAs of familiarizing themselves with the regulatory change, costs to sponsors and Registration Agencies of updating standards for compliance, and costs to SAAs of updating State plans for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship. The following sections present estimates for each of these cost categories imposed by the final rule.
Familiarization With Regulatory Change
To estimate the cost of rule familiarization for sponsors, we multiplied the number of program sponsors in 2026 (26,810), the first year in which the change will be in effect, by the amount of time required to read the new rule (which we estimate to be 1 hour) and by the average hourly compensation of a private-sector human resources manager with fringe benefits included ($113.78). This cost is only incurred in the first year of the change, so the total cost to sponsors for time spent on familiarization is approximately $3.05 million in labor costs.
In response to public comments, the Department also estimated the cost of rule familiarization for SAAs. The Department assumed that for SAAs, both a human resources manager and a lawyer would review the regulatory change in the first year. The Department estimated the cost of rule familiarization by SAAs by multiplying the number of SAA states (33) by the amount of time required to read the new rule (1 hour) and by the sum of the average hourly compensation of a public-sector human resources manager ($92.04) and a State-level lawyer ($98.84). The total cost to SAAs for time spent on familiarization is approximately $6,299 in labor costs.
[
79
]
There are no familiarization costs for future years because sponsors and SAAs will already be familiar with the rule and new sponsors would have had to familiarize themselves with the prior part 30 regulations. Therefore, we estimated the total cost of initial rule familiarization of $3.06 million in labor costs, realized entirely in the first year.
Updating Standards for Compliance
Pre-existing sponsors of Registered Apprenticeship programs will also need to develop language or make adjustments and updates to existing standards to comply with the changes to part 30. The Department estimated that this will be a one-time cost only imposed on pre-existing sponsors that already had standards prior to the publication of the final rule. The Department estimated that updating standards to comply with part 30 will mainly involve removing items currently required by part 30 and therefore estimated the burden will be minimal. Accordingly, the Department estimated the average response time for the projected 26,466 pre-existing apprenticeship programs in 2026 to ensure standards comply with part 30 is 20 minutes (0.33 hours).
[
80
]
We estimated an annual burden of 8,734 hours (26,466 × 0.33). The Department assumed the standards will be updated by an administrative assistant. Therefore, the Department estimated a one-time cost of $315,266 (8,734 × $36.10).
Registration Agency staff are responsible for reviewing and providing input on a sponsor's apprenticeship program standards to ensure compliance with the requirements in part 30. Registration Agencies will therefore incur a one-time cost to review updated standards for pre-existing programs. The Department estimated that the review and input provided by Registration Agency staff for program sponsors will take 10 minutes, which resulted in 4,499 annual burden hours (26,466 × 0.17 hours). Using the State employee wage calculated above, we estimated a total cost to Registration Agencies of this one-time review of $399,891 (4,499 hours × $88.88).
Revision of State Plan
The process of updating a State plan (under current part 30, a “State EEO plan,” and in the final rule, a “State plan for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship”) may potentially involve various people at different stages of implementation. Updating the plan will include drafting the new plan, ensuring conformity and that State laws and practices do not exceed the final rule, and completing all administrative procedures that may apply, such as revisions to a State's apprenticeship law or policy that may require a public notice-and- comment period, training for SAA staff on the revised State plan, and outreach to program sponsors to inform them of the relevant aspects of the revised State plan once it has been approved by the Department. The
(
printed page 70236)
updates to State plans include changing language and existing requirements such that they align with the regulatory changes herein. To calculate the costs, the Department assumed that the process to revise the State plan will take a full year of effort (2,080 hours) to complete.
[
81
]
The Department acknowledges that State plan revisions can involve multi-stage processes and varying legislative timelines, but these assumptions used in the analysis represent the best data available and the Department's best estimate for updating the existing State plan. As noted above, many State apprenticeship laws incorporate part 30 requirements through referencing the Federal regulations and will not need to be updated, likely leading to lower costs for some SAA States than others. However, the Department assumes that all SAA States will experience the same cost. As a result, the Department is likely overstating the true cost of revising State plans. For simplicity, we assumed that an SAA human resources manager will complete the task at an hourly compensation rate of $88.88.
[
82
]
Based on this calculation we estimated a one-time cost of $6.10 million in the first year (2,080 hours × $88.88 × 33 SAA States).
[
83
]
Complaint Referral Procedures
Section 30.4, Complaint referral procedures, directs the Registration Agencies to refer complainants alleging illegal discrimination against apprentices to the appropriate enforcement agency. Since the complaint process is not a new process, the Department does not expect that these provisions will result in any incremental change in the burden on Registration Agencies as these agencies are already required to refer complaints to other EEO agencies under current § 30.14(c)(3). Therefore, the Department does not estimate any additional costs associated with complaint referrals under the final rule.
Nondiscrimination Compliance Reviews and Enforcement
In response to public comment, the section on nondiscrimination compliance reviews and enforcement (§ 30.5) within the final rule adds a requirement that sponsors disclose to the Registration Agency any final determinations by an enforcement entity or court with jurisdiction over an applicable nondiscrimination law that the sponsor violated such law with respect to an apprentice or applicant for apprenticeship. Sponsors must provide this written disclosure within 60 days of the final determination and must include, at a minimum, copies of relevant final determinations, judgments, decisions, and orders. Sponsors must also include, as part of this disclosure, a description of any remedies prescribed by the enforcement entity or court to address the violation.
The Department expects that this requirement may impose some administrative burden on sponsors in the limited circumstances in which a final, non-appealable determination of a violation of a nondiscrimination law has been made. In such cases, a sponsor may need to review the final determination and related orders, prepare a written disclosure to the Registration Agency, and describe any prescribed remedies. The Department expects these activities will involve legal, managerial, or administrative staff time, depending on the sponsor's size, organizational structure, and the complexity of the final determination or ordered remedy.
The Department is not aware of prior instances in which sponsors have been subject to final, non-appealable determinations of nondiscrimination violations that would trigger this requirement, and it expects such events to occur infrequently. The Department does not have data that would allow it to estimate how often enforcement entities or courts will issue such determinations involving apprentices or applicants, nor how often those determinations will result in prescribed remedies that sponsors must describe to the Registration Agency or the extent to which any such disclosures will vary in complexity. Because the requirement is triggered only when an external enforcement entity or court has issued a final determination of a nondiscrimination violation relating to an apprentice or applicant, the Department cannot estimate whether this requirement will be triggered frequently, infrequently, or at all for many sponsors. For these reasons, the Department discusses the potential administrative costs of this disclosure requirement qualitatively but does not include a quantified estimate in the RIA.

8. Regulatory Alternatives
In addition to the final rule, the Department considered three regulatory alternatives: (a) repeal part 30 entirely; (b) only eliminate the additional affirmative action requirements pertaining to sponsors with five or more apprentices while retaining the reminder of the 2016 final rule; and (c) take no action (
i.e.,
leave the 2016 final rule intact).
The Department conducted economic analyses of the three alternatives to better understand their costs and cost savings and the implied tradeoffs (in terms of the costs and cost savings that would be realized) relative to the final rule. Below is a discussion of each alternative along with an estimation of their costs and cost savings. All costs and cost savings use the 2016 final rule as the baseline for the analysis.
Repeal Part 30 Entirely
This alternative yields many of the same cost savings as the final rule but also would remove the cost to Registration Agencies (OA or SAAs) related to the referral of complaints, leading to additional cost savings.
The Department assumed that, when a Registration Agency receives a complaint, it takes 15 minutes (0.25 hours) for a public-sector human resources manager ($88.88 per hour) to refer the complaint to the correct entity. The Department estimated that 421 apprentices will file a complaint in the first year and that the number of complaints rises by 9 percent each year.
[
84
]
Based on this assumption, the Department estimated that the savings to Registration Agencies from not having to refer complaints would be $37,507 in the first year. The Department estimated that this would have an annualized savings of $56,428 and $54,889 (at 3 percent and 7 percent discounting, respectively).
Additionally, removing part 30 would remove the costs associated with deregistering programs and derecognizing SAAs that are violating part 30. However, instance in which a program or an SAA has been deregistered or derecognized because of failure to comply with part 30 (current §§ 30.15, 30.16, and 30.18(d)) are rare. The Department therefore assumed that removing the deregistration or
(
printed page 70238)
derecognition components of the current part 30 rule would create minimal to no cost savings. The Department estimated that the cost savings of this alternative would therefore be the same in each year as the final rule, with additional cost savings from the elimination of referral requirements.
In estimating costs, the Department expects that the elimination of part 30 entirely would remove conformity across the Registered Apprenticeship system by creating an inconsistent regulatory framework across states. If some States left their current apprenticeship affirmative action laws in place, it may be harder for sponsors to navigate and comply with this system and these sponsors may not receive the same amount of regulatory relief. This lack of conformity would therefore create confusion and hinder the deregulatory goals of the rulemaking from being achieved on a nationwide basis. Additionally, if some states retained the use of race- and sex-based preferences in apprenticeship selection and advancement decisions, the apprenticeship system in these states would continue to conflict with the merit-based principles that the apprenticeship system, and overall American workforce, should represent.
Eliminating part 30 entirely also would remove an important standard of apprenticeship that was designed to safeguard the welfare of apprentices. As mentioned previously, a Registration Agency's grant of registration to an apprenticeship program serves as an official recognition of that program's overall quality and represents the conferral of a valuable governmental benefit upon the program sponsor. Accordingly, the Department takes the position that there should be appropriate sanctions available (such as program deregistration) if it is determined that a sponsor has engaged in illegal discriminatory conduct against the apprentices enrolled in its program. Rescinding part 30 entirely would remove this important quality safeguard protecting the welfare of apprentices and the mechanism for holding sponsors accountable for illegal discrimination.
While the Department expects that the costs associated with a lack of conformity and conflicts with merit principles could be substantial, these costs are largely intangible and would be difficult to estimate. As a result, the Department estimated that the only monetized costs would be the one-time cost of removing references to part 30 in apprenticeship program standards, which we estimated to be $715,157, and due to data and other limitations referenced above, there would be no quantifiable costs to repealing part 30 entirely because States would not have to submit updated State plans and sponsors would not need to familiarize themselves with the rule change. Take No Action
This alternative yielded no additional costs or cost savings to society because it does not deviate from the baseline, that is, the 2016 final rule. However, the Department notes that taking no action would prevent the cost savings that would accrue from this final rule. In addition to decreasing the burden on sponsors and Registration Agencies, chief among the cost savings from the final rule is the elimination of regulatory provisions that have the effect of encouraging the use of race- and sex-based preferences in apprenticeship selection and advancement decisions. By removing these requirements, the final rule promotes a return to individual, merit-based evaluation, consistent with the principle that all Americans should be treated as individuals rather than as members of demographic groups. Without this change, the Department is concerned that the public's confidence in the fairness of the apprenticeship system could be undermined, that legal uncertainty would remain for current sponsors, and that prospective sponsors may be deterred by the 2016 final rule's prescriptive and group-based mandates.
Additionally, as noted throughout the preamble, the Department anticipates that the removal of these burdensome requirements from part 30 will spur further growth of the National Apprenticeship System, providing more opportunities for American workers to up-skill and for employers to fill their workforce shortages. While the Department has not monetized these benefits due to data limitations, they are likely to be significant. However, if the Department took no action and did not streamline the part 30 regulation, these benefits would not occur.
B. Regulatory Flexibility Act, Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996, and
Executive Order 13272
(Proper Consideration of Small Entities in Agency Rulemaking)
The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980,
[
86
]
as amended by subtitle D of SBREFA, requires agencies to prepare an initial regulatory flexibility analysis when proposing, and a final regulatory flexibility analysis when issuing, regulations that will have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
The Department conducted the analysis below of the burden on small entities from the proposed rule, and based on that analysis, certifies that the costs of this rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
1. Why Action Is Being Taken
The Department has determined that this deregulatory action is necessary to remove administrative barriers to participation in Registered Apprenticeship. As described throughout the preamble for this final rule, in the Department's view, this final rule's changes to the regulation at
29 CFR part 30
will significantly reduce administrative burdens for existing program sponsors, and will alleviate concerns expressed by employers (including small businesses) regarding the amount of administrative burden they would have to take on to participate in Registered Apprenticeship. The Department is finalizing these changes to the regulation at
29 CFR part 30
because these outcomes will help accelerate the expansion of Registered Apprenticeship, in line with the Administration's and the Department's ambitious goals to grow the system, including in industries and sectors where Registered Apprenticeship is not currently widespread. In addition, the Department is finalizing this deregulatory action in light of the Administration's call for Federal agencies to review their regulations and remove regulations that impose undue or unnecessary burdens on stakeholders. Finally, as discussed throughout the preamble in depth, the Departments finds that the existing part 30 regulations impose mandates that may induce the utilization of race and sex-based preferences in a manner that
(
printed page 70240)
is unlawful and in direct conflict with controlling Supreme Court precedent. Accordingly, the Department is removing these requirements.
2. Objectives of, and Legal Basis for, the Final Rule
A primary objective of the final rule is to alleviate administrative burden for Registered Apprenticeship stakeholders and promote a more straightforward framework for the regulated community to participate in the system and maintain compliance with the governing regulations (at
29 CFR parts 29
and
30
). In addition, this final rule seeks to eliminate a duplicative and ineffective (and, in light of recent case law, legally questionable) regulatory framework for nondiscrimination protections in Registered Apprenticeship. These objectives align with the broader goals of the Administration and the Department to identify and modify burdensome regulations, preserve limited enforcement resources, and keep pace with evolving issues in nondiscrimination law. The NAA stands as the Department's statutory basis for promulgating regulations on apprenticeship.

5. Alternatives to the Final Rule
Regarding significant alternatives to the final rule that accomplish the objectives of applicable statutes and minimize any significant economic impact of the final rule on small entities, there are limited options. Repealing part 30 entirely would still require sponsors that are small entities to update their standards to remove reference to part 30, costing $11.91 per sponsor. There could be lower to no rule familiarization costs for small entities if part 30 was removed entirely, since there would be no rule that entities would have to be familiarized with, but sponsors would still need to be informed of the change and may review the
Federal Register

However, the Department is concerned that removing part 30 entirely would prevent conformity across the National Apprenticeship System, as some states may choose to impose additional requirements for sponsors to conduct legally questionable affirmative action or other EEO activities that expand beyond the scope of the Department's proposed part 30 rule. If part 30 was repealed entirely and states were to impose additional EEO requirements, these new requirements and the resulting confusion from a patchwork of different requirements across jurisdictions could ultimately lead to greater costs for small entities.
[
97
]
Alternatively, the Department considered publishing a direct final rule or an interim final rule to make changes to the part 30 regulation. However, the Department determined that these approaches to rulemaking would have given smaller entities no advanced notice of changes to the part 30 regulation, given that the changes would take effect immediately upon (or soon after) publication, and would have denied small entities the opportunity to provide robust feedback on the changes. Accordingly, the Department determined notice-and-comment rulemaking to be more appropriate, in part because it would allow the Department to better account for small businesses' viewpoint and needs.

E.
Executive Order 13132
(Federalism)
The Department has reviewed this final rule in accordance with
E.O. 13132
and found that it will have Federalism implications because it will have substantial direct effects on States. As stated in the Federalism analysis that accompanied the Department's NPRM, matters of Federalism in the National Apprenticeship System are primarily related to the regulatory requirements established in part 29, Labor Standards for Registration of Apprenticeship Programs, which establishes the requirements for the recognition of SAAs as Registration Agencies. However, this final rule's revisions to the part 30 regulation also have direct effect on a State's method of administering Registered Apprenticeship for Federal purposes. In particular, the final rule requires a State that seeks to obtain or maintain recognition as a Registration Agency to submit State apprenticeship legislation, regulations, policies, and operational procedures that pertain specifically to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship to the Department so that the Department may assess whether any such laws, regulations, policies, and operational procedures conform to the revised part 30 regulation.
The Department has determined that requiring States to submit State laws, policies, regulations, and procedures that pertain specifically to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship to the Department is essential to ensure that SAAs conform to the new requirements of part 30. OA regularly consults and collaborates with State partners and organizations, including on matters pertaining to the Federal regulations governing Registered Apprenticeship at
29 CFR parts 29
and
30
. More specifically, such engagement with State partners often relates to States' conformity with these regulations, in particular those States with State agencies that have been recognized (or are seeking recognition) as SAAs that serve as the Registration Agency responsible for registering apprenticeship programs for Federal purposes in the State. These engagements are critical for determining whether the Department should confer the distinct responsibility of acting as a Registration Agency to a State agency. The Department and OA will continue consulting and collaborating with State partners, which the Department views as central to OA's role in promoting and maintaining quality Registered Apprenticeship programs.
Comments:
The Department did not receive any comments on its Federalism analysis required under
E.O. 13132
. The Department did receive several comments raising Federalism concerns in the context of the Department's proposal to require SAAs to “conform only to” the part 30 requirements in proposed § 30.7. As discussed above in addressing SAA requirements in § 30.7, the Department has considered this issue and has determined to change the language in § 30.7 of this final rule to require that States' laws, regulations, policies, and procedures specific to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship “conform to” to the part 30 regulation. In addition, in this final rule, the Department has made additional clarifications regarding the scope of the Department's analysis of State laws, regulations, policies, and procedures, specifically clarifying that the Department only will assess those laws, regulations, policies, and procedures specific to nondiscrimination in Registered Apprenticeship in determining whether the Department will confer recognition to a State agency as a Registration Agency for Federal purposes.

§ 30.1
Purpose and applicability.
(a)
Purpose.
The purpose of this part is to establish a uniform Federal standard prohibiting illegal discrimination against apprentices (including applicants for apprenticeship) in registered apprenticeship programs. To achieve this purpose, this part sets forth nondiscrimination requirements for program sponsors and State Apprenticeship Agencies (SAAs), and clarifies the scope and content of compliance reviews, compliance assistance, and enforcement actions by Registration Agencies.
(
printed page 70246)
(b)
Applicability.
This part applies to all sponsors of apprenticeship programs registered with either the U.S. Department of Labor or a recognized SAA.
§ 30.2
Definitions.
The definitions in § 29.2 of this title also apply to this part.
§ 30.3
Nondiscrimination standards applicable to all sponsors.
Registered apprenticeship program sponsors must comply with all applicable Federal and State laws and regulations prohibiting illegal discrimination on the basis of race, color, religion, national origin, sex, age (40 or older), genetic information, or disability. Failure to comply with such nondiscrimination laws is grounds for deregistration or the imposition of other enforcement actions in accordance with § 30.5(c), if such non-compliance is related to illegal discrimination against apprentices or an applicant to an apprenticeship program with respect to any benefit, term, or condition of employment associated with an apprenticeship.
§ 30.4
Complaints.
If the Registration Agency receives any complaints from apprentices (including applicants for apprenticeship) alleging illegal discrimination, it will immediately refer the individual to any of the following:
(a) The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission;
(b) The U.S. Attorney General;
(c) A State Fair Employment Practices Agency; or
(d) Another Federal or State enforcement entity with jurisdiction over discrimination issues, as appropriate.
§ 30.5
Nondiscrimination compliance reviews and enforcement.
(a)
Conduct of compliance reviews.
Concurrently with a Registration Agency's review of a registered apprenticeship program for conformity with the requirements of part 29 of this title, a Registration Agency will assess a program's compliance with the nondiscrimination requirement of § 30.3.
(b)
Determining compliance.
For the purpose of determining compliance under this part, the Registration Agency may initiate enforcement actions against a sponsor for failure to comply with the nondiscrimination requirement at § 30.3 in instances where a final determination of a violation of an applicable nondiscrimination law, without any remaining right to appeal, has been made by an enforcement entity or court with jurisdiction over a matter, and authority to issue a final determination, relating to an apprentice or an applicant to an apprenticeship program.
(1) Sponsors must disclose in writing to the Registration Agency any instances when an enforcement entity or court with jurisdiction over an applicable nondiscrimination law has rendered a final determination, without any remaining right to appeal, that the sponsor has violated such laws relating to an apprentice or an applicant to an apprenticeship program within 60 days of the final determination. The disclosure must include, at a minimum, a copy of all relevant final determinations, judgments, decisions and orders.
(2) As a part of the self-disclosure requirement under paragraph (b)(1) of this section, sponsors must include a description of any prescribed remedies mandated by the enforcement entity or court to address the violation of applicable nondiscrimination law.
(c)
Compliance and enforcement actions.
Upon learning of a final determination made by an enforcement entity or court with respect to a sponsor's violation of an applicable nondiscrimination law (as described in paragraph (b) of this section), the Registration Agency may work with the sponsor to develop a compliance action plan that aligns with the remedy prescribed by the enforcement entity or court and brings the program into compliance with this part. If the Registration Agency determines that a compliance action plan is not being implemented in accordance with the remedy prescribed by the enforcement entity or court, the Registration Agency may initiate enforcement actions that will remain in place until the violation is resolved to the satisfaction of the Registration Agency. Enforcement actions by the Registration Agency include:
(1) Suspension of the sponsor's right to register new apprentices; or
(2) The initiation of deregistration proceedings set forth in part 29 of this title.
§ 30.6
Reinstatement of program registration.
An apprenticeship program that has been deregistered pursuant to this part may be reinstated by the Registration Agency upon presentation of adequate evidence that the apprenticeship program is operating in accordance with this part.
§ 30.7
State apprenticeship agencies.
(a)
State laws specific to nondiscrimination in apprenticeship.
Within 1 year of January 5, 2027, unless an extension for good cause is sought and granted by the Administrator, an SAA that seeks to obtain or maintain recognition under § 29.13 of this title must submit a State plan for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship, as described in paragraph (b) of this section, that demonstrates that the State's laws, regulations, policies, and operational procedures specific to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship conform to the requirements of this part and part 29 of this title.
(b)
Elements of the State plan for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship.
(1) The State plan for nondiscrimination in apprenticeship must—
(i) Include all State statutes, regulations, policies, and operational procedures pertaining specifically to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship that conform to the requirements of this part;
(ii) Include a description of any State statutes, regulations, policies, and operational procedures pertaining specifically to nondiscrimination or equal opportunity in apprenticeship which impose requirements in addition to those prescribed in this part;
(iii) Not require any sponsor seeking to register an apprenticeship program with the State for Federal purposes, through any State statutes, regulations, policies, or operational procedures, to engage in any activity that is unlawful under Federal or State nondiscrimination law; and
(iv) Require all apprenticeship programs registered with the State for Federal purposes to comply with the requirements of the State's plan within 180 days from the date that the Office of Apprenticeship (OA) provides written approval of the State plan submitted under paragraph (a) of this section.
(2) Upon receipt of the State plan, OA will review the plan to determine if the plan conforms to this part. OA will:
(i) Grant the SAA continued recognition during this review period;
(ii) Provide technical assistance, if necessary, to facilitate conformity, and provide written notification of the areas of nonconformity, if any; and
(iii) Upon successful completion of the review process, notify the SAA of OA's determination that the State plan conforms to this part.
(3) If the State does not submit a revised State plan that adequately responds to OA's technical assistance within 90 days from the date that OA provides the SAA with written notification of the areas of nonconformity, OA is authorized to
(
printed page 70247)
initiate the process set forth in § 29.14 of this title to rescind recognition of the SAA.
(4) An SAA that seeks to obtain or maintain recognition must obtain the Administrator's written concurrence in any proposed State plan, as well as any subsequent modification to that plan, as provided in § 29.13(b)(9) of this title.
(c)
Recordkeeping requirements.
A recognized SAA must keep all records pertaining to program compliance reviews and any other records pertinent to a determination of compliance with this part. These records must be maintained for 5 years from the date of their creation.
(d)
Retention of authority.
As provided in § 29.13 of this title, OA retains the full authority to:
(1) Conduct compliance reviews of all registered apprenticeship programs; and
(2) Deregister for Federal purposes an apprenticeship program registered with a recognized SAA as provided in §§ 29.8(b) and 29.10 of this title.
(e)
Derecognition.
A recognized SAA that fails to comply with the requirements of this section will be subject to derecognition proceedings, as provided in § 29.14 of this title.
§ 30.8
Exemptions.
Requests for exemption from this part, or any part thereof, must be made in writing to the Registration Agency and must contain a statement of reasons supporting the request. Exemptions may be granted for good cause by the Registration Agency. SAAs must receive approval to grant an exemption from the Administrator, prior to granting an exemption from this part.
§ 30.9
Severability.
Should a court of competent jurisdiction hold any provision(s) of this part to be invalid, such action will not affect any other provision of this part.

AGENCY:
Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA), Department of Agriculture (USDA).
ACTION:
Final rule with request for comment.
SUMMARY:
This final rule considers public comments submitted in response to the proposed rule to remove barriers to online ordering and internet-based transactions in the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) published on February 23, 2023. USDA FNA is issuing this regulatory action to support State innovation and develop and implement modernized systems, while underscoring program integrity. It allows for the use of new technologies to improve the WIC shopping experience while increasing access to healthy foods for WIC participants. This final rule also complements the Program's complete transition to electronic benefit transfer (EBT) by streamlining and modernizing certain WIC food delivery regulations to support current technology and future innovation, and introduces measures to support a modern, data-driven program that uses new technologies for food delivery.
DATES:
Effective Date:
This rule is effective December 7, 2026. Online comments submitted through the Federal eRulemaking Portal must be received on or before January 5, 2027 to be assured of consideration.
Implementation Dates:
See section VI of the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
.
Compliance Dates:
This rulemaking consists of multiple provisions. Compliance for each provision is referenced in section VI of the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section of this final rule and detailed in the section-by-section analysis.
Severability. If any provision of such section promulgated through this final rule, “Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC): Online Ordering and Transactions and Food Delivery Revisions to Meet the Needs of a Modern, Data-Driven Program” (FNA-2026-0595; RIN 0854-AE85) is held to be invalid or unenforceable by its terms, or as applied to any person or circumstances, it shall be severable and not affect the remainder thereof.
ADDRESSES:
The Food and Nutrition Administration, USDA, invites interested persons to submit written comments on this final rule. USDA seeks comment on the impacts to stakeholders, specifically State agencies and their Management Information Systems (MIS), Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT), and vendor system partners. Comments may be submitted to the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
http://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the online instructions for submitting comments. All comments submitted in response to this final rule will be included in the record and will be made available to the public. Please be advised that the substance of the comments and the identity of the individuals or entities submitting the comments will be subject to public disclosure. FNA will make the comments publicly available on the internet via
http://www.regulations.gov
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Allison Post, Supplemental Nutrition and Safety Programs, Food and Nutrition Administration, USDA, 201 14th Street SW, Washington, DC 20227, 703-457-7708 or
sm.fn.WICPolicy@usda.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Overview
This rule sets forth regulatory flexibilities, encourages innovation, and modernizes WIC food delivery regulations. The rule ensures WIC participants have the same shopping options as non-WIC shoppers to transact their WIC benefits as the retail marketplace innovates and evolves. This rule also clarifies requirements so that State agencies can effectively carry out a modern, data-driven program that uses current technologies for food delivery. This final rule considers public comments on the proposed rule “Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC): Online Ordering and Transactions and Food Delivery Revisions to Meet the Needs of a Modern, Data-Driven Program” (
88 FR 11516
) published on February 23, 2023, referred to as “the proposed rule.” The changes finalized in this rule better serve families across the country by improving the WIC shopping experience and ensuring that WIC participants have access to healthy foods, while maintaining security and oversight measures at the federal and State agency levels. This rule:
(1) Removes barriers to online shopping and internet-based transactions in WIC, including a current prohibition of the authorization of internet-based vendors. This provides State agencies the flexibility to determine how to offer online shopping to participants in a way that maintains program integrity. The revisions support oversight measures and policies appropriate for current technologies, and adaptable for future ones (
e.g.,
Europay, Mastercard, and Visa (“EMV”) chip cards, mobile apps), as well as security requirements to support program integrity as the retail marketplace innovates.
(2) Streamlines and modernizes WIC food delivery requirements to reflect the Program's complete transition to electronic benefit transfer (EBT), supports current technology and future innovation, and expands opportunities for WIC participants to utilize innovations in the retail grocery industry. The revisions allow State agencies to use new types of food instruments (
e.g.,
mobile payments) and provide State agencies with more flexibility in the issuance of WIC benefits.
(3) Updates reporting requirements to reflect a modern, data-driven program.
II. Background
This part provides an overview of the WIC Program and key terms used throughout this preamble.
A. Overview of the WIC Program
The WIC Program is administered by 88 WIC State agencies, including the 50 States, 32 Indian Tribal Organizations, the District of Columbia, and 5 U.S. Territories (American Samoa, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, Guam, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands).
[
1
]
WIC is an evidence-based public health program, with a long history of improving health outcomes for nutritionally at risk and income-eligible pregnant, breastfeeding, and non-breastfeeding postpartum women, and infants and children up to age five. In fiscal year (FY) 2025, WIC served an average of 6.9 million participants per month.
[
2
]
As of the most recent published estimates (2023), WIC
(
printed page 70251)
participants included around 40 percent of all infants in the United States.
[
3
]
The USDA provides grants to WIC State agencies to provide supplemental foods, referrals to health care and other social services, and nutrition education, including breastfeeding promotion and support, to WIC participants. WIC participation is associated with purchasing healthier foods and improved diets for pregnant women and children and has been shown to reduce prevalence of childhood obesity.
[
4 5
]
According to their participant category and nutritional needs, WIC participants receive supplemental foods on a monthly basis from one of seven evidence-based food packages. The amounts and categories of foods provided in each package are intended to supplement participants' diets and provide specific nutrients known to be lacking in the diets of WIC's target population.
WIC participants typically access supplemental foods through a retail food delivery system. In such systems, a WIC shopper goes to a WIC-authorized vendor (
i.e.,
a retail grocery store authorized by the State agency), selects foods available in their benefit balance, and uses an electronic benefit transfer (EBT) card to purchase the items. In FY 2023, there were approximately 37,368 WIC-authorized vendors nationwide and, as of August 2024, all WIC State agencies completed the transition from paper vouchers to EBT. This rule does not fully remove references to paper food instruments because when the proposed rule was published in early 2023, there were still State agencies in the midst of implementing EBT. The Department intends to use a future rulemaking to update WIC regulations to reflect that EBT is now the sole benefit delivery method in the retail food delivery system.
WIC State agencies are responsible for making sure the distribution of WIC-authorized vendors in their geographic area provides sufficient access to WIC foods for participants, and vendors stock an adequate amount and variety of WIC foods. The regulatory changes in this final rule aim to reduce some of the burden associated with shopping for WIC foods, and support State agency vendor management operations in maintaining strong program integrity efforts. The Department recognizes that the development and expansion of online shopping is a novel and developing component in WIC. In order to protect both participants and taxpayer funds, the Department is committed to ensuring all available resources are deployed toward increased oversight and prevention of potential vendor fraud and abuse.
B. Introduction of Key Terms
The following are key terms used throughout this final rule preamble:
“WIC shopper” means a person shopping using WIC benefits (
i.e.,
a WIC participant, proxy, or a parent or caretaker of an infant or child participant).
“Online shopping” means the general use of an online, internet-based ordering system, platform, or site. It can encompass online ordering with or without internet-based transactions (
i.e.,
the transaction can occur via the internet, in store, curbside, or at the point of delivery).
“Online ordering” means the process a customer (including a WIC shopper) uses to select food items for purchase via an internet-based ordering system, platform, or site.
“Transaction” means the process by which a WIC shopper exchanges their WIC benefits for supplemental foods.
“Internet-based transaction” means a transaction where the WIC payment is completed through the payment section of the online ordering system, platform, or site. This terminology is being used in lieu of “online transaction” to avoid confusion with transactions that occur using online EBT technology.
“Redemption” means the process in which a vendor submits records of electronic benefit transactions for redemption and the State agency (or its financial agent) makes payment to the vendor.
III. Approach To Rulemaking and Status of WIC Online Shopping
This rulemaking finalizes regulatory changes in consideration of public comments received on the proposed rule published February 23, 2023. In developing the proposed rule, the Department considered technical materials developed by a wide variety of WIC stakeholders, lessons learned from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) online shopping projects that began in 2019, as well as feedback from WIC State agencies, Indian Tribal Organizations, and participants. The following technical resources informed the Department's identification of regulatory barriers to online shopping and provisions in this rulemaking:
Blueprint for WIC Online Ordering: Through a cooperative agreement with FNA, The Center for Nutrition and Health Impact (CNHI), an independent non-profit research institute, developed a comprehensive plan for implementing online shopping in WIC. This Blueprint, which initially identified waivers to federal regulations necessary to begin online shopping projects and provided guidance to begin implementing, has since been revised and republished in May 2026, with up-to-date information to support WIC State agencies as they develop their WIC online shopping projects.
[
6
]
The Task Force on Supplemental Foods Delivery: This task force convened WIC providers, retailers, manufacturers, EBT processors, advocacy organizations, and WIC participants to develop an online shopping Recommendation Report for the Department.
[
7
]
The Department initially supported WIC State agencies in pursuing online shopping projects by issuing waivers under the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA,
Pub. L. 117-2
) authority, which allowed FNA to waive regulatory barriers to support outreach, innovation and modernization in WIC and the WIC Farmers' Market Nutrition Program (FMNP). Online shopping waivers were issued through September 2024 and remain in effect to support ongoing projects. With these waivers, the Department provided State agencies with the necessary regulatory flexibility and technical assistance to pursue online shopping projects, regardless of whether or not they received a subgrant from CNHI. The Department recognizes and appreciates the WIC State agencies and authorized retailers that have developed different ways to provide online ordering to WIC participants. Through the cooperative agreement with CNHI, 22 WIC State agencies have received subgrants to pursue online shopping including the necessary
(
printed page 70252)
development of internet-based transactions.
This final rulemaking permanently removes regulatory barriers to allow State agencies to implement online shopping in WIC and eliminates the need for waiver flexibility; therefore, the online shopping waivers will be superseded by regulation once this rulemaking is effective. Additional waivers supporting mobile pay and remote issuance will also be superseded by this rulemaking once effective.
IV. Proposed Rule Comment Summary
The proposed rule published in the
Federal Register
on February 23, 2023, with a 90-day comment period closing on May 24, 2023. During this time, USDA received 1,664 comments. Five form letter campaigns comprised 881 submissions. There were 752 unique comments of which 216 were substantive, providing specific input on the topics included in this final rule. A total of 31 comments were either duplicates or out of the scope of this rule, as they did not provide feedback related to topics in this final rule. The comments came from a variety of sources, including WIC State and local agencies, state representatives, professional organizations and associations, advocacy groups, health care professionals, universities, the food industry, WIC participants, and private citizens. USDA worked in collaboration with a data analysis company to code and analyze the public comments using a commercial web-based software product. This analysis provided data showing support for or opposition to each proposed change. Over 1,070 commenters provided broad support for revisions to the regulations while approximately 10 commenters provided general comments in opposition to the proposed rule. The Final Summary of Public Comments is available online at
www.regulations.gov
in docket FNS-2022-0015. The Final Summary of Public Comments includes the specific number of comments in support or opposition to each provision in the proposed rule, with a detailed narrative describing the key points made by commenters. USDA used the Final Summary of Public Comments and a supplementary review of individual comments to finalize provisions within this final rule. USDA refers to the Final Summary of Public Comments for numbers of comments received on each provision, with general summaries of comments provided in the preamble of this final rule.
As required under the Administrative Procedure Act, FNA considered all relevant, timely-submitted comments received on the proposed rule. Some comments addressed topics out of scope for the revisions and therefore are not addressed in this final rule.
V. Discussion of Final Rule
The following is a discussion of the provisions set forth in the proposed rule, a summary of the comments received that addressed these provisions, and the Department's rationale for either retaining or modifying the proposed provisions in the final rule. Provisions not discussed in this preamble did not receive significant or substantial public comments and are retained in this final rule as proposed.
This preamble communicates the rationale for modifications to the proposed rule codified in this final rulemaking. The Department re-examined the goals of this rulemaking while reviewing the comments to determine the continued applicability of each proposed change. Unless otherwise stated in the preamble of this final rule, the rationales included in the preamble of the proposed rule are regarded as a basis for the final regulations. Therefore, an understanding of the rationales for the final regulations may require reference to the preamble of the proposed rule.
USDA appreciates the many comments expressing support for the proposed revisions and urging USDA to implement the changes included in the proposed rule. USDA agrees the changes improve access to healthy foods and the efficiency of the WIC shopping experience while ensuring State agencies have the flexibility to oversee new types of vendors and to maintain program integrity and security. Before addressing each provision specifically, the following is a summary of overarching themes related to online shopping that the Department is acknowledging broadly.
(i) Technical assistance to support online shopping: the Department received numerous comments requesting guidance and technical assistance to support the implementation of online shopping in WIC.
The Department is committed to providing ongoing technical assistance and guidance to State agencies to ensure they have the support and resources necessary to implement online shopping and can do so while preserving program integrity. The Department is developing best practices, lessons learned, and technical resources to support State agencies in the implementation of online shopping using the many recommendations and ideas stakeholders provided during the public comment period for the proposed rule.
(ii) Internet vendor authorization: Many commenters expressed concern the State agency-by-State agency approach to internet vendor authorization would be lengthy and cumbersome, and instead recommended the Department adopt a national authorization process for online shopping, including national monitoring and management, similar to that of SNAP.
The Department notes there is a significant difference in how SNAP and WIC are authorized in legislation. The Child Nutrition Act expressly delegates responsibility for vendor authorization, monitoring, and oversight to WIC State agencies. Therefore, the Department did not propose a national process related to the authorization of WIC internet vendors.
(iii) Costs of technology innovations and online shopping: Many comments discussed concerns around the cost of adopting new technologies and stated the need for more federal funding to implement the various changes included in this rulemaking.
The Department notes the majority of the changes in this rulemaking either, (1) increase options and flexibilities for State agencies in vendor management activities without increased costs, or (2) provide the opportunity for State agencies to pursue new technologies at their discretion. The Department recognizes funding is a consideration for State agencies and therefore is not requiring implementation of any new technologies at this time. This rulemaking allows State agencies the opportunity to determine an appropriate and feasible timeline to implement new technologies. The Department recognizes the costs associated with authorizing internet vendors, largely due to the EBT and MIS changes necessary to allow new types of transactions and is therefore prioritizing flexibility and has recently supported State agencies through various funding opportunities, including subgrant opportunities from CNHI.
(iv) Modernizing offline EBT systems: Some commenters questioned how State agencies with offline EBT systems (
i.e.,
chipped EBT cards in which benefits cannot be used or issued online) would be able to implement some of the provisions in this rule, such as those related to online shopping or issuing benefits remotely. Commenters asked for technical assistance and funding to help transition to online EBT systems.
The Department recognizes that offline EBT systems will not be able to operate WIC online shopping or issue
(
printed page 70253)
benefits remotely. The Department is actively working with all offline State agencies to transition to online EBT systems so that they can also take part in these opportunities. The Department also highlights that neither online shopping nor remote benefit issuance are requirements for State agencies under this rulemaking. This rule creates the necessary flexibilities for the State agencies that are interested and able to develop online shopping and encourages the flexible issuance of benefits where possible.
(v) Impact to small vendors and accessibility: Some commenters expressed concerns that implementing online shopping would be especially challenging for small vendors.
To support small vendors, CNHI conducted a survey and hosted listening sessions to hear directly from small, Tribal, and rural vendors, and farmers and farmers' markets, to understand the perceptions, experiences, and potential barriers vendors face in implementing online shopping.
[

The Department recognizes different types of support and guidance may be needed to initiate WIC online shopping. USDA is committed to gathering feedback and learning from implementation projects to develop technical resources and assistance.
Commenters also noted that access to online shopping through the inclusion of alternative languages to English, as well as alternative online formats for persons with disabilities are key to ensuring all participants can access online shopping opportunities. The Department will explore opportunities to provide ongoing technical assistance to ensure that State agencies are encouraging vendors to equip their online platforms to meet the needs of their participants.

There was a significant discussion from commenters regarding the new vendor types, and while many commenters supported the proposed definitions, other commenters shared concerns and requests for clarification from the Department. The following discussion is related to overarching concerns regarding the new vendor types. A discussion on the specific definitions for each vendor type follows.
Commenters requested guidance from USDA on how the creation of new vendor types will impact various State agency vendor management activities such as selection criteria, peer groups, preauthorization, above-50-vendor assessment, cost containment, monitoring, training, and sanctions. Many commenters also provided recommendations for how vendor management activities should take place for the new vendor types. Some commenters requested clarification on whether the authorization of internet and mobile vendors is a State agency option. The Department recognizes adding new vendor types warrants revised approaches to vendor management. The Department appreciates the feedback and recommendations on how to adequately manage the new vendor types and will incorporate this feedback into the development of guidance and technical assistance, expanding on current efforts to develop guidance and technical assistance based on lessons learned from online shopping projects. While the Department confirms the authorization of internet and mobile vendors is a State agency option, the Department also encourages State agencies to consider authorizing these new vendor types to better serve families across the country, including in rural areas.
Many commenters strongly agreed with the Department's proposal that all vendors, regardless of type, must adhere to all regulations pertaining to vendors

and discussed the importance of applying consistent and fair program requirements regardless of vendor type. However, some commenters disagreed and recommended different requirements by vendor type, such as different federal selection criteria or minimum stock for internet and mobile vendors than brick-and-mortar vendors.
The Department recognizes that different vendor types will inherently have different training, monitoring, and investigative needs, and the specific ways in which vendor management activities take place may be different. However, the State agency must hold all vendors to the same federal accountability measures and minimum requirements to ensure effective management and oversight. Therefore, the Department maintains that all authorized vendors, no matter the type, are subject to federal regulations governing authorized WIC vendors, but that State agencies may tailor their vendor management approach depending on vendor type. For example, State agency training for internet vendors may include new content for web designers, such as online shopping navigation and pricing, and may focus less on transaction details which may not be applicable for an internet vendor using automated product compliance controls. Further, as discussed in section 1.e, the Department is introducing virtual methods of oversight to provide State agencies with the appropriate tools for monitoring all vendor types. While different vendor types do not have distinct requirements, vendors of different types may be able to show compliance with requirements in distinct manners. For example, an authorized internet vendor sourcing orders from multiple fulfillment locations would not need to demonstrate that each fulfillment location meets stocking standards so long as the vendor can prove to the State agency that their online ordering operations as a whole meet those standards. Similarly, internet vendors may have different mechanisms for demonstrating compliance with inventory audits, which are just one State agency option for investigating their vendor population.
Some commenters stated that the word “store” as used throughout the current regulations appears to refer to a single, fixed location, and therefore would only apply to brick-and-mortar stores. Commenters requested clarification of the Department's application of the word “store” considering the new vendor types that do not have single, fixed store locations.
The Department clarifies that the word “store” as used throughout the regulation is synonymous with the term “vendor” and applies to brick-and-mortar, internet, and mobile vendors.
Many commenters requested the inclusion of a “hybrid vendor” defined by the Task Force Report as a “physical store location that also operates a virtual platform,”
