Benefits
The provisions under this rule modernize the ways that WIC participants can receive and transact their electronic benefits. An estimated 14 percent of the U.S. population lives in low-income census tracts with limited access to food stores,
[
16
]
and 21 percent of WIC participants report using a means of transportation other than their own personal car to travel to a vendor to use their WIC benefits.
[
17
]
By comparison, 95 percent of higher income households (above 185 percent of the federal poverty line) use their own vehicle to travel to a grocery store.
[
18
]
Once at the vendor, participants also report challenges shopping for WIC foods. Recent USDA survey data indicate that finding the right WIC-approved products in stores, WIC-approved products being out of stock, and feeling embarrassed shopping for WIC foods are some of the most cited challenges among WIC participants who report difficulties shopping for WIC supplemental foods.
[
19
]
Online shopping may alleviate some of these issues for WIC participants and has the potential to provide benefits during supply chain disruptions.
Enabling online shopping in WIC under this rule is expected to ensure that WIC participants have access to innovations in the retail marketplace while maintaining program integrity, and to increase participant purchases of supplemental foods. Online shopping may also expand WIC participants' choices when they shop, particularly for authorized substitutions needed to meet certain dietary restrictions that may not be readily available at the closest WIC-authorized grocery stores. The rule will further make WIC more convenient and accessible by encouraging State agencies to remotely issue electronic benefits and mail EBT cards whenever possible, potentially reducing the number of clinic visits that WIC participants are required to make. The rule also includes provisions that will streamline and modernize WIC food delivery by promoting innovation and ensuring that State agency reporting requirements reflect a modern, data-driven program. These provisions provide necessary measures to ensure that State agencies can deliver a more efficient and effective program for WIC participants.
Finally, preliminary evidence suggests online ordering generally supports higher diet quality or more healthful food purchasing decisions among SNAP participants.

To the extent that this rule facilitates healthier food shopping among WIC participants, this rule is likely to lead to better nutrition outcomes for WIC participants.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. 601-612
) requires Agencies to analyze the impact of rulemaking on small entities and consider alternatives that would minimize any significant impacts on a substantial number of small entities. Pursuant to that review, it has been certified that this final rule does not have a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities.
The provisions of this final rule primarily affect WIC State agencies and WIC-authorized vendors. Otherwise, all other provisions apply to all State agencies administering the WIC Program, regardless of size, and largely can be implemented at State agency option. The Department does not expect this final rule to have a significant impact on small State agencies.
Large retailers may be able to implement WIC online shopping more readily than other store types. However, the Department does not expect the final rule to have a lasting or significant negative impact on smaller WIC vendors as WIC sales represent a relatively small share of these stores' revenue. The Department does not routinely track data necessary to determine how WIC benefit redemptions vary by most vendor characteristics, including indicators for whether the store is a small business or independent grocer. USDA's ERS estimated, by merging WIC and SNAP redemption databases, that 76 percent of WIC retail redemptions occurred in larger stores (super stores, supermarkets, or large grocery stores) in FY 2012; however, the study's definition of supermarkets and large grocery stores is inclusive of many independent grocers.
[
22
]
The Department does not have data on the extent to which small businesses and independent grocers have implemented online shopping to date, but is aware of products on the market being employed by independent grocers to provide online ordering currently for WIC participants (with in-store or curbside transactions).
If smaller WIC vendors (such as convenience stores or small and medium grocery stores) do not adopt online shopping solutions, then they may see some of their WIC revenues lost to larger retailers that provide online shopping. According to ERS data, in FY 2012, small grocery stores, medium grocery stores, and convenience stores accounted for 2.9 percent, 3.5 percent, and 3.8 percent of WIC retail redemptions, respectively. For example, the 3.8 percent of total WIC benefits transacted at convenience stores in FY 2012 amounts to about $228 million. U.S. convenience stores reported an estimated $193 billion in total in-store sales, not including fuel, in 2012, suggesting that WIC redemptions represented only about 0.12 percent of non-fuel sales for convenience stores that year.

As WIC sales make up a relatively small fraction of the total revenue of smaller stores, and especially convenience stores, the Department expects any lost revenue for smaller vendors that do not adopt an online

, establishes requirements for Federal agencies to assess the effects of their regulatory actions on State, local and Tribal governments, and the private sector. Under section 202 of the UMRA, the Department generally must prepare a written statement, including a cost benefit analysis, for proposed and final rules with “Federal mandates” that may result in expenditures by State, local or Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or the private sector, of $100 million or more (adjusted annually for inflation) in any one year. When such a statement is needed for a rule, section 205 of the UMRA generally requires the Department to identify and consider a reasonable number of regulatory alternatives and adopt the most cost effective or least burdensome alternative that achieves the objectives of the rule.
This final rule does not contain Federal mandates (under the regulatory provisions of Title II of the UMRA) for State, local and Tribal governments, or the private sector of $100 million or more (adjusted annually for inflation) in any one year. Thus, this rule is not subject to the requirements of sections 202 and 205 of the UMRA.

Civil Rights Impact Analysis
FNA has reviewed the final rule, in accordance with the Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018, “2018 Farm Bill,” Section 12403, Civil Rights Analyses, to identify and address any major civil rights impacts the final rule might have on participants on the basis of race, sex, national origin, disability, or age. The requirements outlined in the final rule aim to remove barriers to online ordering and internet-based transactions, streamline and modernize WIC food delivery, and meet the needs of a modern, data-driven program that uses current food delivery technologies. The changes impact WIC State agencies, including ITOs, WIC local agencies and clinics, and WIC vendors in ways that are expected to increase equity and access for WIC participants and enhance the overall shopping experience.
In particular, the final rule allows State agencies to authorize new types of vendors and explore modern payment technologies and authentication methods. To comply with revised regulations and implement the changes, staff at State agencies, local agencies, and WIC clinics will need to update operations and communicate these changes to participants. The rule will increase the number of WIC-authorized vendors by allowing different types of vendors (
e.g.,
internet and mobile vendors) to participate in WIC, while also reducing administrative burdens on vendors through the elimination of certain collection requirements. As a result, this rule will benefit participants by expanding participant shopping options and reducing in-person requirements.
To mitigate potential impacts on vital program access for populations with limited English proficiency and persons with disabilities, FNA will provide State agencies with technical assistance aimed at ensuring that online shopping platforms and communications about program changes are available in appropriate languages and in alternative formats for persons with disabilities. FNA will also support State agencies as they work to engage small vendors in online shopping in the WIC Program. After reviewing the potential impacts, FNA does not believe the final rule will result in civil rights impacts on specific groups of WIC participants and applicants. However, the FNA Civil Rights Division will propose further outreach and mitigation strategies to alleviate any unforeseen impacts, if deemed necessary.

Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C. Chap. 35;
5 CFR part 1320
) requires that the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) approve all collections of information by a Federal agency before they can be implemented. Respondents are not required to respond to any collection of information unless it displays a current valid OMB control number.
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, this final rule revises existing information collection requirements currently approved under OMB Control Number 0584-0043, “Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) Program Regulations—Reporting and Recordkeeping Burden” (expiration date August 31, 2027), and contains new requirements for the same information collection. These information collection requirements are subject to review and approval by OMB.
The Department published the proposed rule, “Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC): Online Ordering and Transactions and Food Delivery Revisions to Meet the Needs of a Modern, Data-Driven Program” in the
Federal Register
on February 23, 2023 (
88 FR 11516
). The proposed rule requested public comment on proposed changes in the information collection burden that would result from this rule. The Department received approximately 20 comments on the proposed information collection requirements and associated burdens. Commenters also provided feedback on the burden associated with activities not impacted by this rule, which were incorporated as adjustments into this burden. Based on public comment feedback, the Department revised the burden estimates for this final rule as follows:
Travel time for vendor visits: The Department received feedback that a 20-minute round trip travel time for visiting vendors for various activities was an underestimate. Therefore, the Department is adjusting the estimated travel time for round trip vendor visits to 30 minutes and incorporated this edit into the various activities involving vendor visits.
On-site preauthorization visits: To reflect the feedback received related to travel time for State agencies visiting vendors, the Department adjusted the total burden for this activity from 60 minutes to 70 minutes (1.17 hours).
Vendor applications and agreements: The Department proposed the burden for this activity to be 40 minutes (0.67 hours) per vendor applicant. However, multiple commenters stated that this underestimated the amount of time necessary to complete a full review and completion of vendor applications and agreements. Based on the feedback, the Department adjusted the estimated burden to 120 minutes (2 hours) per vendor applicant for this activity to account for the increased estimate of review and processing of applications and agreements.
On-site routine vendor monitoring: To reflect feedback from stakeholders that routine monitoring takes longer than the proposed 80 minutes including travel time, the Department adjusted the estimated burden to 100 minutes (1.67 hours) per vendor for this activity to account for both increased estimates in travel time and the routine monitoring activities that take place.
Virtual routine vendor monitoring: The Department proposed the burden for this activity to be 60 minutes per vendor. However multiple commenters stated that routine monitoring, including remote monitoring, is likely to take longer. Based on this feedback, the Department increased the estimated burden to 70 minutes (1.17 hours) per vendor for this activity to account for an increased estimate.
On-site compliance investigations: To reflect feedback from stakeholders that on-site compliance investigations take longer than 120 minutes per vendor, the Department increased the estimated burden to 300 minutes (5 hours) per vendor for this activity to account for both increased estimates in travel time and the activities that take place.
Virtual compliance investigations: The Department proposed the burden for this activity to be 120 minutes per vendor. Multiple commenters stated that compliance buys take a significantly longer amount of time, even if done remotely. Based on this feedback, the Department increased the estimated burden to 270 minutes (4.5 hours) per vendor for this activity, removing the 30-minute travel time accounted for in the on-site compliance investigations burden.
System updates to allow online shopping, including return of benefits: The Department did not initially include the burden associated with updates to State agency systems (EBT and MIS) and vendor systems necessary to implement online shopping. Commenters discussed the significant cost and impact related to these necessary changes and based on feedback provided by State agencies currently implementing online shopping projects, FNA estimates that, on average, State agencies will need to spend 50 hours modifying their EBT and MIS to enable online shopping. The Department estimates that internet vendors will also have a 50-hour burden to update their systems to implement online shopping and incorporated that into this burden estimate.
Development of transaction authentication policies: The Department proposed the burden for this activity to be 25 hours per State agency. Commenters stated that this was an underestimate and did not take into consideration the hours that it will take a State agency to clear these types of policies through State level review. Based on this feedback, and to account for modifications to this provision that require State agencies to receive written approval from FNA to adopt an authentication method other than the PIN, the Department increased the estimated burden to 50 hours for this activity.
The Department appreciates the feedback provided and incorporated it into the estimates for the final burden. The Department did not change the estimated burden based on public comment feedback for the following provisions:
Shelf price exemptions: Some State agencies stated that because they utilize shelf price exemptions and do not collect shelf prices, they would not be realizing the benefits of the new provision and therefore the burden estimate was inaccurate. While FNA recognizes that some State agencies have already realized the benefits of not collecting shelf prices through the use of exemptions, the goal of this burden assessment is to recognize the decrease in burden hours from an overall regulatory perspective. As this rulemaking permanently removes the requirement to collect shelf prices, the burden reflects the impact on all State agencies, regardless of if they had an exemption.
Participant travel time to clinic: One commenter stated that the participant travel time to the clinic for benefit pick-up was underestimated. The Department recognizes that the travel time for participants in the commenter's State agency may be different than the Department's
(
printed page 70272)
estimate. However, the Department's estimate was based on a survey data
[
24
]
that represents an accurate sample of participants nation-wide, rather than in just one State agency. Therefore, the Department maintains its estimate for participant benefit pick up travel time.
Reporting requirements: Some commenters stated that the estimated burden impact of quarterly reporting submissions to Food Delivery Portal (FDP) were underestimated. The Department has reviewed this feedback and will incorporate changes to the burden related to FDP in a separate burden revision under OMB Control Number 0584-0401.
The Department has made several additional changes to the estimated burden:
Baseline numbers: The baseline number of hours currently approved under OMB Control Number 0584-0043 have been updated since the proposed rule was published, due to the regular revision of the WIC Program Information Collection Request (ICR). The impact of this final rule on the overall WIC Program information collection burden therefore reflects estimated changes to the updated baseline numbers.
Updated program data: Since the WIC Program ICR was last approved, there has been a decrease in the number of State agencies, an increase in the number of vendors, and an increase in the number of participants. The estimated burden associated with this final rule is calculated using the most recent available program data. Changes to the burden estimates from updated program data are classified as “program adjustments,” while changes to the burden as a result of the final rule are classified as “program changes.”
Revised estimates of online shopping uptake: In the proposed rule, the Department estimated that 80 State agencies would implement online shopping and that each State agency would authorize approximately 5 internet vendors, resulting in 400 internet vendors. These estimates were based on the number of State agencies with online EBT systems and SNAP's experiences with online shopping. The Department is revising these numbers to estimate that approximately half of WIC State agencies (44) will implement online shopping in the first five years following the rule's publication and that each State agency will authorize 2 to 3 internet vendors, resulting in 110 internet vendors. These updated estimates are based on experiences with ongoing WIC online shopping projects.
Correction of error in a previous submission: The currently approved burden for State agency recordkeeping activities related to vendor incentive items has an inaccurate number of above-50-vendors. A more accurate, updated number is used in this revision and therefore the change in burden hours associated with vendor incentive items reflects both program changes from the final rule and adjustments from the updated program data.
Additional implementation burden: The Department has also added a one-time implementation burden associated with activities that FNA may ask State agencies that are changing their food delivery systems to complete, such as status reports, additional trainings, and reviewing guidance materials.
Adjusted for provisions that were not finalized: The Department is not adopting the proposed revisions that would have increased the maximum length of vendor agreement periods and the minimum frequency that State agencies must accept and process vendor applications from three to five years. Therefore, the burden associated with vendor agreements and applications have been adjusted to no longer reflect this decreased frequency.
As summarized above, this final rule changes the information collection requirements that were proposed in the proposed rule. The revisions to the existing information collection requirements and the introduction of new information collection requirements that will take effect with the final rule will result in an overall decrease in burden hours for State and local agencies, applicants for Program benefits and businesses responding to these requirements. These changes are contingent upon OMB approval under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995. When the information collection requirements have been approved, the Department will publish a separate action in the

1. Revisions to OMB Control Number 0584-0043
Title:

0584-0043.
Expiration Date:
August 31, 2027.

Abstract:
This is a revision of existing information collection requirements approved under OMB Control Number 0584-0043 that are affected by this rulemaking. This final rule removes regulatory barriers to online ordering and internet-based transactions in the WIC Program, streamlines and modernizes WIC food delivery, and meets the needs of a modern, data-driven program that uses current technologies for food delivery. This final rule impacts the burden associated with reporting requirements for State agencies, individuals and households, and vendors, as well as the burden associated with recordkeeping requirements for State agencies and vendors. The burden estimates affected by the rule have also been updated to include the most recent available program data, resulting in changes to the number of State agencies (a decrease from 89 to 88), vendors (an increase from 37,267 to 37,368), and participants (an increase from 6,243,960 to 6,866,085) since the last submission of OMB Control Number 0584-0043. The average burden per respondent and the annual burden hours are summarized and explained below.
a. Burden Revisions Related to Internet Vendor Authorization, Monitoring and Oversight, and Training
The final rule allows State agencies to authorize internet vendors, in addition to brick-and-mortar vendors and mobile vendors. In FY 2023, the most recent available year, there were 37,368 WIC-authorized vendors. Using the new definitions, all vendors authorized under current WIC regulations are classified as brick-and-mortar vendors except for one mobile vendor. FNA estimates that 110 internet vendors in 44 State agencies will be authorized initially following the rulemaking (this estimate takes into consideration recent experiences with online shopping projects and the fact that, due to technological constraints, offline EBT systems would not be able to support online transactions), increasing the total number of WIC-authorized vendors from 37,368 to 37,478 vendors. In the proposed rule, the Department had estimated that 400 internet vendors would be authorized by 80 State agencies. These estimates were based on SNAP's experiences and have been adjusted to better reflect information from the WIC online shopping grant projects.
Due to public comment feedback on the proposed rule, the Department removed the requirement for State agencies to justify their use of alternative food instruments in the State
(
printed page 70273)
Plan. Instead, State agencies will have to indicate via a checkmark which food instrument types they are using as part of the annual State Plan submission. This check mark will have a negligible impact on the estimated burden hours needed to submit the annual State Plan and therefore there is no change to the burden associated with State Plan submissions due to this final rule. There is a decrease in the number of burden hours associated with State Plan submissions due to the decrease in the number of WIC State agencies since the previous ICR submission.
WIC regulations at §  246.12(g)(5) require that State agencies visit a vendor prior to their initial authorization in the Program. As noted above, based on feedback on the proposed rule, the Department is estimating that during an on-site preauthorization visit, State agency staff spend approximately 40 minutes verifying information provided by the vendor applicant, and 30 minutes traveling to and from the vendor, for a total of 70 minutes. The adjusted travel time, combined with the decrease in the number of WIC State agencies, results in an increase in the currently approved burden associated with on-site preauthorization by 237.32 total hours. The final rule allows initial preauthorization visits of internet vendors to take place virtually, therefore not requiring travel time for State agency staff. Therefore, the initial authorization of 110 internet vendors would add 73.48 reporting burden hours for both State agencies and vendors.
The proposed rule included a provision to increase the maximum length of vendor agreements and the minimum frequency that State agencies must accept and process applications from three to five years. The final rule does not include this change. Therefore, the only program change reflected in the State agency burden associated with reviewing vendor agreements is the added burden for internet vendors' applications and agreements (72.60 burden hours). In response to the proposed rule, FNA received feedback that the current estimate for reviewing, processing, and approving vendor applications was too low and therefore the Department adjusted the estimated burden from 40 minutes to 120 minutes. This adjustment, combined with the increase in the number of WIC-approved vendors since the previous ICR submission, increases the burden estimate by 16,447.74 hours. Taking the program change and the adjustments into account, the burden associated with this activity would increase by 16,520.34 hours over the currently approved burden, from 8,215.14 hours to 24,735.48 hours.
Additionally, the estimated burden for vendors to submit applications and agreements and the estimated burden for State agencies to maintain records of vendor applications and agreements would increase by 36.30 hours each due to the addition of internet vendors. The increase in the number of WIC-authorized vendors since the previous ICR submission also increases these burdens by 33.33 hours. Taken together, the program change and the adjustments to the number of vendors result in net increases in the vendor reporting burden and State agency recordkeeping burden associated with vendor applications and agreements by 69.63 hours each, from 12,298.11 to 12,367.74 hours.
Although the final rule does not change procedures for vendor oversight, the rulemaking allows routine vendor monitoring and compliance investigations to be conducted virtually so that State agencies may use oversight methods appropriate for the vendors they authorize. As with initial vendor preauthorization visits, the Department adjusted its estimate for round trip travel time to a brick-and-mortar or mobile vendor from 20 minutes to 30 minutes based on feedback on the proposed rule. The adjustment of the travel time, along with the increase in the number of WIC-authorized vendors since the previous ICR submission, increases the burden associated with on-site routine monitoring visits by 634.52 hours. The additional virtual routine monitoring visits of internet vendors authorized under the final rule adds 6.44 more hours to State agencies' reporting burden. The State agency recordkeeping burden for routine vendor monitoring would also increase by 5.27 hours, from 931.68 to 936.95 hours. Of this increase, 2.75 hours are due to the addition of internet vendors authorized under the final rule, and 2.52 hours are due to the increase in the number of WIC-authorized vendors since the previous ICR submission.
State agency staff conduct on-site compliance investigations of five percent of vendors each year. As with on-site vendor preauthorization visits and on-site routine monitoring visits, FNA adjusted its estimate for round trip travel time to a brick-and-mortar or mobile vendor from 20 minutes to 30 minutes based on feedback on the proposed rule. To reflect feedback that the compliance investigations take longer than the Department estimated, the Department adjusted the time to 4.5 hours, for a total of 5 hours including travel time. This adjustment, along with the increase in the number of WIC-authorized vendors since the previous ICR submission, increases the burden hours for on-site compliance investigations by 4,992.94 hours, from 4,349.06 hours to 9,342 hours.
The Department estimated that it would take State agencies 2 hours to conduct virtual compliance investigations of internet vendors each year. Public comments on the proposed rule provided feedback that virtual investigations will take more time. Therefore, the Department increased the burden associated with virtual compliance investigations to 4.5 hours, which adds a total of 24.75 hours to the State agency reporting burden. Additionally, the authorization of internet vendors as a result of this rulemaking would increase the State agency recordkeeping burden for compliance investigations by 11 hours, and the increase in WIC-authorized vendors since the previous ICR submission would add another 10.10 hours to this recordkeeping burden.
The addition of 110 internet vendors under the final rule would increase State agencies' reporting burden for vendor training by 220 hours per year. The Department estimates that it takes two hours for vendors to attend annual training provided by State agencies. Authorizing 110 internet vendors results in an additional 220 hours of reporting burden for those new vendors to receive the training. The Department estimates that it takes one hour for each vendor to subsequently train their staff. Due to the additional internet vendors, this will increase the burden for vendor training of their staff by 110 hours. Each of these estimated burdens for State agencies and vendors associated with vendor training activities would also increase due to the increase in the number of WIC-authorized vendors since the previous ICR submission.
Further, FNA estimates that the addition of internet vendors will result in proportionate increases in both the number of vendors that State agencies must assess for “above-50-percent” status and the number of vendors that demonstrate a pattern of violations during investigations. These changes would result in associated increases in: the State agency reporting burden related to assessing a vendor's food sales data to determine if they are an “above-50-percent” vendor (8.80 additional hours); the vendor reporting burden required to provide such sales data (4.40 additional hours); the reporting burden for above-50-percent vendors who request approval from their State agency to provide incentive items to WIC shoppers (0.98 additional hours); and
(
printed page 70274)
the State agency recordkeeping burden to collect information on above-50-percent vendors' incentive items (0.98 additional hours). Since the previous ICR submission, the number of vendors that State agencies assess for “above-50-percent” status has decreased from 840 to 795, the number of WIC State agencies has decreased from 89 to 88, and the number of WIC-authorized vendors has increased from 37,267 to 37,368. These program adjustments have additional impacts on each of the State agency and vendor burdens listed above.
Per 246.12(l)(3), State agencies are required to notify a vendor in writing when an investigation reveals an initial violation for which a pattern of violations must be established in order to impose a sanction before another violation is documented, unless the State agency determines notifying the vendor would compromise an investigation. Accounting for the addition of internet vendors due to this final rule, the associated reporting burden for this requirement would increase by 0.26 hours and the associated recordkeeping burden would increase by 3.09 hours. These burdens would also increase by 0.23 hours and 2.79 hours, respectively, due to the increase in the number of WIC-authorized vendors since the previous ICR submission.
Finally, vendors are required to maintain inventory records for federal tax reporting purposes, a recordkeeping burden that takes vendors approximately 10 minutes (0.167 hours) to complete. To account for the new internet vendors, the Department estimates an additional 18.37 hours associated with this requirement. The increase in the number of WIC-authorized vendors since the previous ICR submission also results in 16.87 additional hours for this requirement.
b. Burden Revisions Related to Program Modernization
In recognition of the efficiency of using electronic benefit redemption data to analyze the prices vendors charge for supplemental foods, the final rule removes the requirement that State agencies with access to EBT data collect shelf prices from vendors on a biannual basis or seek an exemption from FNA. As all State agencies are operating EBT at the time of this rule publication, removing the shelf price collection requirement for State agencies significantly decreases the reporting burden for WIC State agencies (−149,068 hours for collecting shelf prices and −40 hours for preparing exemption requests) and WIC-authorized vendors (−132,318.79 hours).
To operationalize online shopping, State agencies will have to update their systems to support new technology in alignment with the Department's standards per § 246.12(bb)(1). The proposed rule did not account for this burden and therefore the Department is adding a burden associated with system updates to allow online shopping, including the return of benefits. The Department estimates that these updates will take 50 hours, and therefore would increase the reporting burden by 2,200 total hours for the 44 State agencies implementing online shopping. Additionally, to fully account for any State agency status updates, FNA-provided trainings, or review of FNA guidance materials that may be required to update food delivery systems to incorporate online shopping, the Department estimates a 5-hour implementation burden per State agency, for a total of 220 hours. Similarly, the development of online shopping will require 50 burden hours to update vendor systems to allow online shopping, including returns. Therefore, the vendor reporting burden associated with vendor system updates to allow online shopping will result in 5,500 additional burden hours for the 110 new internet vendors.
State agencies are required to submit requests for approval for costs of capital expenditures per §  246.14(d). The proposed rule estimated that the number of State agencies submitting such requests would increase as a result of the rule. However, based on project costs from State agencies currently implementing online shopping, the MIS and EBT changes necessary to implement online shopping projects are not meeting the cost threshold requiring that they submit approval. Therefore, the Department is no longer estimating that there will be an increase in the number of State agencies submitting requests for approval, and there is no estimated increase in the burden associated with this activity.
The final rule allows State agencies to adopt EBT transaction authentication technologies other than PIN authentication. Regardless of whether State agencies adopt new transaction authentication technologies or maintain use of the PIN, they must develop transaction authentication policies for the technology they use. Additionally, the Department has modified this provision from what was proposed to require that State agencies receive written approval from FNA if they adopt an authentication method other than the PIN. Based on public comment feedback, the Department increased the burden hours associated with this activity from 25 to 50 hours, and adjusted the number of estimated respondents in recognition that all State agencies will be creating policies and, in the future, may request FNA approval to adopt authentication methods other than the PIN. This increases the reporting burden for this activity to 4,400 hours.
The final rule encourages State agencies to issue electronic benefits remotely and mail EBT cards to participants to reduce the number of clinic visits households make to receive benefits. This decreases the burden associated with picking up food instruments and receiving benefits outside of a certification clinic visit by a total of 1,747,698.87 hours. These estimates assume that: on average, WIC households consist of two WIC participants, requiring only one trip to the clinic to pick up both participants' benefits; currently, households in State agencies without an online EBT system are required to travel to a clinic to reload offline EBT cards three times a year outside of another scheduled appointment; and currently, new participants in State agencies with online EBT systems are required to pick up their EBT card in person. With this final rulemaking, only participants who need to reload an offline EBT card would be required to travel to a clinic to receive benefits in person. These estimates also account for a decrease in the number of offline EBT State agencies (from 9 to 8) and an increase in the number of WIC participants (from 6,243,960 to 6,866,085) since the previous ICR submission.
c. Costs Associated With the Final Rule and OMB Control Number 0584-0043
In addition to the changes to the information collection burdens discussed in this section, implementing the final rule is expected to create additional costs for State agencies and WIC participants. FNA estimates that it will cost each State agency approximately $185,000 to update their EBT and MIS to implement online shopping in the year that they choose to do so. Across the estimated 44 State agencies implementing online shopping, these one-time implementation costs would total $8.14 million. After implementation, the Department anticipates that maintenance of such systems will cost approximately $4,500 per month. Therefore, in an average year following implementation of online shopping in 44 State agencies, these ongoing maintenance costs would total $2.38 million.

The final rule adds a provision at § 246.12(h)(3)(xxxiii) that allows WIC participants who choose to shop for supplemental foods online to pay for fees associated with such services using another tender type, as long as those fees are also assessed to non-WIC customers using the same services. Adjusting for annual inflation, the Department estimates that an average online grocery order in 2027 will be assessed $10.66 in delivery and service fees, increasing to $11.63, adjusting for inflation, in FY 2031 (see the Regulatory Impact Analysis that follows this rule as an Appendix for a full explanation of these estimates). Additionally, FNA estimates that once online shopping has been implemented across 44 State agencies, 28 percent of WIC participants in those State agencies, or about 961,252 participants, would make one online WIC order each month. Further, FNA estimates that 33 percent of those WIC online shopping orders (317,213 orders) would be placed for home delivery. On average, each WIC household consists of two WIC participants. Therefore, FNA estimates that approximately 158,607 households would place an online order for home delivery each month, costing WIC participants a total of about $1.84 million per month, or $22.14 million per year in delivery fees if 44 State agencies have implemented online shopping by 2031.

2. Revisions to OMB Control Number 0584-0401
Title:
Food Delivery Portal (FDP) Data Collection.
OMB Number:
0584-0401.
Expiration Date:
1/31/2028.
Type of Request:
N/A.
Abstract:
The Department proposed revising regulations around data submission timelines for information that State agencies must report to FNA using the Food Delivery Portal (FDP). All WIC State agencies are required to submit information on their vendor monitoring and investigation activities, in accordance with § 246.12(j)(5). The revisions in the proposed rule removed the annual submission deadline of February 1 of each fiscal year and proposed to replace it with submission timelines that “may be as frequent as quarterly but not less than annually, based on system capabilities and reporting needs” along with other proposed edits.
FNA received comments on the Department's proposed rule burden estimate incorporating the possibility of quarterly reporting. The comments largely expressed that the Department's estimate that this change would not increase the burden was inaccurate, and instead quarterly reporting would quadruple the workload and burden on WIC State agencies.
After further analysis of the FDP system and the current data upload process, as well as considering the public comment feedback received on the proposed rule and the FDP burden, the Department agrees that an increase in the frequency of reporting would put an unnecessary burden on State agencies.
The Department has removed the language allowing federal reporting requests to be as frequently as quarterly. Instead, the Department is finalizing this rule maintaining the current annual federal reporting requirement. Because of this, there will be no change to the existing information collection requirements in the information collection under OMB Control Number 0584-0401. The Department is confident that the data submitted on an annual basis provides the information necessary to ensure federal oversight and support the research work that uses this data.
a. Summary of Revisions to OMB Control Number 0584-0401
The current approved burden for OMB Control Number 0584-0401 is 3,576 hours and 541 total responses. As this final rulemaking does not implement the proposed changes, the burden due to the rulemaking will have no effect on the total number of burden hours, which would remain 3,576 hours.
E-Government Act Compliance
The Department is committed to complying with the E-Government Act of 2002, to promote the use of the internet and other information technologies to provide increased opportunities for citizen access to Government information and services, and for other purposes.

Federal Aviation Administration
AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The FAA is considering a proposal to change approximately 4.99 acres of airport land from aeronautical use to non-aeronautical use and to authorize the sale of airport property located at the Watertown Regional Airport, Watertown, SD. The aforementioned land is not needed for aeronautical use. The subject property is made up of two parcels of airport property known as the Lot 4 (2.0 acres) and Dakota Tube (2.99 acres) parcels. These parcels are located north of the airport, along the east side of Airport Drive. Both properties are currently being used for industrial purposes and will continue to be used for the same purpose in the future.
DATES:
Comments must be received on or before December 7, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
All requisite and supporting documentation will be made available for review by appointment at the FAA Dakota-Minnesota Airports District Office, David Ferrell, Program Manager, 2301 University Drive, Building 23B, Bismarck, ND 58504, Telephone: (701) 323-7380.
Written comments on the Sponsor's request may be submitted using any of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
Go to
http://www.regulations.gov
and follow the instructions for sending your comments electronically.
Mail:
David Ferrell, Program Manager, Federal Aviation Administration, Dakota-Minnesota Airports District Office, 2301 University Drive, Building 23B, Bismarck, ND 58504.
Hand Delivery:
Deliver to mail address above between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. Monday through Friday, excluding Federal holidays.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
David Ferrell, Program Manager, Federal Aviation Administration, Dakota-Minnesota Airports District Office, 2301 University Drive, Building 23B, Bismarck, ND 58504. Telephone: (701) 323-7380.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
In accordance with section 47107(h) of Title 49, United States Code, this notice is required to be published in the
Federal Register
30 days before modifying the land-use assurance that requires the property to be used for an aeronautical purpose.
On November 4, 1947, the United States of America, acting by and through the War Assets Administrator, transferred the subject properties to the City of Watertown via quitclaim deed as surplus property. The properties are not needed for aeronautical purposes and are currently being used for commercial industrial purposes. They will continue to be used for commercial industrial purposes after the proposed sale of the properties. The Airport Sponsor will receive fair market value for the sale of the subject properties.
The disposition of proceeds from the sale of this airport property will be in accordance with sections 47125 and 47151 of Title 49, United States Code and
14 CFR part 155
, Release of Airport Property From Surplus Property Disposal Restrictions.
This notice announces that the FAA is considering the release of the subject airport property at the Watertown Regional Airport, Watertown, SD, from federal land covenants, subject to a reservation for continuing right of flight as well as restrictions on the released property as required in FAA Order 5190.6C, section 22.13. Approval does not constitute a commitment by the FAA to financially assist in the disposal of the subject airport property nor a determination of eligibility for grant-in-aid funding from the FAA.
Property Descriptions
Plat of Lot 4 of Airport Industrial Addition to the Municipality of Watertown, South Dakota, Located in the South Half of Section 23—T117N-R53W of the 5th PM, Codington County, South Dakota.
Plat of Dakota Tube Airport Industrial Addition to the Municipality of Watertown, Located in the South half of Section 23—T117N-R53W, Codington County, South Dakota.
Issued in Minneapolis, Minnesota, on October 26, 2026.
E. Lindsay Terry,
Manager, Dakota-Minnesota Airports District Office, FAA, Great Lakes Region.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is changing the operating schedule that governs the Puget Sound and Pacific railroad bridge (PS&P) across the Wishkah River, mile 0.1 in Aberdeen, WA. This rule will change the PS&P railroad bridge draw position to the fully closed-to-navigation position. Furthermore, this rule requires 24-hour notice for all drawbridge openings and a bridge operator will no longer be required to be on site.
DATES:
This rule is effective December 7, 2026.

.

.

I. Table of Abbreviations
CFR Code of Federal Regulations
DHS Department of Homeland Security
FR Federal Register
OMB Office of Management and Budget
NPRM Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (Advance, Supplemental)
§ Section
U.S.C. United States Code
GWRR Genesee & Wyoming Inc.
PS&P Puget Sound and Pacific railroad
II. Background Information and Regulatory History
On June 16, 2026, the Coast Guard published a Notice of Proposed Rule Making, with a request for comments, entitled “Drawbridge Operation Regulation; Wishkah River, Aberdeen, WA” in the
Federal Register
(
91 FR 36105
). There we stated why we issued the NPRM and invited comments on our proposed regulatory action related to this regulatory change. We received one unrelated comment during the comment period that ended July 16, 2026.
III. Legal Authority and Need for Rule
The Coast Guard is issuing this rule under authority
33 U.S.C. 499
. The PS&P railroad bridge across the Wishkah River, mile 0.1, at Aberdeen, WA operates in accordance with
33 CFR 117.1065(b)
. Bridge logs have shown a significant reduction in bridge opening requests for ten years and the bridge is mostly cycled for maintenance. This rule is necessary to balance the needs of the railroad by reducing the need to frequently cycle the draw closed for rail traffic and back open for marine traffic while maintaining the reasonable needs of navigation.
This regulatory action is based on the ability for the PS&P railroad bridge to open on signal after the GWRR has received at least 24-hour notice by telephone or VHF radio. This rule allows any vessel that needs a draw opening to transit through the subject bridge with the proper advance notice during clear visibility or reduced visibility.
IV. Discussion of Comments, Changes and the Final Rule
The Coast Guard provided a comment period of 31 days and received one unrelated comment regarding sea lions in California. No changes were made to the content of the rule since publication of the NPRM.
This rule amends the operating schedule of the PS&P railroad bridge found in
33 CFR 117.1065(b)
by allowing the bridge to be maintained in the closed-to-navigation position and requiring GWRR to fully open the swing span with a minimum of 24-hours' notice. When the draw is to be opened or closed the drawtender must sound one prolonged blast followed by one short blast. We will remove the text in
33 CFR 117.1065(b)
, “When the draw of the bridge is closed and the visibility at the drawtender' s station is less than one mile up or down the channel, the drawtender shall sound two prolonged blasts every minute.”
V. Regulatory Analyses
We developed this rule after considering numerous statutes and Executive Orders related to rulemaking. Below we summarize our analyses based on a number of these statutes and Executive Orders.
A. Impact on Small Entities
The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980,
5 U.S.C. 601-612
, as amended, requires federal agencies to consider the potential impact of regulations on small entities during rulemaking. The term “small entities” comprises small businesses, not-for-profit organizations that are independently owned and operated and are not dominant in their fields, and governmental jurisdictions with populations of less than 50,000. The Coast Guard received no comments from the Small Business Administration on this rule. The Coast Guard certifies under
5 U.S.C. 605(b)
that this rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities for the following reasons. While some owners or operators of vessels intending to transit the bridge may be small entities, the Coast Guard has not identified any vessel operators that will be caused significant economic impact as result of the proposed rule change. As noted earlier, only one or two vessels required openings of the drawbridge annually over the last 10 years. They would be able to continue to request openings of the drawbridge with a 24-hour notice.
Under section 213(a) of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (
Pub. L. 104-121
), we want to assist small entities in understanding this rule. If the rule affects your small business, organization, or governmental jurisdiction and you have questions concerning its provisions or options for compliance, please contact the person listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section.
Small businesses may send comments on the actions of Federal employees who enforce, or otherwise determine compliance with, Federal regulations to the Small Business and Agriculture Regulatory Enforcement Ombudsman and the Regional Small Business Regulatory Fairness Boards. The Ombudsman evaluates these actions annually and rates each agency's responsiveness to small business. If you wish to comment on actions by employees of the Coast Guard, call 1-888-REG-FAIR (1-888-734-3247). The Coast Guard will not retaliate against small entities that question or complain about this rule or any policy or action of the Coast Guard.
B. Collection of Information
This rule calls for no new collection of information under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3520
).
C. Federalism and Indian Tribal Government
A rule has implications for federalism under
Executive Order 13132
, Federalism, if it has a substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship between the National Government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. We have analyzed this rule under that Order and have determined that it is consistent with the fundamental federalism principles and preemption requirements described in
Executive Order 13132
.
Also, this rule does not have tribal implications under
Executive Order 13175
, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, because it does not have a substantial direct effect on one or more Indian tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian tribes.
D. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
2 U.S.C. 1531-1538
) requires Federal agencies to assess the effects of their discretionary regulatory actions. In particular, the Act addresses actions that may result in the expenditure by a State, local, or tribal government, in the aggregate, or by the private sector of $100,000,000 (adjusted for inflation) or more in any one year. Though this rule will not result in such an expenditure, we do discuss the effects of this rule elsewhere in this preamble.
(
printed page 70013)
E. Environment
We have analyzed this rule under Department of Homeland Security Management Directive 023-01, Rev.1, associated implementing instructions, and Environmental Planning Policy COMDTINST 5090.1 (series) which guide the Coast Guard in complying with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) (
42 U.S.C. 4321-4370f
). The Coast Guard has determined that this action is one of a category of actions that do not individually or cumulatively have a significant effect on the human environment. This rule promulgates the operating regulations or procedures for drawbridges and is categorically excluded from further review, under paragraph L49, of Appendix A, Table 1 of DHS Instruction Manual 023-01-001-01, Rev. 1.
Neither a Record of Environmental Consideration nor a Memorandum for the Record are required for this rule.

Refugee Program Bureau, Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), Administration for Children and Families (ACF), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Notice of issuance of a single-source cooperative agreement.
SUMMARY:
The ACF, ORR announces the intent to award a single-source cooperative agreement in the amount of up to $3,500,000 to the Welcoming Initiative for Newcomers (WIN) in San Diego, California, for the next phase of the State Capacity and Readiness Initiative. Building on the nationwide baseline assessment and related readiness products completed under WIN's prior cooperative agreement, the proposed project will support an updated assessment of state capacity, support development of training and technical assistance resources, support for pilot implementation and learning, and engagement with states not participating in the pilots. The project will also identify service and capacity gaps and provide recommendations concerning additional grants, contracts, technical assistance, or other resources ORR may need to support a state-centered refugee resettlement model.
DATES:
The proposed period of performance is November 1, 2026, through October 31, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Miro Marinovich, Office of Refugee Resettlement, Administration for Children and Families, 330 C Street SW, Washington, DC 20201. Telephone: (202) 729-3638; Email:
RBfrontoffice@acf.hhs.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
ORR intends to undertake the next phase of the State Capacity and Readiness Initiative to support implementation of a state-centered refugee resettlement
(
printed page 70089)
model. Under a prior cooperative agreement, WIN conducted a nationwide baseline assessment of state readiness and capacity and developed related assessment and planning products. The proposed award will build on that foundational work by moving the initiative from baseline assessment to implementation support, pilot learning, and state and local capacity building.
Under the proposed cooperative agreement, WIN will conduct a nationwide assessment of local resettlement partners and identify the support they will need from states, ORR, training and technical assistance providers, and other entities to deliver services effectively. WIN will also update the assessment of state capacity and readiness to reflect current infrastructure, staffing, partnerships, service-delivery capabilities, and implementation needs.
WIN will collaborate with Switchboard, or another ORR-designated training and technical assistance provider, to inform the development and delivery of training, tools, templates, and other resources that strengthen state readiness and implementation capacity. WIN will support ORR's pilot activities by recommending approaches for information collection and pilot assessment, coordinating regular engagement with participating states and partners, documenting implementation experience, and synthesizing findings and lessons learned. WIN will develop a national data dashboard to support capacity planning.
For states not participating in the pilots, WIN will support ORR and ORR regional staff with meeting coordination, agenda development, briefing materials, and other state-engagement activities. WIN will also identify service gaps, capacity limitations, and unmet implementation needs and provide recommendations concerning additional federal assistance that may be needed to support broader implementation of the state-centered model.
Expected project products will include updated state and local capacity findings, analyses of service and support gaps, pilot-learning summaries, recommendations for training and technical assistance resources, state-engagement materials, and recommendations to inform future ORR program and funding decisions.
ORR will be substantially involved in the project by refining the work plan, identifying priority questions, coordinating engagement with pilot and non-pilot states, reviewing assessment tools and project products, and determining how findings will inform implementation and future federal assistance. This level of federal participation supports use of a cooperative agreement.
ORR proposes to issue the single-source cooperative agreement to WIN because WIN was the recipient of the prior cooperative agreement and developed the baseline assessment, readiness products, analytical approaches, and stakeholder relationships upon which the proposed work will directly build. Through that work, WIN acquired detailed knowledge of the initiative's methodology, findings, implementation context, and state and local capacity needs.
WIN's institutional knowledge and established relationships with state and local refugee-resettlement stakeholders will allow the next phase to begin without requiring ORR and its partners to reconstruct project history, reestablish working relationships, or repeat previously completed engagement and data-gathering activities. Selecting WIN will preserve continuity between the assessment and implementation phases, reduce duplicative start-up activities and information requests, and support timely use of Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 pilot findings in FY 2028 program and resource planning.
The proposed project will strengthen federal, state, and local coordination; provide practical implementation support to states and local resettlement partners; and help ORR target future grants, contracts, and technical assistance toward demonstrated service and capacity needs.
Statutory Authority:
Under section
8 U.S.C. 1522(b)(1)
of the Refugee Act, ORR is authorized to make grants to and contracts with public or private nonprofit agencies for the initial resettlement of refugees in the United States. This action further advances the intent of
8 U.S.C. 1522(a)(2)
by creating mechanisms through which ORR can, to the maximum extent possible, incorporate state recommendations into refugee placement and capacity planning decisions.

Grants Policy Branch Chief, Office of Grants Policy, Office of Administration.

Title:
USDA Professional Standards Training Tracker Tool (PSTTT).
OMB Control Number:
0584-0626.
Summary of Collection:
This is a reinstatement of an expired information collection request. Section 306 of the Healthy Hunger-Free Kids Act of 2010 (HHFKA) requires Professional Standards for state and local school district nutrition professionals. In addition to hiring standards, mandatory annual training is required for all individuals involved in preparing school meals. To meet the training requirements and assist in locating and keeping track of training, the USDA FNA's web-based application tool with a SQL-server database is available to local educational agencies and school food authorities through the FNA public website. While training requirements are mandatory, using the USDA PSTTT to track the training is voluntary. State and local school district nutrition professionals can use any method to track and manage their training. These resources facilitate compliance with HHFKA requirements and are provided at no cost to the state, district, or school nutrition professionals.
Need and Use of the Information:
State and school nutrition professionals can use the PSTTT to keep track of their training courses, learning objectives, and training hours, in accordance with HHFKA requirements. State reviewers can run reports from the PSTTT that they can use in preparation for Administrative Reviews that are conducted onsite at the school food authorities.

Title:
Federal Collection Methods for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program Recipient Claims.
OMB Control Number:
0584-0446.
Summary of Collection:
This is a reinstatement of an expired information collection request. FNA is still legally required to collect this data and thereby continuing to collect it in violation of the Paperwork Reduction Act. Section 13(b) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008 (the Act), as amended (
7 U.S.C. 2022(b)
), and SNAP regulations at
7 CFR 273.18
require State agencies to refer all delinquent SNAP debts to another Federal government entity as third-party disclosure reporting to U.S. Department of the Treasury (Treasury) for collection. The Debt Collection Improvement Act of 1996 (DCIA) (
Pub. L. 104-134
), as amended by the Digital Accountability and Transparency Act of 2014 (
Pub. L. 113-101
), requires that these debts be referred to Treasury for collection when they are 120 days or more delinquent. The Treasury Offset Program (TOP),
31 CFR part 285
, intercepts and offsets payments such as Federal income tax refunds and Federal salaries and applies the offset to the delinquent debt. The amount or percentage that can be offset from any payment type is set by.
Need and Use of the Information:
The information is used to satisfy the requirements at Section 13(b) of the Act, as amended (
7 U.S.C. 2022(b)
), and SNAP regulations at
7 CFR 273.18
, which requires State agencies to refer delinquent SNAP debts to Treasury for collection and notify debtors.
SNAP regulations at
7 CFR 273.18
require that State agencies establish, collect, and efficiently manage SNAP recipient claims within 120 days. Text at
7 CFR 273.18(n)(1)
states that State agencies must submit debts to TOP when they are 180 days delinquent or more. However, DCIA updated this timeframe to require that eligible delinquent debts be referred to TOP within 120 days. While SNAP regulations have not yet been updated to reflect this change, States must comply with the 120-day timeframe. State agencies must submit files containing these delinquent debts to FNA weekly, which FNA then consolidates into one file and sends to Treasury each week.
The information collected under this request is used to assist:
(1) State agencies to identify eligible debts to send to TOP, request addresses for TOP notices, send TOP notices to debtors, and give due process,
(2) FNS forward files to Treasury for action and to provide Federal-level due process, and to ensure that collections are received and applied to the appropriate debt,
(3) Treasury to intercept Federal payments and offset debts, and
(4) Debtors receive, read, and respond to TOP notices.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
The National Estuarine Research Reserve System (Reserve System) is a federal-state partnership program authorized under the Coastal Zone Management Act, as amended (16 U.S.C.
(
printed page 70066)
1461). The Reserve System protects a representative system of estuaries across the nation and is dedicated to improving estuarine science, education, and stewardship. Reserve activities directly inform the local and national management of the nation's coasts and increase the resilience of coastal communities. There are currently 30 reserves across 25 different U.S. states and territories. Together, the national reserves protect more than 1.4 million acres of estuarine habitat for long-term research, monitoring, education, and stewardship.
Each reserve is managed by a lead state agency or university and brings together local stakeholders, scientists, land management professionals, and educators to understand coastal management issues and generate local, integrated solutions. NOAA administers the Reserve System but does not own or manage the land within a reserve. Instead, NOAA provides strategic direction, national coordination, technical assistance, and funding to states to implement reserves at the local level. The designation of a reserve does not add new state or federal regulations. Memoranda of Agreement are used to articulate roles and responsibilities among relevant partners and landowners in the state and NOAA.
The Green Bay Reserve nomination process formally began on March 25, 2019, when the governor of Wisconsin submitted a letter of interest to NOAA. NOAA responded affirmatively on July 19, 2019. Between September 2020 and September 2022, the University of Wisconsin-Green Bay, with guidance from NOAA, undertook a comprehensive site selection process for the proposed Green Bay Reserve. This process was informed by input from the public, affected landowners, state and federal agency representatives, Tribal nations, academia, nongovernmental organizations, and local government units. Through this collaborative process, the state selected a site for the proposed reserve comprising three components (Peshtigo River, Lower Bay, and Sturgeon Bay) and consisting entirely of publicly owned or land trust-held areas. NOAA received the state's nomination of the proposed multicomponent site for the Green Bay Reserve on December 29, 2022. NOAA evaluated the nomination package and found that the proposed site met the Reserve System's requirements. (See
16 U.S.C. 1461(b)
.)
On January 25, 2024, NOAA informed the State of Wisconsin of its accepted nomination and started the formal designation process by publishing a notice of intent to prepare a draft environmental impact statement and hold scoping meetings on the proposed designation. Public hearings were held on March 19, 2024, and written comments were accepted until April 19, 2024.
The National Estuarine Research Reserve System's implementing regulations require the preparation of both a draft management plan and environmental impact statement as part of the designation process. (
15 CFR 921.13
.)
II. Draft Environmental Impact Statement
The purpose of the Green Bay Reserve DEIS is to inform decision-makers and the public about the potential environmental impacts of designating the proposed Green Bay Reserve as the 31st reserve in the nation. NOAA prepared this document pursuant to the National Environmental Policy Act. (NEPA;
42 U.S.C. 4321
et seq.
) Three alternatives were evaluated as part of this DEIS:
No Action Alternative:
As required by the National Environmental Policy Act, a “no action alternative” must be considered. The no action alternative represents the scenario in which NOAA does not proceed with the proposed action. In this case, the no action alternative is the result of declining to designate the Green Bay Reserve and implement its draft management plan.
Alternative A:
Under this alternative, NOAA would designate the originally nominated site as a reserve. Alternative A, including upland, wetland, and open waters, is approximately 37,714 acres in size. The proposed land and waters are organized into three component areas by geography: the Peshtigo Component, the Lower Bay Component, and the Sturgeon Bay Component.
Alternative B:
Under this alternative, NOAA would designate a revised nominated site as a reserve. Alternative B is similar to Alternative A, though with minor modifications. Specifically, additional lands adjacent to the originally nominated site acquired by landholding partners are integrated into the proposed reserve boundary; meanwhile, small parcels that are not closely aligned with the mission of the Reserve System are removed, and the delineation of core and buffer areas are revised. Alternative B is approximately 36,502 acres in size.
These alternatives allow NOAA to evaluate environmental impacts while addressing the proposed action's purpose and need.
Designating and implementing the proposed Green Bay Reserve, under any of the analyzed alternatives, is not expected to result in significant adverse impacts to the natural or human environment. Designating the proposed Green Bay Reserve and implementing its draft management plan provides multiple benefits. First, the reserve would support existing efforts and establish new research, monitoring, education, and stewardship programs to address priority coastal management issues in the Green Bay estuary. Additionally, the reserve would leverage existing authorities to ensure a stable environment for long-term research and provide a framework for coordination and oversight to achieve its goals. Finally, the designation would bring additional financial and staff resources to support estuary management.
Once designated, the Green Bay Reserve would commence operations, with associated education, research, training, stewardship, and monitoring opportunities and activities. The draft management plan highlights activities that, independently or when aggregated with other factors, may contribute to reasonably foreseeable impacts on the affected environment. If a reserve is designated, future federal actions (including actions funded through NOAA cooperative agreements) will be evaluated individually to comply with applicable environmental laws and policies.
III. Draft Management Plan
The purpose of the draft management plan is to set a course for operating the proposed Green Bay Reserve upon designation. The plan provides for administration, research, education, training, stewardship, facilities, and management of the proposed site. (
15 CFR 921.13
.) The draft management plan for the proposed Green Bay Reserve supports the goals of the Reserve System (
15 CFR 921.1(b)
) and addresses issues relevant to northeastern Wisconsin. Specifically, the plan defines four key issues relevant to Northeast Wisconsin and the Green Bay estuary to focus on over the next five years, should the reserve be designated:
Preparing Great Lakes communities for long-term ecosystem change and variability
Restoring sustainable and holistic land-water connections
Preserving biodiversity through improved ecological integrity and ecosystem resilience
Enhancing the Bay of Green Bay's sense of place and connection to quality of life
(
printed page 70067)
The draft plan also defines goals that reflect the priorities of the proposed reserve during the first five years after designation:
Goal 1:
Strengthen community adaptation and preparation for projected impacts of climate-driven hydrologic shifts and changing lake levels
Goal 2:
Reduce excessive sediment, nutrient, and contaminant loadings into the Bay from watershed inputs
Goal 3:
Strengthen the ability of native and noninvasive species to access terrestrial, wetland, and aquatic habitats and improve interconnectedness of ecosystem components
Goal 4:
Restore healthy wetland, submerged aquatic, and benthic habitats and promote diverse species assemblages
Goal 5:
Foster historical awareness and contemporary connections between people and the Green Bay estuary
Goal 6:
Promote sustainable, beneficial uses of the Bay for regional communities
If designated, the Green Bay Reserve—like all reserves in the system—would be responsible for the implementation of programs related to education, research, training, stewardship, and monitoring in service to communities surrounding the Green Bay estuary. The draft management plan for the Green Bay Reserve includes information on its core programs as well as program-specific focal areas, potential for partnerships, needs, and opportunities. If designated, the development and implementation of these reserve programs would be led by the University of Wisconsin-Green Bay, the lead state agency for the proposed Green Bay Reserve.
As previously noted, the Coastal Zone Management Act's implementing regulations for the Reserve System require NOAA to provide notice in the
Federal Register
of the availability of the DEIS (
15 CFR 921.13
), the draft management plan (
15 CFR 921.20(h)
), and associated public hearing(s).

The Facility Access Media (FAM) Request, NA Form 6006, is completed by all individuals requiring recurring access to non-public areas of NARA's facilities and IT network (such as NARA employees, contractors, volunteers, NARA-related foundation employees, volunteers, interns, and other non-NARA federal employees, such as federal agency reviewers) herein referred to as “applicants,” in order to obtain NARA Facility Access Media (FAM). After approval of the request, the applicant is given a FAM, if approved, and is then able to access non-public areas of NARA facilities and IT network. The collection of information is necessary to comply with Homeland Security Presidential Directive (HSPD) 12 requirements for secure and reliable forms of personal identification issued by federal agencies to their employees, contractors, and other individuals requiring recurring access to non-public areas of government facilities and information services. AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Final rule; administrative change.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is revising the format for materials submitted by the State of California that are incorporated by reference into the California State Implementation Plan (SIP). The regulations and other materials affected by this format change have all been previously submitted by the State of California and approved by the EPA. This format revision will primarily affect the “Identification of plan—in part” sections, as well as the format of the SIP materials that will be available for public inspection at the EPA Regional Office and the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA). This action, which only relates to rules applicable within six California air districts, is the fifth and final of a series of actions intended to change the format for the entire California SIP.
DATES:
This rule is effective on November 6, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
The EPA has established a docket for this action under Docket ID No. EPA-R09-OAR-2024-0527. SIP materials which are incorporated by reference into
40 CFR part 52
are available for inspection by appointment at Environmental Protection Agency, Region IX, 75 Hawthorne Street, San Francisco, CA 94105-3901. For information on the availability of this material at the EPA Regional Office, please contact the person in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section of this document.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Doris Lo, EPA Region IX, 75 Hawthorne St., San Francisco, CA; telephone number: (415) 972-3959; email address:
lo.doris@epa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Throughout this document, the terms “we”, “us,” and “our” refer to the EPA. This
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section is organized as follows:
Table of Contents
I. Background
A. Description of a SIP
B. How the EPA Enforces SIPs
C. How the State and the EPA Update the SIP
D. How the EPA Compiles the SIPs
E. How the EPA Organizes the SIP Compilation
F. Where You Can Find a Copy of the SIP Compilation
G. The Format of the California Identification of Plan Sections
