and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 27, 2026, Cboe C2 Exchange, Inc. (“Exchange” or “C2”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Exchange filed the proposal as a “non-controversial” proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act
[
3
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6) thereunder.
[
4
]
The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
Cboe C2 Exchange, Inc. (“C2” or the “Exchange”) proposes to introduce a Trade-by-Trade report for C2 Options and to amend its fee schedule to adopt fees for the Trade-by-Trade report. The text of the proposed rule change is provided in Exhibit 5.
The text of the proposed rule change is also available on the Commission's website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
), the Exchange's website (
https://www.cboe.com/​us/​options/​regulation/​rule_​filings/​ctwo/​
), and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The
(
printed page 70113)
Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to introduce a Trade-by-Trade report (“TBT Report”) for its equity options platform (“C2 Options”), which will be available for purchase by Trading Permit Holders (“TPHs”) and non-TPHs, and to amend the C2 Options fee schedule to adopt fees for the TBT Report, including a free sample. The proposed TBT Report is based on the TBT Report recently adopted by the Exchange's affiliated options exchange, Cboe Exchange, Inc. (“Cboe Options”).
[
5
]
Trade-by-Trade Report
The TBT Report will provide subscribers with comprehensive trade-by-trade level detail for each options transaction executed on C2 Options. The TBT Report will be produced and updated at the end of each trading day and be made available to subscribers overnight after midnight Eastern Time (
i.e.,
T+1), ensuring that the data is strictly historical and cannot be used to influence intraday trading decisions.
Specifically, each row in the TBT Report will represent a single trade event and will include transaction time, underlying symbol, Options Symbology Initiative (“OSI”) details (
e.g.,
root, expiry, strike, call/put), trade size, trade price, market context indicators (
e.g.,
National Best Bid/National Best Offer, C2 Options best bid/best offer), side of the market (
i.e.,
buy or sell), transaction type (opening or closing), and origin (
i.e.,
the Capacity of the order, such as Public Customer, Professional, broker-dealer, and Market-Maker),
[
6
]
as well as, for a subscriber that is a TPH, that TPH's execution IDs for both Simple Book
[
7
]
and Complex Order Book
[
8
]
trades, which will better allow for accurate linkage and reconstruction of trading activity.
The Exchange anticipates a wide variety of market participants would purchase the TBT Report, including, but not limited to, individual customers, buy-side investors, and investment banks. The Exchange believes the proposed TBT Report will aid subscribers in performing detailed transaction-level analysis, compliance checks, and historical market reconstruction. The TBT Report may also serve as a foundation for analytics on liquidity, price formation, and trade behavior at a trade-by-trade level. The proposed TBT Report is a completely voluntary product, in that the Exchange is not required by any rule or regulation to make this data available, and potential subscribers are not required to purchase the TBT Report and may do so only if they voluntarily choose to.
Proposed Fees
The Exchange proposes to provide in the C2 Options fee schedule that firms may purchase the TBT Report on a subscription basis or by ad hoc request for a specified month.
[
9
]
The Exchange proposes to assess a monthly fee of $5,000 for subscribing to the TBT Report. The Exchange also proposes to adopt a fee of $3,000 per month for ad hoc requests of the TBT Report. An ad hoc request can be for any number of months for which the data is available, beginning with March 1, 2019.
The Exchange also proposes to offer a free sample consisting of End-of-Day Trade by Trade Historical Data for the period July 1, 2022 through July 31, 2022. The free sample will be available to both TPHs and non-TPHs who have not previously purchased the TBT Report or previously received a free sample. The Exchange believes the proposed free sample will serve as an incentive for new subscribers to start purchasing such data. Particularly, the Exchange believes it will give potential subscribers the ability to evaluate historical options trading data before purchasing the TBT Report. The Exchange notes that Cboe Options is concurrently filing a proposed rule change to adopt the same free sample for its TBT Report. The Exchange also notes that another exchange offers a free trial for new subscribers of a similar data product.
[
10
]
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act and the rules and regulations thereunder applicable to the Exchange and, in particular, the requirements of Section 6(b) of the Act.
[
11
]
Specifically, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5)
[
12
]
requirements that the rules of an exchange be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in regulating, clearing, settling, processing information with respect to, and facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest. Additionally, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5)
[
13
]
requirement that the rules of an exchange not be designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers. The Exchange also believes the proposed fees are consistent with Section 6(b)(4) of the Act,
[
14
]
which requires that the rules of an exchange provide for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among its members and issuers and other persons using its facilities.
In adopting Regulation NMS, the Commission granted self-regulatory organizations (“SROs”) and broker-dealers increased authority and flexibility to offer new and unique market data to the public. It was believed that this authority would expand the amount of data available to consumers, and also spur innovation and competition for the provision of market data. The Exchange believes that the proposed TBT Report would further broaden the availability of U.S. options market data to investors consistent with the principles of Regulation NMS. The proposal also promotes increased transparency through the dissemination of the TBT Report. The proposed rule change would benefit investors by providing access to the TBT Report, which, as noted above, may aid subscribers in performing detailed transaction-level analysis, compliance checks, and historical market reconstruction. The TBT Report may also serve as a foundation for analytics on liquidity, price formation, and trade
(
printed page 70114)
behavior at a trade-by-trade level. Additionally, trade-by-trade information regarding opening and closing activity across different option series may indicate investor sentiment, which can be helpful trading information. The Exchange emphasizes, however, that such data is not necessary for trading.
The proposed TBT Report is also similar to an existing C2 Options data product, Open-Close Data. Open-Close Data is a data product that summarizes volume (contracts traded on C2 Options) by origin (customer and firm orders), original order size, and the opening or closing position of the order, and is available on an end-of-day and intraday basis.
[
15
]
While there are some differences between Open-Close Data and the TBT Report (
e.g.,
level of detail and timing of delivery), the products serve similar purposes. Specifically, the TBT Report and Open-Close Data both provide information regarding options trading activity on C2 Options, which, in turn, may be used by subscribers to create and test trading models and analytical strategies and provide comprehensive insight into trading on the Exchange. The functional differences are the level of granularity at which a subscriber may view executed options transactions and the timeline on which each product is delivered,
i.e.,
on an aggregated, summary level on an end-of-day or intraday basis (Open-Close Data), or, as proposed, on a trade-by-trade level delivered on a T+1 basis (the TBT Report). By offering the TBT Report as well as Open-Close Data, the Exchange will give subscribers an additional choice for historical trade data, and subscribers may choose to purchase the data that best suits their business needs. Given these similarities, and because the TBT Report is substantively identical to the TBT Report offered by Cboe Options,
[
16
]
the Exchange believes that the proposal does not present any new or novel issues.
The Exchange believes the proposed fees are reasonable. A subscriber may purchase a subscription to the TBT Report for $5,000 per month, and may purchase the TBT Report on an ad hoc basis for $3,000 per month of data. The Exchange currently assesses a fee of $500 per month for a subscription to Open-Close Data, which is the most comparable data product the Exchange offers, and $400 per month for ad hoc requests of historical Open-Close Data. The Exchange believes the higher proposed fees for the TBT Report are reasonable in light of the substantially greater content of the TBT Report. The TBT Report provides data on a trade-by-trade basis, while Open-Close Data provides data on an aggregated basis. While a subscriber to the TBT Report will not receive data intraday, the subscriber will receive additional data points because the data is not aggregated but covers every trade executed on C2 Options, including the time, price, size, market context, side, transaction type, and origin of each trade. Further, the relationship between the proposed subscription fee and the proposed ad hoc fee for the TBT Report is consistent with the relationship between the corresponding Open-Close Data fees, in that the ad hoc fee for each product is lower than the subscription fee. The proposed fees are also lower than the fees Cboe Options assesses for its substantively identical TBT Report.
[
17
]
Furthermore, setting fees for the TBT Report that are not commensurate with its value relative to established fees for similar data products would simply serve to reduce demand for the Exchange's data product, which, as noted, is entirely optional. If a market participant views Open-Close Data as a more attractive offering for its specific business needs, then such market participant can merely choose to purchase Open-Close Data instead.
The Exchange also believes the proposed fees are reasonable as they would support the introduction of a new market data product that is designed to aid investors by providing further insight into trading on the Exchange. The Exchange believes the proposed fees are equitable and not unfairly discriminatory because they will apply uniformly to all subscribers, whether TPHs or non-TPHs.
The Exchange believes that the proposed free sample for TPHs and non-TPHs who have not previously purchased the TBT Report or previously received a free sample is reasonable because such users would not be subject to fees for End-of-Day Trade by Trade Historical Data for the period July 1, 2022 through July 31, 2022. The proposed free sample is also reasonable as it will give potential subscribers the ability to evaluate historical options trading data prior to purchasing the TBT Report and will therefore encourage and promote new users to purchase the TBT Report. The Exchange believes that the proposed free sample is equitable and not unfairly discriminatory because it will apply equally to all TPHs and non-TPHs who have not previously purchased the TBT Report or previously received a free sample. As noted above, Cboe Options is concurrently proposing the same free sample, and another exchange offers a free trial to new users of a similar data product.
[
18
]
Lastly, the purchase of this data product is discretionary and not compulsory.
The Exchange reiterates that the decision whether to purchase the TBT Report is entirely optional for all potential subscribers. No market participant is required to purchase the TBT Report, and the Exchange is not required to make the TBT Report available to all investors. Rather, the Exchange is voluntarily making the TBT Report available, as requested by customers, and market participants may choose to receive (and pay for) this data based on their own business needs. Potential purchasers may request the data at any time if they believe it to be valuable or may decline to purchase such data.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. Specifically, the Exchange notes that both Nasdaq PHLX LLC (“PHLX”) and The Nasdaq Stock Market LLC (“Nasdaq”) offer the PHLX Options Trade Outline (“PHOTO”) and Nasdaq Options Trade Outline (“NOTO”) products,
[
19
]
respectively, and that Cboe Options offers a substantively identical TBT Report.
[
20
]
In this regard, the Exchange believes that its proposal will promote competition by permitting the Exchange to offer a data product similar to those offered by other options exchanges, but that contains more granular data reporting details on a trade-by-trade basis, rather than on an aggregated basis. The Exchange believes the TBT Report represents the type of innovation and competition that Regulation NMS sought to create, and is proposing the TBT Report to keep pace with changes
(
printed page 70115)
in the industry and evolving customer needs.
The Exchange also does not believe the proposed fees would cause any unnecessary or inappropriate burden on intermarket competition, as other exchanges are free to introduce their own comparable reports with additional data points and lower prices to better compete with the Exchange's offerings. The Exchange operates in a highly competitive environment, and its ability to price the TBT Report is constrained by competition among exchanges that offer similar products. Setting fees that are not commensurate with the value of the TBT Report relative to fees for similar data products would simply serve to reduce demand for the TBT Report, which market participants are under no obligation to purchase. In this competitive environment, potential purchasers are free to choose which, if any, similar product to purchase to satisfy their need for market information. As a result, the Exchange believes this proposed rule change permits fair competition among national securities exchanges.
The Exchange does not believe the proposed rule change would cause any unnecessary or inappropriate burden on intramarket competition. The TBT Report is entirely optional and available to anyone who believes the data will be helpful for their purposes, and the proposed fees apply uniformly to any purchaser, in that the Exchange does not differentiate between the different market participants that may purchase the report, other than through the free sample, which is available on equal terms to all eligible purchasers.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange has not solicited, and does not intend to solicit, comments on this proposed rule change. The Exchange has not received any unsolicited written comments from Trading Permit Holders or other interested parties.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
Because the foregoing proposed rule change does not:
A. significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest;
B. impose any significant burden on competition; and
C. become operative for 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
21
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
22
]
thereunder. At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission will institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views, and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments

Send an email to

.
Please include file number SR-C2-2026-029 on the subject line.

All submissions should refer to file number SR-C2-2026-029. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
Title 49 U.S.C. 47105(f) provides that every sponsor of an airport for which AIP funds are apportioned shall notify the Secretary, by such time and in a form prescribed by the Secretary, of its intent to submit a grant application for its available entitlement funds. This notice establishes the annual national deadline and requirements for every airport sponsor to signal their intent to submit applications for FY 2027 AIP entitlement funds. This is necessary to ensure the FAA has sufficient time to convert and carry over (protect) undeclared apportionment funds.
(
printed page 70117)
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Airports AIP Program Branch, at
9-ASE-ARP-AIP-Airports@faa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Pursuant to
49 U.S.C. 47105(f)
, each airport sponsor receiving apportioned funds must inform the Secretary of its intention to apply for these funds, including any unused funds from previous years (protected carryover). Each airport sponsor must submit notifications for each airport receiving an entitlement amount to their FAA Regional Airports Division/Airports District Office by the national deadline of February 26, 2027. This notification is essential for the efficient planning and management of the AIP. The FAA will carry over and protect any undeclared apportioned funds after this date. Undeclared apportioned funds will be unavailable to the sponsor until the next fiscal year.
The notification must be in writing and include the total amount planned for eligible projects during the FY and confirmation of which projects listed in their Capital Improvement Plans for the current FY will proceed.
State aviation agencies in the FAA's State Block Grant Program must also notify the FAA by this date, with information consistent with the latest Memorandum of Agreement. This should include a plan for both entitlement and state apportionment funds.
Funds from previous FYs that are still available may not be immediately accessible to sponsors when the FAA initiates the AIP for a new fiscal year. The FAA can only issue grants when sufficient funds are appropriated.
Airport sponsors must submit applications for entitlement-only grants on or before April 30, 2027. These applications should be based on construction bids (or negotiated agreements) but may be based on estimates. Final bid dates should be coordinated with your local Region or Airport District Office (ADO), as appropriate, to ensure all grants can be issued based on bids. The submitted applications must comply with statutory pre-grant requirements, including the National Environmental Policy Act and Buy American requirements. If you are unable to meet the required dates, please contact your ADO.
Issued in Washington, DC, on October 29, 2026.

Director, Office of Airport Planning and Programming,

Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
AGENCY:
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
ACTION:
Fair Lending Report of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
SUMMARY:
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB or Bureau) is issuing its Fair Lending Report of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (Fair Lending Report) to Congress. This report describes our fair lending activities in rulemaking; supervision and enforcement; interagency coordination; and stakeholder engagement for calendar year 2025.
DATES:
The CFPB released the 2025 Fair Lending Report on its website on October 1, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Dave Gettler, Paralegal Specialist, Office of Regulations, at 202-435-7700 or
https://reginquiries.consumerfinance.gov/​
.
If you require this document in an alternative electronic format, please contact
CFPB_Accessibility@cfpb.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
1. Introduction
In 2025, the CFPB transformed its fair lending program by refocusing its regulatory, supervisory, and enforcement activities on its statutory authority and identified consumer harm. Under previous administrations, the CFPB was weaponized and had gone beyond its statutory mandate. In the area of fair lending specifically, CFPB
(
printed page 70068)
leadership uncovered egregious examples of companies being targeted for protected political speech and exercising their constitutional rights. Throughout the reporting period, the CFPB worked to correct its course and reverse the previous administrations' abuses and overreach of its statutory mandates.
Under President Trump, the CFPB shifted the way it regulates, supervises, and enforces the laws as required under the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (Dodd-Frank Act). The CFPB's fair lending efforts now focus on proven, intentional racial discrimination with actual identifiable victims. The CFPB does not engage in or facilitate unconstitutional racial classification or discrimination in its enforcement of fair lending laws. The Bureau employs its resources
[
1
]
on pressing threats to consumers and in the areas that are clearly within the CFPB's statutory authority, without duplicating work of other regulators. Enforcement also is being guided by a new set of principles so that the CFPB focuses on addressing actual harm to consumers, ensuring due process, seeking collaboration when appropriate, and promoting efficiency.
To guide its fair lending efforts, CFPB leadership prioritized implementation of several executive orders, including directives prohibiting unlawful debanking,
[
2
]
terminating all discriminatory and illegal preferences,
[
3
]
and ending use of disparate impact liability in the enforcement of civil rights laws.
[
4
]
Accordingly, during the reporting period, the CFPB stopped using disparate impact in its supervision and enforcement of fair lending laws and undid previous actions relying on disparate impact. The CFPB also stopped consulting with institutions regarding special purpose credit programs (SPCPs) based on race, color, national origin, or sex and prioritized addressing unlawful debanking.
In support of the President's deregulatory agenda, the CFPB worked diligently to reverse regulatory overreach, reduce unjustified regulatory burdens, and streamline and clarify existing regulations. In 2025, the CFPB prioritized two rulemakings related to fair lending. Both rules were finalized in 2026. The first rulemaking amended Regulation B, subpart A, implementing the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) to affirm that ECOA does not authorize disparate impact liability. The rule also prohibits use of race, color, national origin, or sex as eligibility criteria for SPCPs and clarifies the discouragement provisions, protecting targeted advertising from discouragement claims under ECOA. We made these important regulatory changes to align with the best reading of the law and to minimize risks of impermissible and unconstitutional discrimination. Importantly, the changes help ensure that credit is made available to all without regard to protected class status.
The second rulemaking amended Regulation B, subpart B, implementing section 1071 of the Dodd-Frank Act. It amended the scope of what constitutes a covered financial institution and covered credit transaction, modified the gross annual revenue threshold in the rule's definition of small business from $5 million or less to $1 million or less, removed certain data points not required by the statute, and altered certain requirements related to how data is collected. The 2023 rule had imposed a significant number of requirements that are unnecessary to advance the purposes of section 1071, and the CFPB now asks for only what the statute requires. These updates both reduce unnecessary compliance burdens and result in a substantial cost savings for impacted institutions, including a one-time savings of nearly $100M and an annual ongoing savings between $166M and $181M per year.
As this report reflects, we have made great progress implementing the President's agenda in 2025, and we are very proud of our fair lending accomplishments. These are only a few examples of the CFPB's fair lending work in 2025, as described in this report. Although the reporting period for this report is calendar year 2025, we have also included some activity that took place outside of the reporting period due to its importance and relevance to the covered topics.
2. Shifts in Fair Lending Priorities
During the reporting period, the CFPB made significant shifts in its fair lending work consistent with the current administration and CFPB leadership's fair lending policies and priorities. As explained in further detail in the subsections that follow, these changes were also guided by several executive orders, including Executive Order (E.O.) 14281, “Restoring Equality of Opportunity and Meritocracy”;
[
5
]
E.O. 14173
, “Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity”;
[
6
]
and
E.O. 14331
, “Guaranteeing Fair Banking for all Americans.”
[
7
]
2.1 Terminating Disparate Impact
On April 23, 2025, President Trump issued
E.O. 14281
, “Restoring Equality of Opportunity and Meritocracy,” which directs Federal agencies to stop using disparate impact liability in the enforcement of civil rights laws.
Consistent with
E.O. 14281
, the CFPB no longer uses disparate impact in its supervision or enforcement of fair lending laws. Also, as described in section 5 of this report, the CFPB engaged in rulemaking consistent with these priorities.
[
8
]
In addition, the CFPB has closed all elements of open supervision exams and enforcement investigations that relied on disparate impact liability and terminated CFPB orders that relied on disparate impact liability.
Additional activity related to disparate impact occurred since the end of the reporting period. As discussed in more detail in section 5.1.2 of this report, on April 22, 2026, the CFPB issued a final rule amending Regulation B. Among other things, the final rule removed the longstanding “effects test” language from Regulation B and its commentary and replaced it with statements affirming that ECOA does not authorize disparate impact liability.
2.2 Terminating Consultations on Special Purpose Credit Programs
On January 21, 2025, President Trump issued
E.O. 14173
, “Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity,” which obligates executive departments and agencies “to terminate all discriminatory and illegal preferences” and “to combat illegal
(
printed page 70069)
private sector” race- and sex-conscious programs.
Accordingly, the CFPB no longer consults with institutions regarding any SPCPs that rely on race, color, national origin, or sex. Consistent with
E.O. 14173
and recognizing the broader statutory and constitutional concerns raised by such programs, the CFPB amended subpart A of Regulation B, the regulation implementing the ECOA, to prohibit creditors from offering programs that rely on the race, color, national origin, or sex of the applicant in making eligibility determinations.
[
9
]
2.3 Debanking
On August 7, 2025, President Trump signed
E.O. 14331
, “Guaranteeing Fair Banking for All Americans,” stating that no American should be denied access to financial services because of their political or religious beliefs.
Combating unlawful debanking is a priority, and the CFPB has dedicated resources across the Bureau to implement
E.O. 14331
to ensure banking decisions are made consistent with the law and do not substitute unlawful practices for “individualized, objective, and risk-based analyses.”
[
10
]
Consistent with the E.O., in 2025, the CFPB reviewed its Examination Manual and confirmed that it does not reference reputation risk. The CFPB also reviewed its guidance, regulations, and other materials used to regulate or examine financial institutions under its authority for reputation risk concepts that could result in unlawful debanking. Additionally, the CFPB reviewed consumer complaints, as well as supervisory and enforcement data, for evidence of potential unlawful debanking.
In the debanking context, the CFPB evaluates financial institutions for compliance with ECOA and the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA), particularly the adverse action notice requirements under those laws. The CFPB's debanking efforts also focus on religious discrimination. In addition, the CFPB is working with other regulatory partners, including the Department of Justice (DOJ), as part of the DOJ's Equal Access to Banking Task Force, to address debanking issues more broadly.
3. Correcting Previous Administrations' Regulatory Overreach
The previous administrations' regulatory overreach affected many businesses and necessitated a course correction by the Trump administration. In the area of fair lending, CFPB leadership uncovered egregious examples of companies being targeted for protected political speech and exercising their constitutional rights. In line with new fair lending priorities, and implementing the administration's agenda, including executive orders, the CFPB's focus in 2025 was to undo the regulatory overreach of the previous administrations, including actions relying on disparate impact and other fair lending matters. The actions are listed below.
Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection
v.
Townstone Financial, Inc. and Barry Sturner
(N.D. Ill. 1:20-cv-04176) (not a credit union or depository institution). On July 15, 2020, the CFPB filed a lawsuit against Townstone Financial, Inc., a small Midwest firm with about ten employees and a radio program called Townstone Financial. The CFPB alleged that Townstone violated ECOA, Regulation B, and the Consumer Financial Protection Act (CFPA). The CFPB targeted Townstone based solely on perceived racial disparities in mortgage application and origination statistics. Townstone was targeted for protected free speech. CFPB used an audio mining software to search Townstone's radio show and podcasts finding that they engaged in political speech with which the CFPB's enforcement disagreed. The CFPB identified only 16 minutes out of nearly 79 hours of radio content (.33 percent) that it deemed “disconcerting” and that “could be interpreted as inappropriate, incorrect, or insensitive.” The “disconcerting” conduct was talking about local crime, political issues around freedom of speech, supporting local law enforcement, and telling people to check out a neighborhood before buying a home. There was no evidence of any potential customers reporting Townstone to the CFPB or finding their content offensive. The action was resolved by stipulated final judgment and order on November 7, 2024.
On March 26, 2025, shortly after the new leadership came in, the CFPB filed a motion to vacate a consent order and to return a $100K fine to Townstone, on the grounds that the CFPB discovered within its internal case files indications that the CFPB commenced and continued its investigation and litigation without a substantial predicate of actionable facts and targeted co-defendants Townstone and Townstone President and CEO, Barry Sturner, based on constitutionally protected speech. Although the court denied the CFPB's motion to vacate on June 12, 2025, the CFPB's leadership believes this fair lending case is prime example of the prior administration's weaponization of the Bureau.
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Investigation of Credova Financial, LLC.
The CFPB terminated its investigation into Credova because the CFPB had determined that the investigation was a weaponization against disfavored industries and individuals. Credova's use of innovative financial technology solutions to provide consumer financing to facilitate Americans exercising their Second Amendment rights made it a target for the CFPB. The CFPB's demands were also inconsistent with the realities of how such businesses are run. The investigation is one of numerous regulation-by-enforcement actions for which the CFPB became infamous under former Director Chopra. The investigation was aimed at suppressing activities protected by the First and Second Amendment. It also represents precisely the kind of unconstitutional targeting prohibited by
E.O. 14331
, “Guaranteeing Fair Banking for All Americans.”
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and United States of America
v.
Colony Ridge Development, LLC; Colony Ridge BV, LLC; Colony Ridge Land, LLC; and Loan Originator Services, LLC
(S.D. Tex. No. 4:23-cv-04729) (not a credit union or depository institution). On December 20, 2023, the CFPB, together with the DOJ, filed a complaint against land development companies Colony Ridge Development, LLC and Colony Ridge BV, LLC, affiliate mortgage company Colony Ridge Land, LLC (collectively, the Colony Ridge defendants), and loan origination company Loan Originator Services, LLC (LOS). The CFPB and the DOJ alleged that defendants violated ECOA by targeting Hispanic consumers with a predatory loan product. The CFPB separately alleged violations of the CFPA and Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act. The DOJ further alleged defendants' conduct violated the Fair Housing Act (FHA). On February 10, 2026, pursuant to a joint stipulation of voluntary dismissal, the CFPB dismissed its claims with prejudice. That same day, the DOJ notified the court in a joint motion for dismissal that the DOJ, along with the State of Texas, had reached a settlement resolving the DOJ's claims and the State of Texas's claims in a related matter. Following a hearing on the motion, on April 10, 2026, the remaining parties filed a joint stipulation of dismissal, dismissing the action with prejudice and withdrawing their request for continuing jurisdiction. On April 28, 2026, the court dismissed
(
printed page 70070)
the action with prejudice and denied the joint motion for dismissal as moot.
In re Washington Federal Bank, N.A.
(2020-BCFP-0019). On October 27, 2020, the CFPB issued an order against Washington Federal Bank, N.A., a federally insured, for-profit national bank headquartered in Seattle, Washington, to address violations of the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA). On September 22, 2025, pursuant to the CFPB's authority under
12 U.S.C. 5563(b)(3)
and under Paragraph 75 of the order, the CFPB terminated the order. Washington Federal has fulfilled several obligations under the order, including paying a civil money penalty of $200,000, and creating and implementing a compliance plan designed to ensure that its collection, recording, and reporting of HMDA data complies with applicable Federal consumer financial laws and the terms of the order.
In re Washington Federal
(2013-CFPB-0005). On October 9, 2013, the CFPB issued an order against Washington Federal, a bank headquartered in Seattle, Washington, to address violations of HMDA. On September 22, 2025, pursuant to the CFPB's authority under
12 U.S.C. 5563(b)(3)
and under paragraph 3 of article XII of the order, the CFPB terminated the order. Washington Federal has fulfilled several obligations under the order, including paying a civil money penalty of $34,000.
In re Citibank, N.A.
(2023-CFPB-0013). On November 8, 2023, the CFPB issued an order against Citibank, N.A., which is a national bank headquartered in New York City, New York. The CFPB found that Citibank violated ECOA and Regulation B. As CFPB was aware, there was a large-scale fraud perpetuated by a crime ring of Armenians in Southern California. At the time, several rogue underwriters in one location in Citi Retail Services looked at Armenian surnames as they evaluated credit card applications and credit line increases coming from Glendale, California. As soon as Citi learned of these isolated occurrences, Citi terminated the employees, re-trained its underwriting staff, and began monitoring employee communications to ensure their decision-making was not improperly influenced by an applicant's national origin. This issue affected a very small number of applications and there has been no recurrence of the issue since these measures were implemented in 2021. On October 16, 2025, pursuant to the CFPB's authority under
12 U.S.C. 5563(b)(3)
and under paragraph 74 of the order, the CFPB terminated the order and waived any alleged non-compliance therewith. Citibank has fulfilled certain obligations under the order, including paying a civil money penalty of $24,500,000 to the CFPB as required by section X, making redress payments of nearly $1.4 million required by section IX, and taking steps to implement injunctive relief to prevent future violations required by the “Conduct Provisions.”
In re Bank of America, N.A.
(2023-CFPB-0016). On November 28, 2023, the CFPB issued an order against Bank of America, N.A., which is a national bank headquartered in Charlotte, North Carolina, with branches and ATMs located in 38 States and the District of Columbia. 4. This Administration's Fair Lending Supervision and Enforcement
4.1 Supervision
Title X of the Dodd-Frank Act authorizes the CFPB to supervise certain consumer financial services companies and large depository institutions and their affiliates for consumer protection purposes.
[
11
]
The CFPB's Supervision program assesses compliance with Federal consumer financial protection laws and regulations at banks and nonbanks over which the CFPB has supervisory authority.
During the reporting year, the CFPB rescinded its prior supervisory priorities and redirected its supervision efforts. Consistent with new priorities, including its focus on debanking, the CFPB reviewed supervisory data that included complaints received by institutions, for evidence of potential unlawful debanking.
While redirecting its supervisory resources, the CFPB closed 76 percent of its supervisory actions (nearly 1,500) and a substantial majority of its outstanding open examinations. Approximately 12 percent of the supervisory actions closed related to fair lending.
The CFPB's fair lending supervisory activities focus on financial institutions' compliance with ECOA and the HMDA. ECOA examination work focuses on uncovering direct evidence of intentional discrimination on a prohibited basis, systemic failures to provide applicants with legally required notices of adverse actions, and lenders' systems for identifying risks of non-compliance with ECOA and Regulation B. HMDA examination work focuses on validating the accuracy of key data points collected and submitted by lenders.
During the reporting period, the CFPB did not initiate supervisory activities or cite any fair lending violations.

In April 2025, the CFPB announced its plans to reconsider certain aspects of a final rule published in May 2023 that implemented changes to ECOA made by

(
printed page 70072)

[
21

to change the scope of what constitutes a covered financial institution and covered credit transaction, to modify the gross annual revenue threshold in the rule's definition of small business, to remove certain data points not required by the statute, and to alter certain requirements related to how data is collected. The CFPB also proposed extending the rule's compliance date to January 1, 2028. The CFPB believed these proposed changes would streamline the rule, reduce complexity for lenders, and improve data quality, thereby advancing the purposes of section 1071 and complying with recent executive directives.
Additional activity has occurred since the end of the reporting period. On May 1, 2026, the CFPB issued the final rule.
[
22
]
The rule reduces the scope of “covered credit transactions” by limiting the types of transactions subject to reporting in order to focus data collection efforts on core lending products—loans, lines of credit, and credit cards—that are most utilized by small businesses. Accordingly, the rule sets forth certain exclusions: merchant cash advances, agricultural lending, and small-dollar business credit. The rule also narrows the definition of “covered financial institutions” by raising the loan origination threshold from 100 to 1,000 loans annually and excluding Farm Credit System lenders.
In addition, the rule revises the definition of “small business” by reducing the gross annual revenue threshold from $5 million to $1 million. This will allow the CFPB to focus on collecting data related to micro and small enterprises, which are most relevant to section 1071's goals. The rule also reduces the number of collected data points, extends and adopts a uniform compliance date of January 1, 2028, and simplifies the time and manner of data collection in order to allow institutions flexibility in how they comply with statutory requirements.
The rule updates are necessary to ensure reasonable implementation that does not restrict credit availability for America's small businesses. The 2023 rule imposed a significant number of requirements that were not needed to advance the purposes of section 1071 of the Dodd-Frank Act. This rule recognizes those concerns and takes a more reflective approach, including just what the statute requires. The updates will result in cost savings for institutions and reduce the burden of data collection without sacrificing data availability.
More information is available on our website, including a page compiling key materials related to the CFPB's small business lending rulemaking.

5.1.3 Regulation B, ECOA
On November 13, 2025, the CFPB published a proposal to amend provisions of Regulation B, subpart A, implementing ECOA to facilitate compliance with ECOA by clarifying the obligations imposed by the statute.
[
39
]
The proposed rule provided that ECOA does not authorize disparate impact claims. It proposed to amend the prohibition on discouraging applicants or prospective applicants to clarify that it prohibits statements of intent to discriminate in violation of ECOA and is not triggered merely by negative consumer impressions. It also proposed to clarify that encouraging statements by creditors directed at one group of
(
printed page 70073)
consumers is not prohibited discouragement as to applicants or prospective applicants who were not the intended recipients of the statements. The proposed rule would also amend the standards for SPCPs offered or participated in by for-profit organizations to include new standards and restrictions.
Additional activity has occurred since the end of the reporting period. On April 22, 2026, the CFPB issued a final rule amending Regulation B as proposed.
[
40
]
The final rule removes the longstanding “effects test” language from Regulation B and its commentary and replaced it with statements affirming that ECOA does not authorize disparate impact liability. Disparate impact was first read into ECOA based solely on the law's legislative history. However, under the plain meaning of ECOA's text, disparate impact is not a cognizable theory of liability under the statute and is contrary to the principles of Equal Protection.
The rule also changes the anti-discouragement provision to limit prohibited “statements” to spoken or written words or visual images as opposed to broader “acts or practices” such as branch placement or advertisement targeting. Liability also only attaches to statements that a creditor knows or should know would cause a reasonable person to believe the creditor would deny, or offer worse terms on, a credit application because of a prohibited basis characteristic. This change was designed to protect targeted advertising from discouragement claims, specifically providing that encouraging messages directed at one audience would not be treated as discouraging to others who were not the intended recipients of such messages. Merely controversial or provocative speech is to be distinguished from statements that do convey discriminatory exclusion.
In addition, the new rule prohibits for-profit creditors from using race, color, national origin, or sex (or any combination thereof) as eligibility criteria for SPCPs. For any SPCPs that still use other protected classes as eligibility criteria (such as religion, marital status, age, or public assistance income), the creditor would face new restrictions, including stringent documentation and evidence requirements. The stringent new conditions help ensure that Congress's intent to make these SPCPs available for certain credit transactions “when it has been clearly demonstrated on the public record that without such exemption the consumers involved would effectively be denied credit.”
[
41
]
The regulatory changes to SPCPs now align with the law's intended purpose and minimize risks of impermissible and unconstitutional discrimination.
5.1.4 Rescission of 2020 Advisory Opinion Related to ECOA (Regulation B); Special Purpose Credit Programs
Additional special purpose credit program-related activity has occurred since the end of the reporting period. On June 17, 2026, the CFPB rescinded an advisory opinion issued in December 2020 regarding Regulation B, as it applies to certain aspects of SPCPs designed and implemented by for-profit organizations to meet special social needs. Specifically, the 2020 advisory opinion clarified the content that a for-profit organization must include in a written plan that establishes and administers an SPCP under Regulation B. The advisory opinion also clarified the type of research and data that may be appropriate to inform a for-profit organization's determination that an SPCP is needed to benefit a certain class of persons.
The CFPB rescinded the advisory opinion because it contained statements that conflicted with recent amendments to Regulation B and to avoid any confusion about the appropriate standards and related conditions for SPCPs offered or participated in by for-profit organizations. For example, the advisory opinion stated that all program participants in an SPCP offered or participated in by a for-profit organization may be required “to share one or more common characteristics (for example, race, national origin, or sex)”; the April 2026 final rule, however, prohibits any SPCP offered or participated in by a for-profit organization from using the common characteristic of race, color, national origin, or sex, or any combination thereof, as a factor in determining eligibility for the program.

8.1.4 Referrals to the DOJ
The agencies assigned enforcement authority under section 704 of ECOA must refer a matter to DOJ when there is reason to believe that a creditor has engaged in a pattern or practice of lending discrimination in violation of ECOA.
[
72
]
They also may refer other potential ECOA violations to DOJ.
[
73
]
In 2025, NCUA made four referrals to DOJ involving violations of ECOA or Regulation B. Two referrals involved discrimination based on receipt of public assistance, one involved discrimination based on age and marital status, and one involved discrimination based on age alone. The OCC made one referral to DOJ involving violations of ECOA, Regulation B, and the FHA. The matter involved discrimination on the basis of race, color, or national origin in mortgage lending.
In 2025, the CFPB, FDIC, and FRB did not refer any ECOA matters to DOJ.
9. Statutory Reporting on HMDA
Pursuant to HMDA, the CFPB in consultation with HUD, must report annually on the utility of HMDA's requirement that covered lenders report the number and dollar amount of certain mortgage loans and applications grouped according to census tract, income level, racial characteristics, age, and gender.
[
74
]
The CFPB is currently assessing the utility of this data and expects to publish a separate report to Congress in late 2026.
